profileDesc.creation:
Initially created: 2025-12-11T21:22:12.397+09:00 by chris Translate the following text from Classical Chinese into English.
Requirements: 1. The text contains page numbers in square brackets, such as [01], [02], etc. - These must be passed through unchanged. - Each page number must appear in exactly the same position in the translation as in the source. - The number of page markers in the output must match the input exactly.
2. Personal names, place names, titles, and other proper nouns should be rendered in Hànyǔ Pīnyīn with tone marks.
3. Do NOT transcribe the full Classical Chinese text into Pinyin.
4. Do NOT include explanatory notes, annotations, or commentary — output only the English translation.
5. The target language is English.
Input text:

p.seg: In the declining days of the Zhou state,
six powerful states vied for supremacy,
and eight [regions] contended in invasion.
To the south was King Píng of the state of Chǔ,
a ruler who brought peace to the people and governed with transformative virtue.
The king held court for ten thousand states,
his divine might resonating far and wide,
commanding all the various domains.
Externally, he established the Bright Terrace,
internally, he elevated the palace halls.
To the south, he used Tiānmén as a stronghold,
to the north, the Huái Sea as a barrier,
to the east, reaching the sun and moon as borders,
to the west, bordering the Buddhist lands.
He opened mountains and rivers, [making] the earth’s axis,
harmonized the pitch pipes to distinguish yīn and yáng.
He rode the Purple Pole to fix the heavenly gates,
moved the yellow dragon to come bearing wings.
Six dragons descended as auspicious signs,
the earth yielded bountiful grains,
the wind did not howl through the branches,
the rain did not break the clods.
The streets and roads,
were bustling and orderly,
broad, level, and serene,
leaving a name for ten thousand generations.
The chief minister of Chǔ,
was surnamed Wǔ, named Shē,
versed in both civil and martial arts,
his heart devoted to the altars of soil and grain.
Wielding a three-foot sword,
he entrusted his six-foot frame.
Commanded by all states,
his nature was honest and upright,
his conduct loyal and steadfast,
his will like wind and clouds,
his heart like iron and stone,
constantly vigilant without slackening,
diligent day and night.
Serving his lord, he achieved excellence through gradual guidance,
accomplishing things by following and completing them;
if the ruler had faults,
he would risk offending to remonstrate.
Wǔ Shē had two sons,
who served the lord.
The younger was Zǐxū,
the elder named Zǐshàng.
One served the state of Liáng,
the other served the state of Zhèng,
both entirely loyal and steadfast,
and perceptive in their dealings.
The crown prince of Chǔ,
grown up, had yet to take a wife.
The king asked his officials: “Who has a daughter fit to be consort?
I have heard: a state without an Eastern Palace [heir],
is half a state lying fallow,
like springs overflowing in the Eastern Sea,
a tree without branches,
half the tree dead.
The crown prince, honored as half the state,
has no wife yet—
what say you, my ministers?”
Grandee Wèi Líng addressed the king: “I have heard that the daughter of Duke Mù of Qín,
now sixteen years of age,
is surpassingly beautiful.
Her brows like the crescent moon,
her cheeks like congealed light,
her eyes like shooting stars,
her face like flower hues.
Her hair seven feet long,
her nose straight, forehead square,
ears like pearl pendants,
hands hanging past her knees,
ten fingers slender and long.
I beg Your Majesty to issue an edict,
and consult with the crown prince.
If she meets the sage ruler’s favor,
ten thousand states will harmonize in good affairs.”
Thereupon he dispatched Wèi Líng
to summon and recruit the daughter of the Duke of Qín.
King Chǔ called to Wèi Líng: “I trouble you for the long journey,
braving wind and frost.”
When the king saw the maiden,
her graceful appearance and beautiful qualities,
he suddenly conceived a wolf-tiger’s heart.
Wèi Líng, currying the king’s favor, said: “May Your Majesty take her as your own consort.
For the Eastern Palace crown prince,
seek elsewhere.
Beautiful women are endless—
surely this does not hinder the great way.”
The king, hearing Wèi Líng’s words,
was overjoyed beyond measure,
and took the Qín maiden as consort,
remaining within and not holding court for three days.
Wǔ Shē heard of this and was enraged;
fearing not the might of thunder and lightning,
he loosened his hair and went straight before the hall,
confronting the sage ruler’s feelings to remonstrate directly.
The king, startled and afraid,
asked: “What inauspicious matter is this?”
Wǔ Shē declared: “I now see the king’s lack of virtue,
and fear the loss of state and domain.
Should the state fall into chaos and ministers flee,
would it not be because of the Duke of Qín’s daughter!
To take a wife for your son,
yet take her yourself as consort,
contending with your son for a wife—
is this not shameful before heaven and earth!
This is to confound laws,
overturn ritual and propriety.
I wish to remonstrate and exchange words,
but fear the altars of soil and grain may not endure!”
The king then flushed with shame, his face pale,
ashamed before his assembled ministers: “State Minister,
have you not heard: plans once made are not to be discussed,
spilled water is hard to retrieve;
the matter is already thus,
do not remonstrate again!”
Wǔ Shē saw the king’s lack of virtue,
taking the Qín maiden himself as consort,
fearing not the might of thunder and lightning,
confronted the sage ruler’s feelings to remonstrate directly: “Your Majesty is lord of ten thousand people,
commanding all domains—
how can you trust and accept Wèi Líng’s words!
(text missing below) )
(text missing above) ) filial heart,
[ ] come to save me from distress,
separated by the dark abyss.”
Zǐshàng, receiving his father’s distant letter summoning him,
wept bitterly as King Píng imprisoned him,
the distant letter commanding him,
wishing to save his kind father.
The king said: “Your father now suffers harsh punishment,
imprisoned and bound in the jail.
If you do not save your father,
how can you be called a filial son?
You must go quickly,
do not delay further.”
Zǐshàng then took leave of the King of Zhèng,
and raced day and night to the state of Liáng,
to see his younger brother Zǐxū,
and fully relate the letter’s intent.
“Now because King Píng lacks virtue,
trusting the words of treacherous ministers,
he has imprisoned our kind father,
intending to apply severe punishment.
I have come from afar now,
to summon you, brother, to follow.
This matter cannot long be delayed—
I beg you, brother, to prepare quickly.”
Zǐxū, hearing his elder brother’s words,
remotely knew his father was detained,
(counter) considering the matter’s cause,
the letter likely much falsified,
replied to his brother: “King Píng lacks virtue,
using the words of villainous ministers,
imprisoning our father,
intending to execute and eradicate.
Seeing us brothers outside,
he fears future enmity and vengeance,
forges a letter from our kind father,
from afar falsely trying to lure us down—
in such circumstances,
it is enough to warrant execution.
This urgent letter summoning us
must be deceitful words;
to go and be captured is not to be undertaken,
like a dull bird caught in a net,
a spring fish (
(text missing below) )
(text missing above) ) now returning to fully relate Zǐxū’s words.
If there is any coarseness or negligence,
I beg you, lord, not to blame.”
The messenger, having received these words,
then turned back,
bound himself with rope,
and went to see King Píng.
He addressed King Píng:
“I was commanded to serve as urgent envoy,
day and night rushing through several provinces.
South of Kuàijī Mountain, he caught up with me,
drew his sword intending to cut off my head.
I feared the sword in Zǐxū’s hand,
Zǐxū feared me, and we both desisted.
We faced each other but did not approach,
shouting from afar to explain the matter.
He sends back word to you, King Píng:
‘This very day he raises troops to avenge his father’s enmity.’”
Upon hearing these words, the King of Chǔ
struck the throne and roared in fury: "This rebellious scoundrel—
how can he be tolerated?
A blade of grass, one inch long,
how could it measure the heavens?
A single strand of down,
how could it resist furnace coals?
Wǔ Zǐxū's wild talk
is hardly worth considering;
the idle words of the wind
need not be gathered!
"The King of Chǔ then summoned Wǔ Shē and his son Wǔ Shàng from prison
to be sentenced to execution.
As Wǔ Shàng faced death,
he looked up to the sky and sighed, saying: "Had I not disregarded my younger brother's words,
and come from afar to join my father in execution,
what could be done, what could be done?
What other path is there to know?
After my death,
I pray my younger brother survives.
Should Heaven's way suddenly open,
avenge our father and kill the King of Chǔ."
His final words finished,
he was immediately executed.
Father and son
were put to death together.
The King of Chǔ issued a proclamation,
and then captured Wǔ Zǐxū—how did it happen?
It said: "A minister of the State of Liáng,
the traitor Wǔ Zǐxū,
served his lord as a father,
yet failed in loyalty and diligence,
plotting against the state,
cruel, tyrannical, greedy, and brutal.
Wǔ Shàng, a minister of the State of Zhèng,
has been executed together with his father;
only Wǔ Zǐxū has fled,
and has not yet been captured.
If anyone can capture and deliver him,
they shall be rewarded with a thousand catties of gold,
and enfeoffed with ten thousand households.
Whoever hides him
shall suffer the usual penalties of the law:
first beheading the individual,
then executing the nine clans.
Any official who shows leniency or neglect
shall be dismissed from office and prosecuted;
reports shall be submitted daily,
and the culprit shall be bound and delivered."
Once the order was issued,
it was watertight, leaving no gaps;
prefectures and counties were informed,
and notices were posted along the roads.
Villages and wards were searched thoroughly;
who dared to hide him?
All vied to pursue and capture him,
greedy for the heavy reward.
Wǔ Zǐxū traveled to the wild and desolate mountains,
grasped his sword, and sang a sorrowful song, sighing:
Wǔ Zǐxū, filled with indignation, heaved a long sigh;
a great man in hardship, why sigh in lament?
Heaven's net is vast, yet the road is at its end,
leaving me anxious and with nowhere to flee.
Thirsty and weary, with no food to fill my belly,
across the vast wilderness, I have lost my companion.
From afar, I hear the natural moat, filled with wind and waves;
mountains tower high, touching the Milky Way.
At the remote bend of the river, no boats are in sight;
how can I reach the southern shore of the river?
If Heaven goes against the will of man,
I cannot avoid difficulties here.
The sorrowful song ended,
he journeyed onward again,
following fate and circumstance,
until he reached the Yǐng River.
The wind brushed his ears,
and he heard the sound of laundry beating;
not daring to advance rashly,
he hid his form and stood still.
Wǔ Zǐxū reached the banks of the Yǐng River,
thirsty, weary, and hungry, finding it hard to proceed.
From afar, he heard the sound of laundry beating in the air;
he bowed and turned his body, then halted.
Fearing he might be discovered by people here,
he curled his feet, hid his form, and blended with the trees.
After a long while, steady and cautious, he need not be alarmed;
gradually, he peeked through the trees, stealing a glance.
By the ford, there were no men to be seen,
only a graceful woman beating laundry.
From underwater, he peeked a hundred times;
on the waves, her jade-like wrists lifted a thousand times.
He wished to step forward and beg for food,
but his heart was filled with doubt and hesitation.
Not daring to advance or retreat, he pondered;
hesitating, he was about to lower his head and leave.
The woman beat laundry in the water,
looked up, and suddenly saw a man,
walking in a frantic manner,
his spirit dazed and confused,
his face bearing the look of hunger,
walking with a sword at his waist.
Knowing it was Wǔ Zǐxū,
she said with sorrow: "I have heard that a single meal in the mulberry grove
made Líng Zhé push the carriage wheel in gratitude;
the yellow sparrow, healed with medicine for its wound,
brought a white ring in return.
Though I am chaste and pure,
my substance is without flaw,
and now, beating laundry on the water,
I am fortunate to meet a noble man.
Though my home is not well-prepared,
why begrudge a single meal?"
She walked slowly along the bank
and called out: "Traveler, please stay!
Swordsman, from where do you hail, noble sir?
From which state, a man of talent?
Your appearance and spirit,
your bearing and dignified stature.
For what urgent matter
do you tread this long road?
Lost and flustered, without companion,
your spirit dazed and confused.
Looking at your face,
you must have something weighing on your heart.
If not a knight-errant nursing a grievance,
you are surely pursued by King Píng.
I have a humble offering from a poor home,
and dare to invite you for a meal.
What are your feelings?
I hope you will condescend to step forward."
Wǔ Zǐxū replied: "I am a man of Chǔ,
serving as an envoy to Yuè.
Recently, due to presenting tribute,
I went west to the King of Chǔ,
and met with the states of Liáng and Zhèng to discuss military affairs.
Riding a sturdy horse, I turned back,
but upon reaching a small river,
I was attacked by reckless bandits,
and barely escaped with my life.
Today, climbing mountains and crossing ridges,
my provisions are exhausted.
From the air, I heard the sound of your laundry beating;
I followed the sound, searching everywhere.
In my current wretched state,
I am clumsy in dealing with people,
fearing to delay the king's mission,
I rush on with urgency.
Now, on the road to Kuàijī,
how can I pass through?
I beg for directions;
I dare not hope for food!"
The woman replied: "I have heard the words of the ancients,
and they are not empty talk.
When feelings depart, intentions are hard to retain;
a broken string can still be mended.
Your journey
is surely known to me.
I see you looking back and forth,
your face bearing sorrow as you travel.
The rivers and mountains stretch far,
and you brave the wind and dust.
Now, not disdaining my lowliness,
I dare to invite you for a meal.
My home originally lay in Nányáng County,
my youthful radiance like bright silk.
Beating laundry in the pool, I see my rosy makeup reflected;
the lotus flowers on the water are not as fair as my face.
A traveler is like a boat adrift on the sea,
returning to its nest at dusk, fearing the late day.
If you do not disdain my lowliness,
I pray you make an effort to eat your fill."
Wǔ Zǐxū was about to proceed,
but was repeatedly and earnestly detained;
human sentiment is truly hard to refuse.
By the water's edge, he sat down
and ate the meal.
After three mouthfuls, he stopped eating,
ashamed before the woman,
and prepared to set off again.
Further urged by the woman's persuasion,
he ate his fill.
His shame deepened,
and he spoke of his heart's matter.
Wǔ Zǐxū replied:
"I am Wǔ Zǐxū,
fleeing Chǔ to enter southern Wú.
Fearing pursuit by King Píng,
for this, I travel day and night on this desperate road.
Grateful for the meal that fills my hunger,
I wonder how I can repay you!
Light in body, healthy, with clear eyes,
I am about to bid farewell and take to the long road.
I am a guest who has turned his back on the imperial capital;
now pursued by King Píng.
Your kindness need not be spoken for others to know;
I only hope you understand what lies in my heart."
Wǔ Zǐxū, having spoken, walked forward;
the woman wailed and burst into tears.
"The traveler, lonely and forlorn, truly deserves pity,
crawling in death's shadow yet clinging to life.
A single meal from me is still not enough,
a woman's heart fails to satisfy a husband's feelings.
Though you, noble sir, decline with dignity,
my heart feels ashamed, and my regard for you is not light.
Having spoken, she swallowed her sobs and wiped her tears: "Your honorable countenance is suddenly haggard,
if later you are pursued and captured,
they will surely say a woman brought you down.
At thirty, I have not spoken to a husband,
living with my mother among neighbors,
my delicate beauty and radiant face are here before you,
a chaste woman's loyalty and fidelity are vainly cast away.
Calling out, she said to Minister Wǔ, "Do not doubt,"
then immediately embraced a stone and threw herself into the river to die.
Zǐxū turned his head and gazed long after her,
pitying the woman, his heart filled with sorrow,
seeing from afar her stone-embracing form vanish into the river,
he could not help crying out, 'Injustice!'
For no reason, the Yǐng waters extinguished a human trace,
shedding tears, lamenting with doubled grief:
'If in later days I rise to high station,
I will only bestow a hundred gold pieces to bury and inter you!'
Zǐxū finished weeping,
and proceeded further on his journey.
Wind and dust grimed his face,
flying dust obscured the sky,
his spirit was in turmoil,
when suddenly he reached a deep river.
The water's source had no bottom,
the banks were broad without boundary,
he climbed mountains, entered valleys, winding along streams seeking the source.
Dragons and serpents blocked the road,
he drew his sword and swept them aside;
tigers and wolves filled the path,
he immediately strung his bow.
Hungry, he ate grass among the reeds;
thirsty, he drank from flowing springs beneath the cliffs.
A husbandman, for vengeance, stirs his wrath,
facing death is like sleep to him.
In the riverlands, he suddenly came upon a household,
and immediately knocked on the gate begging for food.
A woman came out in response,
hearing the voice from afar,
she knew from a distance it was her younger brother Zǐxū.
With intimate words, she expressed longing and inquired after him,
but Zǐxū kept his mouth shut and did not speak.
Knowing her brother had been thirsty and weary for a long time,
she fetched a gourd to hold rice,
and also made bitter greens into a pickle.
Zǐxū, a worthy man,
anticipated his elder sister's intent,
carefully pondered,
then understanding, said: "The gourd holding rice means bitter inside, sweet outside;
making bitter greens into a pickle means matching bitterness with bitterness.
In righteousness, you should send me away,
go quickly, go quickly,
you must not linger long."
He then immediately took his leave.
His sister asked her brother, "Now you set forth,
where do you intend to go?"
Zǐxū replied, "I intend to go to the state of Yuè.
Father and elder brother were killed,
I cannot not seek vengeance."
His elder sister embraced her brother's head,
sobbing until her voice grew hoarse,
not daring to wail aloud,
sighing, "How painful!
How bitter!"
She beat her own chest,
wondering what crime she and her brother committed in a past life,
to suffer such loneliness and misery!
"What crime have we committed through vast kalpas,
that now we betray our father and mother?
Though born human and possessing wealth and honor,
father in the south, son in the north, each scattered apart.
Suddenly remembering father and brother, I weep whether walking or sitting,
causing my heart to break inch by inch.
I do not know where my brother goes now,
leaving me alone to suffer desolation.
Now I have nothing left to cling to,
I regret not destroying myself and perishing!"
Zǐxū bid his sister farewell, saying, "Take good care,
do not need to weep a thousand lines of tears.
Father and brother were unjustly executed,
the fire in my heart is more searing than boiling water.
A husbandman now has no share of sky or sun,
his ambitious heart knots resentment, bitter and vast.
If I meet the day when Heaven's way opens clear,
I vow to capture King Píng of Chǔ alive.
Pluck out his heart and slice him piece by piece,
his nine clans shall all perish,
if it is not thus,
I vow never to return home!"
Having spoken these words,
he immediately headed south.
Having traveled over twenty *lǐ*,
his eye then twitched and his ear grew hot,
so he drew on the ground to divine,
the divination showed his nephews coming in pursuit.
He used water to perform a rite on his head,
placed bamboo under his waist,
and also put on wooden clogs backwards,
and drew the Earth Door and Heaven Gate on the ground,
then immediately lay down among the reeds,
chanting a spell, saying: "Those who catch me meet calamity,
those who pursue me perish,
urgently, as the law commands!"
Zǐxū had two nephews, Zǐ'ān and Zǐyǒng.
Arriving at a place where someone had eaten,
they knew it was their uncle Xū,
disregarding their mother's deep affection,
they immediately conceived malicious intent and gave chase.
"If I see the Chǔ emperor to claim reward,
I am sure to gain high promotion.
The rebel is now at our door,
why not capture him?"
Having traveled about ten *lǐ*,
they then rested by the roadside.
Zǐyǒng had some knowledge of yīnyáng arts,
so he drew on the ground to divine,
the divination showed his uncle had water on his head,
destined to fall by the river;
bamboo at his waist,
his grave mound would become desolate;
wooden clogs worn backwards,
he would not advance, wandering aimlessly.
If this hexagram holds true,
he is certain to meet his death.
No need to search further,
let us abandon this and return home.
Zǐxū, restraining himself, observed the signs,
and saw his nephews were not pursuing,
so he immediately hurried on,
not stopping day or night.
In the riverlands, he came upon another household,
its walls exceptionally imposing and splendid,
a solitary estate standing alone,
with no one around for miles,
not shaming his eight-foot frame,
he immediately knocked on the gate begging for food.
Zǐxū knocked on the gate to beg for food,
his wife composed herself and came out to respond.
At a glance, she knew it was her own husband,
and immediately wanted to speak and acknowledge him.
The woman stood straight, carefully considering,
not daring to approach and draw near,
with proper courtesy, she bowed and greeted him,
her voice choked with sorrow as she inquired:
"My humble home lies on the edge of the wilds,
with no neighbors for miles around, I dwell alone.
How did you, noble sir, come to be here,
your face bearing a sorrowful look and a hungry appearance?
Like a startled deer in the grass, frantic as if afraid of people,
restraining yourself, huddling your form to beg for food.
Though I am secluded deep in the inner chambers,
I have a faint acquaintance with your influence and bearing."
Zǐxū replied to the lady, saying:
"I am a man of Chǔ serving as a distant envoy,
traversing mountains and rivers to return to my homeland,
on the road I lost my way and became confused,
unwittingly wandering until I arrived here.
My homeland is far distant, at the western end of the sea,
separated by the vast expanse of three rivers.
Just now I presumptuously intruded upon you,
considering myself, it was truly rash.
Noble people often forget and mistakenly recognize others,
I do not recall ever knowing you, lady.
Now I wish to set forth for Jiāngdōng,
I pray you will kindly show me the way."
His wife then composed a poem using drug names, asking: "I am the wife of Wǔjiā, Xìxīn,
who long ago served in Liáng,
but before the wedding rites were complete, Dāngguī was not timely,
leaving me idle and living alone.
Gāoliángjiāng and jiè,
Zéxiè shows no pity.
Looking up, I sigh over Bīngláng,
when will Yuǎnzhì come?
Recently, hearing that the King of Chǔ is without principle,
he stirred the heart of Cháihú,
causing my family to be destroyed, Mángxiāo,
and forcing me to bend in Gān.
Wēiruí, timid and weak,
Shídǎn is hard to bear,
my husband, fearing to be a fugitive,
Zhūyú managed to escape.
Hiding his form in Jùncǎo,
concealing his shadow in Lílú,
like a chased wild creature,
he made his mad husband Làngdàng.
I recall tears staining Chìshí,
knotting hatred with Qīngxiāng.
At night, sleep is hard, Juémíng,
by day, my tongue dries, Juǎnbǎi.
Hearing your plea, Hòupò,
I cannot help but Zhízhú before you.
Speaking of my husband, Màimén,
made Cōngróng slow his steps.
Looking at your Lóngchǐ,
they resemble my Lángyá.
Júgěng, if it be so,
I wish to present Zhǐké.
" Zǐxū replied: "I am not the son of Wǔjiā,
nor am I a fugitive avoiding disaster,
listen to my story.
I was born in Bāshǔ,
grew up in Huòxiāng,
my father is Wúgōng,
living where Bèimǔ grows,
thus making Jīnyá seek treasure,
Zhīzǐ travel far.
Liú Jìnú is my humble friend,
Xú Chángqīng is my noble companion.
Together we crossed Ránghé,
injured by cold water,
my two companions, Mángxiāo,
only I survived alone.
Every day, Xuáncháng Xùduàn,
my thoughts drift aimlessly.
Walking alone on Héngshān,
Shígāo is hard to cross.
Climbing cliffs, Bājǐ,
several times encountering Cháihú.
Intending Kuǎndōng,
suddenly meeting Zhōngrǔ.
Paying attention to Bànxià,
not seeing Yùjīn.
I then turned back, Dāngguī,
and arrived here, Xiōngqióng.
My Yángchǐ,
are not Lángyá.
The sentiment of Júgěng,
I wish to know its meaning.
" The wife replied: "Do not be hasty, sir,
the road is long and distant.
Even if we have never met before,
what harm is there in mistaken recognition?
I am the daughter of Gōngsūn Zhōngdǐng,
matched with a gentleman in chaste virtue.
My husband’s surname is Wǔ, serving as minister,
he bound his hair and traveled a thousand lǐ to serve his king.
Since we parted, letters have ceased,
missing you, my sorrowful heart feels near to breaking.
The distant road is dark and silent,
my family is not accustomed to long separation.
My youthful beauty has faded, unlike before,
longing and tears have never ceased.
Years wasted guarding an empty chamber,
who can endure the season of fragrant blossoms?
Day and night in the green chamber, my appearance dims,
all because my wandering husband serves in Liáng.
Reluctant to gaze at the bright moon in the courtyard,
sorrowful, I return to the bedchamber to embrace the mandarin ducks.
Sending letters afar by wild geese may not reach,
the cold weather and long road create barriers.
Wishing to weave on the broken loom brings no joy,
ashamed to paint eyebrows before the mirror.
Particularly fond of magpie chatter on the grape trellis,
thinking of swallows nesting in pairs in the white jade hall.
You act like Qiū Hú, not recognizing me,
I also have no heart to learn mulberry picking.
Seeing the double front teeth in your mouth,
for this reason, recognition seems fitting.
A simple meal I would not begrudge,
I beg you to stay and not hurry away.
Zǐxū, being recognized, declined with thanks,
tactfully using soft words to explain:
"Lady, do not rashly interfere,
in this world there are many who look alike.
Your husband’s surname is Wǔ, serving as minister,
I am but a humble man dwelling in the wilds.
If you see your husband, convey a message,
advise him with reason to return home.
Now, due to urgent matters, I must go to Jiāngdōng,
I cannot linger day and night.
The woman, knowing he was planning great affairs,
dared not disturb him further.
She provided for him according to custom,
and sent him off with reason.
Zǐxū, having been recognized by the woman,
said no more.
Before the husband could achieve his aim,
he was recognized by a woman,
how could a small matter
ruin my great duty?
A determined man, carrying a stone,
then knocked out his own teeth.
By day, he watched the sun,
by night, he observed the stars,
traveling without rest,
until he reached the northern bank of the Wú River.
Fearing someone might ambush him,
he hid his body among the reeds,
and, gripping his sword, sang a sorrowful song, sighing:
The river waters vast, waves rising high,
reaching the sky, boiling, now shallow, now deep.
Flying sand billows, obscuring the Milky Way,
the clear wind whips the waves, as if toppling forests.
White grass covers the plains everywhere,
green willows line the banks in rows.
Magpies scavenge for food, crisscrossing,
fish and dragons leap and frolic in chaos.
Otters and water cats play and race,
a thousand times over, I cannot help but sigh long.
Suddenly recalling my father and brother wrongly executed,
my innards feel torn apart.
Thinking of the enmity, pain and sorrow overwhelm me,
today, meeting it, I will not let go.
If my life ends in this river pool,
life or death depends on this night.
I do not begrudge my bones buried in the long waves,
but the vengeance for father and brother must not cease.
The grasses above wither, all by the wind’s will,
yet it is the power of the heavens that transforms all.
The mournful song had ended,
and he walked to the riverbank, gazing into the distance.
He saw only the vast expanse of the river and its pools—
how could he cross!
Stretching his neck among the reeds,
he looked back in silence.
He encountered no boat-rowing guest,
no passenger on a raft in sight.
He saw only river crows leaving the shore,
and white egrets vying in flight;
fish and turtles darting about,
cormorants and wild geese alighting in disarray.
He also saw long sandbars stretching endlessly,
misty shores with surging waves,
fog dark and gloomy,
clouds thick and overcast.
Trees lay broken on the aged banks,
moonlight shone on a solitary hill.
Dragons stirred, turtles startled,
the river churned and waves arose.
If there were a traveler who had lost his homeland,
he would climb the mountain ridge and think of home;
if there were a passenger on a raft,
he would point to the stars to find his way.
A pillar of Mínshān,
like tigers and wolves coiling,
roared like the sound of drums and horns,
yet there was no boat to cross.
After spending another night,
he hid among the reeds.
On the waves, he saw a single person,
singing a song while rowing,
holding a fishing rod and hook,
looking like a fisherman.
He emerged from the reeds
and called out: “You, sir, with the hook and boat,
please come ashore for a moment to see me.
Do not decline due to weariness;
I hope you will show compassion and care.”
The fisherman heard the call,
followed the sound,
and suddenly saw a person among the reeds.
He immediately rowed his boat to the shore.
He put away his rod and reeled in his line,
rested his oar and laid down his pole.
Following the flowing water, he moved gracefully,
singing in the clear breeze and asking: “Where do you intend to go today, sir?
You stand alone by the riverbank and shore,
with no boat-rowing guest in sight,
nor any companion in solitude.
Are you drifting like a wandering tumbleweed?
Standing alone on a desolate isle, by a secluded shore.
Even if you seek a boat to cross,
here there are no boats at all.
I am not ashamed of my lowly, foolish self;
I wish to hear you fully explain your situation.”
Zǐxū replied: “I have heard that people understand each other through shared principles,
and fish recognize each other in rivers and lakes.
I am but a wandering traveler;
how dare I deceive you with empty words!
Now, due to a pressing matter,
I wish to travel to Jiāngnán.
I am clumsy in my dealings with people;
I hope you, sir, will understand my plight.
If you would grant me passage,
I would repay your kindness with my life;
if you cannot allow it,
I will accept it and give up.”
The fisherman replied: “Just now, I observed your appearance and demeanor;
I see you are different from ordinary people.
Your noble intentions are clear;
there is no need for further explanation.
I have heard that parting with a person does not diminish their worth,
and parting with jade does not make one poor.
Duke Mù of Qín bestowed wine as a favor,
and a skilled speaker alone halted three armies,
receiving great rewards with an empty cage.
I see you have endured hardships for a long time,
thirsty and weary for many hours.
You cannot cross the river on an empty stomach;
I wish to offer you a meal.
My home is more than ten lǐ round trip from here;
it will take some time to go and return.
Please do not doubt or find it strange.”
Zǐxū replied: “I only seek passage by boat;
how dare I hope for a meal!”
The fisherman replied: “I have heard that when the qílín gets food,
it travels a thousand lǐ in a day;
when the fènghuáng gets food,
it soars across the four seas.”
After saying this,
he left his boat and went.
He headed home to fetch food.
Zǐxū heard these words
and watched the fisherman’s boat.
Zǐxū thought to himself:
“This person told me he is going home to fetch food;
will he not bring many people to capture me?”
So he abandoned the boat and fled,
hiding again among the reeds.
In a short while, the fisherman
returned to the boat.
The fisherman had brought a jug of fine wine,
five catties of fish and meat,
ten thin cakes,
and a pot of rice.
Arriving at the boat,
he did not see the man among the reeds,
only an empty boat on the shore.
Feelings of concern and attachment
filled him with endless sorrow.
The fisherman sang and called out: “You in the reeds,
why are you hiding?
Come out here and see me;
I truly have no ill intentions.
Do not be suspicious or hesitant;
do not make things difficult.
I have brought food for you;
why do you not come and eat?”
Zǐxū heard the boatman’s words
and knew there was no malice.
He then emerged from the reeds,
ashamed of the trouble taken to fetch food,
and humbly expressed his gratitude.
At that moment, they set out the meal
and ate together.
Then they rowed the boat,
reaching the middle of the river.
Zǐxū, having eaten his fill,
thought to himself: “When an ordinary person receives a meal from another,
they feel indebted;
when they receive two meals,
they exert effort for that person.”
He took out a jade disc from his bosom to give as a gift,
but the boatman, fearing the lateness of the hour and eager to proceed,
would not accept the offering.
Zǐxū worried that his token of trust was too little,
so he took off his precious sword to offer as reward.
The fisherman rested his oar and turned around,
saying to Zǐxū: “Do not act rashly,
but think carefully.
What value does a single meal have?
When a person is in distress,
they are like fish and turtles among a school;
when a nobleman is in difficulty,
they are like dragons and snakes sharing a space.
The King of Chǔ is hunting for you,
offering a thousand in gold for your capture;
anyone who hides you
will be executed and their clan exterminated.
I neither covet the heavy reward from the enlightened ruler above,
nor do I fear the punishment of execution below.
You wish to reward me with a precious sword—
how does it compare to King Píng’s possessions?
The precious sword, Lóngquán,
is for your self-defense;
the jade disc, a treasure of Jīng,
is meant for those you hold dear.
If later you rise to wealth and honor,
do not forget this day.
I blame my own frail, willow-like years;
meeting you so late in life,
regarding the sword and jade,
please keep them no longer.
If you understand my heart,
there is no need for further thanks.”
Zǐxū saw that the fisherman would not accept,
and gradually felt uneasy in his heart.
He thought to himself,
fearing the boatman might find his token of trust too meager.
Though it was a king’s treasure,
what could he do?
So he threw the sword into the river,
and a divine light shone brilliantly.
The sword surged and sank three times,
dancing gracefully on the water.
The river god heard the sword roar from afar,
trembled in fear, and the waves boiled and surged.
Fish and turtles hurriedly burrowed into the mud in fear,
while fish and dragons rushed forth and leaped out.
The river god caught it with his hands,
and in fear, handed it over.
Once the sword left the water,
fish and turtles leaped about,
the sun and moon shone bright and clear,
the mountains and forests gleamed,
clouds parted and mist dissipated,
rosy clouds scattered and smoke drifted,
trees on the shore welcomed the guest,
and the river breeze saw him off.
Gazing into the distance at the white egrets by the sandbar,
at dusk, they prepared to return to the woods.
By the shore, no boat awaited,
and there was no companion for the traveler.
He saw only the solitary hill amidst vast waters,
looked back toward his homeland,
wiped his tears, staining his clothes,
his heart filled with melancholy and sorrow.
As they crossed the river to the southern shore,
Zǐxū asked the boatman: “What is your surname and given name, sir?”
"What is your hometown, and in which province and county do you reside?"
The fisherman replied: "I too have neither surname nor name,
I have long dwelled by the river as my companion.
Across the dry marsh shores,
and by the deep pools where swords are sheathed,
today two fugitives meet;
what need is there to exchange names and surnames!
You are the gentleman among the reeds,
I am the man upon the boat;
our intentions are sufficient to be understood,
there is no need to forget each other in wealth and honor."
Zǐxū said: "I am indebted to you, sir, for saving me;
I shall never forget it.
Even a wounded snake that receives medicine
can still repay the kindness."
The fisherman asked: "Now that you are fleeing,
which state do you intend to seek refuge in?"
Zǐxū said: "I intend to go to the state of Yuè."
The fisherman said: "If you go to Yuè,
Yuè is on friendly terms with Chǔ,
and they have never engaged in warfare;
I fear you may be captured and handed over,
and your desire for revenge will go unfulfilled.
If you go to the state of Wú,
you will surely find a way.
The king of Wú has long been an enemy of Chǔ,
and the two states are not on good terms.
Wú and Chǔ have fought many battles,
and Wú lacks capable ministers;
they would greatly value someone like you."
Zǐxū asked the boatman: "How can I gain entry to Wú?"
The boatman said: "When you reach Wú,
enter the capital city,
smear mud on your face,
let your hair down and feign madness,
run east and west,
and wail loudly three times."
Zǐxū said: "I beg you to explain this method."
The boatman replied: "Smearing mud on your face
signifies appearing turbid on the outside while remaining clear within;
wailing three times
and running east and west
is to seek a wise ruler;
letting your hair down in the market
is fitting for such a situation.
I am no sage,
but I have experienced much."
Zǐxū, having received his instruction,
bowed in gratitude to the fisherman.
Fearing that envoys from Chǔ might encounter them,
they could not linger long;
upon reaching the shore, he departed immediately.
His voice choked and hoarse,
like four birds scattering in flight,
or like three branches of a tree parting ways.
Thus, he bid farewell to the fisherman and headed south,
filled with longing,
his sorrow unceasing.
Turning his head to gaze into the distance,
he suddenly saw the fisherman capsize his boat and drown.
Zǐxū felt ashamed and indebted to the fisherman,
his sobs and mournful cries unending,
and he composed a lament, sighing:
The great river's waters, vast and boundless,
where clouds and water meet and connect.
Oh, the pain, the pain, unbearable;
oh, the bitterness, the bitterness, injustice upon injustice.
Since ancient times, parting is the way of human emotion,
life, death, wealth, and honor are all tied to heaven.
What grievance did you, sir, hold against Xū?
That you capsized your boat in the river.
Waves and boat, floating, sinking, submerged,
singing of injustice, the pain cuts deep.
An inch of sorrowful heart feels as if cut by a knife,
on the road, tears cannot help but soak my robe.
Gazing toward the land of Wú, unreachable,
thinking of my homeland, filled with deep resentment.
If I meet a wise ruler and rise to prominence,
I shall unleash the heart of a hero.
The lament ended,
he pressed onward,
still filled with sorrow.
A man of mettle, through trials and hardships,
why such great adversity?
Loyal and devoted,
serving his lord for nine years,
diligent day and night,
unwavering from dawn to dusk,
now fallen into ruin,
what more is there to say?
Words spoken, resentment held,
anger rising, choking his throat,
karma and fate,
all tied to heaven.
Climbing mountains, scaling ridges,
crossing waters, seeking rivers.
Seeking retreat, yet unable to retreat;
seeking to advance, yet unable to advance.
At every move, threatened by hunger,
life hanging by a thread.
King Píng went too far,
crying out, proclaiming injustice.
Zǐxū, sword at his side,
walked forward on foot.
Reaching the wild and desolate mountains,
where stone cliffs pierce the sky,
and chasms plunge ten thousand zhàng into the earth,
vines and bamboo crisscrossing,
gazing afar at pines and creepers,
the mountain cliffs dark and steep.
Insects and wolves gathering and scattering,
a hundred birds chirping in harmony.
Thinking of his homeland,
he sang a song:
What I long for lies on a long road,
crossing river waters, entering the land of Wú.
Father and brother, lost in darkness, where are they?
Left alone, orphaned, in distress and fear.
A man adrift, following karma's course,
life, death, wealth, and honor, how constant are they?
King Píng wrongly heeded Wèi Líng's words,
trusted slanderers, and killed the loyal and good.
Thinking of my homeland, sorrow hard to cease,
by water, climbing mountains, emotions unending.
The Chǔ emperor, fond of slender waists,
many beauties in the palace died of hunger.
The daughter of Duke Mù of Qín, fair as jade,
at sixteen, her beauty like peach and plum blossoms.
Seeing her grace, he took her as consort;
how could a ruler act with such impropriety?
Since fleeing, ever burdened with worry,
leaving me orphaned, with nowhere to turn.
By day, seeking ghostly paths on the road,
hiding my shadow, my form, always wandering by night.
When will the day come to carve praises on Yānshān?
Braving dust and hardship, my temples turning autumn-gray.
Not fearing to traverse east and west, defying heaven's barriers,
only worrying of thirst and exhaustion in desolate lands.
May I reach my destination safely,
journey unhindered, flowing freely.
If in Wú I meet a wise ruler,
I shall raise an army and first behead Wèi Líng.
The lament ended,
yet still filled with fervor.
Turning his back to the northern pass of Chǔ,
heading south to ascend the lands of Wú.
As darkness fell from the sky,
clouds gathered, overcast and gloomy.
Lost, wandering aimlessly,
mountains and forests blocking the way.
Strange birds flocking together,
insects and wolves forming packs.
Birds crying like xīngxīng,
beasts named fèifèi.
Suddenly, his heart startled,
he drew his sword and marched on.
Light emerged from the scabbard,
illuminating the wilderness brightly,
within it, the sun and moon,
and the seven stars of the Northern Dipper.
Heart bold and fierce,
unafraid of a thousand soldiers.
If King Píng captures me,
the matter will not end peacefully;
if I am seized,
death a hundred times over, no chance of life.
Sneaking along hidden paths,
swallowing anger, stifling cries,
at the rustle of grass in the wind,
immediately hiding my form.
The sword song ended,
he pressed onward again.
Crossing Guǎnglíng in the north,
ascending the lands of Wú in the south,
border passes urgent and strict,
provinces and counties vigilant and severe,
checkpoints crisscrossing,
garrisons continuous.
Hiding his body, avoiding his shadow,
step by step, moving forward.
In less than a month's time,
he reached the state of Wú.
Following exactly the fisherman's instructions,
he let down his hair and entered the marketplace,
smearing mud on his face as he walked,
feigning madness, wailing loudly three times,
running east and west.
The ministers and officials of Wú,
riding horses into the market on patrol,
saw a man of extraordinary appearance and talent,
eight chǐ tall,
and knew it was Zǐxū.
He bid farewell to the others:
"You are all from good families,
who have shared hardships with me.
Looking at you, my feelings are not satisfied,
how can I bear to part and go separate ways?
When will we meet again in the future?
Though parting, our hearts remain as close as kin."
From this point on, we are parted,
Both becoming wanderers in foreign lands.
The wise ministers and high officials
Hurried to inform the King of Wú: “Just after parting from Your Majesty’s dragon countenance,
We wandered in the marketplace,
And saw a foreign gentleman,
Covered in mud and acting wild,
With disheveled hair, weeping bitterly,
Running east and west.
We observed carefully from the side,
And could discern from his appearance—
We beg Your Majesty to summon and question this lingering stranger—
He must be a knight-errant bearing a grievance!”
Hearing these words from his ministers,
The King of Wú felt joy in his heart.
He then assembled all his officials,
Parted the pearl curtain and spoke of a dream: “Last night in the third watch,
I dreamed that a worthy man entered our realm.
Thereupon I felt light in body and vigorous in health,
Leaping with uncontrollable excitement.
You, my ministers, deliberate carefully
And interpret for me whether this dream is auspicious or ominous.”
Upon hearing the king’s words,
All the officials at once danced with laughter,
Joined in singing of peace,
And together proclaimed, “Long live the king!”
“In the marketplace is an eight-foot gentleman
Who perfectly matches Your Majesty’s heart.
Seeing him among the ministers,
We cannot contain our joy and congratulations.”
The King of Wú immediately ordered a swift envoy
To go to the marketplace and summon the worthy minister:
“Convey my words for me:
Though we have not met before,
I wish to see you,
To express my thoughts face to face.”
The envoy received his command,
Galloped straight into the marketplace,
Saw Wú Zǐxū and fully relayed the King of Wú’s words.
Wú Zǐxū, obeying the king’s command,
Dared not delay or disobey,
And followed the envoy immediately.
When he reached the King of Wú’s hall,
He prostrated himself on the ground,
Choking with sobs until his voice grew hoarse,
And only rose after a long while.
The King of Wú, knowing it was Wú Zǐxū,
At once expressed his sorrow and inquired with sympathy: “The King of Chǔ did not heed loyal admonitions,
But wrongly accepted the words of treacherous ministers,
Unjustly killing your father and elder brother.
How cruel and ruthless!
The grief and sorrow are beyond words,
The pain and suffering—
Who could bear it?
Mountains and rivers lie between,
You traversed far through wind and clouds.
My state is small and narrow,
Yet you have troubled yourself to come from afar.”
After a long silence, Wú Zǐxū
Gathered his hair and spoke: “My father and elder brother served their lord without due care,
And were thus executed by the Emperor of Chǔ.
I, unable to continue the family line,
Abandoned my father and left my lord, fleeing for my life.
I have heard that when a state is about to fall,
Disasters arise in competition.
When a tree is about to break,
Wind and frost press upon it together.
Alone, it is hard to stand firm;
Seeing such hardship,
Right and wrong are difficult to distinguish,
Dragons and snakes are intermingled.
I wished to cut my own throat and die,
But would be ashamed to face my ancestors in the underworld.
Therefore, I have come to entrust myself to a wise king,
Hoping Your Majesty will know the sincerity of my heart.
I dwell in the wild grasses,
Grew up in a humble thatched gate,
Unworthy to serve and stand before a king.
I am most fortunate to be received and recorded by Your Majesty.”
The King of Wú replied, saying: “My state is narrow and small,
Lacking in loyal and worthy men.
If I appoint you now as a minister,
Would you feel it a disgrace to bend your principles?”
Wú Zǐxū said: “I am but a lowly man,
Undeserving of such great favor.
To be received and recorded by Your Majesty
Is already an extraordinary act of grace.
If further honored with appointment as a minister,
I would not dare, even if it meant death!”
The King of Wú asked those beside him:
“What do you, my ministers, think?”
All the assembled officials voiced their approval,
Saying together: “The wise king has moved others,
And a foreigner has come to submit.”
He was appointed as a chief minister of support, And the entire state together proclaimed, “Long live the king!”
Zǐxū served as a minister with unwavering loyalty and integrity,
constantly harboring a diligent and tireless heart.
Day and night, he was vigilant and cautious,
serving his lord without a trace of disloyalty.
His words did not wound the spirit,
and his speech was harmonious and tempered,
with people from near and far gathering in crowds,
and officials flourishing in great numbers.
The heavenly troops did not stir,
the warhorses halted their whips,
the four borders returned to peace,
and the eight directions were tranquil and secure.
Calamity and chaos did not arise,
disasters and harm did not occur,
the common people rejoiced,
songs and ballads filled the roads,
akin to the era of Yáo and Shùn.
All proclaimed that our emperor was divinely inspired,
the sacred sun lofty and majestic,
heaven and earth illuminated once more.
In the first year of Zǐxū’s governance,
the wind did not howl through the branches,
and the rain did not break the clods of earth.
In the second year of his governance,
granaries and storehouses overflowed,
the realm was peaceful and prosperous,
officials ceased their greed and cruelty,
and the bureaucracy refrained from tyranny.
In the third year of his governance,
the six barbarian tribes submitted tribute,
and all states pledged allegiance.
In the fourth year of his governance,
auspicious dragons were moved to manifest as omens,
red sparrows carried writings in their beaks,
auspicious grasses grew together,
and bountiful grains flourished in harmony.
Farmers yielded the borders of their fields,
and lost items on the road were left untouched.
The three teachings flourished together,
and the city gates remained unbarred.
There was no need for conscription,
and people lived freely without forced labor.
In the fifth year of Zǐxū’s governance,
the sun and moon shone brightly once more,
markets had no dual pricing,
cats and mice shared the same burrow,
rice and wheat were measured fairly,
and prisons held no inmates.
All spoke of the harmony between ruler and minister,
with praise spreading far and wide,
and gratitude felt for Chancellor Wǔ’s achievements.
The common people all came to Zǐxū’s gate, saying: “We wish to join Chancellor Wǔ in raising troops to attack Chǔ.”
Zǐxū, seeing brave men volunteering,
dared not act on his own authority,
and thus addressed King Wú: “I am but a lowly man,
undeservedly favored with Your Majesty’s grace,
having achieved no merit,
how dare I harbor such ambitions?
Judging myself unfit,
I ultimately dare not proceed.”
King Wú replied: “I have heard that one raises sons to provide for old age,
and accumulates deeds in preparation for decline.
Last year, I considered sending you to seek vengeance,
but feared your heart for revenge had not yet stirred.
The peace and prosperity of recent years
are all due to Chancellor Wǔ’s achievements.
If you do not avenge this wrong now,
how can you be called a filial son?
For my state to raise troops and attack Chǔ
is precisely the right time.”
He summoned the brave men of the state
to join Chancellor Wǔ in seeking retribution.
The summons declared: “Chancellor Wǔ’s father and elder brother
were unjustly executed by King Píng.
Now we intend to mobilize the heavenly troops to punish Chǔ,
recruiting those willing to serve with their strength.
If there are those willing to pledge their lives to follow,
they must urgently enlist.
Generous rewards will be granted first,
with honors and emoluments not light.
Those with such fierce and heroic spirit,
come quickly to declare yourselves,
by petition.”
Once issued,
the news spread far and wide,
and all came forward to submit their names,
vying to enlist.
The Ministry of War selected and trained them,
examining and evaluating their abilities,
until their courage surpassed the three armies,
capable of deciding victory a thousand miles away.
Some lifted gates and wielded logs,
others held square beams in their hands,
carried stones and leaped through the air,
or bent bows capable of piercing seven layers of armor.
After seven days of public notice,
nine hundred thousand elite soldiers were recruited.
They were rewarded with crimson and granted green insignia,
each receiving a thousand bolts of silk.
The officers led them outside the city,
arranging them in goose-wing formation.
King Wú, seeing the warriors arrayed south of the city,
immediately went to console and encourage the troops.
King Wú asked Zǐxū: “Now that we intend to attack Chǔ,
how many troops are needed?”
Zǐxū addressed King Wú: “We need only ten thousand troops.”
King Wú said: “Is ten thousand not too few?”
Zǐxū replied: “I have heard that one man resolved to die
is a match for a hundred;
if a hundred unite their hearts,
they can roam unhindered under heaven.”
King Wú said: “Not so.
Only with nine hundred thousand men
can we begin the campaign.”
King Wú then appointed Zǐxū as Marshal and Grand General, commanding the troops.
Receiving the Son of Heaven’s mandate,
he would avenge his father and redress the wrong.
Thereupon, they slaughtered many cattle and sheep,
feasting south of the city.
There were a thousand hu of wine,
and ten thousand jin of meat,
all distributed equally,
with no distinction between high and low in the feast.
King Wú escorted Zǐxū outside the city, saying: “You must strive diligently,
take care on the road ahead,
for Heaven’s way is forgiving,
and your desire for vengeance will surely be fulfilled.
I will have no worries for the state,
and you will not fail the spirits of the departed.
Once the matter is settled, return early,
and let there be no cause for concern.”
Zǐxū addressed King Wú: “I now lead troops to punish Chǔ,
and will surely achieve my heart’s desire.
May Your Majesty not fret or worry from afar.
The journey I undertake is not long,
within a month or so,
once the matter is settled, I will return with the troops,
and then shall die in gratitude!”
Zǐxū, having taken leave of the king,
immediately mobilized the heavenly troops.
Forty-two great drums resounded to the heavens,
thirty-six horns echoed across the earth,
shaking the surrounding forests for a hundred li,
rumbling and roaring.
The vanguard seized the living,
and first cleared the path.
Battle formations spread across all sides,
the sounds of the field filling the plains,
iron cavalry charging forth in great numbers,
fierce warriors, savage and fierce, vying to break through.
Soaring for a thousand li,
they resembled fish scales;
ten thousand soldiers marched in rows,
like the wings of wild geese.
Long spears stood upright in ranks,
dense as a forest reaching the sky;
rhinoceros horn crossbows were drawn with palms,
curved like the crescent moon.
White banners fell like snow,
war swords gleamed like frost,
crossbows fired like thunderbolts,
drawn blades roaring like swords.
The general issued commands,
so tight that not a drop of water could leak through,
the Grand Commander gave strict orders,
so that even flying birds could not pass.
The troops advanced in vast, surging waves,
crisscrossing for hundreds of li.
Golden armor glimmered,
silver saddles shone brilliantly,
trampling through mountains and forests,
rushing and stirring up chaos.
Foxes and hares fled in fear,
startling dragons and snakes into scurrying away.
The general raised a red flag on horseback,
and the soldiers each followed their orders.
The vanguard cleared the path swift as the wind,
and soon reached the northeastern bank of the Yellow River.
The vanguard led the way,
[□] the road galloping,
arranging boats and ships in order,
the army crossed the water in formation,
those in charge of construction,
rushed across the water like flying reeds.
Once the troops and horses reached the riverbank,
it was necessary to feast the soldiers.
After the officers had eaten,
they immediately crossed the river.
The wind and waves subsided,
the mountains and forests were bright and clear,
the sun and moon shone brightly,
the mist rolled back to reveal the blue sky,
the clouds returned to the vast sea.
Simply because there were many people and numerous hands,
by dawn they had already reached the west of the river.
Zǐxū issued orders to the troops,
they must be vigilant and ready to capture.
This was King Píng’s territory,
they were not yet familiar with the mountains and rivers,
they first ascended the dangerous passes,
sent scouts far ahead,
dispatched patrol officers,
to plunder and roam freely.
They secretly advanced along hidden paths,
scouting for over a month.
As the journey neared its end,
they were about to reach the state of Chǔ.
The King of Chǔ unfortunately died early,
and Crown Prince Zhāo was established as king,
to take charge of the military and state affairs.
When King Zhāo heard that Zǐxū’s troops and horses were about to arrive,
he then mobilized the heavenly soldiers,
selected and trained brave warriors skilled in the five weapons,
bestowed them with much silk and cloth,
to widely establish meritorious deeds.
The state of Chǔ had vast land and dense population,
so they raised an army of a million,
banners and flags blotted out the sun,
armor and clothing filled the sky,
they formed ranks and advanced freely,
intending to engage Zǐxū in battle.
On the city walls, they built battle towers,
each gate was fortified,
chariots were prepared and ambushes set,
they smelted and cast bronze.
On all sides, they placed many rolling logs,
the troops and horses were fully prepared,
with strength to match ten thousand men.
King Zhāo led the brave warriors,
and thus clashed with the Wú army.
Zǐxū then deployed his troops and set formations,
like fish scales.
The conch shells roared and called three times,
the great drums sounded and they advanced.
They arrayed a thousand troops at the Chǔ frontier,
deployed ten thousand formations at Huángchí.
In an instant, swords and blades crossed,
they drew blades and swords roared,
spears were stained with sweat and blood,
arrows fell like maddened deer.
Dust and earth rose to the sky,
iron horses neighed and shouted,
one side fell, the other advanced,
only striving and pressing forward.
Each prepared with a heart for killing,
with no intention of retreating.
The western army was greatly defeated,
corpses lay scattered across the wilderness,
weapons could not be wielded,
men and horses piled upon each other.
Zǐxū fought ten battles and won nine,
not losing a single soldier.
King Zhāo saw his troops being slaughtered,
and in fear fled into the city.
Zǐxū pursued closely behind,
like flying reeds rushing into fire.
The Wú army followed closely in pursuit,
like wind and clouds,
they swept away the Chǔ army in one direction,
like hot water poured on snow.
Zǐxū pointed his whip from afar and said to King Zhāo: “Your father King Píng,
was utterly without virtue,
he took a bride for his son,
but took her as his own consort.
Loyal ministers remonstrated,
and were then executed;
treacherous ministers flattered and caused chaos,
yet were enfeoffed as marquises.
He killed my father and elder brother,
causing them wrongful death and suffering,
now I shall avenge my father’s wrongs,
and thus satisfy my heart’s desire.
If I were to eat your heart now,
it would still not be enough;
even if ten thousand soldiers confront me,
they would not match my single person.
Now I shall take your father’s bones,
and your living body,
to sacrifice to the spirits of my father and elder brother, only then will it be sufficient.
” King Zhāo, filled with fear,
then surrendered with a white flag.
The Wú army shouted loudly,
directly entered the Chǔ city,
searched for King Zhāo,
and burned his palaces.
King Zhāo abandoned the city and fled,
but was then captured by Minister Wǔ,
who bound King Zhāo in return.
“Where is your father’s tomb now?
” King Zhāo said to Zǐxū: “My father King Píng,
has already passed away,
the crime of betraying you,
has sentenced him to the Yellow Springs,
since the matter is thus fitting,
my body shall be sliced to pieces,
father and son replace each other,
what use are the corpses?
Please satisfy your vengeful heart,
as you wish with axe and halberd.
” King Zhāo was tortured,
could not bear the suffering,
endured unbearable pain,
and then revealed his father’s burial place.
Zǐxū captured Wèi Líng,
sliced him and took out his heart and liver,
cut his body ten thousand times,
and exterminated his nine clans.
Zǐxū called to King Zhāo: “My father was killed,
and thrown into the deep river.
” Then he stopped the flow,
retrieved King Píng’s bones,
along with Wèi Líng and King Zhāo,
and took all their hearts and livers,
went to the riverside,
and sacrificed to his father and elder brother’s spirits, saying: “Your son Zǐxū,
is deeply unfilial,
father and elder brother were wrongfully executed,
how painful and distressing!
Because my strength was insufficient before,
so I wasted the years.
Now I have killed him and his son,
and thrown them into the deep river,
to offer sacrifice to father and elder brother.
May the spirits accept it.
” After Zǐxū offered the sacrifice,
he cried out loud,
moved so that the sun and moon lost their light,
rivers boiled and churned.
Suddenly clouds darkened and mist grew thick,
the earth shook and mountains crumbled.
The soldiers wailed and wept,
people felt sorrow and grief,
fish and dragons held their breath,
the river water ceased to flow,
streams dried up and springs withered,
wind and dust were bleak and fierce.
After Zǐxū offered the sacrifice,
he took his own sword,
his hatred grew even deeper,
he again slashed King Píng’s white bones;
the bones bled with the sword’s stroke,
like slaughtering a sheep.
He took fire and burned them,
letting the wind scatter them as fine dust.
Then he took his sword and beheaded King Zhāo,
cutting him into a hundred pieces,
threw them into the river,
for fish and turtles to eat,
just like my father.
Zǐxū searched but could not find his father and elder brother’s bones,
so he set up a tree to represent his father and elder brother,
which still exists today within Bózhōu’s borders, over one hundred and twenty lǐ to the southeast.
Later generations did not know,
now it is Chéngfù County.
Zǐxū gathered his troops and turned back,
intending to attack the two states of Liáng and Zhèng.
He wrote a letter to the King of Zhèng, saying: "King Píng of Chǔ was unprincipled,
unjustly executing my father and elder brother.
Zǐshàng was your minister,
why did you not devise a plan?
You sent him to Chǔ to be put to death,
treating a minister as if he were a ruler.
I will destroy King Chǔ to avenge this,
then turn my troops to punish Zhèng."
When the King of Zhèng received the letter,
he was extremely frightened and anxious,
not knowing what plan to adopt.
He considered raising troops to resist,
but feared his soldiers would not prevail.
So he summoned men of secret strategy: "Whoever can halt Wú's army,
I will share the state and rule jointly with him,
and further bestow a thousand pieces of gold."
Then there was the fisherman's son,
who immediately answered the call and offered his name.
"I can halt Wú's army,
without needing an inch of soldiers or a foot of swords,
only requiring a small boat,
a single oar,
a pair of dried fish,
a bowl of wheat rice,
a jug of fine wine,
placed in the water east of the city.
I have my own method."
The King of Zhèng complied with his words,
immediately sought the boat and other items,
and sent them into the water.
The fisherman plied the oar, singing a long song,
sailing the boat in play.
The King of Zhèng closed the four city gates,
and watched from the city wall to see what plan he would employ,
to halt Wú's army.
Zǐxū's troops and horses,
when they were still over thirty lǐ from the state of Zhèng,
first sent scouts to see how many troops Zhèng had to oppose them.
They proceeded to the state of Zhèng,
and found the four city gates tightly shut.
They then went to outside the east city gate,
where in the pond water there was only a single man,
riding in a leaky, covered boat,
singing with his mouth and saying: "The man in the reeds,
is he not a man in dire straits?
I have a jug of fine wine,
five catties of fish and meat,
ten pieces of flatbread,
a jar of rice,
please come to the boat and eat.
If it is ill fortune, I will bear it myself,
if it is good fortune, then you will know my intent.
Should you serve a wise ruler,
you will gain glory, splendor, wealth, and honor.
If by chance the matter is fitting,
I hope you will not abandon me."
The general, hearing the boatman's words,
immediately turned back,
and went to Zǐxū's side to fully relate the boatman's words.
When Zǐxū heard these words,
he immediately knew it was the fisherman's son.
Zǐxū was overjoyed.
"I have a grievance and enmity,
which I must go and destroy,
but because of him I was saved,
how could I forget his kindness?
To forget poverty after gaining wealth and honor,
even Heaven would not aid such a one.
To not repay kindness received,
how can one be called a man!
To repay kindness if received,
is graceful and refined."
Zǐxū reined in his horse, gathered his whip,
went to the water and embraced the youth,
patting and consoling him, weeping sadly and offering condolences:
"Your father drowned in the deep river,
suffering cruelly, alas, alas,
I hope you bear no hatred!"
The King of Zhèng, afraid and fearful,
came out of the city to welcome and bow to Zǐxū,
stepping forward and saying: "I have heard that General's grievance and enmity have been avenged,
I congratulate you, how splendid!
My crimes now are more than enough for death,
I beg to preserve my humble life."
Zǐxū replied to the King of Zhèng: "My elder brother served you as ruler,
you should have concealed and protected him,
but you twisted things to accord with King Píng's wishes,
sending him to his death;
since my elder brother lost his life,
you must pay with your life."
The King of Zhèng said: "I sent a distant envoy with a letter,
saying to spare your kind father from punishment,
I did not know the details,
I sent him to see.
He said he would return in ten days or a month,
I did not know King Píng would execute him.
I now deserve death,
I am resigned and have nothing to say.
Great General, you have achieved your wish for vengeance,
destroyed their ancestral temple,
how splendid, leaping for joy,
my congratulations are boundless!
I humbly beg your generous mercy,
to let me live."
The boatman spoke up: "Great General!
I was recruited by the King of Zhèng,
because Wú's army came to attack,
whoever could halt Wú's army,
would be given a thousand catties of gold,
and a fief of ten thousand households.
Since I coveted his heavy reward,
what was my intent?"
Zǐxū said: "If you do not demand my life,
I will still let you take the reward for halting the army,
how dare I go against this?"
Zǐxū, seeing the fisherman's persuasion and advice,
then released the King of Zhèng.
The King of Zhèng was overjoyed,
and provided food and drink piled high like a mountain,
for three days and three nights,
supplying Wú's army troops and horses.
Zǐxū then appointed the fisherman's son as Emperor of Chǔ.
The two states of Chǔ and Zhèng,
both then enjoyed peace.
He immediately dispatched his heavenly troops,
to attack the Emperor of Liáng.
When the King of Liáng heard Wú's army was about to arrive,
he slaughtered a thousand oxen,
cooked ten thousand sheep,
food and drink piled up like mountains,
arrayed by the roadside,
with tents set up and spreads laid out.
When Wú's army arrived,
the King of Liáng crawled on his elbows and knees,
bowing and thanking Zǐxū: "I humbly beg your generous mercy,
to let me live.
Now hearing that General is attacking Chǔ,
my congratulations are boundless,
from afar I assist, how splendid,
deeply leaping for joy."
Zǐxū replied: "Because of urgent matters,
I could not devise a plan to keep you,
I bore resentment against you,
therefore I came to attack."
Zǐxū saw food and drink arrayed south of the city,
and asked the King of Liáng,
the King of Liáng addressed the Great General: "This food and drink can supply General's soldiers."
When Zǐxū heard these words,
he immediately ordered his troops to eat their fill.
The soldiers finished eating.
The troops, having eaten their fill,
their spirits leaping for joy,
said to Zǐxū: "Receiving one meal from him,
makes one ashamed before him;
receiving two meals from him,
thanks are not enough."
The officers and soldiers all said: "Great General,
these words are true, how splendid,
do not attack the King of Liáng."
Zǐxū pondered in his heart: "I have a grievance and enmity,
single-mindedly seeking to destroy,
but because of him I was saved,
how could I forget his kindness."
So he forgave the King of Liáng's crime.
Having spoken, they advanced,
gathering the heavenly troops,
traveling until beside the Yǐngshuǐ River,
he lifted his face to the sky,
sighed and said: "I once fled and came here,
and asked a woman for food.
That woman did not refuse,
but embracing a stone, threw herself into the river and died.
Today I have nothing else to repay that woman's kindness."
Following the words spoken while she lived,
he took a hundred pieces of gold and threw them into the Yǐngshuǐ.
Zǐxū made an offering, saying:
"I once fled and entered southern Wú,
on the road we met and I begged for food.
Ashamed that you gave me a single meal,
embracing a stone, you threw yourself into the river and ended your life.
Since we parted many years have passed,
morning and evening I have long remembered you.
Thinking of your spirit and consciousness following the waves,
your wandering soul scattered, following the brambles."
Having spoken, weeping, he announced:
"Spirits of the netherworld, I hope you know my feelings.
Since you could die by throwing yourself into the river with chaste integrity,
in the Yellow Springs, can you not feel desolate and sigh!
The dark road separates us, we do not know each other,
life and death have always followed different paths.
I have nothing else to offer you,
only take this hundred pieces of gold to repay you in burial."
After Zǐxū completed the sacrificial rites,
he turned his troops and marched to his elder sister's home.
He captured his two nephews, Zǐ'ān and Zǐyǒng,
shaved their heads,
cut off their ears,
and knocked out their front teeth.
"When I fled in the past and begged for food,
you tried to capture me and send me to King Píng of Chǔ.
Today I take revenge,
may you forever be slaves."
The heavenly troops have their limits,
they cannot linger long.
His horse then sped like lightning and shooting stars,
traveling to Zǐxū's wife's dwelling,
intending to welcome his wife back to the state of Wú.
He then knocked on the door and called out,
but his wife closed the gate and courtyard,
responding from afar beyond the wall,
refusing to let him in.
Zǐxū said to his wife:
"In the past when I suffered the calamity in Chǔ,
I was ashamed that you came out to meet and welcome me.
Now that I have taken revenge on Chǔ,
I return with the army to see you,
hoping it can be like the old days.
Why do you close the door and refuse me,
not letting me see your face?
Is it because there is another reason,
why are you ashamed of Xǔ and will not accept me?
Since we parted,
I have often thought of your kindness,
my shame and gratitude are not light,
that is why I have come to plead with you."
His wife replied:
"When you suffered the calamity in Chǔ in the past,
passing by on the road,
you knocked on the door and I saw you face to face.
Then I knew of your hardship and distress,
and I repeatedly made inquiries,
but you refused to acknowledge it and would not admit,
and I could not force you to the death.
The bond between husband and wife is weighty,
I hoped you would pledge to die and live together.
You first brought shame not lightly,
so I later resent and will not accept.
When poor and lowly you did not look back,
now rich and noble, why pretend to help me up?
I do not covet favor, salary, glory, or splendor,
I wish you would understand my heart!"
Zǐxū then admitted his capital offense,
bowing and kowtowing in thanks beyond the gate.
His wife, seeing his earnestness,
then opened the gate and let him in.
Their love was as in former days,
and they immediately set off to return together.
Zǐxū ordered the three armies,
to march in single file, leading the ranks.
Now that the world is peaceful and tranquil,
the sun and moon are pure and bright,
jade whips striking golden saddles in unison,
he then sang a song:
"My heavenly troops are matchless,
filling the plains in thousands of ranks.
Sweeping ten thousand li, clearing dust and dirt,
subduing the Chǔ army like shattered tiles.
A true man's way connects with heaven's will,
taking up arms and donning armor to campaign afar.
Warriors fierce and brave as tigers and leopards,
iron cavalry savage and fierce, truly like dragons.
Deploying formations like spreading clouds draping to the ground,
divine banners gathering cranes soaring from the hills to the sky.
Roaming the world without equal,
knowing all states will ultimately be the same.
Joy, oh joy, today's joy,
delight, oh delight, today's delight.
Golden whips beating rhythm in harmonious chorus,
finding the way, they then entered Wúzhōng."
The warhorses mingled in a jumble,
rumbling and thundering,
iron horses whinnying and neighing,
the great army vast and mighty.
Tall pines verdant and lush,
short grass yellow and ripe,
jade ornaments clear and tinkling,
golden saddles gleaming and shining.
Day and night treading the long road,
in a matter of months they reached Wúzhōng.
The King of Wú heard that Zǐxū was victorious,
and immediately came riding to welcome him.
Zǐxū saw the King of Wú coming to welcome him,
dismounted and bowed in thanks to the King of Wú,
loudly announcing his respects, saying:
"Since this foolish minister parted from the dragon countenance,
my unwearied heart has never forgotten.
Your subject, receiving the king's loan of troops to attack Chǔ,
the troops and your subject,
were of one heart together.
Commanding without discord,
driving forward in perfect accord.
The troops reached north of the river,
encamping south of Chǔ.
King Píng unfortunately met his demise,
and Crown Prince Zhāo was established to know the army and state.
Hearing of your subject's troops arriving,
he came out to engage in battle.
Your subject dispatched fierce troops to block the rear,
bold generals to charge the front,
at once wiping out the Chǔ army,
men and horses piling upon each other.
Corpses strewn across the wilderness,
blood staining the mountains and rivers.
Like a falcon striking crows and geese,
resembling a leopard hunting foxes and hares.
As if holding Mount Kūnlún to crush an egg,
how could it not be shattered?
As if grasping a torch to singe hair,
how could it not be consumed?
Seeing his troops routed and scattered,
Zhāo King then fled and ran, hiding in the city.
Your subject then pursued from behind,
and captured him within the city.
Your subject's accumulated hatred was especially deep,
so I cut Zhāo King into a hundred pieces.
King Píng's dried bones,
the sword slashed, blood flowed.
Your subject seeing this wound,
the vengeful heart was finally stilled.
Wú's warriors,
were all safe and sound.
The slain soldiers of Chǔ,
corpses strewn across the wilderness.
The king's power and influence,
have satisfied the vengeful heart.
Ashamed yet grateful to the great king,
I look up to the king without end.
Not losing a single soldier or horse,
armor and clothing all intact.
Among them are brave and fierce men,
I wish the king would reward their merits and grant rewards."
The King of Wú said:
"Since I parted from you,
longing and remembrance have never left my heart.
I feared the Chǔ troops were many,
and the heart seeking revenge might not be achieved.
Heaven's way lent aid,
enabling the destruction of Chǔ and return to Wú.
All merits and achievements,
I myself will generously deal with and assign."
Zǐxū then led his troops into the city,
inspected and collected the weapons,
rewarded merits and granted rewards.
Among them were vanguard fierce generals,
awarded crimson and each given golden fish.
Those holding banners and commanding troops,
all occupied official positions.
The remaining soldiers,
each was rewarded with the merit of Pillar of the State.
For a time they danced and cheered,
all saying the monarch had feeling.
The King of Wú, seeing that Zǐxū had the bearing of a great man,
then established Zǐxū as the state's Grand Councilor.
Later, King Gōujiàn of Yuè
raised troops and mobilized masses,
coming to attack the Wú army.
Yuè's worthy minister Fàn Lǐ advised King Yuè, saying:
"Wú's worthy minister Wǔ Zǐxū,
knows astronomy above,
knows geography below,
versed in civil and military arts,
with which he established himself.
His appearance is extraordinary,
his spirit outstanding and unique.
Wú's Grand Councilor,
the head of the state's steps.
If the king now attacks Wú,
it is certain to bring self-harm."
King Yuè said:
"My strategy is already set,
cannot be abandoned midway."
He then raised troops and mobilized masses,
went to attack the Wú army.
The King of Wú,
with Yuè troops coming to attack,
then dispatched the state's councilor Wǔ Zǐxū to lead troops to attack.
Zǐxū led troops and engaged the Yuè troops in battle,
killed the Yuè soldiers,
corpses strewn across the wilderness,
blood flowed floating the pestles.
King Yuè, seeing his troops being killed,
then together with Fàn Lǐ fled to Mount Kuàijī to take refuge.
King Yuè together with Fàn Lǐ went to Councilor Wǔ's side to present words, saying:
"I see the state councilor avenged his father,
so I came to pay a visit,
with no intention of attacking."
Zǐxū hearing these words:
"If not for the words of the worthy minister Fàn Lǐ,
At that time, King Wú dreamed at night of divine light shining in his palace hall,
second, he dreamed of the city walls lush and verdant,
third, he dreamed of soldiers battling at the city gates,
fourth, he dreamed of blood flowing to the southeast.
King Wú immediately sent Zǎi Bǐ to interpret the dreams,
Zǎi Bǐ said: "Dreaming of divine light in the palace hall signifies abundant fortune and prosperity;
dreaming of the city walls lush and verdant means dew is like frost;
a box under the southern wall and a frame under the northern wall indicate the king's long life;
dreaming of soldiers battling at the city gates means the king's defenses are secure;
dreaming of blood flowing to the southeast signifies the Yuè army will perish."
King Wú then sent Zǐxū to interpret the dreams.
This Zǐxū understood astronomy above,
geography below,
and human affairs in between,
versed in both civil and military arts,
all spirits and deities,
he was thoroughly knowledgeable and adaptable.
King Wú then sent him to interpret the dreams.
Zǐxū said: "I interpret these dreams
as extremely inauspicious.
If the king follows Zǎi Bǐ's words,
the state of Wú will surely face ruin."
The king said: "Why?"
Zǐxū straightforwardly interpreted the dreams: "The king dreaming of divine light in the palace hall means a great person will arrive;
dreaming of the city walls lush and verdant means they will be overgrown with thorns;
a box under the southern wall and a frame under the northern wall mean the king will lose his throne;
dreaming of soldiers battling at the city gates means the Yuè army will arrive;
dreaming of blood flowing to the southeast means corpses will cover the ground.
The king's army and state will be destroyed,
all because of Zǎi Bǐ's words."
King Wú, hearing Zǐxū's words,
widened his eyes in anger,
slapped the throne and shouted furiously: "This old minister, so stubborn,
first curses my state."
Zǐxū, having interpreted the dreams,
seeing King Wú's anger,
then lifted his robe and descended from the hall.
King Wú asked Zǐxū: "Why do you lift your robe and descend?"
Zǐxū said: "Thorns have grown on the king's palace hall,
piercing my feet,
therefore I lift my robe and descend."
The king bestowed upon Zǐxū a sword of candle-jade,
ordering him to take his own life.
Zǐxū, receiving the king's sword,
addressed all the officials: "After I die,
