cut off my head,
and hang it on the eastern city gate,
I will watch when the Yuè army comes to attack Wú!"
After Zǐxū was killed,
Yuè borrowed four million dan of grain from Wú,
King Wú then gave the grain to King Yuè,
delivering the full amount.
Later,
King Yuè steamed the grain and returned it to Wú,
then sent a letter to King Wú saying: "This grain is excellent,
the king should have the people plant it."
The grain returned to Wú had been steamed,
and when planted, none of it sprouted.
The people lost their livelihood,
for one year there was scarcity,
and famine lasted five years.
King Yuè then consulted with Fàn Lǐ: "The state of Wú is now in turmoil,
having mostly followed Zǎi Bǐ's advice,
what strategy can we devise together
to attack the Wú army?"
Fàn Lǐ addressed the king: "Wú's worthy minister Wǔ Zǐxū,
King Wú ordered him to take his own life.
A house without strong beams
is bound to collapse;
a wall without good earth
will soon crumble;
a state without loyal ministers,
how can it not fall?
Now there is the treacherous minister Zǎi Bǐ,
who can certainly be bought with bribes."
The king said: "What bribes should we use?"
Fàn Lǐ addressed the king: "Zǎi Bǐ loves gold and treasures,
loves beautiful women;
obtaining these will surely open the way,
without any doubt."
King Yuè, hearing Fàn Lǐ's words,
immediately sent envoys to fetch gold from Lìshuǐ,
seek white jade from Jīngshān,
gather bright pearls from the Eastern Sea,
and procure beautiful women from the southern states.
King Yuè obtained these things,
then selected brave and fierce men,
sent them to the state of Wú,
to present them to Zǎi Bǐ.
He, seeing these things—
the beautiful women graceful and light,
the bright pearls shining brilliantly,
the gold glittering and splendid,
the white jade flawless—
the gifts from Yuè to Zǎi Bǐ,
he joyfully accepted them.
The king, seeing this treacherous minister accept the bribes,
sought him out.
He again asked Fàn Lǐ: "When King Wú killed Wǔ Zǐxū,
Wú had poor harvests for two years,
the people suffered scarcity and famine,
and it has been five years now."
King Yuè called Fàn Lǐ and asked: "I now wish to attack Wú,
how should we proceed?"
Fàn Lǐ addressed the king: "For the king to attack Wú now,
is precisely the right time."
King Yuè then mobilized an army of four hundred thousand men,
and as they marched halfway,
fearing the soldiers might not be united,

Recalling when Liú and Xiàng rose in righteous struggle for supremacy,
with three-foot white blades,
they brought order to the central plains.
In the east, thinking of Emperor Yǔ,
in the west, subduing mighty Qín.
Saddles never leaving horses’ backs,
armor never leaving generals’ bodies.
Seventy-two major battles,
thirty-three minor battles,
battle after battle lost to the Western Chǔ overlord.
Only Hàn’s high emperor sat grandly in his hall,
summoning his Zhāng Liáng,
to approach before the throne.
Zhāng Liáng heard the summons,
hurried to the throne’s front,
bowed and performed the ritual,
hailing ten thousand years.
The Hàn emperor said to Zhāng Liáng: “The three armies’ officers and men,
cease their sorrowful cries of Chǔ,
and proclaim for me.
Issue orders to the three armies:
those who resent me,
let them ascend the hall,
cut off my head,
and deliver it to the Western Chǔ overlord.”
The three armies heard these words,
choked with sobs and wept bitterly,
all bearing spears and armor,
encamped thirty paces away from the Hàn king.
When night reached the end of the first watch,
left vanguard cavalry commander and censor-in-chief Wáng Líng,
right vanguard cavalry commander and censor-in-chief Guàn Yīng,
the two generals deliberated,
planning to raid the Chǔ camp.
Zhāng Liáng said to Guàn Yīng: “When men raid a camp,
they first take leave from their sovereign;
if they do not take leave from their sovereign,
how can it be called raiding a camp!”
The two generals then approached in the dead of night,
startling the emperor into a cold sweat down his back.
The Hàn emperor said to the two: “Without my decree,
how dare you two approach in the dead of night?”
Then summoning the two ministers near the throne: “Do you think I lack heavenly mandate?
Let anyone ascend the hall,
cut off my head,
and deliver it to the Western Chǔ overlord, if you will!”
Wáng Líng memorialized: “Your servant serves his lord,
how dare he act so!
Your servant sees Your Majesty fighting repeatedly and losing repeatedly,
tonight the two generals plan to raid the Chǔ camp,
hoping to satisfy our king’s true intent.”
The emperor heard the memorial,
his dragon countenance greatly pleased,
opened the treasury to bestow two carved bows,
two hundred precious arrows,
entrusting them to the two ministers: “When done, return early,
do not let me worry from afar.”
The two generals took leave of the king,
then went to the raid site,
from this episode,
began the initial changes.
This was in the eighth or ninth year of Gāohuáng,
since then often serving before the king.
Precious swords sharp, long drawn from sheaths,
carved bows often with three strings replaced.
Líng said: “Grandee, setting out tonight,
all of Chǔ’s army signals must be overturned,
selecting ministers who cannot go,
general, don armor and swiftly mount.”
Grandee Guàn Yīng harmonized:
“Since wielding the sword for Gāohuáng,
major battles experienced dozens of times,
minor engagements at Péngyuán countless,
body covered with sword and arrow wounds.
Not only raiding the camp tonight,
ahead, wind and fire must also be faced.
One hundred new white-feathered arrows,
dragon swords newly sharpened, keen as frost.
If tonight we meet Xiàng Yǔ,
we shall behead him and offer him to our king.”
After the two generals took leave of the king,
they exited the military gate,
leapt onto their saddles.
The men were like lightning flashes,
their horses like shooting stars;
in less than ten days,
they reached the border of the Right Army.
Wáng Líng said to Guàn Yīng: "This is the day the two empresses divide the realm;
twenty li south is the Hàn camp,
twenty li north is Xiàng Yǔ's camp."
Wáng Líng then said: "Left General Dīng Yāo,
Right General Yōngshì,

Dīng Yāo said to Yōngshì: "We will cut off the Hàn generals here,

The two generals, hearing this,
let the Chǔ army pass,
reached the mountain pass road,

Wáng Líng took off his sweat-soaked inner garment,

Great officers must carefully remember,

They waited until purple dusk to listen for the watchword near the gate.
The jade water-clock passed the time,

In Xiàng Yǔ's tent, as he slept deeply,

sweat poured over his whole body.
His men numbered six hundred thousand,

Where the two generals raided the camp,

Under Yǔ were elite troops six hundred thousand,

Three, five, here and there, they wept in secret,

Emperor Gāozǔ of Hàn sat grandly upon his throne,

hurried to the front of the hall.

immediately summoned Lú Wǎn
to deliver the declaration of war.
Lú Wǎn memorialized: "Those sent to deliver letters before and after,
ten thousand go without one returning.
I beseech Your Majesty
to compose the declaration of war;
your servant will then dare to deliver it."
The Emperor finished composing the declaration of war,
sealed it within a casket,
and entrusted it to Lú Wǎn.
Lú Wǎn took his leave of the King,
walked out of the army gate,
mounted his horse and settled into the saddle.
In less than ten days,
he reached the border of the Chǔ territory.
Scouts detected him
and reported to the Hegemon King.
The Hegemon King, hearing the report,
summoned him before the tent.
Lú Wǎn gained audience,
performed the ritual bow and dance of greeting,
and the Hegemon King then asked: "Did the Hàn ruler come in ten thousand blessings?"
He replied: "My lord came in ten thousand blessings."
"You have come from afar;
ascend the tent and be granted wine and food."
The Hegemon King then summoned Zhōng Lí Mò,
ordering him to fetch Wáng Líng's mother.
She was bound with her hands behind her back,
and thirty warriors were commanded,
each holding knives and clubs,
to drive her before the tent,
...to the Hàn envoy.
Seeing Lú Wǎn in the tent asking no questions,
the Hegemon King became exceedingly angry: "Lú Wǎn, drinking and eating in the tent,
did you just now see the person being driven past?"
Lú Wǎn replied: "Your servant reports to Your Majesty,
I saw."
The Hegemon King said to him: "It was no one else
but the mother of that Wáng Líng who, on the night of the twenty-fifth of last month,
led the cavalry general Guàn Yīng
to raid and throw my camp into chaos,
causing two hundred thousand men each to suffer knife and arrow wounds,
and fifty thousand men to die that very night.
Upon the advice of my strategist Zhōng Lí Mò,
I had Wáng Líng's mother fetched.
The one just driven past was precisely Wáng Líng's mother."
Lú Wǎn leaped up and jumped down the steps,
then memorialized to the Hegemon King: "Wáng Líng simply does not know.
If Wáng Líng were to find out,
he would travel day and night at double speed into Chǔ
to rescue his loving mother."
The Hegemon King, hearing this memorial,
his dragon countenance greatly pleased,
opened the treasury and rewarded Lú Wǎn with ten catties of gold.
Lú Wǎn, having received the ten catties of gold,
then took leave of the King of Chǔ: "Your servant must deliver the letter;
there is a strict time limit.
I await Your Majesty's command to proceed or halt."
The King of Chǔ said: "Just bring the Hàn King's letter here.
Mark a line or two at the end:
if they want to fight, then fight;
if they want to divide, then divide."
Having taken leave of the King,
he walked out of the army gate,
mounted his horse and settled into the saddle.
The man was like a bolt of lightning,
the horse like a shooting star.
In less than ten days,
he reached the state of Hàn.
"Lú Wǎn has returned from delivering the declaration of war;
I wish to question him personally."
He called out "Long live the Emperor": "Your servant dares not fail to report: Formerly, on the night of the twenty-fifth of the second month,
Wáng Líng led the cavalry general Guàn Yīng
to raid and throw Xiàng Yǔ's camp into chaos.
Having obtained the counsel of the strategist Zhōng Lí Mò,
they captured Wáng Líng's mother in Cháchéng Village of Suízhōu.
She is now in the camp,
suffering bitter torment.
Your servant dared not fail to report."
The Emperor, hearing these words,
slapped the table in great alarm,
and summoned Wáng Líng to approach the dais: "Your mother is now in the camp,
suffering bitter torment.
If I allow you to enter Chǔ
to rescue your loving mother,
what is your intention?"
"Your servant reports to Your Majesty,
if you allow Líng to enter Chǔ
to rescue his loving mother,
he also requests that Lú Wǎn accompany him."
Having taken leave of the King,
he walked out of the army gate.
In less than ten days,
he reached the border between the two armies.
Wáng Líng's eyelids twitched and his ears grew hot.
He temporarily requested Lú Wǎn to enter Chǔ
to inquire about his mother: "If my mother is indeed there,
I will enter Chǔ to rescue my loving mother.
If my mother is not there,
I and you, Great Officer, will return to the Hàn court
to serve the sovereign of sacred person."
Wáng Líng's mother, seeing Lú Wǎn who had delivered the letter
returning once more,
feared her son would come: if her son were to arrive,
her son would die,
and his mother would also die.
She instructed Lú Wǎn to go back and report to Wáng Líng.
Wáng Líng's mother, before the Hegemon King,
verbally promised to write a letter summoning her son.
The Hegemon King, hearing these words,
his dragon countenance greatly pleased.
"To summon your son,
what need is there for lengthy discussion?"
"I need no other object,
only request the Great King's precious sword Tà'ē from his waist!"
"But since it is to summon your son,
why do you need my precious sword?
For what purpose will it be used?"
"Letters were written before and after to summon my son,
but my son did not believe any of them.
If I may borrow the Great King's precious sword,
to cut off a lock of my hair,
and seal it within the letter,
my son, seeing the hair,
will travel day and night at double speed into Chǔ to rescue his mother."
The Hegemon King, hearing these words,
drew the Tà'ē sword
and handed it to Wáng Líng's mother.
Wáng Líng's mother, having received the sword,
moved more than thirty paces away from the Hegemon King.
"To let my King know."
Wáng Líng's mother then cut her own throat and ended her life.
At that moment, heaven and earth lost their flawless light,
and thus the tale is told.
At that time, wind and clouds were all grievous and bitter,
and a hundred birds, seeing it, wept blood.
The border scouts first reported it to Wáng Líng,
and then fully memorialized to tell Emperor Gāozǔ:
"You, following the general's order to inquire after your kin,
entered the camp and again saw the Grand Lady.
Hearing that the general was at the border,
she raised her eyes to the south, divining, and was surely angered.
In frantic haste she devised a plan like rain ceasing,
fearing the matter at hand might not be true.
Turning her head, she bade me take back this message: 'Instead, set forth from the south and serve the Hàn sovereign.
If one day you bow before the golden palace gates,
do not forget your mother's nursing grace!
Do not blame me for reporting sorrow to your face—
your lady has cut her throat at the gate of the Chǔ camp.'"
Wáng Líng, having heard the messenger's words,
felt his liver and intestines severed inch by inch as if cut by a knife.
He threw himself down as if a mountain had collapsed,
and from his ears and nose, blood sprayed forth.
"Oh, Mother, why must it have come to this?
It is all because your rebellious son's actions were clumsy.
If one day the Hàn house should rise,
raising my hand, I will first behead Zhōng Lí Mò!"
Lú Wǎn had reported the mourning completed,
and together with Wáng Líng they arrived at the Hàn border.
The gatekeeper reported: “Wáng Líng has returned from rescuing his mother.”
Thereupon, he was summoned before the hall,
and after finishing his ceremonial bows,
the King of Hàn said: “I allowed you to enter Chǔ to rescue your kind mother,
were you successful?”
Wáng Líng reported: “Upon reaching the border, my spirit became unsettled,
my mind uneasy,
so I temporarily asked Lú Wǎn to enter Chǔ,
to investigate my mother.
When my mother saw Lú Wǎn arrive,
she drew the Bàwáng's sword and ended her own life.”
The emperor, hearing this report,
slapped the table in great shock: “Summon Zhāng Liáng for me to the vicinity of the hall.
” He ordered the Grand Historian to summon the lady's spirit onto a golden plaque,
and before three hundred battle commanders,
and four hundred thousand assembled ministers,
with a grand feast laid out,
arrays of rare delicacies,
he sacrificed to the mother of the loyal minister Wáng Líng,
bestowing upon her the title of Grand Lady of the State.
Moved, Wáng Líng, before the Son of Heaven,
loosened his hair and wept for his kind mother.
Wáng Líng's mother, from within the Chǔ camp,
riding a black cloud,
in the sky, shamefully thanked the emperor.
How was it described at the sacrificial ceremony?
Alas, bitter indeed, the general's mother,
her heart endured suffering, she bore hardship and toil.
How fortunate am I to have such as this,
constantly aided by loyal ministers.
At that time, Wáng Líng, weeping for his mother, said: Gazing afar at the Chǔ camp, green and dense,
yesterday she surrendered to Xiàng to summon her son,
her reputation under heaven was among countless multitudes.
Wáng Líng, do not worry in the future,
you will surely be enfeoffed as a marquis of ten thousand households.
One scroll of "The Transformation Tale of Wáng Líng from the Eighth Year of Hàn: Chǔ's Fall and Hàn's Rise."
Written and recorded by the Clerk Kǒngmùguān Yán Wùchéng on the sixteenth day of the eighth month of the fourth year of Tiānfú.
The rhymed text of the third year of the Great Hàn: Chǔ general Jì Bù shaming the Hàn king in battle array, the Hàn king's humiliation, the ministers reining in their horses and withdrawing the army:
In former times, Chǔ and Hàn contended for Western Qín,
before distinguishing dragon from snake, two lords arose.
Year after year of warfare churned rivers and seas,
seasons piled upon seasons locked in stalemate, sun and moon grew dim.
Hàn's strategists below were truly like rain,
Chǔ's fierce generals were just like clouds.
Each assisting their own king contending for the realm,
for years they clashed, none yet established as supreme.
Later, in the winter tenth month of the third year,
by the Suī River's banks, armies were raised again.
The two houses, Chǔ and Hàn, finished arraying their formations,
observing winds, divining auras, their momentum poised to devour each other.
Horses bridled with jingling ornaments, men clad in armor,
each anxious about victory or defeat, hesitating.
Chǔ's Jì Bù was skilled in speech,
his office was that of Yùshǐ Dàfū.
He then addressed the Bàwáng, boasting of his quick wit,
claiming, "I have a good plan fitting this auspicious hour.
I see the two sides have finished their formations,
tigers fighting, dragons contending will surely cost lives.
Let me revile the Hàn king three to five times,
without deploying bows or crossbows, I'll make them withdraw their army."
The Bàwáng, hearing this report, said: "According to your words, you are a most loyal minister!
When spears and halberds clash they still do not retreat,
how could they withdraw their army upon hearing insults?
Since your tongue's tip harbors such quick wit,
do not mislead me with wild talk!"
Jì Bù, having received the king's permission to revile,
his intent was like a fierce dragon ready to spew clouds.
He then called the general Zhōnglí Mò,
each taking light cavalry to follow them.
They rode out from the formation, tossing banners a strong hundred paces,
halted their horses, hooves gathered, not stirring dust.
At his waist, wolf-tooth arrows with four fletchings,
on his arm, the Wūháo bow strung with six jūn.
With the wind, he lofted high his low-mou banner,
(against the wind) arrows hung long, brushing his linked-armor skirt.
Gazing afar, he waved his hand at the Hàn king and reviled,
his words could shake heaven and earth.
Loudly shouting directly, he called, "Liú Jì!
You are a man from Fēng County, Xúzhōu.
Your mother knew how to spin hemp, living in a village cottage,
your father could tend herds, dwelling in the countryside.
You once served as a village head at Sìshuǐ,
long suffering hunger and poverty in the marketplace.
Taking advantage after the Qín house's collapse and chaos,
you styled yourself a king, false usurping the true.
How can a crow wear phoenix wings?
How dare a turtle or soft-shelled turtle hang dragon scales!
A hundred battles, a hundred losses, Heaven does not aid you,
your soldiers and officers, three parts reduced by two.
Why not bind yourself with grass rope,
surrender to my lord and beg for lenient grace?
If further you persist, deluded, boasting to fight the enemy,
captured alive, taken prisoner, there will be no reason for release."
War drums not yet beaten, banners not yet waved,
his loud, boastful words were heard one by one.
The Hàn king, reviled, his ancestors dragged in,
ashamed to look left and right, humiliated before his ministers.
A phoenix fears cold crows, dislikes the noisy trees,
a dragon avoids common fish, shuns the muddy waters.
He turned his horse, waved his whip, and promptly fled,
his formation collapsing like a mountain, dust covering the wilds.
Reaching the lower slope, he rested and paused,
rearranged his spear and helmet, and asked his great ministers:
"Yesterday, the two armies arrayed for battle,
suddenly I heard two generals speaking in confusion,
the one before the formation halting his horse, shaking his whip,
who was the man reviling in a loud voice?"
After asking, Xiāo Hé reported: "Yesterday morning, two generals displayed stubborn insolence,
insulting and shaming Your Majesty, humiliating us your ministers,
their reviling touched the dragon countenance, angering heaven and earth.
Fine horses, carved saddles, clad in linked armor,
beneath their banners, clearly recognizable.
It was none other than Jì Bù and Zhōnglí Mò,
we know for certain it was not anyone else."
The Hàn king, hearing these words, harbored deep anger,
slapping the table, frowning frequently, unbearably enraged:
"They cannot aid Hàn to eliminate the wild rebels,
falsely governing, aiding the state, they ruin me.
If I indeed lack Heaven's mandate,
then openly, all matters need not be discussed;
but if I gain a wisp of cloud to shield my head,
Chǔ generals who surrender will all be preserved and settled,
only Jì Bù and Zhōnglí Mò,
roasting by fire, frying in oil would not be enough trouble.
You, together with me, remember this well,
record their names, note their surnames, do not delay.
Should the day suddenly come when I face south and claim sovereignty,
I will capture them alive, grind their bones to dust, and scatter it to the wind."
Later, in the winter tenth month of the fifth year,
meeting at Gāi, Chǔ was destroyed, smoke and dust settled.
Xiàng Yǔ by the Wū River took his own life,
at that time, the four borders were cut off from fragrant growth.
Chǔ's defeated generals came to surrender to Hàn,
the Hàn king bestowed rewards, showing all grace.
Only Jì Bù and Zhōnglí Mò,
then knew the mouth is the gateway to calamity.
Not daring to reveal their names in this sage age,
they fled separately to avoid trouble, hiding themselves.
At that time, the Hàn emperor prospered in his royal enterprise,
ascending the throne at Cháng'ān, uniquely claiming sovereignty.
The people in all four directions were content in their labors, the three borders peaceful,
from the eight directions came revival, the myriad families joyful.
His sage virtue towering, he laid aside arms,
his imperial grace vast, all turned to cultivating culture.
His heart brooded, unable to execute Jì Bù,
often his dragon countenance was clouded, brows unparted.
He then issued an order throughout the land,
dispatching to apprehend the treacherous, fierce, and search for rebel ministers.
Those who captured them would be rewarded with gold and office as a marquis of ten thousand households,
those who hid or concealed them would be executed by the sword, their whole clan beheaded.
Within ten days, the proclamation spread throughout the land,
reaching every province, county, and village.
Jì Bù, learning of the emperor's hatred,
was shocked and frantic, his soul nearly lost.
He lamented only that the world held no place to hide,
heaven wide, earth narrow, greatly distressing a man.
He then entered the valleys within Lìshān's ravines,
stealing life, avoiding death, concealing his person.
At night, he stole meals from village cottages,
at dawn, entered mountain forests, keeping company with beast herds.
He disliked the sun and moon,
loved the stars and constellations,
hiding by day, emerging at dusk, fearing to meet people.
A great man, a hero, suffering this hardship,
all because he failed to recognize the sage and enlightened lord.
Thus morning and evening, grieving over peril and difficulty,
constantly sighing to himself, his breath like clouds.
Ever since the Hàn king ascended the throne of the Nine and Five,
the common people revived, the myriad families joyful.
Only I, with heavy crimes, worry for my life,
in the end, how shall I deal with this body?
Taking my own life or being executed by others—there will surely be a day,
but soaring to heaven or entering the earth—I bitterly lack the means.
Enduring hunger, suffering thirst, in the end hard to pass,
I must seek out old bonds of duty and former close affection.
At the first watch, just as darkness fell and few people walked,
he scaled the wall and went straight into the stable gate.
Deep in the night, he stealthily reached the hall's steps,
in the flower and herb garden, his figure hidden by a tree.
As the Zhōu couple were in the midst of their meal,
in a moment, they felt their spirits stirred.
Stopping their rice, pausing their meal, their ears grew hot with alarm,
twirling chopsticks, laying spoons askew, their eyes twitched strangely.
Suddenly rising, looking toward the door, he asked:
"At the steps, who dares? Is it a ghost or spirit?
If a living person, speak early,
if suddenly a ghost, flee to the grave mound.
Questioned and not speaking, startling your servant,
sharp swords, steel blades will surely harm you!"
Jì Bù from the darkness softly replied: "You can be sure, at the steps there is no ghost or spirit,
It is only because of the old affection and duty between us,
That I bring a thousand gold pieces to you at night.
Zhōu Xuàn, following the sound, asked: “For a thousand gold pieces there must be a favor,
Yet you say you’ve come from afar to repay old bonds—
These words are empty, speak no more of them.
Late at night, he climbed over the wall to enter the house,
In the stillness, with no one around, he spoke the truth.
Jì Bù replied in a low voice: “Do not speak loudly and disturb the neighbors.
If you had not asked, I could not have told you,
But since you inquire, I will explain.
At this late hour, there is no need to ask my name—
I am the man who reviled the emperor’s army two years ago!
Zhōu then knew it was Jì Bù,
He descended the steps to welcome him and exchanged warm greetings.
He asked, “Since we parted, noble sir,
Many seasons have passed, years have gone by.
Since the order was issued to hunt for you,
Where have you hidden, with no news heard?
Jì Bù, hearing this, wept: “Do not speak of the hardships I’ve endured.
Ever since I broke the emperor’s formation with my insults,
I’ve hidden in mountains and grass, suffering bitterly.
Like a bird caught in a net, fearing for its wings,
Or a fish in a cauldron, grieving for its scales.
I risk my remaining life to seek my benevolent brother,
How can you show compassion and grant me safety?
Zhōu, seeing his sincere plea, said: “Noble sir, please set your heart at ease.
Since we became friends like Guǎn Zhòng and Bào Shūyá,
Our deep bond has long transcended worldly dust.
Now you are trapped, heaven and earth seem narrow,
Where else could you turn to find refuge?
If the nine clans were to suffer for defying the decree,
I would give my life for you, do not worry.
Hand in hand, they went up to the hall and sat facing each other,
Called for food and shared several rounds of wine.
Zhōu explained carefully to his wife,
Saying, “He is an old friend with deep affection.
Now, fleeing the nation’s troubles, he has come to seek my help,
Do not speak of it, lest the neighbors hear.
Jì Bù then hid inside a double wall,
Where neither ghosts nor men could know of him.
Zhōu’s name and status were registered in the county,
Every morning he donned his cap and entered the official gates.
He instructed his wife to prepare and send meals,
Treating him with the courtesy due to an elder brother, attentive and diligent.
But the emperor’s hatred burned fiercely,
He opened the curtain and asked his ministers:
“I dispatched orders across the provinces to find Jì Bù,
Why has there been no news for months?
It must be that the officials are negligent,
Thus the rebel remains hidden to this day.
He then ordered the authorities to reissue the command,
Changing the regulations to be more stringent and diligent.
White clay was smeared on walls for sketching portraits,
Paintings were made to capture his likeness even more truly.
Every two households were grouped into one unit for mutual surveillance,
Investigating and reporting any knowledge or lack thereof.
First, dismantle double sheds and remove hidden walls,
Then order the scattering of dust and dirt.
Search mountains and rivers, smoke out caves,
Trample grass, comb forests, and seal tomb gates.
Whoever captures him by matching appearance and name,
Will be rewarded with gold, jade, and a new official post.
Whoever hides him for even a meal or a night’s stay,
Will have his clan exterminated and relatives executed.
He then appointed Zhū Jiě as envoy to Qí,
Who bid farewell at the palace steps and left the capital gates.
Galloping his horse and shaking the whip, he arrived in ten days,
Hoping to capture the villain and bring honor to his descendants.
Arriving at the official lodge in Púyáng,
He fully conveyed the emperor’s will and proclaimed the edict.
The provincial and county officials were all fearful,
Worried about failing the emperor’s favor in the capture.
At that time, Zhōu heard the proclamation,
It felt like a heavy stone had struck his heart.
He had hidden him for so long in his house,
Now his bones chilled, hair stood on end, and he lost his spirit.
Returning to the wall to see Jì Bù,
His face was ashen, brows furrowed repeatedly.
After a long silence, he had no other words,
Only saying that disaster was imminent.
Jì Bù did not know the new envoy had arrived,
And instead reproached his host with words:
“Master, there is no need to frighten me,
I have often heard the common saying:
‘Long stay since ancient times makes one despised,’
And also, ‘Stagnant water grows muddy over time.’
If you find me burdensome and wish to cast me aside,
It will be hard to find another place for this guilty body.
When friendship breaks, human feelings turn cold,
I should end my own life this very morning.
Zhōu replied in a low voice: “Brother, listen and do not be angry.
The emperor’s hatred for you is intense,
He has specially sent a new envoy to proclaim the edict.
Yellow notices are clearly posted in the market,
With rewards piled high and new regulations.
First, dismantle double sheds and remove hidden walls,
Then order the scattering of dust and dirt.
With such strict and urgent orders to hunt for you,
Both your life and mine are in great peril.
Moreover, you once served as a censor,
Virtuous, high-ranking, and peerless in skill.
My family is willing to face the cauldron,
But it would be a pity for you to turn to dust.
Jì Bù, startled and worried, asked: “Who is the imperial envoy now?
Zhōu replied, “The official is a censor,
Named Zhū Jiě, who has received the emperor’s favor.
When Jì Bù heard it was Zhū Jiě,
He nodded slightly, a smile parting his brows.
“If it were someone else, I would fear for my life,
But what is Zhū Jiě and his kind worth discussing?
They say he is incompetent, undeserving of his salary,
Crude in mind, lacking in both martial and literary skills.
Even if a thousand gold pieces are piled as reward,
Or ten thousand ingots of silver heaped high.
Though the imperial edict is strict in its investigation,
Scattering dust and dirt will be of no avail.
Since they have sent Zhū Jiě to hunt for me,
I have a plan to disguise myself and escape.
Zhōu, hearing this, was greatly astonished,
His words were like playing with the ruler of the state.
“The emperor sent an envoy to hunt for you,
How can you possibly escape, brother?
Jì Bù said, “Now I have a plan,
Just watch how I will get out of this.
Shave my head and dress me in coarse short clothes,
Pretend I am a lowly household servant.
Just say I am a guest from a manor in Yǎnzhōu,
Who frequently comes and goes with you.
When Zhū Jiě returns on his way back,
Sell me at the slave market.
If Zhū Jiě happens to buy me,
Bargain with him, but do not argue harshly.
Once he buys me and takes me away,
I will hold the whip and cap without complaint.
If heaven allows me to see the emperor’s face again,
It will be like a sick crane soaring once more among the clouds.
He then took scissors and prepared to cut his hair,
Changing his appearance, his spirit pained.
Holding the knife, about to cut his hair,
His chest filled with emotion, tears fell profusely.
He sighed and said to Master Zhōu: “I regret that my heart and eyes were once blind,
In vain I studied the classics and learned swordsmanship,
Only knowing how to discern the weather and winds.
I served a lawless lord east of the river,
And reviled the righteous ruler of Xiányáng.
Now I cannot even cherish my own hair and skin,
Ashamed to face the sun, moon, and stars.
Once I boasted of loyalty to my master,
Now I have become unfilial, disgracing my family.
With these words, he cut his hair with tears,
Covering his brow, the length even and neat.
Stained with charcoal to resemble scarred flesh,
He swallowed charcoal to change his voice, making it unclear.
Going in and out of doors with Zhōu,
The neighbors believed he was a warehouse servant.
Zhū Jiě, serving as censor in eastern Qí,
Stopped to rest and entered the market gate.
He saw a lowly man, six feet tall,
His whole body flesh-colored as if smoked.
Bewitched and tempted, he thought of buying him,
Planning to show him off like a man from Luòyáng.
He asked, “Who is the master of this lowly man?
I wish to discuss the price—how many strings of cash?
Zhōu came before his horse and saluted,
Following the earlier plan, he reported in detail:
“I bought this warehouse servant because of a shortage,
I will sell him for a hundred gold to save my family from poverty.
If you, noble sir, wish to discuss and take him,
I will follow your terms without dispute.
Zhū Jiě asked Zhōu: “What abilities does he have to be worth a thousand gold?
Zhōu then boasted of his skills: “Though lowly, he is exceptional.
Since childhood, his parents cherished him,
Because he was born into the household and raised with care.
Skilled in massage, able to soften muscles,
Good at folding fragrant clothes for storage.
He can deliver messages and also read and write,
And knows how to accompany and serve in the school gates.
If speaking of riding, he can handle reins,
Having once herded horses at the manor’s edge.
Do not begrudge a hundred gold pieces, just buy him,
Weigh and consider how to employ him, lest he be stubborn and foolish.”
Zhū Jiě, seeing him praised for such skill,
Then ordered a contract to verify the truth.
The storekeeper took paper and moistened the brush,
And presented characters whose force resembled collapsing clouds.
The inscribed surname and signature were like a phoenix dancing,
The written year and month resembled crows in flight.
Above and below, scattered flowers and waves matched perfectly,
Between the lines, brocade was spread, cursive and standard script.
Zhū Jiě lowered his head to examine the document closely,
His mouth agape, eyes wide, forgetting to close his lips.
After a long while, shaking his whip, he sighed in admiration,
Looking at the document signed with such merit.
Not only was a hundred gold the highest price,
A thousand gold, as stated, should be paid.
Thus he paid the price and bought him,
And immediately sent him off through wind and dust.
Jì Bù, receiving his guidance and support,
Held the whip and cap, not shunning hardship.
What did Zhū Jiě escorting the good man resemble?
It was like misty shadows atop a mountain ridge.
In less than ten days, they returned to the court,
And fully reported that in Eastern Qí there was no such person.
The emperor, hearing there was no Jì Bù,
Said, “You have toiled in vain through wind and dust.
I allow you to rest and return to your private residence,
For my grievance has not yet been resolved.”
Zhū Jiě, hearing the emperor’s words before the hall,
Worried, bowed and danced his way out of the golden gate.
Returning home, relatives and old friends came to soothe his weary feet,
Setting out a feast with a lavish spread of delicacies.
Having bought the storekeeper for his cleverness,
He boasted of him in the hall to visiting guests.
In leisure, they often discussed past and present,
In boredom, they spoke before the hall of ancient texts.
From then on, Zhū Jiě’s heart grew fond and protective,
Often praising him to his wife:
“Though I bought him as a simple servant,
He is truly knowledgeable and widely learned.
Heaven punished him with shackles and a short coarse garment,
Like jade hidden in a mountain or a pearl within a clam.
His intentions are sincere and understanding,
I should raise him up and settle him elsewhere.”
They discussed granting him the Zhū family name,
Removing his shackles and coarse garment, replacing them with new clothes.
Now that they had taken him as their own flesh and blood,
They ordered the inside and outside to report to all relatives.
Do not call him storekeeper, a lowly title,
Always call him the eldest young master.
They tried teaching him to ride a horse and wield a polo mallet,
Suddenly striking and passing others with ease.
On horseback, twirling spears and playing with swords,
Drawing the bow and shooting arrows, surpassing Líng Jūn.
Reining in the bridle and saddling up, two horses galloping together,
Leaping and standing alone as if divinely alive.
Swinging the whip, displaying his dignified appearance again,
Tapping the stirrups, proudly showing his stalwart body.
Circling north and south like a flash of lightning,
Holding east and west like wind and clouds.
Zhū Jiě, at that moment, was greatly astonished,
Stunned, nearly losing his spirit.
Carelessly, he had bought a simple servant,
But see his bearing surpasses that of a general.
The name ‘storekeeper’ must be false,
He must surely be a minister of the Chǔ state.
Calling him before the hall, he asked: “In Púyáng, I acted hastily,
Using a hundred gold to buy you in a rush,
Never carefully asking about your origins.
Seeing your demeanor, you are no commoner,
What is your surname and name, and where are you from?”
Jì Bù, having been carefully questioned,
Pondered in his heart, deciding to tell the truth.
With a voice stirred by emotion, he replied: “Speaking of the origin brings unbearable sorrow!
If not asked, I would say I am a lowly man,
But since asked, you must know I am no inferior.
I am the eloquent scholar and heroic general of the King of Chǔ,
The object of the Hàn emperor’s grudge—Jì Bù himself.”
Zhū Jiě, suddenly hearing him name Jì Bù,
Trembled with fear, worried only that disaster would enter his door.
“Yesterday I saw the astrologer’s memorial to the throne,
The three terraces and eight seats were in great turmoil.
He also reported a traitor’s star appearing by day,
I long suspected it might be among the hundred officials.
Never expecting I myself would encounter such peril,
To whom can I explain this situation!
I would rather be executed and accept death,
But my entire family would suffer calamity.”
Jì Bù, learning of his fear,
Used sweet words and fine speech to reassure him:
“Do not be alarmed and flustered,
Sir, compose yourself and be at ease.
Now the whole empire is searching for me,
Whoever captures me will be enfeoffed and given a hundred gold.
If you but deliver me to the court’s gate,
You will surely be promoted to a new rank.”
Zhū Jiě, careless and short-sighted,
Intended to call his attendants to send him away.
Jì Bù spoke up and frightened him: “Sir, you seem utterly drunk and confused!
Obediently accepting favor without consideration,
You will surely face Emperor Gāo’s stern decree.
Whoever captures me will be enfeoffed with ten thousand households,
But the family that hides me will have all six relatives executed.
Moreover, having hidden me in your home for a month,
Sending me away now, you first worry about your own family’s destruction!”
Zhū Jiě, hearing this,
Panicked, turning and losing his spirit.
“Hiding you endangers my life,
Sending you away means the destruction of my family.
The world says you are full of schemes,
Now, how can I avoid this calamity?”
Jì Bù then said, “Now I have a plan,
Surely it will save both me and you.
Tomorrow, arrange a feast in the hall,
Summon all the great ministers from the court.
Among the seats, speak only of Eastern Qí affairs,
Say that my crimes are numerous.
I will then step forward and personally beg for my life,
There must be a way to escape disaster and calamity.”
They managed to invite Xiàhóu and Xiāo Hé,
Who ascended to the feast, yielding to precedence.
Zhū Jiě, because of his inner fear,
Brought up the matter of Jì Bù from Eastern Qí.
Hóu Yīng, at that moment, was startled and suspicious,
And exchanged frequent glances with Xiāo Hé.
The two ministers, seated, spoke up: “We have deeply troubled you with such precious flavors.
The emperor ordered you to capture Jì Bù,
Yet you openly hide him in your residence.
Such a lavish feast is hard to eat,
Sitting long may harm people.”
The two ministers brushed their sleeves and rose,
Zhū Jiě, anxious and afraid, grew increasingly flustered.
The two chancellors had just mounted their horses at the gate,
When Zhū Jiě personally came to urgently invite them back:
“In my residence, there is no Jì Bù,
I only wish for you to leisurely drink a round.”
Hóu Yīng, seeing there was no Jì Bù,
Observed his expression and listened to his voice to verify the truth.
Dismounting from their saddles, they returned to the feast,
Since there was no Jì Bù, the matter was dropped.
At that moment, wine was passed to Xiāo Hé’s hand,
Music began, and only new songs were heard.
Jì Bù emerged from behind the curtain,
Greeted them with bows, and exchanged pleasantries.
Approaching the hall, he clasped his knees and kissed their feet,
Prostrating himself, begging for his life repeatedly.
“I, Bù, once insulted the battle array and belittled Gāozǔ,
I should face the three lights and take my own life.
Hiding until now has prolonged my humble life,
Regret and remorse leave only traces of blood and tears.
Bearing my guilt, I await your judgment,
My life or death now depends on your grace, my lords.”
The two chancellors, seated before him, met him: “We are ashamed before you, a hero and minister of Chǔ.
Recalling the day you waved your whip and insulted the battle array,
In helmet and armor, your spirit was like clouds.
How is it that today you suffer such defeat,
Your appearance changed, your body reduced to a lowly man?
But Emperor Gāo’s desire for vengeance is intense,
How can we save you?”
Jì Bù bowed and addressed them: “My lords, please try to memorialize the enlightened ruler:
Simply say you passed by Zhū Jiě’s residence,
And heard that the households in Eastern Qí are impoverished,
The prefectural officials and county magistrates are all anxious and fearful,
Fine fields and fertile lands are overgrown with brambles.
Because a thousand gold was offered to search for Jì Bù,
Every family seeks reward and has ceased farming.
If Your Majesty would cease the search,
Spare the gold and jade, and show compassion to the people.
If these words reach Emperor Gāo’s ears,
He will surely order the provinces to retract the decree.”
Hóu Yīng and Xiāo Hé deeply appreciated the plan: “According to your excellent strategy, it is most ingenious.
To have him pardon your crimes and retract the decree,
Half depends on the Son of Heaven, half on his ministers.
Today we will memorialize in person for you,
So that later generations will know what it means to be human.”
Xiāo Hé then entrusted Hóu Yīng to memorialize,
Facing the heavenly steps to see the supreme ruler.
They fully reported, “The people of Eastern Qí have lost their livelihoods,
Hoping for gold and rewards, they have ceased farming.
If Your Majesty would cease the search,
Spare the gold and jade, and show compassion to the people.”
The emperor, hearing that the people had lost their livelihoods,
Exclaimed, remembering the words of the *Shàngshū*:
“The people are the foundation of the state; bestow kindness and benevolence,
When the foundation is firm, the state is at peace—nourish the people with grace.”
I, the emperor, for an old feud laid waste to the land,
As time passed, I made the four seas impoverished.
Following your memorial, I shall cease the pursuit,
Resolve grievances, release entanglements, and end all discourse!"
Hóu Yīng bowed and danced, then left the golden hall,
To see Jì Bù and bring him joyful news.
"The emperor has pardoned you,
You may now live carefree and unrestrained!"
Hearing this, Jì Bù's heart grew even bolder,
"I have long harbored resentment for the suffering endured.
Although the memorial has halted the pursuit,
I should still lie low and remain in obscurity.
Unless there is an edict of a thousand pieces of gold,
How could I risk appearing and facing execution?"
Hóu Yīng, upon hearing these words, felt angry: "How could I dare present a golden edict to a rebel minister!"
Jì Bù bowed deeply and spoke again: "If you memorialize once more, the grace of Yáo and Shùn may be opened.
Simply say that Jì Bù's heart is stubborn and unyielding,
Unashamed of the imperial virtue and ungrateful for the emperor's grace.
Knowing my crimes are grave, I fear the cauldron and boiling oil,
And dread fleeing to the Róng and Dí tribes beyond the rivers.
Should I gather reckless troops to invade the land of Hàn,
The border regions would inevitably stir with dust and smoke.
It would be like the rebirth of Xiàng Yǔ in the east,
Or the resurgence of the western Qín dynasty.
If Your Majesty issues a golden edict to summon me,
I will surely assist and serve as a loyal minister."
Hóu Yīng, hearing such words, said: "Based on your words, you could move the stars.
I shall memorialize again on your behalf,
But when the memorial is presented, the emperor may grow angry."
He waited until the early court session to enter the palace,
And presented the memorial with the earlier words to the emperor:
"Yesterday, by Your Majesty's merciful decree, Jì Bù was pardoned,
Bringing peace to the state and joy to the people.
I worry that Jì Bù is stubborn and rebellious,
Unashamed of the imperial grace and ungrateful for the emperor's favor.
If Your Majesty halts the pursuit upon ascending the throne,
He may flee to the Róng and Dí tribes beyond the rivers.
Should he gather reckless troops to invade the land of Hàn,
The border regions would inevitably stir with dust and smoke.
It would be like the rebirth of Xiàng Yǔ in the east,
Or the resurgence of the western Qín dynasty.
I have heard that Jì Bù is full of schemes,
Skillful in strategy and adept at employing troops.
In battle, he is like frost withering leaves,
Breaking formations like wind scattering clouds.
If a golden edict is issued to summon him,
He will surely repay the state's grace with loyalty."
The emperor, hearing this, was greatly pleased: "I am grateful for your loyal and frequent memorials!
I suffered wounds in the struggle for the throne,
My body covered with oil sores and arrow scars.
In dreams, I still tremble at the memory of the Chǔ army,
How much more should I fear Jì Bù shaking the world?
Following your memorial, I shall issue a golden edict,
Swearing by the mountains and rivers to record his merits."
Jì Bù, having received the summons with crimson silk,
Immediately changed his sorrowful heart and drafted a memorial.
The memorial read: "I, your subject, deserve to be ground to dust for my crimes!
I lived in Dōngqí, simple and sincere,
Born in humble lanes and raised in a thatched gate.
Unaware of Your Majesty's dragon-like destiny,
I assisted the fierce lord of Jiāngdōng.
With reckless plans, I cursed in battle and implicated my ancestors,
Bringing upon myself the torment of cauldron and boiling oil.
Your Majesty, upon ascending the throne, brought a sage era of peace,
Spreading the sun of Shùn and the clouds of Yáo.
My gratitude is profound and difficult to express.
I beg to spend my remaining years in farming,
Bringing life, death, and glory to the joy of my nine clans."
At that time, he followed to the court gates,
Where the officials led him into the golden hall.
The emperor lifted the curtain to look at Jì Bù,
Recalling the battle curses and suddenly growing angry.
He ordered the warriors to seize him: "Boil him in oil for me, spare him not!"
As he was brought outside the palace walls,
Jì Bù's loud voice was heard in the hall:
"A wise and enlightened son of heaven deserves assistance,
But what worth is there in deceiving the ruler?
Clearly, a golden edict was issued,
Only to lure me to the court and then kill me.
Though my execution is deserved for my crimes,
How will Your Majesty face the judgment of later generations?"
The emperor, hearing these words at once,
Turned anger into joy and ordered him spared.
"I admire your many strategies and schemes,
Let the old wrongs be forgotten entirely.
I bestow upon you brocade, silk, and precious jade,
And appoint you as the governor of Qízhōu.
I send you back to your hometown in embroidered robes,
Bringing glory, rank, and honor to your clan."
Jì Bù, having received the official post, gave thanks,
Bowing and dancing on the palace steps with renewed joy.
He secretly informed Zhū Jiě first,
And clearly expressed gratitude for the kindness of Púyáng.
Striking the stirrups, he sang and returned home,
Shaking the whip, joyful to escape the dust of the world.
If one speaks of gaining high rank by cursing in battle,
Throughout all ages, he is the only one.
The *Book of Hàn* has been compiled and completed,
Do not say the poet's song is untrue.
One scroll of *The Song of Jì Bù Cursing in Battle in the Third Year of the Great Hàn*.

Day after day, she did not weave at all,

On the brocade, golden patterns appeared in pairs,
pair after pair of mandarin ducks facing phoenixes.
Once the brocade was woven, she cut it off,
folded it, and placed it in a chest.
The master saw the contents of the chest,
and thought of this woman's woven patterns.
Such a woman is not found in the mortal world;
she must have grown up in heaven.
Once the required amount of silk and satin was woven,
he released the two to return to their hometown.
The two bid farewell and were told to go well,
not to harbor resentment toward the master.
The two bid farewell and set out on the road,

When they reached the place where they first met,
"I bid you farewell and return to heaven!
The lady then rose on clouds and departed,
leaving instructions for the young boy before parting.
She only said, "Take good care of the child,"
and parted from Yǒng with a thousand lines of tears.
Dǒng Zhòng grew to seven years old,
playing games by the roadside.
The child, lingering and playing, was scolded and insulted,
all saying Dǒng Zhòng had no mother.
He ran home to tell his dear father: "Why do I have no mother?
"Back then, I sold myself to bury my parents,
and moved a heavenly maiden to help repay the debt.
Now you miss your mother,
tears streaming from your eyes in thousands of lines."
Dǒng Yǒng let his son go seek his mother,
and he went straight to Sūn Bīn's side.
The master came to divine with the yarrow stalks,
This man must be seeking his mother.
She came to bathe by the pond,
First hiding secretly beneath the trees.
Three women were together as companions,
Hurrying straight to the water's edge.
They removed their heavenly robes and entered the water,
In the center, he grabbed the purple garment.
This one was Dǒng Zhòng's mother,
At this moment, ashamed to see her young son.
"My child is young, how could he know this place?
Sūn Bīn surely possesses excellent yīn-yāng arts.
I intend to take my child to raise,
But my son should not stay in this place.
Take the golden vase and return to the mortal world,
Place the golden vase beside Sūn Bīn."
Heavenly fire suddenly appeared ahead,
The master lost it and fled in haste.
Thinking it was all burned at that time,
But upon searching, sixty sheets were found.
Thus, he did not know the affairs of heaven,
All because Dǒng Zhòng sought his mother.

A thousand lǐ north of Dūnhuáng, west of the town Yīzhōu city lies Nàzhí County,

In the tenth year of the Dàzhōng era,
the Great Táng dispatched the Commissioner for the Enfeoffment of the Uyghurs, Vice Censor-in-Chief Wáng Duānzhāng, bearing the imperial tally to proceed to the Chányú.
Below him was the Officer-in-Charge Chén Yuánhóng, who fled as far as the Shāzhōu border region,

Chéngzhēn suddenly, in the midst of the open wilderness,

Chén Yuánhóng stepped forward

I humbly beseech the General to consider my plight with compassion."
Chéngzhēn, realizing he was an envoy of the Hàn court,
had him brought on horseback to Shāzhōu

Chén Yuánhóng bowed and knelt in greeting,
fully recounting the circumstances,

The Vice Director asked Chén Yuánhóng: "Where did the envoy encounter the bandits?

Yuánhóng stepped forward

who, bearing the imperial tally by decree, proceeded north to the Chányú

While traveling to the southern slopes of the Snowy Mountains,
we encountered over a thousand mounted rebellious Uyghurs,

the Vice Director was filled with great anger.
"How dare these bandits act with such audacity,
indulging in violence and harm!"
He said to Chén Yuánhóng: "The envoy may return to the official guesthouse for now;
we will promptly investigate the matter."
Before troops could be dispatched,
on the fifth day of the eighth month in the eleventh year,
Wáng Héqīng, the Prefect of Yīzhōu, sent a mounted courier,
who reported: "There are over five hundred tents of rebellious Uyghurs,
led by Chief Zhái and others, who have already brought the Uyghur people to the vicinity of Yīzhōu.

In the era of Emperor Yáo's enlightened rule,
a thousand auspicious signs appeared daily.
Emperor Shùn had his own birth mother living at home;
Lèdēng Fūrén was her name.
Lèdēng Fūrén fell ill,
remaining bedridden for three years without recovery.
The lady called to Gǔsǒu and said: "I have orphaned sons and daughters,
left in the hands of their brother-in-law.
I hope my husband will not allow them to be whipped and shamed."
Gǔsǒu replied to his wife: "[All] people in the world fall ill;
you, my lady, must take great care to recuperate."
Having said this, she passed away.
Shùn observed mourning for three years,
wearing plain garments for a thousand days.
Gǔsǒu called to Shùn and said: "My son Shùn, having lost your mother at a young age,
there is no one to manage the household.
If your father takes a stepmother,
how would you, my son, feel about it?"
Shùn, clasping his hands, addressed his father: "If Father brings a stepmother home,
she will be no different from my own birth mother."
Gǔsǒu took a stepmother,
and before ten days had passed,
Gǔsǒu called to Shùn and said: "The troops of Liáoyáng City have descended;
this year offers excellent opportunities for trade.
I will go to Liáoyáng for a while,
to seek some profit along the way.
I leave you, my son, to manage the household affairs."
When he left, he said it would be for one year,
but for three years he did not return home.
The son, longing for his father, was heartbroken;
he placed a zither on the mat.
While Shùn was playing the zither,
an old man stood at the gate.
Shùn hurried out the door: "May the venerable elder enjoy boundless blessings!
From where has the elder come?"
The old man replied to the young master: "I came from Liáoyáng City yesterday,
and now have a letter from your father."
Shùn entered the house gate,
and knelt and bowed four times to his mother.
When the stepmother saw Shùn kneeling and bowing four times,
a venomous, angry heart arose within her.
"It is neither a festival day,
nor is there any joyous news from afar.
To kneel and bow four times at midday—
what kind of ghostly sorcery have you learned!"
Shùn, clasping his hands, addressed his mother: "Father went to Liáoyáng for a while,
leaving me to manage the household affairs.
When he left, he said it would be for one year,
but for three years he has not returned home.
Your son, longing for his father, is heartbroken;
he placed a zither on the mat.
While I was playing the zither,
an old man came to the gate,
who came from Liáoyáng City yesterday,
and now has a letter from Father.
Two bows were to inquire after Mother's well-being,
two bows were to share joyous news with Mother."
When the stepmother heard that Gǔsǒu was returning,
she immediately devised a plan.
She called loudly to Shùn: "If your father is truly coming,
the household is sadly unprepared.
I see that the peaches in the back garden,
are exceptionally fine,

If my [son] could pick some peaches,

Hearing about picking peaches,

Shùn climbed the tree to pick peaches;

She loosened her own hair bun,
took a golden hairpin in her hand,
pierced her own foot,
and called loudly to Shùn: "You are a filial son;
surely you will come down the tree to see your mother's wound."
Hearing this, Shùn
believed it to be true and without deceit.
Shùn hurried down the tree.

Later, when the stepmother saw Shùnzi,

Gǔsǒu replied to his wife: "Since human life is of utmost importance,

The stepmother replied to Gǔsǒu: "If we do not beat and humiliate him, all matters will cease;

Within two or three days,
the stepmother devised a successful plan.
The stepmother said to Gǔsǒu: "I see the empty granary in the backyard,

have that Shùnzi repair the granary,
set fire on all four sides to burn him to death."
Gǔsǒu replied to his wife: "Though you are a woman,

Gǔsǒu called Shùnzi and said: "Your father sees the backyard granary,

When Shùnzi heard about repairing the granary,

He mixed a pile of mud and water,

The stepmother asked Gǔsǒu: "Is it your enemy who repairs the granary,

As soon as Shùnzi went up to the granary,

The first torch was from the stepmother,
followed by Gǔsǒu with the second,

With three torches burning at the base,

Shùnzi feared for his life,
so he used the two bamboo hats as wings,
and soared into the air, flying down from the granary.
Shùnzi was a virtuous ruler,
moved the earth god to support him,
thus he was not burned and not a hair was harmed.
He returned to the study courtyard,
first reciting the *Analects* and the *Classic of Filial Piety*,
then reading the *Máo Poetry* and the *Book of Rites*.
Later, when the stepmother saw Shùnzi again,
a malicious heart of the five poisons arose.
"Since my husband went to Liáoyáng,
he left me to manage household affairs.
The children from the previous marriage are unfilial,
the eastern courtyard's banquet hall is often open,
the western courtyard's study is often closed.

Gǔsǒu replied to his wife: "Since human life is of utmost importance,
how can we just punish him?

The stepmother replied to Gǔsǒu: "If we do not beat and humiliate him, all matters will cease;

When Shùn heard about cleaning the well,

The heavenly Emperor Shì,
secretly sent down five hundred silver coins,

Shùnzi then placed the silver coins in a mud jar,

After counting them,
he reported to his father and mother: "The well is full of water and the coins are all out,

Emperor Shì transformed into a yellow dragon,

Shùn called out from above,

Shùn then wept and bowed,

as for the other Yáo families,

Shùn immediately knew these were his parents and younger brother.

Shùn came to Lìshān,

Shùn took the money from his mother but pretended to forget,

Gǔsǒu found it strange

The wife led Gǔsǒu to the market,

Gǔsǒu said to him: “Who are you, kind sir,

Shùn said: “Seeing you, old sir, are elderly,

Gǔsǒu recognized his voice and said: “Doesn’t this sound exactly like our Shùn?”
Shùn said: “It is I.”
He then stepped forward and embraced his father’s head,

Shùn wiped his father’s tears,

His mother also regained her wisdom,

The people in the market saw this,

At that time, Shùn brought his parents back to their home.
Gǔsǒu wept and said: “My son is filial.”
