he gathered neighbors and relatives,
intending to kill the stepmother with a knife.
Shùn clasped his hands and addressed his father: “If you kill my mother,
then I, Shùn, would have no filial piety at all—
please consider this, father.”
The neighbors were filled with sorrow,
for such a thing had never been heard under heaven.
After the father spared the mother’s life,
they were all of one heart and mind, joyful,
and their fame spread throughout the land.
Emperor Yáo heard of this,
and gave him his two daughters in marriage,
the elder named Éhuáng,
the younger named Nǚyīng.
Yáo then abdicated the throne to Emperor Shùn.
Yīng gave birth to Shāngjūn,
who was unworthy.
For this reason, Shùn abdicated the throne to King Xiàyǔ.
A poem says:
Gǔsǒu filled the well and became blind,
Shùn from then on plowed at Lìshān.
Bringing rice to Jìdū, he met his parents,
and by licking their eyes, restored their sight.
Another poem says:
Filial piety toward parents moves Heaven,
Shùn cleaning the well obtained silver coins.
His parents pressed stones upon Shùn,
yet moved, the well connected to the eastern neighbor’s home.
One scroll of “The Transformation Text on Shùn’s Utmost Filial Piety.”
It is found in the “Poem of a Hundred Years,” which says: “Shùn, at twenty, pursued learning.
At thirty,
Yáo raised him up.
At fifty,
he greatly administered the affairs of the realm.
At sixty-one,
he succeeded Yáo and ascended the imperial throne.
He reigned for thirty-nine years,
made a southern inspection tour,
and died in the wilds of Cāngwú,
at the age of one hundred.
He was buried south of the [river] at Jiǔyí,
which is Línglíng.
Shùn’s surname was Yáo,
and his courtesy name was Chónghuá.”
It is also found in the “Record of Emperors,” which says: “Shùn was known as Yǒuyúshì,
his surname was Yáo,
and his eyes had double pupils.
His father’s name was Gǔsǒu,
his mother was known as Wòdēng,
descendants of Zhuānxū,
and ninth-generation descendants of Huángdì.
His capital was Píngyáng,
later moved to Púbǎn.
Xiàyǔ succeeded him.”
Kǒng Ānguó said: “Shùn reigned for fifty years,
and lived to be one hundred and twelve years old.
He died,
and was buried in the wilds of Cāngwú at Jiǔyí Mountain.
The first year of Emperor Shùn’s reign was wùyín.”
Completed on the fourteenth day of the month of Ruíbīn in the year of jǐyǒu, corresponding to the fifteenth year of Tiānfú.
In the past, there was a worthy scholar,
surname Hán, given name Péng,
who was orphaned at a young age,
having lost his father due to mourning,
and alone cared for his elderly mother,
conducting himself with filial piety.
His mother, considering his future, urged him to take a distant official post.
Concerned about his mother living alone,
he took a virtuous wife,
Chénggōng Sùnǚ,
who was just seventeen years old,
named Zhēnfū.
She was already wise and sagely,
radiant and peerlessly beautiful,
with a graceful and elegant figure,
unmatched under heaven.
Although a woman,
she was well-versed in the classics,
and in all she did,
she conformed to heavenly principles.
Three days after entering the household,
they agreed to live together,
and made a vow to each other,
each to guard their own integrity.
The husband would not take another wife,
like fish and water;
the wife would not remarry,
serving one husband until death.
This is scroll B, numbered 3227,
the original text complete at the beginning but missing at the end.
Hán Péng went traveling,
serving in the state of Sòng,
expecting to be gone three years,
but six autumns passed without his return.
Péng's mother missed him,
her heart was troubled and resentful.
His wife thought of him,
within herself she stirred her heart,
suddenly took up a brush,
and wrote a letter word by word.
Its script was elegant,
its phrases like shattered gold,
like pearls, like jade.
She wished to send the letter by a person,
but feared people's many words;
she wished to send it by a bird,
but birds always fly high;
she wished to send it by the wind,
but the wind dwells in emptiness.
If the letter has feeling,
let it go straight before Péng;
if the letter has no feeling,
let it fall scattered among the grass.
The letter had feeling,
and went straight before Péng.
Hán Péng received the letter,
read and understood its words.
The letter said: "Vast are the white waters,
swirling waves that flow.
Bright is the clear moon,
floating clouds reflect it.
Lush green are the waters,
winter and summer have their times.
If you miss the season and do not plant,
grain and beans will not grow.
All things sprout and transform,
not defying heaven's timing.
Long have we not seen each other,
my heart is full of longing.
A hundred years together,
yet joy lasts but a moment.
Do you not remember your kin,
your old mother's heart grieves.
Your wife alone is frail,
nights often spent in solitude,
ever harboring great sorrow.
I have heard that when birds lose their mates,
their cries are mournful;
at dusk they roost alone,
the long night is desolate.
When Tàishān first arose,
high and low, towering and steep.
Above were a pair of birds,
below was a divine turtle,
playing day and night,
always returning together.
What crime have I now committed,
to be alone without light?
The sea waters surge and swell,
waves arise without wind.
Those who complete others are few,
those who ruin others are many.
On the southern mountain there is a bird,
on the northern mountain a net is spread,
the bird flies high of itself,
what can the net do?
If you are but safe and well,
I too have no other wish."
Hán Péng received the letter,
his feelings stirred, his heart grieved,
for three days he ate not,
nor did he feel hunger.
Hán Péng wished to return home,
but had no means to do so.
Carrying the letter carelessly,
he lost it before the palace hall.
The King of Sòng obtained it,
and greatly loved its words.
He immediately summoned his ministers,
and also the Grand Historian: "Who can fetch Hán Péng's wife for me,
I will bestow a thousand catties of gold,
and a fief of ten thousand households."
Liáng Bó spoke up to the king: "Your servant can fetch her.
" The King of Sòng was greatly pleased,
and at once brought out an eight-wheeled carriage,
and swift-footed steeds,
with attendants before and after,
numbering over three thousand.
Setting out on the road,
swift as wind and rain.
Three days and three nights,
they arrived at Péng's home.
The envoy descended from the carriage,
knocked at the gate and called out.
Péng's mother came out to look,
her heart startled and afraid.
She asked the caller: "Whose envoy are you?
" The envoy replied: "I have come as an envoy from the state of Sòng,
a friend of Péng's.
Péng serves as a Merit Officer,
I serve as a Registrar.
Péng has a private letter,
to deliver to his bride."
The old woman turned and spoke to the bride: "As this guest says,
Péng is now an official,
and moreover on a successful path."
Zhēnfū said: "Last night your bride had an evil dream,
vague and indistinct.
I saw a yellow snake,
coiled around the legs of my bed.
Three birds flew together,
two birds fought each other.
One bird's head was broken, its teeth fallen out,
feathers drifting down in profusion,
blood flowing in streams.
Horses' hooves trampling,
ministers imposing and grand.
Above and below, I saw not the neighbors,
much less a guest from a thousand miles away.
A guest coming from afar,
in the end cannot be trusted.
Clever words and sharp speech,
forging Péng's letter.
If Péng's words are truly from abroad,
let the bride come out to see.
Mother-in-law, reply to the guest,
simply say the bride lies ill in bed,
unfit for medicine or treatment."
Receiving the words, she thanked the guest,
for his toil in coming from afar.
The envoy replied: "When a wife hears of her husband's letter,
why is she not joyful?
There must be another affection,
among the neighbors."
Péng's mother was old,
unable to discern the meaning.
The bride, hearing the guest's words,
her face turned green, turned yellow: "If the guest speaks thus,
saying there is another affection,
if I wish to question his intent,
I will instead lose all reason.
Sending me to see the guest,
the mother loses a worthy child.
From now on, the mother-in-law will also lose a daughter-in-law,
and the daughter-in-law will also lose a mother-in-law."
Then she stepped down from the golden loom,
bade farewell to her jade shuttle,
for a thousand autumns, ten thousand years,
never again to weave with you.
Well waters deep and clear,
when will I draw from you again?
Cauldron and stove,
when will I cook upon you again?
Bed mat and inner chamber,
when will I lie upon you again?
The courtyard broad and empty,
when will I sweep you again?
Garden vegetables lush and green,
when will I gather you again?"
Going out and in, weeping mournfully,
the neighbors felt heartache and sorrow.
Head bowed, stepping backward,
tears falling like rain.
She ascended the hall to bow to the guest,
the envoy helped her into the carriage.
Zhēnfū mounted the carriage,
swift as wind and rain.
Péng's mother behind her,
called to heaven, cried to earth,
wailed and wept loudly,
the neighbors startled, gathering around.
Zhēnfū said: "What good is calling to heaven,
what use is crying to earth?
Once the team of four horses departs,
how can I ever return!"
Liáng Bó swiftly departed,
each day growing more distant.
Upon first arriving in the state of Sòng,
a journey of over nine thousand lǐ,
a light shone in the palace.
The King of Sòng found this strange,
and immediately summoned his assembled ministers,
including the Grand Historian.
He opened the books to consult the divination,
puzzled by the reason for it.
The Erudite replied: "Today is jiǎzǐ,
tomorrow is yǐchǒu,
when all the ministers gather,
the king will obtain a beautiful woman."
Before his words had finished,
Zhēnfū arrived.
Her face was like congealed lard,
her waist like a bound skein of silk,
possessing elegant grace.
Among the palace ladies and beauties,
none could compare.
When the King of Sòng saw her,
he was immensely delighted.
For three days and three nights,
his joy knew no bounds.
He immediately enfeoffed Zhēnfū,
making her his queen.
Attendants before and behind,
entered her palace quarters.
Once Zhēnfū entered the palace,
she grew haggard and joyless,
falling ill and unable to rise from her bed.
The King of Sòng said: "You were the wife of a commoner,
now you are the mother of a state—
what is there to be unhappy about?
Your clothes are of damask and gauze,
your food is whatever pleases your palate.
The Gentleman Attendant at the Yellow Gates,
is constantly at your side.
What is there to be unhappy about,
that you also take no joy?"
Zhēnfū replied: "I left my family and parted from my kin,
to serve Hán Péng.
Life and death have their place,
nobility and baseness have their distinctions.
Reeds and rushes have their ground,
brambles and thorns have their thickets,
jackals and wolves have their companions,
pheasants and hares have their pairs.
Fish and turtles have their water,
they do not delight in lofty halls.
Swallows and sparrows fly in flocks,
they do not delight in the phoenix.
Your handmaid is the wife of a commoner,
she does not delight in being the consort of the King of Sòng."
The lady remained sorrowful and joyless,
and the king said: "The lady is grieving and longing—
who can advise her?"
Liáng Bó replied: "Your servant can advise her.
Péng's years are not yet thirty,
just over twenty,
his form graceful and slender,
with black hair and fair skin,
teeth like jade pendants,
ears like suspended pearls.
It is because she thinks of him
that her heart is joyless.
We must swiftly bring harm upon Péng's person,
making him a convict."
The King of Sòng then followed his words,
immediately having Hán Péng's two front teeth knocked out.
And dressing him in old, tattered clothes,
sent him to build the Qīnglíng Terrace.
When Zhēnfū heard of this,
her liver and intestines were cut with pain,
her heart filled with vexation and resentment,
thinking of him without cease.
Zhēnfū petitioned the King of Sòng: "Since the Qīnglíng Terrace is now built,
I beg permission to go briefly to see it."
The King of Sòng granted it.
He bestowed an eight-wheeled carriage,
a piebald horse,
with attendants before and behind,
over three thousand people,
they went and arrived below the terrace.
Then she saw Hán Péng,
chopping grass to feed the horses.
Seeing his lady, he felt shame,
and took grass to cover his face.
When Zhēnfū saw him,
tears fell like rain.
Zhēnfū said: "If the King of Sòng has clothes,
I will not wear them;
if the king has food,
I will not taste it.
I long for you, my lord,
as thirst longs for broth.
Seeing your suffering and pain,
cuts my heart and intestines.
Your appearance haggard and worn—
I am determined to repay the King of Sòng.
Why feel shame,
take grass to cover your face,
avoiding me and hiding?"
Hán Péng replied: "In the southern mountains there is a tree,
named the bramble.
One branch, two stems,
leaves small, heart at peace.
My appearance haggard and worn,
I have no heart for feelings.
I have heard that east-flowing waters,
and fish of the western sea,
leave the lowly for the noble—
what meaning is in that?"
Hearing his words, Zhēnfū
lowered her head and stepped back,
tears falling like rain.
She immediately tore a three-inch strip from the front of her skirt,
bit her finger to draw blood,
and composed a private letter,
tied it to an arrowhead,
and shot it to Hán Péng.
Upon receiving this letter, Péng
immediately took his own life.
When the King of Sòng heard of it,
his heart was startled and alarmed,
and he asked his various ministers: "Did he die by his own hand,
or was he killed by someone?"
Liáng Bó replied: "When Hán Péng died,
there were no wounds or injuries on his body,
only a three-inch plain letter,
tied beneath Péng's head."
The King of Sòng immediately took it and read it.
Zhēnfū's letter said: "Heaven's rain falls continuously,
fish swim in the pond,
the great drum has no sound,
the small drum has no tone."
The King of Sòng said: "Who can interpret this?"
Liáng Bó replied: "Your servant can interpret it.
'Heaven's rain falls continuously' refers to her tears,
'fish swim in the pond' refers to her thoughts,
'the great drum has no sound' refers to her anger,
'the small drum has no tone' refers to her longing.
All under heaven is in her words,
their meaning is profound indeed!"
Zhēnfū said: "Hán Péng is already dead,
what more is there to say?
I only wish that Your Majesty would show grace,
and bury him with proper rites—
would that not benefit later generations?"
The King of Sòng immediately sent men east of the city,
to dig a pit one hundred zhàng deep—
the burial rites of the Three Dukes.
Zhēnfū begged to go and see it,
not daring to linger long.
The King of Sòng granted it.
He ordered her to ride in a plain carriage,
with attendants before and behind,
over three thousand people,
they went and arrived at the burial site.
Zhēnfū descended from the carriage,
circled the tomb three times,
wailing and weeping bitterly,
her voice entering the clouds.
Approaching the pit, she called to her lord,
but her lord could not hear.
Turning her head, she bid farewell to the hundred officials: "Heaven can repay this kindness.
I have heard that one horse does not bear two saddles,
one woman does not serve two husbands."
Before her words had finished,
she immediately went to the chamber,
soaked her clothes in bitter wine,
then became brittle as scallions,
left and right she swayed,
and vanished at a touch.
The hundred officials, alarmed and fearful,
all beat their breasts.
They immediately dispatched messengers,
to run and report to the King of Sòng.
Upon hearing these words, the king
was greatly enraged.
He took a sword from his bedside
and killed four or five ministers.
Messengers rushed about,
and all the officials gathered.
Heavy rain fell from the sky,
water flowed into the tomb,
making it difficult to retrieve anything.
Minister Liáng Bó advised the king, saying: “There is only ten thousand deaths,
not a single chance of life.”
King Sòng immediately sent people to dig it up.
They did not see Zhēnfū,
but only found two stones,
one blue and one white.
King Sòng looked at them
and had the blue stone buried east of the road,
and the white stone buried west of the road.
East of the road grew a cassia tree,
west of the road grew a paulownia tree.
Their branches perfectly matched,
their leaves intertwined,
their roots connected below,
and beneath them flowed a spring,
blocking the path.
King Sòng saw this while traveling
and asked, “What trees are these?”
Liáng Bó replied, “These are Hán Péng’s trees.”
“Who can interpret them?”
Liáng Bó replied, “I can interpret them.
The perfectly matched branches are their mutual affection,
the intertwined leaves are their mutual longing.
The connected roots are their shared spirit,
and the flowing spring below is their tears.”
King Sòng immediately sent people to cut them down.
For three days and three nights,
blood flowed in abundance.
Two splinters fell into the water
and turned into a pair of mandarin ducks.
They spread their wings and flew high,
returning to their homeland.
Only one feather remained,
exceptionally beautiful and perfect.
King Sòng obtained it
and began to stroke it against his body.
It shone with great brilliance,
except for his neck, which remained unaffected.
When he stroked it against his neck,
his head immediately fell off.
He forcibly took another man’s wife
and unjustly killed the virtuous.
Before three years had passed,
the state of Sòng perished.
Liáng Bó and his son
were exiled to the borderlands.
Doing good brings blessings,
doing evil brings calamity.
One scroll of “The Ballad of Hán Péng.”
Written by Zhāng Dào on the eighth day of the third month in the year Guǐsì.
(text missing earlier) Where have the Three Dukes come from?
Square and round are sufficient,
where is gold not found?
I see that the noble ministers in court
all come from diligent study□□□□□□□.
If one studies far away for two or three years,
if one does not ride in a carriage and wear an official seal,
one swears not to return to one’s hometown.
If one does not follow this□□□□□, one becomes dust.
”Having said this,
he straightened his appearance
and walked to the front of the hall.
With hands clasped, he addressed his mother: “I have heard that in ancient times, there was Sīmǎ Xiàngrú,
who studied at□□(Zǐtóng) Mountain,
and achieved fame and prominence.
Sū Qín studied not at Guǐgǔ,
yet he wore the seals of the six states and did not return without them.
I have heard: learners are as numerous as ox hairs,
but those who succeed are as rare as unicorn horns.
The classics and decrees of old
cannot be mastered in a single reading;
□□seeing home,
cannot be reached in a single step.
I now bid farewell to you, Mother,
to study far away for two or three years.
I beg you to grant me permission!”
His mother, hearing these words,
could not hold back her tears.
She called to Qiū Hú: “Come closer,
and listen to your mother’s words.
External texts say: when parents are alive,
a son should not travel far,
and if he must travel, he should have a fixed destination.
Moreover, you lost your father at a young age.
I raised you alone,
and brought you to adulthood.
Now you wish to leave me to pursue studies.
You must reconsider carefully.
Think of yourself wandering destitute abroad—
what use will regret be then?”
Qiū Hú addressed his mother again: “I have heard that Zēng Shēn was supremely filial,
yet he left his parents to serve Zhòngní,
without□weariness,
devoting his days to studying the Three Histories,
mastering the Nine Classics,
thus bringing honor to his ancestors
and leaving his name for ten thousand generations.
I have also heard that Tàigōng□was poor but loved learning,
and eventually met King Wén,
later rising to the rank of the Three Dukes.
What use was his former wife’s regret then?
Now I wish to pursue studies,
with diligence matching the ancients.
In two or three years,
I will surely return home!”
His mother, hearing these words,
wept and replied to her son: “You and I are mother and son,
bound by deep affection and duty.
I do not refuse to let you travel for study,
but if you study at home,
why worry about not mastering skills?
Even if I let you seek a teacher□,
how could you immediately become an official?
You would do better to endure and stay at home,
plowing deep and sowing shallow,
expanding your silkworm work,
studying during the three spare times.
Would that not lead to success?
It would be good to stay with your mother,
and often see your young new wife.
Share joys together,
and bear hardships yourselves.
Laugh and talk in shared happiness,
with feelings of shyness and affection.
If you leave your mother,
she will be lonely and desolate,
walking alone with hidden tears.
Even if you succeed abroad,
when you return, how could you see me again?
You now insist repeatedly
on abandoning me to travel for study.
Strive diligently,
and return home early.
Do not make me worry.”
Qiū Hú bid farewell to his mother
and went to his wife’s room.
Her brows were unpainted with sorrow,
her appearance completely altered.
Her disheveled hair hung long,
and tears filled her eyes.
Qiū Hú addressed his wife: “The bond between husband and wife is most important,
its propriety aligns with heaven and earth.
Above, it joins like golden orchids,
below, it shares the same coffin.
Two bodies become one,
flesh and blood in harmony,
bones attached, bodies buried together,
with you, my wife, turning to dust together.
Now, with my mother’s permission,
I am to travel for study.
I do not know if you, my wife, will grant me permission or not?”
His wife, hearing her husband’s words,
felt sorrow in her heart,
her speech filled with grief.
She replied: “Husband!
In life, I am not a member of this family;
in death, I will not be a ghost of this house.
Though I am the wife of a respectable family,
I am not a person inspected by your parents.
I was raised here for fifteen years,
yet there is always a sense of parting.
A daughter’s heart turns outward;
she follows her husband a thousand miles.
Today, I am matched to you, my husband.
Whether good or bad, I obey your decisions.
If you, my husband, go to pursue studies,
this aligns with my own feelings.
Once your studies lead to success,
return home as soon as possible!”
After bidding farewell to his wife,
he took ten volumes of texts,
including the *Classic of Filial Piety*, *Analects*, *Book of Documents*, *Zuǒ Zhuàn*, *Gōngyáng*, *Gǔliáng*, *Máo Poetry*, *Book of Rites*, *Zhuāngzǐ*, and *Literary Selections*.
He then set off on his journey.
Without passing a full month,
he traveled to Shèng Mountain,
and immediately entered it.
This mountain was also different from other mountains: its peaks were steep, piercing the sky,
roaming alongside the sun and moon,
its cliffs hung ten thousand fathoms high,
vines dangled a thousand arm-spans long,
ravines and valleys twisted and converged,
deep streams intertwined,
bird paths were impassable,
and human traces were utterly absent.
When Qiū Hú reached this mountain,
he ascended the streams and entered the valleys,
winding around ravines and patrolling the forests,
the road rugged and uneven,
with springs dripping and streams flowing.
Arriving at the deep ridges,
the terrain was strategically positioned,
the mountain peaks lofty and bright,
with tens of thousands of trees,
flowers and medicinal herbs flourishing among them,
all being white sandalwood and black poplar,
cinnamon, camphor, and sappanwood,
catalpa, sandalwood, and tengnǚ,
their scents diminished by the wind,
peach, plum, and olive trees,
holding beauty and longing,
their fragrance not that of yìzhì or betel nut.
Qiū Hú walked to the foot of the forest,
and saw a stone hall.
Inside was an immortal of several thousand years,
thoroughly versed in the Nine Classics,
and clearly understanding the Seven Summaries.
Qiū Hú immediately paid his respects,
and then served him respectfully for three years,
achieving mastery of the Nine Classics.
After completing his studies,
he bid farewell to the master and left the mountain,
but did not return home,
instead heading to the state of Wèi,
intending to seek an official post.
With disheveled hair, he wandered about,
feigning madness and acting foolish,
submitting a memorial to King Chén,
vowing not to seek office,
to demonstrate his loyalty as a subject.
The memorial read: "Your subject has heard that before a tiger's stripes are revealed,
its spirit of devouring an ox already exists;
when a swan spreads its wings,
does it rely on the force to part the clouds?
Dù Zhòu traveled to Lǔ,
and the Marquis of Lǔ summoned and employed him.
Tàigōng fished at eighty,
and King Wén appointed him as prime minister.
Your subject was born in the land of Lǔ,
and grew up in the rivers of Wèi,
not having learned the merits of Cháo Fù,
but roughly understanding the intentions of Xǔ Yóu.
Your subject now leaves his hometown and country,
to serve at Your Majesty's dragon court.
If Your Majesty shows kindness and benevolence in the court,
how could a mere plot of land be begrudged?
Bowing my head, I await death for my offense."
The King of Wèi received the memorial,
and was exceedingly pleased.
"I have heard that since the existence of heaven and earth,
it is fitting to have the assistance of ministers.
I am the head,
and the ministers are the limbs.
Seeing a worthy minister from Lǔ,
now coming to aid the state,
I immediately appoint him as Left Minister,
bestowing three thousand households.
Brocades, damasks, and silks,
and additionally granting one hundred thousand,
singing and dancing beauties,
to be selected at will,
fine and strong servants,
as many as desired."
Since Qiū Hú arrived in Wèi,
several years had passed,
(he) slaughtered border barbarians,
crushed the wicked and pacified bandits,
leaving no grievance unresolved,
no envoy not paying tribute,
travelers singing praises,
all proclaiming the emperor's influence.
As for Qiū Hú's wife,
since her husband left to study,
six years had passed,
with no letters exchanged,
and news completely cut off.
His wife did not know whether her husband was still alive or not.
Since then, she diligently served with filial devotion,
acting as a servant outside,
and as a maid inside,
enduring the cold in winter,
and the heat in summer,
raising silkworms and weaving,
to serve her mother-in-law,
diligently day and night,
without a moment's rest.
Qiū Hú's mother,
ashamed to see her daughter-in-law alone in an empty room,
with no other thoughts in mind,
called her daughter-in-law and said: "My son was supposed to leave
for three years originally,
why has it been six years without return?
Could it be that his life has been lost?
I am ashamed that you, my daughter-in-law, have no husband,
sharing poverty and hardship with me,
it is too much to bear!
I cannot let you sleep alone in solitude,
cannot let you long guard an empty room.
You may remarry someone else,
I dare not keep you any longer.
I do not know what you think in your heart?"
When the daughter-in-law heard these words from her mother-in-law,
she could not help but feel deep pain in her heart,
and immediately shed tears,
stepping forward to address her mother-in-law: "My parents matched me,
originally intending for me to serve you diligently;
since your son has not returned from his studies,
I should only devote myself to supporting you for life,
how could I consider remarrying,
which would cut my heart?
If you instruct me, mother-in-law,
I dare not disobey;
but if later your son suddenly returns,
how could I explain myself?"
When the mother-in-law suddenly heard these words,
she could not help but burst into loud crying,
tears streaming down,
and both of them composed themselves.
After another three years had passed,
making six years in total,
it suddenly became nine years.
On the third day of the third month in the ninth year, Qiū Hú attended the morning court.
Remembering his mother, he wept tears filled with sorrow.
With hands clasped before his chest,
he knelt before the king and bowed four times,
then spoke these words: "Your servant addresses Your Majesty: I have heard that for the weight of the vast heavens,
one may fast from drink for seven days;
for the toil of boundless parents,
one may weep tears of blood for three years.
Dǒng Yǒng sold himself to bury his parents,
and a heavenly maiden came to repay his kindness;
Guō Jù buried his son and was granted gold,
for August Heaven observed and judged.
A child clothed in fine garments
does not complain of frost and cold;
a son of Cháo Fù
would rather die guarding [his principles] than refuse.
I lost my kind father early,
and only my mother remained alone.
She nursed and raised me,
and now I have achieved standing.
I have also heard: the filial crow returns to feed its parents in repayment,
the lamb kneels to its mother in gratitude,
the cow cherishes the feeling of licking her calf—
how could mother and son not feel mutual longing?
I left my hometown,
and now nine years have passed.
Whether my kind mother lives or dies, I do not know.
I now serve the king with loyalty and fervor,
but those at home have no way of knowing my circumstances.
Great King, your compassionate clouds
spread widely with sweet dew,
nurturing all the people,
so that the common folk harbor no resentment.
If I receive great rewards,
it is like wearing brocade at night.
I specially hope for your heavenly grace,
to allow me to return to my country,
back to my native village.
Would this not be the king's compassionate kindness?
Only by seeing my mother and repaying her kindness
can I then know I am her son.
I humbly await your imperial decree—
what is my crime, if any?"
Hearing these words, the King of Wèi
shed tears and assembled all his ministers,
to speak of this official: "I have heard that where there is heaven and earth,
the myriad things are born.
A ruler is established,
and [his] ministers assist and support.
I am the head,
and they are my limbs.
In this kingdom of mine,
Qiū Hú has spread his fame and talent to aid the state.
Since being enfeoffed as chancellor,
he has shown both filial piety and loyalty,
steadfast as metal and stone.
His awe-inspiring reputation spreads for ten thousand *lǐ*,
his countenance stands out alone,
his talent and virtue are exemplary.
He remembers and longs for his kind mother;
now I wish to let him return.
Though I feel reluctant to part,
it is fitting to bestow one hundred ingots of gold
and one thousand bolts of patterned silk.
I temporarily release him to return
and serve his honored mother.
When your affairs are settled,
see your mother and return early."
Having received the king's command, Qiū Hú
felt both joy and sorrow—
sorrow at leaving the king's court,
joy at being able to see his kind mother.
After bowing to the king,
he immediately set out on his journey.
He reached his own country
at the time of mulberry-leaf picking.
Riding in his carriage, he wore a purple robe,
a golden belt at his waist,
and was accompanied by mounted attendants.
Passing through the mulberry groves,
he changed his clothes and proceeded.
The trees spread their shade over the ground, swaying,
their branches intertwining and screening.
Wishing to find someone,
to ask for news from home.
Raising his head, he suddenly saw his chaste wife,
alone among the mulberry trees picking leaves.
Her appearance had changed,
her face was without makeup,
her disheveled hair hung long,
her heart burdened as she picked mulberry leaves.
Qiū Hú suddenly saw his chaste wife.
For a long while he gazed at her.
Her graceful beauty,
her face like white jade,
her cheeks tinged with red lotus,
her waist like willow branches,
her slender eyebrows finely drawn.
He briefly halted his horse,
stepped forward to look at her closely.
Only because he did not recognize his wife,
he presented her with a poem:
"A jade face reflecting red adornment,
golden hooks hidden while picking mulberry.
Eyebrow tints emerge between the strands,
silk jacket concealed among the leaves.
Cheeks outshine spring peach and plum,
body like white snow and frost."
Qiū Hú called out, saying: "Young lady!
Have you not heard it said: Picking mulberry is not as good as meeting a young man,
tilling the fields is not as good as a bountiful year!
I offer you two taels of gold,
a bundle of patterned silk.
I beg the young lady for a brief moment in my embrace—
I wonder if the lady will grant this or not?"
The woman descended from the tree,
composed her demeanor,
not recognizing her husband,
and addressed him, saying: "Sir, my husband has gone to study,
and now nine years have passed.
No news has come through,
messages have been cut off.
My mother-in-law is old,
sitting alone in the hall.
I would rather endure cold in winter,
endure heat in summer,
tending silkworms and weaving,
to serve my mother-in-law.
One horse does not wear two saddles;
a single ox, how could it pull two carts side by side?
Though our home is poor and humble,
I would rather guard my hunger and die,
how could I take pleasure in gold as important?
If suddenly one morning my husband were to arrive,
what would I, your handmaid, have to say?
Even if gold were piled halfway to the sky,
patterned silk heaped like hills and mountains,
would I, your new wife, have a heart that clings to them?
I can guard my poverty and choose death."
Hearing these words, Qiū Hú
wore a face of shame,
and passed by in his carriage.
After walking a few steps,
he sighed in his heart, saying: "I have heard of chaste husbands and virtuous wives
from ancient times till now, by hearsay only;
now before my eyes I have been taught.
Which family's wife is worthy of entering the historical records,
transmitting her name for ten thousand generations?"
Before his words were finished,
he arrived at his home.
He saw his kind mother sitting alone in the empty hall,
not knowing her son had come.
She then sighed, saying: "Qiū Hú,
you went away to study,
originally set for three full years.
Why has it been nine years now?
Was it that fate brought decline and scattering?
Or that your body turned to the Yellow Springs,
your life carried off by the wind?
Or that you pursued pleasure and did not return?"
Before her words reached their end,
she then saw her son,
wearing a purple robe,
standing before his mother.
Fearing his mother would not recognize him,
he entered the hall,
knelt and bowed to his mother: "Do you recognize your son?
I am Qiū Hú.
Now my affairs are settled,
I have come to repay my mother's nursing and rearing kindness."
Hearing her son's words, his mother
called out, saying: "Qiū Hú,
I thought of you, not speaking of it,
speaking as if in another life.
How could I expect to see you face to face?
Mother rejoices in your gold and silks,
not because she covets your official glory,
but I am ashamed for your wife, who for nine years has slept alone in solitude.
That you now attain nobility
is not due to your diligent study and toil,
but is the merit of my filial daughter-in-law's work." She sent someone to go to the mulberry grove
to summon her daughter-in-law.
Before the messenger had gone far along the road,
he saw her returning from picking mulberry leaves.
A villager reported: "Your husband has arrived.
By your mother-in-law's instruction,
I am sent to call you back."
Smiling, she immediately returned home,
to meet her husband face to face.
Suddenly hearing that her husband had arrived,
she was overwhelmed with joy,
joy in her heart,
her face beaming with a smile.
She walked to the house,
seeking her husband in the northern hall,
and saw her kind mother-in-law.
The bride wished to bow and thank her mother-in-law,
so she then entered her room,
took the mirror stand to adorn her appearance,
and went to meet her husband.
She painted her eyebrows dark,
then applied lotus-pink makeup,
wore the clothes from her wedding day,
covered her face with a silk fan,
wishing to resemble the time of her first marriage.
She walked to the front hall to perform the rites,
assisting her mother-in-law in her joy.
Seeing the bride arrive,
the mother-in-law, ashamed, thanked her for nine years of filial care and effort,
then descended the hall steps,
weeping and calling out: “Bride!
My son has come,
his studies completed,
with official seal at his side,
he has become the state minister,
with gold and silks,
I am ashamed to thank you for your filial kindness,
I hope the bride will accept them.”
Hearing her mother-in-law’s words, she turned to bow to her husband,
looked closely at him,
and it was the nobleman who had given her gold among the mulberry trees.
In her heart, she was displeased,
her face changed, tears streaming down,
choked with emotion, unable to speak.
The mother-in-law was very puzzled,
and asked the bride again: “My son has been away for nine years,
the bride has now gained a reputation for filial piety,
why is it that now, seeing my son return,
you suddenly appear displeased today?
The bride must have a secret affair,
with someone in the neighborhood,
why not confess the truth early?
If there is no other heart,
this should not be so!”
The bride, hearing her mother-in-law’s words,
tears flowing,
again wished her mother-in-law to listen to the reason for her displeasure.
“The bride truly has no secret affair,
only resents two things about your son that are not right: first, he is unfilial at home,
second, he is disloyal to the state.”
The mother-in-law called out to the bride: “If my son is disloyal to the state,
how could he return home with official honors?
If he is unfilial at home,
he should not even see me with gold and silks.
If there is no other heart,
why speak such groundless words?”
The bride addressed her mother-in-law: “If your son were filial and kind at home,
heaven’s grace would bestow gold,
instructing him to bring it home,
to repay his mother’s nurturing kindness.
Now, before even seeing his mother,
he has already given it away among the mulberry trees,
thus he is disloyal to the state,
and unfilial at home.
The bride’s parents,
matched her to him,
she served for nine years,
her support was often lacking,
the rituals were few,
the mother-in-law wished for a filial and kind bride (

During the reign of Emperor Huìchāng,
there was no reverence for the Three Jewels,
monasteries were destroyed,
causing all monks and nuns in the land,
to return to lay life and avoid persecution.
It is said among them was a monk named Fǎhuá Héshang,
whose home was in Xíngzhōu,
knowing the ruler was unrighteous,
he then wrapped the sutras,
and went straight to hide in the mountains of Suízhōu,
temporarily dwelling in a thatched hut.
He never failed to recite daily,
and read sutras every day.
He moved eight people,
who did not reveal their names,
to come daily to listen.
One morning,
seven came first,
one arrived later.
Fǎhuá Héshang, suspicious in his heart,
spoke up and asked: “I ask the elder,
where do you reside?
What is your surname and name?
Every day, eight come together,
why does the gentleman arrive late?”
The elder replied: “We are not others,
we are the eight great sea dragon kings,
knowing the monk reads a volume of the ‘Fǎhuá Jīngyì□’,
transferring the merit to us, the aquatic kinsfolk,
all equally sharing in the blessings.
We kinsfolk,
have no way to repay,
fearing the monk might face calamity,
specially came to protect and assist,
please do not mind the late arrival.
For Yáng Jiān of Suízhōu,
within a hundred days’ limit,
is destined to have heavenly mandate,
but wearing the flat-heaven crown is unstable,
we must go to replace his skull.
If the monk does not believe,
the governor currently suffers from brain pain,
with no one to heal him.
We eight brothers have no other way to repay,
have a box of dragon ointment to give to the monk.
If you go before the governor of Suízhōu,
apply the ointment,
he will surely recover.
If he is cured,
you must entrust him with this matter:
within a hundred days’ limit,
there will be an imperial envoy summoning him,
advancing one day means death,
retreating one day means injury.
If later he becomes ruler,
he must revive the Buddhist Dharma,
that is our wish fulfilled.
We now bid farewell to the monk.”
Having spoken,
they suddenly vanished.
Fǎhuá Héshang, seeing the dragon kings gone,
went straight to the Suízhōu government office.
The gatekeeper reported inside: “Outside is a monk,
skilled in marvelous arts,
claims to heal,
dare not fail to report.”
The governor, hearing this,
ordered the monk to ascend the hall and sit.
He spoke to ask: “I suddenly suffer from brain pain,
have exhausted all prescriptions,
could not be healed.
Knowing the monk now has marvelous arts,
if cured,
I will surely not fail you.”
Fǎhuá Héshang, hearing this,
took out a box from his sleeve,
applied the dragon-immortal ointment to the crown of his head.
It is said before this ointment reached the crown,
there was no effect,
once it touched the skull,
it was like a Buddha’s hand pinching it away.
The governor, cured,
bowed repeatedly in reverence,
addressed the monk: “Although the court has clear orders,
not to hide monastic teachers,
please stay in my office to avoid notice,
would that not be good?”
Fǎhuá Héshang, hearing this,
remembered the dragon kings’ entrustment,
dared not stay long.
Addressed the governor: “Within a hundred days’ limit,
you are destined to have heavenly mandate.
If an imperial envoy summons you,
advancing one day means death,
retreating one day means injury.
If later you become ruler,
you must revive the Buddhist Dharma,
that is this humble monk’s wish fulfilled.
I now bid farewell to the governor and return to the mountains.”
The governor, seeing the monk gone,
still had doubts in his heart,
so wrote on the wall as a record.
Not more than a few dozen days later,
indeed, the Director of the Astronomical Observatory observed celestial phenomena at night,
and learned that Yáng Jiān of Suízhōu, within a hundred days,
was destined to have the Mandate of Heaven.
He submitted a memorial to report this.
When the emperor read the memorial,
it was as if a great pestle struck his heart.
He then dispatched a high-ranking palace attendant directly to Suízhōu to proclaim the imperial edict.
The Prefect, having received the edict,
dared not delay,
and immediately set off on the journey with the arriving envoy.
They traveled swiftly without stopping,
until they reached Cháng'ān, lodging at the Chánglè Post Station a little over ten *li* from the city.
Just as they had settled to rest,
the Prefect suddenly remembered the instructions of the Fǎhuá monk: within a hundred days,
he was destined to have the Mandate of Heaven.
Advancing a day would mean death,
retreating a day would mean injury.
"If I go to court for an audience today,"
I am sure to fall victim to his murderous scheme."
Having thought this,
he then ordered the imperial envoy to discuss with him,
to have the audience on the following day.
The imperial envoy assented,
and submitted a memorial to report this.
When the emperor read the memorial,
he was greatly pleased, his imperial countenance beaming.
Only Consort Yáng had tears streaming from her eyes.
As soon as the emperor saw this,
he asked the Empress: "The crime concerns Yáng Jiān alone,
it does not involve the Empress."
Consort Yáng bowed in thanks,
then went to the rear palace,
pondering in her heart: "My father will have an audience tomorrow,
he is sure to fall victim to his murderous scheme.
I, as Empress,
what glory is there for me?
It would be better to take poison and die first,
to avoid seeing the Prefect suffer."
Having thought this,
she bathed in fragrant water,
changed her clothes,
and filled a cup with poisoned wine, placing it before the dressing mirror.
The Empress re-combed her cicada-wing hair,
and redrew her moth-eyebrows.
While she was in the midst of dressing,
she suddenly saw a person in the mirror,
turned her head to look,
and it was originally the Sovereign,
who rose from his seat.
The emperor asked: "The Empress is dressing as usual,
what is the wine for?"
Consort Yáng, thus questioned,
a plan descended from heaven,
and she addressed the Sovereign: "When your handmaid dresses,
she must drink a cup of this wine;
first, to soften the hair,
second, to preserve youthful looks,
and moreover, to serve the Sovereign,
there is no other reason."
When the emperor heard this,
he was overjoyed: "The Empress herself preserves her looks,
if I, the solitary one, drink it, will I not also become handsome?"
Consort Yáng, hearing this,
hurriedly held up the cup,
and addressed His Majesty: "When your handmaid drinks it,
it is called 'Hair-Dressing Wine'.
If the Sovereign drinks it,
the name of the wine should be changed,
what should it be called?
It is called the 'Ten Thousand Years Cup'.
May the Sovereign live ten thousand years, and ten thousand times ten thousand years!"
The emperor, unaware it was poisoned wine,
took it and drank.
Before the wine was drunk, nothing was amiss,
but as soon as it reached his mouth,
his head split and he died.
Consort Yáng, seeing this,
dragged the coffin,
and placed it beneath the dragon bed.
For the moment, she used a screen to block and conceal it.
She then went to the front hall,
and dispatched a palace attendant,
straight to summon Yáng Jiān.
The Prefect, having received the summons,
felt as if a great pestle struck his heart,
but dared not disobey the imperial command.
He went for an audience at once,
proceeding directly to the palace gate.
The official in charge entered to report,
Consort Yáng heard the report,
and ordered him to be granted an audience.
The Prefect, granted the audience,
passed through the screen wall,
and performed the ceremonial bow, calling out "Ten thousand years!"
Consort Yáng, seeing him,
instructed those around her: "Help the Prefect up,
and grant him permission to ascend the hall."
Yáng Jiān raised his eyes and suddenly saw the Empress,
pondering in his heart: "Can I escape this calamity today?"
Having thought this,
he ascended the hall.
Consort Yáng asked: "Father, do not fear,
the Sovereign has returned to the vast sea,
today you shall become the ruler of ten thousand chariots."
Yáng Jiān heard this,
but was still doubtful.
"If you do not believe,
go to beneath the dragon bed,
see his coffin,
then you can believe."
Yáng Jiān addressed the Empress: "My strength is weak,
how can this be done?"
The Empress asked: "Father, with whom in the court are you usually on good terms?"
"I have a connection with the Left and Right Imperial Guards."
The Empress, hearing this,
since the authority of these two men was in her grasp,
why worry that the great matter would not succeed?
She then went to the front hall,
and dispatched someone to summon the Left and Right Generals of the Imperial Guards, Hú and Lǎng.
The two men, having received the summons,
proceeded directly before the hall,
and suddenly saw Yáng Jiān,
becoming suspicious in their hearts.
The Empress asked the generals: "I know you have a connection with the Prefect.
The Sovereign has already returned to the vast sea,
now we plan to enthrone the Prefect as ruler,
what is your opinion?"
Lǎng addressed the Empress: "Enthronement is possible,
but what about all the court ministers,
how can this be done?"
The Empress asked: "Generals, tonight muster five hundred imperial guards,
they must have broad-bladed long swords,
and lie in ambush beneath the armor screens.
I will go to the front court tomorrow,
and question them myself.
If they agree to enthrone the Prefect as ruler,
all is well;
if there is one word of dissent,
kill them all before the hall,
and establish another as minister,
would that not be a good thing?"
The generals assented,
and mustered five hundred imperial guards,
lying in ambush beneath the armor screens.
On the following day at court,
all civil and military officials and ministers were gathered before the hall.
The Empress announced: "The Sovereign has already returned to the vast sea,
now we plan to enthrone Prefect Yáng of Suízhōu as master of heaven and earth,
what is your opinion?"
Having said this,
she flicked her sleeves and left.
All the civil and military officials and ministers, unable to fathom the limits,
were suspicious in their hearts,
and gazed towards the hall,
seeing a white goat, its body twelve feet long,
baring its teeth and sharp mouth,
descending from the hall,
roaring like thunder,
intending to devour all the court ministers.
Everyone, seeing this,
knew that Yáng Jiān was destined to have the Mandate of Heaven,
and together they performed the ceremonial bow,
calling out "Ten thousand years!"
Thus he was enthroned,
proclaiming himself Emperor Suí Wén.
He moved the four barbarians to submit,
and the eight tribes to come and surrender.
At that time, there was King Chén of Jīnlíng,
who, upon learning that Yáng Jiān had become ruler,
felt deep resentment.
He issued an edict summoning all the court ministers,
gathering them before the hall,
and at that moment proclaimed: “I now intend to raise an army,
to subdue the arrogant Qín,
what are your thoughts?”
At that time, the Guardian General of the State, Rén Mánnú, stepped out from the ranks and
addressed the throne, saying: “I report to Your Majesty,
I am willing to be appointed as commander,
to lead the troops in battle,
and once we have taken Western Qín,
Your Majesty may proceed in person.”
King Chén, hearing this, said: “It shall be as you propose.”
He then appointed Xiāo Móhē and Zhōu Luóhóu as commanders,
to subdue the arrogant Qín.
The two men received the decree,
bowed and gave thanks for the imperial grace,
and led an army of over four hundred thousand,
setting out on the march.
Within less than ten days,
they reached the mouth of the Guō River, where they encamped to rest.
The two commanders deliberated
and decided to advance in two columns,
each with over two hundred thousand men.
Xiāo Móhē would attack Sòng, Biàn, Chén, and Xǔ,
while Zhōu Luóhóu would take Ān, Fù, Táng, and Dèng.
Once they entered the border regions,
the villagers and commoners submitted memorials to inform the emperor.
The emperor read the memorials
and felt as if struck in the heart.
He then ordered the bells rung and drums beaten,
gathering all civil and military officials,
assembling them before the hall.
The emperor proclaimed: “I lack virtue,
and have presumptuously taken the throne.
Now, Chén Shúbǎo of Jīnlíng has rebelled,
defying my authority.
I now intend to appoint a commander
to lead the troops in battle.
Who is willing to go?”
At that time, the Left Garrison General Hè Ruòbì stepped out from the ranks and said: “I report to Your Majesty: I am willing to lead the army.”
Just as Hè Ruòbì volunteered to lead the army,
there was one person who refused.
Who was it?
It was none other than the renowned general Hán Xióng’s son,
who had lost his father at a young age
and had given himself the name Qínhǔ.
Feeling deep resentment,
he stepped out from the ranks and said: “I report to Your Majesty,
a puddle of water
cannot contend with the vast waves of the sea;
even if ants gather in heaps,
how can they pose a threat to heaven?
I am willing to lead the army,
and within days, capture King Chén alive to present to you.
I dare not fail to report this.”
The emperor, hearing this,
saw that Qínhǔ was only thirteen years old,
still smelling of milk,
yet already showing great ambition.
Why should I worry about the state?
He intended to appoint Hán Qínhǔ as commander,
but feared it would obstruct Hè Ruòbì.
If he appointed both as commanders,
they were already at odds in the court;
if they led troops abroad,
they would surely contend for personal glory.
He told the two men: “Return to your residences for now,
and come to court another day,
when I will issue further decrees.”
Later, on the appointed day,
all the court ministers gathered before the hall,
and gold seals were cast.
First, Yáng Sù was appointed as Chief Commander,
second, Hè Ruòbì was appointed as Deputy Commander,
and third, Hán Qínhǔ was appointed as Field Commander of Cavalry and Infantry.
The three men received the decree,
bowed and gave thanks for the imperial grace,
left the court gates,
and led an army of over three hundred thousand,
setting out on the march.
They advanced swiftly without pause
until they reached Zhèngzhōu.
The vanguard scouts reported that Xiāo Móhē was leading over two hundred thousand troops
and had encamped at Chénliú.
They returned with a full report.
Upon hearing this, General Yáng Sù
immediately set up camp there,
ascended his command tent, and took his seat.
He then summoned the two commanders,
gathering them before him,
and asked: “Emperor Suí Wén declared in court
that you are to capture Jīnlíng.
Now the enemy forces are pressing close,
who is willing to go?
If you return victorious,
submit a memorial to report it.”
As soon as the general asked,
Hán Qínhǔ stepped out from the ranks and said,
addressing the general: “I am willing to go.”
“How many troops do you need?”
“Thirty-five thousand cavalry and infantry.”
They were immediately assigned to him.
Having obtained troops, Qín Hǔ
advanced his army and set out,
moving swiftly without pause.
Arriving at the border of Zhōngmóu,
he stationed his army and halted.
Qín Hǔ ascended his command tent and sat,
then summoned an officer and soldier to stand before him,
repeatedly instructing him: "You are tasked with reconnaissance,
acting solely on the general's orders.
Once you have ascertained the enemy's military situation,
return quickly and early,
and you will be heavily rewarded."
The officer assented,
changed his attire,
disguising himself as a commoner.
Carrying a basket of steamed buns,
he went straight into Xiāo Móhē's camp,
and immediately began selling them.
Having learned the military situation,
he returned at once.
Arriving before the general's tent, he bowed and reported.
Qín Hǔ asked the officer: "What is the enemy's military situation?"
The officer replied: "Their cavalry uses black flags with sea-eye designs,
their infantry uses red flags,
with the character 'shèng' (victory) in the center.
Their camp gates are wide open,
allowing commoners to come and go freely for trade."
Hearing this,
Qín Hǔ knew that Xiāo Móhē was not a seasoned combat general.
Since ancient times, it has been said: "If the army is lax, the general will perish;
if the ruler is negligent, the state will fall."
Having spoken these words,
he ordered his men,
to change their banners and flags.
When night fell at dusk,
they set out on the march.
About twenty *li* from Xiāo Móhē's camp,
they slipped past by a hidden route,
moving swiftly without pause.
Arriving at the banks of the Jīnlíng River,
they seized boats by force,
and led the army across.
Upon reaching the southern shore,
all the boats
were sunk in the water,
and then they raised their own banners and flags,
displaying Qín Hǔ's name prominently.
Leading the army to raid,
they advanced straight to Shítóudiàn.
The households reported the emergency,
submitting a memorial to inform the king.
King Chén read the memorial,
feeling as if struck in the heart by a large pestle.
He then ordered bells rung and drums beaten,
gathering all civil and military officials and ministers,
assembling them before the hall.
King Chén proclaimed and asked: "I, your servant, am without virtue,
presumptuously occupying the throne.
Now the Suí army has arrived,
who can withstand them?"
As King Chén was questioning,
the renowned general of thirty years, Great General Zhènguó Rén Mánnú, stepped forward from the ranks: "I report to Your Majesty: I do not know how many Suí troops there are.
Since Qín Hǔ leads thirty-five thousand soldiers,
I request thirty-five thousand troops.
Without needing to deploy formations or unfurl banners,
upon hearing my name, Rén Mánnú,
they will surrender immediately."
Hearing this,
King Chén ordered a muster of troops,
commanding no delay.
Mánnú then led thirty-five thousand soldiers,
advancing straight to face Qín Hǔ's formation.
With a unified shout and banners raised,
he demanded battle with the Suí troops.
At the sight,
Qín Hǔ led his troops forward,
and asked loudly: "What is the name and surname of the opposing general,
and what is his official rank?"
The general replied: "My surname is Rén, given name Mánnú,
holding the office of Great General Zhènguó."
Hearing this,
Qín Hǔ's eyes filled with tears.
He remembered: "My late father instructed: 'If you later become a general,
and reach Jīnlíng,
there will be a famous general named Rén Mánnú who studied in the same hall as your father,
copying texts and transcribing books together.
When you meet him,
you must absolutely observe the propriety due from son to father.'
Who would have thought we meet today!"
Having reflected thus,
he came forward and addressed the general: "However, I, Qín Hǔ, bear three staffs of authority on my person,
and cannot kneel in obeisance.
I beg the general not to take offense."
Hearing this,
Mánnú realized this was Hán Xióng's son,
and thought to himself: "A father cannot engage in battle with his son."
He asked Qín Hǔ: "Withdraw your army and return.
I, Mánnú, will memorialize King Chén,
to send an envoy for peace negotiations,
establishing a state of propriety and righteousness.
Would that not be a good thing?"
Hearing this,
Qín Hǔ felt it unacceptable,
and addressed the general: "However, on the day I took leave of Emperor Suí Wén,
I pledged to subdue Jīnlíng.
This task is not yet accomplished.
To return, I must obtain three things
to present to Emperor Suí Wén;
only then can I withdraw."
Mánnú asked: "What is the first thing you require?"
Qín Hǔ replied: "My first requirement: I want the geographical territory and mountains-and-rivers of the Chén state,
and the census of its households.
Only then will I withdraw."
Hearing this, Mánnú said:
"[This is a minor] matter.
Allow me to memorialize King Chén." Mánnú asked: "What is the second thing you require?"
Qín Hǔ replied: "My second requirement: I want the military provisions and treasury stores,
to reward the three armies.
Only then will I withdraw."
Mánnú asked: "What is the third thing you require?"
Qín Hǔ answered: "My third requirement: I want Chén Shúbǎo's head to present to Emperor Suí Wén,
only then will I withdraw."
Hearing this,
Mánnú knew the son was being discourteous,
and suddenly grew furious.
Seeing this,
Qín Hǔ drew his sword and brandished it,
declaring to the general: "This sword in my hand, Qín Hǔ's,
was bestowed by imperial decree before Emperor Suí Wén's hall.
Its blade contains frost and snow;
when meeting the enemy in battle,
it does not recognize kinship or strangers."
Hearing this,
Mánnú turned his horse and deployed a 'Left Covering, Right Pacifying' formation,
demanding battle with the Suí troops.
Seeing this,
Qín Hǔ broke into a slight smile,
and asked his officers: "Do you recognize this formation?"
None of the officers recognized it.
"Although I, Qín Hǔ, am still young,
I have also extensively studied my late father's military texts.
This is the 'Left Covering, Right Pacifying' formation.
See the red flag at the ferry crossing ahead,
below it are all [deer lanes],
inside are [entangling] hooks and snares.
Do not get caught by them;
be sure to remember this.
Observe the right pacifying part of the formation:
there are many men there,
and at the front are all crossbows." Qín Hǔ gave the order: "Raise banners and shout,
lower banners and advance together in unison.
If even one man retreats,
all officers will be executed.
Do not say you were not warned!"
Having spoken,
they raised banners and shouted,
and charged forward together.
This formation, with a single strike,
immediately crumbled.
Mánnú led the remaining battered troops,
and entered the city.
Upon hearing this, King Chén
was greatly enraged.
He ordered his attendants
to have him seized.
Dragged and pulled,
he was brought straight before the hall.
The king rebuked him, saying: "This traitor is intolerable!
On the battlefield, in the midst of combat,
he recognized kinship ties
and ruined my state.
A general who leads a defeated army
cannot be allowed to live;
a minister of a fallen state
deserves no pardon.
Drag him outside the army gate
and execute him, then report back."
Rén Mánnú, without protest,
raised his head: "I deserve ten thousand deaths from Your Majesty.
I beg to lead troops once more
and engage the Suí army in battle."
Hearing this, King Chén,
considering the renowned general's peerless achievements,
ordered his attendants
to release his head.
Mánnú bowed and danced in gratitude,
then addressed the king: "Your servant wishes to lead the army
and fight the Suí forces again.
If I return victorious,
I will support Your Majesty
in ascending the throne facing south as sovereign—
would that not be a great thing?"
King Chén, upon hearing this,
ordered a muster of the troops in the city
and commanded that they be handed over.
Mánnú took command of the army,
his heart filled with discontent.
From the city, he deployed a "Dragon Emerging from Water" formation,
advancing straight to the front of the Suí army's lines.
With flags raised and a great shout,
he demanded battle.
Qínhǔ, seeing this,
broke into a slight smile
and turned to address his generals: "Mánnú is indeed a peerless renowned general.
Having just suffered defeat, his heart is discontent.
From the city, he has deployed a grand formation—
do you recognize it or not?"
The generals replied to the general: "We only know how to obey orders;
we are not versed in military texts.
What does the general think?"
Qínhǔ replied: "Though I am young,
I have studied my late father's military texts.
When facing the 'Dragon Emerging from Water' formation,
one must deploy the 'Five Tigers Pressing the Mountain' formation."
As soon as he finished speaking,
this formation was completed.
As no general came to surrender,
he grew suspicious in his heart.
Looking back at this formation,
he saw the tigers lacked claws and fangs—
how could they be fierce and sharp?
So he drew five hundred archers from the rear guard
to serve as claws and fangs.
At what time and season was this formation deployed?
It was in the yín year, yín month, yín day, and yín hour.
Once this formation was complete,
it aligned with heaven and earth.
When Mánnú saw it,
he lost sight of the Suí troops—
all he saw across the wilds were great tigers,
baring sharp teeth and opening wide jaws,
coming to devour Jīnlíng.
Mánnú pondered in his heart: "To counter the 'Five Tigers Pressing the Mountain' formation,
one must deploy the 'Three Hundred Sixty Thousand Human Spears' formation.
Even fighting for ten days and ten nights,
victory or defeat would still be uncertain.
With the few troops I have,
like a single piece of meat
placed in a tiger's jaws,
it would be chewed and devoured
in the blink of an eye—
all would be utterly destroyed.
I have heard: those who achieve merit depart;
those yet to come may rest.
It would be better to turn my weapons
and remove my armor to surrender."
Having thought this through,
he bound himself with straw ropes,
fastened his elbows with hemp cords,
and went straight before General Qínhǔ's horse.
Upon seeing him, Qínhǔ
ordered his attendants
to raise Mánnú up,
saying: "Those who resist are slain;
those who come to surrender are of one family.
Allow me to report to Emperor Wén of Suí
and request that you be treated as an uncle, cared for with grace—
that would fulfill Qínhǔ's wish."
Having said this,
he led the army into the city.
When King Chén saw the Suí troops arriving,
he fled and hid in a dry well.
But the gods did not aid him,
and it turned into level ground.
The officers and soldiers saw this,
captured him on the spot,
and brought him before the general’s horse.
They rebuked him, saying: “How dare you, rebel, harbor thoughts of betrayal,
disturbing the Central Plains?
Now that we have captured you,
what explanation do you have?”
King Chén, being rebuked,
remained silent and speechless.
He was then placed in a prison cart and transported,
to be presented together at court to Emperor Wén of Suí.
They advanced swiftly without stopping,
until they reached the border of Xīn’ān.
The vanguard scout reported that Zhōu Luóhóu was leading over two hundred thousand troops,
intending to rescue his lord.
Upon hearing this, Qínhǔ
ordered King Chén to be reproached, saying: “To betray one’s lord
is not blessed by Heaven.
First, we shall behead you,
then enter the central camp
and await battle with Zhōu Luóhóu.”
Hearing this, King Chén
addressed the general: “Allow me to write a letter to Zhōu Luóhóu urging him to surrender.
Would that not be a good thing?”
Qínhǔ, upon hearing this,
ordered him to write the letter.
King Chén wrote: “When I, your servant, ruled in Jīnlíng,
I governed over fifty prefectures,
more than three hundred counties,
held ten thousand lǐ of rivers and mountains,
and commanded a million troops.
I intended to dominate the world,
proclaiming myself sovereign.
But I did not expect Qínhǔ’s troops to arrive and strike—
my forces crumbled instantly,
and I was captured on the spot.
Even if you, sir, command your own army,
you cannot fight against the Suí.
If you harbor doubts,
Heaven will not bless you.
Now, this letter from King Chén is delivered into Zhōu Luóhóu’s hands to be opened.”
After finishing the letter,
he sent a junior officer directly to Zhōu Luóhóu’s camp to deliver it.
Luóhóu received the letter,
tears streaming from his eyes.
He pondered in his heart: “My lord has already been captured.
Even if I were to win and return in triumph,
where would the credit go?”
After thinking, he said: “A true man
adapts to circumstances.
It would be better to surrender.”
First, he sent two hundred thousand sets of military armor,
then bound himself with a straw rope,
and went directly before the general’s horse.
He addressed him, saying: “I am a defeated general.
Whether I live or die,
I beg for your judgment.”
Hearing this, Qínhǔ
replied to the general: “Those who resist are killed;
those who come to surrender are treated as one of us.”
Having obtained both enemy commanders,
they set out on the journey,
traveling day and night without stopping,
to present them together at court to Emperor Wén of Suí.
The emperor read the memorial,
his dragon countenance greatly pleased.
He then ordered an audience granted.
Qínhǔ, granted the audience,
first presented the two enemy commanders,
then passed through the screen wall,
bowed, danced, and shouted, “Long live the emperor!”
The emperor saw this,
his dragon countenance greatly pleased: “I grant you permission to return to your private residence and rest.
Wait until Yáng Sù arrives;
there will be further decrees.”
Qínhǔ bowed, danced, and thanked the emperor for his grace,
then left the court gate
and rested at his private residence.
Not ten days later,
Yáng Sù returned victorious after defeating Xiāo Móhē,
and went straight to the palace gate.
The officials in charge reported his arrival,
and the emperor, upon hearing the report,
ordered an audience granted.
Yáng Sù, granted the audience,
passed through the screen wall,
bowed, danced, and shouted, “Long live the emperor!”
The emperor saw this,
then summoned all the court ministers
to gather before the hall.
With gold-colored seals cast,
he appointed Hán Qínhǔ as Duke of Kāiguó,
remotely governing as military commissioner of Yángzhōu.
Second, he appointed Yáng Sù as留守 of the Eastern Capital.
Third, he bestowed upon Hè Ruòbì brocades, silks, damasks, and gold and silver vessels.
The three generals received the decrees,
bowed, danced, and thanked the emperor for his grace,
then left the court gate
and returned to their respective private residences.
Not ten days later,
the Great Chányú of the Northern Barbarians, Dàxià, sent a Turkic chieftain as an envoy
straight to Cháng’ān,
demanding to wage war against Emperor Wén of Suí.
The emperor, hearing this,
gathered all civil and military officials and ministers,
assembling them before the hall.
The emperor asked: “The Chányú demands to wage war against me.
What are your thoughts?”
As soon as the emperor asked,
the barbarian envoy, unfamiliar with court etiquette,
stepped out of line: “I report to Your Majesty: Among us barbarians, archery is supreme.
We propose a shooting contest right here before the hall.
If you can match my arrow,
we will send tribute every year
and acknowledge ourselves as subjects for generations.
But if you cannot match the arrow,
right here before the hall,
we will decide the fate of your state.”
The emperor, hearing this report,
immediately had a target set up before the hall,
with two deer painted on it,
and ordered the shooting contest to begin.
The barbarian, seeing this,
was overjoyed beyond measure.
He bowed and thanked the emperor,
then shot immediately.
The arrow left the string,
its force like splitting bamboo,
neither east nor west,
but striking right in the center of the deer.
The emperor saw this
and asked his ministers: “Who can match this?”
At that moment, the left general Hè Ruòbì said: “I am willing to match the arrow.”
The emperor, hearing this,
said, “As you propose.”
Hè Ruòbì then took up his bow,
selected an arrow,
nocked it to the string,
and shot immediately.
The arrow left the string,
neither east nor west,
and struck through the same hole.
The emperor saw this,
his dragon countenance greatly pleased.
All the court ministers
bowed and danced together,
shouting, “Long live the emperor!”
At that moment, Hán Qínhǔ, seeing the arrow unmatched,
refused to bow and dance,
standing alone before the hall.
The emperor asked: “What are your thoughts?”
Qínhǔ reported: “I am willing to match the arrow.”
The emperor, hearing this,
said, “As you propose.”
Qínhǔ bowed in thanks,
then took up his bow,
selected an arrow,
nocked it to the string,
and shot immediately.
The arrow left the string,
its force like thunder roaring,
neither east nor west,
but striking the barbarian’s arrow nock,
piercing from shaft to tip,
passing straight through,
flying more than ten paces beyond the target,
and embedding three feet into the ground.
The barbarian, seeing this,
was extremely frightened.
He hurried forward
and bowed respectfully.
Qínhǔ, seeing this,
rebuked him, saying: “How dare you, little beast,
harbor treacherous intentions,
disturbing the Central Plains?
Now, here before the hall,
what explanation do you have?”
The barbarian general, hearing this,
was extremely frightened.
He immediately took his leave
and set out on his journey.
Emperor Wén of Suí, seeing this,
appointed Hán Qínhǔ as envoy to make peace with the barbarians.
Qínhǔ received the decree,
bowed, danced, and thanked the emperor for his grace,
bade farewell to the emperor,
and set out on the journey with the barbarian general.
In less than ten days,
they reached the border of the Tǔfān territory.
The Chányú received the imperial envoy,
ascended his tent and sat down,
then summoned the thirty-six princes who shoot eagles,
all gathered before him to give orders: "Since the imperial envoy is here,
and we have no singing or music,
the Tǔfān way is to rely on bow and arrow—
shoot eagles and bring down geese,
to entertain the imperial envoy.
" The princes acknowledged the order,
mounted their horses at once.
Suddenly, an eagle was seen approaching from the north;
as soon as a prince spotted it,
he immediately shot an arrow.
Once the arrow left the string,
it flew neither east nor west,
but passed by the eagle's front wing.
When the Chányú saw this,
he suddenly flew into a rage,
ordered his attendants,
to seize the prince,
and rip open his belly to take out his heart,
saying, "You have shamed the ancestors of our Tǔfān people."
Seeing this, the imperial envoy
stepped forward to intervene,
addressing the Tǔfān king: "Spare the prince this time.
I myself wish to borrow a bow and arrows,
to shoot an eagle and present it to the Chányú."
Hearing this, the Chányú
then handed a bow and arrows to the imperial envoy.
Qínhǔ took them,
and as he was pondering,
suddenly a pair of eagles
came flying, fighting over food.
When Qínhǔ saw them,
he was overjoyed,
bowed to the Tǔfān king,
and immediately prepared to shoot.
Qínhǔ rode his horse for ten paces,
at twenty paces he nocked an arrow on his arm,
at thirty paces he took the arrow,
at forty paces he fitted the notch to the string,
drew the bow into a full circle,
and at fifty paces he turned his body and shot backward.
Once the arrow left the string,
its force was like splitting bamboo;
it flew neither east nor west,
but pierced the throat of the leading eagle,
passing straight through,
and then struck the heart of the trailing eagle,
both eagles falling together before the horse.
When the Tǔfān king saw this,
all exclaimed in admiration.
The imperial envoy seized the moment to intimidate: "But Qínhǔ's archery is only a minor skill;
Emperor Suí Wén has a corps of one hundred and twenty who shoot geese with finger signals,
all of them master archers."
Hearing this, the Tǔfān king
hurriedly dismounted,
bowed and danced toward the Southern Dynasty from afar,
shouting "Long live the Emperor!"
After bowing and dancing,
he selected a hundred fine horses,
a thousand camels,
gǔduō (rams), deer, and musk,
to provision the imperial envoy.
Qínhǔ then took his leave,
and set out on the journey.
In less than ten days,
they reached Cháng'ān,
going straight to the palace gate.
The officials in charge entered to report,
and when the emperor heard,
he immediately ordered an audience granted.
Qínhǔ, granted the audience,
passed through the screen wall,
bowed, danced, and shouted "Long live the Emperor!"
When the emperor saw him,
he was overjoyed,
and bestowed upon Qínhǔ brocades, silks, and fine fabrics,
gold and silver vessels,
a pair of beautiful women,
ordering him to return to his private residence to rest,
and that further instructions would be given after a month.
Qínhǔ bowed, danced, and thanked the emperor for his grace,
then went to his private residence to rest.
Before twenty days had passed,
he suddenly felt uneasy in spirit,
his eyes twitching and ears burning,
pondering in his heart,
he ascended the hall and sat down.
Before he had settled in his seat,
suddenly the ground split in a cross shape,
and a man emerged,
clad in golden chainmail armor,
wearing a phoenix-winged helmet,
holding a triple staff,
bowing his head and loudly announcing his presence.
When Qínhǔ saw him,
he immediately asked: "Who are you, sir?"
The divine man replied: "I am the General of the Five Paths."
"Why have you come?"
"Last night at the third watch, I received a heavenly mandate,
that you, General, are to become the ruler of the underworld."
Hearing this, Qínhǔ
replied to the Great God of the Five Paths: "But I request a three-day leave,
is that possible?"
The Great God of the Five Paths addressed the General: "Because the spirits and the underworld
have no one in charge,
not a single moment can be spared."
Hearing this, Qínhǔ
suddenly flew into a rage,
asking: "Under whose authority are you?"
"I am under Your Majesty's authority."
Qínhǔ rebuked him: "If not for the fact that I have not yet taken leave of my sovereign,
I would give you a hundred iron blows under the left armpit."
Hearing this, the General of the Five Paths
was so frightened that sweat poured down his back: "Your subject reports to Your Majesty: not to mention three days,
a month's leave can certainly be granted."
Qínhǔ instructed the General of the Five Paths: "Quickly go to the underworld to inspect the spirits,
and wait upon me again after three days."
The General of the Five Paths acknowledged the order,
and his form vanished like a shadow.
After seeing the General of the Five Paths depart, Qínhǔ
then wrote a memorial to inform Heaven,
detailing the matter and reporting it to Emperor Suí Wén.
The emperor read the memorial,
and was extremely astonished,
summoning Qínhǔ,
straight to the front of the hall.
"Due to my lack of virtue,
I presumptuously occupy the throne,
unaware that you, General, are to become the ruler of the underworld.
What will become of my state?"
Qínhǔ reported: "Your subject reports to Your Majesty,
if great calamity arises,
simply know to report and pray,
and your humble subject will surely lead the underworld army to assist."
Hearing this report, the emperor
then ordered all court ministers to feast for three days,
only to bid farewell to Qínhǔ before the hall.
Just as the third day arrived,
in the midst of singing and joy,
suddenly there was a man in purple,
and suddenly a man in crimson,
riding a black cloud,
standing before the hall,
loudly announcing their presence.
When Qínhǔ saw them,
he said, "Who are you standing before the hall?
Answer immediately."
"We two are from the heavenly court and the earthly underworld,
come to fetch the Great King,
for no other matter."
Hearing this, Qínhǔ said: "First, grant them wine and food to manage,
and stand aside for now."
The two acknowledged the order,
each taking a side.
Qínhǔ then bade farewell to the Sovereign,
took leave of all the court ministers in person,
entered his own residence,
entrusted his wife, children, and all members of the household, noble and humble,
and prepared to depart.
Having spoken these words,
he rushed to his bed and lay down.
As soon as he was covered with the brocade quilt,
he mounted his horse by the saddle,
and ascended the cloud path,
arriving before Emperor Suí Wén's hall,
to take leave of His Majesty and depart.
When the emperor saw him,
tears filled his eyes,
and he raised a cup, poured a libation of wine, and offered a sacrifice, saying:
The illustrated tale is now complete,
with nothing omitted or abridged.

the female Daoist priests □□ all understood talismanic registers,
and further followed the teachings of the Supreme Venerable Sovereign.
Jìngnéng admired them upon first sight,
and immediately became attentive,
residing within the temple,
□ a Daoist priest.
Day and night he diligently cultivated,
studying with earnest toil.
At the age of twenty,
he formally entered the Daoist order.
His person was robed in a Daoist cap and yellow cape,
scrolls never leaving his hand,
his sincere devotion moved the spirits,
and thus he was able to see a divine being,
Jìngnéng also did not know from where he came.
The text says: Jìngnéng was young,
wholly devoted to the Daoist path,
he moved the Emperor of the Great Canopy Palace,
who dispatched a divine being,
to deliver this one volume of talismanic texts to Jìngnéng,
ordering Jìngnéng to study with a sincere and diligent heart: "Do not let others know.
If you achieve mastery,
there will be nothing you cannot accomplish,
Venerable Master, should you suddenly wish to ascend to heaven,
you may go when you wish to go,
and come when you wish to come.
You can push over the Five Sacred Mountains in an instant,
command the great ocean's waters to flow backwards,
penetrate the hidden and fathom the subtle,
control and bind the cosmos,
within the work of creation,
no one can be your equal.
If you do not hold the profound heart of the Daoist methods,
you will be harmed by the talismans.
In heaven and on earth,
the names of all numinous spirits,
are recorded within this volume of talismanic texts,
I also cannot speak of it,
fearing that people will know celestial patterns.
After bidding farewell to the Venerable Master,
we shall meet again
in the Great Canopy Heaven."
In a moment,
Jìngnéng could no longer see the divine being.
At that time, his heart was wholly devoted to the Dao,
with no thought of turning back.
He then opened the talismanic text and read it,
the footnotes were clear,
all annotating the names of ghosts and spirits,
discussing the various specters of the world.
Not only minor evils,
should one suddenly wish to uproot the earth or move mountains,
one need only use a single divine talisman.
Jìngnéng then practiced the refined arts within Kuàijī Mountain,
above responding to the heavenly gate,
below penetrating the principles of the earth,
all the ghosts and spirits under heaven,
were all summoned by Jìngnéng,
and no deity or spirit dared not obey his commands.
