Jìngnéng then, within Kuàijī Mountain,
ordered divine beings, ghosts, and specters to gallop and race,
there was nothing that did not accord with his will.
He could summon them when he wished to summon,
and command them when he needed to command.
If one is proficient in the Dao,
and most exceptional in talismanic registers,
within the cosmos,
none surpass Yè Jìngnéng.
Moreover, the Daoist priest was handsome in appearance, clear and fluent,
his disposition broad and leisurely.
When facing great matters,
his nature could match both urgency and ease;
once he wished to travel,
his heart's desire could be fulfilled in an instant,
traveling thirty to fifty thousand *li* in a day.
If he did not eat,
he could easily go thirty or fifty days;
if he wished to eat,
he could at once consume sixty or seventy portions and still not be satisfied.
Sometimes he would conceal his form and vanish his shadow,
at other times he would transform into a hundred people.
Now he encountered the Son of Heaven of the Táng dynasty,
since the opening of heaven and earth by the Three Sovereigns and Five Emperors,
none have been as sage and enlightened as our Xuánzōng Emperor.
The ministers and high officials of the court,
spoke without flattery or deceit.
His reign era was called Kāiyuán.
Since the Emperor often cultivated the Dao,
he ordered the empire to construct venerable images,
along with temple halls and buildings,
further exalting the Daoist teaching.
Jìngnéng went from Kuàijī Mountain to Cháng'ān,
leaving his name.
After traveling for several days,
the Great Canopy King transformed into a river,
the river was about five *li* wide,
and there was no bridge or boat to ferry people across,
thus testing Jìngnéng.
He then wrote a single talisman,
and threw it into the water,
the river dried up,
and Jìngnéng proceeded on his way.
After several days,
they arrived about five li east of Huáyīn County in Huàzhōu.
In the fourth month of that year, the official appointments were made,
and everyone proceeded to their posts.
There was a magistrate of Wúxī County in Chángzhōu named Zhāng Lìng, who was passing by the temple of the Mountain God of Huàyuè with his wife and children.
This Magistrate Zhāng,
with wine, dried meat, and a camel-horse,
made offerings to the Mountain God, seeking blessings.
It so happened that on this day, the Mountain God in his temple lacked a Third Consort,
and having arrived at the inn,
when the night reached the third watch,
he sent someone to take her.
At the third watch and third point,
she suddenly died.
The magistrate did not know that the Mountain God was taking her (taking her away),
and cried out to heaven, weeping bitterly,
his emotions deeply entangled.
Jìngnéng was staying at a nearby inn,
and suddenly heard the sound of crying, very intense.
Jìngnéng then asked, "Why are you crying?
" Zhāng Lìng said, "My wife died suddenly tonight.
" Jìngnéng said, "She must have been taken by the Mountain God!
" He wished to bring Zhāng Lìng's wife back to life.
Zhāng Lìng said, "I beseech you, Venerable Master: if you can transform and save her, bringing her back to life,
I would not dare to disobey even at the cost of my own life,
(I will) obey the Venerable Master's command.
" Jìngnéng asked the official, "Did your wife have any prior illness?
" Zhāng Lìng said, "She had no prior illness,
she just died here on her own.
If Jìngnéng can rescue her,
I swear I will not betray your kindness.
" Jìngnéng then took a brush and wrote a black talisman,
blew it into the air,
and it transformed into a black-clad deity,
swift as a cloud,
arriving immediately before the temple of the Mountain God.
The gatekeeper saw him,
ran and reported to the Mountain God, saying, "An envoy from the Great One has arrived.
" The Mountain God then bowed,
and had the envoy enter directly before the hall,
saying, "The Great One sends word:
Why have you taken another man's living wife,
separating husband and wife,
destroying their love?
" The Mountain God addressed the envoy, saying, "I have all received matches from the Heavenly Ministry,
and she is to be my Third Consort;
this is not a matter for the Great One.
" He then sent the envoy back,
instructing him to report accordingly.
The envoy assented,
and immediately returned,
fully reporting the Mountain God's words.
Jìngnéng's expression changed to anger,
and he again took a vermilion brush to write a talisman,
blew it into the air,
and it transformed into an envoy,
dressed in vermilion robes.
In an instant, the envoy arrived.
The Mountain God hurried down from his hall,
and respectfully faced the envoy.
The envoy said, "You should not have taken another man's living wife as your own;
the Great One is extremely angry.
Where have you taken Magistrate Zhāng's wife now?
" The Mountain God addressed the envoy, saying, "How dare I arbitrarily take another man's living wife as my own?
I have all received matches from the Heavenly Ministry;
I humbly beg the envoy to report this clearly,
and I will be ever grateful.
" The envoy said, "Do not let this woman cost you, the Prefect, your life,
and implicate the Heavenly Ministry!
" The Mountain God said, "I humbly beg the Great Envoy
to speak well on my behalf,
and I will never dare to betray you.
" The envoy returned to the inn to see Jìngnéng,
fully conveying the Mountain God's words,
saying that he had all received matches from the Heavenly Ministry,
and she was to be the Third Consort;
he dared not act arbitrarily.
Hearing this, Jìngnéng
changed expression and showed emotion,
angrily scolding the envoy, saying, "This is no small matter!
" He shouted and set him aside.
He then took realgar and two chi of white silk,
drew a talisman and blew it into the air,
and it transformed into a great general.
Clad in golden armor,
(wearing) a helmet,
his body ten feet tall,
his waist several arm-spans wide.
He then drew a sword,
roared like thunder,
his eyes glaring fiercely,
like flashes of lightning.
In the blink of an eye,
he arrived before the temple of the Mountain God.
At that moment, Magistrate Zhāng's wife was just in the midst of the wedding ceremony,
and the envoy shouted loudly with a stern expression: "Hah!
Why have you, Prefect, taken another man's living wife as your own?
The Great One is extremely angry,
and orders me to take your head!
" Without allowing the Mountain God any explanation,
he drew his sword and ascended the hall,
intending to behead the Mountain God.
Seeing the envoy ascend the hall, the Mountain God
was filled with panic and fear,
not knowing what to do,
and immediately fled.
The relatives came forward,
pleading and bowing in sorrow,
begging the envoy to just take Magistrate Zhāng's wife away.
The relatives reported back to the Prefect,
saying not to keep this woman,
lest it provoke the Great One's anger.
The Mountain God himself hurried down from the hall,
knelt and bowed deeply,
pleading with the envoy.
At that time, he then led Magistrate Zhāng's wife back to the inn,
and before long,
Magistrate Zhāng's wife revived.
She reported to her husband, saying, "While I was in the midst of the wedding ceremony before the Mountain God,
suddenly a general appeared,
clad in golden armor,
(wearing) a helmet,
drew his sword and ascended the hall,
intending to behead the Mountain God;
the Mountain God feared him,
and so released me to return.
" Hearing his wife's account, Magistrate Zhāng
was overjoyed,
and together with his wife, he bowed in thanks to Jìngnéng,
saying, "Venerable Master, you have saved my wife and brought her back to life;
your kindness is as weighty as Mount Yuè,
I do not know how to repay you.
" Magistrate Zhāng then took twenty bolts of silk from his trunk and offered them to the Venerable Master.
Magistrate Zhāng said, "I only have this silk,
and I am but a poor orphan.
My person and my wife
should become your eternal servants,
to thank you for your kindness;
I humbly hope, Venerable Master,
you will accept this meager gift.
" Jìngnéng said, "In the Dharma gate of the Dao,
one does not hold material things in mind,
does not seek the heart of sensual desire,
does not covet glory and wealth;
only saving people in the world from illness,
that is the Dharma gate.
Because the official and his wife have deep affection,
Jìngnéng thus saved her life;
you should just proceed to your post,
take the silk to use for your journey ahead,
do not insist further.
Jìngnéng will go west to Cháng'ān,
and there will be wealth there.
" The husband and wife then bowed and took leave of Jìngnéng.
Jìngnéng immediately took up his staff and set out on the road.
In less than ten days,
he reached Cháng'ān,
and settled in the Xuándū Temple.
After a full month had passed,
he did not leave the temple grounds,
only playing the qin and whistling long,
to express his feelings.
The temple's servants,
often secretly watching,
saw no kitchen,
nor any place for eating and drinking.
Groups of five or three peers
came to pay respects and inquire about his Daoist arts,
and Jìngnéng fully explained the power of talismans and registers,
and how to cure illnesses caused by spirits, demons, and evil entities;
there was nothing he could not speak of.
Thus it came from one person's mouth,
and entered ten thousand people's ears.
In less than two nights,
the common people of Cháng'ān's two markets
all knew that within the Xuándū Temple was a visiting Daoist priest,
skilled in curing spirit-induced illnesses,
and possessing the power of talismans and registers.
At that time, among the commoners of Chóngxián Ward, Kāng Tàiqīng had a daughter aged sixteen or seventeen,
who was possessed by a wild fox spirit.
She would sometimes laugh, sometimes cry,
sometimes run about, sometimes sit still,
or go out into the streets wandering aimlessly,
and would then curse people with foul language.
At that time, a neighbor reported to Kāng Tàiqīng: "In Xuándū Temple,
there is a visiting Daoist priest who can cure illnesses caused by wild foxes."
Upon hearing this, Kāng Tàiqīng
went with his wife
to the courtyard of the temple,
paid respects to Jìngnéng,
and described the symptoms of the illness: "We beseech the Venerable Master to save and heal her;
even if she dies, we will not forget your grace."
Jìngnéng said: "This illness is caused by a wild fox.
To cure it completely,
just bring a piece of felt,
four large nails,
and I will heal her immediately."
Kāng Tàiqīng then returned home,
fetched a piece of felt and the nails,
and brought his daughter along to the temple.
When Jìngnéng saw the girl,
he immediately knew it was an illness caused by a wild fox.
Jìngnéng then took a sword in his left hand,
seized the girl with his right hand,
and cut her into three pieces,
with blood flowing all over the ground.
Everyone in the courtyard
was utterly shocked.
Kāng Tàiqīng and his wife wailed to heaven and earth,
shouting loudly as they ran,
and went to the county office to report that a Daoist priest from Xuándū Temple had killed someone with a sword.
Jìngnéng showed no panic or fear;
he covered the girl's corpse with the felt,
nailed it down at the four corners,
and blood continued to flow beneath the felt.
Countless onlookers
all said that within the imperial city,
how dare such a thing happen,
who would not cry out?
Jìngnéng, however, remained in his room,
playing the qin and whistling leisurely,
paying no heed to the matter.
Shortly after,
the arrest officers and the officials in charge of apprehending criminals
all arrived in Jìngnéng's courtyard,
asking: "Where is the Daoist priest who killed someone?"
Jìngnéng replied from his room: "Here!
Why are you officials in such a hurry?
I, Jìngnéng, was curing an illness caused by a wild fox;
ignorant bystanders
falsely claimed that I killed someone."
The officials turned to ask,
and Kāng Tàiqīng addressed them: "There is a person under the felt."
When the officials saw blood flowing profusely from under the felt,
they said to Jìngnéng: "The evidence of the murder is right before our eyes,
yet you still dare to resist!"
Jìngnéng said to the officials: "Why not lift the felt and examine it?
Then enforce the law on this reckless act!"
The arrest officer then ordered his subordinates
to lift the felt and examine it,
and they said: "Kāng Tàiqīng's daughter is lying together with a wild fox;
the girl is completely unharmed,
while the wild fox has been cut into three pieces."
When the arrest officers saw this,
they were utterly astonished.
Kāng Tàiqīng and his wife prostrated themselves in reverence.
Their daughter's possession illness
was cured on the spot.
The arrest officers reported the full details of the incident to their superiors,
and the prefect came to the temple in person to pay his respects,
inquired about his name,
and regarded him with the utmost admiration.
The prefect spoke of this miraculous event,
recorded it in a memorial, and reported it to the emperor.
Emperor Kāiyuán favored Daoism,
and did not revere Buddhism;
he then ordered a palace envoy to go to Xuándū Temple to summon Jìngnéng with an imperial decree.
Receiving the decree,
he went straight to the front of the palace hall,
and as soon as the emperor saw him,
Jìngnéng expounded on Daoist teachings,
which were pure, profound, and subtle,
greatly pleasing the emperor.
The emperor was inclined toward the art of immortality and eternal life,
and Jìngnéng memorialized: "There are talismanic registers that enable one to ascend to heaven and earth,
and eliminate illnesses caused by spirits, demons, and evil entities;
refining divine elixirs
should not be hindered.
If Your Majesty seeks the ultimate principle of immortality and eternal life,
it will also be easy to attain."
Emperor Xuánzōng, hearing Jìngnéng's memorial,
was delighted in heart and mind,
and said to Jìngnéng: "I wish to become your disciple;
let the Venerable Master be my teacher,
and be accommodated within the temple."
The temple selected a courtyard for him,
and arranged for daily provisions.
The emperor came in person every day to Jìngnéng's courtyard,
to discuss Daoist teachings with him.
Even the ministers and high officials of the court
all wished to visit.
Since then, among the common people,
all revered Daoism.
Suddenly one day,
the emperor desired to seek immortality,
and summoned Jìngnéng to the palace for consultation.
Jìngnéng memorialized: "Your servant and Your Majesty will remotely gather immortal herbs."
Jìngnéng's original body remained in the temple,
while he transformed another body to fetch the immortal herbs for Your Majesty.
Traveling to the Qiántáng River,
he saw the water deep and vast,
broad and boundless, its limits unfathomable.
In the river was a fierce giant clam,
and boats did not dare to cross.
Jìngnéng then wrote a talisman,
and threw it into the river;
the river water cleared for three days,
washing the fierce giant clam onto the sandy shore.
As soon as Jìngnéng saw it,
he immediately cut it into three pieces.
He then crossed the river,
obtained the immortal herbs,
and presented them to the emperor.
The emperor was greatly pleased.
Only Gāo Lìshì did not believe they were immortal herbs,
and so memorialized: "Your servant fears that this medicine
is not genuine;
your servant wishes to test it!"
The emperor said: "How will you test it?"
Lìshì memorialized: "Your servant proposes that within the palace walls,
we dig a tunnel and beat five hundred drums.
Your Majesty will then summon Jìngnéng,
saying that there are demons causing disturbances in the palace;
how will the Venerable Master eliminate them?"
The emperor agreed to the memorial,
and Lìshì had people dig the tunnel,
and beat five hundred drums inside.
The emperor then summoned Jìngnéng,
who received the decree and came to the front of the hall.
The emperor granted him permission to ascend the hall,
and said there was the sound of demonic drums in the palace.
Jìngnéng, receiving the order to eliminate the sound of the demonic drums,
requested a bowl of water,
and facing the emperor,
sprayed it while performing a ritual.
As soon as the water left his mouth,
clouds and mist darkened the sky,
transforming into a giant serpent,
which entered the tunnel.
Its eyes were like hanging mirrors,
its mouth like a blood-filled basin,
its poisonous breath forming clouds;
the five hundred men all made sounds as if suffering from severe chills,
and dared not beat the drums.
When Jìngnéng heard the sounds cease,
he memorialized: "Your servant reports to Your Majesty,
it is not the sound of demonic drums."
The emperor said: "If it is not the sound of demonic drums,
then what sound is it?"
Jìngnéng memorialized: "Your Majesty was testing your servant's talismanic power,
by having people beat drums."
Hearing this memorial,
the emperor felt ashamed before Jìngnéng,
and returned to the temple.
For three days before and after,
the emperor summoned Jìngnéng to feast in the palace,
and music was played, stirring the melodies of Xiāosháo.
It was the time of early autumn,
and cool winds gradually encroached.
Inside the palace, feasting and enjoyment,
amusing with the consorts and concubines,
drinking several rounds together,
singing and piping in profusion.
Yet the emperor’s heart was not joyful,
and he said to Jìngnéng: “I am feasting now,
but it is not at all satisfying;
does the Celestial Master have a charm or command
to make the banquet joyful and delightful?”
Jìngnéng, accepting the emperor’s command,
rose to his feet,
and facing a painted jar from Jiànnán in the southwestern barbarian lands in the western corner of the hall,
which could hold about one dàn,
Jìngnéng shifted his mind and performed magic,
secretly seeking joy,
wishing to please the emperor’s heart,
to warm his spirits with roasting.
Thereupon Jìngnéng took a brush from his bosom,
and on the jar painted a Daoist priest,
holding a wine cup and drinking,
and pasted it onto the jar.
That jar then transformed into a Daoist priest,
three chǐ tall,
still wearing a coarse cap and yellow robe,
standing in the western corner of the hall.
Jìngnéng addressed the emperor: “I see Your Majesty drinking but not enjoying it;
I have invited a drinking companion for Your Majesty,
and this feast will surely be joyful.”
The emperor, hearing this,
said to Jìngnéng: “What kind of drinking companion is this,
who understands my wishes?”
Jìngnéng replied: “He is a Daoist priest,
skilled in charms and commands,
and also adept at feasting,
discussing the present and speaking of the past,
there is nothing he does not know,
versatile and capable,
familiar with all things human.”
The emperor summoned the Daoist priest,
and the Daoist priest, receiving the summons,
hurried from the western corner of the hall straight to the front of the hall,
repeatedly calling himself “your subject.”
Emperor Xuánzōng, seeing him,
was greatly pleased, his dragon countenance beaming,
and the consorts, empress, and palace maidens
all laughed joyfully.
The Daoist priest did not neglect court etiquette,
and the emperor then granted him to ascend the hall,
saying, “Sit beside me and converse.”
The emperor also asked: “Venerable Master, how great is your capacity for drink?”
Jìngnéng replied: “This venerable one has a large capacity,
truly a drinking companion;
each round he can add thirty or fifty cups,
and still hardly get drunk.”
The Daoist priest drank whenever the round reached him,
without any refusal.
The emperor was extremely happy,
sitting together in high spirits,
and the consorts, empress, and palace maidens
all urged him to drink three shēng.
The Daoist priest, being urged quite a lot,
did not miss a single round.
From the sì hour drinking until the shēn hour,
the Daoist priest drank about one dàn,
and the wine jar was just full.
In the wine vessel there were five shēng of wine left,
and Jìngnéng, wishing to show off the Daoist priest,
addressed the emperor: “Your Majesty’s feast is about to end,
the remaining wine I intend to urge the Venerable Master to drink,
humbly hoping Your Majesty will grant my request.”
The emperor said: “Granted!”
The wine was then bestowed upon the Venerable Master,
but the Daoist priest strenuously refused,
saying: “I fear losing court etiquette and violating ritual propriety.”
Jìngnéng said: “I know the superior one has a large capacity,
why refuse?”
The Daoist priest replied: “I have already had my fill of wine,
I truly cannot drink more!”
Jìngnéng, seeing his strenuous refusal,
before the emperor changed countenance and angrily said: “This Daoist priest must be beheaded!”
The emperor said: “What crime has he committed,
that he should suddenly be beheaded?”
Jìngnéng replied: “Because he has provoked me greatly.”
The emperor, complying with the request,
ordered Gāo Lìshì to take a sword and behead the Daoist priest.
His head fell with the sword,
and was cast aside.
The head was originally the lid of the wine jar,
the body was the body of the painted jar,
on which was painted a Daoist priest,
with a charm pasted on it.
Because the wine jar was just full, it appeared drunk.
The emperor, seeing this, laughed heartily,
and the consorts and empress together congratulated the emperor on his delight,
while the palace women exclaimed and laughed incessantly.
Gāo Lìshì looked again and again but could not distinguish,
gazing repeatedly with sighs.
Emperor Xuánzōng and the court ministers
admired Jìngnéng as surpassing the ancients and exceeding the present,
his transformations reaching the limitless,
displaying talismans and registers,
profound and mysterious as a sage,
rare in the human world,
unfathomable in his transformations,
no different from the Supreme Elder Lord.
Xuánzōng devoted his heart to the Dao,
concentrating on seeking immortality,
baring his gall and laying open his liver,
longing for eternal life.
He also greedily sought the wonders of talismans and registers.
The emperor again dreamed at night of a divine being,
who brought dragon liver,
and the emperor asked the divine being: “Where does this liver come from?”
The divine being said: “The upper realm ordered me to deliver it.”
The emperor, dreaming, obtained dragon liver,
its flavor extremely delicious,
but suddenly he awoke with a start,
and there was nothing at all.
The emperor, pondering the dream,
summoned Jìngnéng to ask about it.
Jìngnéng replied: “Your Majesty should get to eat dragon meat.”
The emperor said: “How can it be obtained?”
Jìngnéng replied: “Fetch a basin of water.”
He placed a sword across it,
performed magic and wrote a charm,
threw it into the basin,
and clouds and mist darkened.
After a long while,
the mist cleared and the clouds dispersed,
and in the air was a divine being,
who delivered a dragon leg,
weighing over thirty jīn.
Jìngnéng received it,
and presented it to the emperor.
The emperor, seeing the dragon meat,
was greatly pleased, his dragon countenance beaming,
and the court ministers all said: “Since ancient times there has been none like Jìngnéng!”
In the thirteenth year of the Kāiyuán era, the world suffered severe drought,
and the emperor summoned all officials.
The emperor said: “Beyond the passes there is severe drought,
within the passes there is no rain,
what will you all do?”
The prime ministers Jǐng and Chóng addressed him:
“Why does Your Majesty not ask Yè Jìngnéng to seek rain?”
The emperor, hearing this,
summoned Jìngnéng for an audience,
and he received the summons and went straight to the front of the hall.
The emperor said: “The world suffers severe drought;
how will the Celestial Master seek rain for me,
to save the myriad people?”
Jìngnéng replied: “I will summon the gods of the Five Peaks to question them.”
The emperor said: “Then go and ask.”
Jìngnéng, before the emperor,
set up an altar for performing magic,
wrote five charms,
first summoning the direct officials of the Five Peaks to demand rain,
and the Five Peaks said: “It all depends on the Celestial Ministry.”
Jìngnéng then summoned the Celestial Ministry,
which stated: “It is precisely because the people discarded their flour and rice cakes
that there has been severe drought for three years.”
Jìngnéng said: “Because the emperor needs rain,
where is there surplus rain?
Quickly order it to fall!”
The Celestial Ministry said: “Rain follows heaven’s will.”
Venerable Master Yè then ordered the Five Peaks and Four Rivers to confer,
and quickly bring rain together.
For three days before and after, rain fell in abundance,
the hundred grains ripened plentifully, and the myriad people sang in praise.
In the fourteenth year,
the emperor issued a great amnesty to the world,
allowing the common people to light lamps for offerings.
The various palaces viewed the lanterns,
and there was extraordinary merrymaking.
There was also an order: the people of the wards and markets,
were all permitted to light lanterns,
and the night curfew was not to be enforced.
After viewing the lanterns and returning to the inner palace,
the emperor asked: "Are all the prefectures and counties like this?"
Jìngnéng reported: "Shǔdū has lanterns,
and the offerings are extremely lavish;
I humbly fear the capital cannot compare!"
The emperor asked again: "How far is Jiànnán from here?"
Jìngnéng reported: "It is three thousand lǐ from here."
The emperor asked: "How do you know about that place?"
Jìngnéng reported: "Your subject has just returned from viewing it there.
If Your Majesty does not believe what I have reported,
going there yourself would be difficult;
but if you go with me,
we can arrive in an instant."
The emperor said: "If you take me there,
what attendants should I bring,
and how many people should accompany us?"
Jìngnéng reported: "One person would suffice."
The emperor said: "And what color clothes should we wear?"
Jìngnéng reported: "Those in attendance
should all wear plain white clothes."
The emperor said: "Then order Gāo Lìshì and others to make urgent preparations,
and quickly go with you to Jiànnán to view the lanterns."
Gāo Lìshì and others received the imperial command directly,
and immediately arranged and prepared.
Then, performing magic,
he took the emperor and the attendants accompanying the imperial carriage,
and together they went to Jiànnán to view the lanterns.
Swift as flying clouds,
like a flash of lightning.
The emperor and his attendants arrived at Jiànnán in a moment,
patrolling the streets and avenues,
touring various places together.
They also saw the wards and markets set up with lanterns,
offerings crisscrossing everywhere,
music at its peak,
greatly pleasing the emperor's feelings.
Jìngnéng then took the emperor to the Shǔwáng Hall,
and the attendants accompanying the imperial carriage viewed it together,
whereupon he ordered several pieces of music to be performed.
The emperor said to Jìngnéng: "Celestial Master,
the night is growing late,
I intend to return to Cháng'ān."
Jìngnéng reported: "Your Majesty has toured Shǔchuān today,
but has not yet seen it all;
if you wish to return to the capital,
we can go now."
Jìngnéng reported again: "Your Majesty has graced this commandery with your presence,
you should let the people of Shǔ commandery know that you viewed the lanterns,
and performed music in the Shǔwáng Hall."
The emperor said: "How can we let people know that I personally came to view the lanterns?"
Jìngnéng reported: "Your Majesty must leave one piece of clothing worn on your body in the Shǔwáng Hall.
Later, the military governor will surely send people to search the hall,
and upon seeing this undershirt,
will certainly dispatch someone to report it.
Your Majesty can then say that you personally viewed the lanterns and enjoyed music,
and intentionally left the undershirt,
as proof that it is not false.
Then the people of Shǔ and the officials and commoners,
will all know that Your Majesty viewed the lanterns,
would that not be excellent?"
The emperor then left one small undershirt,
in the Shǔwáng Hall.
Jìngnéng saw that the emperor had left his clothing,
and performed magic,
in a moment,
they arrived together at Cháng'ān.
Jìngnéng reported: "This is the inner palace."
The emperor, turning over in his mind, felt ashamed,
seeking the way of immortality,
marveling that Jìngnéng's abilities were unfathomable,
his talismans and registers unmatched in the world.
The emperor devoted himself to seeking the art of immortality and avoiding death,
when suddenly he heard the inner palace drum strike four times,
the night watch clearly marked,
the emperor replied to Jìngnéng: "Celestial Master, return to your temple for now,
tomorrow morning Jìngnéng shall see me."
Jìngnéng received the command,
and returned to his temple.
The emperor said to Gāo Lìshì: "The road to Shǔ is far,
blocked by mountains and rivers,
yet in the blink of an eye,
we reached the various prefectures and commanderies."
That night, the military governor, officials, and commoners,
again heard music in the Shǔwáng Hall,
lasting until dawn.
The people of Shǔ commandery were deeply suspicious,
redoubled their searches,
suspecting it was an extraordinary person.
They pursued in great confusion,
fearing it was a spirit or monster.
They also recovered one small undershirt.
After several days of searching,
there was still no trace.
The Jiànnán military governor did not dare conceal it,
so he recorded a memorial to report,
presenting the strange event,
respectfully dispatching his aide, concurrently Censor Zhái Cháng to present the memorial.
In less than ten days,
they reached Cháng'ān.
The emperor perused the memorial,
spread it on the jade table,
and read it once through.
Seeing the undershirt again,
his imperial countenance greatly pleased,
(he) knew it was not false.
The emperor personally inquired about the matter,
the messenger reported in detail: "On the night of the fifteenth day of the first month, during the second watch,
carriages, horses, and attendants,
all wearing white clothes,
numbering over a hundred people,
went to the Shǔwáng Hall to perform music,
and left when the music ended.
They left behind one undershirt,
and after searching, there was no further trace.
This is a strange and auspicious event,
my superior ordered your subject to report it."
The emperor said to Zhái Cháng: "On the night of the fifteenth day of the first month last,
I, along with Yè Jìngnéng and the attendants accompanying the imperial carriage, rested in the Shǔwáng Hall,
and so ordered music to be performed.
When the performance ended and the music stopped,
and as we were about to return,
fearing the Shǔ commandery would not know of my tour to view the lanterns,
I intentionally left the undershirt.
You quickly report to your superior,
I will personally issue a separate generous reward edict."
Zhái Cháng bowed and took leave of the emperor,
and immediately set out on the journey.
His heart full of joy,
the rain and dew moistening his body,
his six relatives gaining honor,
his nine clans all celebrating.
In less than ten days,
he reached Shǔzhōng,
and relayed the imperial edict in detail.
The officials, clerks, and commoners of Jiànnán,
all said the emperor communicated with spirits throughout the universe,
touring the world,
not only the territory of Shǔchuān,
the various prefectures and offices did not dare arbitrarily enforce laws and orders.
The emperor personally inquired about Jìngnéng's Daoist methods every day,
Jìngnéng constantly presented methods,
the emperor never neglected any matter.
Suddenly one day,
the empress, having no son,
intended to request of Jìngnéng: "I have heard that Yè Jìngnéng's magical arts communicate with spirits,
I wish to seek a son,
and dare not not report it."
The emperor then summoned Jìngnéng and asked: "Before I ascended the throne,
I already had an empress;
but since ascending the throne,
there have been no offspring at all.
Celestial Master, a monk of the black robe,
seek a son for me,
for the sake of the state's plans.
I and the empress,
dare not fail the Celestial Master."
Jìngnéng reported: "Having children is due to past karma,
how can Jìngnéng seek it?"
Jìngnéng then inquired of the celestial offices,
and sent a dispatch to the underworld.
Jìngnéng then drew a talisman for the emperor,
blew it into the air,
and it immediately transformed into a spirit,
and then ascended to heaven.
He also wrote a talisman dispatch to inquire of the underworld.
In a moment, the celestial offices and the underworld both reported: "The empress in this life is not destined to have a son."
Jìngnéng reported this in detail.
On the night of the fifteenth day of the eighth month,
the emperor, along with Jìngnéng and his accompanying attendants,
was enjoying the moon from a high place.
The emperor said to Jìngnéng: "The affairs within the moon—
can they be fathomed?"
Jìngnéng replied: "Even if I were to speak of them, I fear it would be of no benefit.
I wish to take Your Majesty to the Moon Palace for a visit—would that be acceptable?"
The emperor said: "How can we go there?"
Jìngnéng replied: "Your Majesty cannot go alone,
but if you go with me,
what difficulty is there in that?"
The emperor was greatly pleased, his imperial countenance beaming.
The emperor said: "Can the attendants accompany us?"
Jìngnéng replied: "Viewing lanterns in Jiànnán is a place for ordinary people;
the Moon Palace is an upper realm,
different from the mortal world.
Because Your Majesty possesses an immortal destiny,
you may go there temporarily."
The emperor asked further: "What color of clothing should I wear?"
Jìngnéng replied: "You may wear white brocade padded garments."
The emperor said: "Why wear white brocade padded garments?"
Jìngnéng replied: "Because there are crystal towers and halls there,
and the cold air is piercing."
The emperor dressed accordingly and prepared to go.
Jìngnéng performed his magic,
and in an instant, they arrived at the Moon Palace.
Observing the towers, halls, terraces, and pavilions,
they were unlike anything in the mortal world;
the doors, windows, and openings
were entirely different from those of the mundane realm.
The emperor, his heart set on viewing the towers and halls,
entered through the layered gates,
and saw palaces and pavilions beyond the towers,
all the way to the great hall.
Everything was made of crystal, glass, and agate,
with no discernible boundaries.
Windows were made of crystal,
and towers and terraces were also of crystal.
They also saw several beautiful women,
clad in garments of three-zhū weight,
each holding crystal trays in their hands.
On the trays were vessels,
all crafted from crystal and the seven treasures.
Upon seeing the emperor, they all maintained proper decorum.
Jìngnéng led the emperor straight to the side of a shāluó tree to view it.
The emperor saw that the tree's height was immeasurable,
its branches directly covering the three-thousand-great-thousand worlds.
The color of its leaves
was no different from silver,
and its flowers were like the color of clouds.
As the emperor strolled leisurely beneath the tree,
he paused and stood for a moment.
The cold air was piercing,
and the chill penetrated to the bone.
The emperor said to Jìngnéng: "The cold is severe;
I wish to return to the palace."
Jìngnéng replied: "Accompanying Your Majesty on this excursion
is truly an immortal splendor,
unlike the world below.
Your Majesty need not hurry;
please leisurely enjoy the moon and the sights.
Then we shall return—
would that not be excellent?"
The emperor leaned against the tree,
but felt the cold intensify.
He asked Jìngnéng again: "I can no longer endure the cold;
I wish to return now.
If we delay any longer,
I fear it may become unbearable."
Upon hearing the emperor's words again,
Jìngnéng could not help but smile slightly.
He then performed his magic,
and in an instant, they returned to Cháng'ān.
The emperor, wholeheartedly seeking the Dharma,
clasped his hands and stepped forward,
addressing the celestial master: "Show me the Daoist methods;
for the rest of my life,
I shall eternally receive heavenly blessings,
and you shall be my teacher."
Jìngnéng replied: "My humble Daoist methods
are all achieved through the power of talismans and registers—
how could they be worthy of transmission?"
The next morning,
when the officials gathered for court,
the emperor said: "Last night at the third watch,
I went with Celestial Master Yè to view the Moon Palace.
I saw that inside and out, the clear skies were utterly distinct;
the towers, halls, terraces, and pavilions were all extraordinary,
adorned entirely with the seven treasures."
The officials together congratulated the emperor: "Since the Three Sovereigns, Five Emperors, Zhōu, and Qín,
there has been none like Your Majesty.
As for Daoist methods connecting with the divine,
and the absolute marvel of talismans and registers,
there is none in the world surpassing Celestial Master Yè!"
The emperor then commanded the Grand Historian
to record this in the "Táng Records."
Several days later,
Jìngnéng saw a palace woman within the inner court
of exceptional beauty,
who often received the emperor's favor.
Jìngnéng then returned to his temple,
wrote a talisman,
and transformed it into a deity.
Every night at the third watch,
this deity would bring the palace woman to the temple to sleep,
and just before dawn,
would return her to the palace.
As days passed and months went by,
half a year had already elapsed.
The beauty was dazed as if drunk,
completely unaware of what was happening.
Suddenly, she reported to the emperor: "I am now with child;
only awaiting the difficulties of childbirth,
I dared not fail to report this."
Upon hearing this report,
the emperor knew it was Jìngnéng's doing through magic.
He ordered someone to fetch her.
He then instructed the beauty not to speak of this to anyone.
The emperor summoned Gāo Lìshì to discuss
a plan to kill Jìngnéng within the great hall.
Jìngnéng, in his temple, already knew of this early on.
The emperor said to Gāo Lìshì: "Yè Jìngnéng can move mountains and overturn seas,
alter heaven and earth,
control the cosmos,
ascend into the void at will,
and transform without difficulty.
I intend to kill him,
but fear it may be difficult.
What plan do you have
to kill him for me?"
Lìshì replied: "Yè Jìngnéng's ascension into the clouds and travel back and forth
all rely on the power of talismans and registers.
Now, if we devise a plan to kill him within the great hall,
how would Jìngnéng know of it?
Your Majesty need only summon Jìngnéng to the hall, grant him a seat,
and secretly station five hundred swordsmen behind the hall.
Your Majesty can calmly inquire about the Dharma;
while Jìngnéng is expounding the Daoist methods,
calmly display your imperial majesty.
I will secretly give the signal,
and the five hundred men will simultaneously rush into the hall with swords drawn,
and surely kill him."
The emperor said: "This plan is excellent."
Lìshì, having received the command,
then took five hundred men from the Imperial Guard,
their swords gleaming like frost and snow.
They hid behind the hall,
letting no one know.
The emperor then summoned Jìngnéng.
Jìngnéng already knew of the ambush behind the hall,
but paid it no mind.
Upon arriving before the hall,
the emperor granted him a seat,
and he expounded his Daoist methods.
The emperor said: "What other methods are there?"
Jìngnéng, knowing the emperor was pressing him about magical techniques, said: "Their number is extremely vast.
If Your Majesty intends to inquire about them all,
you will never reach the end.
What I have seen is only this much!"
Upon hearing Jìngnéng's reply,
the emperor's expression changed to one of anger,
and his imperial majesty flared in great rage.
Gāo Lìshì then dispatched the five hundred men,
who rushed into the hall simultaneously,
intending to behead Jìngnéng.
Seeing the five hundred men drawing their swords and entering the hall,
Jìngnéng showed no panic or fear.
He walked slowly and calmly before the emperor: "I too shall not hurry!"
The five hundred men simultaneously raised their swords,
bearing down upon Jìngnéng.
Jìngnéng focused his mind and performed magic,
instantly transforming and entering a pillar of the hall,
with no trace to be seen.
The emperor, startled and flustered,
circled the pillar several times, looking for him.
He called out repeatedly: "Celestial Master!
Celestial Master!
I had no such intention;
Gāo Lìshì conceived this treacherous plan.
I earnestly hope the Celestial Master will recognize my sincere and pure heart."
Jìngnéng, from within the pillar, replied: "I originally wished to serve Your Majesty for your entire lifetime,
but who knew Your Majesty would harbor such treacherous thoughts midway!"
The emperor then ordered Gāo Lìshì to take a sword and cut into the pillar to look.
Gāo Lìshì obeyed and cut into the pillar.
When about half of the pillar had been cut through,
it became clearly visible,
yet there was still no trace of Jìngnéng.
Jìngnéng, from within the pillar, spoke again: "I shall now return to the Great Luó Heaven!"
The emperor and Gāo Lìshì saw a streak of purple qi
ascend into the sky and depart.
The emperor's regret was too late.
The court officials and generals
all said the emperor had hastily accepted Lìshì's [plan],
causing the Celestial Master to no longer dwell in the mortal world
but instead return to the upper realm.
This was certainly not Jìngnéng's fault.
From this time onward, the Emperor
day and night thought of him with longing,
unable to rest or eat in peace.
Within ten days,
a palace messenger, about a hundred *li* or more into Shǔchuān,
suddenly saw Yè Jìngnéng walking slowly at a leisurely pace.
Jìngnéng saw the messenger,
and called out loudly: "Messenger, stop!
" The messenger, hearing the call,
dismounted from his horse,
stepped forward, bowed in greeting, and asked the Celestial Master,
saying: "May Your Holiness be blessed with boundless fortune tomorrow.
" The messenger said: "How did you come to be here?
" Jìngnéng said: "I am returning to the Dàluó Palace.
My departure was hasty,
and I had no time to bid farewell to the Emperor.
Messenger, please relay my words to His Majesty:
Jìngnéng is on the road,
and has no time to prepare a memorial.
I humbly beg His Majesty to understand.
If you wish to see your servant again,
you must wait until the seas run dry and the rivers wither,
until mountains move and the earth sinks.
" Having spoken these words,
in an instant,
he was nowhere to be seen.
The messenger then returned to the palace court,
and upon seeing the Emperor, first reported the matters concerning Shǔchuān,
then reported: "When your servant was returning from Jiànnán,
about a hundred *li* from Shǔchuān,
I encountered Yè Jìngnéng walking slowly at a leisurely pace.
He called to your servant to relay a message to Your Majesty: His departure was hasty,
and he had no time to bid farewell to Your Majesty.
Moreover, being on the road,
he had no time to prepare a memorial.
If Your Majesty wishes to see him again,
you must wait until mountains move and the earth sinks,
until the seas run dry and the rivers wither.
He ordered your servant to deliver this message orally,
and I dared not fail to report it.
" The Emperor, hearing the message Jìngnéng had entrusted to the messenger,
faced the palace hall and gazed toward Shǔchuān,
his eyes filled with tears as he wailed loudly, saying:
"My Yè Jìngnéng,
there is no second like him in this world.
He diligently cultivated the Dàoist teachings,
pure, empty, and of profound will.
He refined the divine elixir of nine transformations,
attaining immortality and deathlessness.
Taking but a single pellet of it,
its potency is beyond compare.
The Primordial Tàiyī divine talismans,
could move Heaven and Earth at will.
He could summon the Five Offices to come and converse,
command the Five Peaks to follow his hand's direction.
If Creation needed shifting, he shifted it;
if Heaven and Earth needed halting, he halted them.
He could also take me to view the Moon Palace,
and again roam and play in Shǔchuān.
I, however, conceived a treacherous heart,
and prepared weapons of war.
Yet when called to the hall,
he showed no fear or apprehension.
Questioned about his arts of the Way,
he declared them peerless.
Blades covered his body,
yet he cast his form into a pillar.
I searched for him but found no trace,
how could I fathom his intent?
The messenger from Jiànnán returns,
yet he had already arrived there long before.
He ordered an oral message relayed,
able to preserve the bond from beginning to end.
I have truly wronged you, my minister,
I wish you to know my heart.
Gazing afar toward Shǔchuān,
in vain my twin tears flow.
Since the separation of Heaven and Earth,
there has been but one such man.
For me, inscribe his name,
and record him in the annals of history.
" *The Ballad of Yè Jìngnéng*.
In ancient times, Master Fúzǐ journeyed eastward,
and arriving at the foot of Jīngshān,
he met three young boys on the road.
Two boys were playing games,
one boy was not playing.
Fúzǐ, finding this strange, asked: "Why are you not playing?
" The boy replied: "Great games lead to killing each other,
small games lead to injuring each other.
Playing games yields no merit,
only torn clothes and empty bellies.
Following each other to throw stones,
is not as good as returning home to pound grain.
Above, to my parents,
below, to my brothers,
I only wish not to report them,
yet fear receiving their discourtesy.
Having pondered this matter well,
therefore I do not play.
Why do you find it strange?
Xiàng Tuō then followed along, piling up earth to build a city,
and sat inside it.
Fúzǐ said to the boy: "Why do you not avoid the carriage?
" The boy replied: "I have heard the sages of old say: They know astronomy above,
geography below,
and human affairs in between.
From ancient times until now,
I have only heard of carriages avoiding cities,
never of cities avoiding carriages.
" Fúzǐ at that moment had no words to reply,
and so ordered the carriage to avoid the city and take the lower road.
He sent someone to ask: "Whose child is this?
What is his surname and given name?
" The boy replied: "My surname is Xiàng, my given name is Tuō.
Fúzǐ said: "Though you are young in years,
your understanding of affairs is great.
" The boy replied: "I have heard that fish, three days after birth,
swim in rivers and seas;
rabbits, three days after birth,
circle an area of three *mu*;
horses, three days after birth,
can already keep up with their mothers;
humans, three months after birth,
recognize their parents.
Heaven bestows this naturally,
why speak of great or small!
Fúzǐ asked the boy: "Do you know which mountain has no stones?
Which water has no fish?
Which gate has no barrier?
Which carriage has no wheels?
Which ox has no calf?
Which horse has no foal?
Which knife has no ring?
Which fire has no smoke?
Which man has no wife?
Which woman has no husband?
Which day is insufficient?
Which day has surplus?
Which male has no female?
Which tree has no branches?
Which city has no envoy?
Which person has no courtesy name?
" The boy replied: "An earthen mountain has no stones.
Well water has no fish.
An empty gate has no barrier.
A sedan chair has no wheels.
A clay ox has no calf.
A wooden horse has no foal.
A chopping knife has no ring.
Glowworm fire has no smoke.
An immortal has no wife.
A jade maiden has no husband.
The winter day is insufficient.
The summer day has surplus.
A lone male has no female.
A withered tree has no branches.
An empty city has no envoy.
A young child has no courtesy name.
Fúzǐ said: "Excellent!
Excellent!
Shall I travel the world with you,
would that be acceptable?
" The boy replied: "I will not travel.
I have a stern father,
whom I must attend;
I have a kind mother,
whom I must support;
I have an elder brother,
whom I must obey;
I have a younger brother,
whom I must instruct.
Therefore, I cannot follow you, sir.
Fúzǐ said: "In my carriage, I have a backgammon board,
shall we play a game together?
" The boy replied: "I do not play games.
If the Son of Heaven loves gaming,
wind and rain become untimely;
if the feudal lords love gaming,
state affairs fall into disorder;
if officials love gaming,
documents and cases are delayed;
if farmers love gaming,
plowing and sowing miss their seasons;
if students love gaming,
they forget to read books and poetry;
if children love gaming,
they are whipped and beaten for it.
These are unprofitable matters,
what use is there in learning them!
The Master said: "If I were to level the world with you,
could it be done?"
The child replied: "The world cannot be leveled.
There are high mountains,
there are rivers and seas,
there are nobles and ministers,
there are slaves and servants,
therefore it cannot be leveled."
The Master said: "If I were to level the high mountains with you,
block up the rivers and seas,
remove the nobles and ministers,
and discard the slaves and servants,
the world would be vast and empty,
wouldn't it be level then?"
The child replied: "If the high mountains are leveled,
beasts will have nowhere to rely;
if the rivers and seas are blocked,
fish will have nowhere to return;
if the nobles and ministers are removed,
people will create right and wrong;
if the slaves and servants are discarded,
whom will the gentlemen employ?"
The Master said: "Excellent!
Excellent!
Do you know why pines grow on roofs,
reeds grow before doors,
rushes grow on beds,
dogs bark at their masters,
wives sit while their mothers-in-law serve,
chickens transform into pheasants,
and dogs transform into foxes?
What is the reason for this?"
The child replied: "Pines growing on roofs are the rafters;
reeds growing before doors are the door screens;
rushes growing on beds are the mats.
A dog barking at its master
is because there is a guest nearby;
a wife sitting while her mother-in-law serves,
is because she has just arrived under the flowers;
a chicken transforming into a pheasant
is due to the mountains and marshes;
a dog transforming into a fox
is due to the hills and mounds."
The Master said to the child: "Do you think husband and wife are closer,
or parents are closer?"
The child said: "Parents are closer."
The Master said: "Husband and wife are closer.
They share the same bed and pillow in life,
and the same coffin in death,
their affection is extremely deep,
are they not close?"
The child replied: "What kind of talk is this!
What kind of talk is this!
A person having a mother
is like a tree having roots;
a person having a wife
is like a cart having wheels.
If a cart breaks, you can make a new one,
and it will surely be new;
if a wife dies, you can marry again,
and you will surely find a virtuous family.
If one tree dies,
a hundred branches wither;
if one mother dies,
all her children become orphans.
To compare a wife to a mother,
is that not perverse?"
The child then asked the Master: "Why can geese and ducks float?
Why can swans and cranes cry?
Why are pines and cypresses evergreen in winter and summer?"
The Master replied: "Geese and ducks can float because their feet are flat;
swans and cranes can cry because their throats and necks are long;
pines and cypresses are evergreen in winter and summer because their hearts are strong."
The child replied: "That is not so!
Frogs can croak,
is it because their throats are long?
Turtles and soft-shelled turtles can float,
is it because their feet are flat?
Bamboo is evergreen in winter and summer,
is it because its heart is strong?"
The Master asked the child: "Do you know how high the sky is?
How thick the earth is?
How many beams does the sky have?
How many pillars does the earth have?
Where does the wind come from?
Where does the rain start?
Where does frost come from?
Where does dew appear?"
The child replied: "The distance between heaven and earth is 99,999 lǐ,
the thickness of the earth
is equal to that of the sky.
Wind comes from Cāngwú,
rain comes from high places,
frost comes from the sky,
dew comes from the hundred grasses.
The sky has no beams,
the earth has no pillars,
they are supported by the clouds from the four directions,
therefore they serve as pillars,
what is strange about that?"
The Master sighed and said: "Excellent!
Excellent!
Now I know that the younger generation is truly to be feared."
The Master and Xiàng Tuō conversed,
and in every aspect, the Master was inferior to Xiàng Tuō.
The Master harbored thoughts of killing Xiàng Tuō,
and thus composed a poem:
Sūn Jìng hung his head and pricked his thigh,
Kuāng Héng bored through the wall to steal light at night.
Zǐlù was fond of bravery by nature,
Zǐzhāng was greedy for reading poetry and books.
Xiàng Tuō, at seven, could speak eloquently,
and replied to Kǒng Qiū with great strength.
Xiàng Tuō went into the mountains to study,
and clasped his hands before the hall to bid farewell to his mother.
"Under the hundred-foot tree, the child studies,
there is no need to send anything."
His parents grew old and confused,
and sent two cartloads of grass to the Master.
The Master was gone for years,
and Xiàng Tuō's parents did not expect him.
They took a hundred bundles to burn,
and saved the rest to feed the cattle and sheep another day.
The Master suddenly came to demand the grass,
and his parents' faces turned pale.
They immediately offered to pay double the price,
three strong ingots of gold per bundle.
"Gold and silver coins are of no use,
where is my child, Xiàng Tuō?"
"My child has been gone for years,
studying under the hundred-foot tree."
When the Master heard these words,
his heart was filled with joy beyond measure.
The Master rode his horse into the mountains,
climbing peaks and crossing ridges with great effort.
Every tree measured less than a hundred feet,
and the kudzu vines intertwined, very long.
The Master had someone take a shovel and pick,
and digging into the ground, they found a stone hall.
Inside the first gate were stone lions,
outside the second gate were stone guardians.
Entering the middle gate, he listened carefully,
and pairs of students were reading in lines like wild geese.
The Master drew his sword and swung it to cut,
but the people were not harmed.
They turned into stone men, all silent,
and the iron sword cut, blood flowing profusely.
Xiàng Tuō's remaining breath was not yet exhausted,
he turned his head and looked back, calling to his mother:
"Collect my red blood,
and carry it home for more than seven days."
His mother could not bear to see her child's blood,
so she carried it and poured it beside the dung heap.
On the first and second days, bamboo took root,
on the third and fourth days, the bamboo grew lush.
The bamboo poles grew densely, a hundred feet tall,
and each joint had soldiers and horses like divine kings.
Bows, knives, and weapons were carried on their bodies,
and the treasured swords at their waists were white as frost.
The two of them immediately sought victory,
but who knew that Xiàng Tuō had already perished.
The Master was very frightened at the time,
and the prefectures and counties clearly established a temple hall.
One scroll of "The Book of Questions Between Confucius and Xiàng Tuō."
In mid-spring, the second month,
pairs of swallows soar,
wishing to build a house,
husband and wife discuss.
They measure east and west,
and divine north and south,
only avoiding the General and the Grand Duke,
naturally receiving blessings without calamity.
Taking high-headed rafters,
piling mud to make a nest,
climbing up to the beams and rafters,
using grass as a bed.
They settle without considering danger,
not nesting in green curtains;
divining a favorable place to dwell,
they entrust themselves to the great beam.
The arrangement is just completed,
they briefly go to the embankment pond.
Then there was a yellow sparrow,
with a sharp, pointed head,
leaning against streets and alleys,
bullying the weak by force,
seeing the swallow was not home,
he entered to plunder.
Seeing his house clean and tidy,
he simply occupied it himself.
Women, children, men,
all rejoiced together,
boasting of their cleverness: “Thanks to his efforts,
the farmer hunts rabbits,
the shoemaker eats meat stew—
the old saying is clear,
and indeed not wrong.
Clenching fists hard,
baring arms forcefully,
if the swallow comes in,
we’ll beat his legs with sticks.
He’s alone and single-handed,
how dare he challenge us recklessly?
And with his lips stammering,
we’ll make him piss himself in the end.”
Before the words were settled,
the swallow returned,
stomping the ground and shouting.
The sparrow came out,
without asking good or bad,
raised his fist and struck.
Pushing left and shoving right,
twisting ears and slapping cheeks.
The child pulled his feet,
the wife bit with her mouth.
The swallow was beaten,
a pitiful sight.
His head could not lift,
his eyes could not open.
Husband and wife faced each other,
breath choked, voices mournful: “We never offended the leopard’s tail,
why did we suffer this bird disaster unjustly?”
So they went to the phoenix,
submitting a petition for judgment: “The swallow is poor and alone,
built a house,
but was forcibly seized by the sparrow,
who also threatened us further.
Saying: ‘By official decree, vagrants are registered,
entered into the proper rolls.
You, fugitive off the register,
never seen you perform royal service.
In the end, officials will beat your back,
exile you to Dān, Yá, Xiàng, Bái!’
And saying: ‘The magpie is my uncle,
the turtledove is my elder,
the prefect and county officials,
are melon-vine relatives.
If you petition against me,
I fear it will do you no good in the end.
Leave my door quickly,
or soon you’ll get a beating.’
” The swallow, not resigned,
demanded justice.
Then he was seized by the head and dragged,
clothes grabbed and torn.
Fists flew wildly,
blows crisscrossed fiercely.
Father and sons, several in number,
joined in beating him.
The swallow was struck,
feathers injured, wings broken,
unable to move,
life hanging by a thread.
Humbly beg for examination,
bruises green and purple are visible.
Unable to bear the injustice,
beg Your Majesty to punish the crime.”
The phoenix said: “The swallow’s petition,
words and reasoning earnest,
the sparrow’s tyranny,
beyond description.
Eventually, both parties
must face each other to clear things up.
Only by knowing right and wrong
can judgment be made.”
Specially sent the wren to arrest him.
The wren, receiving orders,
dared not delay.
Half running, half galloping,
swift as a shooting star.
Arriving outside the door,
stood listening for a long while.
Just heard the sparrow,
speaking from inside the hole.
The sparrow said: “I had a bad dream last night,
this morning my eye twitched,
if not a private fight,
surely official scolding.
Lately, corvée duties
have been levied frequently.
Probably the swallow
submitted a petition.
Command the children,
do not open the door.
If someone looks for me,
say I went to the east village.”
The wren called from outside the door: “You, don’t hide recklessly!
Just now I heard what you said,
come out quickly and reason with me.
Why seize his house,
and still beat him injured?
The phoenix ordered your arrest,
you yourself must bear the responsibility.
Even hiding in a hole won’t save you,
no matter how much you scheme.”
The sparrow, terrified,
trembled in fear and panic;
the whole family, young and old,
all startled and flustered.
Then he came out, kneeling to the wren,
calling him “Eldest Brother, Second Brother”: “You’ve come from afar in the heat,
please come into the hole to cool off.
A sudden guest lacks a sudden host,
sit awhile, let me arrange household hospitality.”
The wren said: “This fellow is utterly foolish,
completely unaware,
just seeing leniency,
trying to delay past the time.
Don’t talk of food,
I’m not hungry either.
Must go urgently,
lest the king blame the delay.”
The sparrow, already worried,
valued lingering,
delaying and not leaving,
hoping to escape trouble.
Empty talk, forced words,
begging a thousand, pleading ten thousand: “Allow postponement till tomorrow,
there’s still a little gift.”
The wren grew angry,
grabbed him by the waist.
The sparrow distressed,
eyebrows furrowed.
Seized and taken away,
in a moment reached the court.
The phoenix saw from afar,
asked who it was.
Immediately he bowed his head and knelt,
saying: “Commoner sparrow,
slandered by the swallow seizing the house,
yesterday received the king’s summons,
crawled and ran,
dared not come late.
The swallow’s document,
is all false words,
confusing high and low,
beg the king to confront and examine.”
The phoenix said: “This rogue is shameless,
eyes envious and harmful,
how can he be tolerated?
All are under my command.
Strip his back bare,
pull out his left leg,
crack open his skull.”
The sparrow, scared out of his wits,
repeatedly cried “death penalty,”
begged to call the swallow to confront.
Swallow suddenly popped out its head,
bowed and explained: "Sparrow seized my dwelling,
now you see me settled,
the injuries I suffered,
are not exaggerated,
eyewitness evidence confirms the truth,
how can it be called false?"
Sparrow, knowing its own guilt,
face full of shame,
begged to swear an oath,
with many excuses: "If I truly seized Swallow's home,
may I suffer lifelong poverty.
In the morning meet hawks seizing,
in the evening encounter owls,
walking caught in nets,
sitting struck by pellets,
endeavors never succeed,
dwelling never peaceful,
bury one each day,
whole family not spared."
Though a hundred curses were made,
Phoenix was not easily deceived.
Swallow said: "Men in distress burn incense,
dogs in distress leap walls.
Just like your festering sores and scabs,
bury your corpse!
All are evasive curses,
merely trying to deceive the king."
Phoenix grew very angry,
after hearing the case, pronounced judgment: "Sparrow's crime,
cannot be denied,
investigating the cause,
still shows resistance.
Considering the circumstances, sentence five strokes,
cangue the neck and imprison."
Swallow cheered,
overjoyed without end: "Seized my home,
caught and beat me,
thought you'd have good fortune to the end,
who knew heaven would repay you!
Now it's your turn,
five strokes is just the beginning."
Then Jílíng (wagtail) was nearby,
being Sparrow's sibling,
feeling great urgency and distress,
stayed close to attend.
Seeing Swallow cheer,
immediately stepped forward to intervene: "My elder brother offended you, sir,
I am deeply ashamed.
I've heard 'when the fox dies, the rabbit grieves,'
hating harm to its kind.
All under heaven are brothers,
how much more those sharing the same scent.
Today we can argue ourselves,
let the authorities handle it.
No need to beat a dead sparrow,
why curse after the fact."
Wife heard Sparrow was caned,
couldn't help feeling dispirited,
only knew to beat her chest,
shaking head, thinking of the trouble.
Two steps as one,
hurried to the prison to see.
Saw Sparrow lying on the ground,
face like dust.
Back sewn with a patch,
seemingly a foot and a half high.
Seeing Sparrow in distress,
tears fell like rain.
Poured urine into his mouth,
pasted old paper on the wounds.
At that time ( ) advised,
turned away, not listening.
Unnecessarily making a fuss,
indeed saw him argue in court.
Now cangued and imprisoned endlessly,
what good is it for you?
It's bringing trouble upon yourself,
can't blame others (as) ancestors.
Sparrow, putting on a tough front,
still talked wildly: "A man, a husband,
if things go wrong,
back beaten raw,
what more is there to fear?
Live but once,
die not twice.
As the saying goes: Better face ten wolves, nine tigers,
than meet a fool's rage.
Now encountered this reckless bluster,
all because of that black rascal's doing.
I'm now in prison,
rather die than be shamed.
You should go quickly,
call for Qúyù (mynah).
He's sharp-witted,
rely on him to find a way,
bite the powerful,
ask him to intercede with Phoenix.
Just know to avoid more beatings,
give him a bundle of Qímó."
Sparrow, imprisoned for days,
begged the jailer to remove the cangue.
Jailer repeatedly refused,
Sparrow sweet-talked (to dissuade): "Officially not a needle's gap, privately a cart's space,
kowtow and remove it by evening court,
no need to stubbornly refuse,
the one bringing food will surely have hairpins."
Jailer said: "You're not yet cleared,
so you remain in the yellow sand.
I, though unworthy, am the chief officer,
how can I accept bribes?
If it reaches the king's ears,
smashed like sesame seeds.
I'd rather you be upset,
than let me remove the cangue."
Sparrow sighed: "In ancient times, high officials suffered under jailers,
I see it today myself.
Must only chant Buddha's name,
make vows in heart,
if the case can be resolved,
vow to copy the Heart Sutra once."
Then he fawned on the clerk,
hoping for a little leniency: "Officials above and below,
speak of your fairness and strength.
Today,
beg for some convenience.
There's paper and brush for duty,
don't say empty-handed and cold-faced."
Clerk said: "You want to play dumb,
or are you backing down?
Seized his home,
showed no humility,
acted violently,
beat him till he's distressed.
You're a criminal under royal law,
Phoenix ordered me to interrogate.
Tomorrow morning present the case,
surely another beating.
Ten strokes already passed heaven's gate,
death is not half an inch away.
Just prepare your back to bear it,
why whisper secretly ( )."
Sparrow was reprimanded,
even more choked with anger,
received the interrogation points,
especially more depressed.
"Question: Swallow built a house,
intended for its own survival,
how dare you act so rudely,
brazenly seize by force?
Answer!"
"But Sparrow, named Nǎozi,
was chased urgently by the old crow,
fled without choosing danger,
entered any hole encountered,
temporarily entered Swallow's house,
to avoid capture.
Truly due to避难,
the matter was urgent,
not forceful seizure,
hope the king understands."
"Another question:既然称避难,
why threaten,
and further beat,
causing broken wings?
The state has constant penalties,
should cane one hundred strokes.
What other reason,
to explain yourself?
Answer!"
"But Sparrow only because Nǎozi避难,
temporarily lingered in Swallow's house.
Seeing it empty,
rested briefly to卸下.
Swallow arrived,
immediately wanted to上前道歉.
Not knowing the situation,
cursed at sight.
Father and son together,
involved all around.
Anger ignored danger,
immediately fought.
Swallow claims broken wings,
Sparrow now also limps.
Both sides injured,
彼此相当.
If truly discussing house occupation,
beg to compensate its price.
Now wishing to judge by law,
truly dare not argue.
I have the rank of Shàngzhùguó勋,
请求赎罪价."
"Another question: Seizing a dwelling through intimidation is a crime that cannot be tolerated.
Since you have high merit,
where did you first achieve merit?
Answer truthfully!"
"This Sparrow says: In the nineteenth year of the Zhēnguàn era,
the Great General campaigned against Liáodōng.
Sparrow enlisted to serve as an attendant,
and was assigned to the vanguard at that time.
I did not ride a horse,
nor did I bend a bow.
I carried mugwort fire in my mouth,
and delivered it upwind.
Gāolì was thus destroyed,
and for this I achieved merit.
I was uniformly granted the title of Shàngzhùguó,
and now possess several certificates of merit.
If you insist on verification,
please consult the 'Classic of Mountains and Seas'."
The Phoenix judged:
"Sparrow is bald and scruffy,
forcibly seized the Swallow's house.
Investigating the root cause,
he originally showed no submission.
However, since he holds the Shàngzhùguó merit for redemption,
he cannot be detained long in prison.
He should be released immediately,
without further burdening the case files."
Sparrow, having gained his release,
was overjoyed beyond measure.
He then called Swallow,
and offered to drink two shēng together.
"My past offenses,
I beg your mercy and compassion.
From now on,
I will serve you differently and respectfully.
In front of others, I will keep to the ground,
and never again..."
Swallow and Sparrow, now reconciled,
went walking to the neighborhood,
where there happened to be a meddlesome Wild Goose,
who asked the two:
"Recently you were in conflict,
Sparrow could not retreat quietly,
opening his eyes to wet the bed,
violating his rules and orders.
Relying on the Phoenix's grace,
you were spared a life of grass.
If a sparrowhawk had caught you,
your hundred years would have ended right then."
He then scolded Swallow:
"You are very stubborn and foolish.
Such a trivial matter,
why make such a fuss?
You directly sought to endanger his life,
acting with such inhumanity.
Both of you lack understanding,
it is fitting that I do not associate with your kind."
Swallow and Sparrow replied together:
"Who would have thought the Phoenix would not be angry,
yet we are reprimanded by a meddlesome Wild Goose.
You also are incapable of settling matters,
in the end, you have few words of substance.
If you truly possess high talent,
we request you compose a poem on a set theme."
The Wild Goose, well-intentioned,
was instead mocked and ridiculed.
He then composed a poem
to present to the two:
"The Wild Goose's heart has long held lofty ambitions,
The Swallow and Sparrow have never understood this.
One morning I shall reach the azure clouds,
In three years, flying and calling, it will be my time."
Swallow and Sparrow replied together:
"The great Peng indeed aims for the south,
The wren nests on a single branch.
Each finds contentment in their own way,
What concern is it of two insects?"
"The Swallow's Fu," one scroll.
This song suits itself perfectly,
Under heaven, none surpass it.
Sparrow and Swallow,
jointly created the 'Kāiyuán Song'.
Swallow is truly hard to match,
able to speak and also clever.
His whole life, heart quick and vigorous,
among birds, none surpass him.
He dwells on the hall's beam,
carrying mud to make his nest.
He seeks friends and companions, his kin,
shunning promiscuous birds.
In autumn and winter, hidden in a rocky cave,
in spring and summer, he is among men.
In the second month he comes to the thicket,
in the eighth month he returns to the mountains.
He carries the herb of long life in his beak,
other matters he leaves at ease.
If he survives the winter,
this year he will come back again.
Soaring and playing among the clouds,
wheeling and flying in the sky.
He returns again to his old abode,
each to their own original nest.
In the thicket he met a bird,
who gave his name as Sparrow.
Shaking his head, talking wildly,
in his words, matters..."
Sparrow was truly cunning,
playing tricks, alternately sinking and floating.
Knowing his nest and burrow were good,
he came right over to invade.
He asked Swallow, 'What mountain bird are you?'
Stamping the ground, making sounds:
'You come seeking my burrow in vain,
let it go and restrain your heart.'"
Swallow said to Sparrow:
"How good you are at acting wrongly!
Hearing your previous words,
I originally did not know you.
I lived here all winter,
keeping my wife and children warm.
You ought to feel ashamed,
yet you complain and argue!"
Sparrow said to Swallow:
"Don't speak so grandly of grace.
Raising your voice is certainly unreasonable,
no need for beak-headed clamor.
The authorities have their principles,
they will see clearly and proclaim.
The empty space I truly sat in,
how could Sparrow claim it for himself?"
Swallow said to Sparrow:
"How good you are at being utterly foolish!
You sat in my house,
yet bullied the master.
Now that I demand it back,
you wildly talk of authorities.
Raising a toad brings illness,
I tell you, this is certain!"
Sparrow said to Swallow:
"It's not up to you to decide with your beak.
I ask you, where do you live and sit?
Originally, what prefecture did you reside in?
The imperial household is now registering guests,
specifically catching fugitives.
The clever ones devise other excuses,
change their minds and just withdraw."
Swallow heard this and clapped his hands, laughing:
"It's not up to you to decide with wild talk.
My great house is situated in the mountain place,
this is indeed my estate.
My native place belongs to Jīngzhào,
my life's ties are in the imperial capital.
Just know to return his burrow,
your wild words are not appropriate.
Even if I had no registered residence,
it still would not concern you.
I obtain long life again,
wherever I go, I settle peacefully.
These words are all true,
the whole world also knows and hears.
If you do not believe these words,
I beg you, ask the scholars."
Sparrow said to Swallow:
"Why bother with such elaborate explanations?
How do you obtain the blessing of long life?
Your words are all empty.
Your spirit is evident in your eyes,
alive, you understand freely.
Where did you gain such skill?
Wild words deceive the village folk.
Your head is like a solitary pestle bird,
your body like a large lacquer form.
Your body stained with bean juice,
your hands and feet like needle points.
Constantly serving the stinking great soap-bag,
you just want to fill the foreign bottle.
How do you know the way of governing the state?
Why envy my name of long life?"
"Once in the hall of the King of Wú,
the swallow made its nest.
Palace maids played at night,
and casually caught and burned the nest.
At that time, having no place to stay,
it lodged for a night on the hall's beam.
The king took pity on it,
showing compassion and great leniency.
Do not scorn its youth and small size,
its spirit is that of a true hero.
On a hundred beams of the hall,
it soars and flits among the clouds.
On water, it swallows floating insects,
in the air, it catches flying bugs.
Truly incomparable,
it was once betrothed to the Dragon Palace of the sea.
The third daughter of the Dragon King,
her hair over seven chǐ long.
Carried in its beak, lying beneath its belly—
how could the swallow not be praised?
Please read the Analects for proof,
ask Gōngyě Cháng,
who at that time was in bonds,
but spared misfortune because of a swallow."
The sparrow said to the swallow: "Listen carefully with attentive ears!
If you want your nest back,
first quiet your beak's clamor.
The red sparrow was anciently deemed auspicious,
its brethren dwell in the heavenly court.
Dukes and kings clasp its hand,
court and countryside all know its name.
Though sharing the same world,
the fruits we receive are not equal.
When wheat ripens, I eat first;
when grain is ready, I taste ahead.
Through cold and heat, coming and going,
have I ever left the imperial domain?
My descendants fill the world,
fathers and uncles are in every village.
Since gaining discernment,
my kind mother's heart has been at peace.
Constantly pondering the ten good deeds,
awakening to the impermanence of desires.
When hungry, I always eat the five grains,
never killing a single living being.
Pitying you as a distant guest,
I thus do not contend with you."
The swallow sighed to itself: "I won't boast to the sparrow.
When hungry, I always dine on ninefold-fermented wine,
when thirsty, I drink cinnabar elixir.
Unable to distinguish the four seas,
my heart yearns for Hóngyá.
Do not wonder why I hide through winter—
it is only for the joy of mountain life.
Staying long makes people despise and scorn,
coming rarely brings delight.
That is why I hide through winter,
not from fear of hunger or cold.
Secluded cliffs are truly joyful,
in mountains and wilds, I wander freely.
I intended to observe others,
but instead became the one observed.
A single tiger, though fierce,
is no match for many dogs.
My nest was seized and taken away,
they threatened to report me to the authorities.
Vain contention is of no benefit,
better to see the phoenix."
The sparrow, seized by the swallow,
was brought directly before the king of birds.
The phoenix sat upon its terrace,
surrounded by a hundred birds on all sides.
Pacing and gazing around,
it saw the swallow holding words in its beak.
"Wrongfully, my nest was forcibly seized;
I accuse by name the sparrow.
Bearing grievance, I come to plead,
begging to inform the great king."
The sparrow and swallow
both stood before the king.
The phoenix personally decreed:
"Let the one with reason speak first."
The swallow spoke first: "Hear my words, Your Majesty.
I will tell the truth of the matter,
recounting the origins and causes.
My home was invaded and I suffered;
though wronged, how dare I speak?
The yellow-headed sparrow, without distinction,
allied with bullies and the strong.
I had a dwelling of my own,
forcibly seized without cause.
Wronged, it is hard to remain silent;
I beg for your consideration.
Though the sun and moon shine bright,
their light does not reach beneath an overturned pot.
Empty words have no power;
who would willingly enter the king's gate?"
The phoenix rebuked the sparrow: "Why did you seize and bully him?
Each has its own nest and home;
how could you suddenly act so wrongly?"
The sparrow stepped forward and addressed the phoenix: "Your Majesty, how can you not know?
Investigate carefully, question in detail—
how can you believe empty claims?
I, the sparrow, am but a bird,
each of us lives in our own village.
Neither had a fixed home;
we settled wherever we could.
I saw an empty, unused nest,
broken and old, not new.
Long seeking, it had no owner;
so I settled there as suited me.
What is accomplished should not be destroyed;
it cannot be moved or altered.
I settled within as was fitting,
cherishing and guarding it securely."
The swallow addressed the king: "The sparrow speaks wildly and falsely.
It is a bird of poverty and oddity,
fabricating words and phrases.
Carrying mud to build a nest,
its mouth grew sores from the toil.
If Your Majesty doubts my words,
ask the original owner."
The phoenix then decreed: "Both birds, come near.
Without speaking, I already know well;
the matter is clear and evident.
You cunning yellow-headed bird,
stop weaving false reasons.
Quickly return its nest to him,
do not delay any longer."
The sparrow addressed the phoenix: "I willingly accept your judgment.
Though the king orders its return,
I beg for some flexibility.
I am a sparrow of the tax-paying household,
not to be equated with outsiders.
The swallow comes and goes with the seasons,
never staying through the winter."
The phoenix said to the sparrow: "Quickly return the swallow's nest.
I have now made my judgment;
the sparrow is in the wrong.
I am the lord of all birds,
my laws are not to be ground down.
Justice demands it be so;
there must be no partiality."
The swallow regained its home,
rejoicing with great delight;
the sparrow, ashamed, wished to die,
with nowhere to settle.
The swallow sought no quarrel with others;
sparrow, do not bear resentment.
I have heard the ancients say:
'Three fights make kinship.'
In the past, King Yáo was sage,
ruling for twenty years.
Zhèng Qiáo served all under heaven,
facing each other, they became kin.
Yuán Bó fell ill at home,
his friend Jùqīng traveled a thousand lǐ to see him.
The King of Yàn resented the state of Qín,
weeping horses turned into unicorns.
Sharing provisions, sitting guard unto death—
for ten thousand generations their tale is told.
Bǎi Yáo remembered the court,
sobbing, tears streaming down.
Even with a king's righteousness to sever a horse,
still they could not part.
Wǔ Zǐxū attacked Chǔ,
two cities had no words.
Unable to emulate ancient virtue,
we two are but birds in form.
For contending over a ruined nest,
we wasted our spirit in vain.
Wealth is like dirt and dung;
benevolence and righteousness outweigh mountains.
Now, swallow, I am truly at fault;
sparrow, do not bear resentment."
The sparrow said to the swallow: "After parting, no need for further talk.
The house is your house;
reasonably so, not falsely claimed.
All winter I spent repairing it,
every crack and flaw made whole.
You ought to feel ashamed,
yet you dragged me before the king.
The phoenix upholds the Buddha's law,
not intending to harm or kill;
but if suddenly punished with beating,
how much would the golden body be shamed?"
The swallow said to the sparrow: "This remark is not out of anger either.
Because you repaired the house,
I did not ask to borrow rent money.
Twelve months in a year,
Five hundred coins each month—
If we were to discuss the rent,
It would surely mean selling yourself."
"The Swallow's Fu," one piece.
Composed by Xiānggòng Jìnshì Wáng Fū.
