I have observed that Shénnóng once tasted all the herbs,
And from this, the five grains were distinguished.
Xuānyuán made clothing,
Passing down teachings to later generations.
Cāngjié created writing,
Kǒng Qiū expounded and transformed Confucian principles.
It is impossible to recount everything in detail from the beginning,
So let us summarize the essential points.
For now, let us ask about tea and wine:
Which of the two has greater merit?
Who should be considered humble and lowly,
And who should be honored as noble?
Today, each must present its case,
The stronger one will bring glory to its kind.
Tea then stepped forward and said: "Everyone, do not make a fuss,
Listen to what I have to say.
I am the chief among all herbs,
The flower of ten thousand trees.
Prized for its buds,
Valued for its tender shoots.
Called fragrant grass,
Known as tea.
Offered to the mansions of the five nobles,
Presented to the households of emperors and kings.
Freshly offered in season,
A lifetime of honor and splendor.
Naturally noble and esteemed,
What need is there for debate and praise!"
Wine then stepped forward: "Ridiculous words!
From ancient times to the present,
Tea has been cheap, wine has been dear.
A single ladle of wine poured into the river,
And the entire army claims to be drunk.
When the ruler drinks it,
He shouts 'Long live!'
When ministers drink it,
They are granted fearlessness.
It soothes death and stabilizes life,
The spirits savor its essence.
Wine and food offered to others,
Never harbor ill intent.
With wine comes rules,
Benevolence, righteousness, propriety, and wisdom.
Naturally, I should be honored as noble,
Why trouble to compare!"
Tea said to wine: "Have you not heard: Fúliáng and Shèzhōu,
Nations from all over come seeking.
Shǔshān and Méngdǐng,
Climbing mountains and scaling ridges.
Shūchéng and Tàihú,
Buying maids and slaves.
Yuèjùn and Yúháng,
Gold and silk as sacks.
Plain and purple for the Son of Heaven,
Rare even among mortals.
Merchants come seeking,
Boats and carts jam the routes.
Based on these facts,
Who should be considered lowly?"
Wine said to tea: "Have you not heard: Qíjiǔ and Gānhé,
Exchanged for brocade and fine silk.
Pútáo and Jiǔyùn,
Moistening the body.
Jade wine and qióngjiāng,
Cups and goblets for immortals.
Júhuā and Zhúyè,
For kings to entertain guests.
Zhōngshān and Zhàomǔ,
Sweet and delicious, bitter and astringent.
One drunken stupor lasts three years,
Passed down from ancient times to now.
Promoting courtesy in villages,
Harmonizing military headquarters.
You, with your head,
Need not struggle in vain."
Tea said to wine: "My fragrant grass,
Is the heart of ten thousand trees.
Sometimes white as jade,
Sometimes like yellow gold.
Famous monks and great virtues,
Secluded in Zen forests.
Drinking it while conversing,
Dispels drowsiness and dullness.
Offered to Mílè,
Presented to Guānyīn.
Through thousands of kalpas,
All Buddhas revere it.
Wine can ruin homes and scatter households,
Widely leading to wickedness and debauchery.
After drinking three cups,
People only sink deeper into sin."
Wine said to tea: "Three coins for one [unit],
When will you ever become rich!
Wine connects with noble people,
Admired by dukes and ministers.
It once made the Zhào ruler play the qin,
And the Qín king strike the fǒu.
You cannot invite songs with tea,
Nor teach dancing for tea.
Drinking tea only causes back pain,
Drinking too much makes people suffer stomachaches.
Drink ten cups in one day,
And your belly swells like a drum in the yamen.
If you consume it for three years,
You will develop edema as retribution."
Tea said to wine: "I achieved fame at thirty,
Dressed in belts and headwear.
Crossing seas and riding rivers,
I come to pay homage to the golden chambers.
Brought to the marketplace,
Arranged and displayed.
People come to buy me,
Wealth overflowing.
Instant riches upon speaking,
No need to wait for tomorrow or the day after.
You, wine, cause confusion and disorder,
Drinking too much leads to much grumbling.
Framing innocent people on the streets,
Receiving at least seventeen lashes on the back."
Wine said to tea: "Have you not seen the talented scholars of old,
Composing poems all saying: 'When thirsty, a cup
Can nourish and sustain life.'
Also saying: 'Wine is the medicine to dispel sorrow.'
And also: 'Wine can nurture the worthy.'
The dregs of the ancients,
Now passed down to this day.
Tea is cheap: three coins for five bowls,
Wine is cheap: half a cup for seven coins.
Offering wine to thank for a seat,
Courtesy and deference in social interactions.
The music of the state,
Originally meant for wine feasts.
If we only drink your tea all day,
Who would dare to play any pipes or strings!"
Tea said to wine: "Have you not heard it said: 'Boys of fourteen or fifteen,
Should not become close to wine houses.'
Have you not seen the xīngxīng bird,
Who lost its life because of wine.
You claim that tea drinking causes illness,
While wine drinking nurtures the worthy.
Yet we see there is wine-induced jaundice and wine sickness,
But we never hear of tea madness or tea insanity.
Āshèshìwáng, because of wine, killed his father and harmed his mother,
Liú Líng, because of wine, was dead drunk for three years.
After drinking, eyebrows raised and eyes glaring,
Angrily fighting with fists raised.
The indictment only speaks of rough drunkenness from wine,
Never mentioning tea drunkenness.
Inevitably, head in cangue and beaten with rods,
The bailiff demanding money.
Large cangue around the neck,
Beams thrown on the back.
Then they burn incense, swear off wine,
Chant Buddha's name, and pray to heaven,
Vowing never to drink again for life,
Hoping to avoid calamity."
The two were fiercely arguing over who was superior,
Unaware that water was right beside them.
Water said to tea and wine: "You two,
Why such haste?
Who allowed you
To each claim merit?
With words you slander each other,
Arguing east and west.
The four great elements of life,
Are earth, water, fire, and wind.
Without water, tea—
What form would it take?
Without water, wine—
How would it appear?
Eating dried rice and yeast
Harms the stomach and intestines.
Chewing dried tea leaves
Only scrapes the throat.
All things depend on water,
The ancestor of the five grains.
Above, it corresponds to celestial signs;
Below, it aligns with fortune and misfortune.
The Jiāng, Hé, Huái, and Jì rivers—
With me, they flow freely.
I can flood heaven and earth,
And also dry up rivers, killing fish and dragons.
The nine-year disaster in Yáo’s time
Was only because I was within it.
I moved all under heaven to revere and serve,
And the myriad people to rely and follow.
Even I do not boast of sagehood—
What use is it for you two to contend for merit?
From now on,
You must be harmonious and united.
Let wine shops prosper,
And tea houses never be poor.
Be brothers forever,
And maintain this from start to end.
If one reads this volume,
They will never suffer from wine madness or tea folly."
One scroll of "The Debate Between Tea and Wine."
Recorded by the disciple of the Institute of Techniques, Yán Hǎizhēn, on the fourteenth day of the first month in the rénshēn year of the third year of the Kāibǎo era.
Seat-Settling Text of "Subduing the Demons"
Year after year, time silently shifts,
Yet no one awakens to this in their heart.
Just yesterday, cheeks were rosy and bright,
But now, white threads appear on the head.
Though honored and lofty, with a thousand promises,
All are hurriedly compressed into a single dream’s span.
Further, see the elderly with bent backs,
Still toiling tirelessly for wife and children.
Do you not see that from birth to death,
It is like ants moving in cycles?
For clothing and food,
It is like silkworms spinning cocoons.
Even if there were a man of strength to lift mountains and tripods,
He would still be buried under three feet of earth.
Even those adorned with jade and gold embroidery
Cannot avoid becoming a handful of ashes.
Do not cling to long abiding—
Look instead to the time of departure.
Though we speak of the highest heavens,
All must reach the land of impermanence.
A young wife’s affection may be deep,
But she cannot take your place at death’s gate.
Love for a child may be profound,
But in the end, they cannot bear your suffering.
In this bustling, turbid world,
Why cling to prolonged dwelling?
In the vast, dim confusion,
How can one plan to leave?
If you do not gather the tree of constant intention,
The flower of awakening will wither early.
Where there is heavenly palace joy,
Hell must also lie below.
Do not lament death, Bōzhā—
After leaving, life returns again.
All should sigh in sorrow—
How can you not reflect?
A lifetime is like a flickering lamp, vain and empty;
A hundred years are like a spring dream, bitter and hurried.
Hold it in your heart and ponder carefully:
Worldly affairs have never lasted long.
Even if gold and silver fill the treasury,
At death, can you take any with you?
Rosy cheeks gradually wrinkle like chicken skin;
Dark hair soon turns to crane-feather white.
Even those you knew before
All grow old, sick, and impermanent.
Spring, summer, autumn, winter—the four seasons urge haste,
Causing the cycle of rebirth in the human world.
On a thousand mountains, white snow clearly lies,
While ten thousand trees’ red flowers are about to bloom unseen.
Swallows come and go, time pressing urgently;
Flowers bloom and wither, competing in succession.
Hearing this, you must directly awaken,
So that in the future you may avoid rebirth.
If you wish to ask whether such things exist,
The sūtra’s title and name will be chanted forth.
With this, we open and praise the merits born of the Mahāyāna,
Reverently dedicating them to adorn our present emperor’s noble position.
We humbly pray that Shùn’s sun may long hang high,
And Yáo’s years be preserved forever.
Extending the phoenix city for a thousand autumns,
Protecting the dragon chart for ten thousand years.
We humbly address our prefectural lord, the Púyè:
With divine endowment of upright spirit,
And heroic essence descended from the mountains.
Holding deep benevolence that aids all beings,
Embracing the grand task of harmonizing the primal forces.
His family transmits noble lineage,
Nurturing the common people.
Upholding the pure regulations of state teaching,
Balancing the weighty position of land and water.
Since he came to govern the city and countryside,
Every household is like spring.
All sing songs of good governance,
Together celebrating the transformation toward peace.
Thus, the years bring abundant harvests,
And the entire region is tranquil and serene.
Grain stores pile like mountains, flowing like rivers;
The sound of trade spreads through city and town.
We reverently offer praises of merit,
Dedicating them to adorn our prefectural lord, the Sītú.
We humbly pray that the great river may flow again,
Its waters forever encircling heaven and earth;
That the purple sash may last a thousand years,
His achievements long supporting the altars of state.
Next, we offer praises of merit,
Reverently dedicating them to adorn the imperial mother, the holy celestial princess.
We humbly pray that the vermilion cassia of the southern mountains
May not change through the four seasons;
That the cold plum of the northern ridges
May bloom alone, a singular splendor.
Again, we offer praises of merit,
Dedicating them to adorn all the young ladies and noble sons of the household.
May the sons, with red tassels, serve the state,
Assisting and supporting the sagely court;
May the young ladies, with brows aligned to dragon towers,
Personally approach the imperial gates.
May the gate hold many beautiful jades,
The residence receive auspicious blessings.
May a thousand calamities not descend upon the courtyard,
And ten thousand virtues all gather at the noble house.
Then, for the great generals before the yamen,
May they be filial and loyal to the utmost;
For the officials in attendance,
May they be pure and upright.
For the city god, community temples,
Local earth spirits, and sacred altars—
May high peaks be preserved for a thousand autumns,
And all within the seas be called peaceful.
[Again, we offer praises of merit,
Dedicating them to adorn our chief monastic supervisor, the Heshang.
We humbly pray that he may long receive the emperor’s grace,
Becoming a state preceptor of abhiṣeka.
May he forever stabilize the steps of the throne,
Assisting the enlightened king in governance and transformation.]
The golden immortal (Buddha) manifested in form
Originally in the Zhōu dynasty;
The spread of the image-dharma
Began in the Hàn dynasty.
In King Zhāo’s time,
An auspicious dream foretold a thousand autumns;
In the rénwǔ year,
He renounced the imperial palace for the Snowy Mountains.
Six years of ascetic practice,
The four wisdoms perfected all around.
He defeated nine million demon armies,
Achieving the eighty minor marks of excellence.
Thus, in heaven above and earth below,
Only the Buddha is honored alone;
Within the three realms,
Truly none can compare.
Now, at the clear and bright festival season,
Mid-spring with its warming scenes,
It is the day the Buddha wearied of the royal palace,
And the household gathers on this auspicious day.
Beholding the Buddha’s jade-curl mark,
What blessing does not arrive?
Seeing the golden one’s supreme form,
What calamity does not vanish?
Through three great asaṃkhyeya kalpas, his vows are firm;
The six pāramitās’ practices are fully perfected.
A hundred thousand meritorious qualities fill his body,
The eighty secondary characteristics near completion.
If he does not come here to save and deliver,
Then where shall we await the opportune cause?
At that time, not remaining in other lands,
He manifested temporarily, dwelling in the Tuṣita Heaven.
Our Buddha, in order to deliver all beings,
abandoned the royal palace,
and cultivated the Way in the Snowy Mountains.
Now, after six years of ascetic practice,
his four wisdoms were perfected and complete.
On the morning of the eighth day of the twelfth lunar month,
he descended the mountain to bathe in the Xīlián River,
washing away the filth accumulated over many years,
and attaining the golden body of purple-gold luster.
Emerging from the pure river of desire,
he encountered an auspicious elder.
The elder generously spread a grass seat,
and made diligent offerings.
At this time, a cowherd girl presented milk,
and on this day, the Four Heavenly Kings offered alms bowls.
As soon as he ascended the seat,
the demon palaces trembled.
At that moment, what words did the Demon King speak?
What words did the Demon King speak?
"For six years he practiced austerities in the mountains,
his four wisdoms perfected, his attainment of the Way firm.
He descends the mountain wishing to save beings from suffering,
washing away defilement and filth in the Xīlián.
Just emerging from the river, he meets an elder,
who generously spreads a grass seat, forming a good connection.
The cowherd girl personally offers milk in供养,
the Four Kings bring alms bowls to the riverbank.
As soon as he sits firmly,
he shakes the heavenly palaces,
thus we know his holy power is boundless and inexhaustible.
The Demon King immediately looked down upon the lower realm,
and then knew the Tathāgata had appeared in the world."
Thus, the Demon King, having observed the lower realm,
saw neither men of the five heinous crimes,
nor filial and obedient sons.
He only saw that in our southern Jambudvīpa, King Śuddhodana's Prince Siddhārtha was about to attain perfect enlightenment.
The Demon King thought to himself: "If he is allowed to teach and deliver beings,
our followers
will turn to the Buddha.
It would be better to seize the opportunity, first gather our troops,
inspect the demon palaces,
harass Gautama,
and prevent him from appearing in the world."
What words did the Demon King speak at that time?
"The Demon King, furious and restless,
widely summoned all demonic spirits and ghosts.
Seeing the Tathāgata now appearing in the world,
his ambitious heart could not bear it, and anger arose.
Not understanding his own kind are evil spirits,
he lifted mountains and overturned seas to destroy the golden man.
Ordering the ghosts and spirits to obey his command,
to seize the Tathāgata and vent his own feelings."
Thereupon, the Demon King struck a golden bell,
assembling a million followers.
He then appointed the Horse-Headed Rākṣasa as temporary patrol general,
the Swift Yaksa as vanguard commander,
the Kumbhāṇḍa ghosts arranged spears and halberds to advance ahead,
the Piśāca spirits led armored soldiers following behind.
Summoning the Asura army as shock troops,
their eyes flashing with ferocity;
ordering the Preta spirits to follow after,
they were by turns angry and pleased.
Furthermore, there were Yaksa officers,
Rākṣasa patrol chiefs,
with sword-like teeth and halberd-like fangs,
sharp fur and bronze claws,
holding iron clubs,
and girded with red snakes.
Driving specters and goblins ahead,
demons and ghosts followed behind.
Yama, King of the Dead, served as commander-in-chief,
overseeing all armies.
The Great God of the Five Paths also served as chief guard general,
and knew beheading and chopping.
Calling the Wind Master and Rain Master to form one camp,
summoning the Epidemic Ghost King to form a separate troop.
Ten thousand kinds of demonic hags,
with ears that do not hear;
a thousand types of weapons,
never before seen by the eye.
Then, deploying two battle arrays,
dividing into four flanks,
surrounding left and right, shielding front and rear,
advancing ahead and cutting off behind.
Using thunder as war drums,
spreading lightning flashes as crimson banners,
releasing fierce winds to sweep forward,
restraining poisonous dragons to follow behind.
Vipers coiled and knotted,
filling the ground and overflowing streams.
Gods and ghosts crisscrossed,
shaking spirits and startling eyes.
Furthermore, there were flying sky demons,
unfathomable in form.
Some with five eyes and six tusks,
three bodies and eight arms,
four shoulders and seven ears,
nine mouths and ten heads,
yellow hair and red beards,
pointed heads and broad foreheads.
Some with thick wrists and thin arms,
small heads and long feet.
Waving their banners across mountains and rivers,
breathing out and spitting clouds and mist.
Shaking the sun and moon,
rocking heaven and earth.
Making chirping and chattering sounds,
spreading cries of 'bozha'.
The Demon King personally led the troops,
coming to the forest.
First spreading dense, dark clouds,
then releasing ink-splashing rain.
Square beams and rolling logs,
blocked the empty sky.
Holding rocks and lifting mountains,
darkening and obscuring the sun and moon.
A violent wind suddenly arose,
uprooting trees and blowing sand,
heaven and earth could no longer distinguish east from west,
in the darkness, how could one know north or south?
At one command,
they descended from the heavens.
In an instant,
they reached beneath the Bodhi tree.
"Inspecting a million kinds of demons,
planning to seize the Tathāgata as if it were trivial.
Before the army, ordering all gods and ghosts,
'Unless Gautama is dead, do not return.'"
The Demon King acted as supreme marshal,
commanding all armies according to his direction.
Dense, dark clouds spread through the sky,
splashing down black fog like an ink pond.
Raindrops striking like arrows hitting their mark,
hailstones meeting people like swinging hammers.
Mountains lifted and placed in the palm,
rivers pinched and poured straight down.
Chaos in the sky,
alarm in the world,
only the cry of 'Kill!' heard in the commands.
Where red banners were furled, sunset clouds arose,
where black standards hung, blue clouds flew.
Gods and ghosts in the clouds were all fierce,
the Demon King from time to time shook with might.
Surrounding the Buddha's body in millions of circles,
planning to seize the Tathāgata to vent their slave feelings."
Then, our Buddha beneath the Bodhi tree,
with right mindfulness, thought: "All these heretics have arrived,
how should I prepare?"
Thereupon, he aroused the power of compassionate good roots,
and skillfully subdued the heretics,
without resorting to weapons of war,
nor troubling soldiers and horses.
The implements and weapons held by the Tathāgata
were entirely different from theirs.
He donned the armor of patience,
grasped the sword of wisdom,
bent the bow of meditation,
aimed the arrow of compassion,
mounted the steed of the ten powers,
and wielded the whip of diligence.
Before the sword of shame was even raised,
the demon generals were startled and panicked;
before the sword of wisdom was even swung,
Māra was afraid and fearful.
Those who breathed smoke and spat flame
were instead burned by their own fire;
those who carried rocks and lifted mountains
sank and fell by themselves.
The heretics' bows, when drawn, had strings that snapped,
arrows, when about to be shot, sprouted flowers,
spears, before being whirled, broke of themselves,
swords, before being swung, lost their blades,
thunder turned into Brahmā's sounds,
hailstones transformed into pearls.
Red banners appeared and vanished,
fragrant breezes arose of themselves,
fierce fires and black smoke
turned into sandalwood mist descending.
Our Buddha manifested his power of concentration,
the heretics and Māra had no means and were afraid.
The larger ones fled, lost in the fog,
the smaller ones fought, shaken within the clouds.
Seeing this, the Demon King
temporarily withdrew his army.
The Rākṣasas kowtowed,
crying out, 'We deserve death!'
Turning their weapons, they then departed,
returning to the demon palace,
their venom not yet gone,
still generating anger, and so on."
"The Demon King exhausted all his supernatural transformations,
but could not shake our Tathāgata.
Precious swords, when brandished, lost their blades,
bows, when drawn, had strings that snapped.
Lifting mountains and scooping seas, displaying supernatural powers,
square beams and rolling logs filled the empty sky.
Planning to harm the Tathāgata, lord of the three realms,
was like fallen leaves meeting the autumn wind.
The Demon King acted as supreme marshal,
but in fear and urgency, hid himself with nowhere to hide."
Then he personally issued commands before the army,
urgently withdrawing troops to return to the palace.
Not considering that they themselves were of the demonic kind,
they compared themselves to the great World-Honored One in heaven.
Although the Arhats are minor saints,
their strength rivals that of countless heavenly demons.
The ghosts and spirits,
in myriad forms,
exhausted their strength transforming like the Tathāgata.
No matter how many transformations you make in front,
the Tathāgata does not move a single hair.
Seeing the battle formation seemed lost,
the demon king withdrew his army
and returned to heaven.
Not recognizing his own inferior strength,
he still intended to harass and harm the Tathāgata.
His wrathful feelings
had not yet subsided.
Then he sat upright in the main hall,
leaning back against the incense bed,
clenching his wrist and raising his eyebrows,
his lips pursed in unbearable anger.
The demon king had three daughters,
who suddenly saw their father unhappy,
so they stepped forward and addressed the king:
"Recently, your appearance seems changed,
why are you so troubled and unhappy?
Is it because the heavenly beings are causing trouble?
Or is there unrest in the palace?
Or are you worried about affairs of the kingdom?
Or are you concerned about your daughters?"
We only wish our father would have compassion,
and now tell us the reason."
The king replied:
"It is not concern for my daughters,
you all have naturally grown up;
nor is it worry about affairs of the kingdom,
what worries could there be in the joyful heavenly palace!
It is because of Jìngfàn's Siddhārtha,
who recently attained perfect enlightenment.
It is unbearable to see him now in the world,
I fear he will convert all my followers.
If he is allowed to teach and convert,
he will convert all my disciples and followers.
What plan can I devise now,
to eliminate him and prevent him from appearing in the world?"
Then the three daughters stepped forward,
and addressed their father:
"Gautama spent his youth in the deep palace,
how could he resist the pleasures of sensual realms?
Moreover, he is young and handsome,
this is precisely the time for pursuing pleasure and joy.
We now wish to descend to Jambudvīpa,
to harass him and prevent him from attaining enlightenment.
We will surely make him retreat in heart,
and fail to achieve the supreme great bodhi."
Hearing this plan,
the demon king was extremely pleased.
From the treasury, silks and satins
were given to the maidens for adornment.
They combed their cicada-wing side locks,
slantingly inserted phoenix hairpins,
draped themselves in fine silks,
and wrapped their arms with jeweled necklaces.
The beauties of the eastern neighbors
truly could not compare;
the charming women of the southern lands
were clearly inferior.
Their jade-like faces resembled snow,
vainly boasting the beauty of Luòpǔ;
their rosy cheeks were like flowers,
idly speaking of the charms of Wūshān.
They moved like drifting clouds and rain,
capable of toppling cities and kingdoms.
They wore robes of five colors,
and garments of three zhū weight shone in the sun.
Heavenly maidens followed behind,
holding jeweled canopies to accompany them;
weaving maidens led the way,
fanning fragrant winds to fill the path.
Summoning the colorful maidens of the six palaces,
they were arranged on the left;
commanding the ladies of the kingdom,
they were placed on the right.
Directly from the upper realms,
they came before the Buddha.
Singing and dancing together,
pipes and strings competed in performance.
In sentiment, they were truly silken-clad beauties,
in appearance and demeanor, uniquely surpassing spring.
They wore heavenly palace garments of three zhū weight,
their feet treading on a piece of Wūshān cloud.
The first daughter said: "World-Honored One!
World-Honored One!
Human life in this world,
how long can it last?
If one does not seek glory and splendor,
one merely lives in vain.
My beauty,
is truly without equal.
I should not boast myself,
but such is rare in the human world.
Thus I have come to serve you,
vowing for a thousand years.
Do not reject my lowliness,
let me forever be your zither and lute."
(The daughter said):
"I advise you not to seek the great bodhi,
why must you stubbornly cling with a troubled heart?
I have left my loving parents to descend to this world,
willing to give myself to be your wife."
(The Buddha said):
"I now vow to attain the great bodhi,
preaching the Dharma to convert the deluded masses with my heart."
The second daughter said: "World-Honored One!
World-Honored One!
Of the golden-wheel royal lineage,
imperial sons and princely grandsons,
you have abandoned your royal position,
alone in the mountains in solitude.
My intention in coming here,
has no other purpose,
I wish to accompany you in the mountains,
sweeping the ground, burning incense, and fetching water.
When the World-Honored One is not present,
I can watch over the home and guard the dwelling."
(The daughter said):
"I love wearing silken garments,
without applying heavy musk, naturally fragrant.
I have left my loving parents to descend to this world,
vowing to sweep your golden bed with my delicate hands."
(The Buddha said):
"My every thought now is of impermanence,
where is there any place that does not burn incense?"
The third daughter said: "World-Honored One!
World-Honored One!
I am young in years,
especially cherished by my parents,
of peerless端正 appearance,
rare in intelligence.
Indra and Brahmā,
frequently came to inquire,
but my parents considered their status lowly,
and did not allow me to become a bride.
I see the World-Honored One is upright,
and also the son of King Jìngfàn,
complete in the three excellences and six arts,
fully equipped in both civil and military abilities.
Therefore I left my parents,
and came to Jambudvīpa below,
not daring to be the Buddha's wife,
but willing to forever hold your sitting mat."
(The daughter said):
"I, your servant, am fifteen springs old,
just like a lotus emerging from the water's edge.
Seeing you complete in both civil and military arts,
the six arts and three excellences surpassing the crowd.
I have left my loving parents to descend to this world,
not wishing to make myself a monastic teacher."
(The Buddha said):
"You should have long abandoned your female body,
only because of past obstacles to the Buddha's cause."
The demon daughters did not believe the World-Honored One's words,
uttering presumptuous arguments,
lightly troubling the Buddha.
Then the World-Honored One extended his golden arm,
pointed at the demon daughters' bodies,
and all three instantly transformed into old women.
Their eyes were like vermilion cups,
their faces like fire pots,
their foreheads broad and heads pointed,
chests high and noses crooked,
hair yellow and teeth black,
eyebrows white and mouths blue,
faces wrinkled like skin wrapped around skulls,
necks long like chopstick handles.
Their bodies' fine brocades
turned into two pieces of cloth skirts;
the combs and hairpins on their heads
became a tangled mass of snakes.
Their bodies hunched and necks shrunk,
just like freezing old owls;
waists bent and legs long,
like crickets past autumn.
Their entire bodies were objects of ridicule,
truly like corpses.
The three looked at each other,
their faces devoid of color.
Unconvinced in their hearts,
they took mirrors to look,
only leaving behind forms of a hundred uglinesses,
no longer seeing their thousand charms' appearance.
The three sisters
said these words:
"It was not heaven's doing,
all came from our own making of disaster.
Where have the lovely appearances gone?
Ugliness has come at this time.
Eyes blazing like fire within,
Wishing to return to the heavens above,
They were ashamed to show their ugly faces.
Three demon maidens,
Had transformed the appearance of Cháng'é,
Ashamed of their own hideous forms,
Too embarrassed to face the celestial palace,
They sought to return but could not.
Then they knelt before the Buddha,
And pleaded again and again.
At that moment,
What words did they speak?
Unaware of the deep karmic hindrances from past lives,
They came directly to the mortal realm to visit the twin groves.
For the sake of their parents' profound kindness and righteousness,
They did not expect the demonic power to be weak.
Disturbing the Tathāgata brought many karmic obstacles,
Their appearances changed, and they suffered resentment and sinking.
They only hoped that Śākyamuni would show compassion,
To forgive and not hold onto thoughts of resentment.
The Buddha's heart is vast with compassion,
He grants wishes and fulfills them,
Releasing them from past transgressions,
Allowing them to repent and atone.
Restoring their former beauty,
Even surpassing it;
Their graceful and lovely appearances returned,
More radiant than before.
Our Buddha's compassion is vast and his vows great,
For the Dharma, he manifests forms to spread it far and wide.
The three demon maidens displayed their charms,
Transforming their original upright appearances.
Earnestly they bowed and addressed the Tathāgata,
Temporarily abandoning the demon palace, their hearts turning to goodness.
The ugly maidens regained their proper forms,
Their verbal transgressions repented and forgiven.
The demon maidens regained their proper forms,
And returned to their original heavens.
As they were about to depart,
What words did they speak?
The demon maidens repented and returned to the heavens,
Overjoyed, they paid homage to the sages.
Thus, we know the Buddha's power extended to them,
The three sisters surpassed their former selves.
The maidens saw the demon king and spoke of their true feelings,
Speaking of the Tathāgata's attainment of the fruit of the Way.
All three of us have transformed,
How could we not return once more?
With sincere hearts, they bowed and sought repentance,
Only then were their appearances restored and their karmic hindrances lightened.
At this time, the World-Honored One attained perfect enlightenment,
And the demon king henceforth ceased his clamor.
Intending to speak,
But pausing for now,
Look, the sun sets in the west.
Before the Buddha's seat, receive the verses,
In the future, you shall surely sit upon the lotus.
But I, a direct descendant of the meditation river,
Strive diligently in my later cultivation.
Lacking the ability to guide and transform,
I mistakenly occupy a position of praise.
My body and mind tremble with anxiety,
How can I find peace in my fear and caution?
I hastily recount these rough words,
To express virtuous qualities.
Since the commander-in-chief pacified this region,
He continued the legacy of banners to assist the great Liáng.
His filial piety and benevolence surpass Shùn and Yǔ,
His civilizing strategies exceed Yīn and Tāng.
Dividing lands and worrying about all sides,
He toils late into the night for the sake of the realm.
The scriptures clearly state,
Guānyīn Bodhisattva manifests as a benevolent king.
Guānyīn appears in the form of an official,
The governor is solely the guardian of the state.
South of the Jade Pass, malignant energies are dispelled,
West of the Yellow River, smoke and dust settle.
Borders are restored as before,
Walls rebuilt, renewed and strengthened.
The sage ruler and wise ministers are transformed by the Bodhisattva,
All living beings become people of peace.
The ruler's virtue and ministers' wisdom spread across the four seas,
Barbarians turn to civilization, and turmoil subsides.
Neighboring states send envoys to make peace on all sides,
Sailing across the seas, reaching the highest heavens.
Greatly benefiting all beings with rain and dew,
Extensively spreading the Buddhist teachings, praising the flowers of Dharma.
This humble monk wishes to speak of the merits of the sutra,
And further pray for the commander-in-chief's longevity of ten thousand years.
One volume of "The Subjugation of Demons Transformation."
Written on the tenth day of the Yellow Bell month in the cyclical year Jiǎchén, the ninth year of Tiānfú, with cold condensation, exhaling to warm the brush while recording.
Written by Yuànróng, a Śramaṇa and Dharma Master of the Jìngtǔ Temple.
It is heard that when the Tathāgata expounds the Dharma,
it is as numerous as the countless sands of the Ganges;
when the Bodhisattvas transmit the scriptures,
it is across thousands upon thousands of worlds.
Beginning in the Deer Park,
he delivered the five companions;
finally, at the Twin Sāla Trees,
he subdued the ten Brahmanical ascetics.
Expounding subtle words, he calmed the waves of the river of craving;
discussing Prajñā, he toppled the mountain of afflictions.
He united the three points at the true source,
and purified the six dusts in the human realm.
Therefore, within the great city of Śrāvastī,
he arose with compassionate thoughts to deliver all beings;
in the garden of the Elder Anāthapiṇḍada,
he upheld the lamp of wisdom to transmit the seal of the Dharma.
The Tathāgata, donning his robe and holding his bowl,
strode forth in the early morning,
and when it was time for the meal,
he returned to his original place.
Begging for food cultivates the karma of great merit;
going in sequence demonstrates the compassion of equality;
washing the feet reveals the merit of upholding precepts;
spreading the seat is for calming the mind in meditation.
Then, humans and devas gazed up and gathered around,
while dragon spirits reverently and joyfully listened.
Subhūti, with dignified demeanor, emerged from the assembly,
adjusted his Dharma robes, and earnestly expressed his sincerity.
Wishing to initiate a discourse on signlessness,
he raised a question born of doubt.
Thus, he was called "rare" by the son,
and praised with "excellent" by the Buddha.
Thereupon, the profound gate was widely opened,
and the treasury of meaning was greatly revealed.
Those who hear the scripture are enabled to keep the four minds unwavering,
their five eyes shining brightly,
and the four fruits...
Dispelling the self and others, the three sages
attain to roam in the eightfold right path;
the self and others, the four marks,
are realized to be empty in their essential nature;
the six classes of sentient beings
all return to extinction.
The giving at the beginning, middle, and end cannot be considered abundant;
the extent of the ten directions' emptiness cannot be known.
All marks are no marks,
thus one sees the Dharma-body of the Tathāgata;
birth is non-birth,
attaining the equality of true and false.
Yet, even if one exhausts the seven treasures of the great thousand worlds,
compared to the four lines, it is entirely light;
afterwards, the beings of the five turbidities,
equal to one hearing, surpass the supreme realm.
Then, even the Dharma should be relinquished,
clinging to the raft leads instead to sinking.
Blending self and other in emptiness,
extinguishing right and wrong in marvelous existence.
Not stained by the realm of the six dusts,
one awakens to Bodhi.
Even when seeking through the six consciousnesses,
all phenomena are encompassed within Prajñā.
The Buddhas of the three times,
arise from this scripture;
the most sublime Bodhi,
emanates from this scripture.
Moreover, it encompasses all teachings,
acknowledged as the essential summary of all scriptures.
Transmitted and translated into China,
for over several hundred years.
Although it has been recited and circulated widely,
with commentaries and subcommentaries proliferating,
there remains fear that the meaning may not accord with the sage's mind,
or the principle may deviate from the Middle Way.
I humbly consider our great Táng Hàn sage sovereign, the Kāiyuán Tiānbǎo Shèngwén Shénwǔ Yìngdào Huángdì Bìxià,
whose transformation surpasses the ancient past,
whose reputation exceeds that of a hundred kings.
In literature, he encompasses the subtleties of the five classics;
in martial prowess, he subdues the courage of the nine barbarian tribes.
The eight directions are unified under his non-active transformation,
the four quarters sing of the customs of Yáo and Shùn.
Moreover, in the wake of his harmonious influence,
he constantly promotes the three teachings.
Sometimes exploring Confucianism and Daoism,
exhausting their nature and probing their origins;
annotating and interpreting the Buddhist tradition,
his sentences are profound and far-reaching.
The sage's grace surges like the sea and springs;
the heavenly palace is as bright as the sun and moon.
Because of this, the Daoist teaching is revitalized,
and the Buddha-sun shines brightly once again.
Upon the treasure grove,
the palm leaves joyfully vie to unfold;
within the garden of Dhāraṇī,
the Dharma-clouds richly moisten.
Now, the title heading "The Diamond Prajñā Pāramitā Sūtra":
"Diamond" is a metaphor for hardness and sharpness;
"Prajñā" is designated as wisdom;
"Pāra" is the other shore,
arriving is broadly named "Pāramitā";
"Sūtra" means stringing together as its meaning.
It is the model of good governance,
hence named "The Diamond Prajñā Pāramitā Sūtra".
The Greatly Awakened World-Honored One, in the Jetavana garden of Anāthapiṇḍada in Śrāvastī,
proclaimed this scripture,
opening our secret treasury.
The fourfold assembly surrounded him,
hosts of immortals protected and upheld him,
heaven rained down the four flowers,
clouds cleared the eight directions.
Such is the marvelous power of the Tathāgata,
difficult to describe in words!
Sudatta was charitable and kind by nature,
fond of giving aid to the orphaned and poor,
therefore he was named Anāthapiṇḍada due to his conduct.
Spreading gold to purchase land,
he built a monastery,
invited the Buddha and extended hospitality to the monks,
thus his name is recorded within the scripture.
Jeta, observing his reverence for the Dharma,
donated trees to jointly establish it,
but because the sovereign is weighty and the minister light,
the order of naming reflects priority.
The complete details of the events
are narrated below.
In the past, there was a great kingdom in Southern India,
named Shèwèichéng.
Its king’s might shook the nine heavens,
his influence spread to the eight directions,
the three borders were calm,
and the four frontiers were clear of dust.
The worthy prime minister who assisted the state was named Xūduōduō,
skilled in strategy within his heart,
and perceptive of the opportunities of his time.
People called him the pillar of the state,
his virtue as valued as salt and plum.
Yet he always harbored heretical views,
and did not revere the Three Jewels.
He did not crave glory or position,
but aspired to cultivate himself with diligence.
He had several sons at home,
the youngest of whom was not yet married.
During a festive occasion,
he suddenly thought to himself: “Now my household lacks nothing,
and I am honored within the kingdom.
My youngest son is of marriageable age,
and it is proper to arrange a wedding in due time.
If there is no suitable match in our own kingdom,
we shall send envoys to foreign lands to seek one.”
That day, he instructed his household,
and had them open the treasury,
taking a thousand taels of gold,
several rings of white jade,
soft brocades and light silks,
thousands upon tens of thousands of bolts,
a hundred strong elephants,
and set out on the journey that very day.
“You must accomplish the task ahead,
travel day and night without delay,
with success as the limit,
spare no expense.
Just satisfy my son’s heart’s desire,
and upon your return, you shall be richly rewarded!”
After bidding farewell,
they assented and departed immediately.
Traveling day and night,
they soon reached their destination.
They roamed the streets and alleys,
listening attentively with keen interest.
During their journey,
they happened to encounter Ānán begging for alms.
Having never seen such a sight before,
they were astonished beyond measure.
Holding a staff and a bowl,
he called out loudly for alms.
Hùmí’s household upheld the ten virtues,
and often personally invited Buddhist monks;
young and old were of one mind,
all revering the Three Jewels.
Though the young lady stayed within the women’s quarters,
she suddenly heard the sound of alms-begging,
and out of deep respect,
she rushed out beyond the gate,
prostrated herself with five limbs touching the ground,
and paid homage to Ānán.
She inquired about the hardships of his missionary work,
and expressed her reverence for the Buddha’s benevolence.
The envoy, peering from behind the wall,
saw her extraordinary beauty,
which even Xīshī could not match in grace,
nor could the goddess of the Luò River rival her splendor.
He wanted to gaze directly,
but feared breaching etiquette;
so he slowly stepped back,
and calmly asked a neighbor: “Whose residence is this?
The woods are dense and lush,
with a grand gate in front,
and long spears displayed outside.
Jade towers and precious pavilions,
resemble a royal palace;
with singing halls and pond terraces,
quite different from commoners’ homes.”
The neighbor said: “Have you not heard of the prime minister who assists the state,
named Hùmí?
He assists in governing the court,
and receives a daily salary of ten thousand coins.
Apart from the king,
he is the second most honored,
and in matters of state policy,
he is consulted on every detail.”
Hearing this, the envoy
was startled and awed,
and asked the neighbor further: “I am most fortunate
to have met someone as virtuous as you.
I wonder how many children
the prime minister’s family has?
I am a visitor from afar,
sent here on a mission;
please do not hesitate to tell me,
and briefly describe the affairs of the prime minister’s household.”
The neighbor said: “The prime minister has
three daughters in total: two are already married to royal grandsons,
and one remains unmarried.
Her beauty is exceptional,
unmatched in the kingdom,
her demeanor elegant and virtuous,
unparalleled in past or present.”
Hearing this, the envoy
was overjoyed and relieved,
and immediately sent word,
delivering a letter.
The envoy was then ushered in,
and paid his respects with greetings.
Before expressing his heartfelt intentions,
he first exchanged pleasantries about the weather.
As host and guest, they observed formalities,
and feasted for several days;
but regarding the marriage proposal,
he had not yet received consent.
Suddenly one night, the elder
and his household bustled about,
sweeping and cleaning the halls and rooms,
tidying the courtyards and grounds,
applying fragrant mud for decoration,
with exquisite and rare adornments.
Banners were hung around every courtyard wall,
and every room was spread with carpets and cushions.
Xūduōduō, seeing them rise early,
and restless in sleep;
and observing the elaborate preparations,
was puzzled and asked the reason: “Is it for a gathering of relatives?
Or to entertain the emperor?
Why is the whole household in such haste,
making such splendid arrangements?”
The elder said: “It is neither for a gathering of relatives,
nor to entertain the emperor.
I intend to invite the Buddha and the monks,
and make offerings with sincere devotion.”
Xūduōduō had long cultivated good habits,
and had once been close to Buddhist monks;
hearing the Buddha’s name suddenly,
sweat poured from his body like fine rain.
Xūduōduō asked: “What divine wonders does the Buddha possess?
What virtues and abilities do the monks have?
That upon hearing their names,
I break into a cold sweat?
Where do they reside?
Please tell me in detail.
I regret having long followed heretical paths,
and not knowing the true way.
Now I deeply yearn to learn,
and wish to hear the origins.”
Hùmí said: “The Buddha is no ordinary man;
he is the son of King Jìngfàn of Jiāpíluóchéng.
His ancestors in succession
ruled with the golden wheel of a thousand ages;
generations of honor,
descendants of phoenixes.”
Hearing this, Xūduōduō
was astonished and awestruck,
his yearning and reverence
firmly rooted in his heart.
He wished to visit the place,
and behold the venerable countenance.
Hùmí replied to the elder: “The Buddha is not far away,
he is at Qíshéjuéshān,
leading the eight divisions of dragons and devas,
expounding the principles of the three vehicles.
It is already night now,
but going tomorrow morning will not be too late.”
Hearing of the Buddha’s virtues and abilities, the elder
could not rest peacefully,
earnestly yearning and revering,
fixing his thoughts on the compassionate one.
The Tathāgata, seeing his sincere devotion,
emitted a ray of light that illuminated everything,
making heaven and earth bright as day,
like the radiance of a thousand suns.
Xūduōduō, seeing the light suddenly,
thought it was dawn,
and followed the light straight to the city gate,
which was still locked.
Xūduōduō then realized the Buddha’s power,
and his reverence doubled,
thinking of the Tathāgata,
he sighed deeply and lamented:
Lofty towers rise high, gates shut tight below,
the path at quiet night blocks the way to and fro.
Longing to see the venerable face, yet not in sight,
hesitating, gazing afar, strength fails to climb the height.
Often regretting born in a land of heretical views,
not yet struck by the wisdom mallet that falsehoods brews.
May the compassionate one deign to guide and lead,
with focused heart I wait to bow before the noble deed.
After Sudatta had finished his sigh,
the Tathāgata, with his divine ear, heard from afar,
and with his mind-reading ability, knew immediately,
with no obstruction across ten thousand miles.
He also emitted divine light to illuminate,
and the city gate suddenly opened by itself.
Seeing the gate open,
Sudatta followed the light straight to the Buddha’s place,
circling around dozens of times,
exhausting his focused and sincere heart,
fixing his gaze to behold the revered face,
where joy and sorrow intermingled—how to describe it?
Sudatta, upon hearing the Buddha, had his mind enlightened,
and tears fell from his eyes in thousands of streams.
"This disciple was born in a land of heretical views,
all day accumulating sins in service to Māra.
I humbly beseech the Heavenly Teacher to accept my invitation,
descend to bless Śrāvastī and serve as a bridge."
The Buddha knew his virtuous roots were mature,
fit to be transformed and easily guided,
so he complied and accepted,
agreeing to his request.
He called out, saying, "Elder:
I am the lord of the three realms,
the most supreme and honored.
My movements are calm and dignified,
with heavenly dragons as attendants and guards,
Brahmā on the left,
Śakra leading in front,
heavenly immortals filling the empty sky,
and the fourfold assembly rushing like clouds along the roads.
It is necessary to widely construct halls and pagodas,
and build many chambers and rooms.
My disciples are now numerous,
and their dwelling places are cramped and small.
You have also long followed heretical paths,
and do not know the proper rituals.
Take my Śāriputra with you,
and ask him about each and every rule and form."
Having received the Buddha’s consent to his invitation,
and now accompanied by the sage,
Sudatta selected two strong elephants,
upon which he set up pavilions,
and within a few days,
arrived at the city of Śrāvastī.
Together with the sage,
he surveyed the land for a monastery.
First, going east of the city,
he saw from afar a garden,
with abundant flowers and fruits,
and very fine ponds and pavilions.
Sudatta urged his horse forward,
and asked the monk, 'Is this garden suitable?'
Śāriputra said to the elder,
'Though the garden is good,
there is too much garlic,
its foul stench reaches the heavens,
and sages and worthies cannot dwell here.'
Sudatta turned the elephant around,
and went to the west of the city,
where, raising his eyes, he suddenly saw a garden,
with trees far surpassing the previous one.
Sudatta composed himself, joined his hands,
and asked the monk, 'Since the previous one was deemed unsuitable,
is this garden fit for dwelling or not?'
Śāriputra said to the elder,
'This place was once a horse market,
where many beings were slaughtered,
foul with blood and stench,
and truly unfit for dwelling.'
Pulling the reins, he turned the carriage,
and went to the north of the city,
where he saw another garden,
with lush and flourishing trees.
He asked the monk, 'Is this garden suitable?'
Śāriputra said to the elder,
'Though the garden is good,
and the trees are dense,
there are many taverns and houses of debauchery,
increasing the delusion of beings,
nourishing the root of the sea of suffering.
This place is unsuitable,
we must choose elsewhere.'
The elder had toured three places,
and the venerable one had declared all unsuitable.
The Buddha had no affinity with these lands,
perhaps due to many lifetimes of karmic obstacles.
Sudatta, ashamed and restless,
uneasy beyond measure,
turned the carriage in frustration,
and went out to survey the south of the city.
Not too far from the city,
clearly visible along the road,
he suddenly saw a garden,
with bamboo and trees unusually lush.
In the third month of spring and the ninth of summer,
the scenery was fragrant and fresh;
at the end of winter and beginning of autumn,
the fading flowers were still luxuriant.
The grass was green and emitted verdure,
the flowers shone brilliantly and bloomed red.
There were a thousand kinds of ponds and pavilions,
and ten thousand varieties of fruits and herbs.
Fragrance wafted and assailed the nose,
birds chattered noisily and sang in harmony.
The trees stirred, proclaiming the name of the Three Jewels;
divine bells resounded with the sound of ending suffering.
Auspicious phoenixes and lucky luan birds
vied to display the splendor of their brocade-like feathers;
jade maidens and immortal boys
competed in playing music of eternal life.
Seeing this garden,
the elder was deeply pleased in his heart,
so he composed himself
and asked the monk, 'The previous three places
were all deemed unsuitable;
now, this garden—does it meet our wishes or not?'
Śāriputra said to the elder,
'I am of small fruit,
my spiritual power is humble.
Wait for me to enter meditation and observe,
then we can know its goodness or evil.'
Śāriputra gathered his mind and entered meditation,
collecting his thoughts for a moment,
observed this garden and pavilion,
and found it entirely without fault.
Hundreds of thousands of past buddhas
had all dwelt here,
preaching the Dharma and liberating people,
countless as the sands of the Ganges.
Seeing this,
Śāriputra was overjoyed in body and mind,
smiled and relaxed his expression,
and replied to the elder, 'This garden is not only fit for our teacher in this lifetime,
but a thousand Tathāgatas of the present fortunate eon
have all dwelt here.
It is the most auspicious and supreme,
and nothing surpasses it.
To build a monastery,
only this land will do.'
How did Śāriputra and the elder deliberate?
The elder, having received the sage’s protection,
had all his deluded thoughts completely enlightened.
Śāriputra accompanied him to establish the place of practice,
intending to invite the Tathāgata to expound the four-line verse.
Having toured three sides of the city and found none suitable for dwelling,
the elder was troubled and hesitant in heart.
Riding the elephant, he pondered as he went forward,
and suddenly saw a garden with lush flowers and fruits.
Sudatta and Śāriputra rode the white elephant,
turned and looked toward the south of the city.
Suddenly they saw several thousand jeweled trees,
with flowers blooming in extraordinary colors, unmatched.
Auspicious clouds and canopies filled the empty sky,
white phoenixes and blue luan birds soared in the air.
Sudatta sighed in great wonder,
gazed at the revered face and asked the monk.
Śāriputra turned his head and replied to Sudatta,
'This garden is exquisite and rare, hard to encounter.
Sacred bells manifest among the trees,
heavenly immortals in the sky hold offerings.
Past buddhas first dwelled here in peace,
liberating beings beyond count.
Clearly knowing the inconceivable power of the sage,
this is where the Tathāgata preaches the Dharma.'
Hearing this, Sudatta was greatly astonished and doubtful:
'Looking at this garden, it is rare within the country.
I do not know who the original owner is,
how can I buy it by any means?
Good things in the world are loved by all,
it is very hard to expect someone not to sell.'
For a long time he pondered, displeased,
his heart uneasy and ashamed.
He called the gardener to ask:
'Who is the owner of the garden now?
I have urgent business and must meet him,
quickly tell me in full without delay.'
The gardener joined his hands and explained in detail:
'The garden owner is wealthy and noble, not ordinary.
He is currently the crown prince of the eastern palace,
and comes every day to see it himself.
Xūdá addressed the monk, saying: “Is this garden suitable?”
Śāriputra said to the elder: “Not only does my original teacher, Shìjiāmóuní, delight in this place,
but also the countless Buddhas of the past
have dwelt here.
Those heavily defiled,
treading this ground, become pure.
Divine bells and heavenly music,
without being struck, constantly sound;
rare fragrances and celestial flowers
vie in profusion, falling in disarray.
Venerable sir, please return to your place for now,
while your disciple temporarily goes to the Eastern Palace
to pay respects and inquire,
to see if it can be obtained or not?
If they are willing to sell,
we will not haggle over the price, high or low;
if they stubbornly refuse,
we must skillfully find a way to persuade them.
By a thousand schemes and ten thousand plans,
we must not rest until it is done.
Xūdá took his leave and set off,
going straight to the gate of the Eastern Palace.
He entered at an unusual hour,
going directly to see the crown prince.
The crown prince, seeing the important minister from afar,
immediately descended the steps to welcome him.
The crown prince said: “You are a minister of state who assists the ruler;
why, in all the affairs of my lord,
for what urgent matter
do you suddenly seek an audience with me at this unusual hour?”
Xūdá wished to speak directly,
but found it somewhat difficult to begin;
so he temporarily devised a deceitful tale,
replying to the crown prince: “Yesterday, while traveling,
I happened to come to Your Highness’s garden,
and from afar saw ominous disasters arising in contention,
and strange birds flocking and crying.
I then halted my horse to observe,
and suddenly felt my spirit tremble with fear.
The ponds and pavilions were withered and dry,
the flowers and fruits sparse and凋零.
If Your Highness does not believe my words,
send an envoy to observe the truth of the matter.
” The crown prince, hearing this,
was not greatly alarmed.
“Since I purchased this garden,
many years have passed.
In the third month of spring, the supple willows
are surrounded by green翠 and hang with branches;
in the height of summer, famous flowers
shine brilliantly throughout the ponds and pavilions.
They are fully capable of dispelling sorrow and relieving melancholy,
delighting the heart and refreshing the spirit.
That you now suddenly utter such words—
is it not deceptive and false?”
Xūdá adjusted his demeanor,
and addressed the crown prince: “Your Highness is most exalted and noble,
the crown prince of the state.
Your humble servant serves at the jade steps,
as arms and legs to the royal house.
How could I dare to deceive and mislead?
What difference would lying make?
If there were the slightest discrepancy,
how could I, your servant, remain whole?
If Your Highness does not believe,
deign to go in person to observe,
verify the truth of the matter,
and thus manifest your servant’s loyalty and integrity.
” The crown prince said: “You are a loyal minister;
you must not be false and crafty.
If this matter is truly so,
how can it be averted and remedied?”
Xūdá addressed the crown prince: “If an object causes anomalies,
it must be sold to another.
Your Highness should post notices at the four gates,
announcing that the garden is for sale.
The mouths of the multitude can melt metal;
the calamity and inauspiciousness will naturally dissipate.
If someone intends to buy,
demand an exorbitant price: the flat ground spread with黄金,
the tree branches filled with silver coins.
Since people treasure wealth,
surely there will be no one willing to buy.
” The crown prince, hearing this,
complied and agreed.
That very day, he posted notices
at the four gates of the city.
Xūdá’s secret plan now accomplished,
he took leave of the crown prince.
Then, at the four gates,
he took down the notices and brought them,
went straight into the Eastern Palace,
to see the crown prince.
The crown prince, indignant at this matter,
mounted his horse and left the city,
going in person to observe.
Accompanied by Xūdá,
they went straight to the garden.
Looking all around,
it was no different from before;
gazing in all four directions,
there were no strange anomalies.
Inquiring of the garden’s caretakers,
there had been no changes at all.
The crown prince then grew angry,
and sternly rebuked Minister Xūdá: “You now conspire against the state,
intending to collude with foreign countries,
inciting ruler and minister,
sowing discord between father and son.
The ruin of families and loss of the state
would surely be because of you!
As for the gentleman,
at home he fulfills filial piety,
in service to the state he fulfills loyalty,
conducts himself with reverence and caution,
is frugal and follows the laws.
Thus he preserves his emolument and position,
and ends his life in wealth and honor.
How can a minister be disloyal,
utter words lacking in trustworthiness?
Not only does he bring calamity upon himself and invite disaster,
he also brings shame upon his ancestors.
If I report to the heavenly grace,
you will be left with no place to hide.
Rise and fall, glory and disgrace,
lie only in a breath’s time.
Though face to face, a thousand miles apart;
undeservedly occupying a position of honor,
drawing salary without merit—
this is what you are now.
I shall report to the heavenly court,
and you will suffer ten thousand executions!”
At that time, for the sake of the Dharma, he defied emotion,
unafraid of losing his life.
Ruler and minister both contended,
each intending to see the king.
The god Śuddhāvāsa, hearing their words from the sky,
thought to himself: “If I do not admonish these men,
this good deed will surely encounter obstacles.
” Concealing his divine form,
he transformed into an old man,
with white hair and beard,
leaning on a weak staff,
he went straight before the crown prince’s horse,
and called out loudly ahead: “Stop,
young master!
Good and evil have their reasons;
why use clamorous dispute?
High and low each have their propriety;
noble and base must observe the rules.
How can you block streets and截 lanes,
breathing angrily and raising your voices!
Each state your original intent;
in reasoning, you must rely on truth.
Even the Son of Heaven serves the three elders;
in ancient times, the aged were cared for and their words sought.
Do not rely on false and fabricated words
to disturb the public authority.
This old body will judge fairly,
hoping certainly to reach an impartial verdict.
” The crown prince dismounted,
indignant at the deception,
and recounted the origins in detail,
stating his case to the old man.
The old man, hearing this,
sternly rebuked Minister Xūdá,
listing a thousand kinds of transgressions,
hundreds of faults,
glaring with angry eyes,
scolding Minister Xūdá,
to dispel the crown prince’s anger,
and prevent obstacles to the good deed. How was it?
The crown prince, seeing the garden free of disasters and anomalies,
knew immediately that Xūdá had spoken deceitfully.
“You, a loyal minister, utter false words,
skillfully trying to trick me out of my garden.
I shall draft a memorial to the king for his decision,
and in a moment, beheaded, your life will not be spared.
Before the two had finished disputing,
midway they suddenly met Śuddhāvāsa.
His face, once ruddy, now had a thousand wrinkles,
cold tears in his eyes like a spring.
Leaning on a thousand-year灵寿杖,
trembling, he came to meet the crown prince.
“This is the place for the crown prince’s banquets;
a short distance, not far from the heavenly countenance.
The gentleman truly should contend with virtue;
the wise do not need clamorous speech.
If there is a matter, tell it all to this old man;
I will judge fairly and not allow bias.
The crown prince clasped his hands and addressed the elder: “Please listen briefly to my explanation, do not be angry.
I, though only the crown prince,
when coming and going, half my retinue always accompanies me.
Minister Xūdá has shallow wisdom,
and does not uphold the duty between ruler and minister, high and low.
Without cause, he devises deceitful schemes and hidden plots,
skillfully intending to raise the ambition of usurping the state.
I humbly hope that you, venerable elder, will consider and see clearly,
Who among those who recklessly speak of calamities and auspices is not like this?"
The old man, hearing this, pressed his voice in anger: "Recently I have heard that you are a loyal minister,
But your words are inconsistent and unreliable,
Falsely benefiting from the state's governance while oppressing the common people.
Why must you recklessly speak of calamities and auspices arising?
Your deceitful nature is impure in conduct.
Based on this crime, it is difficult to forgive your transgressions,
If the king knew, you would be cut in half and reduced to dust."
The old man, with a gentle expression, said to the crown prince: "When a ruler speaks, his words should not be contradictory.
It is better to set a high price that is hard to meet,
Than to say you will sell and then refuse, going against others' expectations.
I, an old man, have seen many things in my time,
And I speak frankly to advise fairness and reason.
From now on, let there be harmony and no more disputes,
Let ruler and minister serve each other well (in mutual respect)."
Xūdá addressed the old man: "Can one hand clap alone?
It takes two hands striking together to make a sound.
A single word can bring ruin to a state,
For error lies within a hair's breadth.
In ancient times, a single promise,
Was valued more than a thousand pieces of gold and remained unshaken.
To speak is easier than turning one's hand,
But to retract one's words is harder than moving a mountain.
How can one's earlier words not match what is said later!
The crown prince issued a proclamation,
Declaring he would sell the garden,
But when it came to discussing the terms,
He immediately said he would not sell."
The old man's original intention,
Was to favor Minister Xūdá,
But to comply with the crown prince's wishes,
He pretended to gnash his teeth in anger at Xūdá.
Xūdá, in his anxious state,
Stepped back several paces,
Then bowed to the crown prince and stepped forward: "Though I am but a humble subject,
I am not yet of the age of understanding (sixty).
A gentleman serves even at the age of fifty,
As the Master inquired in the Grand Temple.
A household relies on the eldest son,
A state depends on loyal ministers.
A boat moves because of water,
Lips and teeth rely on each other.
When lips are parted and teeth exposed,
When water dries up, the boat stops.
If a ruler lacks ministers,
On what can the state rely for stability?
It is well known that going against reason and lightly provoking,
Only leads to private harmony through compliance.
A harmonious household can nurture winter silkworms,
Advancement and retreat must both follow propriety.
The crown prince's garden is surely vast,
With dense and abundant trees,
If the ground were covered with gold,
And silver coins hung from every branch,
Even if you emptied the granaries and exhausted the treasury,
There would still be no time when anyone would be willing to buy it.
If the transaction does not succeed,
The garden will remain as it is."
The crown prince, hearing these words,
Followed the advice,
And thus said to Minister Xūdá,
Demanding this impossibly high price.
Xūdá complied immediately and obediently,
Without any hesitation,
Right there they discussed face to face,
And on the spot drew up the contract.
With many guarantors,
And heavy penalties for reneging.
Fearing the crown prince might change his mind,
And thwart his original intention.
Immediately he opened the treasury,
And brought out purple refined gold.
Selecting a hundred strong elephants,
To carry and deliver it.
But by the power of the sage's blessing,
In a moment it was nearly complete.
Only a few paces remained,
And it was almost entirely covered.
How was the gold-laying scene?
Xūdá, having received the old man's judgment,
Knew to match his expression to his true intent.
He then selected strong elephants from among them,
Opened the treasury and loaded them with pure purple refined gold.
High ridges and steep peaks were all arranged,
Perfectly distributed without room for a needle.
All family members, noble and humble,
Chanted the sound of Mahāprajñā.
In an instant, it was fully laid out,
The power of the sage, truly profound, was clearly known.
Xūdá had nearly finished laying the gold,
Only a small amount of work remained,
But in his heart he pondered anxiously,
Wondering which treasury to open next.
While he was deep in thought,
The crown prince grew suspicious,
And addressed the elder: "If your heart hesitates,
It is not too late to regret,
But why have you stopped the work,
When you had already begun?"
Xūdá said: "Even if I had to lay out my own flesh and blood,
I would not shirk the labor;
How much less would I dare to be stingy
With mere trivial wealth before the Buddha!
The Buddha's era is hard to encounter,
Meeting him once through countless kalpas.
If I do not strive with utmost sincerity,
What use will regret be later!"
The crown prince said: "You now treat wealth as dirt,
And value virtue as treasure,
But with such determination to buy the garden,
What purpose do you intend?"
Xūdá said: "What I am buying now
Serves another purpose.
Recently, due to a marriage alliance, I was fortunate to meet
And encounter the Great Sage.
His father is called Shuddhodana,
His mother is named Māyā,
He awakened spontaneously,
Without a teacher among humans or gods,
He is known as the Self-Enlightened One.
His body is sixteen feet tall,
With a halo around his head and back,
Like the radiance of a thousand suns,
Hard to compare with anything else.
He can also shake heaven and earth,
Yet keep all beings safe and peaceful.
He can move mountains and rivers,
Without any sense of coming or going;
He can swallow wind and inhale fire,
Without the slightest harm to his body.
When danger and calamity press upon you,
Calling his name brings immediate relief.
I now roughly describe his virtues,
Speaking only in brief.
To fully extol the Great Sage's abilities,
Would take countless kalpas and never be exhausted."
The crown prince, hearing this,
Trembled and broke into a sweat.
"If he truly possesses such great virtue,
I deeply wish to pay him homage.
The remaining uncovered area,
Please cease the work;
The silver coins on the trees,
I will also donate."
The ruler led and the minister followed,
Perfectly matching the principles of harmony;
Seeing the virtuous and aspiring to emulate them,
Accords with the teachings of the ancient sages.
With united hearts and minds,
They together built the monastery.
Is this not like a boat relying on water,
And neighboring boats helping each other?
Having pondered this,
He then accompanied Śāriputra,
Measuring the land east and west,
Surveying north and south.
Suddenly they came upon a nest of ants,
Crawling densely all over the ground,
In numbers beyond count.
Śāriputra, seeing these ants,
Smiled and relaxed his expression,
And explained to Xūdá and Jeta the causes from past lives:
Xūdá had bought the crown prince's garden,
His body and mind leaping with joy unceasing.
He then invited Śāriputra into the garden,
To measure the land by pacing and observe its extent.
Before they had finished surveying east and west,
They suddenly encountered a nest of ants.
Śāriputra turned and said to Xūdá: "Look at these beings of evil karma,
From the time of Buddha Vipaśyin's appearance,
They have long been born here as ants.
Today they again encounter Śākyamuni,
This time their evil conditions should be abandoned.
They will receive the ten precepts and take the three refuges,
And be bestowed the nectar of bodhi water.
From now on they will forever leave behind
Their rebirth among the heavenly hosts."
The elder resolved to build the monastery,
With lecture halls and courtyards all fully prepared.
In Tuṣita Heaven the music resounded,
From afar they saw their bodies reborn there.
Having finished laying the gold, they gazed with reverence,
Urgently needing to construct the monastery's design.
Sparing no precious treasures, gold or silver,
They posted notices summoning skilled craftsmen from across the land.
At the triple gate tower, vajra guardians were sculpted,
In every courtyard, painted images were made.
Side towers, meditation halls, and cloisters,
Even seeing them could remove calamities and obstacles.
Lutes and zithers hung at the four corners,
The wind blowing through produced myriad clear sounds.
There were also flutes, pipes, and konghous,
Cymbals, pipas, and paired chimes.
The high seat for preaching the Dharma was adorned with jewels,
Incense burners offered ox-head sandalwood as offerings.
The nine grades of rebirth according to one's wishes,
The kalaviṅka birds soar through the sky.
The elder devoutly builds a pure abode,
Buddhas and bodhisattvas gaze from the heavens.
Prince Jītā resolves with great determination,
Wishing for the Bodhi sprout to gradually grow.
After Sudatta completed the purchase of the garden,
He and the prince then returned.
Suddenly, on the way,
They encountered the six heretical teachers.
Without inquiring into the details,
They glared angrily at the sight: “The prince is the heir to the kingdom,
His travels should be accompanied by a grand procession;
The elder holds the honored position of prime minister,
A minister who assists in governing the state.
How can you disgrace the state and belittle yourselves,
With attendants numbering no more than ten riders?
Though Yao’s rafters were left unhewn,
It was to promote the reputation of frugality;
Though Shun’s cooking pots lacked rich flavors,
It was to curb the dangers of extravagance.
Moreover, long tassels and wide sleeves
Enhance the majesty of a powerful state;
Golden pillars and jade steps
Display the honor of former kings.
These are recorded in the *Book of Songs* and *Book of Documents*,
Not merely personal opinions.
Why then are your belongings so hurried,
And your persons so lightly attended?
Is it to plot against the state?
Or perhaps there are other intentions?
This matter must be reported to the king,
To seek his judgment and decree.” Now observe how the matter is explained when questioned:
“The prince is second in honor in the kingdom,
His comings and goings must be prepared by all officials.
Why are his riders no more than ten,
Riding hastily to this place?
Tell me truthfully,
Do not hide the good or the bad.”
The prince dismounted and replied to the revered teacher: “You are unaware that Sudatta has bought a garden.
We intend to invite the Tathāgata to preach here,
For I sincerely admire and wish to take refuge.
Having just overseen the gold-laying, the matter is settled,
And so we are now returning.
These words are all true,
I bare my heart and liver, hoping you will understand.”
The six teachers laughed uncontrollably upon hearing this,
“Gautama’s illusions are hardly worth comparing.
With sweet words and honeyed tongues, he deceives people,
His mother died just seven days after his birth.
Unable to endure the jade halls and towers,
He abandoned his father and fled to the deep mountains.
The words he speaks are called scriptures,
He praises himself as uniquely golden.
If he comes to this state, he will harm the common people,
We cannot open our eyes and let him trample us.
Tomorrow morning we will submit a memorial to the king,
The merits and faults must be tested before the throne.
Do not rashly compare ox-nose slobber
To my vast rivers and seas!”
Upon hearing the invitation for the Buddha to reside here,
The six teachers grew furious,
Their cheeks puffed up high,
Their eyebrows fiercely raised,
Gnashing their teeth,
Extremely bitter and resentful.
“Better to risk death once
Than to live in vain twice.
My disciples have all been deceived,
Leaving me no path to survival.
Everywhere I am bullied,
All day long they treat me with contempt.
Even emperors bow to him,
How much more so ordinary folk.
To whom shall I now voice my grievances?
I must lay my complaint before the king.”
The six teachers hurried anxiously,
Striding roughly with great steps,
Rushing to the dragon court,
To strike the grievance drum.
The king dispatched officials
To inquire into the matter.
The six teachers choked, their voices hoarse,
Remaining silent for a long while.
Then they addressed the king: “Your Majesty, I have heard that since the creation of heaven and earth,
There have been rulers and subjects.
The sun and moon shine brightly,
Relying on the sage ruler’s transformative influence.
Now the eight directions are sincere,
And the four seas come as guests.
Only rebellious sons and traitorous ministers
Plot against the king’s governance,
Harboring wickedness and flattery,
Disregarding public opinion.
They undeservedly hold the honor of prime minister,
Vainly consuming ten thousand measures of salary.
I have heard that treacherous ministers destroyed six states,
And treacherous wives turned six relatives against each other;
Sudatta and Jītā
Are precisely such today.
How could they, without informing the heavenly court,
Summon foreign barbarian gods?
Deceiving the common people,
He calls himself Buddha.
He does not honor his parents,
Constantly neglecting the duty of filial care.
He does not revere the king,
Violating the rites of a subject.
He does not diligently pursue livelihood,
But shaves heads upon meeting people.
He falsely speaks of hell and heaven,
With no one having witnessed their roots.
If he comes here,
I fear it will harm the state and ruin families.
I now bare my heart and liver,
Hoping Your Majesty’s sage wisdom will examine this.” Now observe how the accusation against the Tathāgata is explained:
“The royal prince, honored in the state,
Should not summon foreign barbarian gods.
The traitorous minister Sudatta leads the way,
Stirring up falsehoods to confuse the true.
Simply because Gautama excels in illusions,
He shows no loyalty or filial piety to the ruler.
The king does not bow to his parents,
Disrespecting the noble while honoring fools.
I beg Your Majesty to open the precious mirror,
And let its light shine upon me today.”
The six teachers pleaded again,
Bowing with bent back and lowered head: “The supernatural powers we have attained
Have been accumulated over many years.
A thousand wondrous manifestations appear,
The whole state knows our abilities.
Reflect on our merits,
Each learned from our teachers.
Today I report to the king,
Hoping for heavenly grace and protection.”
The six teachers addressed the king again: “I now speak truthfully of the matter.
Traitorous ministers and rebellious sons plot in secret,
Fearing the state will be ruined and people destroyed.
Sudatta’s original intent is to invite barbarian gods,
Planning to spread evil throughout the city.
They ruin our inconceivable true Dharma,
Inviting vile and inferior wickedness from afar.
This is depraved and unworthy of reliance,
I beg the wise ruler to examine this.”
The king said: “Monks,
Listen carefully,
Do not be anxious.
I will investigate the root cause,
And examine the facts.
If there is any error in judgment,
Both shall face ten thousand deaths.”
The king’s officials
Captured Sudatta alive,
Along with Prince Jītā,
Surrounding them with punitive staves.
Now observe how they are questioned while standing:
The king asked: “Sudatta, for what reason
Did you rashly buy a garden to build a temple?
Intending to invite Gautama here,
The six teachers say disasters will arise.
I, deep in the palace, knew nothing of this,
You must explain fully without evasion.
How does Gautama compare to my six teachers?
Choose the good and act accordingly.”
The emperor sat upright in the glazed hall,
Ruling with folded hands, facing due south.
Elegant scholars managed yin and yang,
Valiant warriors held precious fans.
They seized Sudatta and asked the reason: “Why have we not seen you for days?
We hear you are summoning foreign barbarian gods,
Your crimes are hard to forgive.”
Sudatta pleaded in response: “I have served the jade steps for many years.
With bared heart and liver, ever cautious,
Never acting falsely in the slightest.
To compare heretics with the Tathāgata
Is like comparing fine grain to weeds.
The Buddha’s majestic body stands sixteen feet tall,
While heretics are like faint fireflies.
The four great seas fit on a hair tip,
Five-colored divine light issues from his mouth.
Brahmā and Indra always lead before him,
The eight kinds of dragon gods follow behind.
How can a single sweaty shrimp
Dare to contend with the great sage, the qilin!”
The king heard the praise and commendation,
but had not yet ascertained the root cause,
so he summoned Sudatta forward: “You must investigate the truth,
and not allow any discrepancy;
glory and disgrace, rise and fall,
lie only in a moment’s span.
I, as the ruler of a kingdom,
govern all the nations;
you must exhaust your loyalty and preserve your integrity,
and not follow old ways and change your resolve.
When the Son of Heaven is angered,
he can cause a million corpses to lie prostrate,
and blood to flow for a thousand li.
From whose family lineage does the Buddha come?
Did his ancestors have a family of renown?
From whom did he learn and receive the teachings?
What virtues and powers does he possess?
Do not conceal anything,
