but speak truthfully and let me see.
If there is the slightest discrepancy,
you will personally face the law at my hands.
Sudatta addressed His Majesty: “The Tathāgata’s former generations
produced a thousand wheel-turning kings;
branch and leaf succeeded one another,
and honor and glory never ceased.
From his grandfather to his father,
all held the dignity of ten thousand chariots;
his outstanding sons and distant descendants
are all called the direct line of phoenixes.
His father was called Śuddhodana,
the most honored among eight kingdoms;
his mother was named Māyā,
peerless among the five heavens.
The Tathāgata was born in the land of Southern India,
and grew up in the city of Kapilavastu.
From birth to death,
from death to rebirth,
there is nothing he did not do,
nothing he did not accomplish,
nothing he did not experience,
nothing he did not undergo.
He grew up in King Śuddhodana’s palace,
and was named Siddhārtha.
After passing nineteen years of age,
he understood life and death;
before reaching twenty,
he soared over the palace walls.
Beneath the Bodhi tree,
he was not stained by worldly passions;
through diligent hardship for many years,
he emaciated his form.
Daily eating hemp seeds and barley,
he prolonged his life.
Crows and magpies nested on his head,
and raised their young to maturity.
His head was like a tangled nest,
his neck like a needle’s point;
his ribs were like rafters of a decaying house,
his eyes like stars at the bottom of a well.
His body was frail and weak,
in the shape of a hungry ghost.
Accumulating merit and virtue,
he achieved the Bodhi path.
His body was sixteen feet tall,
his neck and back radiant and full.
On his chest was the svastika mark,
clear and distinct.
He had the sign of a broad, long tongue,
and his forehead was broad and level.
His chest was like a lion king’s,
with hair curling in spirals.
The Tathāgata is extinguished yet not dead,
quiescent yet not born.
Stirred, he does not become turbid;
clarified, he becomes pure.
Hidden, he is not dark;
darkened, he becomes bright.
Looked at, his form cannot be seen;
listened to, his voice cannot be heard.
High, he is not perilous;
low, he does not incline.
He can stir rivers and seas and turn them into cream and cheese,
transform the great earth into lapis lazuli and crystal.
He can lift Mount Sumeru and know its weight in catties and taels,
chop the four seas and turn them into dry pits.
Closing his eyes, he travels ten thousand li;
opening them, he stops at once.
He manifests a great body pervading the world,
or manifests a small body,
hiding his form within a mote of dust.
The Tathāgata, when cut with a knife, feels no resentment;
when medicine is applied, feels no pain.
Finding something, he does not rejoice;
losing something, he does not weep.
In a great assembly, he does not feel the noise;
sitting alone, he does not feel lonely.
Both minds are of one kind,
equally and uniformly level.
He divides his body into a hundred million parts,
and everywhere receives alms.
One name is Siddhārtha,
the second title is Tathāgata;
he is the teacher of gods and humans,
possessing all wisdom.
Among the four kinds of birth and the three realms,
he is the most supreme and honored.
I have now briefly described his abilities,
which even over countless kalpas could not be fully praised.
Your Majesty!
The king heard these words,
and his joy was hard to contain.
“Although you have praised these abilities,
you have not yet demonstrated their actual truth;
we must test them face to face,
and only then can we determine right and wrong.
The teacher you follow—
can he match my monk or not?
Sudatta addressed His Majesty: “A thousand-jūn crossbow
is not triggered for a mouse;
a hundred-foot blazing furnace
is not ignited for a single hair.
Without even needing my great sage, the heavenly teacher,
even his smallest disciple
can match him.
The king asked: “Who is this disciple,
that he can face my monk?
Sudatta addressed the great king: “The Buddha’s disciple
is no other person—
it is Śāriputra.
The king said: “Śāriputra
is my monk’s nephew.
He recently left home,
and his study of the Dharma is still shallow;
considering his merit and practice,
he has not spent much time.
The young and old cannot stand shoulder to shoulder—
how can he face my monk!
“Though Yàn Yīng was small,
he could outwit tiger and wolf ministers.
Virtue does not depend on advanced age;
without wisdom, a hundred years are in vain.
Constructing empty falsehoods
is not as good as testing to obtain the truth.
Gold refined a hundred times
shines with ever-increasing radiance;
lead and tin placed in the furnace
instantly turn to ashes.
I humbly hope you will clearly proclaim,
issue an order to gather widely,
announce to all officials,
and hold a great contest to see,
and only then determine victory and defeat.
If the six teachers win,
I will accept ten thousand beheadings,
and my family will be confiscated by the state.
The king then ordered all officials: “Quickly make preparations;
on the eighth day of next month,
establish a site for the contest south of the city.
If the Buddhist side is stronger,
I and all the people of the kingdom
will together follow and serve the Buddha;
if there is the slightest error,
both of you must be executed.
Sudatta, having received the decree,
felt in his heart not a little anxiety and fear.
He then returned home,
frowning and with knitted brows.
Śāriputra saw his worry and fear,
and his appearance changed from normal,
so he exclaimed in surprise,
and asked wonderingly: “Elder, why are you worried and afraid,
and your face and appearance changed?
”Sudatta said: “This disciple today entered the court,
and personally received the clear decree,
ordering that on the eighth day of next month,
south of the city a site for the contest be established,
each displaying supernatural powers,
to determine superiority and inferiority.
If the Buddhist side wins,
the king and ministers all plan to submit sincerely;
if the six teachers are stronger,
the crown prince and this humble one will both be executed.
I am now an ordinary person with shallow wisdom,
and cannot measure the high and low of the sage.
I earnestly wish for your compassion,
and hope you will truthfully inform me of the prospects!
”Śāriputra, to relieve his worries,
spoke boastfully and manifestly as follows:
Sudatta addressed Śāriputra: “The decree orders that on the eighth day of next month,
south of the city a great site for the contest be established,
and supernatural powers each be displayed in every way.”
The king personally oversees to witness his abilities,
All officials deliberate to discern gains and losses.
We earnestly hope the Venerable will speak his mind,
Clearly stating his position, advancing or retreating, in one account."
Śāriputra smiled and replied to Sudatta:
"All false appearances must be severed.
The heretics compete with me in supernatural powers,
Like pitting a fish against an otter.
The bright moon cannot be compared to firefly light,
Seawater cannot be measured by the peck or handful.
It is like summer sun melting spring ice,
Or refined gold compared to wood shavings.
The followers of heresy are all chaff,
Once a great wind rises, none can be gathered.
I now subdue demons, determined to prevail,
And will transform them all into Bodhisattvas."
Śāriputra smiled and relaxed his expression,
Replying to Sudatta: "Though I am now but a lesser saint,
I do not decline to receive instructions from on high.
As for manifesting righteousness and crushing falsehood,
It is truly a minor task.
Even if demons numbered in the hundreds of millions,
Filling the empty sky,
They could not stir a single hair,
Let alone the six teachers, mere mosquitoes and gnats,
How could they possibly stand against me!
I now sharpen my blade and feed my steed,
Awaiting only the trial of combat.
There is no need for delay,
Only haste is required.
Elder, petition again,
Eight days is too long,
Like a rabbit darting into a burrow,
Who can endure cooked food for long?
Tomorrow we must act,
Please hasten the eight-day deadline."
Sudatta then petitioned the king again.
The king granted his request,
Issuing a decree to all officials:
"Tonight, by dawn,
All preparations must be completed.
For the Buddhist assembly grounds,
You, ministers, must make ready;
What the six teachers require,
I myself will provide.
At dawn tomorrow,
The contest must begin."
Once the proclamation was issued,
Sudatta immediately returned home.
Arriving at his house,
He could not find Śāriputra.
Sudatta clapped his hands in shock and lamented,
Crying out: "Disaster!
A great calamity has occurred.
Tomorrow morning we are pledged to contest with saints,
Yet today he has fled secretly.
Even if he judged himself incapable,
He should not have left without word.
I, your disciple, for the Dharma's sake,
Am willing to sacrifice my life;
But the prince's person,
What crime has he committed to suffer death!"
In frantic haste he searched,
Not knowing where he had gone;
He asked throughout the streets,
But none knew his whereabouts.
Then he met a young cowherd,
And questioned him closely:
"When you went into the wilderness,
Did you happen to meet my master?"
The boy bowed and said to the elder:
"Yesterday, driving the cattle to graze,
I chanced to reach the edge of Qīlǐ Jiàn,
And saw a bald-headed youth,
Clad in crimson robes,
Sitting serenely under a tree, asleep.
I do not know what manner of being he is.
Elder, you should go see for yourself."
Hearing this, the elder knew it must be he.
For in this kingdom,
There are none others who shave their heads.
The elder urged his carriage swiftly onward,
And arrived at the edge of Qīlǐ Jiàn.
Going straight to the Nyagrodha tree,
Approaching its left and right,
He clasped his hands and stepped forward,
Addressing the Venerable:
"Your disciple personally heard the sacred decree,
The constraints are severe and strict.
Master, you yourself urged haste,
Promising to contest with saints tomorrow.
How can you be unaware of urgency,
Coming to this place,
Unmindful of leisure or busyness,
Walking here to sit and sleep?
The slightest negligence,
And both our lives will be forfeit.
Even if I, your disciple, am to blame,
How could you, Master, bear to see it!"
How did he plead?
The elder joined his palms and addressed the Ācārya:
"Your disciple, foolish and ignorant, did not realize.
I scattered gold to buy the garden without hesitation,
But the heretics seize and torment me with harsh penalties.
Your disciple personally received the command,
That Raudrākṣa wishes to contest divine powers.
Fearing hesitation might arise along the way,
Hence my worry and fear, my furrowed brow."
When Śāriputra heard Sudatta's words,
He entered samādhi and reflected within.
Clearing his spirit, purifying his thoughts, calming his mind,
Subduing false notions, ceasing all errors.
The six thieves run rampant but cannot defile him,
Thus knowing the power of concentration is inconceivable.
Yet ever fearing the strength of a Śrāvaka is feeble,
He humbly wishes the Tathāgata to grant protection.
Śāriputra, without leaving his seat,
Exercised his supernatural powers,
And arrived at the peak of Vulture Peak,
Weeping tears of sorrow,
Choked with sobs, his voice hoarse,
Circling the World-Honored One
Several tens of times.
How did he seek the great sage's majestic empowerment?
Śāriputra tearfully addressed the Dharma King:
"The Tathāgata commanded the building of a monastic dwelling.
Before sincere efforts could complete its adornment,
The six teachers and their followers grew somewhat formidable.
Your disciple, a humble man, has feeble divine power,
I beseech you to bestow care and lend majestic light.
If they can be subdued in one moment,
I shall cause them all to enter the monastic order."
The Buddha told Śāriputra: "Do not grieve,
It is because your Śrāvaka power is slight."
Then he called Ānanda to his side,
"From the rack, fetch my saṅghāṭī robe.
Through countless kalpas subduing demons, it has served you,
Supernatural powers and wisdom need not be exerted.
Take my golden-hemmed kasāya,
Countless good spirits will guard it.
At the sight of it, demons will all be subdued,
The Dharma-nature pure, realizing the unconditioned."
Śāriputra suddenly arose from concentration,
Looking left and right, he saw no others,
Only the minister Sudatta,
Along with the eight kinds of dragon spirits and divine beings,
Surrounding him front and back,
Encircling him on all sides.
Asuras held the sun and moon to lead the way,
Kinnaras grasped spears and followed behind.
Then the wind deity stirred the winds,
The rain deity poured down rain,
Wetting the dusty clamor,
Smoothing and leveling the road.
Divine kings held clubs,
Vajrapāṇis grasped pestles,
Selecting the brave and heroic,
Arranging them in ranks and files.
Then they blew the Dharma conch,
Struck the Dharma drum,
Brandished spears and blades,
And stirred majestic wrath.
Moving like thunderbolts,
Advancing like spreading clouds.
There were also Snow Mountain elephant kings,
Golden-maned lions,
Glaring eyes and raised brows,
Bared teeth and gnashing jaws,
Bristling fur in fierce vigor,
Shaking heads and swinging tails.
Banners and standards reflected the sky,
Spears and halberds covered the ground.
Each vied to display divine might,
How did they empower the Tathāgata's great disciple?
Śāriputra bid farewell to the assembly,
That day he set out upon the road.
Virūḍhaka Devarāja held golden banners,
Dhṛtarāṣṭra Devarāja bore jade tablets.
Armor and weapons were all of gold,
Blades and arrows were wholly of iron.
Blue-faced Vajrapāṇis, dark and somber,
Fire-headed Vajrapāṇis, wrath unceasing.
Bells and drums roared, shaking the heavens,
Auspicious vapors bright and gleaming clear.
Heavenly immortals scattered famed flowers in the sky,
Chants of praise rose in overlapping waves.
From the demon-subduing pestle, flames arose,
By the wisdom blade, frost and snow formed.
May all Buddhas only stir compassion,
Soon the banners of falsehood will all be shattered.
Divine power required not a snap of the fingers,
In an instant, they reached the royal city gates.
King Pòsīnì saw Śāriputra,
and immediately addressed his assembled officials,
"Each of you must pay attention.
The Buddhist side is to the east,
the Six Masters are to the west.
We, the sovereign, are to the north,
and the officials and commoners are to the south.
Regarding the two paths of victory and defeat,
each must clearly record them.
If the monk is victorious,
strike the golden drum and lower the golden tally;
if the Buddhist side is stronger,
ring the golden bell and mark the character 'shàng' (尚).
Each of you, take your positions,
and then proceed as you will."
Śāriputra walked slowly and composedly,
ascending the lion throne.
Raudrākṣa, residing within a precious canopy,
was surrounded and supported on all four sides.
Śāriputra then ascended the precious seat,
like the king of lions,
and uttered an elegant and wondrous voice,
declaring to the fourfold assembly: "However, within my Buddhist Dharma,
no mind of self and others is established.
To manifest the correct and crush the false,
I provisionally employ expedient means.
What transformations can Raudrākṣa manifest?
Let him proceed as he will!"
Upon hearing these words, the Six Masters
suddenly transformed and produced a jeweled mountain,
several yojanas high.
Lofty and steep with green jade,
towering with white silver.
Its peak pierced the celestial river,
with dense bamboo, fragrant and fresh.
To the east and west were the sun and moon,
to the north and south were the stars.
There were also pine trees reaching to the sky,
and countless vines and creepers.
On its summit, recluses dwelt in peace,
and furthermore, various immortals wandered and observed.
Riding cranes and mounting dragons,
their immortal songs were in delightful confusion.
Who in the fourfold assembly was not astonished and sighed?
All who saw it praised and marveled.
Although Śāriputra saw this mountain,
in his mind there was no fear or difficulty.
In a brief moment,
he suddenly transformed and produced a vajra-being.
What form did this vajra-being take?
This vajra-being's head was round like the heavens,
the round heavens could barely serve as its cover;
its feet were square, spanning ten thousand leagues,
the great earth was just sufficient as its anvil.
Its eyebrows (verdant and lush) were like two layers of green mountains,
its mouth was as vast as rivers and seas.
In its hand it held a precious pestle,
from the pestle flames soared to the sky.
With one motion toward the heretical mountain,
it was instantly smashed to pieces.
The mountain flowers withered, faded, and scattered,
the bamboo and trees were nowhere to be found.
All the officials sighed in unison at this wonder,
the fourfold assembly all at once cheered in delight.
Thus it is said: The place where the vajra-being's wisdom pestle shattered the heretical mountain—how was it?
The Six Masters' angry feelings were hard to stop,
they transformed a jeweled mountain, incomparable.
Precipitous cliffs could be several yojanas high,
purple vines and golden creepers covering the ground.
Mountain flowers, lush and emerald, formed brocade patterns,
lofty rocks and crags rose amid azure clouds.
Upon it were Wáng Qiáo and Dīng Lìngwēi,
fragrant waters flowed within the jeweled mountain.
Flying immortals often scattered famous blossoms,
the great king, seeing from afar, was filled with joy.
Śāriputra saw the mountain enter the assembly,
composed and unmoving, he abided in samādhi.
Timely, he transformed and produced a great vajra-being,
with high eyebrows, broad forehead, and a massive body.
In its hand a golden pestle, flames soaring to the sky,
with one motion toward the heretical mountain, it was smashed to powder.
The heretics choked, their voices hoarse,
the fourfold assembly all at once cheered in delight.
At that time, the emperor was astonished,
the fourfold assembly was joyful.
Since this round was not equal to his,
they wondered what divine transformation would come next?
At that time, the elder Sudatta then struck the great bell,
holding a golden plaque in hand,
petitioned the king to demand the 'shàng' character.
The Six Masters saw the jeweled mountain destroyed,
their indignation soared to the heavens,
further arousing their wrathful minds,
they again petitioned the king, saying: "However, my supernatural transformations
have no end or limit.
Although this one round was not equal,
appearing again, I surely know how to achieve victory."
Raudrākṣa suddenly, within the assembly,
transformed and produced a water buffalo.
This buffalo had horns gleaming, propping up the sky,
its four hooves like the swords of Lóngquán;
its dewlap hung down, dragging on the ground,
its pair of eyes bright like the sun and moon.
With one bellowing roar,
thunder startled and lightning roared.
The fourfold assembly sighed in admiration,
all saying the heretics were strong.
Although Śāriputra saw this buffalo,
his spirit and demeanor remained completely unmoved.
Suddenly he transformed and produced a lion,
fierce and courageous, difficult to withstand.
This lion had a mouth like a deep ravine,
a body resembling a snowy mountain,
eyes like shooting stars,
teeth like frosty swords.
Vigorously and swiftly it roared,
and charged straight into the arena.
The water buffalo saw it,
lost its soul and knelt on the ground.
The lion first broke its neck bones,
then twisted its spine and heels.
Not allowing time for chewing,
its form and bones were smashed to pieces.
The emperor gasped in amazement,
the officials and commoners were dumbfounded.
The Six Masters were then terrified and alarmed,
the crown prince was then overwhelmed with celebratory joy. The place—how was it?
The Six Masters, angry before the king,
transformed a water buffalo, most pitiable.
Charging straight into the arena, startling the fourfold assembly,
grinding its horns, digging the ground, bellowing continuously to the sky.
The heretics in unison all cheered 'good!',
"Our Dharma shall be spread throughout the land."
Śāriputra on his seat was not alarmed or hurried,
all because his wisdom was exceedingly profound.
Adjusting his robes, settling his mind,
he transformed the majestic and awe-inspiring lion king.
Roaring, its two eyes like stars and lightning,
sharp teeth, swift claws, keen as frost.
With heroic spirit it shook its tail,
charging forward, aiming directly to wound the water buffalo.
Breaking and crushing, instantly it was dissolved,
even its bones chewed, completely vanishing.
Twice the Buddhist side had been victorious,
the heretics, minds at their limit, had no plan.
The Six Masters, having twice been inferior,
their spirits gradually increased in shame and distress.
Forcing their stubborn, thick-skinned faces,
within the assembly they transformed a pool of water.
Its four banks adorned with the seven treasures,
inside, golden sand covered the ground.
Duckweed and water chestnut plants,
all over the green water vied to grow;
supple willows and lotus flowers,
encircled the numinous pond, lush and misty.
Śāriputra saw the pool's wondrous marvel,
yet was not startled or amazed.
He transformed the king of white elephants,
its body vast and broad,
eyes like the sun and moon.
Its mouth had six tusks,
each tusk emitted seven lotus flowers.
On the flowers were seven heavenly maidens,
hands plucking stringed instruments,
mouths singing string-accompanied songs.
Their voices elegant, wondrous, fresh, and clear,
their postures graceful and beautiful.
The elephant then slowly began to move,
walking straight into the pool,
trampling east and west,
circling north and south.
Using its trunk to suck the water,
the water then dried up.
The banks collapsed, dust flew,
transforming into arid land.
At that time, the Six Masters lost color,
the fourfold assembly gasped in amazement,
the entire country's officials,
in unison sighed in wonder. The place—how was it?
That pool had seven treasures for its banks,
agate and coral vied in dazzling splendor.
Fish in the pool leaped, all wearing crowns (or: strung together),
turtles, soft-shelled turtles, giant salamanders, and crocodiles vied to dive and flee.
Lotus flowers in the water shone radiantly,
those who saw could not help but be startled in mind.
The heretics themselves sighed, 'most rare and strange!',
"See me this time contend for strength and weakness."
Śāriputra raised his eyes and looked south,
transformed the six-tusked great fragrant elephant.
Its gait resembled a snowy mountain moving,
its body vast and broad, difficult to fathom its size.
In its mouth, precipitous, it emitted six tusks,
each tusk one hundred zhang high.
On each tusk were seven lotus flowers,
in the flowers, jade maidens, none could match.
Hands plucking qin and se, playing stringed songs,
elegant, wondrous, fresh and clear, voices harmonizing in resonance.
Together they praised the Land of Ultimate Bliss of Amitābha,
joining hands, they earnestly urged all to go there with one heart.
The elephant then stepped into the pool,
trampling east and west along the banks.
It sucked up all the water with its trunk, leaving it dry,
leaving the six masters choking with sorrow and regret.
The six masters repeatedly suffered defeat,
their hearts growing ever more vexed.
Today, strange that they are no match for him,
last night their dreams were all topsy-turvy.
Their faces turned ruddy and sallow,
their lips and mouths unusually parched.
Their bellies burned as if scalded by boiling water,
their guts ached as if churned by knives.
Though Gautama is a vicious wolf,
he cannot withstand the bites of a pack of dogs.
Śāriputra, with his modest wisdom and clumsy schemes,
shows his skill before Lǔ Bān.
If this time he happens to gain strength,
he will shatter all that came before.
Unwilling to endure the humiliation,
suddenly he transformed into a poisonous dragon.
Its mouth spewed smoke and clouds,
darkening the sky and obscuring the sun.
With raised brows and darting eyes,
it shook the earth with thunderous roars.
Lightning flashed, now dim, now bright,
auspicious clouds now stretched, now curled.
Terrifying the fourfold assembly,
alarming the common people.
The entire nation saw it,
marveling at its supernatural strangeness.
Śāriputra sat calmly on his precious throne,
utterly without a fearful heart.
He transformed into a golden-winged garuḍa king,
with extraordinary feathers and unusual bones,
beating its twin wings,
obscuring the brightness of sun and moon.
Its claws and spurs slender and long,
no different from the swords of Fēngchéng.
Descending straight from the sky,
like a shooting star from heaven.
Spotting the poisonous dragon from afar,
it seized it in several rounds of combat.
Though not enough to fill me for one meal,
it at least staved off my hunger.
The bird first pecked out its eyes,
then devoured its four limbs.
With two movements of its beak,
not even the bones remained.
The six masters trembled with fear and sighed in astonishment,
their spirits bewildered and dazed:
On this day, the six masters grew increasingly wretched,
filled with resentment, not knowing where to turn.
Though they fought fiercely and resisted stubbornly,
in the end they knew they would topple themselves.
Once more they transformed into a poisonous dragon body,
spewing smoke and clouds, harboring violent fury.
Thunder roared, lightning flashed, fog darkened the sky,
cracking sounds echoed like fiery explosions.
The assembly trembled with fear and gasped in awe,
looking at each other, all exclaiming in admiration.
As soon as Śāriputra saw the poisonous dragon arrive,
he manifested the extraordinary golden-winged bird.
Crushing its head and tail was no difficulty,
its first bite then pecked out the brain.
Ribs shattered into fine dust,
the six masters were at a loss for words.
The awesome power of the Three Jewels is immeasurable,
the demon king trembled in battle, beset by vexation.
The king said: "Monk, you have boasted wildly,
with a thousand kinds of skill and art;
yet before others, in contest,
you are incapable of a single feat.
What other divine powers do you have?
Quickly manifest them!"
The six masters forced themselves to rally their spirits,
and addressed the king: "Within my dharma,
spiritual transformations are endless."
Suddenly, amidst the crowd,
he transformed into two demons.
Their forms were ugly and vile,
their bodies rugged and grotesque.
Their faces, bluer than indigo, turned even darker,
their eyes, redder than cinnabar, grew even brighter.
Fire issued from their mouths,
smoke rose from their nostrils,
they moved like galloping lightning,
swift as whirling gusts,
raising eyebrows, blinking eyes,
terrifying all around.
Those who saw them felt their hairs stand on end,
but Śāriputra alone remained serene.
Śāriputra hesitated, pondering deeply,
when Vaiśravaṇa appeared before the king.
Majestic and awe-inspiring in might,
armor and weapons gleaming bright,
earth spirits supported his feet,
a precious sword hung at his waist.
At the sight of the two demons,
they begged for their lives incessantly. How was it then:
The six masters claimed to be without equal,
yet transformed into two yellow-headed demons.
Their heads were of strange kind, their corpses ugly,
frightening all around, causing terror.
Śāriputra raised a thought and briefly reflected,
and Vaiśravaṇa, the heavenly king, arrived of his own accord.
The heavenly king turned his gaze, his eyes flashing like thunder,
the two demons fell dazed and prostrate on the ground.
On that day, the heretic (Śāriputra) defeated the demon army,
the six masters cowered, their souls utterly lost.
Thanks to the compassion of Śāriputra,
who endured and exhausted all awesome power.
Only when donkeys and mules bear heavy loads on long roads,
does one realize they can be compared to dragon scales.
Merely because the mind is deluded on petty, wrong paths,
they are transformed and led to take refuge in the great dharma gate.
Though the six masters had lost five times,
they still would not surrender.
"Let us try once more and see,
later success may make up for past failure.
If we happen to fail again,
we will willingly bow and submit to him."
Having finished this thought,
suddenly amidst the crowd he transformed into a great tree,
with luxuriant branches and leaves,
shading the sun and touching the clouds,
its towering trunk and fragrant boughs,
reaching heights of ten thousand ren.
Auspicious birds and phoenixes,
filled the branches and leaves with harmonious song;
emerald leaves and fragrant flowers,
spread for miles around, vying in splendor.
Those who saw it then,
could not help but gasp in amazement.
Śāriputra suddenly, amidst the crowd, transformed into the wind god,
clasped his hands and stepped forward,
addressing the monk: "The three-thousand-great-thousand world,
I can blow away in an instant without difficulty;
how much less this tiny, insignificant tree,
dare stand against my wind's path!"
Having spoken these words,
he opened his bag and blew.
Then the earth rolled up like cotton,
stones shattered like dust,
branches and twigs scattered to other realms,
trunk and stem vanished without a trace.
The heretic had no place to hide,
the fourfold assembly cheered as one. How was it then:
The six masters repeatedly lost five times,
yet before the king they transformed into a tree.
Its height could be several yojanas,
its branches lush and luxuriant, flourishing abundantly.
Śāriputra's power of the Way is inconceivable,
his supernatural transformations exceedingly rare.
Leaving the Buddha, he came especially to subdue the heretics,
then in turn summoned a great wind to blow.
The divine king's cry was like the roar of thunder,
the long snake struck the tree, leaving no branch intact.
In the blink of an eye, it completely dispersed and vanished,
the heretic drifted aimlessly, with nothing to rely on.
The six masters were blown, their feet off the ground,
incense burners and precious vessels flew with the wind.
The precious throne tilted perilously, about to topple,
the heretic, terrified and desperate, all rushed to support it.
One by one they discussed the six masters' weakness,
how could a mustard seed compare to Mount Sumeru!
Then the king addressed the monk: "I, in recent days,
have vainly shown you respect and honor,
lavishly bestowed jade and silk,
wastefully expended the state's treasury.
Thus I know true gold from counterfeit brass,
by sight and examination one can distinguish;
dragons and snakes mixed together,
only then can their abilities be discerned.
Monk, your strength is exhausted, your power spent,
in every matter you are weak,
you must lower your heart and bend your will,
submit and yield to him.
Cease vainly exalting yourself,
discoursing on heaven and earth."
The six masters, hearing these words,
could only assent and comply.
Their faces wore shame and embarrassment,
they had no place to hide themselves.
Śāriputra, seeing the heretics subdued,
felt joy and ease in heart and mind.
It was not due to my own robust strength and ability,
but all due to the empowerment of the Tathāgata.
Then he soared straight upward,
leaping into empty space,
to the height of seven tāla trees.
Fire issued from his head,
water flowed from his feet,
sometimes manifesting a giant form,
filling the entire sky,
sometimes manifesting a tiny form,
as small as a mustard seed.
With supernatural transformations,
he displayed eighteen kinds,
the entire nation's people,
all gazed up in reverence. How was it then:
Śāriputra suddenly displayed his supernatural powers,
Leaping up to stand in the empty sky.
Sometimes manifesting a vast form pervading the Dharma-realm,
Sometimes shrinking his body to hide within a mustard seed.
Raudrākṣa stood astonished, palms joined,
Thinking, "How can my dharma compare with his?"
"Let us together abandon falsehood for the true path,"
They humbly and shamefully expressed their gratitude.
"Since contending with the sage, we have been utterly inferior,
How dare we not turn our hearts and follow?"
Each resolved to repent and take refuge in the Three Jewels,
No longer giving thought to serving the fire-dragon.
For years we wasted our strength in vain,
All day long moving from emptiness to emptiness.
Now each withdraws to serve the Buddha,
To avoid being pounded by the iron mortar in the future."
One scroll of "The Transformation Text on Subduing Demons."
If any errors are seen,
When someone reads it,
Please correct them accordingly.
"The Second [Scroll] on Dhṛtarāṣṭra (Bodhisattva)"
The sutra says: At that time, Māra Pāpīyas, with twelve thousand heavenly maidens,
In the guise of Śakra, with drums, music, strings, and songs,
Came to where I was.
At that time,
Pāpīyas devised a plan,
Arraying many court ladies and consorts;
Wishing to vex the sage,
He displayed extravagant beauties.
Rare demon maidens,
Twelve thousand in number;
The most exceptional pearls,
A thousand kinds of adornments.
The transcendent bodhisattva,
Is not easily disturbed;
How could the venerable Dhṛtarāṣṭra
Be made to retreat?
All were adorned with great beauty,
None lacking in grace.
If seen, they were taught clever words,
Surely causing retreat and defeat.
These demon maidens,
Each like a blooming lotus,
Every one like flawless jade.
Their bodies soft, as if newly descended from Wūshān,
Their appearances graceful, as if just leaving an immortal cave.
All bore peach-blossom faces,
All shared willow-leaf eyebrows.
Moving slowly like the wind brushing lotuses,
Walking gently like water swaying lotus stems.
Vermilion lips, delicate and lovely,
Able to be crimson, able to be red;
Snow-white teeth, even and neat,
Able to be white, able to be pure.
Light gauze wiping their bodies,
Exuding rare fragrances;
Thin silk draped over them,
Trailing extraordinary emerald colors.
Arranged to the right of the seat,
Standing within the palace.
Like the five-colored clouds spreading across the blue sky,
Like a thousand flowers blooming in a jade pond.
Rare, rare,
Marvelous, marvelous.
Merely sending demon maidens to tempt him,
I fear cannot stir him.
Better to divide into several groups,
Each displaying their grace.
Those holding fresh flowers diligently offer them,
Those burning rare incense earnestly show devotion.
Joining jade fingers in repeated bows,
Uttering clever words with feigned sincerity.
Some hold musical instruments,
Some chant poems;
Some exhibit elegance,
Some sing songs.
Do not boast of the Yuènǚ,
Nor speak of Cáo É.
No matter how firm Dhṛtarāṣṭra's heart,
Upon seeing them, he must retreat.
Excellent, excellent,
Rare, rare.
Such beautiful grace,
How could it not stir thoughts?
Even seeing them oneself,
One's soul becomes bewildered;
Others beholding them,
Surely will have disordered minds.
No matter how diligent his practice,
Surely he will turn his head;
Even if his heart were made of iron,
Upon seeing them, it would shatter.
The demon king said: "If I go as I am,
Surely the bodhisattva will recognize me.
Better to form a procession like Śakra's,
And question Dhṛtarāṣṭra Bodhisattva."
Then the demon king greatly adorned himself,
Prepared to leave the palace city,
Descending from heaven.
Surrounded and escorted,
A hundred layers, a thousand circles.
Melodies, strings, and songs,
Divided into twenty-four groups.
Step by step leaving the heavenly gate,
Far, far from their original palace.
Pāpīyas led the way,
The demon maidens followed behind.
Those holding instruments noisily played tunes,
Echoing to the azure heavens;
Those burning incense sent smoke curling,
Misty in the blue sky.
Vying in extravagant beauty,
Each displaying graceful charm.
Those holding fresh flowers matched the flowers' hues,
Those bearing pearls were no different from the pearls.
On pipa strings,
Melodies harmonized with spring orioles;
In flute and pipe,
Notes sang like calling phoenixes.
Sticks beating the jié drum,
Like scattering broken jade on a plate;
Hands playing the qín zhēng,
Like arranging wild geese on strings.
Gentle strings and bamboo,
Even the finest court music could not compare;
Vast singing voices,
How could foreign tunes match them?
Enchanting appearances grew more splendid,
Beautiful forms even more abundant.
Group after group like four-colored flowers blooming,
Team after team like five-colored clouds radiant.
Circling the blue sky,
Winding through the azure heavens.
Seen from afar, minds scattered, hearts startled;
Beheld up close, souls flew, eyes dazed.
Descending from heaven,
Like heavenly flowers raining chaos upon the world;
Fresh from the demon palace,
Like immortal maidens scattering fragrance throughout the universe.
Heavenly maidens all leaped with joy,
The demon king himself was delighted.
Now the scheme seemed sure to succeed,
Dhṛtarāṣṭra's practice surely to retreat.
Appearance just like Śakra,
Dignity exactly like Brahmā.
The sage would surely have no doubt,
Dhṛtarāṣṭra would likely not suspect.
Heavenly maidens each applied the six pitches,
Everyone tuned the five notes.
Singers pretended devout hearts,
Those making offerings feigned reverence.
Do not let the sage become aware,
Do not allow the bodhisattva to perceive.
When speaking, carefully pause,
When tempting, be sure to act prudently.
Each please hold fresh flowers in your palms,
For me burn aloes and musk in the censer.
Show pearl-like faces, flaunting enchanting looks,
Reveal jade-like countenances, adding even more beauty.
Vast flute and sháo music leading the way,
Noisy melodies and harmonies sounding together.
All at once descending from the clouds,
Entering the meditation chamber entirely.
(Chant): The demon king's procession left the heavenly palace,
Seeking to vex the sage, descending to the world.
Extensively setting out incense and flowers to make offerings,
Adding also music and string songs.
Clear, cold, empty realm, melodies clamorous,
Chaotic among clouds, sounds resounding brightly.
Foreign tunes could not compare,
Kuí zī music could not match them.
Far, far, music led them from the demon palace,
Faintly arrayed within the celestial river.
Incense burning, smoke flying, blending with auspicious air,
Flowers held in disarray, stirring propitious clouds.
On pipa strings playing with spring orioles,
In flute and pipe crying like brocade phoenixes.
Jié drum sticks beating broken jade,
Qín zhēng strings dropping pearl treasures.
Each adorned in beauty, displaying grace,
All revealing jade faces, boasting enchanting forms.
Every one like flowers bursting into bloom,
Each person like the moon goddess flying.
Descending from heaven, filling heaven and earth,
Leaving that palace, covering the universe.
At first sight, everyone's soul and courage shattered,
Upon first glance, each person's heart startled.
(Rhyme): Pāpīyas that day came forth from heaven,
Music groups arrayed in azure sky and blue expanse.
Jade maidens' looks like flowers splendidly blooming,
Immortal maidens' forms like the moon hanging open in the sky.
Enchanting peaches forcefully tempting the bodhisattva,
Beautiful forms vainly boasting to vex the sage's heart.
Drums, music, strings, songs, thousands of groups,
Following, crowding, vying to linger.
Boasting enchanting forms,
Flaunting figures,
Graceful as flowers opening toward the sun.
Ten fingers slender as carved jade,
Paired eyebrows faintly like knives trimmed.
Holding musical instruments,
blowing flutes once more,
they gradually descend from the clouds, winding and turning.
The sounds of flutes and pipes drift from afar,
the notes from the pipa strings are mournful and sorrowful.
Songs drip and flow,
laughter rings out joyfully,
encircling Póxún, arranged in rows.
Their formation is just like that of Indra descending,
their dignified bearing resembles that of Brahmā arriving.
One must conceal and examine,
not let others guess,
feigning devout reverence before the Dharma platform.
Do not let questioning cause alarm,
be diligent and avoid any transgression.
Agarwood and musk,
lifted in hand,
offered temporarily with heartfelt intent.
Truly waiting until the sage’s mind is confused,
then, following his movements, they will come to disturb.
One must remember this,
take it to heart,
not allow the Dharma eye of practice to open.
If Chíshì attains the Way,
the demon’s kin will surely be destroyed.
Skillfully adjusting and tuning,
well arranged,
forcefully using words to express intentions.
When encountering forms, the mind falls into decline,
following emotions and desires, they lure him back.
Songs and music,
competing in blowing flutes,
mixed and clamorous, overflowing the path in rows.
Demon maidens and demon kings enter the chamber,
□ giving rise to disturbance, they sing of what is to come.
(The scripture says): With their retinue, they bow at my feet,
join their palms in reverence,
and even cultivate steadfast Dharma.
At that time, Póxún has a verse:
(Poem): For the sake of deep meditation, I come to this abode,
today I specially descend from the celestial paths.
Reverently adhering to precepts, pure as the moon,
mindful of lofty purity, solitary as a mountain peak.
In meditation, unaware of how long the practice has been,
seated in Zen, uncertain of what the Dharma is like.
Now bringing my retinue to pay respects,
I inquire, Venerable Brother, are you well and blessed?
(Prose): At that time, Póxún said to Chíshì: “Venerable one, you have practiced for many days,
spent much time in meditation.
Firmly upholding the virtues of Dharma,
binding the mind and spirit to maintain resolve.
The thatched hall is silent and still,
the stone chamber secluded and empty.
I imagine you know the solitude of morning and night,
and reckon the daily toil and weariness.
The gate of Zen is deep and far,
the Dharma of emptiness difficult to comprehend.
I do not know the depth of your realization,
nor what merits and practices you have.
I leave the realm of emptiness,
descend from the celestial palace.
Thinking of your virtues, no different from others,
recalling your solitary loftiness, unique and distinct.
Today, joyfully meeting,
I humbly hope the great sage will be compassionate,
and speak with me briefly on the flavor of Dharma.”
(Plain poem): Temporarily casting aside the five desires, I descend from heaven,
to pay respects to my brother at his meditation platform.
Drum music and string songs express offerings,
incense, flowers, and rare fruits convey heartfelt intent.
Joyfully gazing upon the great being a thousand times,
happily paying respects to the lofty one a hundred rounds.
Humbly hoping for compassion to proclaim the wondrous Dharma,
I now wholly wish to extinguish the dust of defilements.
At that time, Chíshì did not recognize the demon king,
mistaking him for Jiāoshījiā,
wrongly identifying him as Indra,
therefore
(The scripture states): I said it was Indra,
and spoke to him: Welcome,
Jiāoshījiā!
Even to cultivate steadfast Dharma.
(Prose): That day, the Bodhisattva Chíshì addressed Indra, saying: “The lifespan and blessings of the celestial palace have their limits,
do not mistake wealth and luxury
for something eternal and enduring.
Rising and sitting, there is spontaneous music,
pleasing songs and pipes.
Thus, there are many exotic fragrant flowers,
following one’s will freely.
Celestial men and women,
attend without cease;
jeweled trees and forests,
roaming without rest.
Wherever the mind goes,
there are towers and pavilions;
wherever intention moves,
jeweled fragrances arise naturally.
Flowers blooming become daylight,
flowers closing mark dusk.
Thinking of clothing brings layers of silk and brocade,
desiring food brings hundreds of rare delicacies.
Such wealth and luxury,
truly extravagant.
All are but fleeting causes and conditions,
all are impermanent blessings.
Indra,
Indra!
You must know,
you must know!
Do not fix your mind on the five desires,
do not indulge recklessly in the celestial palace.
Although the lifespan is long,
it is still not ultimately enduring;
although wealthy and luxurious,
how can there be a place of permanence?
When lifespan ends and strength is exhausted,
one ultimately returns to the three evil paths of hell;
when blessings are exhausted,
one enters the path of轮回.
Like a blazing fire,
when the wood is gone, it turns to dust;
like an arrow shot into the sky,
when its force is spent, it ultimately falls to the ground.
Not escaping birth and death,
not transcending impermanence.
Quickly relinquish inner and outer treasures,
attain the wondrous fruit of non-action.
Diligently practice the Buddha’s Dharma,
realize true suchness.
Less attachment to glory and splendor,
fully understand it as a source of affliction.
Deeply troubling Indra,
I will now explain the path.
With you, I shall briefly expound the profound,
to realize transcendence over birth and death.”
(Ancient chant, upper and lower): The celestial palace cannot avoid impermanence,
blessings slight, one falls nonetheless.
Wealth and luxury ultimately do not last long,
indulging in songs and music is not steadfast.
However much one praises the jade maiden’s beauty,
however much one flaunts the moon maiden’s allure,
however much you indulge in luxury and freedom,
in the end, you cannot avoid impermanence.
However much one boasts of brocade and embroidery in layers,
however much you savor hundreds of rare delicacies,
however much all your needs are met,
in the end, you cannot avoid impermanence.
However much blessings adorn the body,
however much your retinue surrounds you long,
however much you follow emotions in joy,
in the end, you cannot avoid impermanence.
However much clear music plays strings and songs,
however much towers and pavilions appear wherever you go,
however much consorts and concubines follow in attendance,
in the end, you cannot avoid impermanence.
However rare and extraordinary your beauty,
however wealthy the celestial palace,
however much flowers bloom, filling the path with fragrance,
in the end, you cannot avoid impermanence.
Do not indulge body and mind in the upper realms,
do not sink deep into the five desires in heaven,
do not take pride and luxury as ultimate,
do not cling to wealth and neglect practice.
Know that there is collapse and ruin there,
like an arrow shot into the sky, falling to the ground.
If you can understand within body, life, and wealth,
your practice will not transcend impermanence.
(Summary): Troubling Indra to descend from heaven,
deeply thanking the arrangement of string songs and drum music.
Jade maidens all awaken and realize,
beauties each must emerge from the dust.
When will the wealth of the celestial palace end?
The torments of hell repeat tens of thousands of times.
If you can comprehend within body, life, and wealth,
you can long transcend the three calamities.
Remember this,
take it to heart,
return to the upper realm, the celestial palace.
The mountain of karma from the five desires diminishes daily,
the peak of delusion and obstruction crushes with time.
Establish a firm treasury within the body,
remove the defiled seeds of affliction from the heart.
Indra, moved by the elder brother’s exposition of Dharma power,
how shall he respond? Sing of what is to come.
(Scripture): Then he said to me, “Noble one, accept these twelve thousand celestial maidens,
to prepare for sweeping and sprinkling.”
(White): At that time, the Demon King addressed Chíshì, saying: "I have temporarily left the Realm of Desire,
descending from the celestial palace.
Delighted to behold the majestic bearing of the Bodhisattva,
I have arrived within the meditation chamber.
Fortunate to receive your compassionate thoughts,
you have graciously bestowed teachings.
I deeply understand that the five desires are not steadfast,
and I have briefly realized that the celestial existence is not long-lasting.
The defilements surrounding the body,
from now on should be removed;
the dust and dirt upon the mind,
from this point onward should mostly be kept at bay.
Having been moistened by the Dharma rain,
washing away the dust of toil;
having drunk the clarified butter,
suddenly dispelling the heat of afflictions.
Feeling the convenience of a thousand lifetimes,
I am ashamed of the kindness of ten thousand virtues.
I now have no rare treasures or jewels to repay,
to recompense your venerable virtue,
I only offer twelve thousand celestial maidens to you, Elder Brother,
as recompense for your teaching of the Dharma.
I humbly hope for your compassionate acceptance,
I beg you, Great Being, to allow them to stay.
Moreover, let them serve daily,
available for morning and evening tasks.
The meditation hall is secluded and quiet,
the empty room is silent and lonely,
let them add incense morning and evening,
day and night warming the meditation hall.
Do not give rise to worry or concern,
I am pure (without invitation) and free from doubt and suspicion.
Elder Brother, please accept them,
this disciple now makes this offering.
The false Indra had a verse to address Bodhisattva Chíshì:
"Out of admiration for your virtuous conduct, I left the celestial palace,
able to pay respects to the compassionate countenance of the great sage.
Joyfully drinking the clarified butter dispels the heat of afflictions,
thoroughly moistened by the Dharma rain, washing away the dust of confusion.
Coming here, I did not bring various precious treasures,
how can I repay the merit of your Dharma teaching?
Twelve thousand celestial maidens,
Elder Brother, please accept them and let them serve respectfully.
Chíshì addressed the false Indra, saying: "I am a practicing Bodhisattva,
I am a transcendent noble one.
My single body is already more than sufficient,
why would I need so many celestial maidens from you?
I have already departed from defiled desires,
I do not dwell in worldly sentiments,
knowing that clamor and noise are the cause of birth and death,
realizing that beautiful forms are the root of saṃsāra.
Moreover, these celestial maidens,
are all bodies indulging in arrogance, extravagance, and defiled desires.
Those who are attached and deluded will certainly enter birth and death,
those who are inclined toward them will surely sink into hell.
I have already cultivated the Buddha fruit,
attained the true vehicle,
I do not reside within the dusty world,
nor do I seek within worldly sentiments.
Cultivating meditation and contemplation,
it is fitting to be quiet and reduce conditions;
gathering the mind and clarifying the heart,
why would I need so many people from you?
Indra,
Indra!
You must know,
you must know!
Why bring these beautiful people,
and offer them before me?
I only hope you will take them back yourself!
Instead, I request you to return,
quickly go back to your original celestial palace,
leave this meditation chamber early.
Do not let ordinary sentiments cause alarm,
do not allow shallow and hasty doubts and suspicions.
Saying my meditation is not firm,
saying my practice has declined and failed.
The forest is quiet,
please return early;
the chamber is secluded and tranquil,
it is not suitable to stay long.
I wish to cultivate the Buddha fruit,
you must quickly ascend to the celestial palace.
Do not present these maidens,
my household certainly knows not to accept.
" Chíshì had a verse:
"Deeply troubling Indra to descend from the edge of heaven,
personally coming with attendants to ask me.
In the chamber, sparse and quiet, discussing the Dharma for long,
the celestial palace is delayed, the road forks and is distant.
In the mountains, as evening approaches, the green forest darkens,
on the peak, the light shifts, the red sun slants.
Indra, at this time, do not stay long,
lead the celestial maidens home early.
The Demon King said thus: "I have heard that those who cultivate practice,
do not oppose human sentiments;
those who are Bodhisattvas,
skillfully adapt according to capacities.
To sprout the seeds of budding growth,
one must sprinkle the spring dew;
to open the door of the hibernating household,
one should await the thunderclap.
I now have aroused intention,
and am determined to turn my mind.
Wishing to repay the merit of your Dharma teaching,
how can you not accept this offering?
Moreover, these celestial maidens,
each one has a form like white jade,
each one has a countenance resembling fresh flowers.
Enchanting peaches that surpass Cháng'é,
beautiful forms that put Dájǐ to shame.
They can sing in tune,
moving clouds cannot help but hang low;
they understand playing music,
the Weaving Girl suddenly stops her loom.
Embroidering into coiled phoenixes,
facing lotus flowers, how can they not blush with shyness;
stitching out mandarin ducks,
alongside peonies, how can they be without shame?
Hairpins slantingly falling,
tilting phoenix buns like flowers leaning on medicine railings;
jade-like faces frequently relaxing,
plain moth eyebrows like wind blowing lotus leaves.
They can also serve and attend,
particularly understanding how to respectfully receive.
Lowering their eyebrows, they already understand human sentiments,
moving their eyes, they early know matters of the heart.
For the four seasons, medicinal decoctions,
they also know how to prepare;
daily vegetarian meals,
they deeply know warmth and coolness.
Sweeping and cleaning the meditation hall,
clear wind does not raise dust;
arranging the secluded chamber,
the full seat quickly becomes auspicious air.
The aforementioned celestial maidens,
roughly know the Buddha Dharma,
deeply possess the mind of the Way.
Their households wish to serve diligently,
also hoping for compassionate employment.
Bodhisattva,
Bodhisattva!
Elder Brother,
Elder Brother!
Now, do not hesitate further,
at this moment, I hope you will condescend to accept them.
When bored, have them sing in harmony,
when idle, send them to sing songs.
In the meditation hall, do not let it be lonely,
in the secluded household, do not allow it to be desolate.
I reside in the upper realm,
descending from the celestial palace.
Deeply concerned that the great virtue has no one,
only fearing that Elder Brother is lonely.
Twelve thousand celestial maidens,
each and every one fully possesses the mind of the Way.
I am now determined to give them up,
I cannot take them back to heaven.
Accept them,
accept them!
Do not doubt,
do not doubt!
They vow to be disciples of the Bodhisattva's gate,
they wish to become Elder Brother's disciples.
" Indra addressed him:
(Side): Bodhisattva, compassionate, do not doubt or worry,
the meditation hall is quiet, without reliance or support.
Cultivating practice directly moves the celestial palace,
entering samādhi subdues dragons and tigers.
I have come now,
receiving the Dharma rain,
the dust of toil has already vanished, the mind is opened and awakened,
how can I repay the kindness of your Dharma teaching,
Elder Brother, accept the celestial maidens.
Leaving the heavenly gate,
descending the cloud road,
coming here, I did not bring various precious treasures,
able to pay respects to the compassionate great Dharma King,
Elder Brother, accept the celestial maidens.
Understanding song and sound,
able to follow musical tones,
the Sháo music directly causes dark clouds to spread,
day and night having them warm the Dharma hall,
Elder Brother, accept the celestial maidens.
Skillful at cutting and sewing,
able to embroider and mend,
stitching coiled phoenixes requires sweet rain,
each one can make a hundred-patched robe,
Elder Brother, accept the celestial maidens.
Understanding people's hearts,
clever with words,
how can you bear to let them return empty-handed,
in the meditation hall, employing them for good service,
Elder Brother, accept the celestial maidens.
Countenance like flowers,
body like plain silk,
like snow, like flowers, and the flowers also speak,
One fit to be a student in the meditation hall,
Elder brother, accept these heavenly maidens.
I have now specially descended from the heavens,
To see my elder brother's meditation session open,
Joyfully bowing to the noble one a hundred times,
Happily gazing upon the Bodhisattva a thousand turns.
Having received the proclamation of Dharma's flavor, granting understanding for the fast,
Resting and bathing in discourse to resolve my heart.
In return, I have no other rare treasures,
Only offering heavenly maidens as my tribute.
Accept them for me,
Do not doubt or guess,
From now on, I have no wish to return to the upper realms.
I vow to be my elder brother's disciple,
Forever serving the Bodhisattva, circling the flower platform.
Relying on the power of the Way,
I beg for your compassionate mercy,
Fulfill my sincere feelings and understand my heart.
If you have a vow to bestow, you must accept,
Without fault in perception, certainly without fault.
Within the meditation hall,
There is no arrangement,
Solitude should be known as hard to share.
Day and night, teach them to sing grandly,
Morning and evening, ensure they are joyfully happy.
They have needlework skills,
Exquisite and hard to match,
Serving and attending to please your heart's desire.
Unafraid to mend, spin, and embroider,
They can also prepare incense offerings daily.
Presenting a hundred kinds,
Offering a thousand times,
Moved by my elder brother's opening of Dharma teaching,
Twelve thousand heavenly maidens,
Do not decline to accept them—sing them forth!
(Sutra says): I say, Jiāoshījiā,
Do not use these improper things
To entice us, the Śramaṇa disciples of Śākyamuni.
This is not fitting for me.
(Plain speech): At that time, the Bodhisattva Chíshì said to the god Śakra: "I have heard that when the moon in the sky darkens,
It is because there are floating clouds;
When a precious mirror loses its luster,
It is all due to dust and grime.
Not yet attaining Buddhahood,
Is because of greed and anger;
Not escaping the cycle of rebirth,
Is entirely due to defiling desires.
Moreover, these heavenly maidens
Are all roots of greed and anger,
Remnants of hell's calamities,
Not fitting for a Bodhisattva's demeanor,
Not the view of a Śramaṇa.
Those who cultivate the path
Focus intently on ascetic practice,
With will purified and spirit clarified,
Considering fleeting glory as the light of flint,
Viewing human life as a candle in the wind." Chíshì told the false Śakra: "I have cultivated for a long time,
My understanding of Dharma is clear,
I cannot accept your human sentiment,
Causing me to sink again into evil paths.
Moreover, these women and such,
Bound by the three obediences to the body,
Entangled by the five hindrances.
They take the body as the ultimate body,
They take the form as the ultimate form.
Therefore, I reject them like dust and dirt,
Relying on my own strength to cultivate.
Now I see I am about to realize (Bodhi),
I cannot allow myself to fall back.
Chíshì refused to accept the heavenly maidens,
There is a verse:
(Break): The three obediences and five hindrances are at their side,
The ten evils repeatedly entangle and bind them.
Buddha-nature grows dim and retreats because of this,
The true vehicle goes astray, pulled by them.
The cultivating Bodhisattva's heart can renounce,
The world-transcending eminent monk's mind does not look.
How many coming and going sink and drown,
All because defiling desires lose the root source.
(Plain): At that time, Chíshì said to Śakra: "I do not escape the three evil paths,
All because deluded by craving and attachment;
The fruit of Buddhahood not yet attained,
Is entirely due to desire's downfall.
I have already cultivated meditation contemplation,
Not defiling the dusty mind,
Wishing to transcend the world,
Hoping to seek benefit and happiness.
Śakra, do not speak to confuse me,
Jiāoshījiā, do not trouble people.
Do not give heavenly maidens to a Śramaṇa,
Do not bestow charming forms upon a Bodhisattva.
They are not what I love,
Nor should Chíshì be attached to them.
If I now love and accept them,
I will surely be slandered by others!
Śakra,
Śakra!
You must know,
You must know!
Take back your retinue,
I do not want the heavenly maidens.
The meditation hall is narrow and cramped,
Truly hard to accommodate;
The secluded dwelling is not spacious,
Without a door to receive them.
Moreover, on the path of cultivation,
Many people are not needed;
The gate to transcend the world
Should be quiet and still.
I have already transcended life and death,
Do not dwell in the river of craving,
Far removed from worldly toils,
Cast aside, residing beyond the sea of hindrances.
The filth of defilement,
Not a speck of impurity can stain;
The dust-covered □,
A tiny bit cannot adhere.
Wisdom perfected, I see the realization of Bodhi,
Outflows exhausted, desire clarifies the Dharma-eye.
If I accept now,
It is like a wild goose entering the net again;
If I receive today,
It is like a white deer caught once more in the tether.
I dare not,
I dare not!
How could I,
How could I!
Causing me to lose two stages,
Making my cultivation regress and fail.
Thank you for coming to my humble room,
Troubling you to leave the heavenly palace.
In the mountain forest, there is nothing to offer respectfully,
In the secluded room, I am ashamed of lacking proper hospitality.
The heavenly gate is extremely far,
The journey to the upper realms is distant.
White clouds gradually rise on the ridge,
The red sun is about to set.
I do not invite you to stay long in the room,
I urge you to return quickly;
Do not linger here,
Vainly wasting your energy.
A thousand times,
A thousand times!
Return quickly,
Return quickly!
Śakra, do not utter wild words,
I do not accept the heavenly maidens now.
(Chanting up and down): Do not give heavenly maidens to a Śramaṇa,
Do not trouble a Bodhisattva with retinues.
I have cultivated seeking to transcend the world,
Not allowing defiling desires to cling to body and mind.
The heavenly palace is far from here,
The return journey to the upper realms is also long.
The red sun is about to vanish behind the mountain,
White clouds again appear on the ridge.
You, Śakra, must return early now,
Take your retinue and go back.
Do not stay long in the room,
Do not utter wild words within the forest.
Those who cultivate should not doubt,
Bodhisattvas altogether do not want them.
A secluded room cannot retain retinues,
A meditation hall does not need many people.
I have heard that craving and attachment certainly lead to rebirth,
Defiling desires and retinues sink one into life and death.
I have already cultivated and attained the fruit of the Way,
Take these heavenly maidens back instead.
(Level tone): In the room, do not hesitate further,
The upper realms are distant; it is time to go.
Heavenly maidens' extravagance is not the matter,
Music and songs are also not suitable.
White clouds emerge faintly on the ridge,
The red sun gradually hangs on the mountain peak.
Do not stay here long,
Lead the heavenly maidens and return early.
I do not want them,
Take them back instead,
I do not wish for songs and music to disturb my heart.
Sitting peacefully should only be silent,
Cultivating meditation requires no one to come.
Thank you for the offering,
I am grateful in my heart,
Heavenly beings in a secluded room are hard to arrange.
Cleaning and sweeping would surely make people wonder,
Serving and attending would certainly cause others to guess.
Standing in the room,
Circling the meditation platform,
For you, I expound and open the meaning of Dharma.
Do not let charming forms defile me,
Do not bring heavenly maidens to trouble people.
I have cultivated long,
Emerged from the dust,
Already seen the true thusness, the path opening.
Accepting human sentiment would cause downfall,
Receiving your heavenly maidens would certainly lead to rebirth.
Do not stay long,
Must return quickly,
A thousand times, understand my heart today.
The heavenly maiden at that time refused to go,
so who will rescue and sing it forth?
"The Bodhisattva Dharmadhātu" Volume Two.
(The sūtra says): "The Buddha addressed Mañjuśrī,
'You go to Vimalakīrti to inquire about his illness.'"
(Narration) The words "the Buddha addressed"
are the Buddha's words of command.
Because at the assembly,
the Buddha addressed all the sages and worthies,
the five hundred śrāvakas,
the eight thousand bodhisattvas,
asking them one by one,
all said they were not up to the task.
All were reprimanded and scolded,
no one dared to go.
Considering talent and eloquence,
it must be Mañjuśrī.
Those other minor figures,
truly are not difficult to send.
Just now Śāriputra,
also was not capable.
Now relying on Mañjuśrī,
he is specially sent to inquire.
Thereupon, he spoke to Mañjuśrī, saying:
(Verse) Throughout the three thousand realms his name is known,
all say Mañjuśrī's arts and understanding are refined.
His form is like a lotus blooming alone,
his mind like a bright mirror reflecting a clear pool.
Constantly proclaiming the wondrous Dharma, evil mountains crumble;
explaining and expounding the true vehicle, obstacle oceans subside.
Today at the feast he must be appointed,
to act as my envoy to the city of Vaiśālī.
(Narration) Thereupon, at the assembly in the Jeta Grove,
he called to Mañjuśrī: "I trouble you to rise briefly from the flower dais,
and listen to my command this day.
I, for the great being Vimalakīrti,
who is ill in Vaiśālī;
the exalted one, the Golden Millet,
lies resting in his chamber.
In the assembly are eight thousand bodhisattvas,
at the feast are seen five hundred śrāvakas.
From the beginning, all were asked and dispatched,
up to the Buddha, yet no one dared to go.
Śāriputra, foremost in wisdom,
pleaded his case, saying he was utterly unable to bear it.
Mahākāśyapa, most venerable in virtue,
declined, citing old age and frailty.
Ten were asked,
all claimed to fear meeting Vimalakīrti;
the whole assembly was tasked,
those tasked feared the householder.
I also asked Maitreya,
and also the exalted Dharmadhātu.
Vimalaprabha declined in a thousand ways,
Śāriputra begged off with ten thousand pleas.
Capable of being the envoy,
it must be Mañjuśrī.
To match wits with Vimalakīrti,
only Wonderful Virtue can suffice.
You now act as my envoy,
personally go to Vaiśālī,
inquire into the root cause of the illness,
convey the Golden Immortal's sincere intent.
For my sake,
do not decline further;
heed your master's words,
and accept the task.
Moreover, you long ago achieved perfect enlightenment,
fulfilled the fruits over three incalculable eons,
are the teacher of the seven Buddhas,
the compassionate father of the four kinds of birth.
You left the Land of Wonderful Joy,
to aid my teaching mission.
Descended to the Sahā world,
manifesting in the form of a bodhisattva.
Your body adorned with jeweled necklaces,
radiant like the moon stretching across the sky;
your head covered with a golden crown,
pure as a lotus reflecting in water.
Your name alone surpasses the Dharma assembly,
the multitude of sages cannot match;
your eloquent discourse resounds throughout the feast,
praised throughout the five regions of India.
Your compassionate practice is widely spread,
encompassing the three wretched paths and six destinies;
your heart of rescuing the suffering is universally applied,
pervading the lands within the three thousandfold world system.
On the day of your birth,
ten auspicious signs appeared.
Manifesting the bodhisattva's supreme dignity,
displaying the great being's matchlessness.
Moreover, your eyebrows are curved like spring willows,
graceful and delicately fragrant;
your face is like the autumn moon,
bright, clear, and shining brilliantly.
With such virtue and conduct,
you are well-suited to face Vimalakīrti;
possessing such great renown,
you are fit to enter his chamber.
Moreover, the householder,
is afflicted with lingering illness,
long in speech and his calculations are not up to the task,
in debate he would likely be no match for you.
Do not decline,
but respectfully proceed forward.
Lead the great assembly and quickly leave the Jeta Grove,
display your dignified demeanor and promptly go to the chamber.
Dragon deities are all instructed to lead the way,
accompanying you together;
humans and devas all go along,
surrounding you on both sides.
Arriving there, see the householder,
convey the words of the compassionate father,
say my concern and affection run deep,
therefore I sent me to inquire.
The Buddha spoke a verse praising Mañjuśrī:
Again proclaimed at the assembly of the Muni,
to inquire of illness in Vaiśālī, the truth must be revealed.
Accept, and hope to leave the Dharma assembly,
follow my words, do not offer excuses.
Vimalakīrti in his chamber thinks of me earnestly,
lying ill, groaning, already half a month.
I hope you today understand my intent,
temporarily act as a comforter.
There is another verse addressed to Mañjuśrī:
(Verse) The assembly of eight thousand bodhisattvas is hard to match,
all say Mañjuśrī's eloquence is sufficient.
Long have you been the teacher of the seven sages,
your name marks the three times, titled Thus-Come One.
With spiritual power you can destroy evil mountains,
with wisdom you can melt away obstacle oceans.
To act as my envoy to the chamber,
you must quickly go and leave the flower dais.
(Alternating meter) At the World-Honored One's assembly, he addressed Mañjuśrī: To act as envoy, go today to the chamber.
Convey my intent to Vimalakīrti's place,
extend my earnest inquiry, do not delay.
Earlier in the assembly, all the śrāvakas,
each declined, saying they would not go.
All spoke of the great being Vimalakīrti,
all said of Vaiśālī, "I am not up to it."
Among them, Maitreya also declined,
at the feast, Vimalaprabha earnestly pleaded.
Eight thousand great beings, none would go,
five hundred hearers (śrāvakas), not one went.
You now please quickly prepare,
by all means act as my envoy and go.
A dignified procession follows along,
heading to Vaiśālī to inquire of Vimalakīrti.
The bodhisattva, as teacher of the seven Buddhas,
long ago verified complete merit, Buddha of the three times.
Personally left the pure land to come to the mortal world,
to aid me in proclaiming and turning the Dharma wheel.
Majestic, his body like a golden mountain,
magnificent, unmatched among the multitude.
Eyebrows distinct, bright as the three autumn moons,
face depicted, fragrant as the nine summer lotuses.
Fit to be a comforter in the chamber,
fit to engage in debate with Vimalakīrti.
Fit to lead the great assembly from the Jeta Grove,
fit to be an envoy to Vaiśālī.
Follow my command and proceed ahead,
please now leave the Dharma assembly.
If you meet the great being Vimalakīrti,
inquire into the origin and cause of his illness.
Mañjuśrī's virtue is heard of in the ten directions,
Wonderful Virtue's spiritual powers are spoken of throughout a hundred koṭis.
Able to crush non-Buddhist paths, all return to the right,
able to dispatch demon armies, all hide away.
Follow my command and quickly go forward,
follow my direction and go to the chamber.
Earnestly comfort and inquire of Vimalakīrti,
skillfully use words to ask Vimalakīrti.
Then the holy lord stirred like spring thunder,
myriads of dragon deities arranged on all sides.
Seeing that Mañjuśrī would personally inquire of the illness,
the assembly of humans and devas rejoiced heartily.
Then he rose and stood in the feast,
palms joined respectfully, approaching the precious dais.
Because praising Vimalakīrti, his name is extolled to the utmost,
how then to the Buddha also sing it forth?
(The sūtra says): "Mañjuśrī" up to "go there to inquire about his illness."
This recitation of the sūtra text is divided into three parts: First, Mañjuśrī modestly declines and addresses the Buddha;
second, he praises the householder.
The sūtra says: "That exalted one" up to "all have been liberated";
third, relying on the Buddha's spiritual power,
he dares to go inquire about the illness.
The sūtra says: Even so,
I receive the Buddha's holy decree.
Now the first,
Mañjuśrī, receiving the Buddha's address,
rose in the midst of the feast,
wishing to express the debt to his teacher,
modestly declining his own capability.
Joining his ten fingers in reverence,
standing in the feast,
he addressed the compassionate honored one of the three realms,
before the assembly.
Mañjuśrī spoke a verse to the Buddha:
(Verse) Specially favored by the compassionate father, who proclaimed in the assembly,
Feeling gratitude toward Móuní, how could I not be devoted?
I reflect on my own emptiness and lack of eloquence,
My wisdom and discernment are not yet complete.
The golden envoy has already been sent to the Vimalakīrti’s chamber,
The wondrous virtue must follow the great enlightened sage.
If I go, I will not refuse to serve as the envoy,
Fortunately relying on the holy power to bestow grace and compassion.
There is also a verse in praise of Vimalakīrti:
(Verse) Vimalakīrti of the chamber possesses ample eloquence,
His words flow like a vast river, difficult for the multitude to match.
He can speak wondrous dharma, shattering the mountain of evil,
He expounds the true sutras, turning back the ocean of obstacles.
Each day for the six realms, he spreads the net of teachings,
Constantly saving those in the three wretched paths from the cycle of rebirth.
Though he is a layperson like ordinary folk,
His mind is like the autumn moon shining through the mist.
(Prose) Expressing feelings and humbly declining,
Many serve as envoys to Vaiśālī;
Praising that Pure Name,
Shows the difficulty of facing that superior being.
Five hundred śrāvakas,
Attained the eight wisdoms within themselves;
Three thousand bodhisattvas,
Transcended the ten stages in the assembly.
Though Mañjuśrī received the sacred decree,
That day he pondered a thousand thoughts.
He only intended to decline within the feast,
But feared going against the Tathāgata’s words.
He only wished to serve as envoy to the chamber,
But felt ashamed before the eminent ones in the assembly.
If the World-Honored One sends me,
Today I will certainly go to the chamber.
Then Mañjuśrī spoke a verse:
(Verse) Since I have received the earnest command from the holy lord,
I dare not decline but will speak before the assembly.
Bearing the decree, I will go to the chamber,
To proclaim grace and see the honored Pure Name.
Where the golden crown moves, auspicious light appears,
When the moon-like face relaxes, auspicious colors renew.
On this day, all sages and worthies will go,
I, as the leader, will accompany them all.
(Prose) Mañjuśrī received the Buddha’s instruction,
Rose from the flower platform,
Adjusted his crown of a hundred jewels,
Moved his necklace of eight treasures.
The fragrant wind rustled,
Shaking jade pendants with a tinkling sound;
Auspicious colors swirled densely,
Causing pearl garments to glisten.
Just now, the compassionate holy lord,
Proclaimed in the assembly;
The great enlightened Móuní,
Spoke words at the feast.
A thousand praises,
How could I bear them?
A hundred discussions,
Truly make me apprehensive.
The World-Honored One sends me as envoy,
To go and inquire of Vimalakīrti;
That superior being,
Is difficult to respond to.
Moreover, though Mañjuśrī holds the position of a bodhisattva,
In principle, he is not fully knowledgeable;
Within the Buddha’s assembly,
His words are not outstanding.
The World-Honored One sends me as envoy,
I dare not decline.
Bearing the Buddha’s command, I fear I may not be competent,
Relying on holy power, I surely can go.
I submit that Vimalakīrti, the layperson,
Possesses four kinds of eloquence,
Said to be unmatched;
Displays vast supernatural powers,
Rashly not easy.
Deeply penetrating true reality,
Well attuned to the minds of all Buddhas;
Unobstructed in verbal skill,
A model for the speech of bodhisattvas.
Holding all secrets,
There is nothing he does not know;
Sounds of upper, middle, and lower classes,
He fully comprehends them all.
If I go to inquire now,
I am truly ashamed of my incompetence;
I must rely on holy majesty,
Then I can go.
Thus, Mañjuśrī accepted,
The great assembly rejoiced,
Hastily discussing in the Āmrapālī Garden,
Following Mañjuśrī to the chamber.
(Side chant) Mañjuśrī addressed the compassionate lord,
Received the Buddha’s full instruction in the assembly.
Sent to Vaiśālī to inquire of Pure Name,
Ashamed of my shallow words, how can I go?
The World-Honored One’s instructions are earnestly detailed,
I dare not express my sincere feelings at the feast,
If sent to Vaiśālī to inquire of Pure Name,
From afar, I rely on the great sage to bestow protection.
Vimalakīrti,
Lord of Golden Millet,
Long possessed the merit of four wisdoms and three bodies,
If sent, I must inquire of Pure Name,
From afar, I rely on the great sage to bestow protection.
Unobstructed eloquence is Vimalakīrti,
Deeply penetrating the intent of all Buddhas,
Inquiring of illness in Vaiśālī, I fear incompetence,
From afar, I rely on the great sage to bestow protection.
The World-Honored One specially proclaimed in the assembly,
Sent me to go to the chamber in Vaiśālī,
Facing Vimalakīrti as an opponent, I fear incompetence,
I must rely on the great sage to bestow protection.
My current understanding of arts is truly inadequate,
Unworthily receiving the Tathāgata’s sheltering grace,
Inquiring of illness in Vaiśālī, I fear incompetence,
From afar, I rely on the great sage to bestow protection.
Honored Golden Millet,
Named the Tamer,
Manifesting as a layperson dwelling in Vaiśālī,
Since receiving the Tathāgata’s instruction to inquire,
From afar, I rely on the great sage to bestow protection.
Going to Vaiśālī,
Bidding farewell to the transforming lord,
Hesitating means setting out on the journey,
Today bearing inquiry to Vimalakīrti,
From afar, I rely on the great sage to bestow protection.
(Verse) Since I have received the earnest command from the holy lord,
Today I shall be the one to inquire of illness.
Bearing the decree, I should leave the dharma assembly,
Holding grace, I must go to proclaim and state.
At this time, through debate, remove deluded attachments,
In this discourse, expound and reveal the true reality.
Surely causing dragons and gods to open the eye of dharma,
Teaching the eight classes to awaken to profound causes.
(Sutra) Mañjuśrī, in the assembly, expressed his feelings,
From afar, praising Vimalakīrti’s ample eloquence.
This time, certainly bearing the decree to go,
Fully relying on our Tathāgata.
In the śrāvaka assembly, noisy clamor,
In the bodhisattva feast, vast urging.
Though not yet departed from the holy lord,
Who will discuss and chant what is to come?
(Sutra says): “Then in the assembly” up to “all wished to follow.”
Thus, Mañjuśrī accepted,
To serve as envoy to Vaiśālī.
To convey the words of the holy lord,
To inquire of the great being Vimalakīrti.
In the assembly were eight thousand bodhisattvas,
In the feast five hundred śrāvakas,
Seeing Mañjuśrī going to inquire of illness in Vaiśālī,
All wished to accompany as companions.
In threes and fives,
All wished to follow the vehicle.
Regardless of gods or yakṣas,
All said they would serve as attendants.
Then humans and gods were vast,
Dragon multitudes clamorous.
In the sky, scattering a hundred kinds of flowers,
On the ground, arranging the seven treasures.
The assemblies of Śakra and Brahmā,
Held jade banners before the lion throne;
Dragon kings and yakṣas,
Held precious streamers around the bodhisattva.
Though not yet departed from the Buddha’s assembly,
Their majesty had already left the Āmrapālī Garden.
Conch shells and cymbals struck with clanging sounds,
Music played with resonant melodies.
Asuras tuned the clear-sounding pipa,
Kiṃnara kings struck the variegated drum.
Gandharva multitudes blew wondrous tunes in the clouds,
Garuḍa kings played flute music in the sky.
At that time, in the Āmrapālī Garden assembly,
Holy beings were boundless.
Mañjuśrī was about to bid farewell to the World-Honored One,
The great assembly all spoke of accompanying.
Bhikṣuṇīs vied to burn sandalwood incense,
Upāsikās each competed to burn dragon brain.
All begged to follow the great being,
In unison addressing the World-Honored One.
Wishing the Buddha to permit following Mañjuśrī,
To go inquire of the layperson Vimalakīrti.
The compassionate lord permitted,
The great assembly rejoiced.
Surrounding the patriarch of the seven Buddhas,
