Passing to the stone chamber of one zhang.
(Side chant) Vimalakīrti lies ill in the chamber,
The Buddha sends Mañjuśrī specially to inquire.
Proclaimed to dragons, gods, and spirits,
Filling sky and road, people without measure.
The Buddha descended,
Arranged the ceremonial guard,
Śakra and Brahmā kings also ordered to go.
Regardless of Garuḍas or Gandharvas,
Drum music and clear songs freely played and sung.
Kiṃnaras,
Yakṣa generals,
Wanting to go, the Tathāgata does not obstruct.
Praising dharma, crushing evil, arranged left and right,
Vast and clamorous, all joyful and elated.
Heroes arrayed,
All resist and oppose,
Their majestic divine forms make demons lose courage.
Outwardly radiating awe, inwardly harboring compassion,
At that time, all wished to approach the abbot's chamber.
Tens of thousands, all gallant and unrestrained,
Their momentum like the vast ocean pushing giant waves.
Chaotic and surging, all willing to proceed,
Group after group, each with its own distinct appearance.
Bodhisattva monks,
Small or tall,
All, under the compassionate Venerable One's vow, follow along.
Devout men and women also accompany,
Each and every Tathāgata without hindrance.
Arranged in order,
Extremely clear and bright,
The sounds of flutes, zithers, harps, and reed pipes resound.
Incense burners emit sandalwood and precious blended fragrances,
Tens of thousands, all with palms joined in reverence.
Mañjuśrī is modest,
The World-Honored One praises,
Bodhisattvas and śrāvakas, the small serve the great.
They must lead the multitude on their journey,
Without delay or hesitation, lingering for a moment's meal.
Mañjuśrī takes his leave,
All gaze with reverence,
Carrying the command to Vaiśālī to expound the profound teachings.
To witness Vimalakīrti's skill in expounding the Dharma,
Together they bow in farewell to the golden form.
Arriving there,
They see the master of Dharma,
To engage in切磋琢磨, they must be clear and bright,
Universally enabling humans and devas to awaken to true reality,
Together they bow in gratitude to the golden form.
Bathing in the compassion of the Venerable One,
All are granted permission,
To enter Vaiśālī, due to past causes from long ago,
Encountering two venerable ones who discourse on emptiness,
Together they bow in gratitude to the golden form.
Scattering fragrant flowers,
Riding precious elephants,
The golden-maned lion is the foremost,
Going to escort Mañjuśrī to inquire about the source of the illness,
Together they temporarily bid farewell to the golden form.
Voices clamorous,
Music resounding brightly,
The majestic virtue and awe-inspiring presence, supreme among the supreme,
Eight thousand Bodhisattvas and śrāvakas,
Together they temporarily bid farewell to the golden form.
Devas, humans, and Bodhisattvas now arrayed,
Surrounding Mañjuśrī by a hundred million multitudes.
Some hold precious flowers scattering in the sky,
Some present wondrous melodies echoing lingeringly.
Dragon deities stride through mist leading the way,
Ghostly minions fly on clouds urging from behind.
Having left the World-Honored One's Dharma assembly,
Unaware of how their majestic demeanor will be chanted henceforth.
(Sūtra says): "Thereupon Mañjuśrī" up to "entered the city."
(Narration) Mañjuśrī accepts,
Leads the multitude forward.
Five hundred śrāvakas accompany together,
Eight thousand Bodhisattvas serve as companions.
Thereupon, at the assembly in the Āmra Garden,
The listening crowd is boundless.
Accompanying the Great Being, all proceed to Vaiśālī,
Following Mañjuśrī, together passing to the abbot's chamber.
The season is spring scenery,
A thousand flowers vie in smiling within the gardens and woods;
The festival arrives with verdant brightness,
Ten thousand trees all flourish in the mountains and fields.
Thus, Mañjuśrī,
Personally goes into the midst of the abbot's chamber.
Thereupon, establishing majestic demeanor,
Arranging the baggage in order.
Thereupon, a precious crown covers the head,
Jeweled necklaces adorn the body.
Bidding farewell to the World-Honored One on the thousand-flower platform,
To inquire of the layman within the one-zhang room.
Dragon deities lead the way,
Bodhisattvas welcome ahead.
Auspicious energy fills the sky,
Heavenly flowers reflect the sun.
Banners and pennants line the road in pairs,
Dragon standards proceed in rows ahead.
Halo light vies in brilliance with the dazzling sun,
Elegant music blends harmoniously with Brahmā sounds.
Eight thousand Bodhisattvas attend and follow,
Five hundred śrāvakas travel together.
Simultaneously bowing in farewell to the Compassionate Venerable One,
All hasten to Vimalakīrti to inquire about his illness.
At this time,
The crowd is vast,
Voices clamorous.
Chaotically in the clouds,
Jubilant cheers under the sun.
Restraining the auspicious energy of verdant peaks,
Scattering the lingering auspicious glow.
The uṣṇīṣa lofty and towering,
Pearl garments dazzlingly bright.
Dragging the exquisite robe of six śarāvas,
Wearing the seven-jeweled head crown.
Gathered golden threads layered heavily,
Moving fragrant breezes trailing continuously.
Leading the mighty lion,
Each step can prolong the wind.
Seated on the thousand-petaled lotus,
Containing the emerald hue of misty waters.
Leading the multitude of heavenly followers,
Departing from the Buddha's assembly in the Āmra Garden.
Heavenly maidens and heavenly youths,
Welcome ahead and encircle behind.
Transforming objects in the sky,
Gazing from afar within the clouds.
Orderly and majestic in demeanor,
Directing and commanding the followers.
All people in the city of Vaiśālī see,
All proclaim the supernatural powers are immensely awe-inspiring.
Mañjuśrī's procession is truly praiseworthy,
Temporarily parting from the holy abode of Māṇi.
Welcoming and leading immortal youths by thousands of troops,
Accompanying Bodhisattvas numerous as Ganges sands.
Golden crowns and jade pendants shine under the azure sun,
Cloud-like robes and pearl necklaces attract emerald clouds.
Lions, robust and sturdy, lead before and after,
Turning their bodies to sit upon the precious lotus.
(Interlude) The procession, high and low, lines the entire road,
Layer upon layer, section after section, reflecting the golden platform.
Golden censers and jade tables appear in the sky,
Dragon standards and banners unfold within the mist.
Bodhisattvas following along all leap with joy,
Śrāvakas from behind happily chuckle and laugh.
Before allowing eyes to open and see clearly,
They have already arrived at Vimalakīrti's assembly.
Truly rare,
The King of Dharma,
Manifesting traces, temporarily as Mañjuśrī.
Gold and purple illuminate the treasures within the robe,
Between the brows, at times emitting white hair-tip light.
The auspicious form on the flower platform appears from time to time,
The lotus seat, wondrous and extraordinary, has another name.
In an instant, they pass the abbot's chamber,
Eagerly hastening, wishing to pay respects to the King of Dharma.
(Interlude) Śrāvakas vast and numerous fill the empty sky,
Bodhisattvas clamorously enter the room.
Canopies and parasols descend from cloud-tops filling the road,
Banner flowers within the mist resound delicately.
Dragon deities, distinguished and eminent, all snap their fingers,
Praising Mañjuśrī's purple-golden countenance.
Filling Vimalakīrti's abbot's chamber everywhere,
Be they ordinary or sage, by thousands upon thousands.
(Interlude) The accompanying listeners number boundlessly,
All stand before Mañjuśrī's precious seat.
The eight classes cease chanting the fish-Brahmā tune,
The four heavenly kings' processions encircle the golden lotus.
In the sky, only heavenly flowers are seen falling,
Within the clouds, only camphor smoke is smelled.
Trillions of listening followers, vast and boundless,
Thousands of groups of holy multitudes, noisy and clamorous.
(Sūtra) Mañjuśrī's procession is truly marvelous,
Ordinary and sage accompanying, a hundred million multitudes.
Bodhisattvas surround the precious seat on both sides,
Śrāvakas encircle the flower platform on four sides.
From the Āmra Garden assembly, gazing and paying respects from afar,
Within the abbot's chamber feast, auspicious colors unfold.
The layman sees Mañjuśrī enter the room,
How it is arranged, also chant henceforth.
Regarding the fifteenth day of the seventh month,
the gates of heaven open,
the doors of hell are unlocked,
the karmic retributions of the three evil paths are extinguished,
and the ten virtues increase and grow.
It is the day when the monastic community concludes the summer retreat and engages in self-disclosure,
a day for gathering blessings,
when all deities, the eight classes of beings, dragons, and devas
all come to seek blessings.
Those who receive offerings gain blessings in the present life,
while the deceased are reborn in superior realms.
Thus, the Ullambana offering of a hundred delicacies
is respectfully presented to the Three Jewels.
Relying on the compassionate radiance of the great assembly,
it rescues those in dire straits, hanging upside down in suffering.
In the past, when the Buddha was in the world,
there was a disciple named Mùlián.
Before leaving home to become a monk,
his name was Luóbǔ.
He deeply believed in the Three Jewels
and revered the Mahāyāna.
Once, intending to travel to another country for trade,
he divided his wealth and treasures,
instructing his mother to hold vegetarian feasts in his absence,
making offerings to the Buddhas, the Dharma, the Saṅgha, and all who came begging.
After Luóbǔ departed,
his mother developed a miserly heart.
All the assets entrusted to her
she secretly concealed for herself.
Before many weeks or months had passed,
her son completed his affairs and returned home.
His mother told him: "As you instructed,
I prepared vegetarian feasts to cultivate merit."
Thus, having deceived both ordinary people and saints,
upon her death she fell into the Avīci Hell,
enduring severe sufferings.
After Luóbǔ completed the three-year mourning rites,
he went to the Buddha, left home, and became a monk.
Due to past habitual causes,
he heard the Dharma and attained the fruit of Arhatship.
He then used his divine eye to search for his beloved mother
throughout the six paths of birth and death,
but could not find her anywhere.
Mùlián arose from meditation
and, filled with sorrow, inquired of the World-Honored One: "In which direction does my kind mother now experience happiness?"
At that time, the World-Honored One replied to Mùlián: "Your mother has already fallen into Avīci,
where she is undergoing various sufferings.
Although you have attained the holy fruit,
what do you intend to do?
Unless it is the day when the Saṅgha of the ten directions concludes the summer retreat and achieves liberation,
only through the collective power [of the Saṅgha] can she be saved."
Therefore, out of compassion,
the Buddha opened this expedient means,
establishing the Ullambana basin offering—
this is the matter at hand.
After his parents passed away, Luóbǔ
completed the three-year mourning rites with ritual weeping.
Hearing music brought no joy, his appearance wasted away;
eating delicacies brought no sweetness, his sinews and bones pained.
Hearing that the Tathāgata was at the Deer Park,
where all humans and devas received solace,
he thought, "I shall now seek the Way and find the Tathāgata,"
and went to the Twin Sāla Trees to inquire of the Buddha.
At that time, the Buddha himself paced slowly,
and [Mùlián] bowed his head to the Teacher, the One with the Twofold Honor.
To his left and right were the great assemblies of Śakra and Brahmā,
east and west the great generals and the god Sañjaya.
On his chest, the svastika mark shone like crystal;
behind his head, a circular halo resembled the disc of the moon.
To know the hundred jewels and thousand flowers upon him
was like gazing upon five-colored clouds at the edge of the sky.
"This disciple, foolish and dwelling in the five desires,
cannot abandon and leave behind greed and anger.
Simply because my past transgressions are heavy,
misfortune has reached my kind mother, drawing her into the gate of the springs [of the underworld].
I fear only the pressing of impermanence,
sinking in the sea of suffering, the ford of birth and death.
I pray the Buddha in his compassion will deliver this disciple,
that I may concentrate on learning the Way to repay my two parents."
When the World-Honored One heard Luóbǔ speak,
he knew he was upright, his heart not deviant.
First, bending his fingers, he expounded the Four Noble Truths;
later, he spoke of what should be avoided—the seven disqualifications.
Even if one amassed treasures reaching the clouds and Milky Way,
it would not equal teaching someone to leave home, even temporarily.
It is like a blind turtle encountering a floating log;
it is like a lotus flower emerging from a great fire.
The blazing house of fire is hard to escape;
the vast sea of suffering is boundless and shoreless.
Precisely because sentient beings make distinctions,
the Tathāgata therefore established the three vehicles.
The Buddha called Ānanda to shave his head;
his garments transformed into monastic robes.
Instantly he realized the fruit of Arhatship,
and later received the Prātimokṣa precepts.
At that time, Luóbǔ stood before the Buddha;
from the golden censer, puffs of incense smoke arose.
Six kinds of jeweled forests shook the great earth;
four types of flowers, their forms marking purity, adorned the clear sky.
A thousand kinds of brocade spread over seats and couches;
ten thousand strands of beaded banners hung suspended in the air.
The Buddha himself declared, "This is my disciple,
named the Great Mùlián of Supernatural Powers."
At that time, Mùlián, beneath the Twin Sāla Trees,
attained the fruit of Arhatship.
Why is this so?
According to the Lotus Sūtra: "The poor son first received his wages,
and afterward removed the dung"—
this is precisely it.
First he attained the Arhat fruit,
and afterward practiced the path.
Observe the place where Mùlián sat in meditation deep in the mountains:
After Mùlián shaved off his hair and beard,
he took himself deep into the mountains.
In a secluded, pure place where no people dwelled,
he contemplated emptiness and sat in meditation.
Sitting in meditation, contemplating emptiness, he knew good and evil;
subduing the mind, fixing the mind, without attachment.
Facing objects, clear and still, unmoving, unshaken,
the left foot still must press upon the right.
Sitting upright upon a flat rock,
the tongue placed against the upper palate.
White bones all become empty;
breath and energy do not clash.
At that time, herds of deer rested in the chanting forest,
drawing near the clear pond, gazing toward the sea's edge.
Bright moonlight in the courtyard listened with the Dharma-eye;
green mountains under the pines—there only meditation sat.
At the horizon, sea-mists transformed like radiant clouds;
beyond the ridges, green hills looked toward frontier towers.
The autumn wind rustled through the forest;
yellow leaves drifted and floated on the water.
Mùlián sat peacefully in the realm of emptiness,
purifying mind within and without, gradually cultivating.
Penetrating the Śrāvaka vehicle, he dwelt in the holy ground;
entering and leaving the mountains, he attained freedom.
Mùlián emerged from concentration,
swiftly performing supernatural feats.
Coming like a sudden clap of thunder,
going like a gust of wind.
Sea geese cried, fearing the bowstring;
wild geese escaped the netted cage.
In the pool, mist and haze were jade-green;
the sky pure, the distant road crimson.
With supernatural powers, he gained mastery;
tossing his alms bowl, he soared into the sky.
Then in a single direction,
he ascended to the Brahmā heaven palace.
Mùlián went straight to the heavenly court,
where his ears heard only the sounds of drums and music.
Vermilion towers half-reflected golden halls;
jade-green windows, all perfectly formed of white jade.
His monk's staff knocked three or five times at the gate;
unconsciously, tears brimmed in his breast.
An elder came out and spoke with him,
joining palms, first discussing feelings of loyalty and filial piety.
He addressed him: "Elder, do you recognize me?
This humble monk is from Jambudvīpa in the south.
From youth, I suffered the loss of my parents.
My family was greatly wealthy but had few children or descendants;
alone and solitary, I also had no companions.
My kind mother was named Qīngtí,
my father was named Fǔxiàng.
Throughout their lives they cultivated many fields of merit;
having passed away, they should be reborn here in this heaven.
Alas, this place of wealth, honor, and luxury—
gazing upon it fills one's heart with joy and ease.
Bells and drums resound in harmonious, elegant tones;
zithers and lutes also sound clear and bright.
Endlessly, the toils of parental care never cease;
the kindness of nursing and nurturing is hard to forget.
After parting, have you been peaceful and well?
I have come here to this place to seek and visit."
The elder, hearing his words, seemed sorrowful in intent;
his heart troubled, he spoke slowly:
"This disciple in Jambudvīpa had a son,
but I do not recall having a son who left home.
Venerable monk, do not take offense at my earnest questioning;
in the world, human relations are of several kinds.
At first glance, speaking out may seem easy;
but when gathering one's thoughts, it becomes somewhat difficult.
In the mundane world, there are many with the same name;
similar appearances number in the hundreds.
I do not recognize your features as having met before;
simply pondering, I find no place to settle [this recognition].
Ācārya, you insistently come to claim recognition;
speak further of the affairs and circumstances of your home."
Mùlián arrived at the celestial palace to search for his father,
reaching a gate where he saw an elder,
and addressed him: “In my youth,
my name was Luóbǔ.
After my parents passed away,
I took refuge in the Buddha and left home,
shaved off my hair and beard,
and was given the name Mahāmaudgalyāyana,
foremost in supernatural powers.
” Hearing the name from his youth,
the elder immediately knew it was his son: “It has been so long,
have you been well?
” Luóbǔ Mùlián recognized his compassionate father,
and after exchanging greetings and inquiries: “Where is my compassionate mother now, enjoying happiness?
” The elder replied to Luóbǔ: “While your mother was alive,
her actions differed from mine.
I cultivated the ten virtues and five precepts,
and after death, my consciousness was reborn in heaven.
Your mother, during her lifetime,
committed numerous sins.
After her life ended,
she fell into hell.
You should go to the dark paths of Jambudvīpa,
inquire about your mother,
and you will know her whereabouts.
” Hearing this,
Mùlián bid farewell to the elder,
and descended swiftly to southern Jambudvīpa,
heading toward the dark paths.
He searched for his mother but could not find her,
and instead saw eight or nine men and women,
idle and with nothing to do.
Mùlián stepped forward to ask about the situation:
please, do not bow.
Who are you, virtuous ones,
gathered here together?
Idle with nothing to do,
you roam outside the city walls.
This humble monk has come here today,
and in my heart, I deeply wonder.
The people replied to the monk:
“Only because we share the same name and surname,
we were mistakenly summoned here.
After being examined for just three to five days,
we were released without issue and sent back.
But our wives and children had already sent us to the graves,
leaving us alone in the desolate wilderness.
With no relatives or companions around,
foxes, wolves, crows, and magpies competed to scatter us.
Our homes are ruined with nowhere to turn,
and our pleas to the king are filled with sorrowful voices.
Judged to become idle ghosts with nothing to do,
what further calamities await us from our remaining retribution?
Now, the paths of life and death are separated,
once the gate of the springs is closed, it never opens again.
Even if there were a thousand kinds of food on the grave,
how could it ever relieve the hunger in our bellies?
Wailing and crying are ultimately of no use,
only vainly troubling others to burn paper as money.
Send a message to the men and women at home,
urging them to cultivate blessings to rescue us from infernal calamities.
After a long while, Mùlián spoke: “Do you know a Lady Qīngtí?
” The people replied: “None of us know her.
” Mùlián asked again: “Where does King Yánluó reside?
” The people replied: “Monk,
walk north a few more steps,
and from afar you will see a triple-tiered gate tower,
with thousands of strong men holding knives and clubs—
that is the gate of King Yánluó.
” Hearing this,
Mùlián walked north a few more steps,
and immediately saw the triple-tiered gate tower,
with strong men driving countless sinners inside.
Mùlián stepped forward to inquire about his mother but could not find her,
so he wept loudly by the roadside,
and after crying, he continued forward,
until he was brought before the king by the officials.
The gate officers led him in to see the great king,
who asked Mùlián about the matter:
When the great king saw Mùlián enter,
he clasped his hands and hesitated, about to stand.
“Monk, what brings you here?
” He hurriedly bowed from behind his desk:
“I am ashamed that the ācārya has come here,
Your disciple resides in the dark paths,
interrogating sinners about life and death.
Although I do not know the monk personally,
I have long known his name.
Have you come here as an envoy of the Buddha?
Or is there some personal matter?
The judgments of Tàishān are difficult to alter,
all are recorded by the celestial and earthly scribes.
The retribution of sinners arises according to their karma,
who can hastily save them?
The stench of blood and fat lingers in the long night,
defiling the ācārya’s pure robes.
You must not stay long in the dark paths,
I implore the ācārya to depart early.
Mùlián spoke: “Do not say that,
does the great king not know?
In my life, I had parents,
who observed fasting daily and abstained from food after noon.
Based on their deeds in the human world,
after death, they should have been reborn in the pure land.
In heaven, only my father resides,
but my compassionate mother is nowhere to be found among the heavens.
She should not have passed through hell either,
I only fear the heavens have unjustly condemned her.
I have searched everywhere between heaven and earth,
sighing long with grief and regret.
If her retribution has brought her to this realm,
would the great king know of it?
When Mùlián finished speaking,
the great king summoned him to the hall,
and there he saw the Bodhisattva Dìzàng,
and immediately bowed in reverence.
“Have you come to seek your mother?
” Mùlián replied: “Yes, I have come to seek my mother.
” “While your mother was alive,
she committed numerous sins,
immeasurable and boundless,
and is destined to fall into hell.
You go ahead,
I will arrive shortly.
” The great king then summoned the karma officials, life monitors, and record keepers,
who arrived immediately.
“This monk’s mother is named Lady Qīngtí,
how long has she been dead?
” The karma official reported to the great king: “Lady Qīngtí has been dead for three years,
her assigned sin records are all in the celestial registry office, the Tàishān commandant’s ledger.
” The king called the two童子 of good and evil,
and sent them to Tàishān to check in which hell Lady Qīngtí was located.
The great king said to the monk: “Accompany the童子,
and inquire with General Wǔdào,
he should know the whereabouts.
” Hearing this,
Mùlián bid farewell to the great king and left.
After walking a few steps,
he reached the banks of the River Nàihé,
where he saw countless sinners,
taking off their clothes and hanging them on trees,
wailing loudly several times,
hesitating to cross,
turning back and forth in panic,
in groups of five and three,
holding their heads and weeping.
Mùlián asked about the situation:
The waters of the Nàihé flow swiftly westward,
the path is rugged with sharp rocks, difficult to traverse.
Clothes are taken off and hung on tree branches,
driven relentlessly, not allowed to stand still for a moment.
Hearing their names called by the riverbank,
tears unconsciously soak their chests and clothes.
Only today do they realize they have died,
clinging to trees in pairs, weeping in long sorrow.
In life, I cherished my treasures in my home,
golden carriages with four horses and vermilion wheels.
Thinking they would never change for ten thousand ages,
who knew they would turn to dust so soon.
Alas, the pain in my heart,
only burying white bones to build high mounds.
The dragon-horse from the southern stable is ridden by descendants,
the fragrant carriage by the northern window is used by wives and concubines.
All say it is beyond words,
sighing long, what more is there to resent?
Those who commit sins fall into hell,
those who do good are sure to be reborn in heaven.
Now each follows their own karma,
surely it will be difficult to meet again later.
Holding hands, urging each other to strive,
turning back, wiping tears, gazing at each other intently.
In their ears, they only hear urgent calls,
thousands upon thousands driven forward.
Ox-Head holds a club on the south bank of the river,
jailers raise tridents on the north side of the water.
Those in the water gaze with longing eyes,
those on the shore shed streams of tears.
Had they known the hardships after death,
they would regret not cultivating fields of merit while alive.
Mùlián asked the people under the Nàihé trees: “Heaven and hell are not empty illusions,
committing evil is not only condemned by heaven,
but also punished by the spirits of the underworld.
My compassionate mother did not accumulate good deeds,
and her departed soul has also fallen into the three wretched paths.
I heard she was to enter hell,
do you know any news of her?
The sinners all saw Master Mùlián,
everyone weeping, their brows furrowed in distress:
“We disciples died not long ago,
and truly do not know of the monk’s compassionate mother.
We committed many sins while alive,
and only now, suffering, do we begin to regret.”
Even if wives and concubines fill the mountains and rivers,
Who would be willing to die in their stead?
When will they ever leave the gate of the underworld,
To report to my descendants at home:
Do not need jade for coffins,
Nor waste gold to bury in the grave mound.
Long lamentations and sighs are ultimately of no benefit,
For I cannot hear the music of drums, strings, or songs.
To free the deceased from suffering and hardship,
Nothing surpasses cultivating blessings to save the souls in the underworld.
The monk then returned,
To convey the message to all,
Instructing them to create blessings,
To save the deceased.
Apart from the Buddha alone,
No one else can save them.
May the monk attain Bodhi and Nirvana,
Everlasting and undiminished.
Transporting all sentient beings,
Sharply honing the sword of wisdom,
Sweeping away the forest of afflictions and destroying them,
Practicing universal compassion in the world,
Is the great vow of all Buddhas.
If one escapes the hells,
It is due to the monk’s universal compassion descending.
After hearing this, Mùlián
Proceeded further ahead.
After a while,
He arrived at the seat of General Wǔdào,
To inquire about his mother’s whereabouts:
General Wǔdào’s nature is fierce and terrifying,
His golden armor gleaming, sword lights crisscrossing.
To his left and right are over a million,
All swift and agile in movement.
Their shouts are like thunder, shaking the heavens,
Their angry eyes flash like lightning, dazzling as cranes.
Some have their bellies split and hearts exposed,
Some have their faces skinned alive.
Though Mùlián is a sage,
Even his soul is startled and courage fails.
Mùlián weeps, thinking of his compassionate mother,
His divine powers swift as wind and clouds.
If one speaks of the crucial places in the underworld,
None surpass this great general.
To his left and right, spears block the main road,
East and west, over ten thousand stand with staffs.
Even if one raises their eyes to gaze southwest,
They will see the towering god of the five paths.
Guarding this road for countless kalpas.
Thousands of troops and masses determine punishments,
Each from beginning to end follows their karmic deeds.
“My compassionate mother, a lay devotee,
Her soul drifts along the paths of the underworld.
If asked where the three evil paths are most painful,
All say it is the ghost gate of the five paths.
The paths of beasts and evil are crowded,
While the path to heaven is idle morning and night.
All sinners pass through here,
I humbly beg the general to search for her.
The general clasped his hands and addressed the monk: “Do not weep and harm your dignified appearance.
Countless as the sands of the Ganges pass this road,
Suddenly asked, who knows Qīngtí?
Tàishān holds many registers of names,
Verified with the heavenly and earthly offices.
Official documents each have their names,
Orders come down and pass through here.
Today, your disciple is an underworld official,
(Temporarily) helping the monk search and look.
If indeed her name is found,
Tracing her whereabouts will not be difficult.
The general asked his attendants: “Have you seen a Lady Qīngtí?”
An official on the left addressed the general: “Three years ago,
There was a Lady Qīngtí,
Summoned by warrant from the Avīci Hell,
Now suffering in the Avīci Hell.”
Hearing this, Mùlián
Addressed the general: “General, please inform the monk,
All sinners are judged by the king,
Only then do they descend.
Why has my mother not seen the king’s face?”
The general replied to the monk: “In the world, two kinds of people do not see the king’s face: The first kind,
During their lifetime,
Cultivated the ten virtues and five precepts,
After death, their consciousness ascends to heaven,
〔They do not see the king’s face〕.
The second kind,
During their lifetime,
Did not cultivate good deeds,
Widely committed various sins,
After their life ends,
They enter hell directly,
And also do not see the king’s face.
Only those half-evil, half-good,
Will see the king’s face for judgment,
Only then are they reborn,
Receiving retribution according to their karma.
Hearing this, Mùlián
Went to search for his mother in the various hells:
Mùlián’s tears fall, remembering far and wide,
The karmic retribution of sentient beings is like drifting wind.
When his compassionate mother reached this arduous place,
Her soul had long since dissipated.
Iron wheels often descend from the sky,
Fierce flames constantly burn beneath their feet.
Hearts and intestines everywhere are scattered,
Bones, when sought, are like charred ruins.
Copper birds in tens of thousands peck at hearts,
Molten iron pours a thousand times over their heads.
If asked about the suffering of the sword tree ahead,
How does it compare to being ground and cut at the waist?
Beyond description,
Congealed fat and shattered blood like broth.
Vast and expansive, spanning hundreds of miles,
Towering downward for a yojana.
Iron pikes and ten thousand swords below, smoke and fire a thousand layers blocking the four gates.
If asked what crimes are here,
Only the killing sins of Jambudvīpa.
After speaking, Mùlián proceeded further ahead,
In a moment,
He reached a hell.
Mùlián addressed the hell warden: “Is there a Lady Qīngtí in this hell?
She is my mother,
I have come specifically to search for her.”
The hell warden replied to the monk: “This hell contains only men,
And no women.
Go ahead and ask at the Mountain of Knives hell,
You will surely find her there.”
Mùlián went ahead and reached another hell,
Named Mountain of Knives on the left,
Named Forest of Swords on the right.
Within this hell,
Blades and swords face each other,
Blood flows in streams.
He saw the hell warden driving countless sinners into this hell.
Mùlián asked: “What is the name of this hell?”
The rākṣasa replied: “This is the Mountain of Knives and Forest of Swords hell.”
Mùlián asked: “What sins have the sinners in this hell committed,
To fall into this hell?”
The hell warden replied: “The sinners in this hell,
During their lifetime,
Encroached upon and damaged the monastery’s property,
Defiled the temple grounds,
Misused the monastery’s water and fruits,
Stole the monastery’s firewood.
Today, they are made to climb the sword tree with their hands,
Every joint and limb shattered and scattered:
White bones strewn haphazardly on the mountain of knives,
Thousands upon thousands of heads on the sword tree.
To avoid climbing the mountain of knives,
Nothing surpasses filling the temple with good soil.
Planting fruit trees in the temple grounds,
Donating seeds double the monastery’s store.
Ah, you sinners, unspeakable,
For kalpas upon kalpas suffering retribution, countless as the sands of the Ganges,
Since the Buddha’s Nirvana, still not freed.
This hell spans hundreds of miles east to west,
Sinners run chaotically, shoulders bumping.
Karmic winds blow flames forward to burn them,
Hell guards rake and stab from behind.
Bodies and heads shatter like tiles in an instant,
Hands and feet turn to powder at once.
Boiling iron gleams, scorching their mouths,
Piercing left and right, leaving holes.
Copper arrows fly sideways, shooting their eyes,
Sword wheels descend straight from the sky, cutting through.
They say they will not be human for a thousand years,
Yet iron rakes gather them and revive them again.”
Upon hearing this, Mùlián
wept and lamented,
stepping forward to ask the prison warden: “In this hell,
is there a Lady Qīngtí?”
The warden addressed the monk: “What relation is she to you?”
Mùlián replied: “She is my compassionate mother.”
The warden answered the monk: “In this prison, there is no Lady Qīngtí.
Ahead in the hells,
they are all women;
you should be able to see her.”
Having heard this, Mùlián
proceeded further ahead.
Arriving at a hell,
its height and depth were about one yojana,
black smoke billowed,
and foul odors filled the heavens.
He saw a horse-headed rākṣasa,
holding an iron trident,
standing with an imposing air.
Mùlián asked: “What hell is this called?”
The rākṣasa replied: “This is the Hell of Copper Pillars and Iron Beds.”
Mùlián asked: “The sinners in this hell,
while alive in the world,
what sins did they commit,
that they should fall into this hell?”
The warden answered: “While alive,
women with men,
men with women,
committed lustful acts on their parents’ beds,
disciples on their teachers’ beds,
slaves on their masters’ beds—
they shall fall into this hell.
They cannot move east or west;
men and women,
half of them harmonize together.
Women lie on iron beds, nails piercing their bodies;
men embrace copper pillars, their chests rotting away.
Iron drills are long, sharp as blades;
greedy teeth are swift like awls and drills.
When their intestines are empty, iron pellets are stuffed in;
when they cry out in thirst, molten iron is poured down.
Thorns enter their bellies, splitting them like knives;
swords and halberds in the air leap like scattered stars.
Knives carve flesh and bones, slicing them piece by piece;
swords cut livers and intestines, severing them inch by inch.
It is beyond words;
hell and heaven stand opposite each other.
In heaven, day and night, joy resounds;
in hell, no one comes to rescue them.
If parents, while alive, perform good deeds,
one-seventh of the merit may be obtained.
Even if the Eastern Sea turns into mulberry fields,
those suffering punishment will still not emerge.
Having spoken, Mùlián
proceeded further ahead.
In a moment,
he arrived at another hell,
and addressed the warden: “In this prison,
is there a Lady Qīngtí?”
The warden replied: “Lady Qīngtí—
is she the monk’s mother?”
Mùlián replied: “She is my compassionate mother.”
The warden told the monk: “Three years ago,
there was a Lady Qīngtí
who also came to this prison.
She was summoned by a warrant from the Avīci Hell,
and is now in the Avīci Hell.”
Mùlián fainted and fell to the ground;
after a long while, he regained his breath,
gradually moving forward,
when he encountered a rākṣasa guarding the path and asked:
Mùlián’s steps were filled with sorrow and distress,
swords and blades by the roadside like wild grass.
Turning sideways, he heard from afar within the hells,
the simultaneous howling of wind and fire.
Thinking of his compassionate mother, his intestines felt torn;
the road ahead was not far, and he soon arrived.
Suddenly, he came upon the king of yakṣas,
sitting on the ground with a sword, blocking the main road.
Mùlián addressed him: “This humble monk is a disciple of Śākyamuni Tathāgata,
who has witnessed the three insights and transcended birth and death.
My pitiful compassionate mother, named Qīngtí,
after her death, her soul fell here.
Just now, I toured the other hells,
and those I asked all said she was not there.
Recently, it is said she was taken into Avīci;
great general, you must know of this matter.
Tell me truthfully, without hesitation;
in the human world, the kindness of breastfeeding runs deepest.
Hearing of my compassionate mother’s suffering pains my very marrow;
who can hastily understand this humble monk’s heart?”
The yakṣa, upon hearing these words, felt fearful,
and spoke frankly, without concealment:
“Monk, your filial piety is rare throughout the ages;
you fear not to personally traverse the dark paths.
Lady Qīngtí seems to exist,
but her trace cannot be fully pinpointed.
its walls are cast from iron, its barriers made of copper.
Karmic winds and thunderous roars blow in an instant,
those who arrive there are left in disarray like scattered wolves.
I advise you, ācārya, to return home early,
it is futile to search for her here.
Better to go early and see the Tathāgata,
what use is beating your chest in regret?”
Hearing of the hardships of hell, Mùlián
immediately turned back.
He threw his alms bowl and soared into the sky;
in a moment,
he arrived at the Śāla grove,
circled the Buddha three times,
then sat to one side,
gazing at the revered face,
not taking his eyes away for a moment.
He addressed the World-Honored One:
“Separated from the Tathāgata for many days,
I have searched everywhere between heaven and earth.
Although my father was reborn in heaven,
I have not yet reunited with my compassionate mother.
I hear she is suffering in Avīci,
thinking of it, my liver and intestines feel torn.
Fierce fires, dragons, and serpents block the way forward;
hastily, I have no means to find a solution.
The Tathāgata’s divine power can move mountains and seas;
all sentient beings deeply cherish it.
A subject in urgency naturally turns to his lord;
how can I reunite with my compassionate mother?”
The World-Honored One called out: “Mahā-Maudgalyāyana,
do not grieve and weep.
The sins of the world are like ropes,
not twisted by others’ hands.
Quickly take my khakkhara staff,
it can dispel the eight difficulties and three calamities.
Just diligently recite my name,
and hell will open for you in an instant.”
Relying on the Buddha’s power, Mùlián
soared downward,
swift as an arrow in the wind.
In a moment,
he arrived at the Avīci Hell.
In the air, he saw fifty ox-headed and horse-faced beings,
rākṣasas and yakṣas,
teeth like sword trees,
mouths like blood pools,
voices like thunder,
eyes like lightning,
on duty for the heavenly court.
Encountering Mùlián,
they called out from afar: “Monk, do not come!
This is no good path,
this is the road to hell.
In the black smoke to the west,
all are poisonous vapors from the prison;
if they touch the monk, he will turn to dust.
Monk, have you not heard of Avīci Hell?
Even iron and stone passing through will suffer calamity.
Where is hell said to be?
In the raging black smoke to the west.”
Mùlián recited the Buddha’s name like the sands of the Ganges;
hell, after all, is my home.
Wiping tears, he shook his khakkhara staff in the air;
ghosts and spirits immediately fell like scattered hemp.
Cold sweat flowed like drenching rain;
dazed and unconscious, they sighed in despair.
They dropped the three-edged clubs from their hands,
and threw the six-tongued tridents from their arms.
The Tathāgata sent me to see my compassionate mother,
to rescue her from suffering in Avīci Hell.
Mùlián, without stopping, soared past;
the prison guards watched, not daring to block him.
Mùlián walked forward (walked ahead),
arriving at a hell,
still over a hundred paces away,
he was sucked in by the fiery air,
and nearly fell backward.
That Avīci Hell,
with its iron walls towering high,
vast and boundless, connecting with the clouds,
forests of swords and halberds,
layers upon layers of blades and spears.
Sword-trees thousands of xún tall swaying and brushing against each other,
needle-like thorns scraping and rubbing;
knife-mountains ten thousand □ stretching horizontally,
jagged and precipitous, chaotically collapsing.
Fierce flames flickering and roaring like thunder,
leaping and dancing across the sky;
sword-wheels clustered densely like bright stars,
dust and ashes covering the ground.
Iron snakes spewing fire,
scales spread out on all sides;
copper dogs inhaling smoke,
barking and shaking on three sides.
Caltrops raining down chaotically from the air,
piercing the chests of men.
Awls and drills flying sideways from the sky,
gouging and stabbing the backs of women.
Iron rakes stabbing eyes,
crimson blood flowing westward.
Copper forks grinding waists,
white marrow drawn eastward.
Upon □ knife-mountains,
entering furnace coals,
skulls shattered,
flesh and bones rotten,
sinews and skin torn,
arms and shoulders broken.
Shredded flesh splattering outside the four gates,
gushing blood overflowing by the prison walls.
Cries and howls reaching the heavens,
perilous and vast.
□□ thunderous earth,
faint and looming.
Upward, smoke and mist scattered and spread;
downward, iron clanging chaotic and disorderly.
Arrow-haired ghosts scurrying and darting,
copper-beaked birds shrieking and calling.
Prison guards numbering over ten thousand,
all with ox-heads and horse-faces.
Even if your heart were made of iron or stone,
you would still tremble with fear at the sight of lost souls:
Mùlián grasped his staff and stepped forward to listen,
his thoughts turning to Avīci, growing ever more profound.
In all other hells there is some respite,
but this Avīci knows no pause.
Multitudes like the sands of the Ganges enter simultaneously,
all transforming their bodies into a single form.
If by chance one enters alone,
their body too fills the iron-walled city.
Case after case, difficult, difficult to shake the iron,
perilous clouds in the sky,
rumbling, clanging, overwhelming the earth with might.
Long snakes gleaming, three layers black,
great birds with cliff-like wings, two wings blue.
Ten thousand red furnaces fanning broad coals,
a thousand layers of crimson flames shooting out shooting stars.
Iron drills east and west, cruelly piercing chests and ribs,
copper arrows left and right, striking eyes.
Golden awls raining down chaotically like wind and rain,
molten iron pouring from the sky like a deluge.
Alas, how bitter, how unbearable,
and further, long nails driven through belly and back.
Mùlián, seeing this, exclaimed in wonder,
wholeheartedly reciting the Buddha's name thousands of times.
The wind blew poisonous air from afar, breathing it in,
watching as his body turned into a pile of ashes.
With one shake, the black city's locks fell,
with a second shake, the two gates of the underworld opened.
Mùlián, over there, still had not called out,
when the prison guard raised his fork and came out:
"Monk, whose news do you seek?
This city is vast, ten thousand yojanas wide,
hastily, no one can close it.
Swords and blades gleaming brightly,
the suffering people full of sorrow.
Great fires blazing, illuminating the ground,
smoke and mist billowing, darkening the sky.
Suddenly seeing the ācārya standing here,
yet never having met before.
Considering the reasons, there should be no one else,
it must be the compassionate power of the Three Jewels."
The prison chief addressed the monk: "For what reason have you opened the gates of hell?"
He replied: "If I, a humble monk, do not open them, who will?
The World-Honored One sent an object to open them."
The prison chief asked: "What object was sent to open them?"
Mùlián told the prison chief: "He sent the twelve-ringed staff to open them."
The prison chief asked again: "Monk, for what reason have you come here?"
Mùlián replied: "My mother's name is Qīngtí Fūrén,
therefore I have come to search for her."
The prison chief, hearing this,
returned into the prison, to the high tower,
raised a white banner,
struck the iron drum,
"Is Qīngtí Fūrén in the first section or not?"
"Not in the first section."
Proceeding to the second section,
raised a black banner,
struck the iron drum,
"Is Qīngtí Fūrén in the second section or not?"
"Not in the second section either."
Proceeding to the third section,
raised a yellow banner,
struck the iron drum,
"Is Qīngtí Fūrén in the third section or not?"
"Also not."
Proceeding to the fourth section, also not.
Then to the fifth section to ask,
also said not.
Proceeding to the sixth section,
also said Qīngtí Fūrén was not there.
The prison chief went to the seventh section,
raised a blue-green banner,
struck the iron drum,
"Is Qīngtí Fūrén in the seventh section or not?"
At that time, Qīngtí Fūrén was in the seventh section,
forty-nine long nails piercing her body,
nailed onto an iron bed,
not daring to answer the prison chief.
The prison chief asked again: "Is Qīngtí Fūrén in the seventh section or not?"
"If you seek Qīngtí Fūrén,
this guilty body is she."
"Why didn't you answer earlier?"
"I feared the prison chief would take me elsewhere to suffer,
therefore I did not dare answer."
The prison chief reported: "Outside there is a member of the Three Jewels,
shaven beard and hair,
clad in monastic robes,
claiming to be your son,
who has come to visit you."
Qīngtí Fūrén, hearing this,
after a long while of thought,
replied to the prison chief: "I have no son who left home,
is this not a mistake?"
The prison chief, hearing this,
turned back and went to the high tower,
reported to the monk: "For what reason
do you falsely claim a prisoner here as your mother?
Why speak such nonsense?"
Mùlián, hearing this,
wept bitterly, tears like rain,
addressed the prison chief: "This humble monk misspoke earlier.
In my youth, I was named Luóbǔ.
After my parents passed away,
I took refuge in the Buddha and left home,
shaved my beard and hair,
and was given the name Mahāmaudgalyāyana.
Prison chief, do not be angry,
please ask once more."
The prison chief, hearing this,
returned to the seventh section,
reported to the prisoner: "The member of the Three Jewels outside, in his youth named Luóbǔ,
after his parents passed away,
took refuge in the Buddha and left home,
shaved his beard and hair,
and was given the name Mahāmaudgalyāyana."
Qīngtí Fūrén, hearing this: "The member of the Three Jewels outside,
if in his youth named Luóbǔ,
then he is my son.
This guilty body, every inch of intestine, my dear son!"
The prison chief, hearing this,
helped Qīngtí Fūrén up,
pulled out the forty-nine long nails,
iron chains locked around her waist,
a cangue surrounding her,
drove her outside the gate,
where mother and son met:
the cangue's scales gathered like clouds.
The sins of a thousand years, unknown,
from her seven orifices, blood and fluid flowed.
Fierce flames issued from her mother's mouth,
caltrops step by step entered from the air.
Like the sound of five hundred broken carts,
how could her waist and spine bear to be gathered?
Prison guards raised forks, shielding left and right,
ox-headed ones held locks, standing east and west.
Stumbling forward, one step, one fall,
Mùlián embraced his mother, wailing and weeping.
He cried: "Due to my lack of filial piety,
calamity reached my kind mother, casting her into the three wretched paths.
Families that accumulate good deeds have surplus blessings,
but Heaven above only kills the innocent.
Mother, in days past, more beautiful than Pān'ān,
now haggard and suddenly ruined.
I had heard hell is full of suffering,
today I finally know the difficulty of the path.
Since disaster struck and my parents died,
daily at their graves I offer constant sacrifice."
Mother, have you received any food to eat?
Your entire countenance looks utterly haggard.
When Mother heard Mùlián’s words,
Alas, she beat her breast, tears streaming down.
“Yesterday, my child, life and death separated us,
Who knew today we would reunite?
In life, your mother did not cultivate blessings,
All ten evil transgressions she fully committed.
At that time, she did not heed her child’s words,
And now suffers in this Avīci hell.
In former days, Mother was glorious and splendid,
Moving behind silk curtains and brocade screens.
How could she endure this hellish suffering,
Transformed into a hungry ghost for a thousand years?
Her tongue is pulled out a thousand times,
Her chest plowed a hundred times with iron plows.
Bones, joints, sinews, and skin break everywhere,
Without need of sword or blade, she withers away.
In a single moment, she dies a thousand deaths,
Then, as they chant, she returns to life.
All who enter this hell suffer alike,
Regardless of noble, commoner, or high official.
You at home diligently offer sacrifices,
Gaining only a filial reputation in the village.
Better than pouring libations of wine at the grave
Is to copy out a single line of scripture.”
Mùlián choked with sobs, weeping like rain,
And immediately turned to consult the hell warden:
“Though this humble monk is one who left home,
My strength is small—how can I save my kind mother?
Within the five degrees of mourning, concealment is permitted—
This is the ancient saying of sages and worthies.
I only beg the warden to release my mother,
Let my body take her place in enduring long suffering.”
The hell warden, by nature stern and unyielding,
With anger darkening his countenance, replied:
“Though your disciple serves as hell warden,
All judgments come from the King of Impartiality.
If Mother has sins, Mother must bear them;
If the Master has sins, the Master must bear them.
The golden tally and jade tablet bear no erasure,
And no subordinate may alter them arbitrarily.
The time for receiving punishment has now arrived,
She must be taken to the hall of blades and spears.
If the monk wishes his mother released,
Better return home and burn precious incense.”
Mùlián’s kind mother, her voice sorrowful,
Was urged on by hell guards with tridents on both sides.
About to fall before reaching the prison gate,
She then cried out in lasting grief, “Farewell, my child!”
Lady Qīngtí, with one hand
Holding the prison gate, turned her head to look back.
Saying: “Farewell, my child,
This sinful body’s own tender son!
In former days, Mother acted with stinginess and envy,
Fearing not the karmic retribution in the life to come.
Speaking as if heaven existed but no hell,
She slaughtered many pigs and sheep to sacrifice to ghosts and spirits.
Seeking only the pleasure before her eyes,
How could she know the underworld would torture the dead soul?
Now that she suffers this hellish pain,
Only then does she know regret for her own deeds.
But what use is regret when regret comes?
Spilled water cannot be gathered—so says the common proverb.
When will she escape the suffering of hell?
How dare she hope to become human again?
You, Master, are a disciple of the Tathāgata Buddha,
Fully understanding the kindness of parents.
If one day you suddenly attain sage enlightenment,
Do not forget Mother suffering hardships in hell.”
When Mùlián saw his mother depart,
He wished he could destroy himself on the spot.
He threw himself down like a great mountain collapsing,
Blood streaming from all seven orifices.
He cried out: “Mother, do not enter yet,
Turn your head and hear one more word from your child.
The bond between mother and child is by heavenly nature,
The kindness of nursing and feeding is natural.
Today your child parts from Mother,
When shall we know we will meet again?
How can I bear to hear of this hellish suffering?
My heart is pained and constantly anxious.
Hell does not permit substitution,
I can only cry out loudly in lament.
Since I cannot save you,
I too will die before the prison gate with Mother.”
When Mùlián saw his mother return to hell,
He was heartbroken to the bone,
Choking, his voice grew hoarse.
Then he threw himself down,
Like five great mountains collapsing,
Blood gushed from all seven orifices.
After a long while, he died,
Then revived once more.
Pressing his hands on the ground, he rose,
Adjusted his robes,
And soared through the air to the World-Honored One’s place:
Mùlián’s mind was utterly dazed,
Human speech seemed faint, as if unheard.
After long silence and reflection, he awakened,
Cast aside his alms bowl, soared into the sky, and questioned the World-Honored One.
Mùlián complained bitterly to the Buddha,
Fully describing the mountain of blades and forest of swords:
“By the Buddha’s divine power and remaining majesty,
I was able to see my kind mother in Avīci.
Iron walls, smoke, and flames blazing high,
Forests of sword blades, tens of thousands of layers.
Human fat, minced flesh mixed with molten copper,
Flesh splattering, fat congealing in blood.
How could my kind mother’s appearance endure it?
Through the long night, assaulted by blades and swords.
White bones climb the sword-tree ten thousand times,
Rosy cheeks ascend the blade-mountain a hundred times.
Of all things under heaven, what is weightiest?
The kindness of parents’ affection is deepest.
The Tathāgata is the kind parent of all beings,
I beg you to illuminate this deluded heart of mine.”
The Tathāgata, fundamentally greatly compassionate,
Hearing this, sorrowfully knit his brows:
“Beings emerge and vanish in the wheel’s net,
Just like a rabbit caught in a silken snare.
Your mother in former times committed many sins,
Her spirit fell at once into Avīci.
This sin, through kalpas, has not yet been expiated,
It cannot be known by any but the Buddha, not by ordinary men.”
The Buddha called Ānanda and the assembly of disciples,
“I shall go to the dark path to save her myself.”
The Tathāgata, leading the eight classes of dragons and devas,
Surrounded before and after,
Radiated light that shook the earth,
To rescue the suffering places of hell:
The Tathāgata’s sagely wisdom is fundamentally impartial,
With compassion he rescues beings from hell.
Countless dragon-gods and the eight classes of beings,
Followed in one retinue, advancing forward.
Majestic and awe-inspiring,
In heaven and on earth, none can match him.
Sinking on the left,
Submerging on the right,
Like a towering mountain emerging from the clouds.
Lofty and grand,
Heaven and hell open simultaneously.
Moving like rain,
Shaking like thunder,
Like the full moon rising over the sea.
Alone, with the lion’s majestic stride,
Tigers stride boldly, elephant-kings turn.
In the clouds, heavenly music plays ‘Willow Branches,’
From the sky, fragrant petals fall like ‘Plum Blossoms.’
Indra steps forward holding a jade treasure,
Brahmā follows behind, presenting a golden tally.
Ineffable among the ineffable,
The Tathāgata’s divine power rescues the gate of the springs.
Left and right, devas and the eight classes of beings,
East and west, guarding and serving, the gods of the four quarters.
The ūrṇā hair between his brows shines with a thousand hues,
Behind his neck, a halo of five-colored clouds.
Hell, touched by the light, entirely dissipates,
The forest of swords and mountain of blades turn to dust.
Hell guards, touched by the light, all kneel,
Joining palms single-mindedly, they pay homage.
Today the Tathāgata arises in compassion,
Hell is crushed and utterly destroyed.
Iron pellets transform into maṇi jewels,
The mountain of blades becomes lapis lazuli ground.
Molten copper turns into water of merit.
Cool and clear, winding around the pond it flows,
Geese, ducks, mandarin ducks glide on rippling waves.
Red waves, each night, give rise to blue mist,
Green trees, each dawn, raise purple clouds.
All sinners are reborn in heaven,
Only Mùlián’s mother becomes a hungry ghost.
Everything in hell transforms and changes,
All due to the majestic power of Śākyamuni, the Holy Buddha.
Mùlián, by the power of the Buddha,
was able to see his compassionate mother.
Her roots of sin were deeply entangled,
the force of karma difficult to dispel;
though she escaped the bitterness of hell,
she fell into the path of hungry ghosts.
Her sorrow and suffering were unlike any other,
her pain and joy worlds apart.
Compared to her former state,
it was diminished a hundred thousandfold.
Her throat was like the eye of a needle,
not a drop of water could pass through.
Her belly was like Mount Tài,
even three rivers could not fill it.
She never heard the name of broth or water;
month after month, year after year,
she endured the suffering of hunger and emaciation.
From afar, she saw cool, clear water,
but as she drew near, it turned into a river of pus.
Even if she obtained delicious, fragrant food,
it would immediately transform into raging flames.
"Mother is now starving and in distress,
her life hangs by a thread.
If you do not arise with compassion,
how can you be called a filial son?
Life and death are separated by a road,
a future meeting is hard to expect.
To save her from the danger of a hanging thread,
the matter should not be delayed."
"According to the way of the monastic life,
one relies on alms for sustenance.
Even if there were permanent food and drink,
I fear it would be difficult to digest.
Your son bids farewell to Mother and goes to the city of Wángshè,
to fetch food and meet with Mother."
Mùlián took leave of his mother,
tossed his alms bowl and soared into the sky;
in an instant,
he reached the city of Wángshè.
He begged for food in order,
and came to the gate of a wealthy elder.
Seeing Mùlián begging at an improper time,
the elder questioned him about his lingering: "Reverend, the alms time has already passed,
the meal time is over;
for what purpose do you beg for food?"
Mùlián addressed the elder:
"After my poor mother passed away,
her soul fell straight into Avīci.
Recently, she was rescued by the Tathāgata,
her body like dry bones, her breath like a thread.
My poor heart and intestines are broken inch by inch;
the pain is so sharp, how could others know?
It is indeed improper to beg at an untimely hour,
but it is to feed my compassionate mother."
Hearing this, the elder was greatly astonished;
pondering impermanence, his mood turned somber.
The golden saddle forever severed the heart of crystal pearls;
jade-like beauty had no reason to enter the dressing chamber.
Just sing,
just rejoice,
human life is fleeting like a turning candle.
Why seek the pleasures of heaven?
Only hear that sinners in hell are many.
Sometimes eat,
sometimes wear,
do not learn from the foolish who hoard and accumulate.
Better to widely create future causes,
for who can guarantee life from morning to evening?
Looking at each other, unaware of death,
do not spare wealth for the body.
Once hands part and enter the long coffin,
what use is pouring empty libations on the grave mound?
The wise use money to create much merit;
the foolish use gold to buy fields and houses.
A lifetime of toil seeking wealth,
after death, it is all divided by others.
Hearing these words, the elder suddenly grew alarmed and doubtful;
the field of merit of the Three Jewels is hard to encounter.
He urgently urged his attendants not to delay,
to fetch food from home and give it to the Ācārya.
Suddenly, hell dissipated completely;
clearly knowing the inconceivability of all Buddhas.
The elder held the food in his hand,
and handing it to the Ācārya, made a great vow:
"Not only for the reverend to offer to his compassionate mother,
may all sinners in hell be fully satisfied."
Mùlián begged and obtained rice and millet,
carried the alms bowl to present to his compassionate mother.
At that time, he traveled to the vast wilderness,
holding a golden spoon to feed her himself.
Though Lady Qīngtí suffered the pains of hell,
her stinginess and greed were ultimately not eradicated.
Seeing her son bringing the food bowl,
she immediately felt miserly and possessive.
"What comes are the Three Jewels,
that is my son,
who fetched food from the human world for me.
All of you, each of you, calm your minds.
I will heal myself now,
how much more with additional aid."
Mùlián presented the food and bowl to her;
fearing it would be snatched away,
Mother looked around at her companions,
covered the bowl with her left hand,
and scooped food with her right.
Before the food entered her mouth,
it turned into raging flames.
Though the elder's vow was weighty,
it could not overcome her deep stinginess and obstructions.
Seeing his mother like this,
Mùlián felt as if his liver and gallbladder were cut by a knife.
"My power as a śrāvaka is weak,
my wisdom small, my strength meager.
Only by inquiring of the World-Honored One
can I know the path to salvation."
Observe the place where he fed his mother:
Seeing the food, the lady approached;
stingy and greedy, before eating, she fought emptily.
"My son fetched food from afar in the human world,
bringing it to heal my pit of hunger.
Eating alone is still not enough to satisfy;
all others, calm your minds, do not hope for it."
Lady Qīngtí's stinginess and greed, the force of karma heavy;
as it entered her throat, raging flames arose.
Seeing his mother's food turn into raging flames,
Mùlián collapsed and threw himself down like a mountain crumbling;
blood flowed from his ears and nose,
crying, "Heaven! My mother!"
From Jambudvīpa, this food was offered;
on the food was a divine light seven feet high.
It should have been fragrant, delicious food and drink,
but before entering the mouth, it became fire.
Only because her stingy, greedy heart remained unchanged,
therefore she endured its punishment year after year.
Now the pain is sharp, with no other way;
karmic retribution does not allow substitution.
People of the world, do not harbor jealousy;
once fallen into the three evil paths, sins are not yet ended.
Fragrant rice not yet reaching the throat,
raging flames issued from Mother's mouth.
In the mundane world, sins fill Sahā;
only stinginess and greed are the most numerous.
Fire, without cause, comes from the mouth;
clearly knowing karmic retribution is not due to others.
Always practice the mind of equality,
and also concentrate on reciting Amitābha.
Only by abandoning the mind of greed
can one reach the Pure Land or heaven at will."
Lady Qīngtí called out: "Filial son,
this sinful body does not perish by itself.
If not for the Master practicing filial piety,
who would endure hardship to save Father and Mother?
Seeing food, unable to scoop it into the mouth;
great fire, without cause, instead causes harm.
How can stinginess and greed be borne in mind?
It must be that past remnants of calamity remain.
Master is Mother's filial son;
give me cold water to relieve my empty intestines."
Upon hearing his mother ask for water, Mùlián
was choked with sobs and his voice grew hoarse.
As he pondered,
he suddenly recalled that south of Rājagṛha there was a great river,
vast and boundless,
named the Ganges River,
which should also be able to relieve his mother’s suffering from the fire torment.
The sentient beings of Jambudvīpa see water
as cool, refreshing water.
The devas see water
as a lapis lazuli treasure pond.
Fish and turtles see this water
as a flowing stream.
Qīngtí sees water
as a river of pus and raging fire.
When she reached the water’s edge, before hearing her son’s prayerful vow,
she immediately supported herself on the bank with her left hand—truly due to stinginess,
and scooped water with her right hand—truly due to greed.
Precisely because her stingy and greedy heart did not cease,
the water turned into fire before it even entered her mouth.
Seeing his mother’s food turn into raging fire
and water turn into raging fire, Mùlián
beat his chest and stamped his feet,
wailing and weeping in sorrow.
He came before the Buddha,
circumambulated the Buddha three times,
then stood to one side
and said: “World-Honored One,
your disciple’s mother committed all manner of unwholesome deeds,
and fell into the three wretched paths.
Through the World-Honored One’s compassion,
she was saved from her suffering.
But now, when she eats food it turns to fire,
when she drinks water it turns to fire—
how can she be saved from the suffering of this fire torment?”
The World-Honored One called out: “Mùlián,
your mother cannot yet eat food.
Only after one full year, on the fifteenth day of the seventh month,
when you extensively prepare the Ullambana basin,
will she be able to eat.
”Seeing his mother hungry, Mùlián said:
“World-Honored One,
could it not be done on the thirteenth or fourteenth of each month?
Must one wait until the fifteenth day of the seventh month
within a full year for her to eat?”
The World-Honored One replied: “Not only must your mother wait until this day to extensively prepare the Ullambana basin—
on this day, when monks in the mountains conclude their summer retreat (end of the rains retreat),
when arhats attain the Way,
when Devadatta’s sins are extinguished,
when King Yama rejoices—
all hungry ghosts will universally attain complete satisfaction.
”Receiving the Buddha’s clear instruction, Mùlián
went before the stūpa temple at the edge of Rājagṛha,
recited the Mahāyāna sūtras,
and extensively performed the wholesome roots of the Ullambana.
Only then, from within this basin,
did his mother get to eat one full meal.
Since obtaining that meal,
mother and son have not seen each other again.
Mùlián searched everywhere for his mother but could not find her.
Weeping tears like rain,
he came before the Buddha,
circumambulated the Buddha three times,
then stood to one side,
joined his palms, and knelt.
He said: “World-Honored One,
my mother’s food turns to fire,
her water turns to fire.
Through the World-Honored One’s compassion,
she was saved from the suffering of the fire torment.
But since obtaining that one meal on the fifteenth of the seventh month,
mother and son have not seen each other.
Has she fallen into hell,
or has she gone to the path of hungry ghosts?”
The World-Honored One replied: “Your mother has neither fallen into hell nor gone to the path of hungry ghosts.
Through the merit of your sūtra recitation
and the wholesome roots of preparing the Ullambana,
your mother has transformed from a hungry ghost body
and gone to Rājagṛha to become a black dog.
If you wish to see your mother,
practice an impartial mind,
beg for food in sequence,
without discriminating between rich and poor.
When you come to the gate of a great wealthy elder’s house,
a black dog will come out,
seize your robe in its mouth,
and speak in human language—
that will be your mother.”
Receiving the Buddha’s instruction, Mùlián
immediately took up his bowl and alms vessel,
and went to search for his mother.
Without discriminating between rich or poor neighborhoods,
he walked everywhere,
but still did not see his mother.
When he came to the gate of a certain elder’s house,
he saw a black dog
come out from within the residence.
It seized Mùlián’s robe in its mouth,
and immediately spoke in human language,
saying: “My filial son,
you were able to save your mother from the dark paths of hell—
why do you not save me from the suffering of this dog’s body?”
Mùlián addressed his compassionate mother: “Because your son was unfilial,
misfortune reached you, compassionate mother,
causing you to fall into the three wretched paths.
Would you rather remain in this dog’s body,
or return to the path of hungry ghosts?”
His mother called out: “Filial son,
receiving this dog’s body is retribution for being mute;
whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, I survive.
When hungry, I eat unclean things from pits;
when thirsty, I drink from flowing streams to quench emptiness.
In the morning I hear the elder recite the Three Jewels,
in the evening I hear his wife chant the venerable sūtras.
I would rather remain a dog,
enduring the great earth’s filth,
than hear the name of hell in my ears.”
Mùlián led his mother to before the Buddha’s stūpa in Rājagṛha,
where for seven days and seven nights
he recited the Mahāyāna sūtras
and repented, mindful of the precepts.
Through this merit, his mother
transformed from the dog’s body,
shed the dog’s skin,
hung it on a tree,
and regained a woman’s body,
complete and perfect in human form.
Mùlián addressed his mother: “A human body is hard to obtain,
the central land is hard to be born into,
the Buddha’s Dharma is hard to hear,
a wholesome mind is hard to arise.
”He called out: “Mother,
now that you have obtained a human body,
cultivate blessings immediately.
Mùlián brought his mother under the twin śāla trees,
circumambulated the Buddha three times,
then stood to one side
and said: “World-Honored One,
please examine my mother’s karmic paths since then,
observe and discern from the beginning—
what further sins remain?”
The World-Honored One did not refuse Mùlián’s request.
Examining from the three karmic paths,
he further eliminated her personal sins.
Seeing his mother’s sins extinguished, Mùlián
was greatly joyful in heart,
and addressed his mother: “Come, let us return.
The world of Jambudvīpa is not fit to dwell in.
Birth and death originally have no abiding place;
the Buddha-land of the West is most sublime.”
Moved, devas and dragons led the way before them,
and devīs also came to welcome them.
They went forward to the Trāyastriṃśa heaven to receive bliss.
Initially, verses were spoken to deliver the assembly;
when this sūtra was spoken,
there were eighty thousand bodhisattvas, eighty thousand monks, eighty thousand upāsakas, and eighty thousand upāsikās,
who paid homage, surrounded [the Buddha],
rejoiced, faithfully accepted, and practiced accordingly.
The “Transformation Text on Mahāmaudgalyāyana,” one scroll.
Manuscript by Zhāng Bǎodá.
Our Buddha, in his causal stage,
cultivated through countless kalpas.
He threw himself off a cliff to feed a tiger;
he saved a pigeon as Śivi.
Seeking half a verse,
his mind-ground did not waver.
He cut his body to light lamps,
making offerings to a pratyekabuddha.
Seeking a jewel with a good friend,
he was poor and deluded.
When his royal father was ill,
he offered his own eyes.
The Great Sage, compassionate in his causal stage,
cultivated through countless kalpas with firm resolve.
He also made offerings to a pratyekabuddha;
Śakra devānām indra tested him.
He cut flesh to aid his royal father;
in the mountains, he long subdued his breath.
In past lives, he cultivated through practice;
he is the Teacher of the Three Realms.
The World-Honored One, in his past practice of dāna,
saved sentient beings entangled by karmic obstructions.
He also sought a jewel in the great sea;
Śivi saved a pigeon, forming a good connection.
He traveled back and forth through the three wretched paths and hells,
serving as a boat on the six paths of saṃsāra.
To manifest auspicious signs for his disciples’ sake,
he relied on the Tathāgata’s hidden sacred power.
Our Buddha, in order to save his disciples from the six paths of reincarnation,
acted like a boat,
ferrying all beings
to the other shore.
Only then could one see the Buddha,
and in this life have ample clothing and food.
When the time for cultivation arrives,
one must diligently make vows.
If there is surplus, offer it to the Buddha and the monks;
one will then be able to see the Buddha numerous times.
If one cultivates further at this time,
in the next life one will certainly see auspicious signs.
Our Buddha’s compassion is beyond worldly praise;
he saves and delivers beings as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
All will reach the place of non-action,
and in this life enjoy wealth, honor, and luxury.
The human body is as fleeting as a lamp’s flame;
worldly affairs are empty and fleeting like clouds veiling the sky.
Offering to the Buddha and monks eliminates obstacles;
in the next life one will surely pay homage to the Dragon Flower Tree.
The Tathāgata always taught and urged his disciples
to burn incense and make vows,
diligently recite Amitābha’s name,
observe fasts and perform good deeds.
Giving alms brings much merit,
each act too numerous to fully praise.
Setting up a feast with joy
brings perfect retribution.
If one frowns even slightly over a little,
in the next life one will surely have an ugly face.
In the Buddha’s time,
there was a virtuous woman
who also made offerings to an arhat.
Although she had the karmic connection for giving,
in her heart she felt contempt.
Within three to five days,
she died—what spiritual effect did this have?
After this woman died at that time,
where was she reborn?
She was reborn in the palace of King Prasenajit.
This was the karmic result of her giving,
which allowed her to be born into a royal family.
But her slight of slandering a sage’s deeds
resulted in a retribution,
which manifested in our great king’s queen.
Just three days after birth,
she was presented to the king.
When the king first saw her,
he was utterly astonished.
“Ugliness in the world
is born from poverty and low status.
What karma did she cultivate in a past life
that her appearance in this life is so distorted?”
The king said:
“Upon reflection, it is truly strange;
how could a child of my royal line be like this?
Though ugliness exists among people in the world,
I have never seen such an evil-looking form as today.
Hunched like a turtle,
her whole body resembles wild boar skin.
Even if you were a skilled painter in your heart,
no amount of color could depict her.
Her beast-like head is utterly detestable;
surely there is none like her in the whole kingdom.
Considering this girl’s form and appearance,
who would marry her when she grows up?”
Then the king, ashamed,
sighed in great astonishment.
He then ordered the palace attendants
not to speak of it,
and had her sent to the inner palace,
never to be brought out again,
lest he see her.
The girl’s ugliness was rare in the world;
her whole body was like black leather.
Her feet were twisted and misshapen,
her hair like donkey’s tails, strand by strand.
She turned her whole body to look at people left and right,
her steps never knowing etiquette.
Her ten fingers were slender like pillars,
her eyes like wooden pestles.
The king examined her repeatedly,
sighing several times: “What karma caused such ugliness!”
The princess lacked all grace,
a matter of no small concern.
Her upper lip weighed over half a catty,
her nostrils like small bamboo tubes.
She had never known joy since birth,
it was said she laughed once in three years.
Seeking any graceful movement in her walk,
one found only the gait of a Zhao region sock-foot.
When the king saw his daughter’s ugly form,
he often rested his cheek in his hand with the queen.
Worried, he had no heart to seek a son-in-law,
ashamed, who would find a good matchmaker?
Though she lived in wealth and honor in a tower palace,
the shame was due to her lack of beauty that could topple a kingdom.
He ordered her locked away,
the deep palace gates not to be opened.
At that time, King Prasenajit, thinking his daughter ugly
and inferior to others,
had her placed in the deep palace,
not allowing her to appear often.
Days passed, months went by,
and she gradually grew up.
The queen worried day and night,
fearing the king would not consent to send her off.
Later, during a moment of leisure,
the queen composed herself and stepped forward,
approaching to address the king:
“Your humble consort is always ashamed of this ugly body,
unworthily sharing the palace and kinship with the king.
Daily before my eyes is much wealth and honor,
morning to night only pearls and treasures are used.
Palace maids and serving girls always follow behind,
summoned east and west by inner officials.
Ashamed of this body without virtue or understanding,
yet the king’s favor matches heaven and earth.
I have a matter to personally report now,
may the king be pleased and not angered:
The Vajra Ugly Girl has grown up;
how can we bear not to let her serve a man!”
Then the king, hearing this report,
pondered for a long time.
Before he could speak,
the queen reported again:
“The three sisters are all the same,
their comeliness or ugliness tied to karma.
All are the king’s own flesh and blood,
may the king bestow equal mercy and compassion.
Now grown up in the deep palace,
send her forth and have her come forward.
Her ten fingers, long and short from the start,
each should be tried by biting from the beginning.”
The king, seeing the queen’s repeated urging,
could not help but inform the queen:
“Because I am the body of a country’s emperor,
my family members arise from past karma.
How is it that among them one’s appearance is so poor,
making me ashamed to face the court officials?
I know in my heart she is my own born daughter,
but her ugliness is utterly unlike a person.
Speaking of it still brings shock and fear;
how can she be betrothed to another’s family?”
The queen again addressed the king: “If the king has no intention to send her off,
I dare not speak again.
If you intend to have her serve a man,
listen to my plan today.
Secretly summon a minister,
have him find a lowly fellow,
give him an official post, gold, and jade,
and betroth her to him as husband and wife.”
Then the king adopted his queen’s plan,
summoned a minister,
had him act as a good matchmaker,
and secretly arranged the matter.
The minister, receiving the summons,
hurried to the inner hall,
faced the heavenly decree,
and received the king’s command.
The king told the minister:
“You now listen to my words,
carefully hear the origin:
Because the country’s great king (queen)
has a personally born daughter.
Heaven made her appearance not strong,
only wanting straightforwardness.
Find a young man,
betroth her to him as husband and wife.”
The king also said to the minister:
“You are the minister, I am the ruler,
today we discuss this, just two people.
Morning and evening, you must carefully observe and examine,
sadly, do not let outsiders hear.
Do not dislike if he lacks talent or skill,
do not shun if the road is utterly poor.
By all means arrange the match,
add some dowry, do not argue.”
Then the prime minister accepted,
bowed and left the inner palace,
and secretly went through the markets,
traveled through various regions,
asking people everywhere,
searching day after day.
Later, while passing through streets and alleys,
he saw a poor youth surnamed Wáng.
After repeated inquiries,
he agreed at once.
Led to the inner gate,
he first entered to see the king,
reporting he had found someone.
The emperor, greatly pleased,
then summoned the prime minister,
ordering him to bring the youth quickly.
The emperor sat upon his throne in the jeweled hall,
The prime minister bowed and came to see him:
"Previously, I was ordered to seek a person,
Today I have fulfilled Your Majesty's wish.
There is a young man at the gate,
His nature and conduct are quite kind and benevolent.
He appears with a fine countenance,
Only he has a slight speech impediment, and so on."
Upon hearing this, the king joyfully paced back and forth,
Rolled up the pearl curtains and opened the imperial tent.
Not only did it please the sage ruler's heart,
But also made the empress laugh happily (cough cough).
The imperial consorts and palace maidens were ordered to enter,
The eunuchs hurriedly rushed them along.
Then he wiped his face with his sleeve,
Gathered his spirits and forced himself to come in.
Wáng Láng immediately saw the emperor,
What words were spoken?
Thus the poor scholar, receiving the summons,
Kneeled and bowed to the king.
With hands clasped, he spoke of the cold and warmth,
Immediately causing people to burst into laughter.
He further said he was overwhelmed with gratitude,
