And fortunate to serve his mother-in-law.
He stepped forward to pay respects,
His feelings of gratitude were overwhelming.
At that time, the king gave orders,
To arrange a banquet,
And invite Wáng Láng.
Once he arrived at the feast,
He sent palace attendants to lead the princess to meet Wáng Láng.
At that moment,
What words were spoken?
The bride came out to see Wáng Láng,
But all because her appearance was not very strong.
Palace maidens and consorts surrounded her on both sides,
In front, fans were held, creating a fragrant commotion.
Golden hairpins and jade bracelets adorned her head,
Brocade and silk garments emitted a fragrant scent.
As soon as Wáng Láng saw the princess's face,
His soul seemed to fly away in shock.
Thus Wáng Láng was frightened and fell down,
The palace attendants on both sides,
Immediately supported him,
Splashed water on his face,
And after a long while, he revived.
What words did the palace attendants speak?
"Because in her previous life, her looks were insufficient,
Every time you look, she resembles a beast's head.
Naturally, she lacks the rosy peach blossom complexion,
Even if adorned with the seven treasures.
Her husband was frightened and fell down,
Palace attendants and maidservants supported him at once.
Many palace women sprayed water to rescue him,
In a short while, he revived and woke up."
Then her two elder sisters,
Fearing that Wáng Láng would despise her ugliness,
And unwilling to return;
The palace attendants on both sides,
Were all anxious.
The elder sisters, having no plan,
Thought and then used humble words,
To reply to Wáng Láng, saying:
"Wáng Láng, do not be surprised or laugh,
Only because the bride is still young.
Although my younger sister is not elegant,
She is most skillful at sewing and tailoring.
Wáng Láng, do not worry about official positions,
From now on, you will be wealthy until old age.
Do not mind a little ugliness,
The bride is just in her youth."
Wáng Láng expressed his bitterness,
That matchmaker misled me into coming,
Today, before my eyes,
I see this pitiful matter.
I would rather not have wealth and honor,
Nor rely on your official position.
But at the moment of union,
How could I bear to see her ugly appearance?
After thinking it over repeatedly,
He sank into silence, unable to speak.
The elder sister spoke again:
"Do not complain or speak of bitterness,
How could you get such a bride so easily?
Although her appearance is not strong,
She is still the daughter of a king.
Now she is just in her youth,
And you have obtained the princess of the current court.
Even ghosts and spirits are greatly submissive,
Not daring to linger by the door or near the house."
Thus Wáng Láng could not despise or reject her,
The two were united,
Becoming husband and wife.
Ā Táo saw the marriage completed,
Felt extremely happy in her heart,
Went to the palace,
To pay respects and congratulate her parents.
At that time, she said something like:
"The young lady is now married off,
Saving her parents from worry and trouble.
Pushed the monster out the door,
Let her go to his house to make noise."
Wáng Láng informed the eldest sister: "All matters are settled today,
But I must keep my wife from going out,
For fear my friends will mock and laugh.
Young lady, do not be stubborn or forceful,
Do not show your face or head.
Even if Wáng Láng does not mind in his heart,
The karma from past lives must be accepted."
The wife said to her husband:
"Wáng Láng, do not let your heart wander,
Go out and return home early,
Do not abandon me and not come back,
With whom shall I speak then?
How could I willingly go out the door or leave the house,
Nowadays, times have changed,
Many people pass by the door,
I fear startling their donkeys and horses."
Thus the poor scholar, having become the imperial son-in-law,
Associated with high-ranking officials,
Exchanged letters and messages,
To invite and meet each other.
He then attended banquets of court officials,
Bowed together on the jade steps,
Attending imperial secretaries and courtiers,
Coming and going together.
Prefectural and county magistrates,
Accompanied the imperial son-in-law's feasts,
Ministers and secretaries,
Rejoiced together at the same table.
The various officials mentioned before,
Secretly planned together,
Wishing to see the princess.
Taking turns in rotation,
They invited each other to their homes in succession,
Where it was necessary for wives to come out and urge drinking.
Since there was no impropriety,
It became customary for wives to appear,
And all were received at the feasts.
Each day was not without joy,
Gradually, it came to Wáng Láng's turn to prepare wine and food.
He only worried that his wife's appearance was not strong,
Thinking and feeling ashamed to socialize,
Thus he became mentally unsettled,
Worried day and night.
The wife saw her husband resentful and troubled,
Could not help but question him repeatedly.
Wáng Láng, being questioned,
Then truthfully informed his wife, saying:
"Every day I go to attend feasts,
In every home, wives and daughters socialize.
Their jade-like faces are like flowers upon close look,
Their cicada-wing hair is graceful like immortals.
Court officials invite each other in turn,
Food and drink amount to thousands of varieties daily.
Later, when my household prepares wine and food,
You, madam, must also meet the court officials."
Wáng Láng then explained to the princess,
Telling the whole story: "When I go to their homes,
I see all their wives and concubines,
Urging drinking over several rounds,
Sitting opposite, enjoying themselves.
If the various court officials come to my feast,
You, young lady, must come out to meet them,
I am ashamed of this matter,
Hence my worry,
Resenting myself,
Feeling unhappy in thought."
Wáng Láng said:
"I have no resentment nor anger,
I sigh at the evil karma from my past life.
Only because I think of your many ugly features,
I now feel ashamed to meet the guests.
If court officials come tomorrow morning,
You must still come out to urge drinking rounds.
Once you come out to the feast and meet them,
It will bring shame and drain my spirit."
The princess, hearing this matter,
Choked and could not speak,
Ashamed of her ugly quality,
Swallowed her breath and tears fell.
What karma was planted in past lives,
That in this present life,
She obtained such ugliness?
After her husband left,
She then took the incense burner,
Faced the Spiritual Mountain,
Bowed and made a vow.
The princess, upon hearing, shed several lines of tears,
Her voice choked, turning to sorrow.
Resenting what sins in past lives,
Led to such extraordinary ugliness in this life.
She sighed repeatedly to herself,
[sighed] with no solution,
then ceased her makeup at the dressing table,
her heart recalling the Buddha,
begging for his compassionate protection:
"I lament that in this life my appearance is not strong,
I tightly coil my cloud-like chignon and cease applying rouge.
Who would have thought I lack a dignified countenance,
causing me to suffer secret deliberations.
I cast aside the rouge box,
hairpins and ornaments thrown aside.
With streaming tears, I burn incense, thinking of the Dharma assembly,
and from afar inform the Great Dharma King of Língshān."
Thus, without painting her moth-like eyebrows,
or combing her cloud-like hair,
she faced distant Língshān,
and addressed the World-Honored One:
"Pearl-like tears fall continuously, lamenting and sighing,
a kind of human with a deficient face and appearance.
Jade leaves do not grow into a dignified countenance,
golden vines bear flowers of the wild fields.
I have heard that Móuní is sixteen feet tall,
with eighty secondary characteristics, called Shìjiā.
I only wish the World-Honored One would bless me,
granting me some of the thirty-two marks."
The Buddha, with his mind-reading power,
knew from afar that the Vajra Ugly Maiden was burning incense and making vows.
Then, before the steps of the ugly maiden's dwelling,
he emerged from the ground,
personally bestowing his blessing.
The ugly maiden suddenly saw the great sage World-Honored One (appear) before the steps,
her soul shaken (stunned), she threw herself down,
rose to bow in reverence,
sobbing with sorrowful tears.
Just like four birds separated,
thinking of her own body,
she wished not to vanish and sink into the earth.
She addressed the World-Honored One,
begging for his compassionate protection.
The ugly maiden said to the World-Honored One:
"I sigh at the evil karma from past lives,
causing me to be ugly and inferior to others.
Slandering sages and creating much sin,
I have brought upon myself a face like smoke-stained.
My birth parents often disdain me,
sisters daily seem to scold.
When my husband enters, there is no joy on his face,
relatives have never shown warmth.
Constantly distressed, shedding twin tears,
often sighing and lamenting this body.
Hearing of the Lord of the Three Realms at Língshān,
therefore I burn incense to inform the World-Honored One."
The Buddha, with his mind-reading power and divine eye,
then saw from afar.
Appearing before the princess,
he taught her to repent and make vows.
The ugly maiden repented her sins before the Buddha,
the karma from past lives she herself had brought.
As soon as repentance ended and vows were made,
the karmic retribution then brought blessed fulfillment.
The ugly maiden saw the Buddha appear,
her joy multiplied as usual,
then she praised the Tathāgata: "May my body be no different from the Buddha's!"
The princess saw the Buddha arrive,
his countenance unmatched in the world,
hair dark blue with spiral patterns,
eyebrows like the crescent moon, emerald green,
mouth like the bìmínguǒ fruit,
forty-two teeth,
two eyes clear as the sea,
on his chest the svastika symbol.
The Vajra Ugly Maiden finished praising the Buddha,
circumambulated three times to the right,
and retreated to one side.
The Buddha, with his power of compassion,
extended his golden arm,
pointed at the ugly maiden's body,
and the ugly maiden's appearance
was instantly transformed, and so on:
Having praised the Buddha,
seeking his blessing,
she bowed her head in worship with focused mind.
Her countenance suddenly changed from its former state,
a hundred uglinesses turned into a thousand charms.
The ugly maiden, having received the World-Honored One's blessing,
exchanged her former ugly substance
for today's graceful demeanor.
Her ugly form
transformed into dignified and splendid features.
Moved, her appearance became like spring flowers,
her husband entering did not recognize her.
The princess's gracefulness unmatched in the world,
comparable to Yuènǚ and Cháng'é.
Her rosy face seemed lightly parted,
jade-like substance soft as cotton, white as snow.
The former ugliness came from past life seeds,
today's dignity encountered Shìjiā.
Her husband entering did not recognize her at all,
instead looking for the former ugly old woman.
The wife said: "Do you recognize me?"
The husband said: "I do not."
"I am your wife,
how can you not recognize me?"
The husband said: "Frightening!
Wife, you used to have a beast's head,
making me ashamed before others.
Today, why such a dignified appearance?
Please tell me the reason."
The wife said to her husband: "Since you before,
worried about my ugly body,
ashamed to see other court officials.
I was distressed repeatedly,
then burned incense and prayed to the World-Honored One of Língshān.
Receiving the Buddha's compassion,
he bestowed his protection,
exchanged my ugly form
for dignified and splendid features."
The princess herself said:
"I lament that in this life my appearance is not strong,
deeply ashamed day and night to disgrace the prince.
Thinking from afar of Shìjiā, Lord of the Three Realms,
who did not abandon compassion but descended here.
Then I bowed in worship,
added more incense,
unaware my appearance suddenly changed.
I obtained today's dignified countenance,
grateful to the Great Dharma King of Língshān."
The prince, seeing his wife dignified,
clapped his hands joyfully,
saying several times: "Adorable!
Adorable!"
Entering inside,
he reported to the great king.
The prince clapped his hands joyfully,
entered the great king's palace:
"Father-in-law and mother-in-law do not know,
today it's completely a different matter!
The young lady has now changed,
not the former spirit monster.
If you wish to know the princess's appearance now,
she is just like a bodhisattva before the Buddha."
The great king heard this, his heart filled with joy,
hastily and urgently sought his daughter.
The queen's retinue left the palace,
the great king's imperial carriage reached the long street.
Upon seeing his daughter,
joyfully pacing,
glowing peach blossoms bloomed all over her face.
The great king and queen were delighted and smiled,
therefore specially sent wealth.
The princess, because of the Buddha, became dignified,
must properly thank the great sage,
tomorrow morning quickly go to Qíyuán,
bow in worship with utmost sincerity and reverence.
Thus, banners and flags shone in the sun,
black banners faintly visible,
seven treasures and precious wealth
offered to the Buddha.
Hundreds of officials followed the procession,
thousands of officers carrying orders from behind,
together heading to Qíyuán,
to thank for the daughter's dignity.
After one night,
they reached Qíyuán,
thanked the Buddha for his great kindness,
repeatedly inquired:
Descending from the imperial carriage,
bowing to the golden figure,
again offering treasures to the Compassionate Honored One.
"What sins did my daughter commit in past lives?
Her ugliness is hard to describe.
Relying on the Tathāgata's personal blessing,
she is like a withered tree regaining spring.
I only wish for the Tathāgata's compassionate mindful power,
to explain the causes cultivated in past lives."
The Buddha told King Pòsīnì: "Listen carefully, listen carefully,
I will enlighten you with a matter,
and explain past life causes.
The Buddha said this woman in a past life
had made offerings to a Pratyekabuddha,
although she made offerings,
only said his face was ugly.
The cause of making offerings led to birth in a royal family,
but disrespect toward sages' deeds
resulted in an ugly face and appearance.
Sincere giving
must be done with joy.
If someone slightly frowns (with disdain),
then know the karmic retribution will not follow.
In past lives, because she slandered the Pratyekabuddha,
therefore her form and appearance were deficient.
Because she did not recognize an Arhat,
she ridiculed in various ways, suffering confusion (chaos)."
When evil words are about to be uttered,
Their karmic retribution is never mistaken.
Upon seeing the form of the Buddha and repenting,
At that moment, it was like a cluster of flowers.
Only because of evil speech in a past life,
Today’s karmic retribution is indeed real.
Slandering the fruition of an Arhat’s deeds,
Led to a human form that is incomplete.
Two feet emerged like dew-drenched pillars,
A pair of arms like rough rafters.
After just three or five bows to the World-Honored One,
At once they became white, pure, and soft as cotton.
The above describes the transformation from ugliness.
Composed by Master Yuánjiàn of the Left Street Monastic Registry, bestowed purple robes, Yúnbiàn.
In the world, blessings and wisdom
None surpass the Tathāgata,
With dignified and serene features,
And supernatural powers at ease.
How did the Buddha attain such noble dignity?
Fundamentally, it came from practicing filial piety.
Know that the way of filial piety knows no bounds,
Praised extensively among the three teachings.
If one can be filial to both parents,
A thousand Buddhas will protect one’s conduct.
Mùlián saved his mother Qīngtí,
Our Buddha carried his father, King Śuddhodana, on his shoulders.
History books for generations sing of Emperor Shùn,
For a thousand years, people praise Wángxiáng.
Even the crow feels gratitude when feeding its parents,
The wild goose sets off as soon as it can fly.
Guō Jù was willing to bury his own son,
Lǎo Lái joyfully wore colorful clothes.
Most difficult to deceive is sincere earnestness,
Not easy to lightly cheat Heaven above.
Weeping by bamboo, shoots sprouted—his fame is greatest,
Lying on ice, fish leaped—his righteousness immeasurable.
If one can rid oneself of ridicule and slander,
One avoids being harmed by others’ disparagement.
Dogs understand repaying kindness by (chewing grass),
Horses know their master and lower the reins.
Cease wasting wealth on indulgence and lust,
Do not vex kind parents with drunken revelry.
When children fall ill, their gasping breaths are heard,
Father and mother weep until tears flow freely.
Carrying on both shoulders is not too heavy,
Even circling Mount Sumeru a thousand times cannot repay it.
Diligently serve day and night, knowing their needs,
Attentively observe their complexion, inquiring of peace and health.
Spitting out sweetness, swallowing bitterness for three years,
In the womb, bearing pregnancy for over ten months.
Try going out far, and in dreams they chase you,
Return slightly late, and they stand by the door waiting.
Filial piety surely brings blessings from heavenly palaces,
The five rebellious acts can summon hell’s calamities.
Toil and hardship must be borne as one’s own duty,
Deeply avoid taking wealth into private quarters.
Beware of hidden virtue being worn away,
Do not believe wives and children’s gossip.
If one’s own feelings lack utmost filial piety,
Then blame fate and destiny for hindrances.
Neighbors’ anger spreads the news abroad,
The reputation of the five rebellious acts far and wide known.
If brothers quarrel within the household,
Surely neighbors will secretly move (walls).
Closest kin must share the same food,
Deep friendships still share provisions.
In responding with words, be gentle and considerate,
In receiving teachings, deliberate carefully.
If one errs in judgment, kindness and righteousness are lacking,
If one slightly missteps, order and discipline are lost.
Crucially, show compassion to those under your charge,
Doubly care for widows and orphans.
Aunts, uncles, and their orphaned children,
Take into your home and bestow honor upon.
When relatives and friends are poor, extend aid,
On rugged roads, build bridges.
If the Buddhist path can follow these teachings,
It is called the great path of compassion.
Morning and evening, have sons and wives rise early,
With food and drink, let parents taste first.
Living together, though not far, still means parting,
Seeing each other, though not long, ends in impermanence.
In life, lazily providing tea and water,
After death, vainly offering wine and libations.
Willing obedience is like faith in Buddha,
Kind words and inquiries surpass burning incense.
Gently admonish to please kind parents,
Ugly reputations must be borne by oneself.
In scorching heat, fan the pillow,
In freezing cold, warm the bed.
Declining years change as swiftly as flowing water,
Providing delicacies is as urgent as fire.
If in life harmony is like milk and water,
It surpasses sacrificing pigs and sheep after death.
Why need the lanes openly proclaim it,
The gods themselves secretly record it.
Sharing the same tree and branches, how can they be split,
Born of the same womb and milk, how can they bear separation.
The Tathāgata expounded five thousand scrolls,
Confucius discussed eighteen chapters.
None surpass speaking of filial piety,
All without exception tell of gentleness and goodness.
A filial heart is called a true Bodhisattva,
Filial conduct is named the great path.
Filial conduct is the sun and moon in dark streets,
A filial heart is the ladder and boat in the sea of suffering.
A filial heart forever dwells in a land of cool purity,
Filial conduct always resides in a realm of joy.
Filial conduct is no different from spring rain,
A filial heart is no different from the fragrance of a hundred flowers.
A filial heart is vast like clouds spreading,
Filial conduct is clear like sunlight.
Filial conduct can overcome all calamities,
A filial heart can avert a thousand misfortunes.
Filial piety is the treasure among all wealth,
Filial piety is the king among all virtues.
In Buddhism, filial piety is the root of attaining Buddhahood,
One must practice filial piety toward father and mother.
In this life, satisfaction avoids the cycle of rebirth,
Filial care can dispel all disasters.
If one can fully practice filial piety toward elderly parents,
It is like reciting scriptures all day long.
Kind words should bring joy to family affections,
Delicacies need not be urged by parents.
To resemble the World-Honored One’s dignified appearance,
Without filial piety, how can it be proclaimed?
Emperor Gāozǔ of Hàn summoned Hán Xìn at Péngchéng,
At Gāixià, they fought a battle,
Chǔ perished, Hán triumphed.
Zhāng Liáng saw Hán Xìn killing many people,
Zhāng Liáng memorialized: “Your servant will sing a Chǔ song,
To disperse the Chǔ army.”
The song said:
Zhāng Liáng, following orders, entered the central camp,
Instructing the soldiers to listen quickly:
“Tonight select three to five hundred men,
Who can perform Chǔ songs, all must present them.”
Zhāng Liáng’s strategy was most extraordinary,
That night they surrounded the Chǔ camp.
Just at the third watch, well-trained,
From all sides, Chǔ songs were sung in unison.
The lyrics said:
“This year, the commander crosses Háoliáng,
Jade-like dew abundantly fills the ravines with frost.
A man attains high office and rank,
How can he forget his father and mother?
All people are born from parents,
Children are raised by parents,
If not fed from the breast for three years,
How would a six-foot body grow!
Raising children should only know household affairs,
Throughout the four seasons and eight festivals, provide (delicacies).
(Delicacies) have never been provided at all,
Abandoning father and mother, idly passing through life.
Engaged in warfare for several years,
A hundred battles, a hundred wounds, life turns precarious.
Sometimes in dreams lying beneath spears,
Awakening to find oneself still by the war drums.
Where can the thousands of troops be withdrawn,
When will the goose-foot letters return?
Warhorses are constantly saddled,
A bow is strung every night without rest.
Urgent, urgent, hastening one’s aging,
Swift, swift, hastening one’s early demise.
The pass and mountains, rugged roads hard to travel,
Which one is the road to my hometown?”
Chǔ soldiers, hearing this, shed tears in pairs,
Weapons, spears, and banners all cast aside,
In threes and fives, they all fled in waves,
Each returning resentfully to their camp tents.
Just at half past the third watch,
The King of Chǔ finally awoke,
Gathering stars, drawing his sword, he came out of camp,
Already seeing the five stars contending and crossing.
Relying on the spirit of a great man,
Yet today, defeated at the edge of heaven,
Five or six years of bitter campaigning,
At Péngchéng and Gāixià, meeting one defeat.
The time unfavorable, Heaven forsakes me,
Heaven forsakes, what can be done?
Having the strength to lift mountains and tripods,
If not perishing now, then when?
A thousand gold cannot buy old age’s spring,
Drunk lying before the steps, forgetting poverty,
If in this world such a thing did not exist,
Three parts sorrow would kill two parts of a man.”
《Jì Bù》, one scroll.
Recorded on the fourth day of the fourth month, the fourth year of Tiānfú.
At this time, the second month was nearing its end,
just as the third spring began.
Hundreds of birds fluttered their wings in the forest,
fish played in the water and leaped with shimmering scales.
Flowers shone brightly,
their colors radiant and fresh.
Flowers first bloomed and smiled at the sun,
leaves held fragrance and rose with dew.
In the mountains, the great tiger was the chief,
among birds, the phoenix was the most revered.
At this time, all the birds arrived,
gathering like rain and clouds rushing forth,
arranging their ceremonial guards,
allowing the ruler to emerge.
The white crane served as prime minister,
the mountain partridge (鹧鸪) as the loyal minister who remonstrated directly.
The kingfisher acted as the censor overseeing discipline,
the sparrowhawk as the patrolling general.
The gray eagle served as the strategist of the six armies,
the peacock king was solely in charge of the palace gates.
The guardian marsh bird knew how to assign duties separately,
the small bird served as the messenger official.
The wild goose was solely in charge of the Ministry of Rites,
the swan goose, the grand historian, composed writings.
The sun-and-moon bird observed the stars at night,
the red-beaked crow watched the smoke and clouds by day.
The Tūjué bird temporarily managed the foreign guesthouse,
the old crow solely watched the smoke and clouds.
The tail-marked bird had no talent or skill,
devoting itself to dancing in the villages.
The white ribbon belt,
color like silver,
had long lived apart in the mountains.
Hearing that the phoenix appeared in the forest,
they brought their sons and daughters, all coming to gather.
The Xūnhú bird, the teacher goose,
the swan lady, the wren,
the red-beaked duck, the jade-green chicken,
mandarin ducks as companions,
pairs flying together,
receiving orders to summon,
not daring to delay.
From then on, these birds arrived,
none disobeying.
The pelican bird,
with its feet,
usually searched for fish to eat by the water.
The wild duck saw the horned owl from afar,
diving to the bottom of the water, unable to find it.
The white parrot,
the red chicken, the red (鸂鶒),
their bodies covered in feathers of five colors,
in twos and threes by the water's edge,
viewed from afar in the sunlight, truly like brocade wings.
The clever girl,
so pitiable,
on the treetop,
raising children,
carrying茅花 in her beak,
gathering willow catkins,
who in the nest can take the golden needle?
In the Lǒngyòu region,
parrots are produced,
taught clearly to understand human speech,
among humans, none can compare,
caged and presented to the enlightened ruler.
The鸅鶝 also once acted as a rat,
its body featherless, growing fleshy wings,
just at dusk it emerges,
by day, how could it ever admire wind and rain!
The念佛鸟,
carrying a gourd,
usually said it never tasted wine.
The marsh pheasant had a hundred kinds on its body,
the quail had nothing behind.
The独舂鸟,
with a lowly nose,
by nature preferred high branches.
The sparrow lord, an inch in size,
yet disliked the old crow for lacking feathers.
The吉祥鸟,
most spiritual and joyful,
appeared in the cliffs of Táishān,
suddenly emerging amid colorful clouds,
so that all people bowed in reverence.
The花没鸽,
color so beautiful,
all its life loved treading on temple grounds.
The magpie among households was most spiritual,
bringing good news in advance to deliver joy.
The black鸐 (鸜鹆),
the yellow-flowered building,
flying back and forth by the mountain peaks.
The mountain magpie, with a red beak, won people's affection,
the群神 bird alone flew apart.
The寒号虫,
cried every night,
the青雀儿,
color so blue,
its feathers of five colors very bright.
Hearing that the phoenix appeared in the forest,
all came to bow and dance in the heavenly court, and so it was.
"One Scroll of Hundred Bird Names."
Recorded by Yāyá Suǒ Bùzǐ on the day of the twelfth month in the Gēngyín year.
Now, the Yáchǐ new bride,
was born naturally so.
Fighting with lips and tongue,
she only sought to quarrel.
Bullying children and trampling the husband,
cursing with a loud voice.
When the in-laws spoke to her,
she simply would not listen.
Entering the kitchen in a rage,
overturning porridge and spilling soup,
smashing pots and breaking steamers,
hammering cauldrons and striking pans.
Angry like a water buffalo fighting,
laughing like the sound of a pulley.
If speaking of lifting skirts and wagging tails,
truly unmatched in the world.
Stirring trouble among relatives,
bullying neighbors and driving away villagers.
When the mother-in-law scolded her,
she never answered back.
Banging her head,
pounding heaven and earth.
Touching the bed,
pretending to be sick and not getting up.
Seeing the husband enter,
tears filling her eyes.
The husband asked the reason,
what was the matter.
Unable to explain,
she only said, "Yes, yes.
The in-laws scold me,
treating me like a slave or maid,
only sleeping late at night,
not giving me food to eat,
so hungry I get up on my own."
The mother-in-law said to her son: "You brought such a strange, ugly thing in,
what use is she to me!"
Hearing this, the new bride
suddenly rose from the bed: "Why didn't you dislike me back then,
and still gave betrothal gifts and performed rituals?
Now that you have me,
what do you say I am?
Before I was promised,
you prayed to gods and ghosts;
once I entered,
you speak of me like this!"
The new bride then demanded a divorce letter:
"Abandon me so I can marry another, hateful husband."
Hearing she wanted a divorce letter, the in-laws
were overjoyed: "We'll give you some dowry clothes,
and make another blanket for you."
"I beg you to leave quickly,
hoping never to meet again."
The new bride said farewell and left,
muttering curses under her breath:
"I care not for wealth or property,
just to leave these resentful old ghosts."
The new bride was used to roaming freely in the village,
not learning etiquette,
not loving women's arts.
Only carrying a bamboo basket in hand,
as if picking vegetables by the fields.
Such as her,
must be disciplined and corrected.
If from a reputable family,
she would not need to be taught.
Her nature was Yáchǐ,
even beaten to death, she would not change.
In the future, when choosing a wife for your son,
you must carefully observe and pursue,
do not rely on matchmakers' arrangements.
The mother-in-law's poem says:
The Yáchǐ new bride is very stubborn,
causing relatives to dislike seeing her,
no matter how much you restrain or bind her, she won't listen,
enraging the elders till their guts rot.
The new bride's poem says:
My Yáchǐ nature is known everywhere,
Mother-in-law, why bother grieving so?
If you seek from me a wife's proper conduct,
you must first change my skin a hundred times.
"The Tale of Dual Gratitude," Part Seven.
(Sutra) At that time, the crown prince, hearing these words,
was filled with sorrowful tears.
All beings in the world create the roots of evil,
their sufferings never cease.
The Crown Prince Shèngdà, intending to go on an outing,
instead encountered distress and suffering.
Upon seeing the plowing and weaving and such before him,
he could not help but shed tears that filled his eyes,
and dust and grime covered his body.
He lamented the multitude of karmic deeds,
and pitied the severity of the two sufferings.
The strong bullying the weak—
when will enmity ever cease?
The rich exploiting the poor—
on what day will hardship be eliminated?
Thus, he turned his carriage back onto the road,
and with his retinue in order, returned to the palace.
The music he heard as if he did not hear it;
the dancing sleeves he saw as if he did not see them.
The palace ladies lining the embankment were astonished,
in groups of five and three;
the living beings throughout the kingdom were alarmed and fearful,
thousands upon thousands.
Like clouds swiftly passing,
like birds flying in haste.
While they were still discussing,
he had already returned to the palace hall.
A verse says:
Compassionate thoughts for the deeds of all beings,
sleeves drenched with twin tears, swiftly falling again.
Passing by the dancing maidens as if unseen,
the continuous (section by section) flutes and songs as if unheard.
Drums and war drums shake the green fields,
dust rises to the heavens, entwined with red banners.
The whole city, astonished, came out to watch,
amidst the clamor of people and neighing of horses, all returned together.
Having returned, he was unhappy.
The King asked: “You intended to go on an outing;
why are you now unhappy?”
The Crown Prince said: “Father King!
I intended to go out and see the gardens and parks,
not knowing that the human world held such hardship and toil.
For the sake of providing for flesh and blood,
they inflict harm for food and clothing.
The plowman turns up worms for birds to peck;
the weaving woman spins thread, toiling for her children.
Butchers slaughter oxen and sheep;
hunters trap and hook fish and birds.
Mutually causing harm,
ultimately forming enmity.
Deceiving the mind with false affairs,
the strong bullying the weak.
Therefore, I could not bear to witness it,
and turned the carriage and horses back.
Since the masses are oppressed by torment,
why should I alone seek pleasure?
A verse says:
Only knowing to dwell high in the imperial palace,
unaware of the thousandfold hardships outside the gates.
Boiling and searing, cries of hatred from the butcher;
nets and traps, sighs of sorrow for the old fisherman.
Young women before their carts, long twisting thread;
old crows following the plow, swiftly snatching worms.
All due to killing and harm, along with food and clothing,
therefore, upon returning, I wish not to encounter it again.
The King said: “You are greatly mistaken.
In the human world,
poverty and wealth follow karma;
all must clothe their bodies,
and rely on food to nourish themselves.
Without spinning, how can there be clothing?
Without planting, how can one seek grain and wheat?
As for flying birds and running beasts,
it is largely the same.
Though their forms differ according to karmic retribution,
they are matched by karmic conditions and mutually devour each other.
The mouse killed by the cat—
is not taught by humans;
the butterfly caught in the spider’s web—
all follows heavenly decree.
Do not grieve and sigh;
this is the usual rule.
If you trouble my spirit,
how can that be called filial piety?
A poem says:
Heaven assigns human life—how can it be free?
There are kin, there is love, there are enemies and grudges.
Deep blessings come entirely from much planting in the past;
meager share is all due to not cultivating broadly.
Poor women make clothes, toiling at spinning and weaving;
farmers plant and cultivate, tending the fields.
Considering it, it is always the ordinary way;
why must you return alone and bring worry?
The Crown Prince said: “If it is so,
I dare not disobey the King.
I wish to report to you above,
and beg for one wish.”
The King said: “You need only follow my will,
enjoy music for your own pleasure;
whatever you require,
I will grant it all to you.
I have only you, whom I especially cherish;
even a kingdom full of gold is not worth your worth.
Why alone worry about worldly hardship and toil?
Why especially pity people driven to labor?
In Jambudvīpa,
according to karmic power,
just be peaceful and do not torment yourself.
Again, you speak of a different, vast-hearted wish;
I will comply with whatever you want, without opposition.
At first, seeing you return laden with sorrow,
I could not fathom the reason, filled with deep doubt.
Nobility and lowliness are not determined by this life’s deeds;
short and long are all followed from past causes.
Why needlessly scratch your cheeks, adding grief and regret?
Just broaden your heart and maintain it well.
If you have a wish, speak it quickly;
I will comply with whatever you want, certainly without opposition.”
The dragon countenance frequently gazed, the matter hard to decide;
the son had not yet expressed it, forever tying his heart.
Each step filled with doubt—when will it end?
Twin brows knit with resentment—when will they open?
Ministers and officials, cautious, watched according to rank;
palace ladies, careful, lined up outside the hall.
Only awaiting the officials’ words in reply,
everyone safe and joyful, singing what is to come.
(Sūtra) The Crown Prince spoke plainly: “I wish to obtain all the treasures, food, and drink from the King’s treasury,
to give alms to all.”
The Crown Prince said: “The King is my father,
I am the King’s son;
since I have a private wish,
I should carefully detail my petition.
I wish to obtain the King’s food and drink,
to relieve the hungry;
I wish to obtain the King’s pearls and gold,
to give alms to the poor.
So that weaving women need not toil at the loom,
farmers cease labor with plow and ox,
fishermen break their hooks by rivers and lakes,
hunters unbend their bows in forests and wilds.
Butchers release the lives of pigs and sheep,
not forming enmity;
gatherers and trappers spare the lives of swallows and sparrows,
eliminating fear.
All shall be made sufficient,
universally brought to peace and tranquility.
I humbly beg your sagely compassion,
to permit the opening of the treasury.”
A verse says:
“I am bound by the suffering of living beings,
all due to food and clothing creating hardship.
Plowing and mulberry everywhere busy in the three realms;
officials and administrators at every gate toiling in the nine thoroughfares.
I wish that all killing and injury be entirely spared,
desiring that exhaustion and destitution all be revived.
I beg the King’s treasury to be fully distributed,
but do not know if the heavenly heart is willing to give or not?”
The King said: “Whatever you want,
I will not oppose your wish.”
The Crown Prince then rejoiced,
selected a day to open the treasury and move the goods.
With five hundred elephants, they carried them outside the four city walls,
proclaiming throughout the kingdom:
whoever has any need,
their wish will not be opposed,
as fully stated in the sūtra text.
Then locks and keys were all opened,
seals and labels all broken.
Pearls and jewels unloaded (piled),
treasures and gems divided into mounds.
Working together, they transported them to the heavenly court;
hands gathered, they moved them from the imperial treasury.
Exquisite silks and embroideries,
all tributes from mighty vassals paying court;
auspicious brocades and fragrant damasks,
all gifts of gratitude from great commanderies.
Jade belts and girdles piled like houses;
gold vases and bundled ornaments arranged like mountains.
Carved and flowered silks, how endless!
Raised-pattern boats, too many to count.
Copper coins piled (in boats) sharp, incalculable;
variegated silks together with seawater just level.
Five hundred elephants carried them, night continuing into day;
four city gates piled high, from top to bottom.
Summoning the orphaned and destitute,
the roads were like flowing streams;
sounding bells to gather farming folk,
villages and gardens vied to assemble.
According to what each wanted, they freely took away;
following their hopes and needs, no obstruction to coming and going.
What need to speak of years of great abundance?
Far surpassing an age without worry.
The monarch, for his son, emptied all treasuries;
five hundred elephants lined the four roads.
Coins, silks, damasks, brocades, generally piled high;
gold, silver, pearls, jade, how endless the count!
Summoning distant vassals,
proclaiming to nearby supports,
imperial decrees flowed widely throughout heaven.
But the poor and destitute quickly spread the news far and wide.
Regardless of beauty or ugliness, all must come together.
The king, in accordance with his vow, thought of the living beings,
The crown prince bestowed wealth to aid and relieve them.
Once they came seeking, there was no obstruction,
Allowing whatever they desired without hindrance or protection.
Everyone knew,
All rushed and gathered,
Their forms clustered like stars, pouring in like a torrent.
Replacing the young, orphaned, destitute, and lacking people,
All were taught to be satisfied without greed or envy.
Elephants carried out treasures and circulated them widely,
The sage ruler searched and had them proclaimed.
First, to show the emperor’s cultivation of pure charity,
Second, to manifest the crown prince’s forging of good karma.
Gathering scholars in due time, they came like clouds,
Day after day, moving wealth like ants in circles.
Surely every household was joyful,
Door to door, comparing households, scattering piles of money.
Every prefecture and county was rich with treasures,
Only caring for music and songs, drunk with jade cups.
Suddenly abandoning farming and mulberry, busy with the passing years,
Forever casting aside business to roam the dusty world.
Ashamed of the emperor’s grace spreading far and wide,
Grateful for the prince’s opening of the treasury.
Just as the people were taking turns in order,
Who would dare to advise and sing of the future?
(Sūtra) Then the treasurer entered and reported to the king: “All the treasures in the treasury,
The crown prince has now used one-third,
Your Majesty should consider this.
This minister was upright in heart,
Loyal and filial in character,
Not out of miserliness for treasures,
But rather to diligently serve the king.
Worried about the emptiness of the state treasury,
He feared the collapse of the court’s order.
Thus he reported to the king, saying: “The crown prince takes treasures to give alms to the poor,
For several months now,
One-third has been used,
I dare not obstruct,
I must fully report and inform.
I beg Your Majesty to admonish him,
Do not let him go beyond the proper limits.
Ministers and rulers should be loyal with precious wealth,
Guarding against emergencies requires timely provision.
Preserving locks and keys costs physical effort,
Investigating and detecting wickedness allows no leniency.
Prefectures and counties wither and decline, filling the treasury with taxes,
The fat and blood of the living beings enter the royal palace.
In tens of days, the crown prince transported and gave alms,
Already one-third has been emptied.
The king said: “My son,
I do not wish to oppose or refuse him.
” After another ten days,
He took even more.
The various ministers and officials discussed with worry and distress,
Saying: “For any state or city,
It must rely on the treasury,
If wealth and treasures are exhausted,
How will the state’s strength be?
We cannot conceal and begrudge human feelings,
We must further report to the heavenly ear.
” The chief treasurer reported again.
A verse says:
“Wrongly unworthy, I serve as the king’s treasurer,
Wearing the fish tally and purple robes, I enter the court gates.
To begrudge words would be disloyal and unfilial,
When there are matters, I speak directly and report first.
Punish me as you will, even if I die under the blade,
Executing my family, why fear being burned in fire?
Just now I checked the various treasures,
The crown prince has exhausted two-thirds.
The king heard the minister’s report,
And again said: “I do not wish to oppose or refuse my son.
However, you, sir, have delayed a little,
Not matching his heart’s desire,
What is valued is to seize the time and not take it anymore.
” Though the various treasurers temporarily left according to the king’s order,
The crown prince, according to the day and time, opened the treasury without hindrance,
And angrily said: “How dare these petty men oppose my will?
It must be my father the king who taught them.
” The crown prince then thought a little more,
Saying: “To be a filial son,
One must not oppose the ruler’s heart.
I cannot selfishly seek to create karma,
Exhausting my parents’ treasury.
I must seek wealth and treasures elsewhere,
To rescue and aid the poor,
If I do not devise plans and schemes,
How can I be called a donor?
I now vow not to take the various treasures from the treasury,
I wish to gather many wise people to discuss other operations.
Loyalty and filial piety in serving ruler and parents,
Should not oppose the king’s will.
Ashamed to be a man of stature,
How can I oppose heaven and earth?
If one has a compassionate heart, pitying the haggard and weary,
One must directly have other innate wisdom.
To avoid troubling the ruler’s heart with vexation,
And prevent ministers’ words from boiling over.
Only wealth and strength must be personally sought,
Only blessings and karma do not rely on shelter.
I wish to gather all the elders in the city,
To separately plan and operate in cultivating charity.
To avoid incurring wicked opposition and troubling the king’s feelings,
And again have the treasury full as before.
Immediately making all ministers and officials fully satisfied,
Forever removing the chief steward, leaving no name behind.
Deeply knowing my own faults are human errors,
Do not cling to others’ grievances when issuing orders.
How about gathering worthies to discuss and take,
Together applying wisdom and schemes for livelihood?
To aid others, one must have abundant wealth oneself,
How much, at the time, according to one’s will.
If much, I can give alms to satisfaction,
If little, they will not add to it.
Anger and dislike—how can karma be accomplished thus?
Joy and delight can open wisdom.
I dare ask the ministers and chancellors at court,
Which side is sufficient and beneficial? Sing of the future.
(Sūtra) At that time, the good friend crown prince gathered the various ministers and hundreds of officials to discuss together, saying: “In which undertaking is seeking wealth most excellent?
The crown prince first thought,
Then chose a day to go ask the various ministers:
“Assisting court ministers, the world sings together,
Famous in all states, schemes are hard to surpass.
Supporting the state, all are loyal and upright,
Molding living beings, all are harmonious.
Governing chaos, the realm does not harm the masses with violence,
Taxing fields, the people do not complain of burdensome exactions.
Calculating, they should also know the path to seeking wealth,
Which gate yields the most profit?
As soon as the crown prince asked,
Among them, the first minister said to the crown prince: “I hear that for wealth expansion, nothing surpasses farming.
This year, originally sowing five shēng,
Next year, profitably harvesting ten hú.
Not requiring people’s distant plans,
Only needing oxen to plow and cultivate.
Mostly comes from heavenly timing,
Mostly also depends on earth’s moisture.
Moisture and growth in village fields cannot be surpassed,
Regardless of summer wheat or autumn grain.
Three shēng this year on three mǔ of ridges,
One grain next year yields one stalk.
On sowing day, driving oxen though weary,
At ripening time, arranging ears, nothing can compare.
Since receiving the crown prince’s gracious question,
Only farming yields the most profit.
Shànyǒu then replied,
A verse says:
“Deeply thank the strong advice and scheme coming first,
Considering, it is not truly excellent words.
If relying on ripening, who would be ashamed of the land?
Suddenly if drought comes, one must hate heaven.
Morning sun is still hard to expect for evening sun,
This year, early or late, reaches next year?
Lately fearing to see the people’s hardship,
Specially teaching people to farm instead.
Another minister said: “If not wanting to farm,
Nothing surpasses raising livestock.
Whether oxen, sheep, camels, horses,
Or geese, ducks, chickens, pigs,
Following water and grass to multiply,
Following grazing to grow fat and strong.
Oxen then for pulling carts and transporting loads,
Horses then for traveling roads and riding,
Pigs and sheep for sacrificing to gods,
Geese and ducks for serving ministers and chancellors.
Those who want must buy,
Not a day’s pause.
This shows great profit,
Nothing surpasses this.
A verse says:
“Raising depends entirely on water and grass’s richness,
Deep in the palace, the crown prince should also know.
Oxen on main roads, public and private transport,
Horses at court gates, entering and exiting riding.
Geese and ducks cooked and roasted for ministers,
Pigs and sheep slaughtered for sacrificing to gods.
If households need them, they must be taught to buy,
Profit is especially great, doubt no more.
At that time, the crown prince heard this,
And again replied:
“This scheme, considering, is even less worthy,
Greatly capable of wrong views flooding the court.
Speaking, you make me ask again,
Plugging ears, you turn people to lazily listen.
Tying hair, lamentable, vainly receiving salary,
Wearing fish tallies, regrettable, confusing dukes and ministers.
Lately fearing karma, disliking debt of grievances,
Specially now, instead killing living beings.
This did not meet the Crown Prince's wishes,
until finally there was one great minister,
spirited and clear-minded,
eloquent and articulate.
Bending his body, he stepped out from the ranks,
raising his eyes to speak frankly: "Crown Prince!
I see that the Crown Prince is no ordinary man;
you possess compassion and mercy,
wisdom and insight.
You detest killing and creating karmic debts,
and do not wish to kill;
knowing the toil of farming,
you do not wish to farm.
Your intention now is to universally enable all sentient beings
to live in peace without troubles,
clothed in garments of nature,
fed by heaven-bestowed rice.
To break the dwelling of greed, anger, and ignorance,
and escape worldly toils;
to revere the body of precepts, meditation, and wisdom,
and perfectly penetrate the practice of the Dharma.
Why not enter the great sea,
pay homage to the Dragon King,
and seek the Maṇi jewel,
to benefit all beings?
If food is needed, it will rain food;
if clothing is needed, it will rain clothing;
if gold and silver are needed, it will rain gold and silver;
if pearls and jade are needed, it will rain pearls and jade.
It harms no living creature,
and requires no scheming of the mind.
Unless a Bodhisattva can accomplish this,
it is difficult for an ordinary person to attain.
I know the Crown Prince laments birth and old age,
and broadly exercises great compassion and capability.
How could this be the achievement of an ordinary person's understanding?
It is truly the cultivation of a Bodhisattva's path.
Though it may take time,
and efforts may seem hasty,
you will surely remove the afflictions of sentient beings.
If you wish to free all from suffering and toil,
nothing surpasses obtaining the Maṇi jewel.
The sea dragon's jewel is called Maṇi;
thousands seek it, but few obtain it.
If food is needed, it pours forth fine food;
if clothing is required, it instantly rains renowned garments.
All kinds of silks and brocades can be produced,
and every sort of gold and silver follows.
If you resolve to go personally and obtain it,
this is called the Crown Prince's inconceivability.
The Bodhisattva's practice,
moreover compassionate,
cannot be known by petty ordinary people.
The Crown Prince comes and goes without obstacles,
his merit and capability even more inconceivable.
Though urgent,
and taking time,
good deeds often do not waver.
Yet I fear sentient beings have meager merit,
and may not encounter the Crown Prince, causing you to return.
Though I, your minister, have devised this plan with humble intent,
whether to go or stay, decide appropriately at the time.
Rather than seeking safety and hoping for rewards,
do not let the king's displeasure bring disaster.
Anxious and disoriented, I am only ashamed and worried,
trembling and sweating, not daring to retreat.
When the Crown Prince first heard these words,
whether pleased or not, he chanted what was to come.
(Sūtra) The benevolent friend Crown Prince said: "Excellent!
Excellent!
Only this is truly delightful.
" He then entered the king's palace,
and addressed his father the king.
The Crown Prince now wishes to enter the great sea to seek fine jewels.
Hearing this minister's words, the benevolent friend
was exceptionally joyful.
For a time, he excitedly praised with "excellent,"
repeatedly turning to commend with "delightful."
Thanking him again and again,
he truly was a wise man.
Unconsciously raising his whole body,
he joined his palms and praised in verse:
Only now do I believe the court has a wise man;
such a lofty plan I have never heard.
On the Bodhi path, I meet a good friend;
in the city of afflictions, I behold the cloud of wisdom.
Truly we share the mind to cultivate benefit and aid,
truly named as joining strength to save the drowning.
May my journey be without obstacles,
and I will dedicate half the merit to offer to you.
After the benevolent friend Crown Prince spoke this verse of praise,
he entered the king's palace,
and said to his father the king: "To aid the poor,
I opened the king's treasury;
yet fearing it would be exhausted,
I did not wish to deplete it.
Since I am powerless and without means,
I wish to enter the sea to seek jewels.
I ask the king to permit me to go,
and not to worry.
At most half a year,
and I will return to pay homage.
I now enter the sea to seek pearls and jewels,
to universally aid the orphans and elderly in Jambudvīpa.
Greatly altering suffering and distress,
broadly removing poverty and hardship.
The days are not far,
the road is full of people,
with suitable travel provisions, I should arrive.
Specifically I come to bid farewell to the king, my father,
hoping the king will let me go without worry or distress.
The level road is without mountains,
merchant companions are plentiful, not making it difficult.
Going, I plan to seek for several weeks;
returning, I will be back within half a year.
Why need relay stations arrange household feasts?
I have travel rations to eat as I wish.
I only hope the king deeply understands,
and does not use worry to obstruct.
Maintaining peace and goodness, I will return,
surely no dragon god will bring disaster.
Harming others' hearts ultimately leads to calamity;
benefiting beings, the heavenly eye should open.
In time, I will send word when the days are slightly extended;
temporarily borrowing your grace, do not be concerned.
Imagine the king hearing these words—
he must be greatly displeased, so chant what is to come.
(Sūtra) The king heard these words,
like a person choking,
unable to swallow,
and unable to spit out.
He said to the Crown Prince: "The kingdom is yours,
the treasury's precious jewels,
take as you wish.
Why devise a means
to enter the great sea yourself?
You are my son,
grown in the deep palace,
sleeping with curtains and canopies,
eating to your heart's content.
Now you speak of traveling far on roads,
hunger, thirst, cold, and heat—
who will know of it!
Moreover, in the great sea,
dangers are not few.
There may be evil ghosts, poisonous dragons,
swift waves, fierce winds,
whirling currents, surging eddies,
mountains of water foam,
Makara great fish.
Of those who go, thousands and tens of thousands,
only one or two arrive.
How can you now wish to enter the sea?
I do not permit you.
The Buddha's Sūtra of Repaying Kindness, scroll seven.
The Sūtra of Repaying Kindness, scroll eleven.
(Sūtra) Having reached this shore,
he saw his younger brother, the malevolent friend,
and asked: "Where are your companions and fellows now?"
The benevolent friend, having been sent to the seashore by the Dragon King's ghost soldiers,
after being sent, they returned.
Seeing his younger brother, the malevolent friend,
he asked: "The five hundred merchants,
where are they now?"
The following sūtra answers:
"Benevolent friend!
The ships sank,
all perished,
only I, your younger brother, clinging to a dead body, was saved,
the companions' wealth and goods all lost.
The verse says:
"Short or long life cannot be determined,
mist obscures even what is close, how can one distinguish?
Long accustomed to ships, it was still tolerable,
but suddenly seeing the waves, the soul must be lost.
Overturned, one speaks of heavenly treasures,
in peril, what care for the honored of the land?
The many merchant companions all sank,
only I, cultivating the mind, happened to survive.
Shànyǒu, upon hearing this, said: "I am deeply pleased, deeply pleased.
Wealth and treasure are trivial matters.
What the world values most
is none other than one's own self.
If only one can keep oneself safe,
why worry about pearls and jade?"
Èyǒu said: "I am not like that.
I would rather die wealthy now
than live in poverty.
How do I know this?
I once went to a graveyard
and heard the corpses and ghosts
discussing thus:
'What I value most is treasure;
I do not value the body.'"
The original intent of the scripture was to lure his elder brother into revealing the whereabouts of the pearl.
He then spoke a verse to his brother:
"Elder brother, you regard gold and pearls as trivial;
but for me, abandoning them is most difficult.
Only by returning to the country with wealth will my heart be satisfied;
coming back empty-handed, my spirits will be utterly low.
Not knowing this matter makes one seem perpetually dull;
seeing others and speaking little also becomes a vexation.
How can it compare to dying wealthy and honored,
which far surpasses living in poverty in this world?"
Shànyǒu's heart was trusting and straightforward;
what he valued was to ease his younger brother's mind.
Fearing that the treasures might sink into the sea,
he felt doubly distressed.
Soon he said to his brother: "Do not be distressed.
Even if the ships and vessels sink,
it is truly trivial.
I have already obtained the Dragon King's wish-fulfilling pearl."
Èyǒu immediately asked his brother: "Where is the pearl now?"
He replied: "I obtained the precious pearl,
and it is now within my topknot.
I guard it day and night,
vigilant in every action.
It is precious to fulfill our parents' compassionate concern,
and also to relieve the poverty of living beings.
To share in your joy and celebration,
do not trouble your heart.
When the time comes to rain down treasures,
all will enjoy wealth and honor.
The precious pearl is always in my topknot;
today I clearly tell you, my brother.
From dusk to dawn, I endure hardship and toil,
guarding it with care, I must keep it hidden.
Raining down pearls and gold,
broadly providing relief,
benefiting all beings equally, removing poverty and distress.
Do not let reckless people know of it,
lest it be robbed, breaking my vow.
This journey has already been preordained;
the bustling travel must not be delayed.
Whenever I recall leaving the country back then,
how could I have hoped to return with the pearl now?
With utmost sincerity, I greatly practice compassion,
raining treasures specifically to rescue the impoverished and endangered.
Besides entrusting it to you along the way,
if others inquire, do not let them know."
For this, both sorrow and joy filled his heart;
his great vow today has been fulfilled.
Since there is the hard-to-conceive treasure within the pearl,
why cling to the wealth in the sea?
Seeking beyond one's lot is deeply mistaken;
losing what is ordinary is not worth grieving."
Hearing his elder brother speak thus,
Èyǒu calculated and should have devised a plan—now let it be sung forth.
(Scripture) The younger brother, hearing these words,
felt jealousy arise in his heart,
vexed and resentful.
He thought thus: "Our parents have always been partial, loving and doting on him;
now he has also obtained the maṇi pearl treasure.
As for me, my parents now despise and disdain me,
worse than tiles and rubble."
Because of these thoughts, Èyǒu
then conceived a heavy intention.
Verse:
Shànyǒu receives favor, admired by all;
everyone pities and cherishes him, adding more affection.
When he walks, a thousand flowers follow with palace ladies;
when he lies down, canopies and curtains are adorned with a hundred treasures.
Before he arrives, mother-of-pearl seats are already arranged;
from afar, crystal curtains are rolled up.
Now that he has obtained the pearl and returns,
look at me—treated like an enemy, increasingly disliked."
Just after silently reciting this verse in his heart,
he immediately rose, joined his palms, and said to his elder brother: "Excellent!
Truly excellent!
To have obtained this precious pearl.
On this dangerous road,
we must guard it carefully."
Shànyǒu, with a straightforward heart,
said to Èyǒu: "Take this pearl and
diligently protect it.
If I rest,
you should watch over it;
if you sleep,
I will keep watch myself."
Thus for several days they accompanied each other,
all as said before.
The precious pearl is taken down for you to receive;
guard it attentively with care.
Walking and sitting, focus together on keeping it safe;
when sleeping, properly entrust it to each other.
Beware of evil people,
watch the dangerous road,
for those who see or hear will surely be jealous.
If suddenly something goes wrong and it is lost to others,
by what means can we plead our case?
This pearl is rare, truly hard to obtain;
not from the Dragon King, it is not easily kept.
When you sleep, your elder brother will guard it with full attention;
when I sleep, I entrust it to you, my brother, to keep with care.
Evil people, cunning and deceitful, strive without scruple;
the perilous road, rugged and uneven, unavoidably brings worry.
If through negligence it is lost and falls,
the pāramitā of dāna will be hard to cultivate.
Do not sleep, do not be negligent, do not delay;
do not trust in negligence, do not make false excuses.
Do not let your heart err and mislead your brother;
do not cause loss and make your elder brother suffer.
Many orphans and elders hope for its power now;
countless poor people look to this wealth."
Thus accompanying each other for several days—
who will be the one to keep watch? Now let it be sung forth.
(Scripture) At that time, it was Èyǒu's turn to guard the pearl.
His elder brother was asleep,
so he rose and sought two dry bamboo sticks,
pierced his elder brother's two eyes,
seized the pearl, and left.
Èyǒu devised his plan,
calculating that his elder brother was asleep,
and it was his turn to guard the pearl.
He sought two dry bamboo splinters.
Verse:
The journey's toil, deep in the night, he slept soundly;
Shànyǒu sank into deep slumber, dreams formed.
Though the noble one intended to guard it,
the evil man's scheme had already arisen in his heart.
Considering the distance, he should be hard to catch up with;
gazing at the Milky Way, dawn must not have broken.
Taking two bamboo branches, he pierced and damaged his eyes;
stole the pearl and set off hastily through the night.
Shànyǒu, having had his eyes pierced and damaged,
repeatedly called Èyǒu's name: "Èyǒu!
Èyǒu!
There is a great thief here,
who has damaged my two eyes."
He did not know he had already left.
Since calling brought no response,
he shouted even louder: "Evil man!
Evil man!
My eyes are already damaged.
If you want the pearl,
take it as you wish.
Do not harm my younger brother;
my younger brother is foolish and young."
He called out to the empty air,
speaking to the thief:
"The sea treasure, the maṇi, take it as you will;
it is only because I did not know how to hide it separately.
But I worry that my younger brother is young and foolish;
I beg you, in your compassion, do not harm him."
Thus he called out and pleaded,
but still no one responded,
so he moved the tree deity.
Therefore, the scripture below says:
Thus he cried out loudly,
his voice stirring the deities,
but for a long time there was no response.
At that time, the tree deity then spoke: "Your younger brother Èyǒu is your evil thief.
He pierced your two eyes,
took the pearl, and left.
Why are you calling for Èyǒu now?"
He spoke a verse to inform him:
"It is no use crying out loudly and frequently;
deep in the night, you only stir the dragon deities in vain.
The one who stole and took the pearl was not the pearl's wish;
the one who damaged your eyes and injured you is your own kin.
Cease wasting words pleading for his life;
vainly showing affection, caring for his body.
If you want to know your worthy younger brother's current whereabouts,
he is the one who took the bamboo and struck with his own hand."
Shànyǒu said: "Alas!
Alas!
How could I have known this!"
Facing the sky, deep in the night, he wept bitterly;
both eyes in pain, pain hard to bear.
It was not easy to know his jealousy;
how could he pull out the dry bamboo?
What enmity, what hatred,
what kinship, what flesh and blood,
that face to face, amid the grass, blood flows and drips.
Just now they seemed true brothers,
who knew such poison lay in the heart?
Mistaken suspicion, mistaken act—thinking thieves had come to invade,
this journey gone awry, lamenting past and present.
The pearl follows the wicked man, gone by starlit night,
blood follows the dry bamboo, dripping on the grass-tips.
Words of many kinds, wounds without end,
weeping cuts off sound after sound, pain turns ever deeper.
Thinking him compassionate, truly my own brother,
who knew he harbored such poison in body and mind?
Body and face together, too lazy to turn back,
a heart of stone would see this and crumble.
Walking beasts, bent hooves, all gaze in dismay,
flying birds, folded wings, all sink in sorrow.
Not only lost unjustly in the eternal night,
but also toward the long road, the master (digs earth) to bury.
The wicked friend, having taken the pearl and gone,
to what country, what land will he return, now sing of what is to come.
(Sutra) At that time, the wicked friend, carrying the jeweled pearl,
returned to his own country,
and met with his parents.
He said to his parents: "By my own virtue and fortune,
I have been completely saved.
Prince Shànyǒu and his companions, due to their meager virtue and fortune,
drowned and all perished."
This is the wicked friend prince stealing the pearl and leaving first,
returning to his own country,
telling his parents:
"Shànyǒu's past karma brought this about,
adrift on vast waves, alone and in peril.
How many pearls and jades were sunk by the wind,
countless merchants met with water's blowing.
Before setting out with provisions, one could still be cautious,
once aboard the ship, regret is hard to chase.
In human life, fate is known to be fixed,
only I, safe and peaceful, have managed to return."
Question: How did the parents hear this?
The following sutra says:
The parents, hearing these words,
raised their voices in great weeping,
fainted and fell to the ground,
splashed cold water on their faces,
and after a long while revived.
They said to the wicked friend: "How could you bring such news?"
Once weeping over, blood fills the cheeks,
liver and intestines cut inch by inch, thousands of times.
Instead letting the wicked man extend his life and fortune,
yet making the good friend cover the spring terrace.
Never harming things, why should things be angry?
Without wrongdoing burdening heaven, why does heaven send disaster?
If carried away by water, should have followed along,
what more to seize today, what comes?
The wicked friend, rejected by his parents,
his heart turned to vexation.
Intending to take out the pearl saying "I obtained it,"
later hearing these words,
then buried it in the earth.
Having suffered his parents' disdain and cruelty,
turning over and over in thought, he gave rise to poisonous malice.
Outside the gate, though walking (though walking) forced to break through,
dwelling in the palace, altogether without reliance.
Doubly grieving and sighing,
secretly pondering,
already as if separated by a life, once indifferent and cold.
Do not rashly give the pearl to him,
better to dig deep in the earth and bury it.
Now if one were to take out the pearl and present it,
it would be hard to avoid sorrowful weeping, only remembering the elder brother.
In every matter, disdain and dislike, not of this world,
in every instance, slander and cursing, arising from many lives.
Wishing to devise a plan to leave the palace,
yet fearing it would spread, weeping throughout the city.
Even if the pearl were wondrous, of a thousand, ten thousand kinds,
thinking it over, still no affection is shown.
How better to dig deep and bury it in the earth,
cutting off many lives, with life destroyed.
Showing affection to me is not the world's wish,
being a son to him is heaven's error.
Half a year leaving the country, a thousand kinds of worry,
one day returning to the palace, a hundred rounds of cursing.
This too is a trivial matter,
ask where Shànyǒu has come to rest, now sing of what is to come.
(Sutra) At that time, Prince Shànyǒu had both eyes pierced,
dry bamboo splinters piercing,
no one to pull them out.
Wandering, turning and twisting,
knowing not where to go.
At that time, in bitter distress,
greatly suffering hunger and thirst,
seeking life but unable to obtain it,
seeking death but unable to obtain it.
Gradually moving forward,
he reached the borders of the kingdom of Lìshībá.
The wicked friend brought the pearl to the palace,
suffered his parents' disdain and revulsion.
The pearl was already buried.
The elder brother behind, supporting his body, gradually walking.
In the grass, lifting his body,
groping, seeking the road.
Confused and faint, though half awake,
how to plead the pain?
Wandering, comforting his own heart,
weary and exhausted, who would care for him?
He was then a blind beggar,
with nothing to protect himself.
How did the foolish, wicked friend give rise to such poison,
suddenly conceiving this heart to pierce his elder brother's eyes?
Though I now walk with slow steps,
I worry he calculates the journey's speed.
His heartlessness toward me is but trivial,
fearing my precious pearl would be harmed.
Foolish youth, all led astray by spirits and ghosts,
looking to heaven, unconsciously weeping continuous cries.
One cry cut off, then weeping another cry,
thinking of his foolish stupidity, sighing at his name.
My heart ultimately does not see his fault,
I wish only to be safe and return to the imperial capital.
May sages and worthies protect, causing no hardship,
may parents, seeing my return, give rise to longing.
When years grow long, understanding reflection,
sooner or later he will come seeking his elder brother.
Thus weeping and crying,
traveling for several days,
he reached within the borders of the kingdom of Lìshībá.
Before Prince Shànyǒu entered the sea,
his father the king had promised marriage to the daughter of King Lìshī,
later learning he had entered the sea and drowned.
The prince, about to reach the country, several tens of miles away,
on the road pretended to be a blind beggar sitting.
He happened to meet the cowherd overseer,
who for the king herded five hundred cattle.
The cattle king then with its four feet straddled the prince's body,
letting the other cattle pass.
With its tongue, it licked his eyes,
pulled out the bamboo splinters.
After a long while,
the cattle king then left.
Later, the cowherd looked back and saw something strange.
Verse question:
I see you though both eyes are blind,
moved to summon a cow to pull out bamboo splinters and walk.
Previous auspicious signs, though trivial matters,
this day's marvel, how can one not be startled?
Could it be you secretly harbor illusion arts?
Or in past lives served divine spirits?
To dispel my various rising doubts,
I hope you will convey: what is your name?
Shànyǒu, hearing the question,
immediately thought to himself,
if I speak the truth,
that wicked friend will surely suffer harm.
For King Lìshī is his maternal uncle.
So he only replied: "I am a blind beggar.
Deeply ashamed of my lowly, base state, without name,
begging for food, by chance I came here.
Illusion arts, all of them, I do not know,
divine spirits, I have never served.
Thanks to the cattle king,
for pulling out the splinters,
it must be this ruined body not yet due to die.
Benevolent one, today why must you doubt?
My body is merely that of an orphaned, poor son.
I have no home to dwell in, again no return,
begging for food, seeking heaven, trusting my feet to act.
In this life, solitary and cold, content with lowliness and baseness,
in past lives, hunger and thinness led to poverty and peril.
Not because bamboo splinters hid deep arts,
all was the cattle king possessing great compassion.
Seeing this form, all can see it,
suddenly how can there be further doubt?
Do not randomly guess about surname and clan,
this body of mine surely lacks talent.
Entrusted to a mother, unknown what appearance,
born into this body, all day walking in dust and dirt.
Encountering bamboo splinters, due to repaying karma,
meeting the cattle king, to cease disaster."
But how could the cowherd not believe,
again and again, with compassionate thought, now sing of what is to come.
(Sutra) At that time, the cowherd looked all over his body, observing,
his human appearance was unusual.
He then spoke: "My home is nearby,
I should provide for you."
At that time, the cowherd then took Shànyǒu back to his home,
gave him various foods and drinks,
admonished the men, women, young and old of his household: "You all serve this person,
no differently from me."
Though Shànyǒu explained thus,
the cowherd ultimately did not believe,
and so took him back.
Verse says:
"Though my eyes are blind, I entrust this lowly body to you,
Yet how can I bear not being suited to endure hunger and poverty?
My twin brows, thick and dark, extend into the temples,
My two ears, sharp and pointed, hang like dangling wheels.
My philtrum is level and upright, my mouth high like a phoenix's beak,
Distinctly, on my fingers, swirl the patterns of conch shells.
Do not dislike that I dwell in a village garden,
With this body I shall nurture and care for you."
The blind man thus agreed to leave.
The cowherd took him home to care for him,
Instructing his family, young and old,
Not to treat him lightly or with disrespect.
As mentioned earlier.
After a month had passed in this manner,
His family grew weary and resentful, and there were complaints.
Shànyǒu heard the voices and was displeased.
He then thought to himself,
"Tomorrow morning, I shall bid farewell and wish to depart."
The cowherd said:
"Is it because my family, young and old, have been disrespectful?"
He replied: "It is not so,
It is not that your family, young and old, lack compassion,
But rather that I myself am without merit,
Thus it is not fitting for me to stay long."
A verse of farewell:
"I ponder my hunger and poverty, always humbling myself,
Blind eyes make distant things hard to grasp.
The mat I lie on was given by your wife,
The water for washing my face was added by your virtuous son.
Silently, they grumble and sigh because of my begging,
Clearly, their care for you is strict.
Today, the reason I bid farewell,
Is that I must not wait until they grow to dislike me."
The cowherd said: "You must not leave!"
Shànyǒu said: "It cannot be,
I must leave!"
Thus, again and again,
He could not be persuaded to stay.
The cowherd then asked: "What do you need for your journey?"
The blind man said: "If you pity and think of me,
Make for me a zither,
And place me in a crowded area of the city,
I shall play tunes and beg for food!"
The cowherd then obtained a zither and gave it to him,
Sending him to the market of the kingdom of Lìshīwáng.
Though lingering is heartfelt, I have no mind to stay,
With utmost sincerity, I bow and bid farewell, for I must depart.
The blind scholar knows well the trouble he has caused,
The cowherd cannot help but feel doubt and worry.
"My dwelling is poor,
And in a village besides,
Hard to provide pearls or gold to assist.
I offer a zither from my home,
And send you to a place with many people."
The host's care for the guest is clear,
Rarely is the bond between host and guest as strong as today.
The guest, moved by the trouble caused, speaks earnestly,
The host, ashamed of the loneliness, tears welling up.
At home, we lack food for the three meals,
For the journey, I offer a zither as a token.
Both sides have fulfilled all propriety,
Together they go all the way to Lìshīchéng.
Leaning on his shoulder, he enters the kingdom and sits on the long street,
Bidding the cowherd farewell, asking him to return.
Relying on others, it is hard to dislike the bustle,
Passing through, trusting, he brushes off the dust.
Stroking his head and face, he privately rejoices,
Adjusting the zither strings, he secretly arranges a tune.
How many people come to watch,
How like the sound born (born sound) from his fingers, he will sing it forth.
(Sutra) Shànyǒu was skilled at playing the zither,
His music harmonious and elegant,
Delighting the hearts of all.
All the people provided him with food and drink,
Even to the point of abundance,
In the kingdom of Lìshībá, five hundred beggars were all satisfied.
Once in the kingdom,
He played the zither,
All the people watched,
Including the five hundred poor people.
Playing even more movingly, touching people's hearts,
Yet never revealing his name.
In his tunes, he could early on distinguish rhythm and beat,
On the strings, even more skillfully fitting the sounds.
Not only did it reach the palace, heard within,
But also spread and stirred the kingdom's city.
All the neighbors invited him,
Regardless of high or low, all came to listen.
Thus, the people of the neighborhood,
Passed word among themselves,
Prepared clothing,
Provided tea and food.
Not only was the blind scholar himself fully fed,
But he also universally aided five hundred poor people.
All were blessed by the cause of his tunes,
All sheltered by the virtue of his songs.
Daily in the neighborhood, he played songs,
Everywhere, thousands gathered to watch.
All said he must have another home,
All lamented it was a pity he had no sight.
Bowls full of rice,
Clothing abundant,
Regardless of high or low, all cared for him.
Not to mention the abundance for one person,
Enough to provide for five hundred poor children.
Day after day, sitting in the market, playing strings and singing,
Women flocked like clouds, helplessly drawn.
His elegant tunes were both high and steady,
His clear sounds could be beautiful and harmonious.
Not only was everyone's hunger satisfied,
But also clothing increased day by day.
Five hundred poor men were all warm and fed,
Whose merit could compare to his?
Joyful and pleased, his heart was at ease,
Daily, people filled the six streets to listen.
His appearance suddenly shed its haggardness,
His clothing all changed, free from dust.
Never did his name reach others' ears,
Only his songs blended with worldly wealth.
Just as he was enjoying peace and happiness,
By whom was he invited to sing forth?
(Sutra) At that time, the king had a fruit garden,
The garden was lush,
But often troubled by birds.
The garden keeper said to Shànyǒu: "You shall guard against the birds for me,
I shall provide well for you,
I wish ... ..."
The Eleventh Scroll of the *Sutra of the Buddha's Repayment of Kindness*.
The monk △Bǐ says: A thousand years, the river changes,
Ten thousand chariots, a ruler is born.
Drinking the spiritual light of the sun and moon,
Embracing the righteous energy of heaven and earth.
Yearly on the ninth day,
The crimson court spreads auspicious smoke;
Annually on the Double Ninth,
The world rejoices in this fine festival.
His position honors the nine and five,
His sageliness matches the thousand.
If not the hidden form of a Bodhisattva,
Then the response of a Wheel-Turning King.
Cultivating merit and wisdom causes over countless kalpas,
Only then becoming the ruler of humanity, governing heaven and earth.
If dwelling in the Buddha-land, named the Tamer,
Coming to reside in the Divine Land, called the Most Honored.
Planning the world's peace, promoting the imperial way,
Wishing weapons to rest, descending from the heavenly gate.
But speak of the sun and moon shining upon all,
Where do the living beings not feel gratitude?
Golden autumn, jade dew moistens the dust,
Golden halls, jade steps arrayed with precious terraces.
Sweeping mist, the golden wind blows, the frontiers quiet,
Misty golden chrysanthemums face the sky in bloom.
Golden branches of the imperial family surround the throne,
Golden-robed court ministers present longevity cups.
Wishing to praise golden words, aiding the sage's longevity,
Forever like metal and stone, sing forth.
According to the text,
based on the phrase in this piece, "The sutra title chanted by the lead lecturer just now,
is said to be 'The Prajñāpāramitā Sutra for Humane Kings Who Wish to Protect Their States · First Chapter on the Preface,'"
it can be known that this piece is a lecture text expounding upon *The Prajñāpāramitā Sutra for Humane Kings Who Wish to Protect Their States*,
hence the later title *Excerpts from the Prajñāpāramitā Sutra for Humane Kings*,
where *Prajñāpāramitā Sutra for Humane Kings* is the abbreviated name of *The Prajñāpāramitā Sutra for Humane Kings Who Wish to Protect Their States*,
and lecture texts directly using the sutra name as their title
