is also a common convention among Dunhuang manuscripts.
The former title *Lecture Text for the Yìngshèng Festival at the Zhōngxīng Hall in the Fourth Year of the Chángxīng Era*,
is named according to the occasion of this piece's application.
"Chángxīng" was the era name of Emperor Míngzōng of the Later Táng,
"the fourth year of Chángxīng" corresponds to 933 CE.
"Zhōngxīng Hall" was the place where Emperor Míngzōng of the Later Táng held court,
*Old History of the Five Dynasties · Book of the Táng · Annals of Emperor Míngzōng II* records: "(First year of Tiānchéng) On the day Xīnhài,
the Emperor began holding court at the Zhōngxīng Hall.

" *Comprehensive Mirror to Aid in Government*, annotation by Hú Sānxǐng for the fourth year of Chángxīng of Emperor Míngzōng of the Later Táng, quotes *Essentials of the Five Dynasties*: "In the second year of Tóngguāng of Emperor Zhuāngzōng of the Táng,
the Chóngxūn Hall in Luòyáng was renamed Zhōngxīng Hall.
" "Yìngshèng Festival" refers to the birthday of Emperor Míngzōng of the Later Táng (the ninth day of the ninth month),
*Cèfǔ Yuánguī*, Volume 2, *Imperial Section · Birth of a Sage*: "In the sixth month of the first year of Tiānchéng,
the Secretariat memorialized: The ninth day of the ninth month is the Emperor's birthday,
according to precedent, a special festival name should be established,
designating that day as the Yìngshèng Festival,
with a three-day holiday.
Furthermore, let the capital and the realm set up music,
to express congratulations and wishes for longevity,
this was approved.
" Note: "Tiānchéng" was the era name when Emperor Míngzōng ascended the throne.
Each year on the Yìngshèng Festival, it was customary to summon Buddhist monks and Daoist priests to the Zhōngxīng Hall for lectures and discussions,
to celebrate.
*Old History of the Five Dynasties · Book of the Táng · Annals of Emperor Míngzōng III*: "(Ninth month of the first year of Tiānchéng) On the day Guǐhài,
the Yìngshèng Festival,
all officials set up a vegetarian feast at the Jìng'ài Temple,
and summoned the assembly of Buddhist and Daoist clergy to the Zhōngxīng Hall for lectures and discussions,
following recent precedent.
" The so-called "recent precedent,"
refers to the general practice since the mid-to-late Táng dynasty,
of holding sutra lectures on the emperor's birthday.
The Japanese monk Ennin's *Record of a Pilgrimage to China in Search of the Law*, Volume 4: "National custom: Every year on the emperor's birthday,
invite the great virtuous lecturers from both streets and Daoist priests to set up vegetarian feasts and incense offerings within the palace,
invite monks to discuss the sutras,
and hold debates between Buddhism and Daoism.
" *Brief History of the Sangha*, Volume 2, *Birthday Ceremonies Appendix*: "Using the birthday as a festival name,
began with Emperor Xuánzōng of the Táng.
Emperor Tàiwǔ of the Wèi, in the second year of Shǐguāng, established a ceremonial site,
and by the fourth year of Shén,
decreed that all provinces and towns establish ceremonial sites to celebrate the emperor's birthday.
The Shǐguāng period marks the beginning of the emperor's own veneration of blessings,
the Shén period marks the beginning of ministers offering congratulations for the emperor's longevity.
Since then,
ministers' auspicious congratulations must involve preparing vegetarian feasts and reciting sutras,
called the birthday festival ceremonial site,
which remains prevalent today.
Furthermore,
the lecturer of this lecture text,
that is, the author,
according to Mr. Liú Míngshù's speculation,
should be Yúnbiàn,
as discussed in *Collected Notes on Dunhuang Manuscripts · The Lecturer of the 'Lecture Text for the Yìngshèng Festival at the Zhōngxīng Hall in the Fourth Year of the Chángxīng Era,'*
published in *Collected Essays on Dunhuang Language and Literature*,
Zhèjiāng Ancient Books Publishing House, 1988.
Note: Yúnbiàn was a famous monk of the Five Dynasties period,
also written as Yúnbiàn,
his deeds are recorded in Zhāng Qíxián's *Old Tales Heard from Luòyáng Noblewomen*, Volume 1, *The Madcap Junior Mentor
(Yáng Gōng Níngshì)*: "At that time, the monk Yúnbiàn was skilled in popular preaching,
possessed literary talent,
was quick in response,
if it was congratulatory or prayerful words,
according to the rank and status of the person,
he could compose a thousand words facing them,
all as if prepared in advance.
The Junior Mentor especially esteemed him.
Yúnbiàn was lecturing at the Chángshòu Temple in the fifth month,
the Junior Mentor went to the lecture hall and sat facing Yúnbiàn,
with singers at their side,
suddenly a large spider descended by its thread from the eaves,
right in front of the Junior Mentor and the monk
(this sentence has missing characters),
Yúnbiàn smiled and said to the singer: 'Try to mock this spider,
if the mockery hits the mark,
I will offer two bolts of silk.'
" The singer, without further thought,
responded immediately with a mockery,
the meaning entirely不离 the spider,
yet the mocking words,
actually satirized Yúnbiàn.
The Junior Mentor, hearing this,
was overcome with laughter for a long time,
then shouted loudly: 'Monk, bring five bolts of silk!
" Yúnbiàn smiled,
and thus offered five bolts of silk to him.
The singer mocked the spider thus: 'It eats till its belly is drum-tight,
seeking silk, it circles the temple's path;
in the air it sets its snares,
only waiting to kill all living beings.'
(This satirized Yúnbiàn)
(because he was corpulent and had a large belly).
Master Yúnbiàn's monastic name was Yuánjiàn,
later he became the Left Street Registrar,
and after a long time, passed away.
" Note: Yúnbiàn's works of Buddhist popular literature,
preserved through Dunhuang manuscripts,
besides this piece,
also include S.7, S.3728, P.3361 *Preliminary Verses on the Twenty-Four Filial Piety Exemplars* (included in the first part of this book),
P.2603 *Ten Verses in Praise of Universal Fullness*,
S.4472 *Ten Songs of Soliciting Donations for Building Temple Halls*,
S.4472 *Ten Verses on Compassion*, etc.
Sutra
The Emperor, ten thousand years... ... ... ...
With this, the merits generated from opening and praising the Mahayana,
are reverently dedicated to His Majesty the Emperor, adorned with the honorable title.
Humbly wishing the imperial branches ten thousand leaves,
the imperial lifespan a thousand springs;
as deep and profound as the Bohai Sea,
and as firm and solid as Mount Sumeru.
Dedicated for
(chanting Buddha's name)
the Empress,
humbly wishing her ever-renewing exemplary conduct,
eternally spreading the feminine virtues.
Receiving the favor and glory of the ten thousand chariots,
exercising benevolent love throughout the six palaces.
For the Virtuous Consort,
humbly wishing her longevity comparable to the divine catalpa,
her years as numerous as kalpa stones.
May praises for her extending grace be further spoken,
and her fame for internal governance reach far and wide.
Then, may the ruler lead and the ministers harmonize,
heaven complete and earth level.
May beacon fires cease and the world be at peace,
the sun and moon bright and weapons of war still.
(chanting Buddha's name)
The sutra title chanted by the lead lecturer just now,
said to be *The Prajñāpāramitā Sutra for Humane Kings Who Wish to Protect Their States · First Chapter on the Preface*: Humane,
is the foremost of the five constant virtues;
King,
is the尊 of all states;
Protect,
is the sages and worthies bestowing blessings;
State,
is the thoroughfare connecting the civilized and the barbarian;
Prajñā is perfect wisdom and intelligence;
Pāramitā is crossing over the river of desire;
Sutra reveals and displays the true doctrine.
This briefly clarifies the title.
Now, this sutra is explained thus: The Great Sage, formerly at Líng Mountain,
gathered the sixteen great kings of states,
surrounded by hundreds and thousands of holy multitudes.
At that time, there was the Bodhisattva King of Heaven, King Prasenajit,
who lowered his golden crown amidst the ocean assembly,
and paid homage to the compassionate countenance upon the lotus throne.
He requested the exposition of the ten grounds,
wishing to understand the three emptinesses.
He hoped for golden words that protect the state,
and looked forward to jade verses that bring peace to the times.
Then the World-Honored One proclaimed the wondrous principles,
entrusting them to the enlightened ruler.
In the far-reaching sense, it leads to becoming a Buddha and saving people;
in the immediate sense, it brings peace to the people and order to the state.
Implementing the ten good deeds,
to cease the three calamities.
When the mind's conduct is harmonious, wind and rain also become harmonious;
when laws and decrees are upright, the stars naturally become upright.
True customs and worldly truths proceed together,
like fish and water mutually dependent;
royal law and Buddhist sutras jointly transform,
like clouds and dragons in accord.
Wishing the cosmos forever peaceful and clear,
with purified hearts seeking, listen with devoted minds;
within the state, no error in the timing of rain and wind,
in the heavens, no deficiency in the sun, moon, and stars.
The Tamer and Guide, bestowing compassion, though earnest and sincere,
the monarch seeking the Dharma was even more insistent;
Thus the Tathāgata expounded the method for pacifying the state,
hence named *The Sutra for Humane Kings Who Protect Their States*.
The monarch, earnest and sincere, paid homage at the flower throne,
only hoping golden words would be opened for the multitude;
The sun of wisdom illuminates and destroys the evils in the heart,
the wind of compassion blows away the calamities in the state.
Diligently, I dare hope the Compassionate One will grant,
understanding and realization should then cause the emerald carriage to return;
I do not yet know where this sutra was spoken,
who heard the Dharma? Let it be chanted forth.
Sutra
To explain this sutra,
it is divided into three major sections: first,
the introductory section;
second,
the main body;
third,
the dissemination section.
Among these three sections,
we shall first discuss the introductory section.
Within the introductory section,
according to the *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra-śāstra*,
it is subdivided into five types of accomplishment.
"Thus have I heard,"
is the accomplishment of faith;
the two characters "yī shí" (one time),
are the accomplishment of time;
the single character "Fó" (Buddha),
is the accomplishment of the teaching master;
"dwelt at Vulture Peak Mountain in the city of Rājagṛha,"
is the accomplishment of place;
"together with a great assembly of 1,800 bhikṣus,"
is the accomplishment of the audience.
Now, the first,
"Thus have I heard," is the accomplishment of faith.
When the Tathāgata expounded the Dharma,
he entrusted it to those with faith,
sometimes speaking of causes and conditions spanning kalpas,
often describing meritorious practices as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
Those with shallow roots find it difficult to approach,
only with deep faith can one understand.
Hearing half a verse, one might offer one's entire body;
seeking a single word, one might make offerings for a thousand years.
Only if faith and reverence arise,
will one willingly receive and uphold it.
Faith is the initial gateway to entering the Dharma,
wisdom is the profound means for ultimate realization.
Similarly, our emperor earnestly aspires to the true realm,
with resolve and faith in the gate of emptiness.
He cultivates the causes and effects of the three periods,
and reveres the Buddhadharma of the ten directions.
If it were not so,
how could it be that on every occasion of his birthday,
he specially holds a royal banquet?
On the jade steps, he permits monks and teachers to be seated;
in the golden hall, he respectfully hangs portraits for the porridge offering.
He personally gazes upon the auspicious marks,
and himself lights incense.
All because a single-minded faith is firm,
that he is able to sit and hear the Dharma for half a morning.
The great enlightened Móuní transforms those with affinity,
personally expounding the *Protection of the Nation* at Língshān.
Tens of thousands of disciples hear the golden verses,
sixteen monarchs pay homage to the jade countenance.
We wish to board together the precious ship of wisdom,
and together climb the Bodhi flower tree.
If not for the faithful invitation of the sovereign,
how could the sutra text fill the world?
Now the emperor opens with faith and reverence,
each time relying on the Three Jewels to avert disasters.
The sovereign hears the Dharma ascending the golden hall,
the Buddhist and Daoist masters discuss the sutras upon the precious dais (upon the precious dais).
May his longevity equal the pine and the chun tree, ever increasing;
may his blessings be like the Eastern Sea, ever expanding.
Precisely because the sovereign of ten thousand chariots has faith,
monks and teachers from all under heaven come to offer longevity.
Second,
the two characters "yī shí" (one time) are the accomplishment of time.
It means as soon as the World-Honored One spoke,
the disciples immediately heard,
demonstrating the non-difference between the capable and the object,
revealing the unity of teacher and disciple.
The minds of people eagerly yearn,
the Buddha's mouth proclaims and spreads.
Like the spring wind arriving and flowers blooming,
like autumn waters clearing and the moon appearing.
Similarly, our emperor each year responds to the sacred occasion,
specially spreads a flower banquet,
signifying the time when the eight directions encounter an enlightened ruler,
singing of the day when the sovereign of ten thousand chariots corresponds to the flowing rainbow.
With a single sound of silk and bamboo,
they welcome the Yáo and Shùn-like sovereign temporarily emerging from the deep palace;
with several processions of banners and flowers,
they lead the assembly of monks and Daoists to ascend the precious hall.
Monarch and ministers gather,
inside and outside there is joyful acclaim.
The enlightened sovereign personally pays homage to the three bodies,
the entire hall gazes upon the eightfold brilliance.
Ox-head incense gently wafts,
fish-drum chanting leisurely sounds.
Having passed through the sovereign's ten-thousand-chariot Dharma arena,
it is also a single moment's Dharma realm.
Whenever the Buddha speaks, he expounds great compassion,
humans and devas follow, wishing to dispel doubts.
Having paid homage to the dignified form among the flowers,
in the ears they still hear the words of sweet dew.
The Buddha observes the disciples with a sage's mind,
people see Móuní with ordinary eyes.
Precisely because speaking and hearing have no before or after,
therefore the sutra text is called "yī shí" (one time).
The wind idly scatters incense smoke filling the hall,
everyone has words to wish longevity to Yáo.
The sovereign joyfully leads, ascending the dragon throne,
the Buddhist disciples are announced, entering the phoenix steps.
The sage ruler purifies his mind, gazing upon the moon-like face,
ordinary people cleanse their eyes, seeing the brows of Yáo.
Each year on this day hearing the Buddha's Way,
it is also like the sutra being called "yī shí" (one time).
Third,
explaining the single character "Fó" (Buddha),
is the third, the accomplishment of the teaching master.
The teaching master of the Sahā world,
the great enlightened Móuní,
with a body one zhang six chi tall,
and thirty-two auspicious marks.
Sages and ordinary beings all look up to him,
slander and praise cannot shake him.
Vast and boundless, the great guide of humans and devas;
lofty and majestic, the true compassionate father of the Dharma realm.
Similarly, our emperor is the lord of ten thousand states,
the honored one of the four seas.
In public and private, all respectfully gaze upon his comings and goings;
the sages and worthies, whether in seclusion or activity, all protect and uphold him.
At that Dharma assembly,
the tamer of the four kinds of births was the honored one;
in today's Dharma arena,
the sovereign of ten thousand chariots is the master.
At that Dharma assembly, the Buddha was the honored one,
opening the gate of cool liberation.
The mind-mirror's subtle light contains sun and moon,
the compassionate clouds and Dharma rain sprinkle heaven and earth.
His body manifests the forms of sages and worthies, high and low;
the Dharma accords with the deep and shallow roots of humans and devas.
[But for those who can transcend the three realms,
considering it, it is still the grace of the Dharma King.
Today's Dharma assembly, the emperor is the honored one,
not concealing the gate of governance of Fúxī and Xuānyuán.
His compassion is like clouds and thunder shaking seas and mountains,
his brightness like sun and moon illuminating heaven and earth.
With compassionate pity, he understands and cherishes the foundation of the state and family;
with rain and dew, he can nourish the roots of grass and trees.
But for those who can dwell in peace and happiness,
their foundation is entirely the grace of the sage.
"Dwelt at Vulture Peak Mountain in the city of Rājagṛha,"
is the fourth, the accomplishment of place.
The Buddha expounded the *Protection of the Nation*,
dwelling at Língshān.
A thousand layers of verdant peaks touch the sky,
a hundred streams of cold brooks spray snow.
Moss and lichen are mottled,
competing with brocade-like patterns of flowers;
pines and junipers intertwine,
coiling like the giant claws of a black dragon.
The mountain being lofty and great,
the Buddha often walked there.
The Dharma King sat properly upon the cloud cliffs,
the disciples came hastening through the misty trees.
Similarly, our emperor, on every golden festival,
returns to the vermilion courtyard,
seeing the heavenly countenance before the palace of the upper realm,
arranging the great assembly within the ninefold hall.
At that time, the tamer preached the sutra,
dwelling on the high mountain of Vulture Peak;
today, the sovereign hears the Dharma,
in the precious hall of the dragon palace.
Majestic, the Buddha's form resembles a golden mountain,
afflictions withered away, ten thousand kalpas at ease.
Skillfully displaying compassion to pacify the nation's realm,
adroitly using merit to moisten the human world.
The mind-lamp unobstructed, shines on a thousand gates;
the fruit of wisdom long teaches the masses to climb.
Wishing to speak the *Benevolent King Protection of the Nation Dharma*,
on the summit of Vulture Peak, one sees the compassionate face.
Our emperor's blessings and virtue are weighty as a mountain,
the four seas without dust, his mind naturally at ease.
His sage response, ruling within a thousand years,
autumn abundance and summer harvest within a decade.
The virtue of Yǔ and Tāng can hardly compare,
the benevolence of Yáo and Shùn one might slightly approach.
Every time at the Double Ninth, monks and Daoists,
within the depths of purple mist, see the dragon countenance.
"Together with a great assembly of eighteen hundred bhikṣus" refers to
the fifth accomplishment of the retinue.
The World-Honored One traveled to teach,
with disciples following him.
Brahmā, Śakra, and dragon deities,
kings, heavenly lords, along with men and women,
dignified bodhisattvas,
surrounded and attended the Tathāgata.
Their heads adorned with jeweled crowns and feet upon lotus flowers,
their words flowed like a hanging river and their minds vast as the great sea.
Majestic arhats,
serene true monks.
Two spots of snow on their brows never melting,
a strip of cloud on their robes ever present.
Walking, they followed in orderly ranks;
sitting, they encircled flowered platforms.
Like the sea surging around a golden mountain,
or stars clustered around the bright moon.
Just as our emperor's sacred branches number ten thousand leaves,
the imperial lineage a thousand men,
when he goes forth, all officials rejoice;
when he enters, the six palaces gaze with reverence.
Empresses, consorts, and princesses
linger in the light of the sun and moon;
crown princes and royal grandsons
surround him within the shadow of the imperial carriage.
Cultivated over many lifetimes,
through countless kalpas of causes and conditions.
The Buddha has bodhisattvas and śrāvakas;
the king has golden branches and jade leaves.
Whenever the Compassionate One turns the Dharma wheel,
sages and worthies encircle his purple-gold body.
Compassionate winds ripen the fruits of cultivation,
sweet dew cleanses the dust of arising delusions.
Mountains like emerald screens uphold halls and pavilions;
the Buddha like the bright moon governs stars and constellations.
Only due to cultivation in past lives reaching fruition,
can one long follow those without outflows.
The emperor reigns supreme within the seas;
the sacred branches alone receive the fresh rain and dew.
The palace women's hearts lean on him like the winter sun;
civil and military ranks surround him like the North Star.
In Shùn's hall lingers the lord of a thousand years;
under Yáo's sky, ten thousand layers of kin find shelter.
All because of the meeting of causes and conditions over many kalpas,
can one long remain near the sage.
Your servant hears: it is known that the Buddha's words become sutras,
the king's words become edicts.
If sutras are practiced, one abandons the ordinary and attains sagehood;
if edicts are practiced, the distant are awed and the near are peaceful.
The king's grace reaches scholars, farmers, artisans, and merchants;
the Buddha's kindness spreads to dragons, devas, Śakra, and Brahmā.
The Buddha's mind is pure,
enabling those with spiritual powers to liberate beings;
the king's intent is clear,
dispatching loyal and filial ministers to assist the state.
In the Buddha's assembly of that time,
the harmony of the four assemblies was already evident;
in the king's palace today,
the accomplishment of the five teachings also flourishes.
The causes and conditions of the Dharma assembly reach the imperial palace;
the accomplishment of the five teachings should correspond in affairs.
Buddhist sutras are revered everywhere;
who does not respect and honor the king's edicts?
Understanding and upholding the statutes eliminates calamities;
able to follow the Dharma's words, one attests to spiritual powers.
If not for the emperor's heart being like the Buddha's,
how could this śramaṇa have come here?
Therefore, Emperor Wén of Sòng said to Guṇavarman: "This disciple often wishes to observe precepts and abstain from killing,
but compelled by serving worldly affairs with this body,
I cannot follow my aspiration.
How would the Dharma master instruct me?"
The Sòng emperor, harboring doubts unresolved, opened
and asked the śramaṇa to approach the jade steps.
Knowing the difficulty of practicing the kingly way without partisanship,
he often worried his compassionate heart still had faults.
Confronting our state laws, it is hard to cease killing;
placed in his kingly position, he cannot maintain abstinence.
Today he dares to request the high monk to speak,
with one clear phrase to awaken his mind.
Guṇavarman said: "What emperors and commoners cultivate differs.
A commoner's body is lowly, his name inferior,
his words and commands lack authority.
If he does not labor with his own body,
how will he bring benefit?
An emperor regards the four seas as his home,
the myriad people as his children.
Uttering one good word,
men and women rejoice;
enacting one benevolent policy,
humans and spirits harmonize.
He should certainly not let punishments cut short fate,
nor conscript labor to exhaustion.
Then wind and rain will come in season,
cold and warmth respond appropriately,
the hundred grains will flourish abundantly,
mulberry and hemp grow lush.
Maintaining abstinence in this way is great indeed;
refraining from killing in this way benefits many indeed.
Must one then miss half a day's meal,
or spare one bird's life,
only then can it be called widely saving?"
The emperor stroked his armrest and said: "What the Dharma master says
truly enlightens and clarifies understanding;
it can discuss the boundary between humans and devas.
Excellent indeed is such a man!
Not only does he guide advancement into the gate of emptiness,
but he also aids in promoting the kingly transformation."
Thus it is known that the Tathāgata's wondrous practices
can be cultivated by a state's ruler;
not measurable by lesser sages,
how could ordinary folk compare?
With one word just spoken,
the four seas all receive it.
Dispatched, those embracing loyalty and practicing filial piety broaden the Way and renew virtue;
commanded, those betraying righteousness and lacking benevolence tremble in heart and dread in gall.
The great peng spreads its wings,
crossing ninety thousand li of mountains and rivers;
the jade hare soars into the sky,
illuminating ten thousand layers of the cosmos.
Where it reaches, its transformation
is vast and great like this,
shaking and stirring no different from clouds and thunder,
moistening and nourishing again like spring rain.
The Buddha's conduct and the king's heart can be compared;
clearly profound and vast, praise is unending.
Just half a morning of the ruler's goodness
equals an ordinary person's cultivation for ten thousand kalpas.
Swiftly, imperial decrees pacify the great state;
copious, rain and dew shower the feudal lords.
Draped in robes, sitting upright deep in the palace,
a single compassionate heart covers the nine provinces.
The sage ruler's cultivation of goodness is inexhaustible;
one must know ordinary folk are far from matching it.
Below, he is lord of the cosmos, of Huá and Yí;
above, he accords with the creative work of yīn and yáng.
The four seas' abundant harvests return to his sagely virtue;
ten thousand states' peace and prosperity bear his celestial wisdom.
The ruler's fortune is the fortune of living beings;
holding heaven and earth in the palm of his hand.
Our emperor, wishing to purify the four seas,
first admonished the six palaces.
Making them know the toil of weaving women,
teaching them recognize the urgency of silkworm families.
Faces without adornment,
hands with calluses.
Where the shuttle is thrown is already arduous;
when brocade and damask are worn, let them be cherished.
The silkworm family's hardships are hard to bear;
all day long, how could they ever approach a mirror stand?
Leaves like fly heads, barely big enough;
silkworms like ant legs, raised to maturity.
Half a cocoon finished, new cicadas call;
one strand of silk formed, old debts urge.
Therefore the sage admonished the palace women:
Do not use gauze and damask to sweep dust.
Our emperor, whenever facing fine meals,
often thinks of the plowing men.
Worrying that water and drought are unseasonable,
fearing taxes and rents are hard to manage.
Therefore, whenever ordering delicacies,
he does not demand elaborate cooking.
Valuing each grain as if a pearl,
cherishing living beings as if his children.
Often mindful of farming families busy in four seasons,
striving to fill granaries and storehouses.
Hair at the temples just turning white,
wheat in the fields only then turning yellow.
Evening sun on their bodies, returning to distant homes;
morning orioles in trees, going to open wasteland.
The farmers' toil seen by the officials,
paying taxes, let them measure with their own hands.
Our emperor, in a state of luxury, shows people frugality;
in a state of frugality, shows people propriety.
Therefore, diligent in his position,
cautious and concerned for the people.
His conduct accords with the heart of heaven;
plain and simple, reverently cultivating the kingly way.
His intent is to forever empty prisons,
long extinguish beacon fires.
Promoting the kindness of untying the net,
opening the governance of knotted cords.
Sageliness and wisdom both complete,
awe and love doubly manifest.
Truly the honor of the five phases,
truly the lord of the myriad people.
A level heart summons a clear and peaceful state;
rewards and punishments all follow the way of heaven.
Rain and dew wash away resentment's breath;
imperial winds blow, auspicious mists rise.
Through the years, no word of weapons is spoken;
full ears only hear the sounds of strings and bamboo.
Like Mount Sōng, unmoving,
for ten thousand years constantly guarding Luòyáng city.
I have heard that though rivers flow in myriad streams,
they ultimately return to the waves of the four seas;
though the state is divided into nine provinces,
they must pay tribute to the ruler of the Central Plains.
Thus, moved by the cessation of disasters in the Eastern River region,
the hearts of Western Shǔ turned back.
Gazing from afar at the sun and moon, they returned to the dragon towers;
from afar, imperial decrees descended to pacify and soothe the turtle-shaped commandery.
Cultivating virtue and benevolence, affairs need no judgment;
mountains and rivers, once desolate and obstructed, now open wide.
From now on, merchants will enter through the Jiàngé Pass;
from this time forth, Dāozhōu will bring tribute.
Several envoys of the court were dispatched on imperial orders;
several times, memorials of gratitude were sent back.
After the Sage Emperor further conferred kingships,
he dispelled many disasters in the southwest.
Our emperor rejects extravagance and excess,
having already pacified the eight directions;
with no forced actions and no interference,
he receives the homage of ten thousand states.
As for the two Zhè regions,
though separated by vast blue waves,
they are moved by the great state's immense grace,
and receive titles and emoluments from the enlightened ruler.
For a long time, they have offered tribute;
their integrity and resolve have never wavered.
When imperial envoys travel, wind and water pose no peril;
when tribute arrives, boats and ships remain safe and auspicious.
With dragons supporting and gods aiding,
they cross ten thousand miles of blue waves;
sails unfurled and winds rising,
they proclaim the sage virtue of a thousand years.
How many times have the two Zhè regions proclaimed this?
Completely free from drifting and unforeseen disasters.
People gather at the vermilion palace gates, arriving over a thousand years;
winds kick up light sails, opening ten thousand miles.
The whale's eye glimmers, shaking the sun and moon;
the sea dragon's mist exhales, transforming into towers and pavilions.
Because they know to offer tribute to the enlightened ruler,
how many dragon gods have escorted them here.
Now, to advance and add honorific titles,
to broadcast again the heavenly merits.
To display the complete loyalty of all officials,
to manifest the true virtue of the sovereign.
The words "sage and enlightened,"
honor the merit of seeing far and wide;
the phrase "divinely martial,"
praises the achievement of quelling chaos and securing the state.
Virtue is taken as the model, broadening the Way and expanding humanity;
expanding humanity and broadening the Way are taken.
Civil virtue shines forth, solemnly pacifying heaven and earth;
reverent filial piety is deep, peacefully honoring the ancestral temple.
Virtue surpasses a thousand ages,
beauty permeates Huá and the barbarians.
Proclaiming one virtue, all within the realm rejoice;
adding four characters, all under heaven celebrate.
Because it is seen that the ruler is in accord with heaven above,
advancing and adding honorific titles is just and fitting.
One person surpassing ancient and modern rulers,
four characters encompassing the mystery of creation.
Already showing the state's prosperity and customs' abundance,
now knowing the ruler's sageliness moves ministers to worthiness.
After being honored as "Modeling Heaven and Broadening the Way,"
he will govern heaven and earth for tens of thousands of years more.
Our emperor values the security of the ancestral altars,
and further solidifies the great foundation.
The righteousness of defending the city is now firm;
the heart like a massive rock grows even stronger.
Therefore, several commanderies' wise lords,
on the same day were enfeoffed as kings.
Yáo's winds blow, golden stamens fragrant;
Shùn's rains moisten, jade pools clear and deep.
East, west, south, north,
imperial sons stand arrayed, propping up heaven;
inside and outside, public and private,
congratulating the imperial relatives who support the sun.
Enfeoffing kings in several commanderies, still strong,
already shows the jade branches spreading in succession.
Deep, deep jade pools nourish the great state;
towering, towering golden pillars stabilize all regions.
Just ascending the carriage, they know the grace is extreme;
How to repay the power of heaven and earth?
Only with loyalty and filial piety to serve the ruler.
Our emperor's words are not spoken in vain,
his wishes are not empty statements.
Moved by the hundred spirits dispelling disasters and inauspiciousness,
bearing the blessings prayed for by the Three Jewels.
On Yùquán Mountain,
the Sage again adorned the Precious Lotus Palace;
by the Jīngǔ River,
the empress... the scripture repository hall.
Above, to aid the ancestral temple;
below, to bless the living beings.
Manifesting the shared brightness of sun and moon,
displaying the combined virtue of yīn and yáng.
The temple on Yùquán Mountain is newly rebuilt,
the work done in timely rain is heard throughout the land.
Morning sun on rainbow beams, light already merged;
blue smoke over mandarin duck tiles, colors hardly distinct.
The hall's stone floor reflects the cold water;
the hall's immortal monks are embraced by scattered clouds.
What can the weak Buddhist disciples accomplish?
Rebuilding must meet a sage and enlightened ruler.
Our emperor's palace's western side,
the garden park newly completed.
Obliquely dividing the light of the jade rabbit,
evenly pouring the water of the golden goose.
... heart of terraces and pavilions,
arranged and raised from heavenly design;
the imperial path's woods and peaks,
their rows and order entirely due to imperial wisdom.
Ten thousand kinds of lovely flowers,
casting shadows like brocade padding in the pond;
a thousand types of auspicious birds,
harmoniously singing, presenting music in the groves.
The imperial residence is not far,
heavenly steps frequently stroll there.
Punting boats, they break through lotus and water chestnut;
playing music, they startle mandarin ducks and egrets into flight.
Clear waves like a mirror,
reflecting ten thousand miles of mountains and rivers;
auspicious vapors like clouds,
flowers holding up a thousand-year tower and pavilion.
Exotic trees and rare flowers arrayed in several layers,
a pond always seen as clear green.
Sporting fish move, opening wheel surfaces;
strolling visitors walk around the mirror's edges.
Autumn lotus, brocade of Shǔ land;
deep night stars and moon, narcissus lamps.
Everyone points to the yellow dragon boat,
wishing to see the enlightened ruler ascend it ten thousand times.
Now, four or five leaves of Yáo's calendula grass,
hold mist, graceful and slender;
hundreds and thousands of clusters of golden chrysanthemums,
attract dew, fragrant and sweet.
On this morning of flowing rainbow responding to auspice,
is the day of great lightning encircling the pivot.
Monarch and ministers gather together,
monks and Daoists linger,
expounding scriptures to bring blessings to the dragon chart,
holding discussions to aid the phoenix screen.
Dew sprinkles, wind drives, all phenomena clear;
phoenixes fly, dragons dance, the nine heavens bright.
The blue sky just sent down a ruler for a thousand years;
Mount Sōng and peaks shout "long live" in unison.
Every festival, banners and flowers array the imperial hall;
today, strings and pipes fill the entire world.
One will know heaven mended the ruler of heaven and earth,
just born on the Double Ninth festival day.
This day, people celebrate and congratulate,
everywhere there is cheering.
Above, generals, ministers, princes, and marquises;
below, scholars, farmers, artisans, and merchants,
all gaze upon Shùn's sun,
all wish for Yáo's heavens.
Where there are human dwellings,
incense and flowers are displayed;
where there are monks and Daoists,
fasts and offerings are performed.
Sheltering grace is broad,
devout prayers hearts are one.
Only hoping the land will be forever peaceful,
only wishing the Sage will have long life.
Today, much is heard of string and pipe music,
filling heaven and earth, celebrating the Sage's birth.
Grace like jade dew drips in every household;
nobility like golden flowers appears in every place.
Above the palace, swirling, not heavy mist;
at the sky's edge, swaying, called light clouds.
I, a monk, pray and invoke to aid heaven's calculation,
wishing to see the Yellow River clear a hundred times.
For three years, the King of Qín dispatched me,
today, Shùn's sun is near, Shùn's clouds.
Polishing and grinding one scroll of selfless words,
offering tribute to a thousand-year ruler of the Way.
Only using proclamation to express the ultimate Way,
no other path to display merit and service.
Again, from today, lecturing before the curtain,
my name will still be heard throughout the four seas.
King Sòng, loyal and filial, serves Yáo's heavens;
one can reckon he burns incense, entrusting to sages and worthies.
Not yet receiving the edict's summons, he cannot enter the palace;
his dreaming soul always stays by the Sage's side.
King Lù, heroic and outstanding, sits in Qízhōu,
pacifying and comforting the people, called a ranked marquis.
Since there is a hero supporting the altars of state,
west of the pass is no worry for the Sage.
Utmost loyalty, utmost integrity, serving the enlightened ruler;
several pieces of auspicious clouds hold up the sun's wheel.
Since ancient times, the Odes and Documents clearly say:
one must know the ruler's sageliness moves worthy ministers.
Several families' joyful dreams first come true;
owing official money, names are crossed off.
Those with worries and troubles all become happy;
must make the emperor's field of blessings grow.
At this time, grace and favor penetrate east and west;
merits and virtues, like Ganges' sands, cannot be counted.
Not considering the various prefectures, counties, and towns,
all are startled that prisons are empty at once.
Having received grace beyond the ordinary,
At night, facing the stars, I burn precious incense.
How can I once more express my loyalty and filial devotion?
I open a sutra collection to repay my sovereign.
All beings cultivate practices without error,
Only then may they pass through the emperor's household.
The emperor suddenly bestows a horse,
Teaching his subject to ride it, boasting throughout the capital.
Who does not understand loving glory and splendor?
Fierce and sharp in body and mind, and fond of boasting.
Admirable is the loyal minister Yán Guǎng□,
Who renounced glory, shaved his head, to repay the royal house.
The sage's compassion is like the sun wheel opening,
Its illuminating light shines throughout the nine realms.
All is due to the emperor's grace, in accord with divine Buddhas,
Heaven moved Western monks to come to the dharma assembly.
Journeying over a hundred thousand li of flowing sands,
To the Táng country, coming to court at the emperor's house.
The monastic title and purple robe were bestowed by grace,
Always to be taken back to one's homeland for boasting.
By the river, suddenly seeing a small snake creature,
I tried to pick it up and cast it into the deep water.
Thus, in the emerald pool, it learned to nurture its nature,
Recently, it has also learned to command thunder and wind.
Pitying the fish in a dried-up pond with little water,
I let flowing waves, trickling drops, reach the ditches.
Recently, they somewhat resemble scales and shells,
Yet they claim all dragons are not their equal.
Seeing that parrot speak clearly,
No effort was spared in raising it to maturity.
Recently, knowing its feathers have grown strong,
In the sky, it constantly makes resentful human sounds.
Detestable is the lapdog, its fur fluffy,
Lifted and raised, laboriously fed rich food.
Doting on it, hoping it would guard and protect,
Who knew it would instead bark at its master.
Ducklings on water learn to float and sink,
Following their nature, ultimately without care or attachment.
Pity the hen, her heart broken inch by inch,
How could she know he is an ungrateful fowl?
Spiders each night spin many threads,
Coming and going in the air, weaving their webs.
Thinking they would dwell with single mind in the old place,
Who knew their intent was to seek another nest?
Jade hooves, red ears, by the trough at times,
Fed and reared, truly taught to become plump.
Not hoping for reins to hold or to serve as a mount,
Recently, especially, it has become hard to ride.
Common trees like ailanthus and elm surround the pavilions and terraces,
Felled, why must they be planted again?
It is merely a futile waste of effort,
In the end, they will not become pillars or beams.
Great and small among men, unknown and unheard,
Advancement or withdrawal, surpassing the norm, none remains.
Since the root is inferior, of lowly origin,
How can they be chosen to accompany the noble lord?
Rénwáng Prajñā Sūtra Excerpt
Having ascended the seat,
First recite the gāthā,
Burn incense,
Invoke the names of the Buddhas (and) Bodhisattvas.
Since the great awakening opened the profound gate,
At Deer Park and Vulture Peak, the Dharma wheel was turned.
The five divisions, three vehicles, all ocean treasuries,
Spread throughout the world, all receive grace.
Monks, nuns, the fourfold assembly come to the golden land,
Holding flowers, canopies, like rushing clouds.
This day, having cast aside the burning house,
For a while, do not clamor, listen to the sutra.
The holy teachings of the three vehicles are truly worth hearing,
Each phrase can lighten the burden of karmic obstacles.
Not only will it lead to future Buddhahood,
It must surely crumble mountains of accumulated kalpas of sin.
Day after day, only worrying about family affairs,
When have they ever had a day to hear the sutra?
Assembly, for a while, join your palms,
Listen to the Dharma with one mind, can you or not?
But this humble monk was born in a turbid age,
Unworthily placed among the Saṅgha,
Completely lacking the ability of learning and understanding,
Vainly receiving the faithful offerings of humans and devas.
Traveling east to the splendid capital of the Táng country,
The sage ruler rewarded with purple robes,
Receiving grace, specially granted the title of Preceptor.
Intending at Wǔtái Shān,
To stroll among pines and bamboos;
Before the Mañjuśrī Hall,
To offer incense and flowers, passing the days.
Wishing to contemplate universal conversion,
I then left Zhōnghuá.
Carrying a single staff, I came west,
The journey took several years;
Making the three robes in the sandy deserts,
Far reaching Kūn(gǎng).
Approached Niútóu Shān,
Toured the country of Yútián.
Further wishing to ascend the snowy peaks to the west,
Personally visit the Vulture Peak.
Lamenting my own deep karmic obstacles,
My body encountered illness,
Thus, from afar, holding slight virtue,
I came and reached this place.
Beholding our sacred heavenly Qaghan of the great Huíhú country,
None is not a land broad ten thousand li,
A realm vast with a thousand mountains,
A great state with many soldiers,
People strong, horses sturdy.
The heavenly king's name spreads across the four seas,
His virtue pervades heaven and earth,
For over thirty years,
The state secure, the people peaceful.
Long ago receiving the prediction of the Buddhas,
Relying on the empowerment of sages and worthies,
Temporarily called emperor and sovereign,
In truth, he is an incarnated Bodhisattva.
Already in accord with the nine [five]fold favor,
He then receives the sage ruler's grace.
Upright and peerless,
The heavenly princesses Dèng Lín and others,
None not with beauty surpassing groups of immortals,
Faces like peach and plum blossoms,
Compassionate, benevolent, jade-smooth.
The various heavenly [ministers] especially diligent,
None not with sincere hearts serving the state,
Loyal, filial, preserving their persons whole.
Sweeping away barbarian foes across mountains and rivers,
Requiring only a single arrow's effort;
Quelling baleful auras at the purple frontier,
Needing no bowstrings.
Thus, Gélù, Yàomó,
Differently featured Dádàn,
Competed to come and submit,
Vied in offering pearls and gold.
Dúxī then presented camels and horses,
Tǔfān sent treasures, sent gold.
Báxīmì were originally household-born,
Xiájiásī were originally slaves.
The various barbarian tribes,
Like sparrows fearing eagles;
The nearby prefectures and cities,
Like sheep seeing tigers.
Truly fitting for this country,
Not empty words.
This humble monk is fortunate to be within the Śākya gate,
□ dare to offer praise.
Furthermore, the various chancellors, dágan, dūdū, diāoshǐ, sàwēn, méilù, shǐ, dìlüè,
All are the heavenly king's left and right,
Assisting, supporting the golden gate.
Officials, generals, ministers, and such,
None [not] externally rectifying the state's borders,
Internally serving with loyal diligence,
For the ruler, for the sovereign,
Without complaint, dawn till dusk.
Good men, good women,
Dānapati with faithful hearts,
Upholding precepts, maintaining purity,
Cultivating diligently without weariness.
Furthermore, the various dūtǒng, Vinaya masters, Tripiṭaka masters, legal masters, Saṅgha administrators, temple heads, Chan masters, [head] ascetics, nuns, āyí teachers, etc.,
Cannot name each one individually,
All have precept pearls shining brightly,
Dharma water clear and pure,
Acting as teachers for humans and devas,
Being treasures within the state.
Further wishing to broadly express praise,
Fearful of wasting time,
Unable to discuss in detail,
Hereafter, briefly present confession.
All who listen to the Dharma,
Must seek compassion,
Reveal and confess,
First receive the three refuges,
Then request the five precepts,
Only then may hear the Dharma,
Increase good roots.
Then chant the sutra,
Surely obtaining protection and blessings.
Invoke the Buddha's name three to five times.
(Sons of Buddha)
Long lamenting, kalpas sunk in birth and death,
Revolving in the six paths, when will it cease?
In the three evil paths, hells, receiving bitter toil,
Only because of creating evil karma over many lives.
The sins of killing, stealing, sexual misconduct,
False speech, daily deceiving sages and worthies.
Frivolous speech, divisive speech, uttering evil words,
Unafraid of the future three evil paths.
Greed, anger, wrong views, foolish actions,
Certainly become causes for the three evil paths.
Not encountering good friends to pity them,
Ox-heads, yakṣas, how would they let go?
Cast into cauldrons of boiling water, stoves of charcoal,
Iron forks stir and turn, questioning the root cause.
In previous lives, why did you not cultivate?
Today you still come to harass and disturb me.
Driven to ascend mountains of knives, forests of swords,
Urgently sent walking through fierce fires, stove ashes.
Iron eagles come pecking, piercing the eyes,
Iron dogs compete to eat the heart and marrow.
Black ropes, crosses, vertically and horizontally nailed,
Like a chessboard with a cross grid.
Later, the jailers put on the plowshare headgear,
They gathered, wailing and howling in pain.
If one speaks of the sufferings of the three evil paths,
For a hundred thousand kalpas, it is truly hard to describe.
Even iron men would feel heartache upon hearing this,
How could virtuous men and women not fear it?
It is only because in this life they lacked good friends,
Who did not teach them to repent and regret their past.
Ordinary beings cannot cast aside the ten evils,
But today they must strive to repent.
(Calling themselves disciples of the Buddha)
The ten evil deeds are the hardest to speak of,
For a hundred thousand kalpas, there is no chance of escape.
Today, with one mind, we must repent and give thanks,
And in an instant, when life ends, we will be reborn in heaven.
Disciples and followers,
Since you have come to this Dharma assembly today,
You must strive with great effort,
Unite your minds and join your palms,
And repent with me for the sins of the ten evils and the five heinous crimes,
Washing away defilements and impurities,
Arising with sincere and pure hearts,
So that in the next life we may be reborn in the Western Pure Land,
Transformed from lotus flowers,
Forever abandoning the three evil paths,
And eternally beholding Amitābha.
Are you willing or not?
Are you able or not?
Excellent, excellent!
This accords with the Buddha’s heart,
Making dragons and devas rejoice,
And surely extinguishing sins across three lifetimes.
When all Buddhas were in the stage of causes,
They were all ordinary beings,
But because of good spiritual friends,
They confessed and repented,
And attained Buddhahood.
Past Buddhas have already become Buddhas,
Present Buddhas are now becoming Buddhas,
Future Buddhas will become Buddhas.
Disciples and followers,
Since you understand repentance,
Reform the past and cultivate the future,
In future lifetimes,
You will certainly become Buddhas,
Do not harbor any doubts.
(Calling the names)
Next, we invite the Buddhas of the ten directions to bear witness.
We disciples, so-and-so and others,
Together with all in the Dharma assembly,
From time without beginning,
Have committed all kinds of evil deeds:
Killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, false speech, frivolous talk, divisive speech, harsh speech without restraint,
Creating greed, anger, and delusion,
Drinking alcohol and eating meat,
Killing fathers and harming mothers,
Destroying stūpas and damaging monasteries,
Disrupting the harmony of the Sangha,
Shedding the blood of the Buddha,
Men arising with lustful minds,
Defiling pure nuns,
Women arising with lustful minds,
Defiling monks who uphold pure precepts,
Using body, speech, and mind,
To slander and abuse monks and nuns,
Misusing the belongings of the Three Jewels,
Relying on official power and influence,
Driving and coercing monks and nuns,
Seizing fields and water sources,
Sometimes enslaving Sangha servants,
Or due to royal decrees,
Leading troops to plunder and raid,
Capturing others,
Taking others’ wives and daughters,
Seizing others’ wealth and possessions,
Fishing and setting fires,
Burning forests and mountains,
Digging canals and rivers,
Drying up and killing aquatic beings,
In walking, standing, sitting, and lying down,
Harming sentient beings,
Plowing fields and cutting trees,
Accidentally injuring insect lives,
Releasing hawks and setting dogs loose,
Killing and harming living creatures,
Husbands betraying their wives,
Seeking other beauties,
Wives betraying their husbands,
Coveting other men,
Thus, in these ways,
With body, speech, and mind,
We have committed all kinds of sins.
Today, at this moment,
Before the Buddhas of the ten directions,
Before the Bodhisattvas of the ten directions,
Before the scriptures of the Three Vehicles,
Before the Sangha of the ten directions,
Before the great assembly,
We dare not conceal anything,
But with sincere hearts repent,
Wishing for our sins to be extinguished.
(Recite three times)
Ordinary beings’ sins are as high as Mount Sumeru,
Yet they have never been aware and remain ignorant.
Without repentance, they will surely fall into evil paths,
But if they can repent, there will be no doubt.
Like piling firewood higher than the Northern Dipper,
Even carts and oxen would struggle to carry it away.
But with just a single spark in the wind,
The pile of firewood instantly turns to ashes.
We disciples have cultivated merit over many lifetimes,
And in this life have obtained human birth again.
Morning and evening, we listen to the Dharma and hear the scriptures,
Daily observing fasting and upholding precepts.
Even if there are some remaining karmic obstacles,
Through repentance, they will quickly be eliminated.
With such pure hearts as these,
We will surely encounter the three assemblies of Maitreya.
Having completed repentance,
We now receive the Three Refuges,
And afterward uphold the Five Precepts,
So that our vows and actions support each other,
And our merit and wisdom become complete.
Seeking the fruit of Buddhahood,
We will forever escape the cycle of rebirth.
We must receive the Three Refuges,
To avoid sinking into wrong paths.
Those who take refuge in the Buddha
Will not fall into hell.
Those who take refuge in the Dharma
Will not receive ghostly bodies.
Those who take refuge in the Sangha
Will not become animals.
Disciples and followers,
Having received these Three Refuges,
Are you able or not?
Are you willing or not?
(Calling the Buddha’s name)
(Disciples of the Buddha)
The merit of taking refuge in the Three Jewels is beyond description,
It saves one from falling into the three evil paths and suffering hardships.
Not only will one attain Buddhahood in the future,
But one will surely escape the depths of suffering over countless kalpas.
Namo mūlye,
Namo dharmāya,
Namo saṅghāya,
(Recite three times)
I take refuge in the Buddha, the Honored One of the two perfections,
I take refuge in the Dharma, the Honored One free from desire,
I take refuge in the Sangha, the Honored One among the assembly,
(Recite three times)
Disciples and followers,
When we speak of taking refuge in the Buddha,
In which Buddha do we take refuge?
It is not the Móní Buddha,
Nor is it the Bōsī Buddha,
Nor is it the Huǒxiān Buddha,
But the pure Dharma body,
The perfect reward body,
The hundred billion transformation bodies of Shìjiāmóuní Buddha.
Taking refuge in the Dharma means
The five thousand scrolls of scriptures,
Which are called the Dharma.
Taking refuge in the Sangha means
The four fruits and four stages,
Those who shave their heads and dye their robes,
The two divisions of the Sangha,
True disciples of the Buddha,
Called renunciants.
For example, in India, there are ninety-six kinds of heretics,
While here there are the likes of Bōsī, Móní, Huǒxiān, and Kūshén,
All claiming to have left home,
Forever transcending life and death,
But these are all falsehoods,
Deceiving humans and devas.
Only the disciples of Shìjiā
Are true renunciants,
Worthy of receiving the vast offerings of humans and devas.
(Calling the Buddha’s name)
Alas, the heretics have a hundred thousand ways,
Enduring hunger and thirst, wandering in madness.
Deceiving themselves and others brings no benefit,
How could they ever be reborn in heaven after death?
To be reborn in heaven, one must first purify the mind,
Observe fasting, practice generosity, and enter deep meditation.
Every day, eating alone when the sun sets to the west,
Starving people gaze from afar, their eyes longing.
(Reciting the Buddha's name).
Next, invite the Buddhas of the ten directions,
to serve as great witnesses,
then receive the Five Precepts.
Disciples,
are you able or not?
Are you willing or not?
Excellent, excellent!
Now, the Five Precepts
are the good cause for attaining Buddhahood,
the essential path for entering sagehood.
The three thousand dignified manners,
the eighty thousand subtle practices.
Bhikṣus have two hundred and fifty precepts,
bhikṣuṇīs have five hundred precepts.
Upāsakas,
upāsikās,
the Eight Precepts, the Ten Precepts—
all arise from the Five Precepts.
In heaven they are called the five stars,
on earth they are called the five sacred mountains,
in Daoism they are the five phases,
in Confucianism they are the five emperors,
in Buddhism they are the Five Precepts.
First: Do not kill.
Can you uphold this?
When the Buddha was at Língjiù Shān,
there was an elder Brahmin
who stepped forward, joined his palms, and asked the Tathāgata:
"How does one attain such dignified and majestic physical marks?"
The Buddha said, "Elder, listen to my words:
All Buddhas, Tathāgatas, cultivated for many kalpas,
never intentionally killing a single sentient being.
Because of this, their facial disc is like a full moon.
The thirty-two marks are of golden hue,
the eighty minor characteristics are all perfectly bright.
For each mark and characteristic cultivated in progression,
they first used body and mind to uphold the Five Precepts.
Sentient beings with consciousness cherish eternal life—
how can one bear to kill them with a knife?
Perhaps they are the transformed bodies of Bodhisattvas,
or perhaps they possess the compassionate nature of Buddhas.
Perhaps they are one's parents reborn as animals,
or perhaps one's siblings reborn as oxen or sheep.
Ordinary people do not recognize them as kin,
with fleshly eyes, how could they distinguish the holy assembly?
They slice them with sharp knives to eat,
nourishing the evil-karma bodies of ordinary people.
For hundreds of thousands, millions of kalpas they fall into the three wretched paths.
I earnestly advise disciples: do not kill.
Extensively explaining the karmic results of killing,
for a hundred kalpas proclaiming would be endless.
Good men and good women, you must reflect.
Today you must listen to the Dharma Master's words."
Second: Do not steal.
Can you uphold this?
When the Buddha was in the Deer Park,
his majestic marks were like a golden mountain.
Brahmā and Śakra scattered fragrant flowers,
the eight kinds of dragon deities presented offerings.
A merchant came to make an offering,
and asked the Tathāgata about his past causes:
"Your aura-light shines afar like Sumeru;
what precept did you uphold in the causal stage?"
The Buddha said, "Merchant, listen to my words:
In my past hundreds of thousands of lives,
down to a blade of grass, I never stole,
let alone stealing others' property at dusk.
The eighty minor characteristics surpass human marks,
the thirty-two marks excel those of heavenly beings.
For each mark and characteristic cultivated in progression,
all used body and mind to uphold the Five Precepts.
If a person intentionally steals others' property,
they will surely experience future causes of poverty and low status.
They will become donkeys or horses to repay the debt,
bearing bits and saddles, suffering much hunger and thirst.
Hooves pierced, back [worn], worms gnawing and biting,
a horizontal bone in the mouth preventing speech,
heavily laden, beaten with clubs all over the body—
all because in a past life they stole from others.
Or they become slaves or servants repaying with labor,
never having complete clothing or food.
At night, leaving early angers the master,
at noon mealtime, the mistress beats them.
Bare-headed, barefoot, they watch over sheep and horses,
daring not refuse hardship in winter's cold or summer's heat.
Yearly they are sold and resold as commoners,
like circulating coins without a fixed owner.
Stealing in this life brings shackles and chains,
people see it—it is no empty word.
Repaying debts in future lives is extremely difficult.
Today you must listen to the Dharma Master's words."
Third: Do not engage in sexual misconduct.
Can you uphold this?
When the Buddha was in the Jīvaka's Grove monastery,
five hundred lay devotees offered incense and flowers.
The assembly of humans and gods listened to the sūtra,
good men and good women heard the wonderful Dharma.
The Tathāgata, because there is the offense of sexual misconduct,
which can become the root cause of birth and death,
for hundreds of kalpas, thousands of ten-thousands (of kalpas) one undergoes sinking,
none not due to the realm of lustful desire.
If a wife commits adultery, abandoning husband and children,
in a future life she will experience having no husband,
morning after morning alone guarding an empty room,
day after day solitary with no one to rely on.
If a husband commits adultery, abandoning wife and children,
in a future life his wife will not be faithful and good.
Seeing her husband go out, she will secretly act,
just roaming the streets seeking illicit affairs.
Before life ends, one sinks into the three realms of existence;
the jailer Ox-Head will not release you.
Men embrace copper pillars for sexual misconduct;
women lie on iron beds for running away.
Husband and wife themselves must know the limits,
do not embrace in improper places or at improper times.
If in a monastery or monk's quarters,
engaging improperly constitutes the offense of sexual misconduct.
Sometimes when observing the fast or receiving the Eight Precepts,
or when purified and entering the mandala arena,
if husband and wife touch, breaking dignified conduct,
you should know this also violates the precept against sexual misconduct.
Not following the proper way [according to] male and female forms,
one must not violate the sense faculties elsewhere.
Do not be like a great rock, indulging in foolish ignorance,
not distinguishing front from back.
The Dharma Master today clearly explains,
only fearing disciples remain unaware.
From now on, you must be clear,
do not act carelessly as before."
Fourth: Do not lie.
Can you uphold this?
When the Buddha was in Rājagṛha city,
Devadatta conspired with the king's relative.
An edict ordered throughout the country and its districts:
"First, do not make offerings to the Buddha."
The Tathāgata went begging for alms, circling three times;
all the donors did not open their doors.
An old maidservant came out to greet him,
and gave the Tathāgata a ball of rice.
The Tathāgata and the noble sages,
with clean sandalwood paste, then partook of the meal.
The spiritual power of the Buddhas is inconceivable—
it transformed into the supreme flavor of heavenly nectar.
The Tathāgata personally made a vow for her:
"May this good woman be reborn in heaven early."
The heretical nuns were alarmed among themselves,
gathering together, laughing loudly.
"Gautama deeply understands deceptive speech;
enduring hunger, he cannot utter false words.
A single ball of dry rice is not difficult to give,
how can it yield the fruit of rebirth in heaven?"
The Tathāgata replied to the nuns:
"My Buddha's cause and effect is inconceivable.
It is like a fertile field watered,
one planting yields a thousand [fold harvest].
Unlike the foolish heretical lot,
who deceive and mislead humans and gods to sustain their bodies.
It is like sowing seeds in a field—
planting one bushel yields five [bushels].
The Buddha is like the Nyagrodha tree;
its seed is small, like black sesame.
Its hanging branches rise (a trunk) a hundred thousand fathoms high,
shading five hundred chariots completely.
The Tathāgata then extended his tongue mark,
reaching up to the worlds of the gods.
I, through accumulated kalpas, have not spoken falsely;
therefore I attained unsurpassed enlightenment.
Thus know that truthful speech leads to Buddhahood,
while deception brings the cause of evil karma.
In future lives, the tongue mark will not be perfect;
whatever one says, people will not believe.
Deceiving oneself and others brings no benefit;
in this life, people hearing it are displeased.
One falls into the mountain of swords in hell,
where the tongue is pulled out and cut by sharp blades."
Fifth: Do not drink alcohol or eat meat.
Can you uphold this?
When the Buddha was by the Bhadrā River,
a good woman invited monks for a meal offering.
When it was an Arhat's turn to attend the offering,
the donor, with good intention, urged him to drink wine.
One should know that Arhats have various wind ailments;
he did not give rise to evil thoughts, but the monk became drunk.
After the meal, arriving at the monastery gate,
he smashed his alms bowl, lay down in the street.
His robe dragged upside down, his square skirt torn,
his staff thrown sideways, his hat askew.
Drunk, lying like a dead shrimp,
passersby looked and clapped their hands laughing.
The Buddha immediately assembled the monastic community,
and had him dragged back into the monastery.
Three times they deliberated and established regulations;
from then on, monks and nuns were ordered to abstain from alcohol.
Killing father, harming mother—all because of wine;
destroying stūpas, ruining monasteries—for sweet drink.
Three rounds of drinking, and one becomes delirious,
fearing neither Yama nor the jailers.
Eating meat has never been permitted by the Buddha;
for the sake of fragrance and flavor, they kill to obtain it.
Crush peppers and ginger to fill the bowl,
Add fine wine and sing "Three Terraces."
Fear not future birth in hell,
For now, let the belly hang full.
Cut from your own flesh to eat,
Then know if guilt or innocence is meet.
Perhaps Buddhas become beasts,
Or Bodhisattvas descend in disguise.
If one refrains from eating beings' flesh,
Sages and saints alike praise, "Well done!"
Thus far, with disciples and followers,
We have taken the Three Refuges and Five Precepts.
Now, to expound the boundless Dharma gates,
Endless even through kalpas.
Next, with disciples and followers, we chant the sutra.
Can you or not?
Are you willing or not?
Recite the Buddha's name three to five times.
"The Buddha Speaks the Amitābha Sutra."
To explain this sutra,
We divide it into three parts: first, the introductory section,
Next, the main body,
Finally, the dissemination.
Each phrase, each verse,
Is worth a hundred thousand taels of gold.
I will explain in detail to disciples and followers.
Now, the merits born from this praise of the Great Vehicle "Amitābha Sutra,"
First, dedicate to adorn the Khagan Heavenly King.
Humbly wishing his lifespan equals the sun and moon,
His fate matches heaven and earth.
May barbarians from the four directions come to court,
And all peoples within the eight directions submit.
Dedicated to the Khagan Heavenly King.
(Recite all Buddhas.)
All heavenly princesses,
Humbly wish their immortal grace,
Crane-like purity ever fragrant,
Long receiving the sage ruler's favor,
Forever bathed in the imperial king's grace.
(Recite Buddha.)
All heavenly officials,
Dedicate wishes for lifespans like pine and bamboo,
Free from withering disasters;
Blessings equal to mountains and rivers,
Eternal behind the sage heaven.
All monastic overseers and great masters,
Humbly wish within the Lapis Lazuli Hall,
The Prajñā lamp burns high;
By the Anavatapta Pond,
Eternal praise of the unborn verse.
All ministers,
Humbly wish blessings equal to seas and peaks,
Lifespans facing pines and cedars,
Eternal assistance at the golden gate,
Long illuminating the sage era.
All governors, Meilù, Dágān, envoys, estate envoys, Sàwēn, Dìlüè,
And all officials present in the yamen,
Collectively wish each person increased rank and position,
Each preserving extended years,
Official posts gradually promoted,
Homes ever peaceful and secure.
All monastery Vinaya masters, Dharma masters, monastic administrators, Dharma teachers, Vinaya teachers, monastic assemblies, nun assemblies, Āyí teachers,
Collectively wish at the Three Assemblies of the Dragon Flower,
Together ascend the bed of liberation,
Within the kalpas of the Worthy,
Early realize the fruit of non-action.
All upāsakas, upāsikās,
Humbly wish good roots daily advance,
All encounter the light of a thousand Buddhas,
Unwavering faith,
Also attending the Three Assemblies of the Dragon Flower.
Further, may the three wretched paths cease suffering,
Hell stop torment.
For the sick in bed,
Early recovery.
For those in difficult pregnancy,
Mother and child safe.
For prisoners in jail,
Swift pardon and release.
For travelers in distant lands,
Early return home.
For wayfarers on roads,
No encounter with disasters.
For slaves and maidservants,
May they receive gentle care.
For debtors and creditors,
Kindly settle fairly.
May the deaf hear,
The mute speak,
The lame walk,
The blind see.
Thus speaking,
All four hundred and four illnesses,
Collectively wish eliminated.
All aspiring hearts,
Early achieve fulfillment.
May warfare not arise,
Epidemics cease.
Five grains abundant,
Everyone content in work.
Uphold the ten virtues,
Cease the ten evils,
Together awaken to the true vehicle,
Eradicate wrong views,
Universally together in the future,
Together accomplish Buddha-fruit.
For this cause,
Recite all Buddhas.
(Buddha-son.)
Great Vehicle merits hardest to measure,
First dedicate causes and fruits to the Heavenly King.
Lifespan extended ten million years,
Blessings like sun and moon emit divine light.
From four distances all come to the precious throne,
Seven regions peaceful, celebrating prosperous times.
In this life, ascend the Son of Heaven's seat,
In the future, surely become the King of Dharma.
Princess Dènglín resembles a divine immortal,
Not only mortals, even Buddhas show compassion.
To know her former place of birth,
Know it is always in the Suìtuó Heaven.
Though dwelling in the desire realm, surpassing ordinary rank,
Morning and evening ever before the sage king.
Wish to give rise to right view, eliminate wrong view,
In next life, early sit on the purple golden lotus.
Further wishing to broadly discuss names and forms,
Yet fearing to waste time.
Better to expound the sutra text,
Early attain Bodhi Buddha-fruit.
But because all love sounds and sights,
Thus skillfully produce words.
Do not blame the verses repeated,
Essential to delight disciples.
As for this Sahā world,
One must use sounds and sights as transformation bodies.
The Thus Come One of Fragrant Accumulation above,
Smelling fragrance accomplishes Buddha-fruit.
Some awaken to the Way through taste,
Some arouse the mind through touch.
The Five Great Vehicles,
All five sense-objects accomplish Buddha's work,
All things are indeed Suchness.
Lotus flowers emerge from muddy filth,
Afflictions transform into Bodhi fruit.
Unlike the Great Vehicle's clinging views,
Always generating discriminating minds.
Not knowing the five sense-objects are originally empty,
Then say they obstruct the Way's fruit.
Sounds, scents, tastes, touches originally empty,
Empty and non-empty are always empty.
The Dharma realm originally pure,
Unconcerned with empty or non-empty.
This Sahā world,
Uses sounds as Buddha's work.
The Thus Come One manifests thirty-two marks,
But hearing the sound teaching,
Accomplishes the Way's fruit.
"Vimalakīrti Sutra" says: In the land of Fragrant Accumulation Buddha,
People merely smell fragrance,
And accomplish Buddha-fruit.
"Lotus Sutra" says: Dharma joy and meditation bliss,
Eating is flavor,
Thus know using taste as Buddha's work.
"Avataṃsaka Sutra" says: Sudhana youth,
Visiting wise advisors,
Met a lustful woman.
The lustful woman told the youth:
"I have one method,
Able to liberate all men's afflictions.
Light ones, touch my body,
Accomplish Buddha-fruit;
Slightly heavier afflictions,
Come embrace my body,
Kiss me,
Accomplish Buddha-fruit;
Extremely heavy afflictions,
Sleep with me,
Accomplish the Way's fruit."
Thus know using touch as Buddha's work.
These sounds, scents, tastes, touches,
Awakening to their empty nature,
Is no different from Suchness;
Deluded about their empty principle,
Become the six dusts and afflictions.
The Dharma master uses a few verses of praise,
Transforming people without fault.
Now we shall expound the sutra.
Assembly, will you listen or not?
Can you or not?
Are you willing or not?
The Sanskrit term "Mǔnà"
is translated into Tang Chinese as "Buddha."
Buddha means awakened,
and there are three types of awakening: first, self-awakening,
which surpasses all ordinary beings,
as ordinary people do not awaken themselves.
Second, awakening others,
which surpasses all solitary realizers,
who, though self-awakened,
cannot awaken other beings.
Third, perfect awakening,
which surpasses all bodhisattvas.
Why is this?
Although bodhisattvas cultivate the three awakenings,
they have not yet attained perfection.
How can this be known?
The sutras say that bodhisattvas of the ten stages
view the sun and moon as if through a thin veil,
and perceive the Buddha-nature as if through a cicada's wing.
Thus, it is known that their awakening is not yet perfect,
and their merit and wisdom are still insufficient.
Only the Buddha, the great awakened one,
perfectly illuminates the three awakenings,
transcending the three vehicles,
and is therefore called Buddha.
For example, Śākyamuni Tathāgata, over three immeasurable kalpas,
cultivated myriad practices
and the six pāramitās.
In the first asaṃkhyeya kalpa,
he made offerings to seventy-five thousand Buddhas,
the last of whom was named Ratnajāṭa.
In the second asaṃkhyeya kalpa,
he made offerings to seventy-six thousand Buddhas,
the last of whom was named Dīpaṃkara.
In the third asaṃkhyeya kalpa,
he made offerings to seventy-seven thousand Buddhas,
the last of whom was named Vipaśyin.
Beyond the three immeasurable kalpas,
he cultivated the marks of excellence over one hundred kalpas.
The *Diamond Sutra* says: "Before Dīpaṃkara Buddha,
I encountered eight hundred forty trillion nayutas of Buddhas,
making offerings to them all,
without missing a single one."
The *Avataṃsaka Sutra* says:
"The number of thoughts in a dust-mote kalpa can be known,
the water in the great ocean can be drunk dry,
the void can be measured and the wind bound,
but the merits of the Buddha cannot be fully described."
The Sanskrit term "Āmítuó"
is translated into Tang Chinese as "Immeasurable Life."
It should be noted that it is pronounced "Apóluómǐduō,"
where the character "Ā"
means "without" in Tang Chinese.
The two characters "Póluó"
mean "measure" in Tang Chinese.
The two characters "Mǐduō"
mean "life" in Tang Chinese.
The Sanskrit term "Sùdáluó"
means "sutra" in Tang Chinese,
or sometimes "thread."
The earlier phrase "Buddha speaks"
refers to the golden words spoken by Śākyamuni Tathāgata.
"Speaks"
refers to verbal expression through sound,
thus it is known that in this world,
enlightenment is attained through sound.
"Immeasurable Life"
is the name of the Buddha.
One may ask where this Tathāgata resides.
To the west, beyond ten Ganges sands,
there is a Buddha Tathāgata similar to Śākyamuni.
He attained Buddhahood ten kalpas ago,
and now sits on a lotus in that land.
Although there are sages in the ten directions,
this land is the most praiseworthy.
Unlike this world, filled with afflictions,
it is adorned as the Dharma King's abode.
The ground is gold, the mountains are jade,
the forests are lapis lazuli, and the waters are clear.
In early spring, they eat bimbā fruit,
while here in the fourth month, we bite into raw melons.
In that pure land, people are dignified,
while in Śākyamuni's world, there are hunchbacks and the afflicted.
Kalaviṅka and jīvaṃjīva birds are born in the western land,
while here, there are only crows.
Generally, the land of Buddha Āmítuó
is unlike other heavens.
All afflictions are entirely absent,
and one only hears sutras and recites the Buddha's name.
There is no birth, aging, sickness, or death,
nor separation from loved ones.
Sentient beings there are born by transformation,
unlike the karmic forces of this world.
There are no autumn, winter, spring, or summer,
nor the alternation of cold and heat.
Every morning, they join palms among flowers,
and every day, Āmítuó bestows predictions.
The Amitābha Sūtra chanted above,
in Chinese is called Wúliàng Shòu (Immeasurable Life),
which refers to the immeasurable life of the Buddha during his causal stage,
when he practiced myriad deeds,
the six pāramitās,
and upon attaining the fruition stage,
achieved immeasurable lifespan,
thus named after the fruition.
Next, the term "Immeasurable Life Land"
is named after the transformative lord,
just as "Hàn country"
refers to the Hàn people,
and "country" refers to the territory,
also named after the people.
Now, the term "Immeasurable Life Land,"
also called "Pure Land,"
or "Land of Ultimate Bliss,"
or "Land of Constant Joy,"
or "Land of Peaceful Nourishment,"
has many different names,
which cannot all be listed.
First, speaking of the pure realm,
the term "Pure Land"
has two kinds of purity: first, purity of sentient beings,
second, purity of non-sentient beings.
Regarding purity of sentient beings:
there are no three evil paths,
no ten good or unwholesome deeds,
no four hundred and four illnesses,
no eunuchs or hermaphrodites,
no venomous snakes, scorpions, or various poisonous insects, birds, or beasts.
There are no women,
only men.
There are no one hundred and eight afflictions,
all share the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment.
There are no śrāvakas,
only bodhisattvas.
There are no womb-born, egg-born, or moisture-born beings,
all are transformation-born.
They are not summoned by karmic retribution,
all are in the stage of one lifetime to buddhahood,
tenth-ground bodhisattvas born from lotus flowers.
Unlike other realms where beings experience karmic retribution,
such as maggots or garuḍa birds,
who receive transformation-born bodies.
There are no weapons or warfare,
no slaves or servants,
no deception or oppression,
no famine or hunger,
no kings or officials,
for Amitābha Buddha is the king,
Guānyīn and Shìzhì are the ministers,
Yàoshàng and Yàowáng serve as administrators,
and the transformation-born youths are the common people.
There is no taxation of grain or wheat,
no tribute of wine or cloth.
Only morning offerings of flowers and incense,
and evening recitations of praises,
with no other duties.
Thus,
there are no ten sorrows or eight sufferings,
no unpleasant things of any kind,
only birds like the jīvaṃjīva and kalaviṅka.
These birds are not born from karmic force,
but are manifestations created by Amitābha Buddha,
intended to produce sounds that remind beings to recite the Buddha and the Saṅgha.
As for the term "Land of Ultimate Bliss,"
there are no sufferings,
only the joy of Dharma,
not the impure pleasures of the five desires.
Or called "Land of Constant Joy,"
constantly experiencing the joy of Dharma,
with no suffering or obstruction,
hence called constant joy.
Unlike this land,
where one sings in the morning,
but by noon suffering arrives,
and one cries out in pain.
Or called "Land of Peaceful Nourishment,"
a place of peace and joy for nurturing the spirit.
To elaborate further,
would risk wasting time.
Above is a general discussion of purity of sentient beings.
Next, we discuss purity of non-sentient beings.
Regarding non-sentient beings,
these are earth, water, fire, wind,
and the six dusts: form, sound, smell, taste, touch, and dharmas. … …
Regarding purity of earth:
the ground is made of the seven treasures like gold and silver,
all plants and trees
are fragrant flowers,
or various treasures.
There is no land of thorns, gravel, or saline soil,
no high or low, pits or mounds,
no mountains, rocks, streams, or ditches,
no poisonous plants, trees, or bitter herbs.
Thus,
there are no unpleasant things of any kind,
only pleasant things like fragrant flowers and precious treasures.
Regarding purity of water:
all springs and ponds
possess the eight virtues,
and produce multicolored lotus flowers of various treasures,
as large as cart wheels,
with golden sand at the bottom,
and jeweled trees on all sides.
When the waves move, they produce sounds
that recite the names of the Three Jewels.
There is no muddy silt, foul odors, or aquatic creatures like fish or turtles.
Neither increasing nor decreasing,
neither cold nor hot, turbid nor clear,
it is clear as a mirror,
illuminating the heavens,
and all sages and worthies
praise it together.
Regarding purity of fire:
this refers to fire both within sentient beings and in the external non-sentient world.
Regarding internal fire in sentient beings:
the four elements are harmonized,
with no feverish illnesses, sores, or afflictive fires,
nor the fiery torments of lustful desires.
Although sentient beings possess the four elements,
unlike in this land,
there is no increase or decrease
that disturbs beings.
Regarding external fire in the non-sentient world:
in this Immeasurable Life Land,
since it is a Pure Land,
there are no three calamities,
nor scorching heat.
Unlike this land,
where the three calamities arise from time to time,
seven suns appear together,
burning the desire realm and the second dhyāna heaven,
and the fires in various hells blaze day and night,
burning sentient beings.
Thus,
there is no scorching heat of fire.
Regarding purity of wind:
this also includes wind both within sentient beings and in the external non-sentient world.
Regarding internal wind in sentient beings:
