there are no thirty-six kinds of wind-related illnesses.
Regarding external wind in the non-sentient world:
there are no whirlwinds, black winds, yellow winds, etc.,
that uproot mountains and trees.
Nor when the three calamities arise,
destroying the third dhyāna heaven and so on.
Although the Pure Land has internal and external winds,
the internal wind nourishes sentient beings,
the external wind causes flowers to bloom and fruits to form,
or blows through forests and trees,
producing elegant and harmonious melodies,
reciting the names of the Three Jewels,
and proclaiming the Eightfold Path.
Earlier, regarding purity of the six dusts:
first, purity of form:
among the twenty kinds of form,
let us briefly distinguish:
the four colors blue, yellow, red, and white—
the sūtra mentions four kinds of lotus flowers.
Shadow, light, and brightness are also present,
for the sūtra speaks of forests,
hence there are shadows.
Regarding light: first, the Buddha's light,
second, the light of the saints' bodies,
third, the light of the sun and moon.
Although it is called a Pure Land,
there are still sun and moon,
unlike in the heavens,
where beings illuminate themselves with their own light,
so there is no sun or moon.
How do we know the Pure Land has sun and moon?
The sūtra says: in the early morning,
they take many wonderful flowers to make offerings to countless buddhas in the ten directions,
and by mealtime,
they return to their own land.
The sūtra mentions morning and mealtime,
so we know there are sun and moon.
Without sun and moon,
there would be darkness.
Why is this?
One sun and one moon
illuminate the four continents,
hence there are day and night.
It cannot be that one sun and one moon
remain fixed above the Pure Land
without moving—
this is unreasonable.
Some say it is due to the Buddha's spiritual power
that there is light without darkness—
this is also reasonable.
Smoke, clouds, dust, and mist—
these four kinds of form
should not exist in the Pure Land.
How do we know this?

Sutra: “Beat the drum and proclaim the decree,
seeking the Dharma in all directions.
Who can for me
expound the Great Vehicle?
I shall for life
serve and attend upon them.”
The great king said: “The king has a personal vow,
to seek the sutra without weariness.
”Hearing the Buddha’s name, he received and upheld it;
obtaining the Lotus Sutra, he chanted and recited it.
Then he ascended a high tower,
and struck its bell and drum.
The bell’s sound, booming, was heard by all;
the drum’s echo, rumbling, filled the roads.
Amidst the sounds of bell and drum,
his words issued forth: “Who can explain the Dharma Flower Sutra?
For ten thousand kalpas and a thousand lives, I shall never betray them.”
Upon the tower, striking the bell, a place for the Way was established;
through the six periods, unceasing, famed incense was burned.
Daily, the sky filled with auspicious colors;
constantly, from the four distances, came good omens.
Heavenly dragons repeatedly bestowed their protection;
sages and worthies frequently offered their praise.
All Buddhas came together to encourage him;
simultaneously, they emitted the white-curl light.
Bathed in that light,
his joy was beyond measure;
his fierce and sharp mind opened further.
“When will I be taught to hear the wondrous Dharma?
When will I be freed from the cycle of rebirth?”
Since the great king’s mind was so single-pointed,
the sages and worthies surely all took pity.
It was not yet known who could expound it for him;
what name would be called forth next?
Sutra: “At that time, there was an immortal
who came and said to the king: ‘I have a Great Vehicle sutra,
named the Wondrous Dharma Lotus Flower.
If you do not disobey me,
I shall proclaim it for you.’”
This recitation of the sutra text is about the immortal’s arrival,
questioning the great king:
“Immortals always dwell in the mountains,
in lofty seclusion beyond compare.
The wind blowing through bamboo groves—its melody matches the gōng and shāng notes;
cranes calling from lone pines—their voices harmonize with the jué and zhǐ notes.
Troops of wild apes,
gurgling flowing streams.
With a mind to dwell forever among woods and springs,
no intention to visit the imperial capital even briefly.
Suddenly hearing words from the sky,
and seeing clouds gather before the hermitage.
Pondering, he had not yet grasped the reason;
speaking out, he asked the cause.
From the sky came the reply,
with no other meaning intended:
‘Because there is a great Wheel-Turning King of a great kingdom,
seeking the Dharma, willing to cast aside life and death.
You, immortal, fortunately possess the Lotus Sutra;
why not take him as your disciple?
The great king wishes to pay homage to the immortal;
the immortal should receive him and employ him.’”
Dwelling in the mountains, learning cultivation,
he had not considered following the usual path to the imperial capital.
In the quiet hermitage, he only recited the Buddha’s name;
sometimes in the forest, he only upheld the sutra.
Pairs of auspicious cranes added to the incense seal;
couples of spiritual birds filled the water bottle.
Only the immortal cultivated the supreme practice;
deities and spirits reverently obeyed, each giving careful instructions.
One day,
he sensed an auspicious sign;
suddenly before the hermitage, an auspicious aura arose.
It was said a king sought the wondrous Dharma,
sincerely praying and inquiring with clarity.
The immortal asked the great king:
That day, the immortal
left the mountain wilderness;
reaching the king’s city, he trod only on colored clouds;
going to the dragon tower, did he rely on a crane-drawn carriage?
He displayed no imposing manner,
required no attendants;
alone, he soared through the sky,
arriving beneath the palace gate,
and immediately questioned the king,
asking him to express his innermost thoughts:
“Among humans, your precious throne is exalted;
why do you renounce such wealth and honor?”
The immortal, intending to enter the imperial capital,
a host of auspicious clouds bore his feet as he walked.
Worthies and sages in the sky snapped their fingers in farewell;
heavenly beings along the way offered flowers in welcome.
Not long after,
he reached the king’s palace;
within the palace, an auspicious aura was thick at that time.
The immortal saw the great king, his heart joyful;
the king heard of the immortal’s arrival, his mind reverent and respectful.
“For what reason
do you forsake glory and splendor,
insistently seeking to hear the Wondrous Dharma Flower?
I do not yet understand, great king, for what cause?
In your heart, you seem not at all attached to luxury and extravagance.”
The great king addressed the immortal:
“I see people nowadays,
constantly harboring anger and delight.
Everyone loves agreeable words,
all worry about contrary advice.
When will greed for wealth ever cease?
When can love for sensual pleasures ever stop?
With pipes and songs, ten thousand beautiful women;
with wealth and honor, a thousand sons of the golden wheel.
Clothing perfumed with incense,
brocade curtains, jade shoes.
Men’s spirit soaring to the clouds,
women’s dignified appearance with gleaming teeth.
If speaking of luxury and extravagance,
who can match this?
Before ten days of pleasure have passed,
word comes that someone has died.
In life, they never cultivated blessings;
in death, they fall into the Avīci Hell.
Forever belonging to the underworld officials,
long enduring bitter torments.
Sometimes iron birds peck their marrow,
sometimes copper snakes devour their flesh.
Evil karma manifesting—ten thousand deaths, ten thousand rebirths;
pain and suffering pressing—a thousand cries, a thousand wails.
Sometimes corpses lie buried in hot ashes,
sometimes ground, pounded in mortars.
All day long, oppressed and controlled,
subjected to many kinds of beatings and tortures.
Hungry, they swallow iron pellets;
thirsty, they drink molten copper.
Forests of sword trees, sharp and dense;
mountains of knives, towering and perilous.
To avoid such causes and conditions,
what method is there?
Unless one listens to and receives the Dharma Flower Sutra,
how can such calamities be escaped?”
Pondering the floating world’s affairs is lamentable;
wealth, honor, luxury, and extravagance do not last long.
With intent, one seeks only the perfect Buddha-fruit;
without a mind attached to becoming a Wheel-Turning King.
Even if jewels and treasures pile like mountains,
and silks and satins fill the palace halls.
When the killing ghost suddenly arrives afterward,
who can substitute for me in impermanence?
The great king said: “Considering thus,
I am not attached to glory and splendor.”
Then he prepared and arranged the place for the Way,
and invited the immortal to expound the Dharma.
“Today, having met the immortal,
my mind ultimately dares not delay.
Vegetarian meals are ordered to be prepared in the kitchen;
the place for the Way is ordered to be arranged and spread out.
Incense smoke, thick and curling, forms a canopy;
palace trees, misty and hazy, spontaneously turn to spring.
Although I have not yet heard the Middle Way teaching,
the great king that day was exceedingly joyful.”
Then he bowed in homage,
begging for compassion:
“I wish the immortal must surely know.
If you can suddenly expound the wondrous Dharma,
I shall serve as your slave and servant without disobedience.”
The immortal invited the great king to enter the mountains,
and said:
“The king dwells in palaces,
with music of sháo pipes daily.
Seductive environments are many,
ordinary passions accumulate freely.
Increasing faults and errors,
sufficient for their transgressions.
The Lotus Sutra is difficult to proclaim here;
great king, you must fully understand this.
I dwell in the mountains,
where the scenery is matchless.
Before the hermitage, exotic fruits all grow;
upon the ridges, famed flowers all bloom.”
“The king, dwelling in the palace, has much happiness;
moreover, all day long, pipes and songs are played.
Morning and evening, food and drink are all wine and meat;
pairs of garments are all silks and satins.
Greed and attachment suddenly arise again as before;
cultivation from then on is again wasted.
If you seek to hear the subtle and wondrous Dharma,
follow me to the mountains—will you do so?”
The great king was willing to go:
The king, hearing these words, was overjoyed;
this matter deeply pleased my heart.
If only I can hear the immortal expound the wondrous Dharma,
who worries about enduring hunger and vegetarian fare in the mountains?
He bade farewell to flesh and kin,
wishing to accompany him;
in the palace, family members arose in sorrow.
The great king's heart was filled with joy,
And he followed him, singing as he went.
Sutra: "When the king heard these words,
he was overjoyed and elated,
and immediately followed the sage,
providing all that was needed,
gathering fruit and drawing water,
collecting firewood and preparing food,
even offering his own body
to serve as a seat.
Thus he served him
for a thousand years,
for the sake of the Dharma,
diligently attending to him,
ensuring he lacked nothing.
Regarding this passage of sutra chanting, the Cí'ēn commentary divides it into two parts: "First, the ability to perform difficult practices;
later, the ability to endure difficult circumstances for long."
Thus he served him,
for a thousand years.
Hereafter, the great king bids farewell to the palace.
As the great king was about to depart,
he took leave of his compassionate mother,
along with the crown prince and his ministers,
and also addressed the queen consort and princess: "Now I wish to take my leave,
I pray you grant me permission!"
Upon hearing this, the princess bitterly pleaded for him to stay,
the compassionate mother saw this and earnestly comforted her,
the queen consort wept in sorrow,
the ministers were at a loss,
everyone urged the sage to turn back,
each wished the great king would not go.
Hearing these words,
the queen's tears flowed like rain,
she rose from her dressing table,
and pulling at her husband's beard, she cursed: "Since becoming your wife,
how many winters and summers have passed?
Today you suddenly plan to part in life,
how could heaven and earth ever allow it!"
Rising and sitting together with you always in one place,
planning to go east or west is extremely difficult.
The great king, amid five-colored auspicious clouds,
followed the sage into the mountains to cultivate the Way.
That day, the sage employed his supernatural powers,
welcoming the king out of the imperial palace with colored mist.
Sages and worthies praised in countless clusters,
heavenly beings rejoiced in myriad throngs.
With no desire to cling to the precious throne,
he single-mindedly awaited arrival in the mountains.
In no more than the snap of a disciple's fingers,
the king followed the sage to the azure peaks.
Just as they were about to arrive,
not much time had passed,
when the king told the sage, hoping he would understand:
"Please speak the promised Lotus Sutra now,
do not delay any longer!"
The sage said: "Do not be foolish,
why must you repeatedly press me so urgently?
Wait until your cultivation has reached a certain stage,
then will I expound it for you, is that not so?"
The great king cultivated the Way,
with body and mind fiercely determined,
he abandoned the royal palace,
wishing to dwell in the snowy mountains.
He gathered fruit on high peaks,
and drew water from distant wells.
Diligent and undaunted by spring and autumn,
driven and never shirking from the cold.
The great king sought the Way with utmost dedication,
practicing asceticism without retreating.
Serving the sage, his feelings grew more earnest,
desiring to hear the wondrous Dharma, his resolve remained firm.
Each morning preparing food, seeking the sage's fruit,
each day filling bottles, fetching fine spring water.
With such a heart, never wearying or retreating,
suddenly a thousand years had passed.
While the great king was gathering fruit,
he suddenly encountered the beast king on the road.
Serving the sage,
his mind was not reckless,
diligent all day long,
a thousand years had already passed.
Drawing water from the ten-thousand-zhang sheer cliff,
gathering fruit from the thousand-peak green trees.
Holding the fruit, intending to return to the hermitage,
he saw the beast king blocking the crucial path.
His face showed alarm,
his heart filled with fear,
he explained everything in detail,
repeatedly pleading his case.
He wished to pass before mealtime,
as noon was approaching.
Fearing the sage would blame him for being late,
thus his heart was troubled with worry.
He humbly begged the beast king to let him pass,
to release him to return to the hermitage and serve the great sage.
The beast king then asked: "Your Majesty yourself are the honored one of ten thousand chariots,
with the seven treasures accompanying you,
a thousand officials following in attendance,
music when you travel,
flutes and pipes when you sit,
such manifold wealth and honor,
surely accumulated over many lifetimes of cultivation,
why then do you toil here day after day,
what purpose do you seek?"
The beast king questioned that great king:
The beast king then asked the great king: "How many years have you lived in these mountains?
Each day gathering firewood after dusk,
each morning picking fruit before the meal.
Abandoning the imperial palace, your heart feels no regret,
serving the sage, your mind is instead focused.
Such diligence you can endure,
without retreating or yielding, for what reason?"
The great king replied to the beast king: "It is not that I have attained understanding through cultivation in this life alone,
but over countless kalpas,
I have grown weary and troubled by this body,
having been within the three realms above and below,
cycling through the six paths,
coming and going in birth and death,
unable to escape,
all because I was bound by greed for wealth and attachment to sensual pleasures.
Although I was within the great palace,
I secretly heard that the Wonderful Dharma Lotus Flower Sutra is the good medicine for the illnesses of all beings in the southern Jambudvīpa.
It also says this sutra drives the white oxen and three vehicles,
to lure the children in the burning house,
universally bestowing the rain of Dharma,
moistening the three roots,
removing the poor son's tattered, soiled garments,
tying the treasure of the drunken friend,
therefore I relinquished the throne of the state,
entrusted governance to the crown prince,
taking no pleasure in the luxury of the great palace,
how could I love the joys of the deep palace!
Frequently enduring stars and frost,
considerably experiencing cold and heat,
my bitter resolve unchanged,
hoping to hear the wondrous Dharma."
The great king said to the beast king:
The great king then replied for the beast king to hear: "I dwell in the mountains with a sincere heart.
Toiling without complaint, for no other purpose,
only because I wish to hear the Lotus Sutra."
Seeing this,
the beast king was very pleased,
and urged him to be diligent henceforth.
If he could not retreat from his former resolve,
he would likely soon hear the wondrous Dharma.
When the great king returned to the hermitage,
he was indeed blamed for being late.
The sage said: "Great King!
Great King!
Recently you have not been very diligent,
drawing water, you do not come for a whole day,
gathering fruit, you only arrive at noon.
If your heart has given rise to retreat and yielding,
then please return immediately;
the king can avoid daily toil,
and spare me constant vexation.
If you wish to go, let the king return to his country,
this official certainly will not detain you."
The great king addressed the sage,
and recounted the previous events in full.
"I have not become lax,
nor have I any heart of retreat or defeat.
Today I was late gathering fruit,
only because I encountered an unusual matter.
On the road I saw a lion,
its majestic virtue most extraordinary,
suddenly it spoke with a human voice,
telling of many matters.
It said that I, cultivating under the sage,
have now completed a thousand years,
and it is time to hear the wondrous Dharma,
therefore it manifested to inform me."
"I humbly hope the sage will listen to my words,
today my lateness had a reason.
After gathering fruit and drawing water, on my way back,
I suddenly encountered a fierce beast on the path.
It roared, shaking its might, then just stopped,
and from then began to speak with a human voice.
The Wonderful Dharma Lotus Flower Sutra is to be heard today,
the lion personally proclaimed it with its own mouth.
I dare not deceive with false words,
I only pray the sage will discern my heart!"
That day, the sage was exceedingly joyful.
That day, the sage
spoke words of congratulation.
A thousand years without fearing toil,
in one day, his merit and virtue are fulfilled.
Now is the time to hear the Dharma,
do not be lazy or slack!
If you now wish to hear the Lotus Sutra,
you must seek for me a seven-jeweled seat.
To seek the seven treasures for a lofty seat,
And expound the Lotus Sutra—what difficulty is there?
The great king said: "If I were still on the throne,
Wealth and honor would be beyond compare.
Towers and pavilions built of agate,
Stairways and paths paved with lapis lazuli.
Beams and rafters made of gold,
Pillars and columns carved from white jade.
Windows adorned with crystal,
Doors and gates crafted from mani pearls.
Pearls strung together to form hanging curtains,
Coral arranged to line the paths like trees.
The eight delicacies piled high as mountains all year round,
The seven treasures filling the treasury through the ages.
If a lotus seat were needed then,
Rebuilding it daily would pose no difficulty.
But now I dwell in the mountains,
Having long abandoned my royal position.
Where shall I find such a precious seat?
From where shall I seek a lotus throne?
Immortal, I beg you to show compassion,
And see that I am at a loss in my heart.
Could I use sandalwood to make a seat,
And then begin the exposition—would that suffice?"
"If it were the seven treasures of the mundane world,
I would only teach you how hard they are to obtain.
But could you sacrifice your own body,
To serve as my lofty seat?"
When the great king heard these words,
His heart was filled with immense joy.
Knowing only that the Lotus Sutra would be expounded,
How could he refuse such a thing!
"I beg the immortal to ascend upon my back,
And expound the sutra for me now without delay."
The great king then addressed the immortal:
"Willingly I offer my body as a lofty seat,
Only seeking future perfect Buddhahood,
Undaunted by the hardships of today."
The immortal,
Observing the king's sincerity,
Knew his resolve for cultivation grew ever more refined.
To repay a thousand years of diligent effort,
He expounded the seven scrolls of the Lotus Sutra.
After hearing the Dharma,
He vowed to practice,
Passing through three asamkhyeyas without pause.
Attaining Bodhi, he returned to the Pure Land,
Then arose with compassion to transform sentient beings.
Manifesting three kinds of bodies in the Saha world,
Expounding the Three Vehicles to guide and receive them.
Waiting until the roots of beings matured,
He again proclaimed the Middle Way Lotus Sutra.
Intending for the assembly of listeners,
To know how rare it is to encounter the Lotus.
Extensively speaking of many lives of diligent toil,
For the sake of seeking the Wonderful Dharma without weariness.
I urge those listening to the Dharma today,
Upon hearing the sutra, to give rise to reverence,
Not only to increase blessings as numerous as Ganges' sands,
But also to eradicate boundless obstructive karma.
Why did the king bitterly seek with lamentation?
To escape the long kalpas of cyclic rebirth.
The preceding explanation of the prose is now complete,
Once more I proclaim the verses, singing them forth.
Sutra: "At that time, the World-Honored One,
Wishing to reiterate this meaning,
Spoke in verse:
I recall past kalpas,
For the sake of seeking the Great Dharma,
Though I was a worldly king,
I did not crave the pleasures of the five desires.
Striking the bell, I proclaimed to the four directions,
'Who possesses the Great Dharma?
If you will explain it for me,
I will become your servant.'"
This recitation of the sutra text, according to the Ci'en Commentary, is categorized as two verses on seeking the Dharma.
Therefore:
The Buddha spoke this sutra at Vulture Peak,
Commanding all to honor and revere it.
This Dharma is profound and rarely encountered,
Cultivated through many kalpas before one may hear it.
I recall in past kalpas,
I was a king seeking the Wonderful Dharma.
Forsaking my kingdom, city, and precious throne,
Not craving the five desires, I vowed to cultivate.
All day striking the bell, proclaiming to the four directions,
Constantly beating the drum, resonating through the three realms.
Clouds of incense from the burner never ceasing,
In my heart remembering the Lotus Sutra.
Sincerely entreating the honored ones of the ten directions,
"Who can expound the subtle and wonderful Dharma?
If you can speak the true teaching for me,
Becoming your servant is no difficulty.
If I can but hear a single phrase of the sutra,
Giving up this kingly body is entirely easy.
I vow not to disobey the speaker,
Even if my body is crushed to dust, I will serve diligently."
The king then uttered these words,
Not knowing who would come to speak for him.
Next, we hear of the Dharma-expounding teacher,
What name shall be sung forth?
Sutra: "At that time, there was the Ashi Immortal,
Who came and said to the great king,
'I have a subtle and wonderful Dharma,
Rare in the world,
If you can cultivate it,
I will explain it for you.'"
In Sanskrit, Ashi Immortal,
Here called 'Incomparable Form,'
Because his appearance is incomparable,
His majestic virtue is incomparable.
Ci'en Commentary: "People, through the Dharma, have already perfected virtue;
The Dharma, relying on people, is already widely proclaimed."
The king, seeking to hear, his resolve unwavering,
Day and night striking the bell and beating the drum.
Then moved the immortal to descend,
Coming before the king, promising to expound the sutra.
The immortal said to the king:
"I have the Middle Way Lotus Sutra,
Rarely found within the world.
Like the udumbara flower, of which there are not two kinds,
Difficult to encounter, difficult to meet, and difficult to hear."
When a wheel-turning king appears in the world,
A single udumbara flower blooms;
When a World-Honored One appears in the world,
Once he proclaims the Wonderful Dharma Lotus.
Rare, rare, king of all sutras,
Hastily sought—how could it be easily spoken?
If you can diligently advance in cultivation,
I will certainly expound it for you.
The immortal, having promised to expound the sutra,
Required within the cultivation to eradicate evil karma.
The king, hearing this, complied accordingly,
His heart giving rise to joy, singing forth.
Sutra: "At that time, the king heard the immortal's words,
His heart gave rise to great joy,
Immediately he followed the immortal,
Providing for all his needs.
Gathering firewood and fruits,
Supplying them in due season.
Because his mind was set on the Wonderful Dharma,
His body and mind knew no weariness."
This recitation of the sutra text, according to the Ci'en Commentary, is categorized as seeking the Dharma and complying.
The king, diligently seeking the Dharma with his heart,
The immortal promised to expound it for him.
Urging him to strive in cultivation,
The king's heart gave rise to joy.
Forsaking the dragon towers and phoenix pavilions,
Not dwelling in the royal chariot or imperial palace.
He followed the immortal with his body,
And went to cultivate the path in the mountains.
Serving without giving rise to weariness,
His body no different from a servant.
Obeying the immortal's every direction,
Day and night following his commands.
Gathering fruits to suffice for meals,
Drawing water to wash the bowl and fill the pitcher.
His mind set on the Wonderful Dharma Lotus Sutra,
His reverence grew ever deeper.
Serving the immortal for a full thousand years,
Not a single thought of retreat or defeat.
In the mountains, cultivating with great vigor,
For the Dharma, he never gave rise to laziness.
Every thought seeking the unsurpassed path,
Every wish only to deliver sentient beings.
A thousand years in the mountains, serving diligently,
His body as a bed and seat, seeking to hear the Dharma.
Not for his own body, craving the five desires,
But for all conscious beings, singing forth.

and when the Buddha saw all living beings,
they were like children encountering a loving parent,

The assembled ministers danced,
the Son of Heaven proceeded slowly,

who, upon seeing the World-Honored One, felt such extreme joy it turned to sorrow;

(Chant below):
In the Saha world, suffering and torment,
seeking profit and fame—when will it end?
Clinging to self and clinging to others—for what reason?
All arise from the deluded mind of pervasive discrimination.
It is like a person descending a high platform at midnight,
stepping in the dark on a broken, severed rope.
Suspecting it to be a poisonous snake a foot long,
he orders young and old to bring lamps.
When has a single snake ever been seen?
It is all born from a deluded mind coupled with attachment.
Just like our disciples coveting illusory realms,
the deluded mind, through thought and discrimination, takes them as real.
One must truly understand and realize the self and others,
then it is like the broken rope at night.
Deluded memories of wife and children, attached to their appearances,
are still like suspecting the rope is a poisonous snake.
Call your sons and daughters down from the hall,
light the lamp of wisdom to shine and illuminate.
Destroy the darkness of ignorance and afflictions,
then you will know nothing is solid or lasting.
Forming enmity and hatred is due to delusion and folly,
contending for qi and emptiness arises from karmic obstructions.
Not understanding this body is not ultimate,
worrying about family and state, constantly busy.
Chanting of silk, singing of bamboo, facing red towers,
becoming intoxicated is considered bodily pleasure.
Precisely taking pleasure amidst suffering,
because illusory dharmas stain the mind-king.
One must know wine is the gate of all grievances,
at gatherings, [□□] drink.
Moreover, it is a thing that brings calamity to people,
within it, do not give rise to greed.
The pit of fire, wanting to fill it, never ceases,
the Buddha-way, intending to accomplish it, seems ever distant.
Not falling into the three evil paths to suffer torment,
this is not something for ordinary people.
From the beginning, intending to speak—when will it end?
Birth, death, and transmigration—people all experience.
Taking Śākyamuni, the Taming Lord, as example,
he then transformed sentient beings in this world.
The bodhisattva Hùmíng descended from the heavenly palace,
feigning to take refuge in the womb of King Śuddhodana's palace.
Then, on the Snowy Mountains, he cultivated ascetic practices,
and realized the unsurpassed Great Physician King.
Constantly using wondrous Dharma to liberate sentient beings,
loving to teach us the true cause.
Causing us to awaken to the priceless treasure of true suchness,
aiming for people to transcend the body of deluded conditions.
Throughout the three-thousandfold world, sprinkling amṛta,
within the sixteen kingdoms, pouring the Dharma rain.
That day, intending to lead the various holy assemblies,
in the city of Vaiśālī, he drove the three vehicles.
How many sages and worthies fully accompanied him,
striking chimes, blowing conches, together guiding the Buddha.
The Buddha moved his venerable, lofty body with excellent marks,
śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas all proceeded.
Heavenly men offered celestial flowers in golden bowls,
heavenly maidens presented exotic fruits on jade plates.
Śakra, winding and bending, praised the Holy Lord,
Brahmā King, soaring in order, circled the Compassionate Honored One.
The seventeen assemblies all lingered,
the sky rained four flowers along the long road.
Who envies your spreading of silk and displaying of brocade?
No pity for you in heaven and all directions.
Auspicious clouds densely covered the Saha world,
joyous colors soared, invading the azure vault.
Heavenly music, clear and mournful, resounded through the cosmos,
heavenly beings gathered, filling the world.
Sages and worthies of the ten directions all sang praises,
awesome Śākyamuni Buddha.
Vaiśālī had extremely heavy conditions,
eliciting a thousand kinds of extraordinary events.
The monarch, with his imperial carriage, went out to the suburbs to welcome,
the chief ministers, with their carriages and canopies, went on the road to receive.
Wanting to see the Great Compassionate Lord of the Three Realms,
just like children hoping for compassionate pity.
People, in vast multitudes,
came out of the city,
to gaze reverently upon the dignified hundred-jeweled platform.
With vows, with compassion, coming to teach and transform,
sacrificing body, sacrificing life, countless times.
The red sun bright,
white clouds swirling,
heaven and earth swayed, roaring like thunder.
Profound incense smoke and auspicious energy,
lightly enveloped this day's great Tathāgata.
People leaping,
laughing heartily,
a hundred birds in the sky, their calls like lament.
What matter did the Jīvajīvaka and Kalaviṅka birds discuss?
Chirping and twittering, they praised the Tathāgata.
Many extraordinary events,
truly wondrous!
Even creeping, wriggling beings containing spirit all arrived.
Eyes filled with tears, they gazed upon the Holy Lord,
intending, each wishing to abandon the womb of rebirth.
Why was it like this?
Because the World-Honored One, for immeasurable kalpas, had not the slightest opposition to sentient beings,
thus eliciting such a response.
(And so on).
Also, because the Tathāgata's procession entered and proceeded to Vaiśālī,
sentient beings rejoiced and looked up.
Ask, what was the procession like?
(Recalling the Great Sage Vimala)
(kīrti Bodhisattva).
When the Tathāgata in days past entered Vaiśālī,
the procession's adornments were truly magnificent and fine.
Clouds parted in the azure sky, revealing an auspicious sun,
the road added a pure realm, raining celestial flowers.
The Compassionate Honored One slowly walked, golden lotuses supporting,
bodhisattvas proceeded leisurely, joyous colors like flowers.
Śakra's majestic demeanor, how could it be scattered and disordered?
Brahmā King's retinue, not the least bit irregular.
Auspicious clouds supporting feet, worthy of gazing upon,
auspicious energy gathering on bodies, good to chant and praise.
Flower bowls contending, forming lion bones,
incense plates joined, resembling elephant tusks.
Heavenly immortals, graceful like spring willows,
jade maidens, dignified like evening clouds.
Mist moistened, chest ornaments heavy,
wind swayed, jade crowns tilted.
Śrāvakas all circled the golden marks,
pratyekabuddhas all rode white deer carriages.
Upāsaka men held flowered parasols,
upāsikā women offered purple robes.
Walking in meditation, often spreading yellow leaves,
crossing waters, from time to time seeing old sandalwood.
On the road, traveling, all hurriedly,
approaching the city, (seemingly) somewhat near.
The king, leaving the phoenix palace, majestic demeanor (far-reaching),
the emperor, departing the dragon palace, the road long.
The Buddha's intention originally aimed at teaching and transforming,
people's minds only love glory and splendor.
How could they know it is all like a dream?
Not yet understanding people are like the four poisonous snakes.
Birth and death, coming and going, countless times,
sinking and drowning, submerged like dust and sand.
Lofty Holy Lord, who can compare?
Vast ordinary people, cannot fathom the limits.
The Buddha, upon the lotus platform, proclaimed the wondrous Dharma,
at once causing entry into the Dharma King's family.
High and low,
laughing heartily,
trailing purple, dragging red, filling the ninefold heavens.
Joyous colors, light and deep, enveloped sun and moon,
auspicious clouds, dense and faint, locked towers and terraces.
Resounding through the cosmos,
roaring like spring thunder,
proclaiming our Compassionate Honored One's teaching has come.
Throughout a hundred koṭis, nets of enmity dispersed,
filling the three-thousandfold world, flowers of awakening bloomed.
Heaven and earth,
white and gleaming,
all celestial flowers piled everywhere.
Like brocade, like silk, this [□] evil,
like frost, like snow, covering dust and dirt.
The seventeen assemblies,
arranged themselves,
following the King of Emptiness, few could compare.
High fans, fragrant winds blew away heat and affliction,
lightly misting sweet dew, settled dust and dirt.
People leaping,
urging each other on,
early entering Vaiśālī to extinguish obstructions and calamities.
Offering grass, Brahmā King moved grandly,
holding flowers, Śakra appeared lofty.
Dragons vied in dance,
ghosts and spirits pressed close,
Gandharva kings, a hundred million koṭis.
Frequently playing clear songs illuminating the Four Truths,
or blowing elegant music extinguishing the Three Calamities.
The Garuḍa bird,
With unmatched strength,
Crushes high mountains to dust.
From devouring too many dragons, its body glows like fire,
While demon hordes roar like thunder.
The eight classes of dragons and devas stand majestic,
As the Buddha, like a radiant breeze, comes and goes.
Playing with shadows and forms, turning left and right,
Driving clouds and singing with lightning, its power vast and grand.
Lord of the Three Realms,
Singing wondrously,
This majestic presence has no equal.
To rid the four kinds of beings of their arrogance,
And serve as a ladder for the six paths of rebirth.
Rulers and ministers,
Pay homage to the Tathāgata,
Dare not question the flawless words.
Dancing and burning incense, vying to make offerings,
Purifying heart and mind, circling the flower altar.
Men and women,
Troubled in heart,
Their afflictions likely shattered this day.
Gazing upon the auspicious marks in the golden light,
Bowing a thousand times in the fragrance of the jade-white hair.
Truly wondrous,
Hard to describe,
How many noble and humble awaken to the illusory womb.
The Buddha entered the Āmrapālī Garden to preach this Dharma,
Who is there to hold a canopy and sing forth?
The sutra says: At that time, in the city of Vaiśālī, there was a son of a elder,
Named Bǎojī,
Together with five hundred sons of elders, holding seven-jeweled canopies.
(And so on).
The layman knew the Buddha had entered Vaiśālī,
Because I am teaching sentient beings in this country,
The Buddha wishes to join me in promoting the great teaching,
I must today briefly employ supernatural powers.
With whom is the karmic connection ripe today?
Then I observed Bǎojī and others chasing pleasure and amusement,
I must teach and transform them,
To fulfill their resolve for the Path.
Moreover, flowers scattered in the three springs,
Still rely on sweet dew to wash and cleanse;
The Buddha attained perfect enlightenment,
And relies on bodhisattvas for support.
Thus we know flowers depend on the warm sun,
The Buddha relies on assistance.
The layman exclaimed: Within the three thousand realms,
Amidst a hundred billion dust motes,
There is the uniquely supreme one,
Acting as the transcendent lord beyond the crowd.
Wielding the mallet of compassion,
Able to crush the mountain of arrogance;
Spreading the cloud of wisdom,
Later covering the sea of greed and anger.
The four kinds of birth, the six paths,
The eight difficulties, the three wretched paths,
Saving sentient beings without beginning or end,
Transforming other beings inexhaustibly.
Mind like a great hoe,
Able to uproot the roots of afflictions;
Intention like vast waves,
Splashing to extinguish the fire of ignorance.
Majestic presence rarely matched,
Auspicious marks hard to equal.
The topknot jewel like the autumn moon newly full,
Wrist bracelets like icy coldness suddenly pure.
Upon the lotus throne,
Both brows privately carry a smiling expression;
Within the hall of seven jewels,
Both cheeks long hold a joyful hue.
Being the guide for all sentient beings,
The model for bodhisattvas.
Entering Vaiśālī not for others,
Preaching the wondrous Dharma entirely because of me.
I must today,
Briefly employ supernatural powers,
Observe this city,
With whom is the karmic connection ripe?
Just then I saw golden branches and jade leaves,
Imperial sons and princely grandsons,
Playing sheng and singing within the three palaces,
Moving silk and bamboo within the nine chambers.
Silken curtains for daytime naps,
Concubines adding incense to golden duck burners;
Spring outings in the imperial garden,
Attendants plucking magnolia stamens.
Regardless of season,
Never distinguishing autumn or winter.
Drunk returning before the bright moon curtain,
Awakening from dreams beneath the clear breeze hall.
Mounting fragrant saddles and shaking jade bridles,
Not yet satisfied with high or low;
Drinking fine wine and tossing golden cups,
Only knowing wealth and honor.
The layman shouted from afar,
Admonishing Bǎojī: You are greedy for feasts and pleasures,
Stained with form and sound,
Because the seeds of afflictions are deep,
And the karma of ignorance is heavy.
Utterly shameless,
How could you know of poor and lowly people;
Relying on pure heroic prowess,
Only loving extravagant things.
Storehouses hold fine silks and rare brocades,
Kitchens prepare delicacies and flavors.
A single step requires a thousand attendants,
One word answered by a hundred affirmations.
Clad in embroidered silks,
Do you know the toil of the weaving girl?
Mouth eating delicacies,
Do not think of the farmer's suffering.
These are: Guests passing through the six paths,
People dwelling in the three wretched paths.
Privately foolish and ignorant,
Unable to understand.
I must now teach,
I must guide,
Make them abandon this clamor,
And pursue the attainment of the unconditioned wondrous fruit.
(And so on).
(Reciting the bodhisattva).
Vimalakīrti, unconditioned, suddenly pondered,
The Buddha entered Vaiśālī, for whom else?
Lamenting sentient beings' great arrogance,
Pitying their kindred's abundant foolishness.
Following facial expressions, joy is often scarce,
Thinking the body will last unchanged.
Before reaching the end, old age arrives,
How could one know death will ultimately destroy.
Slow steps, frequent graceful postures,
Leisurely walking, ample majestic presence.
Hands like white jade before an autumn mirror,
Eyes like blue lotuses emerging from dawn ponds.
Guiding sentient beings, never weary,
Supporting all beings without fatigue.
This coming is precisely the day of meeting,
Together with me now, the time for teaching.
I see the sons of the ninefold nobles,
They are five hundred imperial sons.
Greedy for unlocking golden locks at the phoenix palace,
Just then drunk with jade consorts in red towers.
Under windows, dark-browed maidens chant imperial verses,
Among flowers, rosy-cheeked ones sing palace lyrics.
Parrots hide in green willows, morning clouds disperse,
Swallows chirp on red beams, scenes decline.
Peach blossoms by the steps washed by spring rain,
Green bamboo before curtains blown by wild wind.
In the fragrance of silks, lamps dimly lit,
Amid sounds of silk and bamboo, pillows half reclined.
Below the hall, drunk awakening calls "long live,"
Before the courtyard, after drinking, summoning consorts.
Only greedy for lasting pleasure,
Not mindful that human life has flourishing and decay.
I must enter the palace to teach and transform,
Make them take refuge in the great Mauni.
The lay devotee had already formed his intention,
and then entered the royal palace.
Seeing Bǎojī indulging in pleasures and chasing after amusements,
he skillfully spoke words of admonishment and reproach,
making him weary of extravagance and luxury,
and teaching him to take refuge in the Three Jewels.
The lay devotee, in his residence, formed his intention,
and having spoken, he set out.
He took his jíli (thornwood) staff before the curtain,
and donned his black gauze cap by the mirror's side.
He did not bring attendants,
yet his dignified bearing was as usual;
he did not lead household servants,
yet his traveling accoutrements were exactly as before.
His wind-tossed white hair,
his long robe sweeping the ground,
raising his head like stars moving at midnight,
moving his feet like an ancient juniper, a divine tree.
Gazing from afar at the imperial gates,
a thousand layers of auspicious qi rose and enveloped;
looking distantly at the royal palace,
a stretch of propitious clouds shimmered and veiled.
Frequently with slow steps,
leisurely shifting his body.
He saw the willow colors along the imperial moat blending with mist,
beheld the peach blossoms in the forbidden garden smiling at the sun.
Just upon entering within the ninefold walls,
he already heard pipes and songs;
gradually approaching the midst of the three halls,
he observed everywhere silks and brocades.
The lay devotee saw Bǎojī and others,
each displaying martial skills,
fully contending in literary talent.
They captured wind and moon within five-character poems,
discussed demons and folly beneath three-foot swords.
Before the steps, beside the terraces,
clear springs wound around bamboos, murmuring;
beneath the woods, by the stream's edge,
snowy junipers swayed in the wind, rustling sharply.
None failed to boast of their wealth and status,
competing in extravagance and luxury.
They rode fine steeds on long roads,
hung brocade robes on broad paths.
Behind the curtains of consorts and concubines,
spring parrots called out "ten thousand years" voices;
before the halls of palace ladies and eunuchs,
autumn swallows chattered with a thousand kinds of melodies.
And moreover, after revelry in red towers,
returning with fragrant parasols.
Golden whips flicked willow branches and flower boughs,
jade bridles lifted in clear breeze and bright moon.
Accompanied by crimson and purple robes,
voices joined in songs praising the emperor's virtue;
attended by robed and capped officials,
united in singing tunes of gratitude.
Upon coral pillows,
before jadeite curtains,
sobering from drunkenness, they heard a strain of qin music,
awakening from dreams in the third watch's rain.
The sovereign's favor and affection,
specially receiving the grace of rain and dew;
the empress's fondness and care,
repeatedly bestowed with pearls and treasures' bounty.
The lay devotee said to Bǎojī: This is willful indulgence in pride and luxury,
affliction, folly, and delusion.
You consider it the glory and splendor of the world of form,
but I say it is the bitter sea of sinking and drowning.
You may indulge to the utmost in self-amusement and self-pleasure,
but what do you know of the suffering and torment of the myriad people?
Alone noble, alone exalted,
how could you think of the oppression of living beings?
I now specially bring sincere earnestness,
to advise you, deluded ones.
You must directly accept my words,
they are like the Buddha's speech from the flower terrace.
Do you not know that in the Āmra Garden there is the Buddha,
who salvages and rescues all beings.
He has a thousand kinds of meritorious virtues adorning his body,
possesses ten thousand types of dignified deportment in his form.
You should together cast aside greed and attachment,
and develop a mind of goodness.
Abandon the illusory mind of this one lifetime,
and pay reverence to the golden-marked, majestic appearance.
You must discipline yourselves,
be steadfast and watchful,
if by chance favorable conditions ripen through idle causes,
together with you, let us block and chase, then go and come.
(And so on).
(End)
Vimalakīrti, having spoken, left the palace courtyard,
his staff of goosefoot wood taken up, clapped hands and held high.
With slow steps exiting the gate, frequently bowing in reverence,
with smiling countenance taking to the road, greeting dukes and ministers.
Scholars and officials, one by one, courted at the dragon gate,
the lay devotee watched as he approached the phoenix city.
The whole road already met with clamor of carriages and horses,
from the nine thoroughfares afar, the sound of pipes and strings was heard.
On golden steps, coming and going, people recognized acquaintances,
in the jade halls, who ever asked for names?
Just then seeing brothers boasting of skills and accomplishments,
each contending in civil and martial arts, vying in brilliance.
Deep in the palace, joy and pleasure none could match,
coming and going, chasing amusement, with wine poured out.
When flower stamens fell, people were half-drunk,
in the depths of willow mist, rain had just cleared.
From high towers only words of peace and prosperity were heard,
from the twin towers, who heard talk of war and strife?
Colorfully dressed girls laughed and scolded swallows at golden pavilions,
consorts and concubines idly called to parrots in jade cages.
Below Purple Cloud Tower, matching songs to music,
before the emperor's curtain, arranging □□.
Jade mirrors washed makeup, presenting plain faces,
sunlit windows gleaming, playing with red parrots.
Puppies wildly chasing, biting at strangers,
servant boys frequently pinching, startling wild pigeons.
Sunset before the window, flipping game tokens,
moon high by the tower's side, learning to blow the sheng.
Greedy for pleasure, unwilling to worry about aging bodies,
chasing amusement, who could think of life and death?
From afar seeing Vimalakīrti, all went to receive him,
from a distance meeting the lay devotee, all came to welcome him.
Vimalakīrti then said to the royal descendants: Old matters from beginning to end must be changed.
Stubbornly greedy in the sea of deluded desires,
busily pushing into the mire pit.
A thousand minds, fully understanding, yet all like a dream,
two eyes, perfectly clear, yet exactly like blind.
Karmic waters accumulated, waves vast and boundless,
mountains of sin added to, momentum towering and steep.
Not knowing there is the wondrously awakened Buddha of the Āmra Garden,
always speaking of true conditions to ferry sentient beings.
His body like gold, radiating sunlight's hue,
his mind like a bright mirror, reflecting a clear pool.
Teeth arranged densely like mountain snow,
thoughts pure and limpid like water crystal.
The holy sword ever takes up the weight of compassionate vows,
the dharma boat long uses the pole of wisdom to push.
One gaze, one bow removes calamities and obstacles,
a smile or a song all attain equality.
If you wish for glory and splendor, seek to revere the Buddha,
together with you, today, let us practice cultivation.
(Bái) Bǎojī and others, having received the layman’s teaching,
immediately turned their minds.
Facing the layman,
they recounted their past days,
pursuing pleasure through the four seasons,
chasing joy across the eight festivals,
unaware that all was illusory and empty,
mistakenly believing themselves in eternal bliss.
Now, having been admonished,
they follow his guidance,
wishing to accompany the great being,
following him to the monastery to pay homage to the Buddha.
The layman said: Moreover, I have heard that buds sprout and flourish,
all due to the orderly progression of the seasons;
ordinary people’s cultivation,
entirely comes from the Buddhas’ teaching.
As for you all,
you are precisely those who crave pleasure,
vie for glory and splendor.
In the four seasons, you follow the enjoyment in flower-decked towers,
in the eight festivals, you roam the jade halls.
In spring,
willow mist first descends,
enchanting scenes lie hidden deep.
Parrots fluttering with chatter,
flower buds half-open as if splitting.
Rain adorns the terrace’s colors,
wind shakes the curtain’s sounds.
A window full of spring shadows, warm and gentle;
the ground covered with sunlight, soft and lingering.
In the palace, beauties
open doors to emerald ponds adding flow;
in the hall, splendid light,
on the pillow, lofty mountains pile upon sentient beings.
In summer,
one may say the yang harmony is faint,
the summer heat is deep and dense.
A railing of green bamboo sways in the wind,
ten thousand trees of cherries carry rain.
Long-spread bamboo mats,
like a stream of jade-green water newly flowing;
clean-swept jade beds,
as if eight feet of cold ice not yet melted.
Thin gauze for curtains,
light silk for dyed garments.
The hall deep, the sweltering heat does not invade;
the pavilion distant, cool and refreshing naturally.
Idle clouds at the door,
like scattered strange peaks;
old cypress leaning against the eaves,
resembling deep, still cave waters.
In autumn,
one may say frost carves red leaves,
rain drips on sparse paulownias.
High in the sky, geese cry in the cold wind;
far on the steps, crickets chirp under the bright moon.
Vast, vast mountain hues,
crowned with clouds, all enter the dragon tower;
mournful, mournful cicada sounds,
mingled with dew, resound at the phoenix gate.
Crimson courtyard at midnight,
purple forbidden quarters at early night.
Hearing the time when a thousand households pound their washing blocks,
listening to the places where ten thousand homes play pipes and strings.
Golden chrysanthemums by the railing,
their fragrance reaches even the gauze curtains;
cold pines reflecting the pavilion,
their sound and rhythm often pierce the embroidered canopies.
(And so on).
In winter,
one may say frost congeals on jade steps,
ice cleanses golden ponds.
Snow taps at the window by the night pillow,
wind shakes the bamboo in the cold courtyard.
Stars shift across the azure sky,
who knows the cold of the cave chamber?
Lamp shadows on silver screens,
unaware of the chill in brocade quilts.
This: I considered it joy,
I made it glory and splendor.
I thought it ultimately firm and secure,
I made it originally real and existent.
I considered it wealth and honor,
a thousand years just like this moment;
I made myself surpassing all,
ten thousand years only as today.
Bǎojī and others, a hundred lifetimes honored,
countless kalpas hard to repay.
Suddenly meeting the elder Vimalakīrti,
joyfully encountering the lofty layman.
Truly, his dignity is majestic,
his pure breeze shoots forth at people;
his appearance is imposing,
his virtue mountain towering as in days past.
Now, receiving the layman’s skillful expedient means,
guiding and leading us.
Taking a single rope of compassion, firm and secure,
taming the five hundred minds (monkeys) to break free from madness.
From now on, we
will have drums, music, strings, and songs
no heart to enjoy and play in ponds and pavilions,
but intent to transcend and seek the wondrous joy.
The sounds of pipes and songs, dripping,
heard like wind in the ears;
colorful maidens in pairs,
seen like thorns in the eyes.
Golden cups and jade vessels,
not poured before painted boats;
fine green wine and white brew,
not drunk on journeys to red towers.
Red-tasseled white horses,
brocade saddles and red saddlecloths.
A thousand men cannot lead ahead,
ten thousand riders cease to follow behind.
Pepper-scented silver ducks,
no longer adding fragrance in the fifth watch;
powder-pavilion beauties,
not gazing into sunset mirrors.
Thus, foolishness vanishes without trace,
greed and attachment leave no trail.
Together abandoning the gate of defilement,
contemplating the principle of non-action.
All due to Vimalakīrti’s pointing out,
the layman’s teaching and instruction.
Suddenly, with different mouths but one voice,
unconsciously they bow and gaze at the layman.
The layman, moved and grateful, said: Excellent, Bǎojī,
truly a guide.
You are imperial sons and princely grandsons,
you are outstanding worthies and accomplished scholars.
You should only crave glory and love pleasure,
drive carts with shining suns on imperial dikes;
display talent and contend in ability,
race wind-chasing feet on purple paths.
How fortunate that this old man’s light words,
taught the elder’s lofty thoughts.
Briefly offering slight, fresh words,
you receive extraordinary weight.
This is great fortune in life and death,
past kalpas having affinity.
Already receiving your acceptance of these statements,
how dare I further accept your bows of thanks.
It is like a full wheel of bright moon,
yielding light before stars and constellations;
a ten-thousand-ren green mountain,
declining steepness below hills and mounds.
Bǎojī and others, hearing Vimalakīrti’s words,
all spurred their minds and spirits.
This morning they must leave the royal city,
this day they must return to the Buddha’s monastery.
Having finished speaking,
they arranged their dignified demeanor.
Each holding dragon-phoenix garments,
changing into fresh new robes.
Accompanying the layman,
jeweled canopies held themselves.
The court officials of the palace bustling,
processions of maidens from the whole country.
Then they leveled the imperial road,
swept and cleansed the heavenly street.
The spring rain on the nine thoroughfares just ceased,
auspicious smoke from ten thousand wells just gathered.
As for the jeweled canopy,
a thousand treasures combined to form it,
ten thousand jewels vied to complete it.
Like a forest of flowering trees suddenly blooming,
like ten thousand auspicious lotuses already split open.
Gold as its bones,
coral parrots in pairs;
white jade as its strips,
jadeite kalaviṅka birds facing each other.
Its craftsmanship surpasses that of Yǐng artisans and worthy men.
Fine strands stringing branches and twigs,
delicate patterns rising in relief.
Pearl tassels sweeping the ground,
fragrant wind blowing with clinking sounds;
radiant light shining to the sky,
auspicious aura locking in hazy colors.
Then [the layman] led ahead,
Bǎojī followed behind.
Look, they are about to leave the royal city,
not yet knowing where they intend to go.
Choosing exotic brocades to make clothes,
only wishing to adorn impure things.
Even if you pluck eyebrows and eyes,
even if you apply powder and oil.
Xīshī’s seductive charm gains people’s pity,
bewitching King Xiāng to abandon his throne.
The killing ghost one day comes to take you,
no matter your beauty and literary talent.
Even if as handsome as Pān Ān,
fruit thrown filling carts, people all know.
The four phases shift, the body perishes after,
only an empty name left, also impermanent.
Even if Hán Xìn had heroism,
destroyed Chǔ, met at Gāixiá, supported the Hàn emperor.
Each of you, consider carefully in your hearts,
all presented as illusion, a scene of emptiness.
The mighty Fán Kuài, sufficient in merit and ability,
stormed the Hóngmén feast to rescue his lord.
Fierce heart and rough appearance increase my arrogance,
Yet now it all turns out to be empty.
Emperors and kings of ten thousand years,
How many have died, who can count?
Look outside the walls of Cháng'ān,
Hills and fields are filled with imperial tombs.
Vimalakīrti thus transformed the royal descendants,
Urging them all to awaken.
With one voice they thanked the layman,
Grateful for dispelling their deluded minds.
From then on, they realized impermanence,
No longer delighting in worldly pleasures.
I regret my past heavy afflictions,
Chasing pleasures through the seasons without rest.
Though summer brings scorching heat,
In the deep palace, I found comfort.
On the horn mat, a chill stirs,
The jade bed, quietly brushed, feels like light ice.
Autumn scenes with sparse leaves,
Clouds scatter, geese fly, drinking much wine.
The hall filled with autumn wind, dreams awaken,
A bright moon rises as drunkenness fades.
Realizing all dharmas are ultimately empty,
Understanding the Three Vehicles is all there is.
How can it compare to honoring the Lord of the Three Realms,
Or drawing near to Śākyamuni?
The royal descendants then made arrangements,
Until the nine palaces teemed with people.
Beauties and consorts were all left behind,
Officials and lay followers accompanied them.
Holding jeweled canopies, they left the city,
Sweeping the heavenly streets like mirrors.
Rows of music preceded and followed,
Splendid robes bustling on both sides.
Auspicious clouds shrouded the towers,
Spring hues lightly veiled the phoenix gates.
Willow mist on the road catches sweet dew,
Flowering trees along the way play with dawn light.
Countless maidens lined the long streets,
Seeing the Buddha, their hearts leaped with joy.
Wishing to form good ties on this day,
They escorted the prince to the monastery garden.
Heaven and earth,
All grew bright,
The jeweled canopies, majestic and splendid.
Golden threads weave twin phoenixes dancing,
Silver strands form flower-offering immortals.
Polished cold jade makes branches,
Carved glass becomes the canopy top.
Mist disperses as if woven by heaven,
Clouds enshroud as if naturally born.
Carried along, jade rings tinkle,
Passing waves chime like pendants.
On this day, Buddha's voice filled the cosmos,
Then heavenly music pervaded the universe.
A snap of the fingers,
Again reverent,
Transforming Vaiśālī into a land of bliss.
Heaven rains four flowers, showing auspicious signs,
Earth trembles six ways, the Buddha knows.
Truly splendid,
New jade flowers,
Brocade, silk, and seven treasures.
On the fragrant shore, behold the imperial son,
In compassionate light, see Vimalakīrti.
Then Ratnākara's mind awakened to the Way,
All teachings were from Vimalakīrti.
Eyes not gazing at seductive colors,
Ears not listening to pipe and string music.
All holding jeweled canopies left the dragon palace,
Each wearing golden crowns exited the phoenix city.
Royal descendants thronged the roads,
Unknown where they all headed.
Crowds upon crowds,
Myriads upon myriads,
Leaving Vaiśālī to honor the Dharma platform.
Gentlemen and ladies walked gracefully through the streets,
Heroes filled the roads, laughing and lingering.
Auspicious smoke rose from ten thousand households,
Joyful hues opened before a thousand doors.
Intending to meet the sage lord at the assembly,
How to bow and chant what comes next?
The scripture says: Ratnākara and others chanted: Eyes pure, long and wide like blue lotuses,
Mind pure, having transcended all meditative states.
Long accumulated pure karma called immeasurable,
Guiding the multitude with stillness, thus I bow.
"Vimalakīrti Fragmented Gold" in one scroll.
Recorded by Kuāngyìn, scripture lecturer monk of Língzhōu Lóngxīng Temple.
Brought by Yuánzōngjiān,
Especially delayed for days,
Finished copying the text.
As a monastic,
I did not wish to refuse.
Shòufāng Buddhist visitor □
Scripture: The Buddha told Ānanda,
I observe sentient beings,
Though endowed with human form,
Their minds act foolishly and ignorantly,
Not thinking of their parents,
Who have great kindness and virtue,
Not generating respect,
Lacking benevolence and compassion.
This chant of scripture,
Is the World-Honored One's reprimand.
Previously, parents have ten kinds of kindness,
All are the nurturing of parents,
The toil of both parents.
(And so on).
The World-Honored One said: Ānanda,
I observe all sentient beings in the Sahā world,
Though possessing human features,
Do not know their parents have great kindness,
Do not generate repayment,
Do not understand gratitude.
At life's end, they must fall into the three wretched paths,
For endless kalpas, never encountering liberation.
Lamenting the world's men and women,
Grown up, yet unable to reflect.
Not yet cultivating a filial heart,
Vainly studying without basis.
Even if foolish,
Often resisting,
Parents try scolding, slapping spoons and chopsticks.
Only at home indulging their temper,
How know outside their reputation spreads?
Hot times too hot, out of love and care,
Cold times utterly cold, for support and uplift.
When the child is happy, the whole family finds peace,
When the child is angry, the whole house is without cheer.
Exhausted from driving,
Suffering torment,
How can they consider even a little?
Easily abandoning, unwilling to return,
Casually forsaking, going to other lands.
Never forming good acquaintances,
Only carving out wicked companions.
At home, always resenting parents' words,
Outside, trusting others' talk.
Greatly foolish,
Unawakened,
Indulging body and mind, incurring guilt.
The Buddha says such rebellious people,
Will not find a good place for rebirth.
Layer upon layer of hell, for what reason?
Only for the Jambudvīpa's rebellious people.
Do not ask about the torment of cold and boiling,
Nor the years and months of grinding the body.
Knowing oneself without reason, accepting beating and breaking,
Begging for mercy, enduring hardship.
Even if you return to the human world,
From birth to old age, you will be cold and poor.
The Buddha said: Ānanda,
If people commit the five rebellious acts,
At life's end, they must fall into evil paths.
Even if born in the human world,
Disease and poverty,
In all they do,
They will not succeed.
This is all because
(And so on).
If you wish in the next life ten features complete,
Wealth and much fortune,
Clothing and food,
You must in this life,
Practice filial support
(And so on).
If you seek the fruit of perfect features,
Much fortune, wealth, and righteousness,
Actions always meeting auspiciousness,
Deeds never encountering disasters.
At home, a marquis,
Abroad, a general,
Land protected, people respectful.
Regrettable hearts in other schools,
No shortcut surpasses practicing filial support.
If you skillfully attend to parents,
Earth gods and dragons all rejoice.
Disasters not a speck each year,
Auspicious signs many each day.
Actions and rest all as wished,
Coming and going, at ease everywhere.
Even if life ends, returning to the great night,
The three wretched paths still will not hinder.
The Buddha said: Ānán,
if a person understands and practices filial piety,
in this life they will be respected and served by others,
and at life's end, they will not fall into the three wretched paths.
Generally, there are many unfilial people in the world.
At home, they exhaust their parents' spirit and mind;
coming and going, they do not observe proper times.
This causes their father's heart to be filled with sorrow and distress,
and their mother's thoughts to be anxious and fearful.
All day long they lean by the gate,
vainly shedding tears of blood
(and so on).
The classics say: "Store grain against famine,
raise children to provide for old age."
Even when the years have passed and they are grown,
knowing east from west,
they cast aside their father and mother,
heading south or north.
Although sons and daughters are unfilial,
parents never cease to cherish them.
Such kindness and remembrance are greatest;
how can they bear to abandon them and go abroad?
(While parents are alive),
(I urge you not to dwell in other lands).
The world's unfilial people are truly pitiable and lamentable,
treating their father and mother with disrespect and neglect.
They do not recall the extreme hardship and bitterness of pregnancy,
how could they know the weariness of nursing and feeding?
They indulge in wrongdoing,
follow evil companions,
lightly curse their honored parents and slander the good and kind.
The Buddha says of such people,
life after life it will be most difficult to see the face of the Tathāgata.
The Buddha says of ordinary people in this turbid age,
they indulge in wrongdoing beyond discussion.
Even seeing evil men, their hearts rejoice,
but encountering the good, they instead become angry.
When kin advise them, they never listen;
when parents instruct them, it is as if unheard.
They refuse all official duties and enterprises,
constantly idle and lax, indulging in procrastination.
Parents are only anxious all day long,
seeing their sons love companions of bad character.
Chasing pleasure and amusement without rest,
gambling at dice and games without cease.
Every day leaning by the gate shedding tears of blood,
each morning vexation pierces their hearts.
The Buddha says such people are not human sons;
dying and entering the three wretched paths is truly pitiable and sorrowful.
From the beginning of pregnancy to infancy,
until the body grows to six feet tall.
They abandon virtue, turn their backs on kindness, and act unfilially,
chasing sounds and sights, indulging their hearts' desires.
Three years of nursing is truly lamentable;
ten months of pregnancy is fully worthy of grief.
Not remembering the nurturing strength of their two parents' kindness,
ungratefully turning their backs—let this be proclaimed.
The scripture says: They abandon virtue and turn their backs on kindness.
This recitation of the scripture text
is our Buddha, the World-Honored One, describing beings of the five rebellious acts,
who turn their backs on kindness and virtue.
Not being filial to parents,
fleeing to other lands,
abandoning honored parents,
not returning home.
At life's end, the evil paths,
endure great suffering and bitterness.
All because in a previous life they were not filial to parents
(and so on).
The scripture says: In a past age,
there was a sinner
upon whose head a hot iron wheel constantly revolved.
He asked Maudgalyāyana
(and so on),
(all because in a previous life he was not filial to parents),
his emerging form was frightening to behold,
those who saw him all said his karmic obstructions were heavy.
A hot iron wheel revolved upon his head,
regardless of time or season, constant pain.
Unclear why he received this calamity,
all because in a previous life he personally cultivated such seeds.
Towards uncles he felt no reverence or respect,
beside his two parents he did not awaken to sincere devotion.
The Buddha says this ghost's karma is hard to describe,
upon his head long revolves a hot iron wheel.
Every day he suffers all kinds of misery and distress,
each morning without cease he endures hardship and bitterness.
All because he was not filial to his compassionate father,
entirely for being ungrateful towards his mother.
I urge all who hear the Dharma today,
quickly must be filial and obedient, do not procrastinate.
Moreover, in serving and attending parents,
cherishing and remembering brothers,
seeing them must bring joy and happiness,
encountering them should bring appreciation and admiration.
Inquiring after them morning and evening,
day and night respectfully attending,
fanning the pillow, warming the bed,
one must know the proper times.
(This is a true filial son).
If the mind gives rise to unfilial thoughts,
abandoning father and mother,
abroad for years,
with no thought of returning home,
this is not a filial son.
Furthermore, when parents restrain them,
they do not believe their words;
responding with loud voices,
their actions contrary and disobedient.
Sweet and savory delicacies,
their wife and children always eat;
bitter and astringent food and drink,
they give to their father to eat.
(This filial son is not)
(not a filial son)
(indeed).
The classics speak of Zēng Shēn
(and so on).
The Buddha teaches men and women of this turbid age,
when grown up, they must be filial to parents.
Evening reflection, morning attendance, do not dread the toil;
warming the bed, fanning the pillow, do not refuse the hardship.
Do not let father and mother give rise to resentment and anger;
follow their wishes, observe their demeanor, teach them appropriately.
Not only will all people praise you,
it will also cause the sages and worthies to bestow their protection.
Respectfully attending and serving brings peace of mind;
the name of filial piety should be transmitted in the world.
In the classics, Zēng Shēn is spoken of by all;
in the scriptures, Luóbo is widely proclaimed.
All ashamed of the great kindness and virtue of nursing,
fully moved by the sufficient pity of pregnancy.
The Buddha says if one can practice filial nurturing,
in this life and the next there will be no distress or obstruction.
Unfilial people,
hard to describe with analogies,
oppose and overturn their two parents, not like a mother's simplicity.
Within the home, quarreling and noise, defying father and mother;
before the gate, cursing each other, dragging in ancestors.
Just planning to instruct them, and anger rises to the heavens;
trying to pretend to restrain them, they harbor wrath and rage.
The Buddha says such people of the five rebellious acts,
at life's end will find it most difficult to cast off suffering and bitterness.
The Buddha says beings of the five rebellious evils,
their karmic retribution in the future is truly not light.
Within the six paths they come and go,
inside the three wretched paths they die and are reborn.
Simply because they do not feel the virtue of pregnancy,
entirely because they lack all sentiment of nurturing and rearing.
Therefore, within the three wretched evil paths,
for a long time they suffer without cease or rest.
Worthy of pity and remembrance,
and worthy of grief,
forgetting such deep kindness is a great bitterness!
Even birds and beasts still practice filial duty;
as humans, how can they indulge their hearts' desires?
Three years of nursing is still bearable;
ten months of pregnancy—the bitterness cannot be measured.
The Buddha personally said in the scriptures,
saying how to bear a heavy burden—let this be proclaimed.
The scripture says: The mother carries the child,
within the ten months,
rising and sitting uneasy,
as if bearing a heavy burden;
eating and drinking do not go down,
like a long-term sick person.
This recitation of the scripture text
is the World-Honored One further clarifying the hardship of pregnancy.
(Previously, among the ten kindnesses, the first is the kindness of)
(bearing)
(protecting)
(and guarding).
According to the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*,
our bodies are formed by taking our parents' red and white substances,
to become this physical form.
These have five colors;
initially born as kalala
(and so on),
(for thirty-eight sevens of days),
only then do we know that within our mother's womb,
we endure much suffering and bitterness.
The mother's form and appearance become emaciated and weak.
(And so on)
Ten months of bearing, all you disciples,
ten thousand hardships, a thousand bitternesses, day by day.
Rising and sitting, morning after morning, the body like a mountain;
acting and doing, day after day, the heart as if drunk.
Phoenix hairpins and phoenix mirrors never held;
jade-like countenance, flower-like beauty turns withered and haggard.
Reciting Buddha's name, seeking divine aid, there is mind for that;
viewing flowers, chasing pleasure, all without intention.
Ten months of bearing the disciple's body,
like bearing a heavy burden, the hardship is beyond description.
Green eyebrows, peach-blossom face secretly waste away;
jade-like countenance, flower-like beauty suddenly changes spring.
Cloud-like hair uncombed for months on end;
the mirror stand left entirely covered in dust.
Because of greed to protect and cherish the child within the womb,
long frowning with both eyebrows, traces of tears.
Walking, I sigh with regret;
sitting, I grieve in sorrow.
Carrying (the burden) for ten months, enduring a thousand autumns.
Though not drunk in heart, I am ever as if drunk;
though without worry in mind, I am just as if worried.
Hearing speech (and laughter), I have no mind to listen;
seeing places of song and joy, I do not lift my head.
Solely hoping for the peace and happiness of mother and child,
I recite Buddha's name, burn incense, and make a hundred kinds of prayers.
Since the compassionate mother became pregnant,
she has suffered a thousand kinds of worry and distress.
Whether sitting or walking,
it is like carrying a heavy burden.
The food and drink she consumes
have no flavor at all.
She only worries about her life and body for a moment;
how could she have the heart for conversation?
Reflecting on the day the compassionate mother gave birth,
the bitterness and distress, a thousand kinds, are hard to describe.
Tears fall all because of cherishing this body;
sorrow arises only from worrying about the physical form.
Suddenly, if it is a filial daughter or son,
once born, it is extremely swift.
But if it is an enemy coming to seek shelter,
the mother's life may be lost in an instant.
Considering it thus,
it is a matter of suffering,
for a thousand kalpas and ten thousand lives,
repaying is not easy.
One must only receive precepts and listen to scriptures;
beyond this, it is hard to express filial piety and righteousness.
Today, those seated here
must clearly remember it all.
Reflecting on when the compassionate mother nurtured you,
she endured ten thousand hardships and a thousand toils, never refusing.
Her emaciated face became ugly and unsightly;
her flowery appearance changed into frailty and weakness.
Bowing her head, silent, ever as if ill;
resting her cheek, wordless, just as if foolish.
Day and night solely worried about the pain of childbirth,
idly distressed, tears falling in pairs.
Carrying (the burden) for ten months is truly pitiable;
the thousand kinds of bitterness and distress are unbearable.
Reciting Buddha's name and praying to gods, hoping for rescue and protection;
burning incense and making vows, begging for freedom from disaster.
Solely worried about murderous ghosts chasing and seizing,
fearing being urged by impermanence in a single thought.
The scripture says: when the mother approaches the month of childbirth,
she suffers immeasurable bitterness and distress. Now sing it forth.
Scripture: When the month is full and birth comes,
she suffers all kinds of pain,
in a moment, good or bad,
only fearing impermanence,
like slaughtering pigs and sheep,
blood flows and splashes on the ground.
This sings the scripture text,
clarifying the appearance of childbirth.
Before the child descends,
the mother worries her life may be lost in an instant;
and when it is born,
blood flows and splashes on the ground.
The whole household, young and old,
each busily anxious,
only fearing life and body may go awry,
quickly watching for signs of good or ill.
(Scripture) "
(When the month is full and birth comes),
(she suffers all kinds of pain)"
(to the end).
When the month is full and birth first comes,
the compassionate mother feels fear and terror.
Only fearing life may be impermanent,
crimson blood pours and splashes.
Bitterness and distress cannot be spoken;
all matters come to an end.
If care and preservation go against harmony,
then the body goes awry.
At birth, a hundred bones naturally open wide,
frightening the whole household into busy hands and feet.
Before the child descends, the compassionate mother is afraid;
and when born, it is like slaughtering sheep.
A thousand worries and ten thousand anxieties can still be endured;
but the ten months and three years of suffering are even longer.
Since this body has grown up,
one must greatly be filial to father and mother.
Therefore, the books say: Zēngzǐ said: "Of all conducts,
none surpasses filial piety.
Filial piety
is the constant principle of heaven, the righteousness of earth.
Filial piety moves heaven and earth,
and penetrates to the spirits.
When filial piety reaches heaven,
then wind and rain follow order;
when filial piety reaches earth,
then the hundred grains ripen;
when filial piety reaches people,
then distant interpreters come to pay tribute;
when filial piety reaches spirits,
then dark spirits aid and protect."
(Also) "The
(Tàigōng Family Teachings)": "A filial son serves his parents,
inquiring in the morning and attending in the evening,
knowing their hunger and thirst,
knowing their warmth and cold.
In worry, he shares their sorrow;
in joy, he shares their happiness.
When parents are ill,
he does not eat sweet delicacies.
He does not seek satiety in food,
nor comfort in dwelling,
hearing music, he does not enjoy it,
seeing plays, he does not watch.
He does not adorn his body,
nor tidy his clothes and cap,
waiting until the illness is cured,
then tidying is not difficult."
Also, the scripture says: "Of all that is great between heaven and earth, in the world,
none surpass the kindness of parents."
Within the scriptures and books,
all speak of the kindness of parents.
I urge you disciples,
you must greatly practice filial piety.
Scriptures and books each have many principles,
all urging disciples to practice filial piety and righteousness.
Only fearing procrastination and not repaying kindness,
therefore in the scriptures it is clearly proclaimed.
Urging disciples,
all you disciples,
attend diligently morning and evening, serving diligently.
Forever let your good name be spread,
and never encounter calamity and trouble.
Reflecting on the body born within ten months,
the five kinds of form and appearance mutually shift and change.
Looking closely, it is not only worthy of sorrow and sighing;
speaking gently, one must know the hundred kinds of suffering.
When the grass falls, wind touches the body;
sharp cries and screams cannot form words.
Blood flows and splashes on the ground like slaughter;
the mother's life may be lost in an instant, ending a hundred years.
Now that you have grown up to be a child,
in all matters strive to be complete in ten aspects.
I urge you, in all matters you must practice filial piety,
do not regard kindness and virtue as idle.
The virtue of a compassionate mother,
truly pitiable,
for ten months and three years she suffers disasters.
Braving heat and rushing cold, toiling her strength,
turning dry to wet, exhausting her heart and mind.
Worrying and caring not less than a thousand times,
nurturing and rearing, how can one count ten thousand times?
Since there are so many deeds of kindness and virtue,
how can one bear to neglect them? Now sing it forth.
Scripture: Suffering such bitterness,
she gives birth to this body of mine.
Swallowing bitterness, spitting sweetness,
holding and nurturing, rearing and raising.
Washing away uncleanness,
not shunning toil and labor.
Enduring heat and bearing cold,
not refusing hardship and toil.
The child lies in the dry place,
the mother sleeps in the wet place.
Within three years,
drinking the mother's white blood.
This sings the scripture text,
divided into two parts.
First explaining diligent protection,
next explaining turning dry to wet.
The two sections are different;
now first is diligent protection.
