The scripture says, "Such hardship and toil,
gives birth to this body of mine,"
(to) "
(not refusing hardship and toil)."
This is the World-Honored One's admonition to Ānanda: In this Sahā defiled world,
all living beings
are all born from parents,
swallowing bitterness, spitting sweetness,
diligently protecting with whole heart,
holding and nurturing, rearing and raising,
never leaving the bosom.
When washing and cleansing,
how can one refuse cold and heat?
If the family elder is above,
uncles and aunts are difficult in nature.
Day and night not shunning toil and labor,
morning and evening constantly harboring worry and fear.
Braving cold and enduring heat,
is indeed ordinary;
raising sons and daughters,
not refusing hardship and toil.
Face and appearance haggard,
form and appearance frail and weak.
How can one bear, once grown up,
not to repay and answer?
(And so on.)
If it is the severe sky and moon,
bitterness and distress are hard to express.
Hands chilled to the bone, aching to the heart,
ten fingers cracked from tip to base.
On one side, feeding the child,
serving and attending at all hours.
Uncles, aunts, and in-laws,
still find her foolish and clumsy.
Often her tears fall like rain,
constantly her heart feels as if cut.
No place to speak her sincere heart,
how can such bitterness be endured?
All for the sake of the small infant,
washing and cleaning without rest.
Deep into the night, still not asleep,
stumbling and falling, body frail and weak.
Among these hardships, the mother suffers most,
lifting and caring for the child, never tiring of the frequency.
Washing and rinsing, undaunted by cold or heat,
holding and carrying, untiring through hardship and toil.
Constantly blamed by in-laws,
often scolded by uncles and aunts.
All because bound by this infant,
causing her days and nights to expend heart and spirit.
Therefore, the scripture says: "Enduring such suffering,
swallowing bitterness, spitting out sweetness,
holding, carrying, nurturing, and raising"
(and so on) up to "not shunning hardship and toil."
The above describes the first diligence in protection.
Second,
exchanging the dry for the wet.
The scripture states: "The child lies in the dry spot,
the mother sleeps in the wet spot,
for three years,
drinking the mother's white blood."
If it were the nine summers of washing,
it might seem not so difficult,
but it is the three winters
that are exceptionally hard.
If there are servants to command,
one can still manage diligently,
but if there are none,
one must do everything oneself.
The in-laws, uncles, and aunts in the main hall,
must be served daily.
Holding the foolish, naive little child,
and again each morning lifting and caring for it,
on one hand washing away filth,
on the other feeding the boys and girls.
The mother sleeps in the wet spot,
the child lies in the dry spot.
Within ten months,
enduring boundless hardships;
within three years,
drinking immeasurable amounts of blood and milk.
Causing the mother's form and appearance,
to grow frail and weak each day;
the loving mother's face and countenance,
to become thin and haggard each morning.
Exchanging dry for wet is a constant task,
three years of diligent toil, feelings unceasing.
Hardship each morning brings falling tears,
煎熬 each night brings no sleep.
Appearance frail and weak,
form thin and haggard,
phoenix mirrors and hairpins all cast aside.
Often before others she seems like a fool,
constantly within her seat as if drunk.
Only because for so long,
driven and toiling hard,
her form, appearance, spirit, and energy,
have all become disordered.
On one hand attending to in-laws,
on the other binding and caring for children.
Day and night never idle,
often weeping like rain.
Exchanging dry for wet is most arduous,
all day driven and toiling, never resting.
Washing and rinsing regardless of morning or evening,
driving and toiling, undaunted by heat or cold.
Always giving the dry and warm place for the child to lie,
the wet spot the mother routinely sleeps in herself.
Three long years passing always like this,
how can one be at peace without repaying such deep kindness?
Therefore, the scripture says,
the child lies in the dry spot,
the mother sleeps in the wet spot.
Within three years,
drinking the mother's white blood.
From the moment the child is born,
until three years old,
drinks the white milk from the mother's breast.
Gradually leaving the mother's embrace,
becoming a child,
yet still tied to the mother's heart,
with a hundred kinds of worry and concern.
By rivers and wells,
constant fear of drowning;
playing with dogs or knives,
always anxious about bites and injuries.
(and so on)
The child gradually grows into a youth,
the loving mother's worried heart never leaves him.
Near fire, especially fearing red flames burning;
by rivers, fearing falling into clear waves to die.
Chasing butterflies,
following puppies,
playing with dirt and mud in the streets.
Because being spoiled and naive is just the age,
precisely due to foolish youth that they are like this.
Gradually leaving the embrace to become a toddler,
crawling, then first walking beside the steps.
Speech like a delicate oriole first trilling its tongue,
laughter like spring trees and wild flowers blooming.
The whole family's loving care knows no bounds,
relatives' doting affection cannot be measured.
Outside the door, suddenly hearing crying,
the loving mother rushes over early.
The infant gradually grows into a child,
both cheeks like peach blossoms, color radiant.
In fives they follow, riding bamboo horses,
in threes they gather, chasing puppies.
Greedily chasing butterflies, leaving home far behind,
fishing for green moss, forgetting to return.
The loving mother stretches her neck, searching a thousand times,
heart constantly fearing he might be bullied.
Thus we know the loving mother cherishes her infant child,
怜念交招 (怜念 and teaching) occupy her thoughts.
Sun and moon shift, years gradually lengthen,
scholars, farmers, artisans, each find their place.
On one hand instructing and teaching benevolence and righteousness,
on the other seeking marriage, entrusting matchmakers.
The Buddha in the scriptures speaks of this,
following the text, please chant what comes next.
Scripture: Infants and children,
even until their prime years,
are encouraged and taught etiquette and rituals,
marriage, official service, and learning.
For seeking property and wealth,
carrying burdens and hardships,
diligent and toiling to the end,
never speaking of kindness and virtue.
This chanted scripture text,
divides into two parts.
First clarifying growth and teaching,
later saying the mother does not speak of kindness.
Growth and teaching is further divided into two,
first clarifying encouraging and teaching etiquette,
later speaking of marriage, official service, and learning.
Growth and teaching.
The scripture states: "Infants and children,
even until their prime years,
are encouraged and taught etiquette and rituals."
People's sons and daughters,
from small to large,
must be taught etiquette and rituals.
If a boy, from seven or ten years old onward,
he is then sent to school.
(The scripture clarifies it is appropriate)
(to enter school),
(the noble youth must exert effort).
The *Analects* says: "To till the land,
hunger lies therein.
To learn..."
(and so on).
The *Qǔlǐ* says: "If the gentleman wishes to transform the people and perfect customs,
he must certainly proceed through this."
Also, the *Shū* says: "Jade not carved..."
(and so on),
"achievement high comes from utmost..."
(and so on),
there are good sons and daughters,
there are weak sons and daughters.
People's [sons] and daughters are also like this.
(and so on)
Sons and daughters gradually grow into adults,
one by one, father and mother personally instruct and teach.
Lifting and caring, still hoping they establish themselves,
招交 (teaching and instructing) only wishing they cultivate benevolence and righteousness.
Entrusting the teacher,
teaching writing and literature,
filial piety, nurturing, etiquette, and rituals must all be完备.
Before even one or two years of teaching,
casually they read through all the books and histories.
High and low all say they are fine young men,
far and near all speak of their exceptional bone and spirit.
Grown up, their bodies become great men,
refined and elegant, true gentlemen.
Stately six-foot-tall men's bodies,
snow-white robes befitting a jǔrén.
The heavens will surely bestow dew and rain,
passing the highest exams, rising above the dusty world.
Most likely soon encountering new joy,
no different than a dragon shedding its old scales.
Wine ripe, flowers bloom in the third month,
only knowing to arrange and play at the Qǔjiāng spring.
The above discusses the encouragement and teaching of rituals and propriety.
Therefore, the scripture says: "Infants and children,
even up to their prime years,
should be encouraged and taught rituals and propriety.
" What are marriage and official studies?
Marriage is one matter,
official studies are another.
Official studies refer to serving as an official,
while studies refer to scholarly pursuits
(and so on).
Now, speaking of marriage.
The Book says: When a man reaches maturity, he should have a household;
when a woman reaches the age of hairpin, she should follow a man.
Once a man has grown up,
he must seek a marriage partner
(and so on).
(If they are good men and women, and so on).
There is a type of family with sons
who do not practice filial piety,
and do not understand rituals and propriety
(and so on).
Even when it comes to marriage
(and so on),
there is a type of disciple or student
whose conduct is perverse and distant.
They do not cultivate benevolence, righteousness, and the five constants;
they do not care for warmth, kindness, respect, and frugality.
Sometimes they forget to clasp their hands in respect;
their blessings feel as if from a past life.
At the fasting ground, they thank the seat early and follow along;
sometimes they laugh inappropriately during mourning.
How many times has your mother arranged marriages for you?
Speaking of it, no one wants to hear.
Just as they begin to arrange for official service,
they are casually scolded by their superiors.
Otherwise, if they engage in the family business,
the value lies in establishing themselves.
If their property and estates are all depleted,
how can lazy and gluttonous wastrels become proper adults?
The above explains that once a man has grown up,
he must be married.
From then on, a girl is taught and raised from a young age,
and must be entrusted to another family in marriage.
For a woman,
it is even more difficult;
first and foremost, she must be taught needlework.
Competing with thread and needle, her intentions grow;
facing crows and phoenixes, she boasts of her skill and wisdom.
Learning music,
bending to the master,
plucking and tuning strings brings joy to the whole household.
When grown, she is chosen in due time to be married off,
and all relatives and clans rejoice.
Born with exceptional intelligence, unlike ordinary people,
she seems like a cloud descending from Wūshān.
Her hair is like a cicada's wings spread in the cold;
her face is like the full autumn moon.
Her eyebrows hang like willow leaves, green as mist;
her cheeks outshine peach blossoms, fresh with rain.
Married into another family, she brings honor to the nine clans;
such a joyous occasion is hard to describe.
If a person is of little intelligence,
from childhood to adulthood, they are exceptionally foolish.
They do not understand goodness when meeting people;
they have never known rituals and propriety in conversation.
They have no intention of learning embroidery or tailoring;
they have never mixed cosmetics or prepared flour.
Even sewing their own clothes, they find themselves clumsy;
which family would be willing to take them?
A mother's heart,
full of love and compassion,
protects and cherishes all equally.
For a daughter, she seeks a marriage arrangement;
for a son, she arranges a wedding to bring joy.
A man must be literate and possess benevolence and righteousness;
a woman must know tailoring and music.
Only after each one is properly established
can the mother finally rest from her worries.
The above is all the first part,
clarifying the teaching and guidance for growth.
From here, the second part:
the mother does not speak of her kindness.
The scripture says: "Toil and hardship to the end,
without speaking of kindness and virtue."
The meaning of this scripture is simply to say that a loving mother carries the child for ten months,
nurses for three years,
shifts from dry to wet,
swallows bitterness and spits sweetness.
Even when the children grow up,
she shows a thousand kinds of affection,
and ten thousand types of instruction.
Marrying off daughters and arranging marriages for sons,
she ensures everything is complete.
Enduring such hardships,
she never speaks of the kindness of raising them
in front of anyone
(and so on).
It is like the World-Honored One's compassion for all sentient beings in the Dharma realm:
those that fly,
those that walk,
those without feet,
those with two feet,
those with four feet,
those with many feet,
the three wretched paths and six destinies,
the five realms and four modes of birth,
in heaven or among humans,
whether noble or lowly,
high or low,
monastic disciples, nuns,
virtuous women and men,
each one is guided to escape the source of suffering,
and everyone ascends to eternal bliss.
Our Buddha does not intentionally speak of any kindness or virtue,
nor of any hardship,
just as a loving mother in a household
raises all sentient beings, sons and daughters,
without speaking of kindness or virtue—there is no difference.
Through Shìjiā's holy compassion,
all sentient beings are cherished.
Each is guided to attain Nirvāṇa,
without any intention to speak of kindness or virtue.
A mother's heart,
without distinction of favor or opposition,
protects and cherishes all sons and daughters.
Each is taught to establish themselves,
without any intention to speak of kindness or virtue.
The Buddha cherishes sentient beings;
the mother cherishes her children.
Both bestow affection equally,
loving and protecting from the beginning.
The Buddha's heart is no different from a mother's;
a mother's heart can be compared to the Buddha's.
Today, those seated here
must clearly understand this.
Shìjiā, honored in the three thousand lands,
cherishes sentient beings beyond description.
Everywhere, he guides them to liberation;
at every turn, he leads them across the sea of delusion.
He does not favor the foolish or the wise;
he does not treat enemies and loved ones differently.
Each one is guided to become a Buddha,
yet he never intentionally speaks of his kindness.
A mother's virtue,
hard to fully describe,
nurtures the bodies of disciples and students.
Ten months of pregnancy bring suffering;
three years of nursing endure hardships.
She does not grow weary of her daughters;
she does not show partiality to her sons.
Each one is taught and protected with care,
yet she never intentionally speaks of her kindness.
A mother's virtue,
hard to measure,
cannot be matched by ten thousand discourses or a thousand scriptures.
Yet sons and daughters often act against filial piety,
casually running away without returning.
Relatives worry day after day;
the mother's heart is shattered morning after morning.
When the son travels ten thousand miles afar,
the mother's heart follows him—now let it be sung.
Scripture: When the son travels a thousand miles,
the mother travels a thousand miles;
when the son travels ten thousand miles,
the mother travels ten thousand miles.
When sons and daughters fall ill,
parents also fall ill;
when the child recovers from illness,
the parents' illness subsides.
This recitation of scripture
is divided into two parts: first,
the mother's heart never forgets;
second,
the child's illness brings worry;
the two sections are different.
Now, speaking of the mother's heart never forgetting.
The scripture says: "When the son travels a thousand miles,
the mother travels a thousand miles"
(and so on).
After sons and daughters have grown up,
each must engage in official duties or business.
As soon as they leave for another region,
the mother's heart follows.
Guarding the northern frontier,
for three years (three years), her gaze is fixed on the Great Wall;
traveling to Jiànlǐng for trade,
for half a year, her soul follows the Jǐnshuǐ River.
(The Book says):
(One must not be unaware of one's parents' age).
Reflecting on our birth mothers,
who worry and cherish sons and daughters all day long.
When the son goes out to distant places,
the mother weeps with sorrow and no joy.
Whether serving as an official,
holding a position,
separated from parents for years,
seeing the four seasons and eight festivals pass without return,
the mother weeps with sorrow and no joy.
Some pursue trade and business,
Chasing profit as they depart,
Some dwell in other lands or travel the roads.
Though sons may find peace abroad,
Mothers weep with sorrow, their spirits low.
Some serve in the capital,
Assigned to garrison duty,
Guarding the borders for three years, enduring hardship.
News is scarce, the roads are long,
Mothers weep with sorrow, their spirits low.
While the son is far away, the mother suffers first,
Worrying all day, tears falling like rain.
Chanting Buddha’s name, praying to gods, doing all they can,
Hoping only for hidden protection and care.
Their appearance withers,
Their hearts are torn,
Begging for their child’s return to reunite.
Reflecting on the kindness of a loving mother,
How can disciples bear to betray her?
Seeking office and staying in other lands,
Or serving in the army, stationed afar.
Though the son may be safe and well in another province,
The mother at home is constantly anxious.
Her heart follows him a thousand miles, her face grows thin,
Her sorrow lasts three years, her intestines break with weeping.
Only when he returns and they meet again
Does the mother finally regain her spirit.
A mother’s virtue,
Is hard to repay,
The heart’s remembrance never ceases.
I urge all disciples and followers,
Do not abandon your parents to dwell in other provinces.
This is the first,
The mother’s heart never forgets.
Second,
When a child falls ill, the mother worries.
The scripture says: “When sons and daughters are ill,
Parents also fall ill;
Only when the child recovers
Do the parents begin to heal.”
In families, sons and daughters
Are cherished and pitied by parents.
If they suddenly lose care,
And their bodies are afflicted with illness,
It makes the father’s heart ache,
The mother’s mind panic.
They forgo sleep and skip meals,
Neglecting their own lives.
Preparing soups and cooking porridge,
They do not shirk the toil of day and night;
Praying to ghosts, consulting oracles,
They fear no weariness from coming and going.
If the child shows slight improvement,
The parents’ worries instantly ease.
In families, parents’ kindness is especially deep,
For sons and daughters, their love is doubled.
Daily they instruct without wavering,
Morning and evening they protect without retreat.
If suddenly the child is afflicted by illness,
Parents fret and worry, their hearts shattered.
Chanting Buddha’s name, praying to gods for protection,
Seeking doctors, divining, hoping for recovery.
No sleep,
No radiance,
Their minds fried, their appearances altered.
Only when the child’s body is fully well
Does the mother finally feel at ease.
When sons or daughters fall ill, the mother worries,
Before they recover, she must shed tears of blood.
Meals and tea are not taken in order,
She stops applying rouge, neglects to comb her hair.
Seeking doctors and divining without rest,
Praying to ghosts and gods without cease.
Only when the child is safe and healthy
Does the mother finally cease to worry.
Reflecting on human affairs, hard to judge,
Parents’ kindness runs deep, impossible to match.
As soon as they see their child afflicted,
They fear life may end in the grave.
On one hand, they seek medicine and medical care,
On the other, they invite monks to dispel disaster.
Once the illness is over, one should practice filial piety,
Yet some commit the five rebellious acts—this is what will be proclaimed.
Scripture: Raised in this way,
Hoping they would soon grow up,
But when they reach adulthood,
They turn to unfilial behavior.
Speaking with respected parents,
They respond with defiance.
Glaring with angry eyes,
They know neither gratitude nor righteousness.
This recitation of scripture is divided into two parts: one, not remembering deep virtue;
Two, betraying kindness and defying affection.
Two sections
(And so on).
Not remembering deep virtue.
The scripture says: “Raised in this way,
Hoping they would soon grow up,
But when they reach adulthood,
They turn to unfilial behavior.”
The earlier scripture speaks of parents’ various ways of nurturing,
Through countless hardships,
Fearing neither cold nor heat,
Begging for the child to grow up,
And to carry on the family lineage.
But when they reach adulthood,
They lack filial hearts,
Do not repay kindness,
Idle away their days,
And even turn against their parents.
(And so on)
In families, parents show much kindness and nurture,
Worrying endlessly for their children.
Begging for them to grow up and become adults,
To continue the family tradition and bring honor and rank.
Who would have thought that as they gradually learn right from wrong,
They often insult and disgrace their parents?
The Buddha says such people in this world,
Upon death, will surely fall into the Avīci Hell.
Those who are unfilial betray Heaven,
Treating their parents lightly as if they were nothing.
Not a bit of service offered all day long,
But a thousand ways of defiance and idleness daily.
Casually shouting loudly indoors,
Rashly speaking nonsense before others.
The Buddha says when such people’s lives end,
They will sink into evil paths, with no year of escape.
Therefore, the scripture says: “Raised in this way,
Hoping they would soon grow up,
But when they reach adulthood,
They turn to unfilial behavior.”
Above is the first part,
Speaking of not remembering deep virtue.
From here, the second part,
Betraying kindness and defying affection.
The scripture says: “Speaking with respected parents,
They respond with defiance,
Glaring with angry eyes,
They know neither gratitude nor righteousness.”
These are all people who betray kindness and virtue,
The five rebellious ones.
They do not reflect on the deep kindness of nurturing,
Do not remember the great virtue of toil.
Raised since childhood by their mother,
Taught as they grew by their strict father,
Who would have thought that as they near adulthood,
They learn to abandon and betray kindness?
Daily they follow evil companions,
All day they avoid good people.
Often with hands not folded in respect,
Frequently speaking three words of disrespect.
When parents call to discipline them,
They pout and remain silent, growing angry.
Sometimes glaring with angry eyes,
Or answering back loudly.
(And so on)
Those who do not understand gratitude,
Turn against their parents, committing the five rebellious acts.
Speaking loudly in response to others,
Preparing to glare angrily as if to devour.
Accompanying evil people,
Engaging in evil deeds,
Drinking and gambling, hard to admonish.
Always causing loving parents to shed tears of blood,
Often making family members grieve with sorrow.
Śākyamuni, the Honored One,
Left teachings and commandments,
Look at the scripture and examine it carefully.
If one persists in the five rebellious acts,
This body will be hard to find in any scheme.
How can people not reflect carefully,
How can they turn their hearts against their parents?
Answering back loudly may still be forgiven,
But glaring with angry eyes is even more hurtful.
Not thinking of the ten months of pregnancy’s hardship,
Not remembering the three years of busy nursing.
The Buddha says such five rebellious people
Have no chance to see the Dharma Wheel King.
I urge disciples
(And so on),
The crow returns to feed its mother—such is repayment.
(How can people… and so on)
Fortunately, through expounding the words of the Buddhas,
I urge disciples to be filial to their parents.
Even birds and beasts know the kindness of nurturing,
How can people bear to betray it?
Ten months of pregnancy,
Three years of nursing.
Speaking of hardships, there are many;
Telling of kindness and pity, countless times.
Now that they are adults,
They must still repay,
Do not learn from fools,
Who turn to commit rebellious harm.
When disciplined, listen attentively;
When scolded, do not answer back.
Why seek the Western Paradise?
Create your own Land of Ultimate Bliss.
Where is a person’s cleverness shown?
Better than repaying the kindness of nurturing.
Not only will there be long-lasting auspicious celebrations,
But also, weapons of war will never be seen again.
All actions will be harmonious and in accord,
And whatever is undertaken will mostly succeed.
When life ends, one leaves forever this turbid, evil world,
To be reborn within a lotus blossom.
One must heed this exhortation,
And harbor no doubts or suspicions.
Having heard it, one must still change one's disposition.
Do not emulate the foolish who stubbornly resist,
Who fail to practice filial piety and nurture, indulging their contrary nature.
When instructed, they wildly utter a thousand kinds of words;
When restrained, they early on scowl with brows furrowed and cheeks puffed.
Even if they are family and kin,
They still endure curses and insults, which will be sung forth.
The scripture says: Bullying uncles,
Beating and cursing brothers,
Defaming and insulting elders and parents,
Having no sense of propriety or righteousness,
Not obeying teachers and elders.
Exhorting the Common People, Sixth
Written on the seventh day of the eighth month, the second year of Tiānchéng
Yet, alas, they are unfilial at home.
Everywhere they revere and esteem wicked people.
They do not understand the sins and blessings of the human world.
□□□□□ and others,
These are the lowest of the low.
□□□□□ on the thoroughfares,
They clash with the virtuous and good.
□□□□□□ topple,
Moreover, they must endure suffering for a hundred lifetimes.
□□□□□□ share,
When meeting people, how could they understand to practice courtesy and deference?
When urged to manage affairs, they puff out their cheeks.
□□□□□□ feelings,
They leave home with companions, roaming the streets and alleys.
In threes and fives, they idly go,
For ten days or more they vanish, unwilling to return.
The loving mother's heart is filled only with worry,
Fearing her child might fall into wickedness.
If wicked people implicate them in crimes and punishments,
By then, no one will be able to save them.
Leaning by the door, she only hopes for their return,
Countless people pass by, but none of them are seen.
Her silken sleeves are stained with fresh tear drops,
Her heart wholly fixed on the child outside.
People store grain originally to guard against famine,
Raising children is also for the purpose of support in old age.
Who could have foreseen that upon growing up, they would all be unfilial?
Even if there were ten of them, what would be the use?
Beginning from infancy in the embrace,
Growing up to become a person of six-foot stature.
They abandon virtue, turn their backs on kindness, often committing the Five Rebellious Acts,
Only acting unfilially, indulging in foolishness.
Three years of nursing is still a trivial matter,
But ten months of pregnancy is truly pitiable.
Often seeing the two parents treated with disrespect and contempt,
They show no reverence, which will be sung forth.
The scripture says: Showing no reverence,
Abandoning virtue and turning their backs on kindness,
Having no benevolence or compassion,
Being unfilial and lacking ritual propriety.
Ninety-one kalpas in the past,
There was a sinful person who was unfilial to his parents,
Constantly committing the Five Rebellious Acts.
After death, he fell into the Great Pit Hell,
With an iron wheel spinning on his head,
Never leaving the top of his head.
Precisely because his sinful roots were deep and heavy,
All due to being unfilial to his two parents.
From then on, he was cast into the pit,
Constantly having an iron wheel on his head.
Passing through thousands, tens of thousands of kalpas,
He does not know when he will regain a human body.
Once falling into this place for millions of kalpas,
Day and night he constantly suffers hardship.
Because of unfiliality, he fell into the deep pit,
Suffering without cause to pause even briefly.
Day and night an iron wheel rests on his head,
Already passing through hundreds of kalpas and thousands of lives.
I urge you to practice filial piety without delay;
Carefully consider this body of yours.
She endured bitterness and gave you sweetness, raising you up;
Do not let her down,辜负 your mother's kindness.
Serve and obey to set her heart at ease;
Parents will always be happy seeing this.
Filial conduct will forever be recorded in the classics and histories,
Truly causing it to be widely transmitted for ten thousand generations.
Carrying the pregnancy for ten months brings a thousand kinds of suffering;
Rising, sitting, body and mind find no peace morning or night.
The Chief Lecturer and the Ācārya, exert your strength,
As if lifting a heavy burden, sing and look.
The scripture says: When a mother carries a child,
For ten months it is arduous and difficult.
Rising and sitting bring no peace,
As if lifting a heavy burden;
Eating and drinking are unpalatable,
Like a person with a chronic illness.
For ten months carrying the disciple's body,
Day and night it is exactly like holding a heavy burden.
Her emerald brows and peach-blossom face secretly change,
A waxy, sallow pallor comes stealthily.
Walking, she is sorrowful;
Sitting, she is sorrowful;
Carrying the pregnancy for ten months seems like a thousand autumns.
Dazed, not drunk, yet constantly as if drunk;
Listless, without worries, yet exactly as if worried.
Pleasant pipes and strings become grating to the ear;
Bashful, yet here she cannot feel shame.
She must only hope for a safe delivery,
The loving mother's heart at peace only when it is completely over.
For ten months carrying the disciple,
Day and night, body and mind find no peace.
Her appearance daily grows more frail and weak,
Gradually turning more haggard.
Several times relatives kindly urge her to come,
But she has no mind to go along.
Even if guests are entertained at home,
She is truly unwilling to join in the merry laughter.
Her dragon-like hair goes uncombed for months on end;
Her phoenix hairpins go unworn for weeks.
The dressing table is dirty before her eyes;
The phoenix mirror is left to gather dust.
Because of the child in her own pregnant belly,
She does not wish to do her former dressing and grooming.
Reflecting on the ten months of nurturing you so much,
How can one bear to delay and not repay this kindness?
The mother grows thin, her flower-like appearance
Changes, becoming sallow, with many ailments.
Her cloud-like hair goes uncombed for several months;
Her phoenix hairpins are cast aside as a trivial matter.
She does not follow her young sister-in-law to go among the flowers,
Nor lazily accompany her elder sister-in-law chasing the little dog.
Several times relatives urge her to go see the flowers;
Countless times playing the hidden hook game, enjoying laughter at night.
This body, without illness, is like having a chronic illness;
Propping her cheek all day, again and again frowning.
All kinds of delicious flavors hold no appeal;
Even these precious delicacies she does not taste or sip.
Even if she eats something sweet, it tastes like yellow cork-tree bark;
Her mouth bitter, tongue dry, she does not wish to eat.
When the ten months of pregnancy are about to conclude,
The sounds of bitter pain are unbearable to hear.
A thousand times reciting the Buddha's name, seeking added protection;
Ten thousand times burning incense, requesting the World-Honored One.
Approaching the tenth month, fearing bodily disaster,
Only fearing impermanence might hasten her in a single thought.
Over there, the sounds of worshipping the Buddha are clear and bright;
Over here, the golden sutras are opened in sequence.
Together they slaughter pigs and sheep, no different from that,
Blood flowing everywhere, which will be sung forth.
The scripture says: When the full month arrives and birth occurs,
She undergoes all kinds of bitter pain.
In a moment, good or bad,
She only fears impermanence.
Like slaughtering pigs and sheep,
Blood flowing everywhere,
She undergoes such suffering.
I earnestly advise the disciples seated here:
You must greatly practice filial piety and nurture your two parents.
In the morning, inquire after their well-being and daily routine,
And do not lose respectful demeanor.
If parents suddenly give instructions,
Do not immediately answer back to your two parents.
Going out and coming in at sunset with caution and reverence—
This is what makes a filial son.
Weeping by the bamboo or lying on ice cannot compare;
A hundred years of serving and nurturing, do not let it fall short.
For ten long months in the mother's womb,
Begging for a safe delivery to give birth to the infant.
For three days there is joy over a safe delivery;
At the full month, monks are invited to avert disasters.
Neighbors vie to look, never getting their fill;
Relatives gaze with lingering thoughts.
From then on, the mother's love knows no end;
Spitting out sweetness to feed you, which will be sung forth.
The scripture says: Having given birth to this body,
She endures bitterness and gives you sweetness.
Washing what is unclean,
She does not shirk toil and labor.
Enduring heat, enduring cold,
She does not refuse hardship.
The dry place is for the child to lie;
The wet place is for the mother to sleep.
Within three years,
The child drinks the mother's white blood.
Not shirking to spit out sweetness and endure bitterness,
Washing and rinsing are simply ordinary.
Sometimes enduring heat, sometimes enduring cold,
The loving mother does not refuse hardship.
How can one bear, after this body has grown up,
To act wantonly unfilially, forgetting the deep kindness?
Sweet, delicious flavors are given to the child to eat;
The bitter and astringent ones the mother eats herself.
Enduring heat, enduring cold, how could she think of weariness?
Holding and carrying, rising and sitting, she forgets the bitter toil.
Shifting from damp to dry is commonplace,
Three years of nursing, not done in haste.
Who would have thought, grown up, all turn unfilial,
Forgetting the nurturing grace of days past.
Gradually leaving the embrace,
Becoming a child,
Always tied to the mother’s heart,
A hundred kinds of worry and care.
(section missing)
The Western Paradise is good,
Hard to fully describe,
Truly splendid, beyond what we’ve heard.
Suddenly, where will this body be born?
For millennia, never to sink into oblivion.
This turbid world is weak,
No need to discuss,
The eight sufferings and three calamities—how can one bear to hear?
Not a bit of good deeds have been done,
Yet hoping for a thousand springs without following the right path.
Mountains of knives gleam under the sun,
Forests of swords pierce the clouds,
Where is there ever peace and joy?
The fires of karma burn the body.
They speak of ten kalpas, five kalpas,
Never a moment of ease or happiness.
How can it compare to the Pure Land,
With bodhisattvas as neighbors?
Leisurely playing in the waters of the Eight Virtues Pond,
When bored, strolling under the sevenfold trees in spring.
Sometimes ascending the precious halls,
Sometimes paying homage to the sutras.
Sometimes driving peacocks,
Sometimes with Kalaviṅka birds on the arm.
Sometimes rising on auspicious clouds,
Sometimes departing into propitious mists.
Sometimes at dawn ascending the precious halls,
Sometimes at night paying respects to the Compassionate One.
Constantly hearing the wondrous Dharma,
Ever flowing through the ears.
There, forever transcending life and death,
Thus gradually attaining Buddhahood.
As evening falls, one must return,
To the old lady’s house, where dry anger awaits.
Consider, a human life lasts but a generation,
Like a drifting tumbleweed.
Noble and lowly may differ,
But impermanence treats all alike.
From emperors above,
To commoners below,
Wealth and status may vary in rank,
But impermanence comes for all the same.
Thus the *Sutra on Impermanence* says:
“(Rebirth in the highest heaven of non-perception)”
(etc.)
The Three Sovereigns of antiquity,
The Four White-Haired Elders,
Pān Yuè’s beauty, Péng Zǔ’s youth—
Thinking rosy cheeks would last a lifetime,
Yet still driven by white hair to age.
King Wénxuān,
Teaching the five constants,
Boasting of elegant writings and ornate phrases,
Thinking his house would endure long,
Yet still driven by white hair to age.
Speak of Xī Shī,
Dá Jǐ’s looks,
In their day, praised for rosy cheeks and grace,
Only their names remain in the world,
Yet still driven by white hair to age.
Be they monks,
Or Daoist priests,
Holding pure lotus seats, upholding the Buddha’s teachings,
Thinking to escape impermanence,
Yet still driven by white hair to age.
Some engage in trade,
Some in skilled crafts,
Competing in novel designs, displaying exquisite work,
Even if rich as Shí Chóng,
Yet still driven by white hair to age.
Keeping vegetarian fasts,
Truly profound and wondrous,
Listen to the sutras, the Mahayana teachings,
Do not linger drunk and dazed in this turbid world,
In a moment, impermanence arrives.
All must heed the teachings given here,
Reflect, for it benefits oneself,
Do not cling foolishly to the pleasures of the physical body,
In a moment, impermanence arrives.
Great men,
Consider carefully,
Why rush to commit the ten evils?
Seventy years of life are already rare,
Why make plans for a thousand more?
Forcibly listen to sutras,
Take these words to heart,
This illusory body has no true master,
Even if you greedily cling to form and body,
When the limit comes, impermanence will take them.
The Wheel-Turning King,
Lord of the four continents,
Ruling over all directions, nurturing the masses,
No one surpasses the king’s wealth and honor,
Yet when the limit comes, impermanence takes him too.
Shùtíjiā,
Shí Chóng’s riches,
Their names passed down through ages to this day,
Consider glory and wealth but a brief moment,
When the limit comes, impermanence takes them too.
Speak of Héng’é,
Talk of Luòpǔ,
Beauties hard to match in the human world,
Dignified and poised, seeming to last centuries,
Yet when the limit comes, impermanence takes them too.
Great men,
Truly gallant and dashing,
Wanting to strut and cast shadows, eagerly looking back,
Youth, do not further flaunt your cleverness,
When the limit comes, impermanence takes you too.
Be they monks,
Dwelling in temples,
Ancient in appearance, slow like dragons and tigers,
Peaceful abodes in clear skies, fine places to settle,
Yet when the limit comes, impermanence takes them too.
Some enter the Dao,
Seeking immortal companions,
Refining elixirs for longevity, boiling in furnaces,
Even if you have many formulas to preserve youth,
When the limit comes, impermanence takes you too.
Regardless of noble or lowly, high or low,
Be they monks, nuns, or Daoist companions,
Except for the One, Móuní,
All the rest are taken by impermanence.
Having spoken long,
With words well-founded,
The sun slants, unable to stay,
Chant the Buddha’s name loudly and must return,
Only go to the steps to receive the gāthā.
Not cultivating practice,
Not understanding sutras’ meaning,
Chasing after sights, indulging in sounds, lost and drunk,
A human life passes in a blink,
Not cultivating is truly foolish intent.
Whether poor,
Or rich,
First, mind and body must benefit oneself,
When impermanence suddenly comes, life ends,
Not cultivating is truly foolish intent.
Having wealth,
Not giving alms,
Instead planning to hoard for oneself,
Suddenly hands are torn apart to both sides,
Not cultivating is truly foolish intent.
Greatly covering the head,
Clearly seeing profit,
Five concubines, three wives, joy in the heart,
Future consequences all borne by oneself,
Not cultivating is truly foolish intent.
Brothers living together,
Sons still young,
Do not hastily split apart over right and wrong,
Born of same womb, nursed together, grown as persons,
Not cultivating is truly foolish intent.
Not cultivating practice,
Seeking liberation,
A hundred-year human life is like a dream,
Sufferings each borne by oneself,
Not cultivating is truly foolish intent.
Worldly sentiments,
Never ashamed,
Holding to the heart, diligently comparing and contending,
Suddenly losing footing, falling into the three wretched paths,
Not cultivating is truly foolish intent.
All must heed the exhortations given here,
Each must apply their own mind,
Returning home, each reflect on their differences,
Urging each other, directly discuss good matters.
Having spoken long,
The sunlight fades,
Farewell, disciples, rise from your seats,
Come early tomorrow at the appointed time to listen,
Chant the Buddha’s name on the steps and receive the gāthā.
A human life, one generation,
In the blink of an eye,
Like spark from stone, lightning flash,
Unable to long endure.
I urge you, disciples,
Quickly seek liberation.
Urge you, disciples,
Cultivate blessings and goodness,
Do not cling to spring scenes worth admiring,
Consider how long they can last,
After all, for the body, they are great harm.
Many dependents,
Who will care for you?
On the road ahead, you bear the hardships yourself,
Leisurely clasping hands, reflecting on your own,
Infatuated with Xīshī,
admiring the moon-like face,
many revere beauty and respect virtue,
yet restraining the mind and purifying thoughts to ponder,
this too is a great affliction for the self.
Slaughtering pigs and sheep,
ashamed of jade-like delicacies,
forcing relatives to indulge in feasts,
boiling, roasting, and butchering one’s own responsibility,
this too is a great affliction for the self.
A lazy and negligent mind,
difficult to persuade and encourage,
picking and choosing monks based on status and wealth,
distinguishing ordinary from holy with bias,
this too is a great affliction for the self.
A mind attached to life and death,
boasting of cultivating goodness,
reciting scriptures with the mouth while the mind remains unchanged,
the Buddha says such people are icchantikas,
this too is a great affliction for the self.
The teacher Shìjiā,
with skillful means,
expounded the seven scrolls of the Lotus Sūtra,
using countless methods to transform sentient beings,
intending to guide all to reach the other shore.
Diligently,
capable of refinement,
earnestly dedicating body and mind with frequent vows,
not merely seeing Ēmítuó in vain,
but surely ascending to the heavenly palace of Tuṣita.
Further intending to speak,
the sun sets in the west,
disciples seated below each prepare to depart,
suddenly encountering an old vinegar peddler,
fifty eggplants and two baskets.
We disciples,
virtuous men and women,
born in the Sahā world of five impurities and evils,
only cling to life and death,
not realizing impermanence.
(The four marks shift),
(the minor four marks).
Speaking of the five metaphors of attachment.
The sky clears,
metaphor for debate and discussion.
Just like a human life in this world,
greed for sights and sounds is no different,
white hair arrives at the temples,
where can one turn to avoid it?
Deafness, dim eyesight, and back pain,
still worrying about family and plans,
limbs heavy and difficult to move,
appearance haggard and emaciated.
The King of Death suddenly arrives,
what order lies ahead?
When King Yán asks you,
what words will you prepare?
Do not rely on sons and daughters in rows,
hoping for their offerings,
even if they set up daily feasts,
how can it compare to preparing oneself?
Instruct sons and grandsons,
to practice filial piety and righteousness,
worship and chant in the golden hall at all hours,
even if they follow these words exactly,
it is not as good as personally preparing while alive.
Further leaving words,
entrusting and remembering,
painting King Yán and kneeling before him,
even if you kneel a thousand times,
it is not as good as personally preparing while alive.
Advising disciples,
cultivate blessings and benefits,
each one preparing for the afterlife,
to avoid entrusting sons and grandsons after death,
while healthy, personally prepare.
Chant Guānyīn,
seek Shìzhì,
the gate of the Land of Ultimate Bliss opens as desired,
in a snap of the fingers, reach the Western Paradise,
the great sage Ēmítuó sees with joy.
Further hearing the sūtras,
and receiving predictions,
surely in the future encounter Maitreya.
Forever abandoning the turbid world of Sahā’s suffering,
not falling into the three evil paths.
Further intending to speak,
the sun sets in the west,
the principles are profound and numerous.
Early tomorrow, I will speak with you,
for now, receive the verses before the steps.
Five thousand sūtra scrolls recorded by the Buddha,
one must awaken to the urgency of human life.
A hundred years is no different from a spark struck from stone,
a lifetime is like a candle in the wind.
Once awakened,
one must strike and drive out,
cease repeatedly arising greed and desire,
even if gold piles up to the North Star,
the mind remains unsatisfied.
Piling pearls and jewels,
heaping white jade,
a treasury filled with thousands of bolts of silk,
even if more is delivered,
the mind remains unsatisfied.
Buying fields and estates,
building houses,
selling all the fine timber of others,
even if the whole country becomes one’s livelihood,
the mind remains unsatisfied.
Overflowing granaries,
storing wheat and grain,
ten thousand stones and a thousand carts stored for winter,
even if everyone’s harvest is brought,
the mind remains unsatisfied.
Digging extra pits,
gathering all bundles,

Afraid of seeing people,

In the sky are always good dragon spirits,

When speaking truthfully, do not feel aversion,

Frequently cut off karmic deeds,

Respect monastic teachers,

Even if your sons and grandsons line up in rows,

At dusk, chanting Buddha, return home,

The entire Jambudvīpa world is all false,

The wealthy’s greed grows daily,

Gaining wealth and abundance,
without shame,

This is always said in the sūtras,
regardless of poverty or wealth, all sink and fall.
The boiling cauldron cares not for talent,
the furnace of charcoal disregards your will.
White jade in life may win people,
gold after death cannot close the door.
Vain actions,
no way to avoid,
a bit of enmity meets face to face,
thus the Tathāgata advises the world,
better to personally prepare while healthy.
Hoping for sons and grandsons,
entrusting gods and ghosts,

Hoping for sons and grandsons,
burning extra paper,
together reasoning in the underworld,

also not as good as preparing early while healthy.
Hoping for sons and grandsons,
practicing filial piety and righteousness,
covering up my lifetime of mistaken intentions,
even if you cover up without fault,
also not as good as preparing early while healthy.
Hoping for sons and grandsons,

piling up seven-day feasts and distant memorials,

Hoping for sons and grandsons,
practicing charity,
casting statues and copying sūtras with painstaking effort,
even if you cast a thousand statues,
also not as good as preparing early while healthy.
In life, one receives seven parts oneself,
after death, only one part is obtained,
even that one part of action,
often and repeatedly is vainly discarded.
Greed for the body,
greed for oneself,
who remembers the two parents suffering beatings?
Do not speak of the gate of contemplation and salvation,
Eyes uneven and without tears.
All push aside the sun and moon amid human feelings,

Alas, the heart,
Mistaken and dull in planning,
Later descendants will be unbearable.
Hear that while strong and healthy, cultivate early,
Better than relying on oneself…
What one does oneself,
One reaps oneself,
Gradually drawing out calamities one by one.
One must be dull and sincere to avoid hardship,
Hoping for others’ effort is without cause.
I urge disciples to practice truly (true practice),
Must seek a human body on the path ahead.
Remove sin and defilement, do not cling,

Even if this body returns to the great night,

Surely born in Tuṣita, what further doubt?
Then bid farewell forever to Jambudvīpa.
The body adorned with light, feasting on jade delicacies,

Before the eyes only meeting sages,

At dusk, chanting Buddha’s name, return home,
Do not let old age…
Do not boast of jade-like, flower-like beauty,
Years come and go, age quickly arrives,
Know that the floating world is but a moment,
Do not make a tune of lasting a thousand years.
Splitting star words,
Splitting star speech,
When spoken face-to-face, one should wake and clamor,
Why so much white hair on the head?
Just this is impermanence throwing a secret sign.
Planning may create clever schemes,
Fate is not determined by human calculation,
Wealth and honor must come from past seeds,
Now it is certainly hard to reverse.
Do not flaunt cleverness, boast of scheming,
By the time schemes succeed, the body is already old,
Further, eyes dim, back bent,
Just this is impermanence throwing a secret sign.
Only chasing affairs, boasting of grace,
Competing in beauty, displaying sharp features,
Indulging freely in wine, meat, and tea,
Hearing lectures opened, yet losing laughter.
Youthful days,
Seeking only pleasure,
Who listens to your idle sutra teachings?
Look, face wrinkled, still seeking strength,
Still not awakening to impermanence throwing a secret sign.
Do not idle about and be unworthy,
Unworthiness will sink you into evil paths,
Now all act wildly and recklessly,
The underworld’s karma mirror clearly reflects.
At that grinding time,
No resistance,任由 grinding and pounding,

A hundred years of life is the common way,

Just three days after death, arrangements made,

Sent back,
Children clamor,

The burning house pulls and torments long,

Just when illness comes, lying in bed,
No support for the path ahead.
Heart anxious,
Producing hot distress,
Regretting not preparing when healthy,
Moving with difficulty, frequent cries,
Still not awakening to impermanence throwing a secret sign.
As a person, one must have a clear heart,
Do not learn empty boasting, much deceit,
Only grinding greed without end,
Must still prepare for the path ahead.
Do not indulge desires,
All chaotic creation,
Illness comes, fearing not your youth,
Even without illness, old age brings deafness,
Still not awakening to impermanence throwing a secret sign.
Now in the world, much inversion,
Do not just rely on their youth,
Their lifespans each differ greatly,
Shadow and echo, the body first dies young.
Then lonely and poor,
Without reliance,
All day lamenting with regret,
Further adding a bent back to the body,
Still not awakening to impermanence throwing a secret sign.
Not related to matters, do not entangle,
Entangling the body and mind is not good,
Constantly vexed, bound by troubles,
Falling into this body, losing calculation.
Perhaps wearing cangue,
Receiving whip and torture,
Tears like shooting stars, where to complain?
Such disasters are not from heaven,
Misfortune has no gate, people summon it themselves.
From now on,
Do not cause clamor,
Where there are loud voices, do not go,
Teach you a lifetime without calamity,
Where you go, naturally people say good.
Wealth, honor, luxury are not necessarily good,
Much wealth harms oneself, attracts trouble,
Shadow and echo, thus falling from the body,
Only because the greedy heart is unending.
Encounter conflict,
Receive whip and torture,
Deeply hidden underground, told to them,
Each one, you see with your own eyes,
Still not awakening to impermanence throwing a secret sign.
Seeing others’ glory, do not produce vexation,
Wealth, honor, poverty come from past creation,
Only know to steadily use body and mind,
Clothing and food naturally always just right.
Disrespect Buddha’s monks,
Disdain divine ways,
Strive to make this body loved and happy,
Must break until form worse than a ghost,
Still not awakening to impermanence throwing a secret sign.
Ten kinds of principles proclaimed to you,
Incline ear, rub heart, quiet, no clamor,
All are matters on disciples’ bodies,
Quickly must beat and lock the heart-monkey.
Do not as before refuse to discard greed and attachment,
Truly no轮回, gone not returning,
If today we take words,
In the West surely see and bow to the golden immortal.
Born into the lotus Buddha land,
Joy, freedom, beyond compare,
Water flows, wind moves, awakening to non-birth,
Bells ring, trees sway, hearing the four truths.
Kaliṅga form,
Peacock neck,
All are transformations of your Amitābha Buddha arising,
Not like Jambudvīpa’s bird sounds,
Each sound speaks the truth of emptiness.
Rhyme clear and tinkling,
Sound marvelous,
Hearing makes people all leave attachment,
Fully surpassing the five turbidities in Sahā,
Four phases shifting, no fixed stop.
Early seek birth,
Quickly discard this,
Do not tire of hearing sutras frequently, a little,
Know that hearing Dharma is the ferry bridge,
If lacking ferry bridge, how to reach there?
Urge now, within this day urge,

Do not decline warmth and heat, support,
Each hope to open some convenience.
Also say, lectured for several days,
Alms offerings, sadly no large amount.

Respectfully note, sutras say: In the Western Heaven there is a country named Huānxǐ,
With a king, King Huānxǐ.
The king’s consort,
Named Yǒuxiàng.
The consort’s appearance graceful and slender,
Jade-like countenance, light and graceful,
Like spring day’s peach blossoms,
Resembling autumn pond’s lotus leaves,
Luminous plain quality,
Brilliant delicate charm,
Truly can be leisurely,
Particularly pleasing the king’s heart.
Chanting: Since entering the king’s palace serving the sage lord,
High and low all say humbly receiving favor.
If discussing dance excellence, should be ranked,
Even with clear songs, often moving frowns.
Entering and leaving pepper rooms, ladies colorful and chaotic,
Settling palace eunuchs, kindness only new.
All under heaven feel gratitude, embracing the king’s sageliness,
Yǒuxiàng virtuous and harmonious, aiding one person.
This lady's appearance was already beautiful,
Her wifely virtues shone even brighter,
Known wherever the sun and moon shine,
Praised throughout heaven and earth.
The king cherished her,
Day and night never leaving the inner chambers,
Morning and evening joyful in the golden hall.
Such wealth and honor,
Were laughably strict.
Suddenly one day,
Another ill omen was heard:
Side Though the king favored her with affection,

Side Suddenly during a song and dance,

A deep, dark aura,

The sage ruler saw it,

Break Suddenly the lady's complexion grew dim,

The king saw this, startled and alarmed,

This Yǒuxiàng lady's face was fair and upright,

One day she danced in the hall,

Unaware of the reason,

(Shìyīn Púsà)

The monk said: “Lady,
Lady!

Side: Floating life is hard to prolong,

Thereupon, the bhikṣuṇī of the stone chamber advised Lady Yǒuxiàng,

The lady asked the monk: “To be born in the human world,

Good doctrine,
Inconceivable,

The Story of King Huānxǐ, one copy recorded.
Written on the sixth day of the seventh month of the yǐmǎo year by the monk Jièjìng of Sānjiè Temple.
As said in the Sūtra of Lady Yǒuxiàng,

The Chányú personally led ten thousand troops,
arriving at Fàn Fūrén Chéng,
pursuing Lǐ Líng.
Hán Yánnián reported to Lǐ Líng: "Great General, temporarily withdraw the troops,
take a route and proceed."
Hearing this, Lǐ Líng
immediately fled southward,
traveling for three days,
and was then overtaken by the Chányú.
The enemy was at full strength,
the Hàn envoys were half-defeated,
unaware of those behind,
losing approximately over five hundred men.
Lǐ Líng called to his attendants: "Why not fight?"
The attendants replied: "General,
the troops are exhausted,
how can we fight again?"
Lǐ Líng responded: "Those wounded by three or four spears,
carry them on carts;
those wounded by one or two spears,
fight again with double effort."
Before descending (the camp was not yet settled),
during the hasty meal,
Lǐ Líng wished to rally the army,
just as he ordered the drums beaten,
but at that moment, the drums would not sound.
Lǐ Líng sighed to himself: "Heaven has abandoned us!"
Before his sigh ended,
from the third cart,
three black vapors
surged upward toward the sky.
Lǐ Líng ordered his attendants to search,
and they found two women,
aged sixteen,
also before the horses.
He ordered his attendants to behead them,
each cut into two pieces,
yet the drums, without being struck,
roared and cried out on their own.
Yǔ Xìn's poem says: "In the army, two women remembered,
beyond the frontier, Fūrén Chéng."
There is no other text,
precisely referencing this event.
The Hú fled in great haste,
the Hàn also raced in pursuit,
slaughtering the Xiōngnú,
over three thousand cavalry.
They immediately cut off their ears,
carrying them on horseback,
when recording the events,
intending to use them as proof.
At night, they looked northwest,
at dawn, they looked southeast,
taking a route and proceeding,
hoping to escape.
Suddenly arriving at a flat plain,
where the plain was quiet and the grass deep,
Lǐ Líng said to his attendants: "Why not hide in the grass,
to avoid disaster and return south?"
The officers and soldiers, hearing this,
immediately entered the grass.
At that moment, Lǐ Líng suddenly encountered a roaring north wind,
blowing the grass southward.
The Chányú said: "The Hàn traitors will die without being fought."
The attendants asked: "Great King,
the Hàn traitors are not fought,
how will they die on their own?"
The Chányú's men set fire from behind,
the smoke billowed,
the flames soared to the sky.
"Great General,
the fire is coming from behind,
how can we avoid death?"
Lǐ Líng asked: "How far is the fire from here?"
The attendants reported: "The fire is one lǐ away."
"Is there flint in the army?"
Quickly striking fire,
they burned the grass ahead,
when the fire came from behind,
it would extinguish itself.
The fire ahead ignited,
the fire behind went out.
Observe the place where Lǐ Líng and the Chányú fought in the fire:
Lǐ Líng's army pressed forward,
the enemy cavalry swarmed in pursuit from behind.
Battle clouds gathered across the land,
the northern chill over Yānnán obscured the view.
At this time, provisions were exhausted and the troops began to starve,
already worn out from fighting others.
Then the Chányú set fire,
wanting to flee, but where could they pass?
In the plain, surely were wolf and jackal fur,
blown by the wind, night after night with fur.
Red flames fiercely spread and flourished,
each gust blowing them higher.
White snow drifted over the purple frontier,
black smoke columns entered the gloomy void.
The grass ahead was burned, no longer connected,
when the fire came from behind, it extinguished itself.
"It is said that Hàn generals of old faced hardship,
accustomed to much suffering on the Great Wall.
Three hundred thousand troops still feared death,
let alone Lǐ Líng with five thousand men!
When there is trouble in the army, aid must be sought,
several generals march together but do not fight together.
I know well the distant pursuit of the fleeing north,
erasing traces and sweeping clean.
In life, I wished to learn the merits of minor officials,
beyond the frontier, only then did I know the emptiness of the fire's curtain.
Even if the Sage Lord shows mercy today,
how can one know Lǐ Líng's heart?
At that time, the general met with misfortune,
I gathered the remaining soldiers left behind.
If the felt blankets are heavy, discard them,
if light, keep them as you wish.
When encountering water, mix with roasted flour to eat,
when encountering ice, do not let it choke your throat.
Since we are in enemy territory, we must fight to the death,
killing each other, death is the only end.
When will I see the Sage Lord in the kingdom again?
I have not been able to bow to my kind mother at home!
Today I die as a wild goose in Hú skies,
flying ten thousand lǐ toward Bàtóu."
The Chányú said to his attendants: "We have entered Hàn territory,
advanced two thousand lǐ,
gather the troops and return,
each to safety."
Before his words ended,
under Lǐ Líng, there was an officer, the resolute Guǎn Gǎn, a Xiàowèi,
due to negligence in inspection,
Lǐ Líng angrily struck him five times,
"If you neglect inspection again,
I will have you executed to command the army!"
Guǎn Gǎn, fearing Lǐ Líng would behead him,
deserted the army and fled,
straight to the Chányú's tent.
Prostrating and twisting,
dancing and leaping with raised voice,
he pleaded guilty to a capital crime.
The Chányú asked: "Who are you?"
"I am Guǎn Gǎn, an officer under Lǐ Líng."
The Chányú said: "Why have you come?"
Guǎn Gǎn addressed His Majesty: "Lǐ Líng's troops,
have exhausted their arrows and broken their bows,
provisions are all gone,
they are extremely close here,
Great King, why not capture them?"
The Chányú, seeing Guǎn Gǎn surrender,
laughed heartily.
He called to his attendants: "Advance another two or three hundred lǐ,
Lǐ Líng will surrender and become a slave."
The Chányú's attendants, hearing this,
pursued Lǐ Líng,
Lǐ Líng immediately drew his crossbow and shot,
hitting the left eye of the Tūqíshī Fānwáng.
The Chányú, frightened and anxious,
dared not advance,
hesitating on horseback,
said to his attendants: "Hurry and guard against the pursuing enemy,
everyone is exhausted.
Though we have marched a thousand lǐ,
we have lost approximately ten thousand men.
Even if we capture Hàn soldiers,
what use are they?
Better to return early."
The attendants replied: "Great King, you personally led a hundred thousand men,
against five thousand,
it does not cover your glory,
instead invites humiliation,
if we turn back and let them go, they will return later,
if we do not eliminate them when small,
great trouble will surely arise.
If Your Majesty fights again,
the Hàn will surely be defeated and surrender,
before noon,
Lǐ Líng's army will flee and be defeated."
The Chányú, hearing this,
pursued Lǐ Líng.
Lǐ Líng's arrows were exhausted, bows broken,
provisions all gone,
his loyal heart sought only a blade's edge.
Lǐ Líng ordered his attendants,
urgently have people dismantle the carts,
each take a cart spoke as a club,
striking, covering heads and faces with sand.
Where Lǐ Líng and the Chányú fought the third battle,
how shall it be described?
The wild Hú northward shook the horizon,
the great Hàn southward, the road still distant.
Engaging in battle, wishing for favorable winds,
facing the enemy, hating the slanting sun's shadow.
Though the rear troops fought urgently,
the Hàn generals knew their strength was insufficient.
With bows and blades all used up,
they grasped empty hands to shield left and right.
In urgent times, nothing surpasses a club,
urgently have people break the carts.
Each takes a cart spoke as a club,
striking, covering heads and faces with sand.
Instantly, plants and trees were cut down by frost;
That day, mountains and rivers were ravaged by blood.
At night, gazing at the Hu stars flying like lightning,
At dawn, watching the killing aura resembling clouds.
Today, as a general against the yellow-bearded foe,
Year after year, I remain like the red-beaked crow.
How dare you act so unreasonably,
Causing my general to never see home again.
Today, beyond the frontier, all is lost,
With what face shall I meet the capital again!
The battle was over,
In a moment, dusk fell,
Each returned to their camp.
Deep into the night,
Líng came out himself,
Calling to his attendants: "If I do not die today,
I am no brave man!"
The attendants addressed the great general:
"Since tying up your hair in youth,
You have ventured far to capture the Chányú,
Entering the enemy's territory,
Over two thousand miles away.
You vowed to pacify the desert,
To end the clamor and dust,
With these small merits,
To serve the enlightened ruler.
Who would have thought the general would meet defeat,
The soldiers in vain,
Betraying such lofty ambitions,
Deviating from your original intent.
In the present situation,
Truly isolated and imperiled.
Like a fish swimming in a cauldron,
A nest on a curtain,
The cauldron boils, the fish rots,
The curtain moves, the nest falls,
The situation is already untenable,
Logic dictates survival is impossible.
The great general's original intent,
Do not waste efforts in vain,
Please consider a plan,
To seek a way to survive."
Líng said: "I heard that Emperor Gāo personally led three hundred thousand troops,
North to campaign beyond the frontier,
And was trapped at Píngchéng.
At that time, fierce generals were like clouds,
Strategists like rain,
Yet once they entered the Chányú's territory,
The army of tens of thousands,
Made a great march only once.
They relied on Chén Píng carving a wooden woman to deceive him,
And fortunately escaped.
How much more so today, with my five thousand infantry,
Facing a hundred thousand enemy troops,
How can mosquitoes resist a strong wind,
Or ants shake a great tree!"
"Great General,
A snake cannot move without its head,
A bird cannot fly without wings,
An army cannot fight without a general,
Soldiers cannot survive without provisions.
Even if the general possessed Huáng Shí's Three Strategies,
Or Chén Píng's Six Wonders,
The methods of divine tactics,
Ghostly vanishings would still lead to death and loss.
The army has no reinforcements,
Heaven has forsaken us,
It is not the soldiers' fault,
I urge the great general to surrender."
Líng said: "I command the three armies,
Hold the flags and drums of the six ministers,
The Son of Heaven entrusted me with this mission,
To defeat the foe and return to court.
But alas, the Hàn are weak, the Hú strong,
Flags and drums scattered,
Command in disarray,
Though men survive,
The army lacks provisions,
Seeing the food run out,
Reason dictates surrender.
You must go,
Strive to return together,
Do not abandon each other.
Have you not heard: 'For a thousand generations, the ruler of the time,
For ten thousand generations, the hometown,
In good times, share glory,
In bad times, share shame.'
Rest well at night,
Rise early at dawn,
If you reach the Hàn court,
Guard well against the Hú ants.
My fate is thin today,
Such is the will of Heaven.
If you reach the court,
Clearly explain the reasoning.
Pay respects to my kind mother in the northern hall,
Bow again to my sovereign facing south.
Say that Líng lived as a man in a foreign land,
And will die as a ghost lost from home.
Forever parting from kin and friends,
Long farewell to those who know me."
He wished to say more,
But could not continue.
Let us see how Lǐ Líng bid farewell to his soldiers and what he said:
"A man beyond the frontier, his fate decided,
Facing the Hú wolves, the reality is hard.
Bidding you farewell, I intended to cut down the Xiōngnú bandits,
Mounted on a priceless moonlit saddle.
A man losing control, defeated by the wild foe,
Betraying Heaven above and Earth below.
Not only no face to see the Heavenly King,
But ashamed before ancestors in the Yellow Springs.
Alas, sighing and chanting long,
Only because deceiving the Hú plunged me deep into suffering.
What path did Heaven make you know,
Your Majesty should know Líng's loyal heart."
The attendants, hearing this, all shed tears:
"General, today, how many times over!
How could you alone lead five thousand men,
To fight a hundred thousand Xiōngnú cavalry?
Crimson blood flowed like water,
Hú soldiers lay dead everywhere.
Even if you have no face to see the Heavenly King,
Your name should remain in the historical records.
Where is the great man now,
You must feel shame for the nurturing grace.
General, do not act recklessly again,
Let us return together to court to see the Son of Heaven."
Líng, hearing his attendants speak of his mother,
Wailed loudly, tears streaming in ten thousand lines.
"If only I had ten more arrows,
I might still have a chance to see my hometown.
Now, attendants, you must scatter like birds and beasts,
Lost on the road, gazing at the moon as you flee.
If you return south to see the Son of Heaven,
Report Líng's guilt and His Majesty's grace."
Lǐ Líng finished speaking,
Sighed deeply several times,
And said to his attendants: "I hear that birds in the sky
Still rely on their six wings;
If the skin is gone,
How can the feathers cling?
We must employ unfathomable schemes,
Extraordinary strategies,
Surrender first, then emerge,
Slay the foe and return to court.
If the Emperor gauges Líng's true feelings,
Would he not believe?"
So they gathered treasures,
Took down the banners and flags,
Buried them in the ground,
Not letting the enemy see.
Attendants of Lǐ Líng,
Each trusting fate,
If dawn comes,
They will surely be captured.
The attendants, hearing this,
Immediately scattered like stars.
Just as dawn broke,
The Hú soldiers arrived.
Líng's deputy, Hán Yánnián, was struck by an arrow, fell from his horse, and died.
Lǐ Líng had neither bow nor arrows left,
Reined his horse and fled,
Beat his chest toward the Hàn country,
Wailed and wept bitterly.
Eyes red, heart clear,
He swore by the mountains and rivers,
Not to betray the enlightened ruler of Hàn.
Casting aside bow and blade,
He surrendered to the Turks.
Hesitating to speak, fearing anger,
The Chányú loudly rebuked him.
How did Lǐ Líng surrender?
Lǐ Líng, having spoken, surrendered to the foreigners,
Walking to the front of the Chányú's great tent.
"First, regarding yesterday's battle,
I shall fully explain my original intent."
"Armor, bows, and soldiers all exhausted,
I wish to long reside by the Jade Frontier.
If the foreign king shows a glance of favor,
Then I will have no heart to court the Hàn heavens.
Since taking command as your general,
One battle feels like a hundred years.
All engagements were ordered by the Hàn Emperor,
How dare I act on my own as an envoy?
Foolish subject, my crimes reach the heavens,
Now I offer my humble life before the king.
Simply for lacking merit, I apologize to the foreign lord,
Hoping for generous grace to forgive this fault."
The Chányú, seeing Lǐ Líng surrender,
Questioned why he had entered the frontier land.
"Time and again leading troops to attack,
Often commanding masses to tread the battlefield.
Your forces never numbered ten thousand,
How dare you suddenly breach the border?
Recently you could still be called a Hàn general,
Why do you come to surrender today!"
You have newly come from the imperial capital;
has the extermination of Lǐ Líng's family truly been carried out?
Wáng Jìncháo replied, saying:
"I wished to speak, but upon reflection, my breath choked.
Fortunately, the letter-writing official Sīmǎ Qiān,
before the hall, answered and spoke from the heart.
Emperor Wǔ heard this and calmed his anger,
pondering carefully and considering the general's suffering.
Later, he sent Gōngsūn Áo into the barbarian court,
but he lost the troops and returned in defeat.
The fault was shifted onto the general,
and the Hàn military strategy was left to teach the wild barbarians.
It was all due to Gōngsūn Áo's slanderous words
that the general's mother was then executed."
When Líng heard that his old mother had been executed by the sovereign,
he cried out in anguish, wailing until his breath choked.
Twin streams of tears flowed as if about to end,
his liver and intestines cut inch by inch as if by knives.
Those around him wept and supported him,
and in the desert frontier, he vomited blood from his bowels.
After a long while, he was shaken and revived,
and gazing south toward the Hàn state, he lamented with sorrow:
"I recall when I first arrived north of Jùnjī,
the barbarian cavalry gradually pressed in from all sides.
I drew my sword and slashed faces until blood formed rivers—
this was to repay the king's grace and virtue.
Not by my own will did I surrender to the Hú barbarians;
day and night I planned and schemed to return to the state.
Today, the August Heaven should know—
the Son of Heaven of Hàn has betrayed Líng's virtue."
Thereupon, they wept and bid each other farewell,
gradually passing beyond Jùnjī.
They saw steep ridges in a thousand layers,
and towering cliffs ten thousand ren high.
To the east, they connected to the Bó Hǎi Sea,
to the west, they joined Yànmén.
Spring grasses did not flourish,
and in summer, snow still fell.
Gibbons cried as if weeping,
cranes called as if singing.
Wild trees grew withered,
cold flowers scattered in disarray,
white clouds drifted aimlessly,
yellow leaves flew lightly.
In secluded ravines, ice formed,
and wild geese called, seeking their mates.
At times, they heard the Qiāng flute,
listening only brought sorrow to people.
At dawn, they crossed the Hú plains,
covering distances continuously,
occasionally meeting shepherds,
but never seeing woodcutters.
Sū, the great envoy, resentfully saw the Chányú,
while General Lǐ Líng shamefully looked upon the Hàn envoy's tally.
Sometimes grieving, sometimes resentful,
they laughed and chanted in turn.
Knowing the immense value of a thousand treasures,
how much more the barriers of mountains and rivers that blocked their way.
At that time, the three men faced each other and wept,
poured farewell wine by the roadside,
and placed the parting lute upon their knees.
Sū Wǔ raised his wine and turned to thank Hán Zēng, saying:
"I am a general of the Great Hàn,
long lost and trapped on the battlefield.
If not for you coming,
how could I have returned?
Engraved in my flesh and carved in my bones,
how could I dare forget this kindness?"
Before his words were finished,
he turned to look at Lǐ Líng.
And he saw Lǐ Líng
clad in Hú furs,
wearing a Hú hat on his head,
and treading in red thornwood sandals.
He asked Lǐ Líng:
"General, you are a general of the Great Hàn—
did you not hope to remain in Lǒngxī,
where for generations,
your name was renowned to the highest,
with vermilion gates arrayed with halberds,
facing south as a ruler among men?
You entered and left fragrant palaces,
holding high office on broad roads.
How is it, General,
that you wander the desert curtains,
and though like flesh and bone,
you are trapped in the barbarian court?
Are you not laughed at by others?"
When Lǐ Líng heard this reproach,
he felt as if his skin were flayed and bones disassembled.
He had turned his back on his lord and left his kin;
though Líng had strength,
it was excessive to have a body yet say it was acceptable.
Now he had no home to return to.
Clutching his chest with his hands,
he looked to heaven and wept bitterly.
The Hú-style hat that Lǐ Líng wore
was cast aside on the desert sands.
Then he drew a blade from his waist,
and speaking of years past,
they gazed together toward Cháng'ān.
He then spoke, saying:
"I recall when Líng first led infantry,
fewer than five thousand men,
deep into the barbarian court,
fighting over ten thousand...
...marching until they reached south of the Jùnxī (Jùnjī) Mountains,
north of the Lónglè River.
The land was remote, without springs,
empty sands without water.
Before Líng's troops could settle,
they saw the Chányú's troops, over a hundred thousand strong,
advancing like rain,
all at once...
That day, Líng planned to fight,
but they were many and we were few.
Líng planned not to fight,
but Sū Gōng was herding sheep,
and I strongly remembered my worthy friend,
so I could not but follow the banner troops.
The battle formation was named Yuèhuá,
...right shoot right empty.
The Xiōngnú poured forth their masses,
charging forward at that time.
The Hàn generals vied for merit,
drawing swords and rushing in,
watching from afar... the Jade Void and star blades,
slaying barbarians and seizing flags.
On that day,
heaven was moved to raise battle clouds,
earth gave birth to war fog.
The Xiōngnú were defeated,
and immediately withdrew their troops.
The Hàn generals were victorious,
advancing about twenty-some li,
yet they had not turned their banners back.
The unruly enemy immediately withdrew their troops,
and the Hàn generals were victorious.
But then the wild bandits set fires with the wind,
crimson flames reaching to the sky.
Líng was in the midst of the fire,
and the situation was difficult to manage.
He could not but feign surrender to the Chányú,
Líng planned to eat...,
his heart was anxious...,
day and night devising plans,
stirring chaos and mutual killing,
stealing a path to return home.
...Líng... within... destroyed,
yet how could Emperor Wǔ... listen to the words of sycophantic ministers,
saying that from Líng's ancestors onward,
three generations had betrayed Hàn?
He ordered the relevant office
to arrest all members of Líng's household,
every man and woman,
driven into Yúnyáng,
to the horse market's execution ground,
and dealt with according to the law.
Young wives and little daughters,
innocent and wrongfully executed.
Líng had an old mother,
eighty-five years old,
who needed support to walk,
and required feeding by others.
What crime had she committed against heaven,
that she too was executed!
Better to... wander the desert,
miserable in the barbarian court,
than under the northern palace gate,
seeking a sliver of profit like an awl's point,
to kill the Son of Heaven's father—
who could initiate such an affair!
You, sir, are like ten thousand...,
Líng has no intention of returning.
Before my old mother's grave,
diligently pay respects on my behalf at the proper times.
Go before Emperor Wǔ's hall,
and plead on Líng's behalf.
If you meet someone trustworthy,
send a message from time to time;
if you encounter a returning wild goose,
entrust a fragrant line."
On that day,
they drank farewell wine,
struck...,
and sang with songs.
Sū Wǔ, without speaking, disappeared from sight,
and then once again pursued Lǐ Líng.
Reining in their horses and shaking their whips,
each composed a poem:
Cool winds chase... mist,
the traveling wild goose longs for the distant frontier.
Sū Wǔ returns to the southern state,
while Lǐ Líng—what has he betrayed heaven for!
I envy the bird that lost its mate,
alone in the northern frontier, flapping its wings.
The Hàn army beneath the sun... white clouds,
how many thousands of li to the road to Xiányáng?
Sū Wǔ harmonized with a poem saying:
I urge you, sir, to drink the wine bestowed,
For after it passes, I shall worry for you.
If you wish to know where I think of you,
I miss you by the water's edge.
At times, lacking the wings of wild geese,
All the ministers together are filled with sorrow.

Over a thousand Xiongnu,

The edict bestowed upon the Minister,

Gold and silver vessels,

The Minister holding and reading the edict,
