Unconsciously shedding tears, the situation
Was as follows:
Imperial envoys westward heading to the dragon court,
Carriages and horses bustling out of the phoenix city.
Edict bestowing mink caps and the nine bestowments,
Tiger banners and dragon tokens shining with double streamers.
First leaving the Wèi palace, mist and clouds serene,
Gradually passing Xiāoguān, the desert road level.
Because bearing the Son of Heaven's command afar,
Swift riding still longing for the green Lǒng mountains.
Traveling singing under the sage sun facing the desolate fort,
Jade bridles urging doubly the journey ahead.
Gazing afar at Dūnhuáng increasing joyful spirit,
The three peaks' emerald green bright before the eyes.
Upon arrival, the polo ground proclaimed the edict's instruction,
The letter praising and rewarding with further earnestness.
The Minister, having seen the silken edict's words,
Dancing with bowed head felt ashamed yet grateful for the sage's wisdom.
"Your humble servant fortunately encounters the Táo-Táng transformation,
Able again to offer the imperial visage at Yānshān.
Repaying the state wishing to clear the barbarian settlements quiet,
Smoke vanishing for ten thousand lǐ, raising lofty walls.
In this life, who could have expected a personal imperial inquiry,
Specially descending celestial officials from the ninefold heavens.
Bestowed silks difficult to hold and receive,
A hundred lifetimes engraving in bone vowing to devote loyalty!"
The Minister, having received,
Immediately led the heavenly envoys into Kāiyuán Temple,
Personally paying respects to our Xuánzōng Emperor's sacred image.
The envoys saw the former imperial seat,
Solemn as if in life.
Sighing, thinking Dūnhuáng though for a hundred years cut off from Hàn,
Fallen to the western barbarians,
Still revered the original dynasty,
Leaving the emperor's image remaining.
The other four commanderies,
All unable to preserve it.
Also seeing Gān, Liáng, Guā, Sù,
Parapets carved and ruined,
Residents shoulder to shoulder with barbarian ugliness,
Clothing how could forget the left lapel?
Only Shāzhōu commandery alone,
People and culture splendid,
Entirely like the inner lands.
The envoys looking at each other in pairs,
For a moment shedding tears,
Left and right attendants,
None not sorrowful and distressed.
Settling down completed,
Daily setting up singing feasts,
Polo and music banquets and rewards,
Not a day without.
At this time,
Beginning of autumn,
The realm charmingly verdant;
Red peaches first ripe,
Nine-brewed wine like a river.
The envoys, due to royal schedule limited,
Could not delay.
Drafting a memorial thanking grace,
Immediately set forth.
The Minister escorting far beyond the suburbs,
Bowing with memorial, farewell feast,
Azure sky autumn thoughts,
Leaving and staying sorrowful,
Hesitating on frontier grass,
Lingering for two nights.
Shaking hands on the road,
How to part sleeves, the situation
Was as follows:
Since recovery already many years,
Ten thousand lǐ western gates cut off garrison smoke.
Last year official honor, piebald horse administration,
This autumn favored encounter, bestowed mink cicada.
Unexpectedly, Xiǎnyǔn invaded Táng territory,
Leading banners charging across Liùquán.
The sage lord far worried, harboring concern,
Imperial sentiment issuing edict to the barbarian court to proclaim.
Within crimson clouds, envoys difficult to see,
Earthen ridges wind and sand, frontier grass cold.
Trekking the Golden River tiring fine steeds,
Deeply ashamed the constant attendant descended to Lóulán.
Return journey take care, add more meals,
Zhāngyè, Gūzāng lie before the eyes.
Upon arriving at the Golden Luan Hall to present his morning memorial,
He responded with grace and ease, skillfully navigating the court.
How could he ever repay the profound imperial favor he felt?
With military authority, he pacified the borders and pleased the emperor’s countenance.
Once the imperial envoy had departed,
They parted ways, going east and west.
The Minister felt deeply grateful for the emperor’s profound kindness,
And rejoiced at the heavenly fortune bestowed by the court.
It should have been that the surrendered Uighurs,
Were all released to return home.
Their leaders, in haste and panic,
All proclaimed “Long live the emperor!”
Who could have expected that wasps and scorpions are venomous,
And the wolfish nature is hard to tame?
As soon as the imperial envoy passed Jiǔquán,
The Uighur prince led troops westward,
Invading our borders.
Lurking by the shores of the Western Tung Sea,
They gathered like ants and massed like clouds,
Scouting beacon smoke from afar,
And immediately planned to raid.
The vanguard scout commander Bái Tōngjí,
Upon detecting the presence of bandits,
Immediately reported it upward.
When the Minister heard that the Uighurs… the generals reviewed the elite troops,
Preparing to campaign against the Xiongnu.
Advisor Zhāng Dàqìng stepped forward from the ranks and addressed: “The golden…
Troops must not be rashly mobilized.
Advancing westward in late autumn
Is taboo for military strategists.”
The Minister said to the generals: “… broke their promise,
Coming here to spy.
Military treatises state: ‘There are times when troops must act even without full advantage,’
… the situation leaves no choice!
But we shall rely on metal to suppress the royal phase,
Now we must eradicate them.”
Having spoken,
… the army,
He rallied his troops, saying: “The Uighurs have just received imperial edicts,
Yet now they betray this favor.
This is what is called…
It is only right to crush them,
To avenge the court’s indignation.
Officers and soldiers, strive to fulfill your duty,
Together let us sweep away the comets of chaos!”
Once the orders were issued,
They immediately led the troops,
Marching out through the ominous gate.
Like wind galloping and mist rolling,
Not exceeding two nights,
They were already near Western Tung.
The enemy camped by the sea,
Holding strategic positions to gain advantage,
Resisting the imperial army.
The Minister then instructed his generals,
Ordering all to silence drums and lower weapons,
Men and horses gagged.
The east wind whistled fiercely,
Stirring faint dust.
As the six dragons just passed,
They vowed not to return empty-handed.
Vanguards scouted far ahead,
Rear cavalry urged forward.
A thousand companies in iron armor,
Warhorses flying like clouds.
Dividing forces into ten routes,
They simultaneously charged the felt tents.
War drums thundered loudly,
White blades clashed and banners waved.
The Xiongnu lost their courage,
Deer fled in all directions.
Heads fell with sword strokes,
Corpses littered the roads.
The Uighurs were utterly defeated,
Heaven lending its mighty power—
How to describe it?
The Minister heard bandits invaded Western Tung,
Immediately dispatched a flank army past Six Dragons.
All were Dūnhuáng’s brave and chivalrous men,
… who had campaigned to crush Qiāng barbarians.
Frosty blades, hard-used, gleamed under mighty sun,
Tigers and leopards vied in rush, murderous aura thick.
Amid clamor of gongs and drums, strikes fell thick and fast,
Clashing sounds uniform, lightning allowing no gap.
Just at dawn, troops enveloped the foe,
Then arrayed elites to resist the first charge.
Bows drawn like crescent moons, twin-feathered arrows crossed,
Axes hacked… piercing chests outright.
Blood stained autumn grass on the plain,
Whole streams’ flow turned long and red.
South wind aided our army’s fierce might,
Western Sea piled with corpses, layers tens deep.
That day the Minister’s heart grew bold,
Heaven’s favor followed… lord.
Lads fierce in spirit… flesh trembling, long swords wildly slashing
Tigers fight… clubs and hammers… formation broken
Bandits broke through heavy siege… bones struck, precious sword swung
Captured all living prisoners… not a single rider missed
Xiǎnyǔn from then scattered completely,
… songs of joy turned east…
Since the Minister returned to the capital,
I, the Minister, alone presented memorials.
… governing Héxī’s five prefectures,
Virtue’s influence reached even birds and beasts.
Heaven-born divine general… brilliant strategy,
South crushing Western Rong, north sweeping the Hú.
Ten thousand li, he made beacon fires extinguish,
Hundreds of cities, black-haired people celebrated revival.
Several times he reported victories to the imperial domain,
The emperor at the palace hall granted him honors.
“You can protect our mountains and rivers in peace,”
Then saw him honored with chariot and ranked among marquises.
Héxī had fallen into decline for over a century,
Roads blocked at Xiāoguān, wild goose messages rare.
Thanks to the general reopening the old routes,
Once shaking his mighty fame, all under heaven knew.
In youth, not yet twenty, he already achieved eminence,
Single horse, lone spear, charging through ninefold gates.
Once toward Qílián…
Several times in the great desert captured chief villains.
West seizing Yīzhōu…
… restored old territories.
Neighboring states four seasons…
… Táng.
Tuìhún petty villains…

It is heard that the Dharma King’s law is vast,
The Buddha’s teaching lofty,
The king’s law is impartial,
The Buddha’s practice is equal.
The king upholds governance and teaching,
The Buddha expounds the true doctrine.
Both are among the twelve divisions of revered scriptures,
All are Shakyamuni’s guiding ford.
After the Tathagata’s parinirvana,
All sages concealed themselves in the Semblance Dharma age.
There was a monk,
Named Zhāntán.
He had a disciple,
Named Huìyuǎn.
Speaking of this Huìyuǎn,
His home was in Yànmén,
Two brothers in the family,
With no other relatives.
The elder brother named Huìyuǎn,
Renounced the secular life to leave home;
The younger brother named Huìchí,
Remained to care for their mother.
Huìyuǎn, at Monk Zhāntán’s place,
Constantly contemplated the right Dharma,
Often beheld true sutras,
Knowing the joy of the third dhyāna,
He then realized worldly life was not far from end.
Thus one day,
Palms joined, he addressed the monk: “Disciple has served the master,
For many years accumulated,
Yet learning and skills remain desolate,
Considering himself dull and slow.
Now I intend to seek a famous mountain,
Cross streams and ford waters,
Visit the Way and call on monks,
Seclude myself by cliffs and valleys,
To fulfill my lifelong aspiration—this would be good.”
The master said: “Since you now wish to go,
Which mountain do you plan to dwell in?”
Huìyuǎn said: “But disciple cannot distinguish east from west,
How could he know north or south?
Only has the mind to go,
But knows not where to go.”
The master said: “Since you now go,
Simply head to Jiāngzuǒ,
With intent to pilgrimage,
Wherever you encounter a mountain, dwell there,
That shall be your place of cultivation.”
Hearing this, Huìyuǎn
Was overjoyed beyond measure,
Having received the master’s instruction,
How dare he disobey the earnest advice?
Thereupon he stepped forward,
Palms joined, bowing deeply,
Bowed again to bid farewell to the master,
And embarked on the long road.
Venerable Yuǎn journeyed on and on,
carrying a copy of the *Nirvana Sutra*,
traveling to the mountains to cultivate the Way.
At that time,
spring light was bright and radiant,
fragrant colors were lush and abundant,
green willows swayed gracefully in the wind,
gazing at the distant clouds and mountains,
watching the busy return of the cold geese.
Firm in his heart for learning the Way,
he wished to attain the true principle early.
After traveling for several days,
Venerable Yuǎn reached Jiāngzhōu.
He wandered through the streets and alleys,
rested for a few days,
and then set off again.
Traveling westward for over fifty *li*,
just as he was walking,
he encountered a mountain along the way.
He asked someone: "What mountain is this?"
A local replied: "This is Shān."
Venerable Yuǎn said: "When I first bid farewell to my teacher,
he instructed me to dwell wherever I encountered a mountain.
This is precisely the place for me to cultivate the Way."
Moreover, he saw that the mountain was extraordinary,
how wondrous was its unusual scenery?
Venerable Yuǎn, captivated by this mountain,
as the sun was setting in the west,
entered deep into the mountains,
seeking a place to settle.
Then, on the northern side of Xiānglú Peak's summit,
he temporarily built a thatched hut.
Taking a flint from his waist,
he struck the flint,
lit priceless precious incense,
sat cross-legged,
and began reciting the *Nirvana Sutra*,
chanting several scrolls.
At that time,
the sound of sutra recitation was clear and resonant,
heard far and near,
the Dharma melody was elegant,
the Sanskrit sounds vibrated afar.
They moved the great rocks to shake,
the hundred grasses to bow,
auspicious birds and spiritual fowl,
all came to praise and admire.
At that time,
the mountain god in his temple suddenly saw this auspicious sign,
greatly astonished and amazed,
the mountain god said: "Who is on duty today?"
At that moment, the steadfast tree god,
walked to the front of the hall and saluted,
his appearance like a bursting thunderclap,
with one head and three faces,
eyes like hanging mirrors,
holding an iron staff as tall as himself,
said: "It is Mǒuyǐ on duty."
The mountain god said: "Since it is you on duty,
I just now in this temple,
suddenly felt the mountain rocks shake,
birds and beasts startled and hurried.
Patrol and inspect this mountain for me,
to see what auspicious sign there is.
Perhaps a sage from another land
has come to this mountain of mine.
Or perhaps there are strange spirits and goblins
hiding in this mountain.
If they bring peace and happiness to this mountain of mine,
then let them be.
If they disturb the peace of this mountain,
you must immediately expel them from this mountain."
The tree god saluted,
traversed all the mountains and rivers,
searched along streams and crossed waters,
every forest and under every tree,
he searched everywhere,
but found no one.
Returning to the north side of Xiānglú Peak,
he saw a monk,
who had built a meditation hut,
sitting cross-legged,
in the midst of reciting sutras.
As soon as the tree god saw him,
he immediately concealed his ghostly and divine form,
transforming into the body of an old man,
aged like willow and reed,
hair white as mulberry and elm,
he went straight to the front of the hut,
and loudly asked after the monk's well-being.
Venerable Yuǎn said: "Ten thousand blessings."
The old man gradually approached,
bowed and said: "This disciple does not know from where the monk has come,
arriving here,
what do you seek?
I humbly beg for your compassion,
and ask you to tell me."
Venerable Yuǎn said: "This poor monk comes from Yànmén,
and now seeks refuge in this mountain,
to dwell and cultivate the Way."
The old man asked again: "Just now I heard the monk's wondrous sound,
what sound was that?"
Venerable Yuǎn said: "The sound just now
was this poor monk reciting sutras.
If any living beings hear it,
may they all be freed from suffering and attain liberation."
Hearing this, the old man
repeatedly praised, "Excellent, excellent."
He asked the monk again: "Since the monk has come here,
what do you require?"
Venerable Yuǎn said: "If this poor monk could have a temple monastery to dwell in,
to shelter from wind and frost,
that would be this poor monk's wish."
The old man said: "If you want other things, I have none,
but if you want a temple monastery,
that is a small matter.
This disciple lives in the village to the west,
I will return to the village and discuss with the many elders,
then come back to build a temple for the monk."
Having said this, the old man
took his leave from the monk and departed.
Thus, the old man bid farewell to the monk,
and about a hundred steps from the hut,
suddenly disappeared.
At that moment, he changed from the old man's body,
back to his ghostly and divine form,
came before the mountain god's temple,
bowed and saluted: "Your subject, following the great king's command,
traversed all the mountains and rivers,
searched for spirits, foxes, and demons,
but did not find a single one.
Traveling to the north side of Xiānglú Peak's summit,
I saw a monk,
who had built a meditation hut,
sitting cross-legged reciting sutras,
saying he came from Yànmén,
and now seeks refuge in this mountain,
to dwell and cultivate the Way."
Hearing this, the mountain god
exclaimed in great wonder.
"Since countless kalpas ago,
I have guarded this mountain,
and never have I seen a monk come to seek refuge here,
all have brought blessings and warded off disasters for my mountain."
The mountain god asked again: "What does the monk require here?"
The tree god reported: "I asked him just now,
and he does not want anything else,
saying he only wants a temple monastery to dwell in."
The mountain god said: "If he wanted other things, it would be difficult,
but if he wants a temple to dwell in,
that is entirely a small matter.
You need not go elsewhere,
gather the ghosts and spirits of the mountain for me,
and build a temple for this monk."
The tree god received the order,
then on the western slope,
knocked three long times,
clouds and fog darkened,
and all the mountain ghosts and spirits
arrived in full.
That night, they selected and trained divine troops,
with a hundred kinds of lightning flashes,
a thousand types of thunder roars,
noisy until dawn,
ghosts and spirits building a temple.
Until daybreak,
they built a temple,
extraordinarily wondrous.
They saw multi-storied buildings and pavilions,
no different from the Trāyastriṃśa heaven;
precious halls and terraces,
no different from the Western Paradise.
Trees and forests,
lush and blooming,
regardless of the four seasons;
spring water flowing alongside,
never ceasing in spring or winter.
Moreover, there were famous flowers and tender buds,
growing beside the path of enlightenment;
auspicious birds and spiritual fowl,
flying above the monastery.
Then Venerable Yuǎn came out of his hut and looked,
suddenly seeing a temple built,
he sighed in amazement,
pondered for a long time,
Venerable Yuǎn said: "This is not within my power,
it is the mighty power of the *Great Nirvana Sutra*."
Witnessing this rare wonder,
Venerable Yuǎn composed a verse:
"Bamboos rustle, spring throughout the four seasons,
crisscrossing streams, clear and dust-free.
Ivy on the walls, each branch green,
moss covering the ground, each spot fresh.
Secluded wilderness avoids the city's noise,
pure and empty, not mingling with the vulgar.
The mountain god built a monastery here,
to invite monks to turn the Dharma wheel."
Thereupon, Yuǎngōng entered the temple himself,
patrolling every room,
walking through every courtyard,
and found everything in order.
Only water was lacking,
with nowhere to seek it.
Yuǎngōng said: “This temple is very fine and proper,
yet there is no water,
how can one dwell here?
When the monks arrive later,
how will there be water?”
He then descended before the Buddha hall,
and saw a large rock.
Could there be water beneath it?
Yuǎngōng then struck it with his monk’s staff,
and only then obtained water,
which gushed forth from the ground.
To this day it is called the Monk’s Staff Spring.
There is a temple named the Temple of the Transformed City.
Below the temple, a stream flows,
called the White Lotus Pond.
Yuǎngōng settled into the temple to live in peace.
After about several months,
listeners from all four directions
came rushing to this temple.
On that day, Yuǎngōng extensively expounded the meaning of the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* for the assembled disciples.
For a full year thereafter,
the listeners were like clouds,
and offerings fell like rain.
Among all the listeners,
within the assembly,
it was said that there was one old man
who had listened to the sutra for a year.
They said of this old man:
When he came, he never announced his name,
when he left, he never stated his surname.
From the moment the lecture began, he would sit,
and only when the lecture ended would he finally return home.
Yuǎngōng found this deeply strange,
so he ordered his fellow monks to summon this old man for him.
The old man, having been summoned,
came directly before Yuǎngōng.
Yuǎngōng said: “Where does the old man reside?
You have listened to the Dharma for a long time,
yet I do not know your name.
I wish to know it clearly.”
The old man said: “Although this disciple has listened for a year,
he still does not understand the meaning within the *Nirvana Sutra*,
and in the end, he cannot state his name.”
Having finished speaking,
the old man walked out of the temple gate.
When they looked after him,
there was no trace whatsoever.
Who was he?
He was the dragon of the Thousand-Foot Deep Pool of the mountain,
who had come to listen to Yuǎngōng expound the Dharma.
After Yuǎngōng saw the old man leave,
he constantly reflected upon it himself,
and felt regret and self-reproach in his heart: This old man came to listen to the Dharma for a full year,
and still did not understand the principles and meanings within the *Nirvana Sutra*.
How much less could ordinary beings of sudden awakening
who hear it possibly understand?
I must now compose a commentary and subcommentary on the *Nirvana Sutra*.
Having spoken,
he announced to the Buddhas of the Ten Directions: “This disciple now, because sentient beings are deluded in mind and do not comprehend,
and have not awakened to the Mahayana,
intends to create a commentary and subcommentary on the *Nirvana Sutra*,
to enable all sentient beings to open their minds in awakening and understanding,
to gain clear comprehension of the Buddha-Dharma,
to abandon the wrong and return to the right,
and to eternally sever the traces of doubt.”
Thereupon, before the Buddha hall,
taking up the divine brush of purple cloud-fine hairs,
he announced to the Tathāgatas, the Buddhas of the Ten Directions,
and the local earth deities and spirits,
all wishing to bear witness,
saying: “If the various sages and worthies do not permit it,
may the brush immediately fall back down.”
Having spoken, he lit incense and made offerings,
announcing with a devout heart.
He then took the brush and cast it towards the sky.
At that moment, the brush stood firmly still in mid-air.
Yuǎngōng knew it accorded with the minds of the Tathāgatas, the Buddhas.
He then requested the brush to descend from the air.
How do we know this?
To this day, at Jiāngzhōu mountain, the Thrown Brush Peak still exists.
Yuǎngōng then composed the commentary and subcommentary.
For three years thereafter,
he finally completed it.
Still fearing textual errors
or principles not being understood,
he took his commentary and subcommentary, over eight hundred scrolls,
to outside the temple’s east gate, placed the commentary and subcommentary within a fire,
piled high with incense and flames,
and repeatedly announced to the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, sages, and worthies of the Ten Directions: “This disciple now, because sentient beings are deluded in mind and do not comprehend,
have not awakened to the Mahayana,
and wish to resolve doubts,
therefore composed this commentary and subcommentary.
If the sutra and its meaning correspond,
may the fire be unable to burn it.
If the commentary and subcommentary correspond with the sutra (the sutra and the commentary/subcommentary correspond),
may water be unable to drown it.”
Having spoken, he burned the commentary and subcommentary.
At that time, red flames reached the heavens,
black smoke billowed densely,
yet the sutra within
was completely unharmed.
Yuǎngōng knew the commentary and subcommentary deeply accorded with the Buddha’s mind.
Still not fully satisfied in his heart,
he again took the commentary and subcommentary, approached the bank of the White Lotus Pond,
and cast it towards the water.
The commentary and subcommentary, about ten feet above the water,
stood firmly still.
Yuǎngōng knew it deeply accorded with the Buddha’s mind.
Later, he retrieved the commentary and subcommentary and brought it into the temple,
placing it within the sutra repository.
Afterwards, the disciples were not few,
and the listeners were extremely many.
Yuǎngōng then propagated the meaning of the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* for the assembly.
It reached the point where people from all directions came to listen,
like sudden rain and rushing clouds,
competing to come and listen to the Dharma.
From beginning to end, the expounding
lasted nearly several years.
Suddenly, within the boundaries of Shòuzhōu,
there was a band of bandits,
led by a man surnamed Bái, named Zhuāng.
Speaking of this person,
he was brave and reckless in his youth,
often engaging in robbery and theft,
disregarding danger and death,
with a heart inclined toward killing.
In Bái Zhuāng’s ears,
he suddenly heard people say that on a mountain in Jiāngzhōu, there was a temple called Huàchéng,
which was extremely wealthy,
with abundant alms and offerings,
and no shortage of riches and valuables.
He gathered a gang of over five hundred followers from afar,
traveling day and night at double speed,
arriving within the boundaries of Jiāngzhōu,
where they immediately encamped and settled.
Then Bái Zhuāng said to his followers: “Do not speak of this to anyone,
for fear that others may find out.
At mealtime tomorrow,
we will raid this temple.”
The men all assented.
Thus, as the common saying goes:
“If a person makes a good vow,
Heaven will surely comply;
if a person makes an evil vow,
Heaven will surely eliminate it.”
Bái Zhuāng had just made his vow on the spot,
when it was immediately known by the local earth deity,
who secretly manifested his divine power,
coming to the mountain temple to inform the monks.
He informed every room,
and made every courtyard aware.
The earth deity announced from the air to the monks: “At mealtime tomorrow,
a band of bandits will come to raid this temple.
I urge all monks to avoid them at all costs.”
Upon hearing this, the monks,
filled with fear and terror,
each fled east and west to avoid them,
all devising plans to escape.
At that time, all the monks fled in panic,
except for Yuǎn Gōng’s senior disciple, Monk Yún Qìng,
who, out of respect for his master’s teachings and rituals,
and due to deep affection, did not dare to flee east or west.
He went straight to the master’s hut,
and addressed the master: “Just now, a divine being came to report that bandits are coming to raid this temple.
I humbly beg the master, in your compassion,
to flee east or west to avoid them.”
Yuǎn Gōng said: “Even before you knew,
I had already foreseen this matter.
As for the meaning of the Nirvana Sutra,
it is originally without fear;
if there is fear,
how can it be called Nirvana?
You and the other monks
must urgently avoid them.
I, here,
will not be able to leave.”
Seeing that the master repeatedly refused to flee,
Yún Qìng wept bitterly,
left the temple gate on his own,
and fled with the others in panic.
After seeing the monks leave,
Yuǎn Gōng sat alone in his meditation hut,
without any fear.
Soon, Bái Zhuāng led his followers to the foot of the temple.
Bái Zhuāng then deployed his troops across the ridge,
and arranged his soldiers along the long river.
They shouted until the mountains crumbled and rocks split,
running wildly east and west,
charging north and south,
all rushing into the temple,
shouting only to capture alive.
When Bái Zhuāng entered the temple,
expecting vast wealth,
he searched every courtyard,
but found nothing in the temple.
Bái Zhuāng said: “How strange!
When I discussed this yesterday,
no one knew about it.
Who informed the temple,
causing everyone to flee east and west?”
Bái Zhuāng ordered his men: “Search inside and outside the temple for me,
everywhere.
If you capture any monks,
bring them to me quickly.”
The men assented,
searched everywhere,
but found no one.
When they reached the east gate of the temple,
they saw a monk sitting peacefully
inside a meditation hut.
The men did not dare to startle him,
but turned back and entered the temple,
going straight to Bái Zhuāng,
and reported: “Just now, following the general’s orders,
we searched inside and outside the temple for monks,
but found none anywhere.
When we reached outside the temple gate,
we saw a monk,
and dared not fail to report it.”
Bái Zhuāng said: “Where is the monk?”
The men reported to the general: “He is sitting in the meditation hut outside the east gate of the temple.”
Then Bái Zhuāng took the reins and mounted his horse,
going straight to the east gate of the temple,
and indeed saw a monk sitting cross-legged inside the hut.
Bái Zhuāng called out loudly,
ordering his men to bring him before his horse.
He asked Yuǎn Gōng: “What money, valuables, or clothing does your temple have?
Bring them out quickly!”
Yuǎn Gōng stepped forward,
and said to Bái Zhuāng: “This temple has always been poor and empty,
with nothing at all.
Even if there were some alms,
they were always used for daily expenses and offerings,
so there are truly no riches or valuables.
I dare not deceive the general.”
Then Bái Zhuāng carefully observed Yuǎn Gōng,
and felt admiration in his heart.
Because Yuǎn Gōng had the appearance of a bodhisattva,
with a silver-white halo around his body,
a height of seven feet,
hair as black as lacquer,
and lips as red as cinnabar.
At first sight,
Bái Zhuāng said to his men: “This monk
is fit to serve me.”
Bái Zhuāng said: “I want you to be my servant.
Will you agree?”
Yuǎn Gōng stepped forward: “I am willing to give up this body to serve the general as a slave,
and am willing to serve before your horse.”
Yuǎn Gōng said: “There is one more small matter
I must report.
Does the general want my body,
or does the general want my vocation?”
Bái Zhuāng said: “What is the body?
What is the vocation?”
Yuǎn Gōng said: “My vocation is reciting sutras.
If the general wants me to serve,
it is only this body.
If the general wants my body,
you must not hinder my recitation of sutras.”
Bái Zhuāng said: “As long as I have you to serve me,
who would hinder your recitation of sutras?”
Yuǎn Gōng assented,
and followed behind him.
After walking about a hundred steps from the temple,
Yuǎn Gōng again addressed the general: “Allow me to return to the temple,
remove these monk’s robes inside the temple,
and then return here,
willing to follow the general’s banner.”
Bái Zhuāng said: “Return quickly,
do not make me suspicious.
If you are late,
I will send men to capture you,
and have you cut into three pieces before my horse.
Do not say I did not warn you.”
Yuǎn Gōng assented,
entered the temple, and stood before the hall.
At that time, his senior disciple Yún Qìng was on a high peak,
saw his master inside the temple,
rushed down the mountain,
went straight to the master’s presence,
and addressed the master: “Just now, when the violent bandits charged,
I was extremely frightened,
but now I am glad the bandit army has withdrawn,
and I congratulate the master.”
Yuǎn Gōng said: “As for the meaning of the Nirvana Sutra,
it is originally without fear;
if there is fear,
how can it be called Nirvana?
From now on,
you must diligently strive,
and uphold the teachings well.
I am now parting from you forever, as if separated by life and death.”
Yún Qìng asked the master: “Why do you speak such words?”
Yuǎn Gōng said: “I just made a vow outside the gate,
to become a slave to that general,
and can no longer stay here.
You must strive hard in the future.”
Hearing this, Yún Qìng
threw himself to the ground,
and from his seven orifices,
fresh blood flowed.
After a long time, he revived,
and rose from the ground.
Then he composed a verse:
“We are like birds in flight,
the master is like a great tree.
Now that the great tree has been moved,
where shall the flock perch?
Where has the transformed body gone?
Only the words of Nirvana remain.
I pray for the lamp of wisdom to shine,
do not forget the path lost in confusion.”
After Yúnqìng finished speaking,
he turned and wept even more sorrowfully.
Yuǎngōng said, “I fear the general will blame me for delay.”
He walked out of the temple gate,
chased after his banners,
and followed behind him.
Days passed and months went by,
following him for several years.
After Yúnqìng saw the monk depart,
he gathered the monastic assembly again,
opened the lecture hall with the Commentary on the Nirvana Sutra,
and all the listeners
shed tears like rain,
as if seeing the great master no different.
Then Yúnqìng, seeing no news of the monk for several years,
entrusted the Commentary on the Nirvana Sutra to Monk Dào’ān.
After Dào’ān received the Commentary on the Nirvana Sutra,
he took it to the Fúguāng Temple in the eastern capital to open the lecture hall.
Not knowing what kind of person Dào’ān was,
he attracted listeners like clouds,
and offerings fell like rain.
At that time, Emperor Wén of Jin was ruling the eastern capital,
and when Dào’ān lectured,
he caused flowers from heaven to scatter in profusion,
with delightful fragrances.
He caused five-colored clouds to appear,
and the crowd grew even larger,
countless listeners
trampled the lecture hall,
unable to open it.
Dào’ān then wrote a memorial to report to Emperor Wén of Jin: “Your servant, following the decree,
lectured on the Nirvana Sutra at Fúguāng Temple.
The listeners grew too numerous,
disrupting the Dharma assembly,
unable to open it.
I humbly beg for an edict,
to grant separate instructions.”
At that time, it was decreed: “If one wishes to hear Dào’ān lecture,
each person must pay one bolt of silk
to listen for one day.”
At that time, due to peaceful conditions,
all goods were cheap,
and each day, those paying one bolt of silk
numbered about twenty or thirty thousand.
The temple was narrow and small,
with no place to arrange them.
He wrote another memorial to report to the emperor: “Your servant, following the decree,
opened the lecture hall at Fúguāng Temple.
Considering the previous order to pay one bolt of silk,
the listeners grew even more,
making it difficult to control.
I humbly beg for further instructions.”
At that time, it was decreed: “If one wishes to hear Dào’ān lecture,
each person must pay one hundred strings of cash
to listen for one day.”
With such restrictions,
daily attendance did not drop below three to five thousand people
coming to hear Dào’ān lecture in the eastern capital.
Where was Yuǎngōng still?
Yuǎngōng often followed Báizhuāng, plundering every prefecture they encountered,
looting every county they passed,
roaming the rivers and fields by day,
lodging in mountains and forests by night,
with disheveled hair and eyebrows,
wearing coarse short garments,
always following behind him.
After several years,
he longed for the monastic life,
with no way to re-enter.
Moreover, Báizhuāng repeatedly committed evil deeds,
consorting with violent men,
fond of killing and averse to life,
living by robbery.
Suddenly one day,
while in the mountains,
Báizhuāng settled on the eastern ridge,
and Yuǎngōng stayed on the western slope.
At that time,
the autumn wind suddenly rose,
leaves drifted down,
the mountains were quiet, the woods sparse,
frost clung to the grass and trees.
The wind passed through the forest,
rustling bamboo like silk,
the moon shone on the blue sky,
crimson clouds like brocade.
By the flowing water,
he felt melancholy.
Drowsily falling asleep,
he saw in a dream the buddhas of the ten directions,
all appearing among the clouds,
immeasurable sages,
all coming here.
They called out: “Bodhisattva, arise,
do not cling to the sleep of ignorance,
attain the state of nirvana,
why not recite the Nirvana Sutra for sentient beings?”
In the dream, Yuǎngōng paid homage without cease,
Yuǎngōng was a complete ordinary person,
moved by Akṣobhya Buddha to receive a prediction,
calling Yuǎngōng forward: “Do not feel disheartened in your heart.
You have an old debt unpaid,
because in a past life you acted as a guarantor,
in this life you must settle accounts,
the creditor is not far,
it is the current chancellor, Chánglín Xiànggong.
Later, you will sell this body,
obtain five hundred strings of cash to repay Báizhuāng,
then return to the mountains,
and meet with you.”
Yuǎngōng awoke from the dream startled,
extremely disheartened,
then sat up,
and recited several scrolls of the Nirvana Sutra.
Báizhuāng, startled on the eastern ridge,
asked his attendants: “What sound is that from the west?”
The attendants said: “Reporting, General,
it is the sound of the lowly slave captured reciting sutras.”
Hearing this, Báizhuāng
became extremely angry,
summoned Yuǎngōng before him,
and loudly rebuked: “If you were in a temple monastery,
you could recite as you wish.
But now you are following me,
how can you recite sutras!”
Yuǎngōng said: “When the general captured this lowly slave,
he allowed recitation of sutras.”
Báizhuāng said: “When did I ever allow you to recite sutras?”
Yuǎngōng immediately fell silent,
but the attendants said: “General, you did indeed allow him to recite sutras.”
Báizhuāng said: “Reciting sutras is a trivial matter,
we each carry weapons,
and do not wish to hear sutra recitation.”
Yuǎngōng said: “If reciting is not allowed,
may I not recite aloud,
but silently, is that permissible?”
Báizhuāng said: “No,
because when I captured you,
first, I gained no money or goods,
second, I had no followers,
so in anger,
I captured you.
Now I have no shortage of men,
plenty of manpower,
so I will release you back to the mountains,
to practice as you wish.”
Yuǎngōng said: “I gave up my body to serve as your slave,
I must serve you for a lifetime,
to abandon you midway,
what kind of giving up is that?
If you still want service,
I will say no more;
if you no longer want this lowly slave,
then sell me anywhere,
use the money to buy wine and meat for yourself,
is that permissible?”
Hearing this, Báizhuāng
laughed heartily: “You are greatly mistaken,
if I had bought you from somewhere,
I could use the old contract
to sell you.
But since I captured you,
how can I sell you?”
Yuǎngōng said: “If you do not sell me,
I will say no more;
if you wish to sell me,
sell me as a household-born slave,
then there is no contract.”
Báizhuāng said: “Where do you expect me to sell you?”
Yuǎngōng said: “If you wish to sell this lowly slave,
take me to the eastern capital to sell.”
Hearing this, Báizhuāng
became fiercely angry: “This lowly wretch’s mind is unchanged, without cunning.
You plan to reach the eastern capital,
see the high and low officials,
go to the sutra platform to file a complaint,
say I am a bandit,
and have me captured.”
Yuǎngōng said: “If this lowly slave had such intent,
to scheme against you,
may in the future life
I die and fall into hell,
with no chance of escape.
Please, do not worry,
this is certainly not the case.”
Hearing this, Báizhuāng
believed him.
He then dispersed his followers,
keeping only three or five men,
acting as merchants,
taking a few horses,
carrying various goods,
heading straight for the eastern capital,
to sell Yuǎngōng,
to the livestock market to sell.
At this time, Yuǎngōng arrived in the marketplace,
holding a sign and offering himself for sale.
At that moment, thousands upon thousands of people,
could not help but sigh in admiration.
Moreover, seeing Yuǎngōng's sign,
his stature was seven feet tall,
with a radiance like silver,
a broad forehead and high eyebrows,
a face as full as the moon,
hair as black as lacquer,
lips as if touched with vermilion.
His gait was like that of an ox king,
his hands hanging past his knees,
walking with measured steps east and west.
The onlookers sighed in admiration,
none failing to cherish him.
At that time, the spectators formed groups of three and lines of five:
"In my life, I have seen thousands of noble and lowly people,
but truly I have never seen such a one."
Amid their sighs of admiration,
the crowd grew larger.
At this moment, Yuǎngōng felt sorrow in his heart,
resenting his own fate,
knowing that his past debts remained unsettled,
and he waited solely to sell himself to repay Bái Zhuāng.
In an instant,
he moved the Emperor of Heaven to descend in transformed form,
appearing as a servant of Minister Cuī,
coming directly to the livestock market,
calling out loudly to the livestock broker:
"This slave,
must not be sold anywhere else;
only the household of Minister Cuī, the current dynasty's prime minister,
is fit for this person.
If it were any other family,
they could not buy him."
The broker, hearing these words,
fully acknowledged the truth of the matter.
At that time, Bái Zhuāng also followed behind,
and Yuǎngōng said:
"Master, you need not come further;
whatever good or ill lies ahead,
this lowly slave will bear it.
If the minister is pleased,
the money obtained,
you, Master, shall receive every bit."
Bái Zhuāng said:
"You must handle the matters ahead properly,
Yuǎngōng assented.
He then followed the broker,
straight to the minister's gate.
The gatekeeper asked the broker:
"Who sent you here?"
because this slave
dare not be sold elsewhere,
and have specially come to offer him to the minister's household."
The gatekeeper said:
"Wait here for now,
The gatekeeper went to the hall and informed the minister:
"At the gate, there is a slave broker
and I dared not fail to report it."
The minister said:
"Have them brought in."
and the broker led Yuǎngōng in,
straight to the front of the hall,
where he saw the minister,
bowed deeply,
and stood to one side.
At first sight,
"Last night in a dream, I saw a divine being
enter my residence;
today, seeing this slave,
could it be the fulfillment of my dream?"
The minister asked the broker:
"Is this a household-born slave of Bái Zhuāng,
The broker replied to the minister:
"He is a household-born slave of Bái Zhuāng."
"Since he is a household-born slave of Bái Zhuāng,
The minister asked the broker:
"How much money is wanted for this slave?"
Before the broker could speak,
Yuǎngōng stepped forward and addressed the minister:
"If you wish to buy this lowly slave,
The minister said:
"What skills do you possess
That is not a small amount;
briefly describe your skills for me to see."
Yuǎngōng replied:
"This lowly slave can know a family's wealth from three hundred years past,
I can fold clothes,
prepare seasonal decoctions and medicines.
I can convey messages,
and there is no question I cannot answer.
I am roughly familiar with several styles
of various schools of calligraphy.
In single combat,
I am ready for any challenge.
I can hoe crops and reap wheat,
albeit with modest skill.
In matters of trade and exchange,
I know all the ins and outs.
If put to work under your command,
I will come like the wind,
truly not sluggish or negligent.
If you do not believe, Minister,
this lowly slave will personally write a deed of self-sale,
and you will know the truth."
The minister instructed his attendants
to fetch paper and brush and hand them over.
Yuǎngōng received the paper and brush,
then requested an incense burner,
immediately performed the ritual,
bowed in thanks to the minister,
and before the hall wrote his deed of self-sale,
unlike any ordinary one.
Yuǎngōng declared:
"On such-and-such year, such-and-such month, I sell myself to the minister as a slave,
completing a lifetime for my master.
If I am abandoned midway,
in the life to come,
I shall fall into hell.
After suffering my punishment,
I shall be reborn as an animal,
saddled and bridled,
with a bit in my mouth,
bearing my past transgressions.
If I serve my master for a full lifetime,
then in the life to come,
the ten stages of fruition shall be perfected,
and I shall be reborn in the assembly of Buddhas."
Once the deed was written,
he handed it to the minister.
The minister received it,
and could only exclaim in great wonder,
thinking, "Could this be a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva who has come to my home?"
He then ordered money to be fetched and given to the broker—five hundred strings of cash,
which were immediately handed over to Bái Zhuāng.
Bái Zhuāng, having received the money,
dared not stay any longer and returned to the boundaries of Shòuzhōu.
The master purchased the lowly slave,
and immediately ordered the servants of the Western Courtyard to take him and settle him in a room.
Yuǎngōng, knowing he was repaying a debt,
dared not harbor resentment toward others.
In all his comings and goings,
he submitted entirely to being driven by whip and spur.
One day, Yuǎngōng happened to be
sitting alone in his room.
The night was late, the hour deep.
As he trimmed the dying lamp,
he saw the River of Heaven serene and still,
the moon bright in the vast sky.
After sitting for a long while,
he grew drowsy and fell asleep.
Then, in a dream, he saw the Buddhas of the Ten Directions
all manifesting in the empty sky,
and immeasurable saints and sages
gathering like clouds.
They called out: "Bodhisattva, arise!
Do not cling to the sleep of ignorance.
Having attained the state of Nirvāṇa,
why do you not recite sutras for the sake of all beings?"
Yuǎngōng was thus startled awake.
He sat up and recited the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*
until daybreak.
At that time, the master in the main hall
suddenly heard the sound of sutra recitation and arose.
Gradually, walking alone,
he came before the gate of the Western Courtyard
to listen to the recitation.
He then ordered his attendants to respectfully invite his wife.
The wife, having received the invitation,
came to the western gate.
The master and his wife listened to the sutra recitation
until daybreak.
The next morning,
after the master returned from court,
he ascended the hall and sat down,
then ordered his attendants to summon the servants of the Western Courtyard to come.
At that time, thirty servants all arrived before the hall.
The master asked: "Last night in the Western Courtyard,
which servant's voice was that reciting the sutra?"
Then a servant, the head of the group, addressed the master, saying: "Last night's recitation
was certainly not anyone else;
it was the voice of the newly purchased lowly slave reciting the sutra."
Hearing that the newly arrived lowly slave had recited the sutra,
the master asked Yuǎngōng: "Last night's recitation,
was it you?"
Yuǎngōng said: "It was the voice of this lowly slave reciting the sutra."
The master asked: "What is the title of the sutra?"
Yuǎngōng replied: "What was recited last night
was the *Great Nirvāṇa Sūtra*."
The master asked: "How many scrolls of it have you recited?"
Yuǎngōng replied: "This lowly slave has recited one set of twelve scrolls,
all of which were recited through last night."
The master said: "Do not speak idly."
Yuǎngōng said: "How would I dare deceive the master?"
The master then had Yuǎngōng sit down again
to recite the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*.
Thereupon, Yuǎngōng restated the title
and raised his voice in recitation once more.
From the beginning to the end of his recitation,
there was not a single omission or error.
Seeing this, the master
repeatedly praised, "Excellent!"
He then summoned over three hundred people, great and small, noble and base, from the household,
all to gather before the hall.
The master instructed:
"From this day forward,
no one may look down upon
this newly arrived lowly slave.
Moreover, he is given an external name:
he shall be called Shànqìng."
Every day after returning from court,
the minister would often go to Fúguāng Temple to listen to Dào'ān expound the scriptures,
donating one hundred strings of cash.
On the following day,
he brought Shànqìng along to the temple.
Because Shànqìng had just begun serving the minister,
he was not allowed to enter the temple to listen to the sutra,
and only stayed outside the temple gate to watch the horses.
In a short while,
he saw the audience rushing like clouds and rain,
all entering the temple.
Soon the bell ceased ringing,
and the sutra topic was raised,
the Sanskrit sounds resonating far and wide,
gradually reaching his ears.
Hearing this, Shànqìng
felt sorrowful in his heart.
Yuǎngōng said: “I do not know what kind of person Dào'ān is,
that he can expound and praise with such great understanding.
I wish that one day I may again ascend the high seat,
re-attain the fruit of the ten stages,
and dispel calamities for all sentient beings.
Whether with form or without form,
with characteristics or without characteristics,
all are extinguished and liberated through Nirvana.”
In a short while,
the lecture ended,
and men and women dispersed together.
The minister returned home,
and after resting in the hall,
he ascended the hall and sat down.
The lady covered her sleeves and came directly before the minister,
addressing him: “For several years now,
at Fúguāng Temple,
you have listened to the Venerable Dào'ān expound the *Nirvana Sutra*;
what Dharma have you heard?
It is said that the meaning of the *Nirvana Sutra*
is immeasurable and boundless;
how much of the sutra text does the minister remember?
Why do you remain silent and say nothing,
and not even speak a half-verse of gāthā to your humble wife?”
The minister said: “Has the lady ever read the *Lotus Sutra*?”
The lady said: “I have read the *Lotus Sutra*.”
The minister said:
“The sutra states: If one does not request it,
even upon hearing, one will not listen.”
The lady said: “I ask the minister to briefly explain a little to the noble and lowly within the household,
so that our minds may open with understanding.”
The minister said: “Very well,
I will explain the meaning within the *Nirvana Sutra* to the lady.”
The lady then ordered the household to sweep and clean the hall,
set up high seats,
and summoned over three hundred people, noble and lowly, great and small,
all gathered before the hall,
to request the minister to explain the meaning within the *Nirvana Sutra*,
and everyone listened in silence.
That night, the minister first explained to the lady the eight sufferings that torment one another.
First, he explained the “suffering of birth.”
The suffering of birth means that when the body is conceived and sheltered in the mother’s womb,
in the months nearing birth,
it is like butter or cheese.
Within ninety days,
it gradually takes shape;
if a boy, he lies on the mother’s left side,
if a girl, she clings to the mother’s right flank,
close to the heart and liver,
receiving breath to form the body,
and thus endures all sufferings.
Wise and foolish are the same,
noble and lowly also alike.
The kindness of a loving mother
should be without two kinds.
When the mother eats hot food,
it is no different from boiling cauldron water scalding the body;
when the mother eats cold things,
it is just like the icy hell.
If the mother eats her fill,
it is like being between pressing stones;
if the mother is hungry,
the child suffers the agony of being hung upside down.
When ten months are fulfilled,
and birth is about to occur,
all the joints open wide,
like being sawn apart.
Until the four limbs are broken,
the five viscera ache with pain,
no different from being cut by a knife,
how unlike being sliced by a sword.
Through a thousand births and ten thousand deaths,
one faints and knows nothing,
life hangs by a thread,
with no hope of living again.
In a moment, mother and child separate,
blood flows like a slaughtered sheep;
in her dazed confusion, the mother
asks whether it is a boy or a girl.
If told it is a girl,
she is content that mother and child have separated safely.
If told it is a boy,
she completely forgets the pain in all her joints;
in her dazed confusion,
she immediately smiles with joy—
this is called a filial son.
But if it is an unfilial child,
how is the delivery?
Inside the mother’s womb,
it causes the mother distress,
kicking and trampling the mother,
never resting for a moment,
suddenly staying near the heart,
suddenly moving to the waist,
within the five viscera,
there is nowhere it does not reach.
After ten months it is born,
then it grabs the mother’s heart and liver with its hands,
stomps on the mother’s hip bones with its feet;
for three days or five days,
it refuses to be peaceful.
From this, the mother’s life force rapidly declines,
the mother seems near death,
her cries shake the earth,
like a sword carving the heart.
Brothers and mother
do not know what to do.
Enemies and creditors
cease only when life is gone.
Having first endured the child,
she must still die later—
this is called the “suffering of birth.”
That night, the minister also explained the “suffering of old age” to the lady.
The suffering of old age means
that even if a person lives a hundred years,
it is like a spark from a flint.
In a short while,
one reaches seventy or eighty,
with strength and energy declining.
In youth, the voice was clear,
the appearance like spring flowers;
now that old age has come,
how different from autumn grass?
Skin like chicken’s, hair like crane’s,
often dry and withered.
Eyes dim, ears deaf,
unable to distinguish blue from yellow.
The four limbs heavy,
all bones sore and aching.
Drawing farther from heaven,
drawing closer to earth.
Lying on the bed at night,
tossing and turning a thousand times,
unable to do anything.
All worldly affairs
are like in a dream.
Do you not see the peach and plum trees by the roadside,
blossoming year after year?
Where are the beauties of old,
where are they now?
If old age and sickness come to invade,
white hair has no chance to turn black again.
The vigor of youth
withers with the changing seasons;
the beauty of old
alters with the four times.
All people grow old,
noble and lowly alike;
whether wise or foolish,
all share this suffering of old age.
Better to hear early
and cultivate fields of merit;
human life is but an instant,
watch as it passes from the world.
One must be diligent,
and then practice cultivation;
once the human body is lost,
there is no way to regain it.
This is called the “suffering of old age.”
That night, the gentleman explained to his wife the "suffering of illness."
His wife then asked, "What is called the suffering of illness?
"The suffering of illness is this:
within the four great elements,
how could there ever be anything substantial?
They are a provisional combination of various conditions—
earth, water, fire, and wind.
If a single vessel is not in harmony,
illness arises in full.
Suddenly, one is gravely ill and confined to bed;
the hun and pò souls are unsettled;
the five spirits are all lost.
Lips are parched, tongue shriveled;
brain aches, head throbs.
Between all the joints of the bones,
it feels as if being sawn apart.
Suffering day and night,
with no respite,
one cannot seek life,
nor can one seek death.
The wondrous arts of the world
only treat those with life remaining;
how can they save those destined to die?
Even if there were medicine,
it could not heal the damage.
Day after day, night after night,
one endures all manner of great suffering.
Even if Jìpó prepared strong medicine,
or Biǎnquè applied acupuncture,
when the illness of death arrives,
none can avoid it.
People in the world vainly accept false teachings;
before falling ill in bed,
they make offerings to spirits and ghosts,
burn paper money to lift prohibitions,
needlessly killing many beings.
Such people
fall into the hells.
The great limit does not exceed a hundred years;
among these, reaching seventy is already rare.
If three people together live a hundred years,
how much time is that, really?
If, in human life in this world,
there were wondrous arts,
there ought to be people living a thousand years.
Why not carefully reflect three times,
instead of vainly suffering the deceptions and intimidations of masters?
This is what is called the 'suffering of illness.'"
That night, the gentleman explained to his wife the "suffering of death."
The suffering of death is this:
the four great elements are about to return to extinction;
the hun and pò souls are driven and scattered by the wind.
Brothers part forever;
father and mother are eternally separated.
Wife, children, sons, and daughters—
there is no way to meet again.
Friends with whom one associated and visited—
once parted, there is no chance to see them again.
Gold, silver, coins, and goods—
one must let them be divided and taken away.
Inns, shops, manors, and gardens—
one cannot take them along.
Clinging and attachment bring the suffering of death;
the four great elements separate;
the hun and pò souls fly and scatter,
none knows where they go.
When the three inches of breath are cut off,
that is the next life.
Once a person dies,
when will they be reborn?
In life, one contends as a hero;
in death, one's fortune and virtue are discussed.
According to one's karma, one receives
and is assigned wherever it dictates.
One may dwell in the hells,
or in the heavenly realms,
or become an animal,
or become a hungry ghost.
In the six paths of rebirth,
there is no respite.
To regain a human body
is one hope in ten thousand.
This is what is called the suffering of death.
That night, the gentleman further explained to his wife the "suffering of the five aggregates."
The suffering of the five aggregates is this:
Human life in this world
is like day and night.
Pus, blood, skin, and flesh,
though adorned with fine silks wrapping the body—
within the five aggregates,
the seven apertures constantly flow.
Inside, they harbor the stench of filth and putridity;
outside, blood courses over the bones.
Just look at the pus-filled sack, the mucus and saliva—
day and night, they constantly flow.
Everywhere is unbearable,
entirely lacking true substance.
All desires arise from the three inches of breath;
they are the sprouts of the three poisons,
the root of the five viscera and the five desires.
Therefore, the great master has a verse:
A thin-skinned sack of pus and blood,
sinews binding stinking bones.
Observing from head to foot,
the entire body flows with pus.
Such are the many kinds of suffering
that afflict the body.
This is what is called the 'suffering of the five aggregates.'"
That night, the gentleman further explained to his wife the "suffering of not obtaining what one seeks."
The suffering of not obtaining what one seeks is this:
In human life in this world,
each person has their own pursuits.
Those who wish for blessings
seek the unsurpassed bodhi.
Yet within the three periods of time,
how many obtain the fortune of rebirth in the heavens?
How many can enjoy worldly glory,
obtain wealth and resources in the human realm,
only to meet untimely death midway?
If one seeks gold, silver, silks, and cloth,
in kalpa after kalpa, the mind craves glory.
Even if one obtains clothing and food,
it is never enough to satisfy oneself.
Father, mother, brothers—
each must seek their own cure.
Bearing sons and raising daughters,
each goes their own way to seek.
If not planted in a previous life,
not cultivated over countless kalpas,
and one desires worldly glory,
one must cultivate fortune in this present life.
Today, I earnestly urge the listeners
to understand that clothing and food are predetermined by past lives.
Therefore, the great master has a verse:
This year certainly leads to the next;
why not plant the grain for the coming year?
This life certainly leads to the next;
why not cultivate fortune for the coming life?
Such are the many kinds
of this, which is called the 'suffering of not obtaining what one seeks.'"
That night, the gentleman further explained to his wife the "suffering of meeting with the hated."
The suffering of meeting with the hated is this:
In human life in this world,
greed and desire reside in the heart.
Seeing others have wives,
one then desires to seek a wife.
Once a wife is obtained,
within two or three years,
sons and daughters are born.
What does this resemble?
It resembles a butterfly gathering flowers,
circling and hovering in empty space.
Suddenly, it sees a peony blossom,
and goes to gather its fragrant stamens.
Unaware, a spider is upon it,
spinning round and round,
a hundred coils, a thousand layers,
wrapping the butterfly,
trapping it within,
with no way out despite all attempts.
This is the suffering.
Ordinary people's love for beauty
is also like this.
Seeing another's youth,
they give rise to a heart of admiration and longing.
As months and years deepen,
eventually, sons and daughters appear.
Once they grow into adulthood,
they are unfilial to their parents,
their offenses against heaven are extreme,
they do not associate with the wise,
but keep company with wicked fellows.
Their speech shows no forethought;
they insult and disgrace the six kinds of relatives
and even their elders.
If at home,
they immediately exhaust people's energy and resources.
If they go out,
one must constantly worry and fear.
These are called enemies from many lives,
continuing world after world without end.
I earnestly urge with good cause,
so the listeners may understand:
If you wish to have no enemies in later lives,
better cultivate pure conduct in this present life.
Enemies will be forever separated,
not disturbing your heart and mind.
The causes and conditions of sons and daughters—
how much is contained within them?
Therefore, the great master has a verse:
Since time without beginning, receiving the deep current,
in the six paths of rebirth, cycling everywhere.
If not decisively severed in this life,
when will the retribution between enemies ever cease?
This is what is called the 'suffering of meeting with the hated.'"
That night, the gentleman again explained to his wife the "suffering of separation from the beloved."
[The suffering of separation from the beloved] refers to this:
if a family raises a son,
whom the parents cherish like pearls and jade,
and who grows into adulthood,
just as he begins to distinguish east from west,
he immediately leaves his hometown and parts from his village.
Day and night, his parents anxiously long for him,
leaning against the door each morning,
until they weep with sorrow.
From this, longing turns into illness,
and they are cared for and given medicine,
wondering when they will see him again.
Suddenly, when the winter festival and New Year arrive,
with all close relatives gathered before their eyes,
they suddenly remember the son who is away from home,
and their chests fill with choked sobs.
This is what is called the "suffering of separation from the beloved."
That night, after the Xianggong had finished expounding on the eight sufferings and their torment,
all three hundred or so people in the residence, high and low, noble and base,
bowed in gratitude to the Xianggong.
Only Shànqìng shed tears profusely.
Shànqìng did not speak,
but pondered in his heart: I recall in my days in the mountains,
when I first lectured on the title of this sūtra,
it immediately caused the great rocks to shake,
the hundred grasses to bow,
auspicious birds and spiritual fowl
flew and filled the temple.
Auspicious clouds did not disperse,
constantly drifting by the side of the purple halls;
propitious qi swirled,
never leaving the vicinity of the vermilion towers.
The devas heard the Dharma,
the ten classes heard the sūtra,
those with form and those without form,
those with characteristics and those without characteristics,
all proceeded towards nirvāṇa and entered parinirvāṇa.
Having finished his contemplation, Shànqìng
had eyes full of tears.
The Xianggong found this strange,
and asked Shànqìng: "I have been explaining the sūtra to you all,
what reason is there for you to weep so frequently?
Are you perhaps resentful of someone?
If you understand matters, quickly explain the reason;
if you do not speak, you will soon feel the staff."
Shànqìng stepped forward,
and addressed the Xianggong: "This lowly slave does not resent anyone else,
it is only because the Venerable Dào'ān expounds the Dharma,
he is utterly incapable of doing so equally."
The Xianggong said: "That Venerable Dào'ān himself came to the capital to lecture and praise [the Dharma],
princes, marquises, generals, and ministers
listen to him expound the Dharma daily.
You have not yet heard him expound the Dharma,
how can you know that his lecturing and praise are not equal?"
Shànqìng stepped forward,
and addressed the Xianggong: "Last night, Shànqìng followed my lord into the temple,
but was left outside the gate,
and could not hear the sūtra.
That is how I know the Venerable Dào'ān expounds the Dharma unequally.
Although this lowly slave's body resides in lowliness,
I have a slight understanding of the Buddha-Dharma.
Though monastic robes differ,
the Dharma should be without duality.
From this, I know Dào'ān expounds the Dharma unequally;
he does not understand how to transmit the Dharma into the ears of the three grades of people,
nor to the four kinds of birth and the ten classes.
" The Xianggong said: "What are called the four kinds of birth and the ten classes,
and the three grades of people?
Explain them to me in detail,
so that my mind may open in understanding,
and I may grasp the Buddha-Dharma clearly."
Shànqìng said: "The three grades of people are:
first, the sick lying in bed;
second, prisoners in confinement;
third, those who are not free.
The Dharma Master on the high seat does not understand skillful means,
to universally reach and transmit [the Dharma] into the ears of these three grades of people.
Having such a fault,
therefore his exposition of the Dharma is not equal."
The Xianggong said: "What are the four kinds of birth and ten classes?"
Shànqìng addressed the Xianggong: "The four kinds of birth are:
birth from womb, birth from egg, birth from moisture, and birth by transformation.
These are the four kinds of birth.
The ten classes are:

those with form, those without form, those with characteristics, those without characteristics, those not-with-characteristics, those not-without-characteristics, four-footed, two-footed, many-footed, and footless.
These are called the ten classes."
The Xianggong said to Shànqìng: "Because I do not understand,
explain them to me in detail,
and I will abandon the wrong and return to the right."
Shànqìng said: "Birth from womb:
these are people who listen to the Dharma.
Suppose two people come to the temple to listen to the sūtra.
One is without a greedy nature,
enters the temple and listens to the sūtra;
one has a greedy nature,
and immediately turns back and leaves.
The one who enters the temple,
sits settled in the Hall of Good Dharma,
hears a single phrase of wondrous Dharma,
which enters his body and mind,
and immediately his mind gives rise to joy.
Suddenly he remembers the person who did not come,
and immediately his mind gives rise to forgetfulness,
even if words are spoken, he cannot listen and receive them,
depressed and unceasing.
Like a child in its mother's womb,
obscured by floating clouds covering the sun,
gradually, over time,
he falls into birth from womb.
Birth from egg:
these are also people who listen to the Dharma.
They come to the temple to listen to the sūtra,
sit before the Hall of Good Dharma,
their minds wishing to attach to the Dharma Master,
but the Dharma Master does not understand,
and only speaks of external conditions.
What kind of Dharma can he then speak to them?
Sentient beings are confused and dim,
difficult to awaken, difficult to understand,
depressed and unceasing,
thus they fall into birth from egg.
Birth from moisture:
such people mostly receive the Dharma in secret,
obtaining a single phrase or verse,
yet never speak it to others,
greedily cherishing it to benefit themselves,
not understanding how to proclaim it for the multitude.
Because of this cause and condition,
they fall into birth from moisture.
Birth by transformation:
suppose they enter the temple to listen to the Dharma,
obtain a single phrase of wondrous Dharma,
discriminate it into measureless and boundless [meanings],
expound the principles and texts, leading and teaching,
like the sands of the Ganges,
like one lamp lit,
for ten lamps also a hundred lamps,
for a thousand lamps also hundreds, thousands, tens of thousands, millions of lamps,
lamps upon lamps unceasing,
this is called birth by transformation."
Thereupon the Xianggong asked: "What are the ten classes?"
Shànqìng said: "First,
those with form:
seeing clay niches and sculpted images,
they immediately bow with a humble mind,
directly saying the Buddha is like Mount Sumeru,
seeing the form gives rise to the mind,
this is called 'with form'.
Second,
those without form:
not establishing a nature, not seeing a nature,
like the moon in water,
the wind in the sky,
all dharmas are nonexistent,
utterly without anything,
this is called 'without form'.
Third,
those with characteristics:
if on the streets they see a handsome person,
they say it was cultivated in a previous state.
Coming into the temple to listen to the Dharma,
seeing the Dharma Master plump and fair,
they immediately give rise to affection and attachment in their minds,
and are immediately bound by entanglement;
since there is entanglement,
there is false thought;
since there is false thought,
there is ignorance;
since there is ignorance,
there are afflictions;
since there are afflictions,
there is sinking and drowning;
since there is sinking and drowning,
there is hell;
for kalpas upon kalpas they transgress,
body and mind unsettled,
immediately receiving their suffering,
this is called 'with characteristics'.
Fourth,
those without characteristics:
all dharmas are empty,
how could they ever be real?
East and west leave no trace,
north and south leave no trail.
These matters do not pertain to body and mind,
the one substance far transcends the three realms,
this is called 'without characteristics'.
Fifth,
those not-with-characteristics:
when speaking, they exist;
when speech ends, they return to nonexistence;
when established, they exist;
when not established, they return to nonexistence.
When believed, they exist;
when not believed, they return to nonexistence.
All dharmas do not pertain to body and mind,
this is called 'not-with-characteristics'.
Sixth,
those not-without-characteristics:
without speech, without words,
without going, without coming,
without movement, without thought,
without birth, without extinction,
this is Suchness.
Without going, without coming,
then it is the Buddha-nature,
this is called 'not-without-characteristics'.
Seventh,
two-footed:
humans living in the world,
having body and wisdom is superficially called 'two-footed'.
Some have body but lack wisdom,
some have wisdom but lack body.
Only this body and wisdom,
if they do not meet,
therefore sink and revolve in evil paths;
if body and wisdom do meet,
Thus is born the Buddha's path.
Therefore, the great master has a verse:
The body is born, wisdom not yet born;
Wisdom is born, the body already old.
The body regrets wisdom's birth is late;
Wisdom regrets the body's birth is early.
Body and wisdom do not meet;
How many times have they aged?
If body and wisdom meet,
Then one attains the Buddha's path.
Having this body and wisdom,
This is called "two-footed."
Eighth,
"four-footed" means:
The four great elements of human life,
belonging to earth, water, fire, and wind;
the four directions and four seas—
this is called "four-footed."
Ninth,
"many-footed" means:
All dharmas are penetrated,
no affair is not mastered;
worldly matters,
all are completely known.
All sutras and texts,
ask and none go unanswered;
the twelve divisions of the venerable scriptures,
memorized in the heart—
this is called "many-footed."
Tenth,
"footless" means:
Although one is human,
affairs are not understood;
cannot distinguish east from west,
no different from beasts—
this is called "footless."
The ten categories above,
each are different.
If there are still doubts,
the Prime Minister may ask as he wishes.
The Prime Minister, hearing these words,
felt as if sweet dew entered his heart;
the Lady, hearing them,
also as if ambrosia bathed her crown.
The Prime Minister called Shànqìng to approach: "According to your exposition just now,
you are not inferior to Dào'ān.
Speak a little more for me,
so that my heart may open in understanding,
and I may grasp the Buddha's Dharma clearly.
" Thereupon, Shànqìng explained the twelve links of dependent origination to the Prime Minister: ignorance conditions volitional formations,
volitional formations condition consciousness,
consciousness conditions name-and-form,
name-and-form conditions the six sense bases,
the six sense bases condition contact,
contact conditions feeling,
feeling conditions craving,
craving conditions grasping,
grasping conditions becoming,
becoming conditions birth,
birth conditions aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, distress, and despair.
With the cessation of ignorance comes cessation of volitional formations;
[with the cessation of volitional formations] comes cessation of consciousness;
[with the cessation of consciousness] comes cessation of name-and-form;
[with the cessation of name-and-form] comes cessation of the six sense bases;
[with the cessation of the six sense bases] comes cessation of contact;
[with the cessation of contact] comes cessation of feeling;
[with the cessation of feeling] comes cessation of craving;
[with the cessation of craving] comes cessation of grasping;
[with the cessation of grasping comes cessation of becoming;
with the cessation of becoming] comes cessation of birth;
[with the cessation of birth] comes cessation of aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, distress, and despair.
These are the twelve links of dependent origination.
The Prime Minister, hearing this,
repeatedly praised, "Excellent!"
The Lady at this moment sighed with admiration,
gaining immeasurable fields of merit.
Shànqìng then descended from the high seat and addressed the Prime Minister: "It is just like the Dharma Master Dào'ān,
who builds halls and pavilions in empty space—
in the end, they cannot be completed.
Just as they are about to be completed,
they are bound to collapse.
Although this lowly slave's body is of humble status,
the Buddha's Dharma is the same;
clothes may differ,
but the essence is not of two kinds.
This lowly slave now wishes to follow the Prime Minister into the temple,
to debate the meaning with Dharma Master Dào'ān.
" The Prime Minister said: "If you have the heart for it,
I will not hinder you.
" Thereupon, the Prime Minister and the Lady had Shànqìng bathe in fragrant water in the western courtyard,
change into fresh clothes,
and allowed Shànqìng to return to his room to rest,
awaiting the early dawn of the next day,
when further arrangements would be made.
Shànqìng, having returned to his room,
clarified his mind and purified his thoughts,
until daybreak,
without any sleep.
In a short while, at the time of entering court,
Shànqìng also followed the Prime Minister inside.
After the Prime Minister attended court,
he returned to his residence to rest,
then summoned Shànqìng.
The Prime Minister said: "That Dào'ān is a high monk within the country;
you must consider carefully.
" Shànqìng addressed the Prime Minister: "As the common saying goes: 'One who enters the mountains without avoiding wolves and tigers—
that is the courage of a woodcutter.
One who enters the water without avoiding serpents and dragons—
that is the courage of a fisherman.'
If this lowly slave can debate with Dào'ān,
it will be like obtaining broth when thirsty,
like obtaining fire when cold.
I beg the Prime Minister to rest easy without worry.
" He only waited for the lecture time to go.
In a short while, the time arrived;
the Prime Minister first sent two hundred strings of cash,
then brought Shànqìng into the temple.
At that time, the audience was like clouds,
offerings fell like rain;
the bell sound having stirred,
the lecture began.
The lead lecturer raised [the topic],
the overseer chanted hymns,
the fourfold assembly gazed up in reverence,
as if ascending the Vulture Peak Mountain.
Dào'ān, intending to rejoice the mind,
Thereupon, Dào'ān held a ruyi scepter in hand,
sat upon a jeweled dais,
widely burned priceless precious incense,
and proclaimed the wondrous meaning;
raising his voice to chant,
he announced the sutra title: "The Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, Chapter One: The Tathāgata's Life Span.
" Having opened the sutra,
he praised the Buddha's majestic demeanor;
first honoring the sages and worthies,
then speaking of the emperor's virtue.
He humbly prayed that the present emperor's way correspond to the dragon charts,
his virtue shine upon the golden [garden];
may he grasp the golden mirror to illuminate the nine heavens,
and follow the divine light to oversee the eight directions.
May all princes and heirs,
their golden branches be forever firm,
their jade leaves ever spring-like.
Princesses and noble consorts,
may their chastity and splendor shine eternally.
Court ministers and high officials,
may they be utterly filial and loyal.
Commandery and district officials,
may they be pure and upright.
All virtuous men and women present,
may a thousand calamities vanish like mist,
epidemics disperse like clouds.
May disasters not intrude,
merit and virtue be perfected.
The three wretched paths and hells,
may suffering cease and torment stop.
All sentient beings in the Dharma realm,
may they share in this blessing.
After the chanting was finished,
he prepared to announce the sutra title.
At that time, Shànqìng also rose from within the hall,
and called out loudly,
halting the announcement of the sutra title.
The fourfold assembly, seeing this,
were all astonished.
Shànqìng gradually approached,
and pointing, said:
"Venerable Dào'ān,
you are greatly skilled in expounding the Dharma,
the Ācārya opens the sutra to lecture and praise,
proclaiming the Buddha's true teaching.
Broadly guiding the foolish and deluded,
propagating the holy teachings,
your literary expressions are brilliant,
unparalleled within the realm,
benefiting sentient beings,
their number unknowable.
Long have you been in the sea of suffering,
yet you fashion a Dharma vessel,
cultivating great karmic causes,
ferrying people across birth and death.
I have not yet discerned which sutra text you are lecturing on,
what Dharma are you proclaiming for all sentient beings?
Whose commentary and subcommentary,
are you expounding to propagate the true teaching?
Wishing to understand the root source,
I beg you to condescend to explain.
The Dharma Master's lectures and praises,
are renowned throughout the land,
praised and transmitted by the ruler,
foremost in the country.
The Minister is present here,
I merely state this to make it known,
to warm the Dharma assembly,
to serve as Dharma joy.
If the Venerable One would bestow great compassion,
establish the proper form for the future,
not rejecting this humble offering,
it would indeed be a gracious favor."
Thereupon, Dào'ān, hearing these words,
changed countenance and became agitated,
and rebuked Shànqìng, saying:
"Gazing emptily, you make demands!
The wondrous scriptures of my Buddha Tathāgata,
their principles are profound and mysterious,
the Buddha-Dharma is difficult to conceive,
not something you can comprehend.
Though I do not decline to explain it to you,
it would be like placing a stubborn stone in water:
the nature of water is inherently moist,
but the stubborn stone has no way to enter it.
You see your present body,
and are moreover of lowly status,
how then can you attain freedom?
The Buddha-Dharma is entrusted to kings and great ministers,
only the wise can fully understand its meaning.
Have you not heard it said in secular texts:
'Worth speaking to, then speak;
not worth speaking to, to speak is to waste words.'
The Master left teachings,
which even the wise still find thus.
I will not explain to you, a person of inferior foolishness.
Karmadāna, inspect and manage,
do not allow clamor.
The time for listening to the sutra is precious,
if you do not understand, lower your head and do not speak,
apply your mind to listen attentively.
The presiding elder's lecture seat,
the audience proclaims,
all universally hear the Dharma.
Do not act as one who questions the Dharma."
He only knew that those beneath the seat,
would not oppose his will.
If it were others, they would fear you, Dào'ān,
but this is Shànqìng,
who fears you?
Thereupon, Shànqìng, hearing these words,
raised his voice even higher,
pointed from afar at Dào'ān,
and angrily reproached him, saying:
"Ācārya, your conduct,
is also that of one who aspires to the Way and emulates the sages,
yet the words you utter,
