do not accord with the sage's intent.
My Tathāgata left teachings,
the sutras are clearly stated,
even creeping insects containing spirit,
all partake of the Buddha-nature.
Do you still recite the *Diamond Sutra* or not?
Womb-born, egg-born, moisture-born, transformation-born,
the ten classes, the four modes of birth,
having form, without form,
having characteristics, without characteristics,
all attain Nirvana and are said to achieve extinction.
I am a human being,
how can it be that I am unfit to hear the Dharma?
Though I am of lowly status,
the Buddha-nature is not different.
The black robes may differ,
the Dharma should be without duality.
Have you not heard that even Kǒngqiū, though a sage,
long remained confused by the words about facing the sun?
The Greatly Enlightened World-Honored One,
still encountered the difficulty of the golden spear.
The layman Vimalakīrti,
was still scolded by the youth Guangyán.
The Immortal of Forbearance,
had his body cut apart by King Kali.
A nobleman does not deceive in a dark room,
but this is a common saying of vulgar scholars.
This humble slave wishes to question the sutra text,
and the seat master gazes emptily and makes demands.
Just as on steep mountains,
poisonous plants yet grow;
within muddy silt,
lotus flowers are born.
Within a torn cloth bag, there are bright pearls;
what use is chaff contained in a brocade bag?
Seat master, do not go to the mountains to gather wood,
judging by appearance.
If you act thus,
you will still lose your Zǐyǔ.
Just as with the Buddha-Dharma,
its great principle is universally equal,
like descending sweet dew,
universally moistening all.
It cannot frequently nourish only the level fields with shallow grass,
while mounds and hills receive no beneficent moisture.
The rain is originally equal,
naturally without discrimination.
The mind of self and others,
is all without difference.
Have you not seen the Medicine King Bodhisattva,
all mark the four seasons;
the five fruits, peaches and plums,
all follow the eight nodes,
born according to the ground.
In the *Parable of the Medicinal Herbs*,
it is clearly stated.
Great roots, great trees, great branches, great leaves,
each follows its own root and basis,
existing according to the ground.
One cannot say that sweet fruits,
the rain makes sweet;
bitter and astringent fruits,
the rain makes bitter and astringent.
The rain is originally of one flavor,
the receiving natures are themselves different.
Only practice a mind of equality,
and the Dharma realm will naturally be peaceful and joyful.
The Minister is present,
seat master, do not deceive people recklessly,
only know to properly establish the meaning,
in the future, I hope to properly respectfully respond."
Thereupon, Dào'ān, being reproached,
was greatly displeased,
ashamed to face the Minister,
embarrassed before the fourfold assembly.
He then grabbed the boundary ruler,
threw it to one side,
gradually approached,
and angrily reproached him, saying:
"Shànqìng,
have you not heard it said:
'If the fight does not hit the mark,
death is also difficult to bear.'
How can it be that for the fault of a single rat,
one toils to release a thousand-jūn crossbow?
If you see my drum,
I will not decline to answer back and forth.
A cicada and a roc bird,
how can they fly as counterparts?
You vainly expend your energy,
if you understand matters, lower your head and do not speak,
apply your mind to listen attentively.
If this time you do not heed my instruction,
you will inevitably receive a caning decision from the Minister's side,
be driven out of the temple gate,
and not be allowed to hear the sutra.
Speaking wild words recklessly,
what use will regret be then?"
Shànqìng, hearing these words,
raised his voice even higher,
pointed from afar at Dào'ān:
"Xǔgōng, you rashly act disorderly,
seat master, you wear the Dharma robes,
constantly proclaim the true sutras.
You should give rise to immeasurable mind,
possess the practice of the six pāramitās,
generate the bodhi mind,
benefit sentient beings,
transcend the three realms.
How can your mind be without compassion,
your poisonous harm even deeper,
deceiving ordinary people,
intending to request a caning from the Minister's side?
According to this conduct, it does not accord with the true teaching,
the words you utter,
The forgetful neglect the meaning.
How much more so when the morning's words are not spoken,
one must then apply the mind,
do not be careless and coarse.
If the reasoning of the words is mistaken,
then you become a disciple.
Firmly grasp the rope's end,
do not let it slip from your hand.
If even a single word in response is amiss,
then this lowly servant will request the rod from the lord,
be dragged down from the high seat and decided upon,
driven out of the temple gate,
unable to proclaim to the multitude,
do not say it was not forewarned.
Dào'ān, being challenged,
remained silent without words,
ashamed to face the lord,
embarrassed before the fourfold assembly.
After a long while,
he then called Shànqìng to approach: "The words spoken earlier,
were all in jest with you,
you should also not harbor a mind of self and other,
and I will not see your faults.
When I first heard you speak,
I was truly startled and doubtful,
thinking it would disturb the lecture seat,
and trouble the listeners.
Now I know you are truly a capable person.
If you ask about the sutra's title,
I can respectfully answer.
" Shànqìng said: "The ācārya claims himself,
yet says not to harbor a mind of self and other.
The Tathāgata left teachings following sutras,
all because of Ajātaśatru,
the World-Honored One expounded and proclaimed,
which all people can comprehend.
Now you say I may ask,
I dare not disobey.
I only know to first ask the sutra's name,
and later there will surely be questions.
" Dào'ān said: "The sutra text I lectured on earlier,
should be the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra*.
Shànqìng, hearing this,
clearly remembered it.
" Shànqìng asked: "What is called 'great'?
What is called 'nir'?
What is called 'vāṇa'?
" Dào'ān replied: "'Great' means vast,
it must broadly benefit all sentient beings,
lifting them from the sea of suffering.
'Nir' is the meaning of non-birth,
neither born nor extinguished,
thus accord with true suchness;
without coming or going,
then it is Buddha-nature.
The one word 'vāṇa',
ferries sentient beings,
out of the three realms,
enabling them to reach the other shore.
" Shànqìng said: "The three characters above have seven meanings.
" "Shànqìng, hearing this,
must firmly remember.
First,
it is like when the spring sun moves,
all grasses come to life;
regardless of shallow valleys or deep ravines,
everywhere flowers bloom.
Since the wondrous Dharma's sutra name is established,
the Tathāgata proclaims and spreads it,
sentient beings, irrespective of high or low,
hearing the sutra, all alike give rise to goodness.
Second,
it is like the meaning of straightening wood with a rope,
then one abandons wrong and returns to right.
Third,
it is like the meaning of a gushing spring,
deep and clear, neither ceasing nor flowing;
the sutra text long abides in the world,
circulating without rest or pause.
Fourth,
it is like rivers and seas,
able to carry ten-thousand-hú ships.
Sentient beings wishing to cross lakes and rivers,
first must rely on poles and oars.
The sutra text circulates in the world,
able to elevate those who transcend;
those intending to advance on the path and cultivate practice,
first must rely on the sutra's power.
Fifth,
it is like heaven and earth covering and supporting sentient beings;
if heaven and earth were entirely absent,
upon what would the myriad phenomena stand?
Since the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* text exists,
sentient beings rely on it to cultivate practice;
if the sutra Dharma were entirely absent,
upon what practice could one transcend the world?
Sixth,
it is like warp and weft,
able to form brocades and fine silks;
even the great bolts of plain silk and damask,
all depend on its warp and weft.
Since the wondrous Dharma's sutra name is established,
those cultivating the path thereby achieve,
all the way to unsurpassed bodhi,
entirely relying on the sutra's power.
Seventh,
it is like a road or path,
understood by those who come and go.
One who wishes to travel a thousand miles,
sets out relying on its road.
Sentient beings who resolve to cultivate the path,
must first read and recite the sutra text.
Therefore, later sages' paths are taken from here.
All the above seven meanings,
each is different,
together explain the one character 'sutra'.
Shànqìng, hearing this,
must still remember.
" Shànqìng said: "The one character 'sutra',
still has many aspects;
are there further sutra names or not?
" Dào'ān replied: "The meaning of nirvāṇa,
is immeasurable and boundless;
to hastily speak of sutra names,
how could they be exhausted?
For example, the common people in the world,
with ten thousand households and a thousand gates,
upon what are they governed?
Thus prefectures and counties are established,
each dividing land and marking borders.
The one character 'sutra',
separately proclaims the ten thousand dharmas,
therefore they differ.
Prefectures and counties require officials,
the wondrous Dharma must establish sutra names.
If prefectures and counties had no officials,
upon what would the common people be governed?
Those who compose commentaries and extracts for the sutra text,
it is like combing.
For example, tangled hair obtains its combing;
since the ten thousand dharmas establish sutra names,
all sages thereby accomplish the path.
The answers given above,
are all entirely based on the sutras.
If there are further doubts,
you may ask again.
Shànqìng said: "The seven meanings of the sutra,
let us set aside for now,
I ask a little more,
is it permissible or not?"
Dào'ān replied: "This humble monk takes heaven and men as teachers,
meanings flow like a spring,
the Dharma is like flowing water,
if you wish to ask,
simply ask,
now facing your earlier doubts,
speak quickly."
Shànqìng said: "As for the Buddha's Dharma and the master's writings,
they are all gathered like dust added to a mountain,
like falling dew increasing a stream,
drawing from it, one cannot fathom its source,
following it, one rarely reaches its end.
But this lowly servant now asks the master,
it is like fireflies competing with the sun,
a mantis blocking a chariot's path.
Knowing myself to be a wild goose,
how dare I ascend the phoenix terrace.
Under the thunderous voice,
a cloth drum is hard to sound;
before the jasper,
how can a mere inch of iron show itself.
Just as Buddha-nature,
pervades all sentient beings.
I ask again, our Buddha Tathāgata,
what is his essence?"
Dào'ān replied: "Shànqìng, come forward,
do not be overly modest.
Our Buddha takes compassion as his essence."
Shànqìng asked again: "Since you say our Buddha takes compassion as his essence,
why does he not save the icchantika beings?"
Dào'ān replied: "You do not understand the conditions,
listen to my explanation.
Icchantika beings,
due to their own creation of evil karma.
For example, a family raises a son,
who grows to adulthood,
and steals within the village.
When the matter is exposed,
he is captured by the local authorities,
then sent to prison,
to undergo torture.
Once the case is settled,
he confesses his crimes,
is led to the execution ground,
and faces death.
Although his parents have kindness and compassion,
how can the king's law save him?
Although our Buddha has compassion,
how can the Buddha's power compare to the power of his karma?
Such a person,
is difficult to save."
Shànqìng asked: "Icchantika beings,
although they create evil karma,
our Buddha's compassion,
should also save them.
What was said earlier,
all pertains to external conditions.
Our Buddha Tathāgata,
what is his nature?"
Dào'ān replied: "He takes equality as his nature."
Shànqìng asked: "Since you call equality his nature,
why do sentient beings sink into birth and death,
while the Buddha attains the remainderless nirvāṇa?"
Dào'ān replied: "Sentient beings sink into evil paths,
arising from ignorance and delusion;
the Buddha attains the remainderless nirvāṇa,
because all is exhausted."
Shànqìng asked again: "Sentient beings have ignorance and afflictions,
how do they relate to Buddha-nature?"
Dào'ān replied: "Ignorance and afflictions are sentient beings,
where all is cut off is Buddha-nature.
Therefore, sentient beings are not separate from the Buddha,
the Buddha is not separate from sentient beings.
The words spoken earlier,
are all answered in this manner."
Shànqìng said: "The words you just spoke are far off,
your praise and explanation of the sutra text are greatly mistaken,
all are reckless and baseless.
You only wish to please your disciples,
making it pleasant to the ear.
Like rivers, lakes, and the great sea,
within them are many beings,
some are giant turtles,
some are shrimp, dragons, or fish,
such various kinds,
all belong to water.
Although fish and water are together,
between them there is a difference,
fish without water will die,
water without fish remains clear.
Sentient beings separated from the Buddha will sink,
the Buddha separated from sentient beings will enter extinction.
It is said that the Buddha appears in the world, uniquely honored,
in one form, transcending the three realms,
for the sake of compassion,
he saves sentient beings.
If the Buddha were the same as ordinary beings,
all that is said would be incorrect.
The Nirvāṇa Sutra,
where are its metaphors profound and mysterious?
Now before the assembly,
I humbly ask the venerable to explain a little."
Dào'ān replied: "The metaphors in the Nirvāṇa Sutra,
are the most numerous,
major metaphors three thousand,
minor metaphors eight hundred."
Among them,
Shànqìng asked: "What is the meaning of the black wind?"
Dào'ān replied: "The meaning of the black wind,
is the wind of sentient beings' ignorance.
Sentient beings, from countless kalpas past,
have been shaken and unsettled by this wind.
This wind is divided into eight kinds,
leading to the platform of meaning,
but ultimately cannot be fully explained."
Then Shànqìng knew that Dào'ān did not understand,
and could not explain.
Shànqìng asked: "Since you are called the great virtue of the country,
you should answer ten for every one asked.
Although you have a skull,
you lack two eyes.
When ordinary people cross water,
first they must know how to float,
not knowing, they enter the water in vain.
The meaning of the black wind,
who explained it,
whose commentary on the sutra text is it?"
Then Dào'ān's mind intended to answer,
but his mouth could not answer;
his mouth intended to answer,
but his mind could not answer.
His limbs trembled,
he only called out his great fault.
I beg your compassion,
explain it to me.
Shànqìng said: "The meaning of the Nirvāṇa Sutra,
is greatly without fear,
please be at ease,
do not harbor worry.
Not asking about other matters,
I ask the venerable,
where did the Nirvāṇa Sutra commentary come from?"
Dào'ān replied: "It came from Master Yuǎn."
Shànqìng said: "Now,
if you saw Yuǎngōng,
would you still recognize him?"
Dào'ān replied: "Now if I saw Yuǎngōng,
I truly would not recognize him."
Shànqìng said: "Since you say you do not recognize him,
where did the commentary come from?"
Dào'ān replied: "It came from Venerable Yúnqìng, the chief disciple of Yuǎngōng."
Shànqìng said: "If you seek others,
it truly is not;
if you seek Yuǎngōng,
this lowly servant is he."
Dào'ān heard this,
still harboring doubts.
"I heard the great master has extraordinary marks,
his wrist has a flesh ring,
if you are the great master,
show this mark."
Then, to dispel the doubt,
Yuǎngōng rolled up his left sleeve,
indeed his wrist had a flesh ring,
emitting great light,
all the listeners saw it.
Then Dào'ān rose from his high seat,
threw himself to the ground,
from his seven apertures,
fresh blood flowed,
step by step forward,
to repent his earlier faults.
He intended to gouge out his eyes with a sharp knife,
hating himself for being born blind,
not recognizing the venerable.
Tears fell like rain, he wept bitterly,
prostrating, wishing the venerable's compassionate forgiveness.
Yuǎngōng said: "Do not harbor doubts in your heart,
do not grieve and weep bitterly.
You are a complete ordinary person,
how could you understand the meaning of the Nirvāṇa I expound.
It is already entering my teacher's position,
wait for me to thank the minister,
then I will return to proclaim the true Dharma to you."
Thereupon, Yuǎngōng went straight before the Prime Minister,
and addressed him, saying: "But this humble servant has served Your Excellency for only a short time,
and has not yet performed any meritorious service.
Yet I rashly entered the temple,
disrupting the Dharma assembly.
Though I have received Your Excellency's merciful consideration,
and no punishment has been meted out,
now, before this assembly,
I request to be severely beaten with the rod."
Hearing this, the Prime Minister
threw himself to the ground,
prostrating face-down,
and did not rise again.
After a long while, he revived,
stepped forward,
and addressed the Venerable One, saying: "Though your disciple holds the office of Prime Minister,
I am utterly incompetent in all matters.
I was promoted and recommended to fulfill three vows,
and the court rewarded and employed me.
But with the eyes of an ordinary man,
how could I distinguish a sage from a worthy?
My sins reach to the heavens;
please forgive and pardon my faults.
For six years you were a slave,
constantly driven and ordered about within my residence.
At times I even spoke harshly and angrily shouted at the Venerable One.
For such sins,
how can I repent?"
Yuǎngōng said: "Because in a past life, this poor monk acted as a guarantor,
there was a debt that remained unpaid.
Wishing to be free of enmity in this life,
it was fitting that I come here to settle accounts.
Once repaid, all is settled;
the matter is now beyond doubt.
From now on,
look upon me with your former eyes,
and have no more worries."
Hearing this, the Prime Minister
wept even more sorrowfully,
and prostrating himself, wished that the Venerable One, in his compassion,
would speak of past-life causes and effects.
Yuǎngōng said: "In a past life, Your Excellency was a merchant.
Another, Bái Zhuāng, was also a merchant.
Your Excellency then borrowed five hundred strings of cash from Bái Zhuāng.
At that time, this poor monk acted as guarantor.
Later, Your Excellency passed away,
and this poor monk intended to repay the debt,
but unfortunately, I also died.
Through several cycles of rebirth,
unexpectedly we have met again.
Because of this karmic connection,
the guarantor received the debt."
Hearing this, the Prime Minister
stepped forward,
wept tears like rain in sorrow,
and blamed himself for his fault: "Your disciple incurred a debt to another;
it should have been repaid by myself.
Yet I troubled the Venerable One's person.
After your disciple dies,
I will surely sink into hell."
Yuǎngōng said: "Now the debt is repaid;
do not doubt.
From now on,
do not do so again.
I earnestly advise all disciples:
if you owe a debt, you must repay it.
This poor monk, merely acting as guarantor,
still had to be a slave for six years without settling it.
Ordinary people, with shallow understanding,
do not fear sin,
and widely commit many offenses;
how can they repent?"
At that time, the listeners wept tears like rain in sorrow,
sighing for Yuǎngōng,
all filled with melancholy.
A thousand people gazed in reverence,
ten thousand sighed in admiration.
That day, all listeners severed their greed and stinginess.
At that time, as Yuǎngōng's discourse was not yet finished,
he was again requested by the entire assembly below and the Prime Minister
to once more ascend the high seat.
That day, Yuǎngōng was like a withered tree at the cliff's edge,
meeting spring again.
He was also like a fish caught in a net,
released back to the rivers and seas.
His natural spirit and bearing,
were not the same as ordinary men's.
His bone structure and divine demeanor
were rare in the world.
The bells and chimes sounded again,
the sūtra's title was raised once more,
as he expounded for the assembly.
At that time, Dào'ān was also seated among the assembly.
When Yuǎngōng had just begun to speak the sūtra's title,
immediately the earth shook in six ways,
and five-colored auspicious clouds
spread across the vast sky.
Hundreds and thousands of heavenly beings
played music together,
and immeasurable sages and worthies
joined their voices in Sanskrit chants.
The sūtra's recitation was clear and distinct,
the Dharma's rhythm tinkling like jade.
The great assembly witnessed this marvel,
and all listeners exclaimed it was rare.
That day, the Prime Minister again attended the assembly in the lotus palace,
and reopened the feast of fragrant accumulation.
He gathered a great assembly of monks and nuns from both streets,
and then had his hair cut with a golden knife.
That day, the Prime Minister, right within the Fúguāng Temple,
fully recorded this matter
and wrote a memorial to report it to Emperor Jìn Wén.
The Emperor, reading the memorial, was greatly pleased.
His dragon countenance repeatedly praised, "Excellent!"
and he said it was rare.
At that time, an edict was issued: ordering the Secretariat-Chancellery
to arrange the three teachings—Buddhism, Daoism, and Confucianism—
to proceed together to the Fúguāng Temple
to welcome and invite Yuǎngōng into the inner palace for offerings.
Then a further edict was issued:
bestowing upon Yuǎngōng several strings of ruyi beads,
one six-ringed staff,
several sets of monastic robes,
and also sending the imperial carriage
to welcome Yuǎngōng into the inner palace.
Once the edict was issued,
all inside and outside knew of it.
Ministers and high officials made arrangements;
it was no different from a boiling cauldron.
With solemn dignity, they entered the temple directly,
and requested the Great Master to ascend the carriage.
At that time, Yuǎngōng repeatedly declined: "This poor monk is but an ordinary monk.
I must decline the sovereign's invitation;
this monk-servant wishes instead to return to the mountains.
That is this poor monk's desire."
Prime Minister Cuī stepped forward
and addressed the Master: "I prostrate myself and wish for your compassion;
do not refuse the request.
The Emperor within the inner palace eagerly and intently awaits,
gazing up to the Venerable One.
First, for the sake of all sentient beings in the Dharma realm,
second, I hope you will not refuse the Emperor's invitation."
Since Yuǎngōng was repeatedly and earnestly invited,
he then stepped forward to proceed.
A hundred kinds of skill and immortal music welcomed him ahead,
and all ministers rejoiced and congratulated the current ten-thousand-year sovereign.
When Yuǎngōng exited the temple gate,
and had walked about a hundred paces,
he suddenly soared into the sky and departed,
and none knew where he went.
The Prime Minister, worried and fearful, made obeisance,
gazed into the sky, and reverently implored: "The Great Master possesses boundless power;
I prostrate myself and beg you to bestow compassion,
and comply with the sovereign's invitation."
As he spoke his plea,
he proceeded on his way.
That day, Yuǎngōng had already arrived early at the palace gate to respectfully receive the imperial decree.
Thereupon, the Emperor, knowing Yuǎngōng had arrived,
came out of the palace gate,
gazing in reverence a thousand times,
bowing devoutly ten thousand times.
Upon seeing Yuǎngōng,
his dragon countenance was greatly pleased,
and his joy was boundless.
Then the Emperor said: "In my small kingdom,
I am overjoyed to have met the Venerable One's descent.
The peace and prosperity of the nation's people
are all due to the Master."
He was then provided for within the inner palace for several years.
The six palaces revered and admired him,
the five courts were devout and respectful.
The Emperor received from the Master the Three Refuges and Five Precepts,
and complied with all.
After Yuǎngōng, within the inner palace, saw that the various palaces often used written paper for filthy purposes in the latrines,
he reproached all the people,
and composed a verse, saying:
The Confucian youth speaks of the Five Classics,
the Buddhist teaching establishes the Three Vehicles.
Observing ritual, practicing loyalty and filial piety,
they are expelled from the nine agricultures.
"Chángyáng" together with the five policies,
their words are the same as the hidden scriptures.
Not understanding to give them precious respect,
they are used filthily in the latrine.
Awakening destroys sins as numerous as Ganges' sands,
through many lives, repentance cannot contain them.
They will be trapped for five hundred kalpas,
constantly becoming insects in the latrine.
At that time, because of Yuǎngōng's recitation of the verse, the entire inner palace
all cultivated blessings.
Master Yuǎngōng suddenly one day,
recalled that Akṣobhya Buddha had said,
then bid farewell to the emperor: “Your humble monk, within the imperial palace,
has received Your Majesty’s support for several years.
Now I intend to return to the mountains;
I humbly beg Your Majesty’s decision.”
Hearing these words, the emperor
shed tears from his eyes,
and after a long while said to the master: “In my small kingdom,
there is truly no proper support.
For several years, the Venerable One
has dwelt within these walls,
and I have never harbored any intention of disrespect.
Though I am the ruler of men,
I unworthily occupy this position between heaven and earth.
I am ever grateful to the Venerable One
for having come to this small kingdom.
I humbly beseech the master, in your compassion,
to stay a few more days—
may this be granted or not?”
Yuǎngōng said: “As for the meaning of Nirvāṇa,
fundamentally there is no grasping;
if there is grasping,
it all belongs to deluded thought.
I humbly wish Your Majesty
not to harbor sorrow.
This humble monk has a vow to return to the mountains.”
Seeing that Master Yuǎngōng’s words were resolute, the emperor
then knew that sentiment [of departure] was hard to detain.
An edict was first issued to inform the six palaces,
and in secret, arrangements were made for a farewell ceremony.
At that time, the emperor was filled with longing and attachment,
and the ministers were deeply troubled.
All the great officials of the kingdom
together saw him off.
Master Yuǎngōng set out on the road,
leaving the palace gates,
parting from the dragon towers,
gazing at the mountains—the road was long;
beholding the rivers—the way was far.
On that day, Master Yuǎngōng, able to traverse the long road,
then secretly manifested his spiritual powers.
Once Master Yuǎngōng had left Cháng’ān,
clouds arose beneath his feet,
like a strong man stretching his arms.
In a moment’s time,
he reached the mountain.
Master Yuǎngōng also did not return to his old temple;
about ten li away,
on a steep ridge,
he temporarily built a thatched hut.
There, sitting cross-legged and spreading his seat,
he then once again sought out his old scrolls,
and raised anew the sound of scripture chanting.
As time passed gently,
several more months went by.
Master Yuǎngōng suddenly gazed upon a high plain,
and climbing up to it,
found a realm where steep peaks echoed with crane calls,
and ravines below resounded with dragon songs.
A hundred valleys and a thousand peaks
were all, without exception, blooming with flowers.
On level ground flowed long streams of water;
in gardens bloomed undying flowers—
this was a place where the Tathāgata practiced.
Thereupon Master Yuǎngōng sat upright,
entering his samādhi.
Purifying his thoughts and clarifying his mind,
he contemplated the Buddha Way,
reflecting that floating life is brief,
and thinking the mortal world unbearable.
Then, with the sovereign of his own-nature mind,
he built a Dharma ship,
to take refuge in the higher realm.
Master Yuǎngōng built the ship
using no mundane materials,
nor any ordinary kinds.
He himself took the faultless Mahāyāna as the hawsers,
and bodhi-prajñā as the railings.

The Good Child stepped forward, clasped his hands, and addressed the Judge: "The Emperor came without having performed any good deeds,

Cuī Zǐyù again asked the Good Child, who addressed the Judge: "The Emperor issued a great amnesty,

Cuī Zǐyù said: "How much merit is created by releasing thirty-six thousand five hundred and fifty people?"
The Good Child said: "The Commissioner of Merits would know the measure of this matter."

Long ago, Qí’s Yànzǐ was sent as an envoy to the State of Liáng.
King Liáng asked his attendants: “What is that man’s appearance like?”
The attendants replied: “The envoy Yànzǐ
is extremely ugly,
his face is bluish-black.
Moreover, his lips do not cover his teeth,
his hair does not cover his ears,
his waist does not reach his hips,
his face and appearance
are not those of a proper man.”
When King Liáng saw Yànzǐ,
he then called for him to enter through the small gate.
King Liáng asked: “Who are you,
that you enter through my dog gate?”
Yànzǐ replied to the king: “If the king were going to a person’s house,
you would enter through the person’s gate;
since you are a dog’s house,
I enter through the dog gate.
What shame is there in that?”
King Liáng said: “The State of Qí has no men,
that they sent you here!”
Yànzǐ replied: “In the State of Qí there are seventy-two chief ministers,
all of them wise and intelligent;
therefore they are sent to states of wisdom and discernment.
I am the least intelligent,
so I am sent as envoy to a state without intelligence.”
King Liáng said: “I won’t say you lack intelligence,
but why are you so short?”
Yànzǐ replied to the king: “The wútóng tree may be large, but inside it is hollow;
well water may be deep, but it has no fish;
a five-foot great snake fears the spider;
a three-inch linchpin controls the carriage wheel.
What benefit is there in being tall?
What fault is there in being short?”
King Liáng said: “I won’t say you are short,
but why are you black?”
Yànzǐ replied to the king: “Blackness
is the nature of heaven and earth.
The meat of a black sheep—
can it not be eaten?
A black ox pulls a carriage—
can it be without strength?
A black dog chases a hare—
can it not catch it?
A black rooster crows at dawn—
can it be without rule?
The swan and crane may be white,
but they dwell long in the wild fields;
the funeral carriage may be white,
but it always carries the dead.
Lacquer is black, yet it faces forward;
the ink stick is black, yet it stays by the king’s side.
When picking mulberries, the black ones are tasted first.
Considering these words,
what benefit is there in being white?”
Again Yànzǐ said to the king:
“A sword may be only three feet,
yet it can pacify the four directions;
the qílín may be small,
yet it is an auspicious response for a sage ruler;
an arrow may be small,
yet it can kill a fierce tiger;
a small mallet can sound a great drum.
Considering these words,
what benefit is there in being large?”
King Liáng asked: “I won’t say you are short,
but who are your ancestors?”
Yànzǐ replied to the king: “The body is born from mourning and affairs,
fine grain and rice come forth from dung and soil,
the strong man speaks of merit,
the weakling speaks of hardship.
Now I am here speaking with the king—
why trouble to ask about my ancestors?”
The king then asked Yànzǐ: “Do you know the guiding principles of heaven and earth,
the fundamental nature of yīn and yáng?
Which is the male?
Which is the female?
Which is left?
Which is right?
Which is husband?
Which is wife?
Which is outer?
Which is inner?
From where does the wind come forth?
From where does the rain come?
From where does the frost descend?
From where does the dew arise?
How many thousands of miles apart are heaven and earth?
Who is the noble man?
Who is the petty man?”
Yànzǐ replied to the king: “Nine times nine is eighty-one—
that is the guiding principle of heaven and earth;
eight times nine is seventy-two—
that is the fundamental nature of yīn and yáng.
Heaven is male,
earth is female;
the sun is husband,
the moon is wife;
south is outer,
north is inner;
east is left,
west is right;
wind comes forth from high mountains,
rain comes from rivers and seas,
frost descends from the clear sky,
dew arises from the hundred grasses.
Heaven and earth are 99,999,000 miles apart.
The wealthy and noble are noble men,
the poor are petty men.
To speak without exhaustion—
this is called Yànzǐ.”
Yànzǐ composed a poem:
In the distant past,
in ancient times,
there was a great kingdom
named Jiāshī.
The people lived in peace and joy,
the five grains were abundant,
the four seasons were harmonious,
with no disasters or plagues.
The king declared: “This is my fortune,
that has brought about such
peace and order in the realm.”
The king’s consort also said: “This is my fortune.”
The crown prince said: “This is my fortune.”
The three each argued, unable to settle.
The king then asked a cultivated immortal,
to resolve his doubts.
The immortal replied: “It is not due to the king,
nor to the fortune of the consort or crown prince.
In the mountain forests,
there were four creatures—the Jiāpíluó bird, a hare, a macaque, and an elephant—
who became sworn brothers,
practicing kindness and spreading righteousness,
mutually respecting one another;
it is they who have moved heaven to bring this about.”
The king went to see,
and indeed it was as he said.
All the people in the kingdom
came to know of this matter.
How did the elephant, bird, and others
determine their order of seniority?
The bird asked the elephant: “When you first came to this tree,
how big was the tree?”
The white elephant replied: “When I came to the tree,
I leaned against it to scratch an itch,
and the tree was just a bit taller than me.”
Next he asked the macaque: “When you saw the tree,
how big was it?”
The macaque replied: “I was on the tree,
grasping its branches, leaping and swinging about;
it was just a bit taller than me.”
Then he asked the hare: “When you came to the tree,
how big was it?”
The hare replied: “When I came to the tree,
I ate its leaves;
my mouth reached the treetop,
the branches, trunk, flowers, and leaves.”
The bird said: “Long ago in the mountains I ate the fruit of this tree,
and dropped a seed here,
which then grew into this tree.”
Because of this tree,
the four creatures mentioned above
determined their order of seniority.
The bird was the eldest,
the hare was second,
the macaque third,
and the white elephant the youngest.
Thus these four creatures,
because of their kindness and righteousness,
after their lives ended,
all were reborn in heaven.
The god Dìshì and the other deities,
with different mouths but the same voice,
rejoiced and praised them.
At that time, the Tathāgata addressed the great assembly: That bird of that time
is now my own body;
the hare is Shèlì;
the macaque is Mahāmaudgalyāyana;
the white elephant is now Ānántuó.
The four creatures practiced kindness,
and still moved heaven to such vast merit;
how much more so for humans—
can they be without kindness and righteousness?
The Táng monk Tǒng Héshang praised and recounted the “Ode to the Kindness and Righteousness of the Four Creatures”
(first cultivating the cause and effect of filial piety),
(now attaining the conditions for becoming a Buddha),
(the reason is thus).
Marvelous, these four creatures,
able to form a good bond.
Respecting the great, recognizing the small,
taking the tree as measure.
Spreading righteousness, practicing kindness,
humbling the heart, lowering the will.
In movement and stillness they accompanied each other,
never weary of the repeated burdens.
With sleeves linked and robes joined,
even Chén Zhònggōng and Léi Yì could not compare.
Moved by the world's peace and prosperity,
disasters and calamities did not arise.
Wind and rain came in due season,
auspicious signs and favorable omens appeared.
The people of Jiāshīguó,
all were filled with joy.
The holy teachings were proclaimed and exalted,
praised and lauded by the heavenly beings.
Later, he attained Buddhahood,
the cause of his blessings rooted in this.
